52 In D 1.11, Machiavelli observes that the people of Florence, who do not appear to have been either ignorant or coarse, were persuaded by “Friar Girolamo Savonarola that he spoke with God.” Machiavelli does not take a stand on whether it was true or not, “because one should speak with reverence of such a man.” He does observe “that an infinite number believed him without having seen anything extraordinary to make them believe him,” even though in 1.56 he reminds his readers of “how much had been foretold by Friar Girolamo Savonarola before the coming of King Charles VIII of France into Italy.” Machiavelli rather clearly indicated what he thought about the truth of Savonarola’s claims, however, in a letter he wrote to Ricciardo Becchi, the Florentine ambassador to the Holy See on March 9, 1498. In this letter Machiavelli first summarizes two sermons that Savonarola, fearing that the newly elected Signoria would not support or defend him against the pope, gave after he had withdrawn from preaching in the city at San Reparata and begun speaking “boldly” at his home church in San Marco. Taking as his text a passage from Exodus, “but the more they oppressed them, the more they were multiplied,” Savonarola first argued that “when it comes to action, prudence is right-reason,” and right-reason might counsel one to go into hiding, as he had. He then sought to encourage his followers by promising that through suffering good people grow in both spirit and number. He finally provided a bridge to his sermon the next day, by saying that the dissension in Florence might cause a tyrant to rise up among them, but that this tyrant would eventually be driven out of Italy. The next morning he returned to Exodus where it says that Moses slew an Egyptian, and reported that “God had told him that there was someone in Florence who sought to make himself a tyrant [and] . . . to excommunicate the friar.” But after he heard that the Signoria had written to the pope on his behalf, Savonarola dropped all such talk of tyrants in Florence and tried to set the people against the pontiff. “Thus,” Machiavelli concluded, “in my judgment, he acts in accordance with the times and colors his lies accordingly.” Machiavelli and His Friends: Their Personal Correspondence, trans. and ed. James B. Atkinson and David Sices (DeKalb: Northern Illinois University Press, 1996), 9–10.


53 Ridolfi, Life, 15, reports that Machiavelli was elected five days after the execution.


54 See D 3.6, FH 7.22, 8.34; P 3 and 7; P 25 and D 1.27, 3.9, 3.44; D 2.11, 2.19.


55 See C. C. Bayley, War and Society in Renaissance Florence (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1961), 276–84, and Mikael Hörnqvist, “Perché non si usa allegare i Romani: Machiavelli and the Florentine Militia of 1507,” Renaissance Quarterly 55 (2002): 148–91.


56 Machiavelli dispassionately summarizes the events leading to the downfall of the republic and the reinstitution of the rule of the Medici in his Letter to a Noblewoman after September 16, 1512, Machiavelli and His Friends, 214–17.


57 Machiavelli and Vettori had become friends in 1508 when they served together as representatives of Florence in Germany at the court of Emperor Maximilian. The party of aristocrats who opposed Piero Soderini had initially pressured him to send a “well-born” young man instead of his loyal servant, but Soderini found that he could not rely on Vettori’s reports and sent Machiavelli to join him. The conditions were not propitious, but Vettori and Machiavelli became not merely cooperative colleagues, but friends.


58 Francesco Vettori to Niccolò Machiavelli, Rome, November 23, 1513, in Machiavelli and His Friends, 260–62.


59 See Giulio Ferroni, “Le ‘cose vane’ nelle Lettere di Machiavelli,” La Rassegna della letteratura italiana 76 (1972): 231–32.


60 Machiavelli to Vettori, P 111.


61 Machiavelli does not state the connection explicitly, but his account of his thrush hunting could be seen as an oblique reference to the suffering he endured in prison and the failure of a former plea to Giuliano for help. In addition to two sonnets he wrote about his suffering in prison, Machiavelli dedicated a third to Giuliano which began, “I’m sending you, Giuliano, if I might, several thrushes—a small gift, I guess, but good to make Your Lordship think a bit of your poor Machiavello in distress.” Lust and Liberty: The Poems of Machiavelli, trans. Joseph Tusiani (New York: Ivan Obolensky, 1963), 46. In a learned and provocative reading of the letter of December 10, 1513, Najemy suggests that the comparison Machiavelli draws between himself bearing the bundle of cages on his back and Geta, the servant of Amphitryon carrying his master’s books on his back, reveals Machiavelli’s sense of his own plight. Geta e Birria was an early fifteenth-century verse novella that was a remake of a twelfth-century neo-Latin comedy, Geta, by Vitale de Blois, which was in turn adapted from Plautus’s Amphitruo. Machiavelli could assume that Vettori would know the story; there were at least four printed editions in his lifetime. In the novella Geta accompanies his master Amphitryon to Athens to learn philosophy. After experiencing much hardship for the sake of their studies, Amphitryon decides to return. His wife Almena sends their second servant, Birria, to meet her husband and Geta at the port; but seeing Geta trudging home loaded with books, Birria hides in a cave. The first parallel Najemy finds between Machiavelli and Geta is thus that both have books that they want to unload on a friend who ducks. (However, in the letter Machiavelli expresses uncertainty about whether he should give his book to Vettori or present it to Giuliano himself. He has reason to doubt that Vettori will press his case; so far he has not.) The second parallel Najemy finds between Machiavelli and Geta is that both have endured considerable hardship to acquire an arte and scienza that both believe will make all their suffering worthwhile by transforming and immortalizing them, but they cannot persuade or even gain the respectful attention of a former colleague. Pretending not to see that Birria has tried to hide in order to avoid helping him, Geta stands outside the cave and brags about the knowledge he has acquired. He emphasizes the hardship, the hunger and pain he has suffered in order to learn philosophy, but he concludes that what he has acquired now makes him happy, because his name will be spread throughout the world. Once a person has learned something, he further observes, that knowledge can never be taken away. Geta does not succeed in persuading Birria to come out and help him, however, until he throws a stone into the cave. Najemy does not recognize that the similarities between Machiavelli and Geta end there. Machiavelli is not in a position to force Vettori to show his hand. Moreover, in the novella Geta disavows the knowledge he thought he had acquired, after he comes to doubt his own identity as a result of his confrontation with a divine copy of himself at his former home. Najemy does not go so far as to claim that Machiavelli doubted the value of the knowledge he had acquired. He does suggest that “his self-comparison to Geta announces that the letter of 10 December was to be a parable of his year of ‘exile’ and of what he now fears might be a disappointing ‘return’ home with The Prince in hand” (Between Friends, 230). The problem with reading the entire letter in terms of this early comparison is that the comparison occurs in the section on thrush hunting, an activity Machiavelli explicitly says that he has had to give up. He had to try to find other means of economic support and entertainment, and he is taking a new tack in appealing to Giuliano with a new kind of gift. Rather than asking for mercy, Machiavelli is offering instruction and assistance in ruling. He is not approaching either Vettori or Giuliano merely as a suppliant.


62 In his subsequent correspondence with Vettori, Machiavelli admits that the other thing lacking was immediate amorous passion. As later in Clizia, so in his earlier letters, Machiavelli occasionally presents himself in the role of a “fool for love.” Najemy does not believe that Machiavelli actually fell in love with an unnamed and only very generically described woman, who, Machiavelli tells Vettori in a letter of August 3, 1514, led him (like his visits to the courts of ancient men) to “set aside the memory of all [his] afflictions.” Responding to Vettori’s evident failure to act on his behalf and his friend’s attempt to divert their correspondence from politics to affairs with women, in that letter Machiavelli claims to have left behind “the thoughts of great and serious things,” because “neither reading about ancient things nor discussing modern ones gives me pleasure anymore” (Between Friends, 290–92). Yet four months later Machiavelli responded with alacrity to Vettori’s request that he write out his thoughts on the foreign policy the pope ought to adopt, so that Vettori could show Machiavelli’s letter to the pope. Najemy also argues, Between Friends, 295–309, that Vettori’s request for Machiavelli’s judgment and Machiavelli’s advice were both quite misguided in light of (a) Machiavelli’s persistent advocacy of a pro-French policy, (b) the fact that Leo had already allied himself with the Spanish king by the time Vettori wrote Machiavelli, and (c) that only two years had passed since Spanish troops had forced the pro-French Florentine republic to allow the Medici to return.


63 Cf. Apology 38a. See also Haig Patapan, Machiavelli in Love (Lanham, MD: Lexington Books, 2006), 143–46, for a discussion of the similarities and differences between Machiavelli and Socrates.


64 Machiavelli to Vettori, P 110.


65 In Between Friends Najemy contends that the Prince is directed first and foremost to Vettori’s insistence that fortune rules human affairs, the view Machiavelli explicitly addresses in chapter 25 of the work we now know as The Prince. (Many readers have understood Machiavelli’s little treatise as concerning primarily the opposition he draws between fortuna and virtù. Pocock, Machiavellian Moment; Skinner, Machiavelli; and Benner, Prince are a few of the most notable recent examples.) Yet in his letter of December 10, 1513, Machiavelli appears to have thought that Vettori was more valuable as a possible messenger than as an intellectual interlocutor or even as an editor. He certainly does not suggest that Vettori voiced the question that inspired him to write.


66 Responding to Vettori’s initial invitation to visit him in Rome, Machiavelli assured his friend that “if these new masters of ours see fit not to leave me lying on the ground, I shall be happy and believe that I shall act in such a way that they too will have reason to be proud of me. And if they should not, I shall get on as I did when I came here: I was born in poverty and at an early age learned how to scrimp rather than to thrive” (letter of March 18, 1513, Machiavelli and His Friends, 222).


67 In “‘The Discourses,’ and Machiavelli’s Last Days,” Machiavelli Researches 9, no. 1 (1967): 79–107, Cecil H. Clough states that “one of the weaknesses of the Renaissance tracts and treatises on politics, especially the Florentine ones, is that the authors could not detach themselves from the political scene. The solution that each one presents often tended to further the personal and family interest of its author” (87). Although he explicitly wrote about his need to acquire employment, I am arguing that Machiavelli had a much broader and more magnificent understanding of his “self-interest.” He aspired to reform the way in which people thought about politics and thus their practice. In doing so, he could and would benefit them much more than he would benefit himself. Consistent with his principles, he presented himself as acting for his own benefit and thus dissimulated the grandeur of his own ambition in order to obtain the cooperation of others.


Part I


Machiavelli’s Comprehensive Treatises


1


Machiavelli’s New Approach to the Study and Practice of Politics


THE PRINCE


Few works of political philosophy have been so often or so variously read as Machiavelli’s Prince. Failing to discern the underlying argument that ties together the apparently disparate topics he takes up, many commentators have emphasized the importance of one aspect or part.1 By bringing out the argument that culminates in Machiavelli’s passionate call for the Medici prince and pope to free Italy from the barbarians, I show that in The Prince Machiavelli presents an entirely new approach to the study and practice of politics.


The Dedication: Teaching or Testing Lorenzo


All the remaining manuscript copies of De principatibus have the dedication to “the magnificent Lorenzo de’ Medici” attached. We do not know whether Machiavelli ever actually presented a copy of his little book to Lorenzo.2 But whether Machiavelli actually presented his little book to the prince or not, he apparently wanted it to be read as if he were giving it to a Medici prince for the purpose of gaining employment.

At the beginning of the letter of dedication, Machiavelli emphasizes the unusual character of his gift. “It is customary . . . for those who desire to acquire favor with a Prince to come to meet him with things that they care most about in their own possessions or with things that they see please him most” (3). But Machiavelli clearly is not giving Lorenzo what he has seen please the prince. (Hence the anecdote about Lorenzo’s liking the dogs he was given by another man much more than the book.) Machiavelli is giving Lorenzo what in his own possessions he cares most about; rather than trying to please the prince, Machiavelli is acting on the basis of his own understanding of what is important. And that is “the knowledge of the actions of great men, learned by me from long experience with modern things and a continuous reading of ancient ones” (3).

Machiavelli demonstrates that knowledge not by cravenly trying to please the prince, but by recognizing the demands on a prince’s time and attention: he has reduced his thoughts and examinations of the deeds of great men to one small volume so that the prince will be able to peruse it in a short time.3 In one of his several clearly ironical (dissimulating) protestations in this letter, Machiavelli “judges this work undeserving” of the prince’s attention, but appeals to his “humanity.” That “humanity” first appears to consist in Lorenzo’s accepting the book out of a kind of charity or pity, because he understands that Machiavelli’s gift of his knowledge is the greatest gift the poor ex-magistrate is able to present. However, Machiavelli goes on to state that Lorenzo could receive “no greater gift” than “the capacity to be able to understand in a very short time all that I learned in many years with so many hardships and dangers” (4). Machiavelli thus claims, in effect, to know what Lorenzo does not yet but needs to understand in order to be an effective ruler. Rather than a form of generosity, the prince’s “humanity” appears to consist in a willingness to concede his own ignorance by learning from another. Having made this very bold claim in the guise of a suppliant, Machiavelli again emphasizes the unusual form of his gift and the fact that he has not ornamented it as is customary: he does not want it to be honored or to please for anything but the variety of the “matter” and gravity of the subject.4

Machiavelli recognizes that he may seem presumptuous in claiming to know the business of a prince better than the prince himself, but to excuse himself he offers a metaphor: Just as those who sketch landscapes have to place themselves below the mountains to consider the nature of the mountains, i.e., to see the way they tower over and above, and to place themselves on the mountains, conversely, to consider the nature of the plains, i.e., how much flatter, broader, lower, but more fertile they are, so “to know well the nature of peoples one needs to be prince” (to look down from on high), and “to know well the nature of princes one needs to be of the people” (to look up). What, we might ask, are the people able to see about a prince from below that he is not able to see so clearly about himself? The answer would seem to be, the quality of his deeds as prince. Is he ruling well and so benefiting the people, or is he failing to keep order and actively oppressing them? The people are in a position to know the effects of a prince’s rule better than he.5 What the prince sees about the nature of the people from his high position is that they are fearful and that they will, therefore, obey his commands (if and when those commands are backed by force). In P 18 Machiavelli observes that people do not see a prince well from their lowly station and can, therefore, easily be deceived by what he says are the reasons for his actions, although they cannot be so easily deceived about the effects of his acts. Machiavelli indicates in this brief introductory dedication, however, that he is able to see things from both perspectives. He is a member of the people who knows what a prince needs to learn.6

Observers see things differently from different positions, but Machiavelli makes clear in the last paragraph of his dedication that the position from which they view others (i.e., whether they are a prince or a member of the populace) is a matter not of nature or of desert, but of fortune (which, of course, includes the accident of birth into a given family). Even though his book is short, Machiavelli suggests that Lorenzo will have to read it diligently if he is to “arrive at the greatness” that Machiavelli desires for him and “that fortune and your other qualities promise.” The contents of Machiavelli’s little treatise are not so easily understood or quickly mastered as he first suggested; Lorenzo will probably need help. Machiavelli concludes by observing that if Lorenzo looks down from the summit of his height to these low places, he will learn how undeservedly Machiavelli endures a great and continuous malignity of fortune. That malignity of fortune, to which Machiavelli refers repeatedly in his letters, is his exclusion from public office. It consists not merely in his poverty and the contempt that poverty will bring him, but in his lack of opportunity to demonstrate the utility of the knowledge he claims to possess by advising someone who has the power to put it into practice.

In the last chapter of The Prince Machiavelli explicitly states that the “greatness” he desires for Lorenzo is for Lorenzo to become conqueror and thus savior of Italy by freeing her from domination by “the barbarians.”7 Machiavelli explains that Lorenzo has an opportunity to become the redeemer of his nation not only because her people, now suffering from the depredations of foreign powers, will follow a leader who promises to liberate them, but also because he has the good fortune of being a member of the family that also controls the Church. Even more and better than Ferdinand of Spain (P 21), Lorenzo will thus be able not only to fund his wars of “liberation” with the help of the pope but also to justify or cloak his conquests in the name of religion. The “other qualities” that added to the promise of Lorenzo’s greatness probably included his military tastes and ambitions.8 By 1515 he had become the virtual ruler of Florence; he was elected captain general in May. His uncle Giuliano, to whom Machiavelli initially planned to present his treatise, died on March 17, 1516, but Lorenzo continued to show his ambition to rule. He was made duke of Urbino through papal investiture in October 1516. However, as early as February–March 1514, Machiavelli had written to Vettori:

everyone is beginning to recognize in [Lorenzo] the beloved memory of his grandfather because His Magnificence is diligent in his work, generous and agreeable during an audience, deliberate and serious in his replies. His way of conversing is . . . [such] that people attribute no pride to it; nor does he mingle too familiarly so that he generates too low a reputation for himself. . . . In sum, he makes himself both loved and revered rather than feared. . . . In his palace there is great magnificence and liberality, yet he does not stray from decent living. So that in all his activities . . . nobody is aware of anything offensive or reprehensible.9


Machiavelli might merely have been trying to seek favor with a Medici by praising him to a mutual friend and potential go-between. The “qualities” for which Machiavelli praises Lorenzo in this letter are not exactly those he recommends in The Prince. They might be close enough, however, to indicate an inclination on Lorenzo’s part to want to act and be perceived as a “prince” and so a willingness to learn how to do so effectively from Machiavelli.

If, as Machiavelli argues in chapter 22, “there are three kinds of brains: one that understands by itself, another that discerns what others understand, the third that understands neither by itself nor through others,” in giving Lorenzo The Prince, Machiavelli was presenting him with a test.10 If Lorenzo recognized good counsel when he received it, he would prove himself to be prudent. If he did not perceive the wisdom of Machiavelli’s advice and offer him a position, Lorenzo would show that he was not able to understand things either on his own or with the help of others.11


I. The Classification of Principalities—and the Foundations of Political Order


In Discourses 1.25 Machiavelli observes, “if someone who desires to reform a state in a city wishes it to be accepted and capable of being maintained to the satisfaction of everyone, he is under the necessity of retaining at least the shadow of its ancient modes so that it may not appear to the peoples to have changed its order even if in fact the new orders are altogether alien to the past ones” (60). And in presenting his educational treatise for a prince, Machiavelli seems to have retained bits of the outer appearance of the existing genre (as, for example, in Erasmus’s The Education of a Christian Prince): Latin chapter titles and an initial dry, almost scholastic classification of types.12

Despite its classical cover, however, Machiavelli’s classification was, in fact, revolutionary, beginning with the very first sentence: “All states, all dominions that have held and do hold empire over men have been and are either republics or principalities” (5). Whereas previous authors had categorized governments or regimes according to the number of rulers, whether they ruled for the sake of the community as a whole or their own advantage, and whether or not the government was restrained by law, Machiavelli began by dividing “states” or “dominions” simply according to the number of rulers, into republics or principalities.13 Commentators like Benedetto Croce have taken this first division to show that Machiavelli was the first “value-free” political scientist, because he did not categorize governments as good or bad, just or unjust. However, since Machiavelli goes on to make a great many “value judgments” in The Prince, his analysis cannot accurately be described as value-free. Machiavelli drops the traditional distinction between governments that serve the common good and those that serve the good of the ruler(s), because he observes that human beings never act simply or solely for the sake of others. The differences among governments cannot, therefore, be attributed to differences in motive or purpose on the part of the rulers. Individuals may sacrifice their lives or their fortunes for the sake of others, but in doing so they are seeking another kind of compensation—honor or glory. Rulers may—indeed, Machiavelli will argue that they should—seek to benefit their people. But he suggests that rulers will most reliably do so if they think that defending their people and contributing to their greater prosperity will keep them in power, if not make them revered.

Machiavelli’s refusal to classify governments as just or unjust does not explain why he reduces the classification apparently on the basis of number to only two types of command rather than the traditional three (one, few, or many). Does the “republican” Machiavelli not see a fundamental difference between the rule of a few in aristocracies or oligarchies and the rule of the majority or many in democracies? In chapter 9 he says that the desires of the many are more decent (onesto) than those of the great. But, as we have already seen, Machiavelli does not distinguish governments on the basis of their decency or desire to dominate (which would be versions of just and unjust).14 In The Prince Machiavelli gradually shows not only that it is in the interest of the “prince” to seek the support of the people, but also that the people are never safe and secure without an effective leader or “prince.”15 As his explicit denomination of leaders of republics as “princes” in both the Discourses and his Florentine Histories indicates, Machiavelli thinks that all peoples need leaders to establish and maintain “law and order.”16 The fundamental question or characteristic that distinguishes “principalities” from “republics” thus proves not to be whether the first have “princes” and the second do not, but whether or not potential “princes” have to compete with each other for popular support.17

Having drawn the basic distinction between principalities and republics, Machiavelli proceeds to discuss the six types of principalities he lists in P 1.18 The “types” are distinguished primarily by the way in which they are acquired and secondarily by the characteristics of the peoples acquired—specifically, whether the people in question is accustomed to living under a prince or under its own laws in a republic—because these characteristics make any given territory more or less difficult to acquire and retain. The first distinction between hereditary principalities “in which the bloodline of their lord has been their prince for a long time” (5) and new principalities might appear to be temporal, simply between the old and the new, or between established (and hence presumably legitimate) and “upstart” (hence questionable) governments. For Machiavelli, however, heredity is a mode of acquisition.19 His typology embodies the general principle he announces in chapter 3: “Truly it is a very natural and ordinary thing to desire to acquire, and always, when men do it who can, they will be praised or not blamed; but when they cannot and wish to do it anyway, here lies the error and the blame” (14–15). Recognizing that princes will be praised as such only if they retain what they have acquired, in the discussion of the types of principalities that follows Machiavelli combines considerations of how they are acquired with considerations of the relative ease or difficulty of maintaining rule once attained.

Not all ways of acquiring rule are equally onerous. Indeed, it is so easy for a person who is born first in line to inherit that Machiavelli does not even comment on the way hereditary principalities are acquired other than to describe the basis: the blood (or bloodline) of the prince. Instead he emphasizes that “the difficulties in maintaining them are much less than in new states, because it is enough only not to depart from the order of his ancestors, and then to temporize in the face of accidents” (6). An heir to an established line has less reason to “offend,” i.e., to injure, his subjects by seizing their property or lives than a new prince, who has to seize and then maintain his rule. So, Machiavelli reasons, “if extraordinary vices do not make him hated, it is reasonable that he will have the good will of his own [subjects]” (7). As we see in Discourses 1.2, Machiavelli knew that previous writers had emphasized the way in which hereditary leaders tended to become corrupt, hated, and eventually overthrown. He might well have thought the tendency of those who are born princes to succumb to the temptation of believing that they can do whatever they please and so arouse the hatred of their subjects to be ordinary. He merely observes that a hereditary prince will have little difficulty maintaining his rule if he employs “ordinary industry.” So long as “the antiquity and continuity of his dominion extinguishes the memories of revolutions and the reasons for them,” he will be deprived of rule only by “an extraordinary and excessive force” (7). Machiavelli thus recasts what was traditionally considered to be a matter of morality or corruption as a question of the prince’s diligence and his subjects’ memories.

Because people accept what they see around them as “natural” if they have no memory that things used to be different, Machiavelli starts with a consideration of the established, hereditary, or “natural” prince. But he soon begins to take up the reasons for change (and thus the difficulties of both acquiring and maintaining rule) in chapter 3. He observes that the reasons for change become evident in a new principality, but he moves to a consideration of wholly new principalities only in stages. By first considering the “mixed principalities” that result from the acquisition of a new territory by an established prince, he reminds his readers that whatever its current character, all rule has its basis in acquisition.

A prince’s control of his new dominion is uncertain as a result of “a natural difficulty that exists in all new principalities. This is that men willingly change their lords in the belief that they fare better” (7–8). In the guise merely of distinguishing the various types of principalities, Machiavelli thus reminds his readers that human beings are not naturally satisfied with their current condition and are inclined, as a result of their perpetual dissatisfaction, to seek change. But, he contends, such men are deceived in the belief that they will improve their condition by changing masters (or rebelling). The reason is “another natural and ordinary necessity that requires that one must always offend those over whom he becomes a new prince, both with men-at-arms and with the infinite other injuries that a new acquisition brings in its wake” (8). A new prince will have as enemies all those he displaced in occupying that principality, and he cannot maintain as friends those who helped put him there, because he will not be able to satisfy them in the way they hoped.

The most obvious form of the necessity that a prince will harm the people of a province he seizes is that he has to use force to take it. The prince or people who have been in charge will not willingly cede their power to him. In order to maintain his rule, Machiavelli thus insists, a new prince has to eliminate the bloodline of the old.20 If he does not, some of them will almost surely conspire to unseat him. But if the states that are added to the old state of the acquiring prince are “of the same province and the same language,” Machiavelli assures his reader, “they may be held with great ease, especially when they are not used to living in freedom” (9). The new prince should simply eliminate the bloodline of the old rulers and, Machiavelli now adds, not alter the laws or taxes. In that case, his new subjects will hardly notice the change in government.21 Nor will they be given new reasons to rebel. Contrary to Machiavelli’s initial statement, it does not require “infinite other injuries” to take over a state, if one keeps everything the same except for the person occupying the highest office.22 People do not care so much about who is in charge as about the effects of that person’s rule on their own lives.

Machiavelli forthrightly admits that it requires “great fortune and great industry” to acquire and maintain rule in places with different languages, customs, and orders. The first thing Machiavelli suggests a new prince should do under such circumstances is to go and live in his new province, “as the Turk has done in Greece” (10). If a prince is living on site, he can spot problems as they arise rather than having to wait for reports from others. Moreover, his subjects will believe that they can appeal to him to control his own officers, and those who would offend against him and his laws will be more afraid of being apprehended. But, Machiavelli urges, if a prince cannot go to live there himself, he should send colonies rather than try to occupy the province he has annexed with an army.23 Colonists support themselves, whereas the prince has to pay and supply his armies; and he will have to offend fewer of the current inhabitants of a province (and so make them enemies) by seizing their land for his colonists to occupy.24

Since a prince can lose control of a province to an external power as well as to internal rebels, Machiavelli also advises the new prince to make himself leader and defender of the weaker powers in the neighborhood, partly as a way of discouraging them from inviting another power, greater than his, in to defend them.25 Because Machiavelli earlier said that he was not going to reason about republics, a reader might be surprised to see that he uses the Roman republic as the example of the imperial policies he advocates. Machiavelli began his classification of states or empires by asserting that there were only two kinds—principalities and republics. States and empires, he now suggests, both experience the same needs and have the same requirements for controlling their subject populations. Because the new acquisition was, until it was acquired, a foreign power, in a “mixed principality” domestic and foreign policy coincide.

Machiavelli contrasts the success the Roman republic had in annexing Greece with King Louis XII’s failure to conquer and occupy northern Italy. A reader might again be surprised to see Machiavelli, in effect, telling a foreign prince what to do in order to seize and occupy Italy. However, at the conclusion of The Prince, Machiavelli calls upon Lorenzo to do precisely what he has argued the foreign prince should have done. In this chapter, we might understand Machiavelli to be showing his chief purported reader what he needs to do in order to realize the greatness Machiavelli desires for him.26

Louis failed to seize and occupy Italy, Machiavelli first says, because he committed five errors: he eliminated rather than befriended the small powers; he enhanced the power of a neighbor (Pope Alexander VI or the Church); he brought in another foreign power (Spain in order to take Naples); he did not come to live there in person; and he did not send colonies. But Machiavelli then adds that the mistake that forced Louis to withdraw from Italy entirely was his destroying Venice, the last remaining check on the other great powers’ ambitions in Lombardy.27 Machiavelli characteristically does not fault the French king for having turned against the allies who first invited him to come into Italy; he also recognizes that the first two “errors” for which he blames Louis resulted from the king’s abiding by a promise he had made to the pope. He refers his reader to P 18 where he argues that a prince can always find reasons to excuse himself from abiding by a promise. According to Machiavelli, it seems, a prince should not fear divine retribution for breaking an oath—at least, if he wants to retain his position as prince. (In P 18 he explicitly argues that a prince must always appear, but only appear, to be religious.)

Machiavelli concludes his discussion of “mixed principalities” by reporting that after the cardinal of Rouen told him that the Italians did not understand war, he told the cardinal that “the French did not understand the state, because if they understood, they would not have let the Church come to such greatness” (16). In reporting this exchange, Machiavelli points to a difference between the ancient Roman republic he has used as a model of correct policy and the modern European prince to whom he is purportedly writing. Unlike the Roman republic, modern European princes have to deal with an independent power that claims a right to determine what is according to divine will and what is not. And as we are reminded by Louis’s promise to lend the pope troops in exchange for the pope’s granting the king a divorce, such determinations reached the basis or purported grounds of the legitimacy of the European monarchs.28 No one can legally inherit a principality from a father to whom his mother is not legally wed. Two big questions thus arise: If Lorenzo or any other modern European prince is to follow the example of the Romans in expanding his empire in Italy, will he have to destroy the independence of the Vatican by going to live in Rome “in person” the way the Turk went to live in Greece? And if he does, will he have to impose the kind of absolute domination on his current subjects that the Turk exercises over his, so that he will not have to fear that his former subjects will revolt or conspire with a foreign power in his absence?29

Machiavelli takes up the example set by “the Turk” in the next chapter, where readers learn that the types of principalities differ not only in the way that they are acquired but also in the character of the people over whom rule is acquired. These differences are not matters of climate or economic enterprise, language, or culture, moreover; they are results of the previous form of government.

In his initial discussion of the ways in which a prince could acquire and maintain a “mixed principality,” Machiavelli suggested that it would be easy to maintain control of a people who spoke the same language and shared the same customs. But in chapter 4 he withdraws that suggestion. The example he gave in chapter 3 of such an easy annexation was that of Burgundy, Brittany, Gascony, and Normandy by the French king. Purportedly to explain “why the kingdom of Darius which Alexander seized did not rebel from his successors after Alexander’s death,” in chapter 4 Machiavelli points out that “principalities of which memory remains have been governed in two diverse modes: either by one prince, and all the others servants . . . ; or by a prince and by barons who hold that rank not by favor of the lord but by antiquity of bloodline” (16–17). Examples of the two kinds of government are those of the Turk and the king of France. And “whoever considers the one and the other of these states will find difficulty in acquiring the state of the Turk, but should it be conquered, great ease in holding it. So inversely, you will find in some respects more ease in seizing the Kingdom of France, but great difficulty in holding it” (17–18).

The reason the “kingdom” of the Turk is difficult to seize but easy to keep once seized is that he has made everyone else his slave. Fearful for their lives if they disobey, the emperor’s slaves are difficult to corrupt, and even if they are convinced to betray him, they cannot bring any other people with them.30 One thus has to overcome the Turk with one’s own forces in an open battle, rather than relying on the defection of some of his supporters. But if a prince defeats the Turk in an open battle, his servants will become the servants of the conqueror, because they are accustomed to following orders, not to ruling themselves.

In kingdoms ruled like France, where there are barons who have their own state and subjects, not as a grant from the king but on the basis of their own bloodline, there will always be some malcontent anxious to obtain the help of an external power in revolting. Such kingdoms are, therefore, easy to enter, but difficult to maintain. It is not sufficient to eliminate the bloodline of the prince, because the barons retain their independent forces and loyal subjects. And it is impossible to content or to eliminate all of them.

What is true of the independent barons is even more true of states that “are accustomed to live with their own laws and in liberty” (20). In chapter 5 Machiavelli explains that there are three ways of dealing with such cities: The first is to destroy them. The second is to go there in person to live. The third, which initially seems preferable, is to “let them live by their laws, taking tribute from them and creating within them an oligarchical state which keeps them friendly. For, since this state has been created by that prince, it knows that it cannot exist without his friendship and power, and it has to do everything to maintain him. And a city used to living free may be held more easily by means of its own citizens than in any other mode, if one wants to preserve it” (20). However, Machiavelli reminds his readers (again using republics as examples of “princely” foreign policy), the Spartans eventually lost Athens by using the third way. The Romans also tried to rule Greece in this manner, but found that “there is no secure mode to possess . . . a city accustomed to living in freedom” except to destroy it, because it always has a reason to rebel in “the name of liberty and its own ancient orders, which are never forgotten either through length of time or because of benefits received . . . unless the inhabitants are broken up or dispersed” (21).31

By the time readers come to the end of Machiavelli’s discussion of “mixed principalities” (since the discussions of the relative ease of acquiring and then retaining possession of provinces ruled by different kinds of princes and republics constitute a subsection of that general discussion), they have thus acquired a great many fundamental lessons about the nature of political activity. First and foremost, Machiavelli has reminded them that human beings do not accept the government of others gladly or freely, certainly not if they have experienced freedom. In other words, government does not arise naturally or spontaneously. It rests, and presumably always will, ultimately on the ability of some to force others to obey. But not merely can human beings be forced to obey; they even can be brought to believe that the reigning government is natural, if and so long as they are not reminded of the causes of innovation. That cause, Machiavelli states in his description of “mixed principalities,” is the natural desire to acquire. For if all human beings desire to acquire more than they currently have, they will obviously come into conflict with one another. This conflict may be most evident in the case of states, which fight wars to conquer others. But it is also the reason, Machiavelli shows in later chapters, that individuals need governments to secure their lives and property from others in their vicinity.

Both because government is not natural but has to be imposed, and because human beings tend to believe that what they see around them is natural and necessary and thus doubt that anything else is possible, Machiavelli declares in chapter 6 that “the greatest examples” of princes are those who found their states de novo. He does not expect Lorenzo or any other reader in a civilized time and place literally to reenact such a founding. It is not an accident that all his examples of such new princes are from a very distant, if not, strictly speaking, “mythical” past. Precisely because, as Machiavelli observed at the conclusion of chapter 2, men tend to forget the causes of innovation once order has been established, he has to remind his reader of how much virtue it requires, not merely to rise from a private position to become a prince (since that can also occur by mere fortune or chance), but to found a new nation. He names Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, and Theseus as the greatest examples. Recognizing that Moses might appear to be an exception, because he was directed by God, Machiavelli nevertheless points out that if one considers “Cyrus, and the others who have acquired or founded kingdoms: you will find . . . their particular actions and orders . . . no different from those of Moses” (22–23). In other words, Machiavelli is going to give a completely secular account of the origins of principalities, even though he knows (and explicitly recognizes in other works) that the founders he is about to celebrate claimed to have divine guidance, if not birth.32

Machiavelli insists that these founders did not get “anything from fortune other than opportunity, which gave them the matter enabling them to introduce any form they pleased” (23).33 The “opportunity” or “matter” consists in an enslaved, discontented, or dispersed people.34 Such people are willing to follow a self-proclaimed leader who promises to free or otherwise improve their condition, precisely because they are enslaved, discontented, or dispersed. Machiavelli’s famed founders thus all appear in the guise of liberators.

The virtue of the founder is demonstrated by his ability to overcome the two different kinds of opposition he inevitably faces in attempting to establish a new order. First, there are the people who benefited from the old order and so oppose the introduction of a new. Second, those discontented with the current order who thus initially follow the new leader tend to fall away, partly from fear of the opposition, “who have the laws on their side.” (Machiavelli thus acknowledges in passing that where there are enough human beings to reorganize, there must have been some previous form of organization. No one entirely begins from scratch; one has to destroy in order to build. And from the point of view of the old order, these “innovators” are criminals.) The followers of the introducer of new modes and orders also tend to fade away in the face of opposition, because of “the incredulity of men, who do not truly believe in new things unless they come to have a firm experience of them” (23–24). The founder of a new order thus has to use force not only to put down and replace those who benefit from the existing order but also to keep his own supporters in line.35

Because the founders of new regimes have to use force against both the opposition and their own adherents, Machiavelli famously concludes that “all the armed prophets were victorious and the unarmed ones were ruined” (24). He points to Girolamo Savonarola as an example of the fate of an unarmed prophet and cites Hiero of Syracuse as a lesser example of the success of a private man who became a prince “in everything but name” by means of arms. Hiero appears, indeed, to constitute an ancient example of the use of the strategies for which Machiavelli will praise Cesare Borgia in chapter 7: “Hiero eliminated the old military and organized a new one; he left old friendships and made new ones; and when he had friendships and soldiers that were his own, he could build any building on top of such a foundation” (25). Machiavelli does not explicitly observe that the “new princes” he has described would be difficult to distinguish from tyrants like Agathocles, whom he takes up in a later chapter as an example of a prince who attained his principality through crimes. He simply concludes that having acquired rule with great difficulty, those who become princes by means solely of their own virtue maintain control easily. Indeed, he goes so far as to say that they will “begin to be held in veneration, having eliminated those who had envied them” (24). To discover how and why a bringer of new modes and orders becomes revered (as opposed to merely feared), and thus a founder rather than a criminal, we have to turn to the following chapters.36

Apparently proceeding in terms of the binary divisions he sketched in chapter 1, Machiavelli turns in chapter 7 to consider “new principalities that are acquired with the arms and fortune of others” (25). By contrasting them with “principalities that are acquired by one’s own arms and by virtue,” he connects virtue to having “one’s own arms.” He has argued that a new prince has to use force in order to acquire rule by means solely of his own virtue. But the greatest examples of such new princes were legendary founders whose deeds are known, to the extent to which they are known, only in fables; and Machiavelli admitted that Lorenzo could not follow their example. He urged his primary reader simply to aim high so that he could accomplish something more ordinary.37

The two contemporary examples Machiavelli now brings forth of men who became princes through virtue, on the one hand, and fortune, on the other, are neither so distant nor so impossible to imitate. Like the ancients, Francesco Sforza came to power by means of his own arms. This mercenary captain had been promised something like a hereditary succession to the dukedom of Milan in the form of a marriage to the daughter of the reigning duke. But Sforza actually acquired control of the city only after the citizens rebelled against the duke and invited the mercenary captain to take over the city (even though he had betrayed them earlier), because they needed someone with an army to defend them. As a result of his prudent planning, Sforza and his army “happened” to be in the neighborhood.38 According to Machiavelli, Cesare Borgia first acquired a principality in the Romagna by fortune, because he was the illegitimate son of the pope.

In relating how Alexander disturbed the existing orders in Romagna so that his son could become prince, Machiavelli shows that one does not need to wait for an “opportunity” to found a new principality. In other words, even the “opportunity” a new prince needs can be intentionally created—by means of an external invasion or internally undermining the existing government. The Venetians made Alexander’s task easier by inviting the French to invade Italy; and Alexander obtained French troops for Cesare to use in conquering the Romagna in exchange for granting the king his divorce.

Although Cesare acquired his principality by means of good fortune and the arms of others, Machiavelli uses his example to show that it is possible, even in modern times and thus for Lorenzo (who might also be said to have acquired his rule by means of his family relation to a pope), to lay one’s foundations after the fact. If a new prince is not a general of his own army like Sforza, he will, like Cesare Borgia, have to use “the arms of others” in order to seize power. But once he does, like a new prince in a “mixed principality,” he will have to worry about the loyalty of his “friends.” Having used French arms to acquire the Romagna and hired Orsini mercenaries to beat down the Colonna, Cesare saw that the Orsini gave him only lukewarm support in his attack on Bologna and that he was ordered by the French king to desist in his attack on Urbino. Deciding that it was no longer prudent to depend upon the arms of others, Cesare first bribed the adherents of both the Orsini and the Colonna families with large allowances and government posts and brought them into his party. Then he eliminated the heads of the opposition by means of deceit.39 Machiavelli does not explain how Cesare convinced these heads to meet him unarmed at Sinigaglia, where he had them seized and murdered. However, in the next chapter he tells his readers about the way the mercenary captain who had arms with him at Sinigaglia, but was persuaded to leave them behind, had gathered together the heads of the leading families in Fermo for a banquet where he had his soldiers murder them. Although Oliverotto praised the greatness of Pope Alexander and Cesare Borgia, he apparently did not suspect that they would be willing to use the very same tactics he had used against his own family in order to eliminate the opposition. As Machiavelli explicitly concludes with regard to Cesare Borgia, so he shows in the case of Oliverotto da Fermo, his ambitious, cutthroat contemporaries do not recognize their own desires and a willingness to adopt underhanded and bloody methods of satisfying them in other equally ambitious and unprincipled would-be princes.

Before he turns to consider those, like Oliverotto, who have attained a principality through crime, Machiavelli pauses to explain how, after he seized the Romagna, Cesare “judged it necessary to give it good government” (29). In other words, Machiavelli shows that laying firm foundations does not merely entail organizing one’s own (or loyal) armed forces and eliminating the opposition from other armed lords. A new prince also has to benefit the people of his new province by establishing “law and order,” so securing their lives and livelihoods. Finding the Romagna “commanded by impotent lords, readier to despoil their subjects than to correct them,” and the province thus “full of robberies, quarrels, and every other kind of insolence,” Cesare gave a cruel and ready man full power to reduce it to peace and unity. However, once Remirro de Orco had apprehended (killed, imprisoned, and/or tortured) those insolent enough to commit the robberies and murders and, with his reputation for cruelty, had frightened others from following their examples, “the duke judged that such excessive authority was not necessary, because he feared that it might become hateful.” So, in place of his fearsome executioner, “he set up a civil court in the middle of the province, with a most excellent president, where each city had its advocate.”40 And “to show that if any cruelty had been committed, it had not come from him but from the harsh nature of his minister,” he had Remirro’s body cut in two pieces and placed “in the piazza at Cesena with a piece of wood and bloody knife beside him” (29–30). Cesare thus not only satisfied the people’s desire to avenge themselves on the immediate source of their fear and oppression (see D 1.16) but also “stupefied” them. The man they thought stood behind his terrible agent had not merely freed them from the domination of this hateful man; he had also brought them peace and civil government.

Cesare might well, therefore, have come to be revered as a founder, if he had been able to maintain himself. Because his father, Alexander (who had provided him with funds and men-at-arms), died less than five years after Cesare began to acquire his principality, however, the foundations of his rule were not yet firm. He had eliminated the bloodlines of the lords he had supplanted, won over the gentlemen in Rome, and gained influence on the College of Cardinals, but he had not acquired enough of an empire to enable him to resist an attack without support from the pope. If Cesare could not control the selection of Alexander’s successor, Machiavelli argues, he should have made sure that no cardinal who had been injured by him or who had reason to fear him was appointed. Because all the candidates except the Spaniards and the French cardinal of Rouen had reason to fear or hate him, Cesare should have made sure that either a Spaniard or Rouen was elected. He did not; he allowed San Piero ad Vincula, whom he had offended, to become Julius II. (Because he thought that Julius would benefit him in return for a bribe after he was elected pope, Cesare was seized, imprisoned, and finally sent off to die fighting in Spain.) Machiavelli does not describe the results of Cesare’s misjudgment. He simply warns his readers, “whoever believes that among great personages new benefits will make old injuries be forgotten deceives himself” (33). Attributing the beneficial effects of a prince’s rule to an intention on his part to serve them, especially if he professes such, Machiavelli has suggested, the people may in time forget the causes of change after a principality has been firmly established. But ambitious princes do not forget or forgive old injuries—even if they are purportedly Christians. Nor, Machiavelli suggests, should they. The power Cesare had acquired in the Romagna, among the warring factions in Rome, and in the College of Cardinals made him a threat to the new pope, who, understanding how he had to lay the foundations of his own principality after he was elevated by fortune, sought to eliminate the bloodline of the previous prince. Like Oliverotto, Cesare failed to understand that other new princes would act against their competitors the way he had acted against his. As Machiavelli suggested in his dedication to Lorenzo, princes see the character of the people. In particular, princes see that the people can be coerced and deceived. But being men of action rather than reflection, “princes” tend not to understand their own natures. One has to look at a prince from the perspective of the people, i.e., as a potential oppressor, to apprehend the nature of a prince. A willingness to act ruthlessly will not suffice to enable a prince to acquire or maintain rule; he needs to understand what his competitors want and will do to achieve what they desire so that he can forestall their satisfaction at his expense.

Having first suggested that Cesare Borgia provides a model for a man like Lorenzo, who has become a prince largely as a result of his family connections, of the way in which he can lay firmer foundations for his rule after he first acquires it, but then admitted that Cesare failed not simply because of bad luck but because of bad judgment, Machiavelli somewhat surprisingly proceeds to discuss four additional categories or types of principalities he did not mention in his initial classification. All four “types” or chapters concern ways in which a prince may or may not be able to maintain his rule better than Cesare did. All can also be read as covert critiques of the Medici.

Machiavelli first observes that there are two additional ways in which a private man may become a prince that cannot be attributed, strictly speaking, entirely to his virtù or to his fortune. These are by means of crime or through the favor of one’s fellow citizens. In chapter 8 he gives two examples of the former, one ancient and one modern, “for anyone who needs to imitate them” (34).

Machiavelli points out that both Agathocles the Sicilian and Oliverotto da Fermo rose through the ranks of their respective armies on the basis of their demonstrated merit as soldiers. They could both be said, therefore, to have demonstrated a certain kind of virtù. Having become the highest-ranking member of their armed forces, they both decided to seize control of their cities. Whereas Cesare openly seized control of the Romagna with French troops, as if he were a foreign prince, and then sought to eliminate the bloodlines of the lords there, Agathocles and Oliverotto proceeded more covertly and expeditiously. Having arranged for gatherings of the leading men in their respective cities, they both had soldiers waiting in hiding to slaughter these local dignitaries on the spot and so eliminated all sources of internal opposition to their rule at one stroke. Machiavelli does not point out that both “criminals” were overthrowing republics; he simply mentions in passing that Agathocles assembled the people and the senate of Syracuse and that Oliverotto arranged the murder of the maternal uncle who had raised him along with the most prominent men of Fermo “with the help of some citizens to whom serving him was more dear than the liberty of their fatherland” (36).41 The two points Machiavelli emphasizes are, first, that the cruelties a private man who wants to found a new principality must necessarily commit in seizing control should be done all at once and, second, that this cruelty should be aimed at eliminating possible sources of opposition. These “criminals” had their own arms (or armies) and did what a man who becomes a prince on the basis of his own virtue rather than mere good luck must do in founding a new order. But, Machiavelli also suggests, they and their deeds cannot simply be called virtuous, because having seized control, they did not cease using cruel means (as Cesare had with Remirro) and begin to use merely the threat of renewed cruelty in order to establish and maintain a legal order that benefitted their subjects.42 As a result, these “criminals” never received the glory bestowed upon a great founder.43

In chapter 9 Machiavelli thus emphasizes the need for a prince, once in power, to seek popular support. Indeed, he observes that “one who becomes prince against the people with the support of the great must before everything else seek to win the people to himself, which should be easy for him when he takes up their protection. And since men who receive good from someone from whom they believed they would receive evil are more obliged to their benefactor, the people immediately wish him well more than if he had been brought to the principality through their support” (40). Machiavelli thus appears to be continuing to show his reader (Lorenzo or another) how he could succeed better than Cesare did in becoming a truly great, well-regarded, and secure prince.

Machiavelli does not name any examples of princes who came into power with the support of their fellow citizens, perhaps because, as he admitted in introducing this type of principality in chapter 8, “it might be reasoned about more extensively where republics are treated” (34).44 But as in chapter 3 where he used the Roman republic as the model of the policy a prince ought to follow, Machiavelli again shows that the general principles of politics he is announcing in his very short little book apply to republics as well as to principalities. He takes this occasion, in fact, to announce one of his most fundamental observations or principles: “In every city two diverse humors are found,” because “the people desire neither to be commanded nor oppressed by the great, and the great desire to command and oppress the people” (39).45 Because these two “humors” (umori) are obviously opposed, and neither can be satisfied except at the expense of the other, two things follow. First, there will always be conflict at the heart of every city. Machiavelli has already indicated that government has to be imposed on human beings by means of force; now he very clearly states the reason: no one wants to be commanded or oppressed by another. That does not mean, however, that some do not want to command and oppress the rest. Machiavelli’s characterization of the fundamental division means, second, that it exists primarily with respect to rule rather than wealth or economic class. As he observes in D 2.10, those who have arms or force can seize the wealth of those who do not.

Depending on the relative strength of these two “appetites” (appetiti), as Machiavelli also dubs them, there are three possible results: principality or liberty or license.46 In a book purportedly devoted to an examination of principalities, he does not explain why he now suggests three possible outcomes of the fundamental struggle within every city rather than two, i.e., either a principality or a republic. He provides the reasoning on the basis of which he comes to this conclusion, however, in his Florentine Histories:

Cities . . . frequently change their governments and their states not between liberty and servitude, as many believe, but between servitude and license. For only the name of freedom is extolled by the ministers of license, who are the men of the people, and by the ministers of servitude, who are the nobles, neither of them desiring to be subject either to the laws or to men. True, when it happens (and it happens rarely) that by the good fortune of a city there rises in it a wise, good, and powerful citizen by whom laws are ordered by which these humors of the nobles and men of the people are quieted or restrained so that they cannot do evil, then that city can be called free and that state be judged stable and firm: for a city based on good laws and good orders has no necessity, as have others, for the virtue of a single man to maintain it. (4.1)


Delineating the ways in which a single man can acquire and maintain his state in The Prince, Machiavelli observes merely that a principality is caused either by the people or by the great, when either of the humors sees that it cannot resist the other without making someone a prince to defend it. Machiavelli does not attribute the rise of such a prince to his virtue, because he does not seize power himself. He is elevated by his fellow citizens in what “one could call a civil principality.” Since his fellow citizens have presumably chosen him to defend them for some reason, his elevation does not appear to be a matter of pure chance or “fortune.” Machiavelli thus attributes it to a “fortunate astuteness” (astuzia fortunate) that leads such a man to see what needs to be done to protect his supporters from his opponents.

However such a “prince” comes into power, Machiavelli strongly urges him not to rely on “the great” to support him, if he wants to maintain himself. There are two reasons why he should seek the support of the people instead. First, the great will always see themselves as the prince’s equals and demand ever more offices and goods as the price of their support. Attempts to satisfy them will, therefore, necessarily fail and, in failing, add to the prince’s enemies. It is possible, however, to satisfy the people, “for the end of the people is more decent [onesto] than that of the great, since the great want to oppress and the people want not to be oppressed” (39).47 The second reason why it is better to seek the support of the people than of the great is even more radical and points to another of Machiavelli’s fundamental political principles. A prince will never be able to secure himself against a hostile people, because they are many whereas the great are few. As Machiavelli observed in the cases of Agathocles and Oliverotto, the great can be destroyed, but a prince will have no one to rule if he murders all or most of his people. A prince needs subordinates to help him rule, “but he can well do without the same great persons, since he can make and unmake them every day” (40), by giving them lands and offices or, conversely, taking those same lands and offices away along with their lives. The “great” are not different from the many by nature; they are not better or more ambitious or more grasping in themselves. “Greatness” is a matter of position. Those raised to office have more power and goods; and having more power and goods, they no longer feel as liable as those who are subject to the government to oppression by others. Instead, they begin to desire to acquire more by oppressing others.48 And because the “great” always want more, they will always be competitors and potential enemies of the prince, unless they and their positions remain entirely dependent on him.49

Although a prince should seek the support of the people, Machiavelli concludes, he should not rely on them to liberate or protect him from his enemies (the way he needs to protect the people from theirs). A prince may need a people, but his necessity will not be theirs unless he finds a way to persuade them that they need the state and his government.

Machiavelli suggests two ways a prince can convince his people that they need him and his government in the next chapter when he inquires “in what mode the forces of all principalities should be measured” (42). A prince can organize and lead an army to defend a city from attack; or if he is not able to field an army, he can construct fortifications and provide sufficient food and work to maintain the people for a year under siege (in which case it becomes too expensive for another power to attack him and his city).50 In sum, Machiavelli suggests, if a prince provides for both the defense and the welfare of his people, he will reign secure.

It is not obvious, however, why a discussion of the forces a prince has at his disposal belongs in a discussion of the types of principalities, i.e., why chapter 10 comes where it does. But the distinction Machiavelli draws here between princes who have enough men or money to field an army adequate to defend them and those who are compelled of necessity to take refuge behind walls does point to a kind of principality Machiavelli has not yet taken up. As he observes in D 2.19, some of the cities of Germany, officially under the emperor, were principalities; and these princes were effectively free to do as they wished, partly because they were able to defend themselves with walls and supplies so that they could withstand both frontal attacks and long sieges, even though they did not have sufficient numbers to field an army, and partly because the emperor was weak. Unlike the princes Machiavelli will write about in chapter 20, these princes built fortresses not to defend themselves against their people, but to defend their people against foreigners. They did not disarm their people, but rather trained them militarily so that they could repel direct attacks. And because they sought to benefit the people in obvious ways rather than oppressing them with taxes or other burdens, these princes did not make themselves hated.

Machiavelli concludes his consideration of the different types of principalities with what appears to be a limiting case—a principality that can be acquired by either virtue or fortune and maintained without either, “for they are sustained by orders that have grown old with religion, which have been so powerful and of such a kind that they keep their princes in the state however they proceed and live. These alone have states, and do not defend them; they have subjects, and do not govern them; and the states, though undefended, are not taken from them; the subjects, though ungoverned, do not care, and they neither think of becoming estranged from such princes nor can they.” Underlining the general conclusion a reader should draw from this discussion, Machiavelli baldly states, “only these principalities are secure and happy” (45). This conclusion is revealing not so much about the character of “ecclesiastical principalities,” however, as about all others. No other principality, including a hereditary principality that appears to be well-established, is really secure. Nor, therefore, can its prince be happy. Rather than trusting or enjoying the company of his fellows, Machiavelli has shown, a prince has to be constantly on the lookout for possible competitors or opponents. He can never relax or be at peace without endangering the continuity of his reign.51

Since these ecclesiastical principalities “subsist by superior causes to which the human mind does not reach,” Machiavelli says that he will not reason about them. He thus calls his reader’s attention to the fact that he will not treat anything that is not intelligible to the unassisted human mind. He can, however, explain how “the Church has come to such greatness in temporal affairs despite the fact that, before Alexander, the Italian powers . . . held her in low esteem in temporal affairs” (45).

In chapter 12 Machiavelli explains that the withdrawal of the emperor from Italy created the “opportunity” (or lack of order) that made it possible for the Church to acquire its temporal power.52 Alexander VI may have intended to help his illegitimate son by granting him control of the French troops the pope had obtained from Louis to conquer the Romagna, but, Machiavelli points out, in the end Duke Valentino’s conquests redounded (one might say “providentially,” although Machiavelli does not) to the greatness of the Church. Pope Julius found the Church in control of Romagna and the factions of the Orsini and Colonna in Rome, which had previously kept the power of the Church in Rome within bounds, destroyed. And Julius not only extended the armed conquests along with “a mode of accumulating money never used before Alexander”; he also forestalled the emergence of new divisions or competitors in Rome by refusing to appoint members of either the Orsini or the Colonna families as cardinals. “If others made [the Church] great with arms,” Machiavelli concludes, “one may hope that His Holiness Pope Leo with his goodness and infinite other virtues, can make it very great and venerable” (47).53

The lessons Machiavelli draws from his seemingly dry and static classification of the types of principalities thus point directly to his passionate concluding call in chapter 26 for Leo and his nephew to seize Italy and free it from the “barbarians.” Just as Alexander unintentionally used his illegitimate son Duke Valentino, so Machiavelli suggests, Leo should intentionally use his legitimate nephew as his instrument. The pope had already made Lorenzo commander of his troops at the battle of Marignano (1515). He could and, Machiavelli will argue, should now lead them in the conquest and “liberation” of Italy as a whole.


II. Advice to the Prince


A. The Lessons from the Ancients: The Importance of Relying upon One’s Own Arms


Having completed his typology of principalities, in chapters 12–14 Machiavelli turns to examine in more detail the means he has already shown a prince must employ in order to found and maintain his state. Emphasizing the fundamental role of force both in establishing and in maintaining political order, Machiavelli infamously begins by observing that “the principal foundations” of all states “are good laws and good arms. And because there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms, and where there are good arms there must be good laws, I shall leave out the reasoning on laws and shall speak of arms” (48).

Machiavelli explains that “the arms with which a prince defends his state are either his own or mercenary or auxiliary or mixed” (48). And on the basis of an analysis of the economic and political incentives, he argues that mercenary and auxiliary arms are either useless or dangerous.

Mercenary soldiers are not apt to be any good, because the stipend is not great enough to make them willing to die for it. They will, therefore, promise to fight so long as they do not actually need to do so. Italian mercenaries have sought to minimize their costs further by relying on cavalry rather than using infantry so that they have fewer men to feed. They have reduced the risks they face in war by not killing each other in battle, but taking prisoners without asking ransom. They also refuse to attack towns at night or to fight in winter. However, should a mercenary captain prove to be an effective commander, he immediately becomes a threat to the prince or citizens who have hired him and his men, precisely because the mercenaries are armed, whereas their employers are not.54

“A prince should,” therefore, “go in person, and himself perform the office of captain.” Acknowledging that republics (about which he was supposedly not going to speak) have to send one of their citizens to lead their troops, Machiavelli observes that if the captain does “not turn out to be a worthy man, [the republic] must change him; and if he is, it must check him with laws so that he does not step out of bounds” (49–50).55

Good arms do not necessarily make good laws; good laws are necessary to make arms good—at least for a republic.56 Machiavelli’s initial claim was a deliberate overstatement, which he quickly if quietly retracts. What is essential is to employ “one’s own arms” and not those of others. The main difference between ancient republics like Rome and Sparta and modern Italian republics like Florence and Venice is that the former armed their own citizens, who defended their freedom, whereas the latter use mercenaries, who threaten the freedom as well as the empire of the cities that employ them.57

If mercenaries are so bad, the question obviously arises, why have Italians employed them? The answer Machiavelli gives is ignorance and inexperience, two factors he proposes to correct by writing The Prince. When the Italians began to repel the empire, he reminds his readers, the citizens of many Italian cities took up arms against their nobles with support from the pope, who wished to increase his temporal power and reputation. Because neither the citizens nor the priests had knowledge of arms, they began to hire foreigners. Although Machiavelli does not explicitly point it out, the Medici in Florence and Rome were prime examples of citizens and priests who had employed mercenary armies rather than arm their own fellow citizens or subjects.

Mercenary arms tend not to be good or reliable troops, but, Machiavelli shows when he turns to auxiliaries, the goodness or badness of arms does not depend simply on the quality of the arms themselves. It is fundamentally a matter of control. Having discovered how unreliable mercenaries are, Italian princes like Pope Julius II who sought the assistance of troops mustered and controlled by other nations left their own fates in the hands of these auxiliaries. Unlike mercenaries, auxiliary troops may be good in themselves, but they are more dangerous precisely for that reason. If they lose, so do the princes who use them; but if they win, they are apt to follow their own interests or leaders rather than the interests of the prince to whom they were loaned. Both the pope and the Florentines have escaped the dire consequences of using auxiliaries only by good luck.

“A wise prince, therefore, has always avoided these arms and turned to his own” (55). In presenting four examples of the benefits and means of turning to one’s own arms, Machiavelli indicates that by “arms” he means more than armies or troops, because the examples he gives refer to strategy, that is, the intelligent employment and control of both force and fraud rather than, literally, armies and weapons. Once again he emphasizes how Cesare Borgia increased his reputation by using and then jettisoning first his French auxiliaries and, second, the Orsini mercenaries, before turning to his own arms. Machiavelli then reminds his readers of how Cesare treated the heads of those mercenaries by praising Hiero of Syracuse for arranging to have his mercenary army cut into pieces when he could no longer use them. (Hiero’s treatment of these mercenaries thus represents another example of “cruelty well-used,” analogous to Cesare’s using cruel means [Remirro] to bring “good government” to the Romagna and then seeing to it that those means were destroyed in order to separate himself from them in public.) By changing the story of David’s refusal of Saul’s arms so that David uses his own sling and knife instead of the biblical stones and his faith in God, Machiavelli also signals that his insistence that a prince should rely on his own “arms” means that a prince should not rely on divine or other forces beyond human control.58 Finally, in praising King Charles VII for liberating France from England by seeing the necessity of arming himself with his own arms, Machiavelli indicates more concretely how he thinks a prince can obtain and employ the support of his people. He should recruit and train them as men-at-arms or infantry (in contrast to the less popular and less numerous cavalry employed by the Italian mercenaries) and so make them “his own.” Machiavelli claims, indeed, that France would have been invincible if Louis XI had not replaced native infantry with Swiss. He admits that a mixture is better than using mercenaries or auxiliaries, but he insists that it is less good than relying entirely on one’s own arms. He would presumably make a similar judgment about relying entirely on one’s own arms—or wit—as opposed to relying on a combination of divine favor or good luck with one’s own resources. Only the last are fully under a captain’s control.

Machiavelli concludes the chapter by emphasizing that a prince without his own arms is wholly dependent upon fortune.
