Those “arms” include one’s fellow citizens, subjects, or “creatures,” that is, the human beings whose liberty, security, and prosperity depend on the perpetuation of the government they serve. To understand how those arms should be ordered, he directs his reader to “the four examples above.” He seems to mean Cesare, Hiero, David, and Charles, but he might also be referring to the four founders—Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus. It doesn’t matter, because the basic point is the same: a prince who wants to found and maintain his rule securely must rely on his own virtue, which includes understanding the need to organize and use his own forces to keep his own supporters in line as well as to eliminate his competitors.

In light of the emphasis Machiavelli has put on the importance of arming oneself, a reader is not surprised to see him conclude the section of the book devoted to defense by announcing that “a prince should have no other object, nor any thought, nor take anything else as his art but that of war and its orders and discipline; for that is the only art which is of concern to one who commands” (58). The reason is simple: those who are armed control those who are not.

Like the definition of one’s own “arms,” however, the exercise of the art of war that Machiavelli recommends turns out to have a much broader range and content than his reader might initially expect. According to Machiavelli, a prince needs to practice it even more in peace than in war (in order to be prepared for the latter, when his fortune changes), and he must practice in two modes, one with deeds and the other with his mind. The “deeds” include not merely keeping his armies well ordered and exercised, so inuring their bodies as well as his own to physical hardships. These “deeds” also entail a kind of mental training or education. By going on hunts in a variety of locations, a prince should learn the nature of sites. He should seek to discover first how to defend his own country, and from reflecting on how to deploy his own troops and defeat those of an enemy in a variety of terrains close to home, he will learn how to deploy them successfully abroad. He should also teach his subordinates by constantly asking them as they ride out together on hunts how they would defend themselves or attack an enemy in the place where they currently find themselves, examining their opinions and reasoning with them so that they will learn what to do in his absence.59

In addition to these “bodily” exercises, however, Machiavelli also recommends exercise of the mind. This exercise turns out to consist in doing something quite similar to what Machiavelli did in order to write The Prince. He thus implicitly brings his own enterprise and its importance more to the fore. By reading the histories and considering the actions of excellent men, especially how they conducted themselves in war, a prince should seek to discover the causes of their victories and losses, so that he can avoid the latter and imitate the former.

Above all, Machiavelli concludes, a prince “should do as some excellent man has done in the past who found someone to imitate who has been praised and glorified” (60). The examples of excellent men Machiavelli now names are different, however, from the “greatest examples” of the founders of entirely new principalities he urged Lorenzo to imitate earlier so that he would reach his target by aiming higher than he expected to land. Alexander, Caesar, and Scipio are described not as founders but as imitators. Moreover, the individuals they imitated were in at least two cases—Achilles and Xenophon’s Cyrus—more literary creations than actual historical figures. And they were remembered, glorified, and praised, not for the lasting effects of their accomplishments, but as great warriors who made extensive foreign conquests, not for having initiated a new order.60 One wonders, indeed, whether Achilles, Alexander, Caesar, Cyrus, and Scipio have been remembered for what they achieved as much as for what they destroyed. Readers are led to suspect that the imitation of a great general is not Machiavelli’s last word about the necessary content of a prince’s education.61


B. Machiavelli’s New Teaching: How a Prince Ought to Treat His Subjects and Friends


By listing only ancient, pre-Christian examples of famous generals who mastered the art of war by imitating another, Machiavelli suggests that the ancients understood how to wage war against enemies. When he turns to the question of how a prince should treat his subjects and friends, however, Machiavelli explicitly finds all previous “orders” lacking. He proposes, therefore, to do something new and different. He thus claims, in effect, to be founding a new “order.” This new order concerns not the means of acquiring power, which Machiavelli has shown that the ancients understood, so much as the means of maintaining it.

Seeking to determine how human beings ought to live rather than describing what they actually do, Machiavelli observes, many previous writers “have imagined republics and principalities that have never been seen or known to exist in truth.” (Plato’s Republic, Aristotle’s regime “to be prayed for,” and Aquinas’s De regimine principum are often taken to be prime examples.) However, Machiavelli points out, human beings do not live the way these writers have said they should. Desiring to “write something useful to whoever understands it,” he thus proposes “to go directly to the effectual truth.” That truth is that, living among so many people who are not good, a prince who attempts to make a profession of good in all regards will come to ruin. So if a prince “wants to maintain himself,” he needs “to learn to be able not to be good, and to use this and not use it according to necessity” (61, emphasis added).

To learn to be able not to be good and to use that knowledge is not simply to learn to be bad. In contrast to traditional educational treatises like Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics or Cicero’s De officiis, which dealt with the ways in which an individual’s character should be formed as a whole, “the effectual truth” Machiavelli proposes to teach is instrumental. A prince who needs to learn to be able to be bad is not entirely or habitually bad; it sounds, on the contrary, as if he is primarily good. He is a person who needs to learn to be able to do what are usually considered to be bad acts—when necessary.62 He thus also needs to learn what is necessary, why, and when. By proposing to teach something useful to those who understand, Machiavelli suggests that not everyone will.

Like Aristotle, Machiavelli initially treats characterizations of people as “good” or “bad” as matters of praise and blame. But where Aristotle proceeds to seek the true virtue in a mean between two extremes, Machiavelli lists the qualities reputed to be “virtuous” or “vicious” in terms of opposites: liberal or mean, generous or rapacious, cruel or merciful, a breaker of faith or faithful, effeminate and pusillanimous or fierce and spirited, lascivious or chaste, honest or astute, hard or easy, grave or light, religious or unbelieving, and so on. When virtues are thought to be simply in opposition to vices, there can be no middle position. Machiavelli contends, moreover, that it is impossible for a prince to possess all the qualities thought to be good. The virtù he recommends thus represents a mixture of good and bad. The good qualities in his list of opposites appear to include a mixture of classical virtues like liberality and Christian virtues like charity and faith; but neither the opposites nor Machiavelli’s originality arises simply from the mixture.63 The difficulty of making a good choice appears initially to be that a prince who does what is necessary to maintain his state will necessarily incur the infamy associated with some vices. Insofar as “virtue” and “vice” are merely matters of praise and blame or reputation, Machiavelli observes, a “prudent” prince will “avoid the infamy of those vices that would take his state from him,” but not “care about incurring the infamy of those vices without which it is difficult to save one’s state.” He concludes, however, by observing that “if one considers everything well, one will find something appears to be virtue, which if pursued would be one’s ruin, and something else appears to be vice, which if pursued results in one’s security and well-being” (62). In other words, virtù is not merely a matter of opinion or reputation; it can be apparent or real. The difficulty, as Machiavelli somewhat circuitously presents it here, is that people have not understood what is truly virtuous and vicious. He will, therefore, present a new substantive teaching.64


1. Machiavelli’s Redefinition of Virtue and Vice


In chapters 16–19 of The Prince Machiavelli specifies which of the opposed characteristics in the list above traditionally thought to be good should be avoided by a truly virtuous prince and which reputed “vices” he should accept if he wants to maintain his state. The first supposed virtue Machiavelli treats is liberality.65

Generosity has traditionally been praised as a virtue. Machiavelli objects, however, that a prince who attempts to acquire a name for his liberality by generously rewarding his friends and putting on lavish displays will necessarily deplete his own resources; and once he has depleted his own resources, he will have to burden his subjects with new taxes and so arouse their hatred.66 As a result, he will lose the support of many, and having become poor, be contemned by all. It is better, therefore, for a prince to accept a reputation for being stingy or mean in the short run, so that he can conserve his own resources to defend himself from whoever makes war on him without burdening his people. In the long run, Machiavelli concludes, such a prince is truly liberal to “all those from whom he does not take, who are infinite” and mean “with all those to whom he does not give, who are few” (63).

Machiavelli acknowledges that the three historical figures he just told the prince to imitate—Alexander, Caesar, and Cyrus—were not liberal in his sense. In seeking to acquire power, Machiavelli admits, princes like Julius II and victorious generals like these ancients could be liberal in the traditional sense, because they gave their supporters goods seized from others. However, he warns, once these princes came to power, they would not be able to continue giving away the goods of peoples who had become their subjects without arousing their hatred.67

Machiavelli’s discussion of whether a prince should be merciful or cruel, loved or feared follows the same pattern. Not only does he reverse traditional notions of good and bad, but he also advises the prince to secure the advantages of many rather than favoring an aristocratic few. Cesare Borgia again provides a notable example. Cesare was reputed to be cruel, but in using cruelty to punish a few criminals and so bringing peace and faith to the Romagna, “he was much more merciful than the Florentine people, who so as to escape a name for cruelty, allowed Pistoia to be destroyed” (65). Because he has to use force to establish order, Machiavelli reiterates, a new prince cannot avoid acquiring a reputation for cruelty. Machiavelli first urges such a prince “not to make himself feared, and to proceed in a temperate mode with prudence and humanity so that too much confidence does not make him incautious and too much diffidence does not render him intolerable.”68 But Machiavelli almost immediately reverses himself. Admitting that it would be best for a prince to be both feared and loved, as a new prince might be if he established order where there was none, Machiavelli nevertheless observes that since it is difficult to be both loved and feared, it is safer for a prince to be feared. Human beings will promise much out of “love” so long as they are not asked actually to do it; but when pressed to do what they have promised, they refuse and revolt. A prince who founds himself entirely on their words will be lost, because “love is held by a chain of obligation, which, because men are wicked, is broken at every opportunity for their own utility, but fear is held by a dread of punishment that never forsakes you” (66–67).69

Machiavelli brings his arguments concerning the true or effective virtues of “liberality” and “mercy” together by warning the prince that although he should make sure that he continues to be feared, he should not make himself hated. And he will not be hated if he abstains from taking the property or the women of his citizens and subjects. Indeed, Machiavelli shockingly observes, a man will more quickly forget the death of his father (who would have had to die sometime) than the loss of his patrimony. Once again Machiavelli urges the prince to exercise what could be called self-control, lest he be perceived to be rapacious and thus become hated. In making this recommendation, however, Machiavelli does not appeal to a prince’s desire to be reputed to be good or virtuous. He appeals to the self-interest of the prince qua prince by arguing that a prince will maintain his power if and only if he leaves the property of his subjects alone.

As in the case of liberality, so in the case of cruelty and mercy, Machiavelli admits that famous ancient generals constitute exceptions. He observes that Hannibal could not have controlled his large army, composed of greatly different men, who had to fight in a strange land, unless he had used “inhuman cruelty,” and that Scipio would have undermined the discipline and success of the Roman army if the bad effect of his “mercy” had not been undone by the Senate. Machiavelli does not point out that, in contrast to the three generals who founded empires, whom he mentioned as exceptions to his advice concerning liberality, Hannibal and Scipio both served republics—and that both represented threats to the perpetuation of the governments they served. Had Hannibal succeeded in conquering Rome, he might well have been tempted to use his mercenary troops against Carthage in order to seize power for himself. Machiavelli does not relate the details of the incident in which Scipio displayed his “mercy,” but if readers look it up in Livy (29.8–9), they will find that Scipio failed to punish an officer, i.e., another aristocrat, who had destroyed a conquered people. By failing not only to discipline a disobedient officer but also to avenge the people he oppressed, Scipio fostered potential rebellions both in the Roman army and in their subjects. Thinking about Machiavelli’s two apparent exceptions, a reader comes to see that republics have to control both the cruelty and the leniency of their generals if they do not want to see their government and laws overthrown. They must, in other words, rule their generals the way a prince must rule himself if he wants to remain in power. In both cases, readers also see that Machiavelli is criticizing previous writers—in the case of Hannibal for not recognizing the cause of the success they praise, and in the case of Scipio for having tried to teach him “how not to err” (or be virtuous in himself) rather than “how to correct errors” in his subordinates and so, like Machiavelli, how to rule them effectively.

Machiavelli’s virtuous prince will avoid arousing the hatred of his people, but he is not simply their friend. On the contrary, Machiavelli argues in P 18, a prince has to deceive both his allies and his people.

Turning to the question of how a prince should keep faith, Machiavelli insists that princes cannot rely solely on force (or the fear its use can arouse). “There are two kinds of combat,” he observes, “one with laws, the other with force. The first is proper to man, the second to beasts; but because the first is often not enough, one must have recourse to the second.” This lesson was taught “covertly to princes by ancient writers, who wrote that Achilles, and many other ancient princes, were given to Chiron the centaur to be raised.” For “to have as teacher a half-beast, half-man means nothing other than that a prince needs to know how to use both natures” (69). The failure to recognize and deal with the bestial parts of human beings thus appears to be particularly modern or, in Machiavelli’s context, Christian.

Of the methods of fighting characteristic of the beast, Machiavelli recommends that a prince should imitate those of the fox and the lion, “because the lion does not defend itself from snares and the fox does not defend itself from wolves.”70 But, he further observes, “those who stay with the lion [i.e., merely with brute force] do not understand this.” As Machiavelli has already indicated, acquiring and maintaining rule is not simply a matter of mustering physical force; it requires strategic intelligence. That intelligence includes knowing that “a prudent lord . . . cannot observe faith, nor should he, when such observance turns against him, and the causes that made him promise have been eliminated” (69). Precisely because circumstances are always changing, an “astute” prince can always find a reason not to keep his word.

In insisting on the need to use fraud as well as force, Machiavelli might appear to be equating keeping “faith” with “honesty” or abiding by one’s promises. He builds on the association of “faith” with religion, however, first, by justifying his advice with an ironical inversion of the “golden rule” and, second, by naming the pope as one of the “infinite modern examples” of a prince’s never lacking legitimate causes to color his failure to keep faith. “If all men were good,” Machiavelli admits, “this teaching would not be good; but because they are wicked and do not observe faith with you, you also do not have to observe it with them” (69). Although Machiavelli first observed that ancient writers recognized the need to fight both like men and like beasts, and so suggested that moderns might not, the connection he draws between “faith” and “religion” should remind his reader that it would be strange for Christians, who presumably believe in the doctrine of original sin, not to recognize the need to deal with the bestial aspects of human nature. And, in fact, he observes that Christian princes know very well not only “how to use the fox,” but also “how to color this nature, and to be a great pretender and dissembler.” Pope Alexander VI represents an example par excellence of a prince who “never did anything, nor ever thought of anything, but how to deceive men, and he always found a subject to whom he could do it.” Other princes and people tended to believe the pope, especially when he swore by the God he was supposed to represent on earth. Machiavelli merely observes that “there never was a man with greater efficacy in asserting a thing, and in affirming it with greater oaths, who observed it less” (70).

Ancient princes may have been better generals, but, Machiavelli suggests, modern princes are better dissemblers. Having urged modern readers to study the art of war, as it was practiced by the ancients, Machiavelli now advises them to combine this art with the modern art of dissimulation, which he associates particularly with Christianity. Unlike the Roman emperors Machiavelli discusses in P 19, Christian princes could not hope to be proclaimed gods after their death and worshiped by their people as such. They claimed, instead, to be serving God or the people; and when things did not go as desired, they could attribute undesirable results to the “will” of an unfathomable “God.” Rather than accepting blame for the suffering of their people, these princes tried to succor and comfort them in their misery. Machiavelli saw that the most astute of these modern princes knew that it is necessary “to appear merciful, faithful, humane, honest, and religious,” but that “a prince, and especially a new prince, cannot observe all those things for which men are held good, since he is often under a necessity, to maintain his state, of acting against faith, against charity, against humanity, against religion” (70).

Machiavelli insists that a prince should take great care not to say anything that is not “merciful, faithful, humane, honest, and religious,” especially religious. Most people judge by appearances. When the effects of the prince’s actions correspond to his explanations of his purposes and motives, people will believe that he has done what he has done for the reasons he gives. “In the actions of all men, and especially of princes, where there is no court to appeal to, one looks to the end. So,” Machiavelli concludes, “let a prince win and maintain his state: the means will always be judged honorable, and will be praised by everyone” (71). This famous observation has often been inaccurately abbreviated as simply saying that the end justifies the means. In fact, Machiavelli points to one specific end, acquiring and maintaining the state. This “end” justifies the means, moreover, particularly in the eyes of the people. If a state is led by a prince who secures the lives, family, and property of his subjects, his people will believe that the prince is doing what he says he is doing—mercifully, faithfully, humanely, and honestly—for the sake of God and his people. As Machiavelli repeatedly reminds his readers, however, in fact princes act for the sake of acquiring and maintaining their own power and fame.71 (This is what the few who can “touch” him, i.e., feel what moves him in his “heart of hearts,” know that most do not.) In P 9 Machiavelli attributed the rise of a private citizen to become prince of his fatherland with the support of his fellow citizens to a “fortunate astuteness” (without pointing out there, as he does in P 15 and 18, that astuteness or cleverness is the opposite of honesty).72


2. How to Avoid Hatred, Conspiracies, or Rebellions


Having specified the qualities for which a prince should seek to be reputed, in P 19 Machiavelli turns summarily to stating what a prince should not do if he is not to become hated and contemned. In discussing “liberality,” Machiavelli already argued that a prince should not despoil his people of their property or honor if he wants to avoid hatred and contempt. So long as the prince does not despoil his people, Machiavelli now adds, they will be content and the prince will have to contend only with the ambitions of the few.

Princes should have two fears, according to Machiavelli: (1) internal from their subjects, and (2) external from powers who would attack them and seize control. But, he suggests, a prince who maintains the support of his people by arming them will secure himself from both.

Machiavelli has already emphasized the importance of a prince’s organizing his own arms to defend his state (and his people) from foreign aggressors. Now he explains that a prince who maintains popular support also secures himself from internal conspirators. Those who seek to kill or overthrow a prince always hope that the people will rally around them. But if the people are content with their prince, a would-be assassin has to fear the reaction not only of the prince’s bodyguards but also of the law, his friends, the state apparatus, and the people.73

Although Machiavelli says that the ambitions of the few can be checked in many ways, he singles out two that happen to correspond to the two ways of fighting he pointed out in the previous chapter: one with laws like a human being, the other with force and fraud like a beast. As is characteristic of the second half of The Prince, the example he gives of the best way to fight, with laws, is modern whereas the example of how to fight like a beast with force and fraud is ancient.

In order to avoid conspiracies, Machiavelli observes, “well-ordered states and wise princes have thought out with all diligence how not to make the great desperate and how to satisfy the people and keep them content.” The example of a well-ordered and -governed kingdom he proposes is modern France, where there are “infinite good institutions on which the liberty and security of the king depend. The first of these is the parlement” (74).74 By enabling the people to try and judge nobles, Machiavelli explains, the French parlement beats down the ambition and insolence of the great and thus secures both the generality of the people, who fear the great, and the king, who sees the great as his competitors, without his having to take the blame. In P 9 Machiavelli observed that there were three possible outcomes of the conflict between the two basic “humors”—principality, liberty, and license. Here in P 19 we see that both the “liberty and security of the king” and the security of the people depend upon the institution of a court that enables the people to check the great.75

Machiavelli’s praise of the “one who ordered that kingdom” is worth quoting in full:

Knowing the ambition of the powerful and their insolence, and judging it necessary for them to have a bit in their mouths to correct them, and on the other side, knowing the hatred of the generality of people against the great, which is founded in its fear, and wanting to secure them, [he] intended this not to be the particular concern of the king, so as to take from him the blame he would have from the great when he favored the popular side, and from the popular side when he favored the great; and so he constituted a third judge to be the one who would beat down the great and favor the lesser side without blame for the king. (75)


As in the case of Cesare’s use of Remirro de Orco to bring “good government” to the Romagna, followed by his instituting a “civil court” and publicly disowning and destroying the cruel means of establishing order by policing the marauding “great,” so Machiavelli concludes here that “princes should have anything blameable administered by others, favors by themselves” (75). Princes should, therefore, honor the great (while making sure that others check their ambitions), and not make themselves hated by the generality of the people by seizing their property or women or allowing their “nobles” to do so.

Machiavelli recognizes that a reader might object to his insistence on the need for a prince to obtain and maintain the support of his people, without driving the great to desperation, on the basis of the succession of Roman emperors from Marcus “the philosopher” to Maximinus. And in light of the fates of these emperors, Machiavelli modifies his advice in two respects. First and foremost, he points out that these emperors had to contend not only with “the ambition of the great and the insolence of the people” (76, italics mine), but also with the cruelty and avarice of their soldiers. He thus admits, in passing, that the people can threaten the state of the prince as well as can the great.76 Men-at-arms pose a more immediate threat, however, than unarmed subjects. Because most of these emperors were “new men” and the armed soldiers were stronger than the unarmed people, these emperors had to allow their soldiers to oppress the people if they did not want the army to overthrow them.

Of the modest, humane lovers of justice among these emperors, Machiavelli observes, only Marcus lived and died honorably. “Because he succeeded to the empire by hereditary right” and “was attended with many virtues that made him venerable,” he was able to keep both the soldiers and the people within bounds. Machiavelli does not say what Marcus’s “virtues” were, but by referring to Marcus as “the philosopher,” he suggests that the emperor’s virtues included his Stoical teachings and practices.77 Machiavelli does remind his readers that, despite his own contemplative “exercises,” Marcus did not succeed in educating his son to become equally virtuous; on the contrary, Commodus became one of the emperors hated for his cruelty and rapacity. Since Commodus succeeded by hereditary right from Marcus, Machiavelli also lets his readers see, although he does not explicitly say, that it was the virtues which made him venerable rather than his hereditary right that enabled Marcus to control both his soldiers and the people.78 Although Machiavelli wrote in P 2 that a hereditary prince need use only “ordinary industry” to maintain himself, he now reminds his readers (including Lorenzo) that where there is a standing professional army, there is always “an extraordinary and excessive force” ready to overthrow him.79

Machiavelli uses the examples of the other two modest and humane imperial lovers of justice to show that “hatred is acquired through good deeds as well as bad ones.” Not merely must a prince make sure that others fear the consequences of disobeying his commands; he must also recognize that laws and courts will not suffice to preserve him and his state. Pertinax was created emperor against the will of the soldiers, who, accustomed to living in license under his predecessor, Commodus, hated Pertinax for trying to make them return to decency. They also contemned him, because he was old (and thus presumably physically weak). The soldiers likewise hated and contemned Alexander, who did not allow anyone to be executed without a trial in his fourteen years as emperor but was “held to be effeminate and a man who let himself be governed by his mother” (77). As a result, they conspired against him and killed him.

As the example of Alexander shows, fighting like a man with laws does not suffice to check a corrupt people or army. A prince must, therefore, also know how to fight like a beast. Both forms of knowledge prove to be quite rare, however. Just as Marcus was the only humane emperor who did not succumb to a conspiracy, so, Machiavelli points out, Septimius Severus was the only cruel and rapacious emperor who did not suffer a wretched end. Because they acted so bestially and basely, all the others aroused the hatred of the people and became contemned by their soldiers, who then conspired to kill them.

Severus constitutes the most famous example of the successful combination of the fox and the lion, which, Machiavelli emphasizes, is particularly relevant to a new prince (like Lorenzo). Although Severus burdened the people, he was able to rule happily by maintaining the soldiers as his friends. He did so by keeping his army constantly in motion, undertaking a series of surprise attacks on his competitors, always under the cover of righting a wrong. The cruelty that satisfied his soldiers might have led the people to hate him, but his repeated successes made him feared and revered by everyone.80

Severus was no more successful than Marcus, however, in passing on his own virtue to his son Antonius (Caracalla), who, by killing so many Romans and all of Alexandria, became hateful to the entire world. Although the empire he gained and maintained was much larger, Severus’s success does not appear to be much different, in principle, from Agathocles’ acquisition and maintenance of his rule in Syracuse (by “crime”) for the duration of his life.81 None of the bestial emperors Machiavelli mentions seems to have been as “astute” as Hiero, also of Syracuse, who, seeing that the mercenary arms he had used to acquire power had become a threat to him, arranged to have them destroyed in the next battle.82

A reader might wonder, indeed, why Machiavelli introduced the possible objection based on the line of Roman emperors when he concludes that “princes of our own times . . . have less difficulty satisfying their soldiers” (perhaps because modern mercenaries demand much less than the Roman armies for doing less), so that modern princes ought to be more concerned about satisfying their people. Machiavelli notes an exception, however, and the exception indicates the point of what might otherwise appear to be an unnecessary digression. Two modern rulers are not in a position to favor their people more than the soldiers. Because both the Turk and the sultan are surrounded by and thus in the hands of their soldiers, these princes must please the army rather than their people. And, Machiavelli observes, the state of the sultan is unlike all other principalities except the Christian pontificate. The similarity Machiavelli explicitly points out is that neither the sultanate nor the papacy can be called either a hereditary or a new principality, because in both cases the order is old, but the holders of the supreme office are elected by those who have authority to do so. The implication, however, is that neither the sultan nor the pope can establish or maintain a stable secular government. Unlike Marcus, they do not rule by hereditary right or share his Stoic virtues. Nor can they follow Machiavelli’s advice to the leader of a “civic principality” and seek to gain the support of the people after they are elected by a few “grandi,” because they are unarmed captives of their armed guards. Like the Roman emperors after Marcus, these “ecclesiastical” princes must either appear to be contemptibly weak or join their soldiers in oppressing others (as the Turk did in Greece). As Machiavelli reminds his readers, a head of the Church like Alexander VI might have proved to be a dissembler par excellence, but he does not have the force of a lion reliably in his own hands. Nor was he any more able than Marcus and Severus to establish a succession by hereditary right. Alexander wanted to help his illegitimate son acquire a principality, but Cesare’s military gains accrued to the Church, not to the Borgia family. Alexander’s successor, Julius II, led his own armies into battle, but as pope he could no more establish a hereditary succession than could his predecessor. As pope, he could not have a son as his legitimate heir. He was, moreover, elected late in life and thus had a short term of office. And he depended upon foreign—mercenary or auxiliary—troops. Only an armed secular prince can effectively combine the bestial virtues of Severus in founding a new principality, and then imitate the actions of Marcus “to conserve a state that is already established and firm” (82). Machiavelli’s three examples suggest that a prince elected by the representatives of a universal religion will find it particularly difficult to do so, because those who elect and fight to maintain them are not necessarily their subjects or “creatures.”83 And their “faith” is not enough to secure their loyalty.

Machiavelli’s apparent “digression” at the end of P 19 should alert an attentive reader to its possible application to the situation of his presumed reader. As commander of the pope’s troops, Machiavelli intimates, Lorenzo was in a position to hold his uncle the pope hostage. He might also determine the cardinals’ choice of his uncle’s successor the way Augustus and his successors controlled the Roman Senate—not by using force directly, but by reminding them that he commanded the army.84


3. Tactics, Distinction, and Advice


Confounding the commentators who read The Prince as a “technical manual” laying out general maxims for ruling, Machiavelli begins P 20 by observing that princes have tried to hold their states securely in diametrically opposed ways: “Some . . . have disarmed their subjects so as to hold their states securely; some others have kept their subject towns divided; some have nourished enmities against themselves; some others have turned to gaining to themselves those who had been suspect to them at the beginning of their states; some have built fortresses; some have knocked them down and destroyed them” (83). And he concludes that he cannot say what measures or tactics would be best without examining the particular circumstances.

In considering the matter broadly, Machiavelli nevertheless highlights the general principles that inform his previous discussion of the ways in which princes can acquire and maintain states—and thus what should truly be considered to be virtuous and vicious. First, he reiterates, a new prince must arm his subjects. When he shows that he trusts and so honors them, their arms become his arms, to be used against those who were in power previously as well as anyone else who resists him and his rule. If an established prince is acquiring a new territory, however, he must disarm his new subjects; and he should also do whatever he can gradually to render the partisans who helped him enter soft and effeminate. Since, as Machiavelli pointed out in P 3, the prince will never be able to satisfy his partisans’ desires for ever greater wealth and power, they will eventually become his enemies. As Machiavelli has made clear in his discussion of the virtues in P 16–19, a prince cannot successfully acquire and maintain his state merely by benefiting his adherents in order to gain and retain their love, because to benefit his followers either he will have to burden his subjects with taxes and thus arouse their hatred or he will have to lead an army on ever more distant campaigns to seize the goods of others. As the Roman emperors learned to their dismay, this army becomes a threat not only to a prince’s people, but also to him.

Machiavelli argues, second, that a prince should not attempt to acquire and maintain rule by “dividing and conquering”—at home or abroad. Machiavelli has insisted that in every city there is conflict between the two humors, which need to be balanced against each other; and he has presented Severus, who deceived one ally long enough to conquer another, as a model of the necessary combination of the fox and the lion. But Machiavelli does not accept the traditional wisdom of the Florentine elders who say that it is necessary to hold Pistoia with factions and Pisa with fortresses. On the contrary, he points out that “when an enemy approaches, of necessity divided cities are immediately lost, because the weaker party always joins the external forces” (84).

Third, Machiavelli has argued that a new prince should understand that he will not be able to satisfy the ambitions of the dissatisfied individuals who helped him acquire power; he should, therefore, look for support in the people who were content under the former government. But now he adds that these include individuals like Machiavelli himself “who at the beginning of their states were held to be suspect” and “who are of such quality that to maintain themselves they need somewhere to lean.” Because they “need to cancel out with deeds the sinister opinion” the prince has of them, such individuals will serve him all the more faithfully (85). Those willing to accept the rule of a prince who does not oppress them and so arouse their hatred also include the generality of the people. Although it has been the custom of princes to build fortresses to hold their states more securely in the face of potential opposition from their own people as well as external aggressors, Machiavelli urges, “the best fortress is not to be hated by the people” (87).

Machiavelli underlines the largely negative redefinition of the virtues he has given by concluding that he will “praise whoever makes fortresses, and whoever does not make” them, because their utility depends on the circumstances, but he will “blame anyone who, trusting in fortresses, thinks little of being hated by the people” (87). Praise follows success, which is sometimes a product of chance; a prince is justly blamed, however, for not understanding his own situation and necessities. The first and foremost of those necessities, Machiavelli has shown in his redefinition of the virtues, is not to become hated by the people and thus encourage conspiracies. A prince needs to use enough force to establish order and enforce the law, but he should not further oppress or tax his people to benefit his allies or soldiers—unless he is constrained to do so by his army. In the following chapter Machiavelli suggests a way in which a prince can earn distinction not by conquering and betraying others, i.e., “fighting like a beast,” but by benefiting his subjects. Human beings seek to be virtuous, because they want to be praised. Having redefined the virtues as the means of acquiring and maintaining rule, he thus reconsiders and redefines the deeds and characteristics for which princes gain distinction. These turn out to be of two rather different kinds.

The first way Machiavelli suggests that a prince can gain distinction is by undertaking great enterprises and giving rare examples of himself. From a weak king, he notes, Ferdinand of Aragon has become “by fame and glory the first king of the Christians.” By attacking the Muslims at Granada in the south of Spain, Ferdinand was able to divert the barons of Castile in the north from planning other campaigns on their own, while he built up his own army and consequent reputation unnoticed by the barons. Because it was a religious war, he could obtain funds to support it from both the Church and his people. “Ever making use of religion, he also resorted to an act of pious cruelty by chasing the Marranos from his kingdom and despoiling them.” He then “attacked Africa under this same cloak” (88) and expanded his campaign into Italy (Naples) and France, so that he always kept his subjects wondering and never gave anyone time to work quietly against him.

Waging war under a religious cover with the financial support of the Church in order to unite his country and expand its empire, Ferdinand would appear to represent an especially suitable contemporary model for Lorenzo, the nephew of the pope. Yet Machiavelli does not call Ferdinand’s “pious cruelty,” “cruelty well-used.” Although Machiavelli has argued that a prince cannot keep faith (and so, presumably, should not be held to promises to allow converts to remain and hold property within his Christian country, if circumstances require that he seize their goods), Machiavelli says of Ferdinand’s exiling and expropriating the Marranos that “this example could not be more wretched or more rare” (88). (Readers should recall that Machiavelli observed that a prince will always be able to find reasons to seize the goods of his subjects, but that he should not do so; seeing Ferdinand banish the converts and then seize their property, his other Christian subjects might worry that they and their property would be next.)85 When he goes on to cite Bernabò of Milan as a case of a prince’s having given “rare examples of himself concerning internal government,” moreover, Machiavelli explicitly observes that a prince can win a kind of distinction or renown for doing something extraordinarily evil as well as something good. Bernabò seized power with two of his brothers and subsequently cooperated in the poisoning of one of them. Bernabò had been largely responsible for the consolidation of the state of Milan; but he was excommunicated three times, imprisoned, and perhaps killed by his brother’s son Gian Galeazzo. (Contemporary readers might think of Adolf Hitler or Josef Stalin as even more egregious examples of “princes” who achieved a certain kind of distinction as a result of their extraordinarily evil deeds.) Without giving any details and concluding simply that “a prince ought to contrive [ingegnare], above all, in each of his actions, to give himself the fame of a great man and of excellent ingenuity [ingegno]” (89), Machiavelli makes his reader wonder whether this is really the kind of “distinction” or “esteem” a prince wants, if his extraordinary cruelty does not, like “cruelty well-used,” enable him to maintain his control of the state.

Following the example of the perfidious Bernabò, Machiavelli’s further observation that “a prince is also esteemed when he is a true friend and true enemy” appears to be ironical. The argument he gives to show that a prince should never remain neutral circles back on itself. Machiavelli suggests that a weaker state that refuses to ally with the victor in an upcoming struggle will be prey to whoever wins, and that the weaker state retains a claim to just treatment, refuge, and future assistance by the defeated party if and only if it allies with the vanished state before the conflict. However, Machiavelli has already argued that obligations of “love” and in “words” are not to be relied upon. And here he emphasizes that “a prince must beware never to associate with someone more powerful than himself so as to attack others, except when necessity presses. . . . For when you win, you are left his prisoner” (90). An alliance with a state that is apt to lose in a conflict with a stronger one appears to benefit a prince only when he himself has enough power to determine the outcome or has a chance of doing so in the future.

The point of Machiavelli’s insistence on the necessity of taking sides does not appear to be the benefits or virtue of loyalty—or the superior nobility of declaring adherence to one side or another rather than remaining weakly neutral. He has already argued that a prince cannot always “keep faith.” Machiavelli’s point is, rather, that “no state should ever believe that it can always make safe choice,” because “in the order of things, one never tries to avoid one inconvenience without incurring another one. Prudence consists in knowing how to recognize the qualities of the inconveniences and choosing the less bad as if it were good” (91).86 Indecision is never good—or even possible.87 A decision not to take sides or to do nothing is nevertheless a decision that will have consequences.

Machiavelli never retracts his insistence on the importance of a prince’s raising and leading his own army in order to defend both himself and his subjects. But, he now suggests, there is a domestic alternative to conquest as a means of acquiring wealth.

A prince must also show himself to be a lover of the virtues by giving hospitality to virtuous men, and he must honor those who are excellent in an art. Next, he must encourage his citizens to be able quietly to practice their trades, in commerce, in agriculture and in every other human occupation, so that one man is not afraid to improve his properties for fear they will be taken from him, and another is not afraid to open a business for fear of taxes. But he must prepare rewards for whoever wants to do these things, and for whoever thinks to increase his city or his state in whatever way. (91)88


Instead of organizing and leading an army to seize the goods of others that will eventually become a threat to him and his people, a prince should reward the ingenuity and efforts of his people. He should not merely secure their lives and property; he should also publicly reward those who do most and “keep the people occupied with festivals and spectacles,” not by descending to fight with the gladiators himself like Commodus, but by offering himself “as an example of humanity and munificence, while maintaining his dignity” (91).89

A prince will be able to maintain his dignity, as well as a reputation for his intelligence, Machiavelli finally adds, only if he is able to choose good advisors. No one can know everything; it is, therefore, necessary to consult. But, he suggests, there is an unfailing way of determining whether a prince can trust an advisor or not: when a prince sees that an advisor thinks more of himself and his own interests than of those of the prince, he should not be trusted. Machiavelli has demonstrated his own credentials in this respect in The Prince by presenting all his knowledge from the perspective of the needs of the prince.90 Machiavelli now adds that if a prince wants to keep his minister good, he should honor and reward him. For his own sake as well as for his advisor, the prince should also be selective in the advice he receives. He should not allow anyone to approach him without his permission, and he should take advice from only a few trusted counselors. He has to make up his own mind, however, and once he does, he should stick to the decision he has made. He should not, like the Emperor Maximilian, constantly change his mind and policy on the basis of his most recent advice. This is another version of the destructive indecision Machiavelli criticized in princes who want to stay neutral or avoid making any decision at all until they are certain. Such evident indecisiveness destroys a prince’s reputation, if it does not lose him his state.


III. Fortune and the Future


After having laid out the general principles of his understanding of the necessities of politics, as well as indicating the basis of that understanding in an analysis of both recent and historical events, in the last three chapters of The Prince Machiavelli applies these principles to his and Lorenzo’s specific situation in Italy. He promises that if a new prince (presumably Lorenzo) applies what Machiavelli has written above “prudently,” his state will almost immediately look ancient and established. “He will have the double glory of having made the beginning of a new principality, of having adorned it and consolidated it with good laws, good arms, and good examples, just as he has a double shame who, having been born prince, has lost it through his lack of prudence” (96).

Those lords in Italy who have lost their states, like the king of Naples, the duke of Milan, and others, had a common defect as to arms. Apparently oblivious to the difficulties Machiavelli pointed out in P 12–14, these princes thought they could rely on mercenaries or auxiliaries; they did not muster, train, and deploy their own subjects and so gain their own arms.91 They also had a hostile people or, like Cesare, “did not know how to secure themselves against the great.” It is necessary, but not sufficient, Machiavelli emphasizes, for a prince not to arouse the hatred of his people. As he pointed out in P 9 and 17, a prince should not rely on the people (or “love”) to save him from the machinations of his competitors. However friendly, an unarmed people cannot withstand an armed attack. A prince must first muster and train his own arms and then establish institutions that will protect him from possible future attacks, internal as well as external.

Machiavelli recognizes “that many have held and hold the opinion that worldly things are so governed by fortune and by God, that men cannot correct them with their prudence.”92 He does not claim that human beings can control or entirely determine their own fates. “It might be true that fortune is arbiter of half of our actions,” but, he judges, “she leaves the other half, or close to it, for us to govern, so that our free will not be eliminated” (98). Fortune is like one of those violent rivers that, when angry, flood the plain and ruin everything built on it, if no one with foresight has erected dikes and dug canals to divert the water; she “demonstrates her power where virtue has not instituted an order to resist her and turns her impetus where she knows that dams and dikes have not been made to contain her” (98–99).

If we look back to Machiavelli’s description of the human condition, the forces that ebb and flow with more or less positive results appear to be the passions, especially an almost universal fear of death and the unending desire to acquire to which that fear gives rise.93 Unchecked and undirected, these passions have destructive consequences, for states as well as for individuals. As Machiavelli has argued, particularly in his discussion of the true character of virtue, human passions cannot be eradicated or directly controlled by law, much less by moral suasion. They can, however, be directed and checked by a prince who knows both how to fight like a man, by establishing institutions like the French parlement that enable the people to check the great, and how to fight like a beast, by using force to put down rebels and aggressors and fraud to deceive both his competitors and his people. By contrasting the “dikes” erected by virtuous leaders in Germany, Spain, and France with the absence of such in Italy, Machiavelli suggests that the relevant “techniques” might include building walled fortresses with a year’s worth of stored supplies used to protect the people (as in the free German cities), claiming to fight wars for religious purposes and thus obtaining funds from both the people and the Church (like Ferdinand of Aragon), or training an infantry and establishing a court (like the kings in France).

It is impossible to say generally what a prince ought to do to protect his people and maintain his state under all possible circumstances, because circumstances or “the times” change. Under some conditions, it is better to be cautious; under other conditions, it is better to be impetuous. Once again, Machiavelli reminds his reader, he is not providing him with a “manual” or rule book to be mechanically applied everywhere or at all times.

As we saw in the first half of The Prince, Machiavelli’s political science rests on his observation of some fundamental forces or passions that move all human beings. If these passions are not recognized for what they are, and checked or redirected, they produce unending conflict. He has suggested that this conflict can be managed, however, by a virtuous prince who knows how to channel it to produce beneficial results for both himself and his people.94 But now, Machiavelli acknowledges, no individual can ever be prudent enough to adapt his behavior to all possible circumstances. Although human beings generally are characterized by certain fundamental passions, the intensity and direction of these passions vary from individual to individual, depending not only on birth but also on that individual’s formative experience or “conditioning.” Like human nature generally, individual human beings are malleable only within certain limits. Once trained or formed, their characters cannot be changed.95 That is the reason Machiavelli did not write a traditional book on the education of a prince. No education of a single individual will enable that individual to see and do what is necessary under all circumstances. Instead of trying to educate a few people to rule wisely and virtuously, Machiavelli thus tries to show his readers what can and cannot be done with the human “matter” at hand by establishing and maintaining certain kinds of institutions.

In a treatise purportedly addressed to a new prince, Machiavelli does not suggest, as he does in D 1.20 and 3.9, that republics are able to solve the problem of succession and to adapt to changes in the “times” or circumstances better than principalities, because republics can elect leaders who possess the necessary characteristics (and unelect those who do not). Nor does he have to acknowledge that even in republics, people do not always choose the best leaders. In The Prince he has already stated unequivocally that in politics no decision or method is ever entirely safe or certain; there are always “inconveniences.”

Toward the end of chapter 25, Machiavelli thus turns to what has worked most recently in Italy and what the best policy for a young prince generally tends to be. The current Medici Pope Leo’s immediate predecessor, Julius II, “proceeded impetuously in all his affairs, and he found the times and affairs so much in conformity with his mode of proceeding that he always achieved a happy end” (100).96 But pointing to the problem Cesare had experienced with his father’s support and a potential problem for Lorenzo to the extent to which he depends upon Pope Leo, Machiavelli also observes that “the brevity of his life did not allow [Julius] to feel the contrary.” However, “if times had come when he had needed to proceed with caution, his ruin would have followed: he would never have deviated from those modes to which nature inclined him” (101). Nevertheless, although “fortune varies and men remain obstinate in their modes,” Machiavelli famously concludes, “it is better to be impetuous than cautious, because fortune is a woman; and it is necessary, if one wants to hold her down, to beat her and strike her down. And one sees that she lets herself be won more by the impetuous than by those who proceed coldly. And so always, like a woman, she is the friend of the young” (101).97

Machiavelli thus concludes his treatise with a passionate exhortation to the young Florentine prince to take advantage of the “opportunity” fortune has provided him, “to seize Italy and to free her from the barbarians.” Explicitly echoing the analysis of the four great founders he gave in chapter 6, Machiavelli assures Lorenzo that “there is matter to give opportunity to someone prudent and virtuous to introduce a form that would bring honor to him and good to the community of men there” (102). No one would have been able to see the virtue of Moses, the greatness of Cyrus, or the excellence of Theseus, if their peoples had not been, respectively, enslaved, oppressed by their neighbors, and dispersed.98 The Italians now suffer from all these disabilities, “and although up to now a glimmer has shone in someone who could judge that he had been ordered by God for her redemption, yet later it was seen that in the highest course of his actions, he was repulsed by fortune” (102). Machiavelli might appear to be referring to himself. However, he continues: the Italians are nevertheless ready to follow anyone ready to lead, and there is no one in whom they can “hope more than in your illustrious house, which with its fortune and virtue, supported by God and by the Church of which it is now prince, can put itself at the head of this redemption” (102–3).99

For centuries, commentators have asked how seriously Machiavelli made this final, passionate proposal. Did he really believe that Lorenzo could become the conqueror and liberator of all Italy?

On the one hand, Machiavelli insists that although the four founders were “rare and marvelous,” they were nevertheless men, “and each of them had less opportunity than the present.” It would therefore be possible for the Medici to duplicate their greatness, if the Medici princes keep their “aim on the orders” Machiavelli has put forth. He repeats: it will be “necessary before all other things, as the true foundation of every undertaking, to provide [themselves] with [their] own arms” (104), and these arms, composed of their subjects and fellow Italians, will become better if they see themselves commanded by their own prince. This is the way Machiavelli insisted any prince needs to acquire and maintain his rule in the first half of The Prince. As Machiavelli made clear in his discussion of Agathocles, however, merely seizing and keeping control of one’s homeland for the duration of one’s life is not sufficient to bring a prince glory. It is necessary to do something more in order to become honored and revered. In discussing the qualities for which a prince should truly be praised and blamed, Machiavelli argued that he should not be liberal or lavish (as Leo was known to be, and Alexander VI and Julius II had been in decorating the Vatican) and that he should seek not to be loved but to be feared and not hated. He will be feared if he arms his own subjects to fight in their own as well as in his defense, and he will avoid arousing their hatred if he makes sure that the persons, families, and properties of his subjects are secure from oppressive taxes and criminal violence.

Since men can be and have been trained to be soldiers in Italy before, Machiavelli concludes, the reason that no previous prince has been able to seize control and liberate Italy from foreign invasions is not so much “the matter” as “the fact that her ancient orders were not good, and that there has not been anyone who has known how to find new ones” (103). The problem in Italy has been not so much the “limbs” as the “weakness at the head.” Since “head” (capo) can refer both to the leader or captain and to the mind or intellect, Machiavelli is suggesting that Italian princes have lacked the intelligence or knowledge he has been claiming to supply, from his letter of dedication onward. If Lorenzo and Leo follow his advice, they can seize and free Italy. Like Cesare Borgia, they may have to begin by using mercenary and auxiliary troops to conquer contiguous territories. Like the Roman republic, they will have to deceive the current lords or governments of the territories they propose to “liberate” by claiming to make them allies while ultimately eliminating the bloodlines of any established leaders. But the Medici will eventually have to muster and train their own “arms,” including, Machiavelli now adds, an infantry able to resist cavalry as well as other, similarly trained and armed men. (Machiavelli provides the specifics in his later treatise the Art of War.) Most important of all, they will also have to establish new laws and orders, most particularly civil courts to guarantee the security of their people. By not merely assuring their people that their persons and property will be protected, but positively fostering domestic prosperity, these new “heads” can also free themselves from becoming dangerously dependent upon their own armies and ever more distant imperial conquests.100

On the other hand, from the very beginning Machiavelli has raised doubts about whether he believes that Lorenzo would or could follow the advice he was about to give. In his letter of dedication to Lorenzo Machiavelli refers to “the greatness that fortune and your other qualities promise”; and in his concluding exhortation, Machiavelli bases his hopes for Italy’s “redemption” not on Lorenzo’s abilities or promise as an individual, but on his “illustrious house, with its fortune and virtue, supported by God and by the Church” (102).

At the end of The Prince Machiavelli might appear to be urging Leo to undertake a project that was, in fact, already well under way—the consolidation of the Medici’s fortune in Italy.101 Shortly after his election as pope early in 1513, Leo had begun distributing power to his nephew Lorenzo II (who became governor of Florence in August), his first cousin Giulio (who was made archbishop of Florence in May and became cardinal in September), and his brother Giuliano (who was made a patrician of Rome and captain of the ecclesiastical military forces). There was, moreover, rumor of a project to make Giuliano “prince” of part of northern Italy.102 Machiavelli thus had reason to think that the Medici lords might listen to advice showing them how to seize control of Italy as a whole.

The problem with the pope’s projected consolidation of his family’s power from Machiavelli’s point of view was that such openly self-serving power grabs would inevitably arouse the opposition of other lords as well as the peoples of the cities involved. Merely seizing power in a few places would not attract the surge of popular support Machiavelli predicted would arise for a redeemer of Italy. In the concluding chapter of The Prince Machiavelli was thus trying to convince the Medici, pope and prince, to define their ambitions more nobly and more grandly—in order to have a better chance of succeeding. He understood that they would be seeking to satisfy their own natural desires to acquire and would have to use both force and fraud in order to do so. But, as he had insisted in P 18, they should present all their actions in public as “all mercy, all faith, all honesty, all humanity, all religion” (70).103 Machiavelli concludes his treatise by quoting Petrarch: “Virtue will take up arms against fury, and make the battle short, because the ancient valor in Italian hearts is not yet dead” (105; “Italia mia,” lines 93–96).104 He thus gives his advice a less Christian and more classical flavor and, at the same time, obscures the difference between the notion of virtue he has put forward in The Prince and that of the “classical humanists.”

The emphasis Machiavelli has put on the necessity of a prince’s mustering and training his own arms would have made his advice particularly difficult for the Medici to follow. Members of that house had not been averse to seeking popular support. That was the way in which Cosimo had first established and then consolidated his family’s control of Florence.105 Like other Florentine ottimati, however, the Medici had resisted the formation of a civic militia. They feared both that armed workers and peasants would revolt and that a successful captain would seize control of the city from them.106 The Medici had, therefore, consistently employed mercenaries. According to Machiavelli, Lorenzo’s fortune depended crucially, moreover, on having his uncle as pope. Julius II had led his own troops into battle, but he had not mustered and trained his own subjects or citizens. Nor was it likely that any pope as pope could do so. So long as the “prince” of Italy depended upon the support of the pope, whether financial or moral, there would be a divided leadership. According to Machiavelli, it was the priests’ inexperience or lack of training in arms as well as the pope’s interference in the domestic policies of other Italian cities that had kept Italy divided and weak.107

Did Machiavelli really believe that Leo and Lorenzo could be persuaded to depart from settled family policy? Machiavelli’s own observations about the way in which individual human beings become set in their ways, as a result of both their natural dispositions and their past experience, argue against his having had much hope of convincing the Medici to change their inherited inclinations and policies.108 It is certainly difficult to believe that Machiavelli believed his own claim that in Italy “extraordinary things without example” have occurred, “brought about by God: the sea has opened; a cloud has escorted you along the way; the stone has poured forth water; here manna has rained” (103). Most readers would recognize that these were the same miracles that had reputedly accompanied Moses’ rise to power among the Hebrews.109

Lorenzo was a military man, so he might have been tempted to lead a grand campaign to free Italy from her foreign oppressors. But if P 26 was a part of Machiavelli’s original treatise, it was addressed to Giuliano, and Giuliano was known to prefer living at the papal court in Rome to living or ruling or leading an army in the provinces (of Italy!).110 And if P 26 was added after 1515, as some commentators believe, Machiavelli would have known that Lorenzo had already proved unwilling to follow his first piece of advice to a new prince, to go and live in the province he had just acquired.111 By that time Lorenzo had shown that, like his uncle, he preferred life at the papal court to residing in Florence, where Lorenzo had been named captain general. In December 1514 Leo had explicitly solicited Machiavelli’s advice through Vettori about what he should do in the face of the French initiative against Milan, but the pope had then proved unwilling to follow it. Yet that advice was based on arguments similar to those Machiavelli gives in The Prince about the dangers of allying with a stronger power or remaining neutral.112

In sum, there are reasons, both textual and contextual, to conclude that Machiavelli did not think the Medici princes would take up his final plea. They did not have enough foresight, daring, or imagination. P 26 thus stands at least as much as a rebuke to the reigning princes in Italy as it does as a passionate plea to them to take the appropriate action.

We do not know whether Machiavelli actually presented The Prince to Lorenzo, but we do know that he gave copies to his friends and that they appear to have shared their copies with others. Machiavelli explicitly refers to The Prince in the Discourses he wrote and presented to his friends a few years later, so he must have thought that they either had copies themselves or had access to one. And the fact that Agostino Nifo plagiarized much of The Prince in 1523 suggests that many more of his contemporaries had an opportunity to read (and even copy!) Machiavelli’s “little treatise,” which soon made its way into northern Europe as well.113

The Prince attracted readers even before it was published, because in the guise of advice to a petty Italian prince, Machiavelli had presented an entirely new way of looking at politics.114 He had not merely reduced the traditional six types of regimes to two, distinguished solely by the number of rulers, but also differentiated the types of principalities according to the ways in which they were acquired and the difficulties involved in maintaining them. He thus described the different kinds of rule from the point of view of someone who wanted to acquire and maintain it, rather than in terms of justice, service to the common good, or foundation in divine right. Jettisoning both the ancient concern with the education of virtuous rulers and the Christian concern with securing the salvation of both princes and peoples, Machiavelli counseled princes—both actual and potential—to learn how to organize and arm their followers. He urged them to pretend always to be religious but to do what was necessary to retain control after they had acquired it.115

Machiavelli made the revolutionary character of his teaching explicit when he urged princes not to act in ways traditionally thought to be virtuous—to be generous to one’s friends, for example, or to be merciful to the downtrodden, in order to obtain their love. A prince should, on the contrary, seek to minimize the costs of government borne by his people and make sure that everyone—noble or ignoble—fears the consequences of disobeying his laws and orders. Observing that characterizations of virtue and vice are matters of praise and blame, and that fame, glory, and reputation are also merely matters of opinion, Machiavelli suggested that the “effective” truths in politics do not concern the character of the ruler or the basis of his claim to rule so much as the results of his rule on the lives of his people. The people (or later writers who would report their opinions) ultimately determine whether a leader is honored or reviled. Princes who wish to maintain their rule most securely should not continue to use the displays of force (or “cruelty”) by which they may have acquired their position, if they did not ascend to office through heredity or election. A prudent leader would seek to persuade his people, both in speech and in deed, that his government acts to secure the lives and property of its citizens or subjects, so that the people would, in turn, act either under arms or in court to oppose those who would overthrow him.

In The Prince Machiavelli announces the change he is advocating in the moral standards used to evaluate leaders and their governments more clearly than the basis of those evaluations in popular opinion and sentiments. He does not urge princes to serve their peoples, because he does not think that any human beings act on the basis of anything but their perceptions of their own needs or goods. He tries to persuade princes that they will retain rule most effectively by convincing their people that this prince governs in their interest, and he reminds his princely readers that their words will be most persuasive if they are backed up by deeds. Concentrating on the bestial means—force and fraud—every prince must use in order to produce results that seem to be in the common interest (because they satisfy the most powerful though different desires of both the people and their prince), Machiavelli only hints at the kinds of laws and institutions needed to maintain those results.116

Addressing two young Florentine aristocrats, who merely “deserve to be” princes and thus have more leisure to listen than a sitting monarch, in his Discourses on Livy Machiavelli describes these institutions at greater length and in much greater detail. He also makes the popular as opposed to the traditionally aristocratic character of the republican government he is advocating more explicit.

Augustus Caesar refused the title of dictator, which Julius Caesar had adopted, preferring instead the title of princeps, with its strong republican associations. The princeps senatus was a title designating the senior member of the senate, whose name appeared first in the roll of members. . . . The significance of the title is that Augustus wished to preserve republican form. What he established was not a dominatio but a principatus, hence a principate” (9). Just as Augustus cloaked his transformation of the republic into an empire by using an old title, so Machiavelli cloaked the revolutionary character of the new education he is providing to “princes” with his Latin title and chapter headings. Augustus did not fool many, if any, observers, however; nor, we suppose, did Machiavelli think that he would. He is a playful author. The fusion or confusion of titles does nevertheless point to greater closeness between the two types of governments than might first appear.


17 In D 1.20, Machiavelli observes that “through the mode of electing [a republic] has not only two in succession but infinite most virtuous princes who are successors to one another” (54). In contrast to his discussion of all other modes of acquiring rule in his book devoted explicitly to “principalities” (because he has discussed “republics” at length on another occasion), Machiavelli does not give particular examples in the chapter devoted to “civil principalities” in which princes acquire power through the favor of their fellow citizens. If he had, it would have become clear that he was talking about “republics” rather than “principalities”—or, more generally, that at this point, the distinction between the two kinds of regimes breaks down.


18 He will not reason about republics, he explains at the beginning of chapter 2, because he has discussed them at length on another occasion. However, as Benner, Prince, 23, notes, Machiavelli does discuss republics, at least in passing, in subsequent chapters, beginning in P 3. Wootton, introduction to Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, tendentiously maintains that the discussion refers to “the one that took place as he dangled at the end of a rope in the city jail. What were his interrogators interested in, if not his attitude to republics, and his commitment to the republican cause?” One might answer that rhetorical question by responding that their immediate concern was whether there was a conspiracy to unseat the Medici, and if so, who was taking part and how they planned to proceed.
