Machiavelli traces the political divisions within Italy that he is urging Lorenzo to overcome to the Church, not only in his Florentine Histories (written a decade later) but also in his Discourses 1.12.


30 We here learn the reason that the Turk could safely leave his own country and go in person to live in the new as well as the reason the king of a province such as France could not do so.


31 In chapter 4 of Machiavelli and Empire (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2004), “To Destroy Them or to Live There,” 113–31, Mikael Hörnqvist gives an expansive historical explanation of Machiavelli’s one-sentence statement suggesting that the analysis he provides in this chapter could fruitfully be applied to the difficulties Florence experienced in holding Pisa. Although Florence had ruled Pisa for almost 100 years, the latter republic took the opportunity afforded by the French invasion in 1494 to rebel. During his time in the chancery Machiavelli was intimately involved in the politics and policies surrounding Florence’s rule of the cities subject to it. He argued for, trained, and then led the militia that enabled Florence to retake Pisa in 1509. Machiavelli recognized that it was not politic to remind a Medici prince too much of his service to the republic.


32 Machiavelli begins his account of The Life of Castruccio Castracani by observing that “the greater part of those who have achieved outstanding things in this world . . . have been of humble birth . . . or else have suffered to an unusual degree from the travails of Fortune; all of them, indeed, have been exposed to wild beasts, or had such humble fathers that, feeling ashamed of them, they have made themselves out to be sons of Jupiter or some other god” (3). The examples to which he points in the birth story he fabricates for Castruccio are Moses (who was said to be found in the bulrushes) and Cyrus (who was said to have been raised by a dog). In Discourses 1.10, he reminds his readers that in founding Roman religion Numa claimed to have been instructed by a nymph.


33 If one were going to quibble, one might object that Cyrus and Theseus were both recognized to be sons of the previous ruler and so could claim a certain kind of good fortune. Machiavelli would no doubt respond that both had to seize rule with force from other claimants who opposed them. The same is true for Romulus (who had to seize power from his brother Remus as well as the king of Alba) and for Moses (who was opposed by both his adopted father the Pharaoh and his brother Aaron). Machiavelli is bringing out the common “necessities,” while admitting the existence of differences in circumstances that prevent any individual from completely imitating the deeds of any other. As all these examples show, Machiavelli does not follow Aristotle in thinking that political associations develop naturally (smoothly or peacefully) out of families. On the contrary, he emphasizes in D 3.2–5, political ambition often overcomes family affection and ties.


34 Machiavelli’s use of the terms ‘form’ and ‘matter’ is intended, of course, to remind readers of the Aristotelian/Scholastic distinction that he is turning on its head by suggesting that human beings (hitherto thought to be members of a natural species) are merely “matter” to be formed not by God but by an earthly prince or series of princes. One can see here the “seed” of Martin Heidegger’s discovery of the “truth of technology,” i.e., that everything is potentially merely “standing reserve” to be formed or transformed at will. If, as Machiavelli insisted, “the prince acts in a world in which there are ‘no prefigured meanings, no implicit teleology’” (as Sheldon Wolin, Politics and Vision [Boston: Little, Brown, 1960], 224, maintains), then all order is the product of human action rather than an a priori object of human cognition, as Kahn, Machiavellian Rhetoric, 18, suggests.


35 A dramatic example of Moses’ use of force against former supporters can be seen in the way he (with God’s help) put down the rebellion of Korah, Numbers 16:1–41. In Discourses 3.30 Machiavelli observes that Moses had to kill thousands. Benner, Prince, 82, misconstrues the meaning of this passage when she takes Machiavelli to be claiming simply and literally that human beings can be forced to believe. Machiavelli is writing specifically about the new prince’s initial followers and what he must do when they or their “belief” wavers. If and when they question his authority, he must use force to make them act as if they believe in his new order, i.e., obey him, or destroy them.


36 Benner, Prince, 84–85, takes Hiero to be Machiavelli’s true exemplar, because he was elected to office and did not seize control by force. However, Hiero did not establish a long-lasting empire or republic, nor did he come to be revered.


37 As both Eugene Garver, Machiavelli and the History of Prudence (Madison: University of Wisconsin Press, 1987), and Kahn, Machiavellian Rhetoric, point out, Machiavelli appeals to the classical notion of learning by imitating exemplary characters commonly used in earlier “humanist” Renaissance writings in order to subvert it. It is impossible to found or originate a new order by imitating the past.


38 For the details of Francesco Sforza’s acquisition of Milan see FH 5.13, 5.17, 5.19, 6.2, 6.12, 6.17–24. In praising Sforza in contrast to Cesare Borgia, Benner, Prince, 94–97, neglects to mention that Sforza acquired his dukedom with his mercenary army or that he and his son perpetuated the tyrannical rule of Milan.


39 Machiavelli’s account of the career of Cesare Borgia here is both briefer and much more positive than his earlier recitation of the sufferings of Italy from a Florentine perspective in his First Decennial. There he explains that after Duke Valentino conquered Imola and Forlì with French troops, Milan recalled Duke Ludovico and the king of France recalled his troops to attack Milan, “leaving the Pope and his son in a plight” (Lust and Liberty: The Poems of Machiavelli, trans. Joseph Tusiana [New York: Ivan Obolensky, 1963], 161). After defeating Ludovico, the French army came into Tuscany purportedly to help Florence capture Pisa, but withdrew in defeat, for which they blamed Florence. Taking advantage of the enmity between Florence and its sometime French protector, Duke Valentino took Faenza and brought Romagna into disorder again. After attacking the Bentivogli in Bologna, he came into Tuscany and camped in Florentine territory. France joined with Spain in attacking Naples, and while Florence sought protection from the French, the duke seized Urbino. King Louis then called the duke to account. But having exonerated himself with the king, and once again enjoying French protection, the duke came back to Romagna and planned another war against Messer Giovanni Bentivogli in Bologna. He was forestalled by the Orsini and Vitelli whom, as Machiavelli also reports in The Prince, he nevertheless snared and killed by deceit. Fearing both the duke and his enemies, the Florentines sent Machiavelli on a mission to him. Both in the letters he sent back to the Signori (October 9 and November 13, 1502), detailing the duke’s forces, and in his later “Description of the Method Used by Duke Valentino in Killing Vietellozzo Vitelli, Oliverotto da Fermo, and Others,” trans. Allan Gilbert, Machiavelli: The Chief Works and Others (Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1965), 1: 163–69, Machiavelli shows just how tenuous and dangerous the duke’s position was, and how foolish the lords were to accept the titles and provinces he gave back to them as evidence of his own lack of ambition and goodwill toward them. They came to meet him without arms and thus succumbed, necessarily, to his. Viroli, Redeeming “The Prince,” 72–75, suggests that the difference between Machiavelli’s earlier observations as a diplomat and what he writes in The Prince shows that he was intentionally creating a political myth to inspire action. Benner, Prince, 104–10, argues that the difference between Machiavelli’s initial critical accounts of the duke’s deeds and his praise of the same means that the latter is not genuine; his readers would know better. John M. Najemy, “Machiavelli and Cesare Borgia: A Reconsideration of Chapter 7 of The Prince,” Review of Politics 75, no. 4 (2013): 539–56, shows that Cesare did not, in fact, do what Machiavelli claims and that Machiavelli knew that Cesare had not—although he had bragged that he would. However, like Viroli, Najemy sees that Machiavelli altered the historical record in order to recommend the deeds he attributes (unhistorically) to Cesare.


40 Many commentators skip over this crucial step in Machiavelli’s account of Cesare’s founding of “good government” in the Romagna. Ardito, Machiavelli and the Modern State, 53, does not.


41 Nor, Strauss, TM, 26, points out, does Machiavelli mention Agathocles’ pitiable end.


42 Strauss, TM, 47, observes that “Machiavelli says of the criminal Agathocles, in two consecutive sentences, first that he lacked virtue and then that he possessed virtue; in the first case ‘virtue’ means moral virtue in the widest sense which includes religion, and in the second case it means cleverness and courage combined.” However, he also observes that “there is an intermediate meaning according to which ‘virtue’ designates political virtue or the sum of qualities required for rendering service to political society or for effective patriotism. Even in accordance with this intermediate meaning, inhuman cruelty could be a virtue [as Machiavelli argues in the case of Hannibal, P 17] and ambition a vice. In many cases it is impossible to say which kind of virtue is meant.” In the case of Agathocles, however, it seems clear that he possessed some but not all of the qualities that constitute virtù in the full Machiavellian sense.


43 See Victoria Kahn, “Revisiting Agathocles,” Review of Politics 75, no. 4 (2013): 557–72.


44 In chapters 8–11 Machiavelli could thus be said to be treating the ways in which republics are both overthrown and founded. Machiavelli does not make clear, as he does in D 1.9–21, that the successful founding of a republic (for which a prince like Romulus acquires posthumous glory) takes more than one generation and thus more than one prince. Nor does he point out, as he does in D 1.40, that a prince elevated by the people who uses the opportunity to destroy the nobility who previously oppressed them with the blessing of the people will surely become a tyrant.


45 Machiavelli describes the same fundamental division within all republics in D 1.4 and FH 4.1.


46 Like Viroli, Redeeming “The Prince,” 81, I thus see Machiavelli’s “realism” to be based on an analysis of human passions, and not on medieval medicine, which did speak of various “humors” (e.g., bilious) or cosmology, as Anthony Parel contends in The Machiavellian Cosmos (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1992) and “Farewell to Fortune,” Review of Politics 75, no. 4 (2013): 587–604.


47 In D 1.16 Machiavelli qualifies this judgment by observing that a prince cannot satisfy a people’s desire not to be ruled or commanded at all. He can, however, satisfy their desire to revenge themselves upon their previous oppressors, i.e., the great, and garner their support by protecting them from those both within and without the city who would deprive them of their lives, liberties, and property.


48 Readers tempted to object that “greatness” might be a matter of nature rather than simply position should remember that Machiavelli is describing two “humors” or dispositions of groups that arise in cities (and do not therefore simply exist by nature). In P 25 he recognizes that individual human beings have different dispositions and talents by nature although these are shaped by their experience. But, as Manent, Enquête sur la démocratie, observes, “rien dans la compréhension machiavélienne de la nature humaine ne permet de fonder une telle différence naturelle entre les hommes” (316).


49 As Machiavelli states in the title of Discourses 1.46, “Men Ascend from One Ambition to Another; First One Seeks Not to Be Offended, and Then One Offends Others.” McCormick, Machiavellian Democracy, 23–25, characterizes the difference between the grandi and the popolo as one of “opposing natures,” even though he maintains that the grandi are characterized especially by their desire for wealth, which Machiavelli states in P 3 is natural to human beings generally. According to Machiavelli, the difference between the two humors is fundamentally political. It is not natural, because the two humors differ with regard to control of the city or state, and cities are not natural entities, according to Machiavelli. He does not call the humors “natures,” even though each has a distinctive character or “nature” in that sense; and he states explicitly that the grandi can be made and unmade (by giving or taking away offices and wealth). As Miguel Vatter, Machiavelli’s “The Prince” (London: Bloomsbury, 2013), sees, “For him, people and nobles do not designate natural kinds; instead, whoever speaks and acts out of a desire to dominate assumes the standpoint of the nobility, and whoever speaks and acts out of a desire for non-domination assumes the standpoint of the people. One and the same individual may therefore occupy these different standpoints at different moments” (63).


50 Those who criticize Machiavelli for not having taken sufficient account of changes in military technology, particularly the introduction of artillery, should note that he includes artillery here among the necessary defensive precautions a prince unable to field an army should take.


51 Machiavelli’s prince thus resembles the tyrant Socrates describes in Republic 9. 571a–580a.


52 In distinguishing the temporal greatness or power of the human-all-too-human Roman Church from the “orders that have grown old with religion and of such a kind that they keep their princes in the state however they proceed and live,” Machiavelli might appear to be following Augustine, who had distinguished the “city of man,” which keeps order among human beings on earth, from the “city of God,” which exists on earth before and while its members wait to ascend to heaven, but for the sake of their salvation there and not their safety here. The distinction had traditionally been characterized and maintained in Europe as that between the “sword,” the physical power used to keep order on earth, and the “scepter” wielded by the “vicar of Christ,” who leads his flock to their salvation on the basis of a “divine law” that is not known to the unassisted human mind, but depends upon revelation. That distinction had been institutionalized, although never perfectly or without controversy, in the relation between the head of the Holy Roman Empire and the head of the Holy Roman Church.


53 Despite Machiavelli’s suggestion about Alexander VI’s innovation, the sale of indulgences Luther was soon to protest had existed for some time. However, Greg Steinmetz, The Richest Man Who Ever Lived: The Life and Times of Jacob Fugger (New York: Simon and Schuster, 2015), reports, Pope Leo X extended and exaggerated it. He charged the equivalent of $4.8 million in today’s money in 1514 to Albrecht of Hohenzollern, whose family ruled much of Germany, to make him archbishop of Mainz. Albrecht borrowed the money from a banker, Jacob Fugger. And to repay the loan, Albrecht’s men arranged with Leo to sell indulgences, supposedly to be used to restore St. Peter’s. These indulgences were sold by itinerant peddlers who carried Bibles and told worshipers that the indulgences would cancel every sin. The sellers used a “progressive fee schedule,” according to which royalty paid twenty-five florins, laborers only one. Leo and Fugger split the proceeds. Anyone who knew anything about the way in which the former Giovanni Lorenzo de’ Medici lived would know that Machiavelli’s concluding hope that “with his goodness and infinite other virtues” Leo would make the papacy great and venerable was ironic.


54 Machiavelli supplies historical examples that support his general reasoning here in FH 5–6.


55 Nathan Tarcov, “Arms and Politics in Machiavelli’s Prince,” Entre Kant et Kosovo (Paris: Presses de Sciences Po, 2003), points out that “this . . . is the only time in the Prince that Machiavelli explicitly considers an issue from the perspective of republics” (117). However, “the examples Machiavelli gives in Chapter XII are all of republics: Rome, Sparta, the Swiss, the Carthaginians, the Thebans, and the Milanese (during the brief republican period between the Visconti and Sforzas)” (117n2).


56 Nathan Tarcov, “Law and Innovation in Machiavelli’s Prince,” in Enlightening Revolutions, ed. Svetozar Minkov (Lanham, MD: Lexington Books, 2006), 77–90, observes that “good laws thus turn out after all to be the foundation or at least the safeguard of good arms in a republic” (78).


57 Machiavelli reminds his readers that mixtures like the use of citizen captains of mercenary armies by the Carthaginians or a foreign captain for a citizen army in Thebes resulted in their defeat and destruction, respectively, by Rome and Philip of Macedon.


58 Cf. 1 Samuel 17: 38–40, 17: 50–51. Connell, “The Prince” by Niccolò Machiavelli with Related Documents, suggests that “M’s mistake must have been prompted by familiarity with Andrea del Verrocchio’s statue David . . . who holds a small sword that might easily be assumed to be David’s rather than Goliath’s. For many years M passed this statue . . . on the way to work in the chancery” (83n7). It seems unlikely, however, that so careful a writer would forget the original, very well known story, just because he had viewed what is also a very effeminate depiction of its hero, in urging his readers to depend upon their own arms. We now admire the Renaissance generally, and Florence in particular, for its art. Machiavelli had other concerns, as shown by the paucity of references to the art of Renaissance Italy in his works.


59 Benner, Machiavelli’s Ethics, takes Machiavelli’s discussion of hunting as a metaphor for education as “evidence of his affinities with Socratic ethics and political philosophy” (124) without noticing that the texts she cites from both Xenophon and Plato are non-Socratic (Xenophon’s Education of Cyrus and Plato’s Laws). Machiavelli clearly and explicitly embraces Xenophon’s depiction of Cyrus as an exemplary political man; but, as Strauss, TM, 291, notes, Machiavelli hardly mentions Socrates (Xenophon’s other “hero”) or Plato.


60 The empire Xenophon’s Cyrus wins is reported to have broken up quickly after he died, as, Machiavelli reminded his readers in chapter 4, did Alexander’s empire; and Caesar is castigated for having brought the Roman republic to an end. The founding of the empire is usually attributed to his adopted heir, Augustus. For excellent studies of the relation between Xenophon’s and Machiavelli’s presentations and uses of Cyrus as an example of political excellence, see Waller R. Newell, “Machiavelli and Xenophon on Princely Rule: A Double-Edged Encounter,” Journal of Politics 50, no. 1 (1988): 108–30, and Tyranny: A New Interpretation, 186–270; Paul J. Rasmussen, Excellence Unleashed: Machiavelli’s Critique of Xenophon and the Moral Foundation of Politics (Lanham, MD: Lexington Books, 2007).


61 And the “imperialism” emphasized by both Mark Hulliung, Citizen Machiavelli (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1983), and Hörnqvist, Machiavelli and Empire, would appear to be a phase or part but not the whole of either the education of the prince or of Machiavelli’s own political thought. By including at least two literary examples, Machiavelli does emphasize the influence “writers” have had on the formation as well as the subsequent fame of great individual political leaders, aka “princes.” Benner, Prince, 174–75, also raises questions about the exemplary status of individuals whose faults Machiavelli points out at other places in the text. Her further suggestion—it’s not clear that she thinks that it is Machiavelli’s—that Hiero and Philopoemen might be better models for contemporary Italians seems, however, to be a little far-fetched. As she admits, they were much less celebrated by previous writers.


62 In D 1.18 Machiavelli describes the same problem as follows: “Because the reordering of a city for a political way of life presupposes a good man, and becoming prince of a republic by violence presupposes a bad man, one will find that it very rarely happens that someone good wishes to become prince by bad ways, even though his end be good, and that someone wicked, having become prince, wishes to work well” (51).


63 Pace Isaiah Berlin, who finds “The Originality of Machiavelli,” Against the Current: Essays in the History of Ideas (New York: Penguin, 1980), 232–325, in this (untenable) combination. Medieval political philosophers had also advocated a mixture of Christian and ancient elements. What is “original” in Machiavelli is, therefore, not the mixture, but the particular combination chosen on the basis of a new concern not with the character of the prince himself as an individual, but with the effects of his rule.


64 Clifford Orwin, “Machiavelli’s Unchristian Charity,” American Political Science Review 72, no. 4 (December 1978): 1217–28, provides a detailed textual exegesis in support of this conclusion.


65 Machiavelli begins by observing that liberality, “if it is used virtuously and as it should be used, may not be recognized,” referring, it would seem, to the Christian proposition that the left hand should not know what the right hand is doing, i.e., that an individual should not seek recognition for his or her philanthropy. He also skips over the first two virtues Aristotle treats in the Nicomachean Ethics, courage and moderation. He has already suggested that a prince needs to be courageous by insisting that he needs to lead his own troops into war. As he indicates in chapter 17, the definition of “virtue” he proposes here could be understood to constitute a certain kind of moderation; it certainly requires that the prince exercise self-control over any tendency he might feel to be rapacious, lascivious, pusillanimous, or irresolute. Machiavelli does not ask the prince to moderate his passions, however; instead he recommends that the prince calculate the best means of satisfying his passions for the longest possible period of time. Courage and moderation (as well as the “prudence” of the prince who chooses to incur the infamy of vices necessary to maintain his state) thus become instrumental means of achieving the prince’s goals rather than chosen, as in Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics 4.1120a23–28), because they are noble in and of themselves.


66 This advice might be seen to be directed particularly to Lorenzo, whose palace Machiavelli noted in his letter to Vettori of February–March 1514 was full of “great magnificence and liberality.” It definitely constitutes a criticism of the practices of past Medici princes. In FH 7–8 Machiavelli argues that Cosimo became, in effect, prince of the Florentine republic by means of his liberality, but that his grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent was not as successful in commerce and had to use public funds to continue building magnificent edifices and pay mercenary armies, so that the people began to complain about paying more taxes.


67 Hörnqvist, Machiavelli and Empire, 166–88, notes both the dialectical complexity of Machiavelli’s discussion of liberality and the exception of the conquering generals, but he does not take account of the limitation Machiavelli puts on the exception. Instead he argues that the discussion as a whole is intended to serve as a justification for a Florentine imperial policy. Hörnqvist nevertheless recognizes the ultimately republican thrust of Machiavelli’s insistence on the importance of the prince’s seeking to maintain popular support and avoiding hatred.


68 Machiavelli thus seems rather playfully to be equating temperance, prudence, and humanity with what he earlier dubbed “cruelty well-used.”


69 Machiavelli explicitly says that “friendships that are acquired at a price and not with greatness and nobility of spirit are bought” (66). That is, he admits that not all men or friendships are false. His argument is that a person in power cannot rely on the nobility of his “friends,” because human beings are fundamentally fearful.


70 Although Machiavelli does not explicitly cite Cicero, several scholars point out that he took much of the vocabulary and organization of his argument about the virtues from Cicero. See Leslie J. Walker, trans., Niccolò Machiavelli, The Discourses (London: 1975), 2, table 13, 277–79; Marcia Colish, “Cicero’s De Officiis and Machiavelli’s Prince,” Sixteenth Century Journal 9, no. 4 (Winter 1978): 84–85; J. J. Barlow, “The Fox and the Lion: Machiavelli Replies to Cicero,” History of Political Thought 20 (1999): 627–45; and Michelle Zerba, “The Frauds of Humanism: Cicero, Machiavelli, and the Rhetoric of Imposture,” Rhetorica 22, no. 3 (2004): 215–40. Cicero not merely distinguished between the ways of fighting characteristic of men and beasts, but also divided the “bestial” into that of “the lion and the fox” (De officiis 1.31.41). He also asked whether it is better to rule through love or fear (De officiis 2.7.23), as well as whether and how a ruler should be liberal, and advised him not to seize the property of others (De officiis 1.14–1.16.52, 2.15.252–2.18.64). However, as Barlow points out in contrast to Colish, Cicero’s conclusions were almost diametrically opposed to Machiavelli’s. Whereas Machiavelli insists on the need for a prince to know how to fight as a beast, in both ways, and praises Severus in P 19 for doing so, Cicero urges his son not to use such bestial ways unless absolutely necessary in order to achieve the common good and characterizes the deception of “the fox” as even more contemptible than the brute force of the lion. Because, as Colish, 81–83, shows, Cicero’s work was well-known at the time, Machiavelli’s readers would have understood the implicit inversion of Cicero’s arguments.


71 Pace Benner, Prince, 283–84, who argues that “the obligations that help make a state strong are produced by people’s reasoned judgements about the quality of a leader’s action, never by deception or manipulation,” Vatter, Machiavelli’s “The Prince,” observes that “the exercise of a monopoly of violence, even if wielded on behalf of the people against those who engage in domination, cannot but project a ‘bad,’ domineering image of the state that fails to reassure its subjects. Therefore, Machiavelli argues that the modern state or civil prince must follow the path of simulation and dissimulation (see Chapter 18) in order to construct for itself an appearance of ‘goodness’ that stands a chance of satisfying its subjects” (66).


72 As Machiavelli states in the title of D 2.13: “One Comes from Base to Great Fortune More through Fraud Than through Force.”


73 As Strauss, TM, 26, points out, in presenting Nabis as an example, Machiavelli undercuts his claim that a popular prince will be able to withstand any challenge, because, as Mansfield notes, Prince, 72n3, Nabis was, in fact, killed by a conspiracy. Because he is writing to a prince, who could become the target of a conspiracy, Machiavelli does not describe the ways in which conspirators can overcome the difficulties in The Prince, as he does in Discourses 3.6. In the Discourses Machiavelli is writing to citizens of a republic who deserve to be princes, and would have to overthrow the existing regime, i.e., become conspirators, in order to do so.


74 Cary J. Nederman and Tatiana V. Gòmez, “Between Republic and Monarchy? Liberty, Security, and the Kingdom of France in Machiavelli,” Midwest Studies in Philosophy 26 (2002): 83, point out that “many major contributions to Machiavelli scholarship in English have largely overlooked his remarks about the governance of France.” They list Hannah Fenichel Pitkin, Fortune Is a Woman: Gender and Politics in the Thought of Niccolò Machiavelli (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1999); Mansfield, Machiavelli’s Virtue; Skinner, Machiavelli; Maurizio Viroli, Machiavelli (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1998); and Fischer, Well-Ordered License, as examples (83n4), and note that Hulliung, Citizen Machiavelli, 85, explicitly denies the importance of Machiavelli’s comments on the “well-ordered kingdom” of France (84n5). But Wootton, introduction to Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, observes that “orderly government provides what Machiavelli sometimes calls il vivere civile or il vivere politico. Kings can provide this; indeed, Machiavelli repeatedly praises France, where royal despotism and aristocratic tyranny are kept within the law by the parlements” (xxxi). Establishing good institutions is a necessary but not sufficient condition for “good government,” according to Machiavelli. As he shows in P 3, the French parlement did not prevent King Louis from adopting a seriously flawed foreign policy.


75 Hans Baron, “Machiavelli the Republican Citizen,” The Crisis of the Early Italian Renaissance (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1966), 116–17, takes the fact that in Discourses 3.1 Machiavelli praises the French parlamenti for securing the people by enforcing the law against both nobles and princes, whereas in The Prince he praises it as a means of securing the king, as evidence of the entirely different character or spirit of the two works. But Hörnqvist, Machiavelli and Empire, 225, points out that Machiavelli is presenting the same institution of a mixed or constitutional government in the two works from the two different perspectives of their immediate addressees.


76 Cf. D 1.37, where Machiavelli explains that the people can become as ambitious, greedy, and oppressive as the “great,” if and when the people acquire enough power.


77 Machiavelli does not remind his readers that Marcus wrote his Meditations while he was serving as general of the Roman army in Germany, where he and his men killed thousands, or that Marcus countenanced, if he did not promote, the persecution of Christians in Rome.


78 In The Prince, addressed to a “prince” of Florence who acquired rule on the basis of his family ties or “heredity,” Machiavelli does not point out that Marcus was adopted. Writing to republican sympathizers in D 1.10, Machiavelli uses a longer line of emperors, including Marcus, to show that only those who were adopted succeeded, and thus that hereditary succession is bad, a judgment he shares with previous writers who saw the corruption of hereditary successors as the reason for the degenerative cycle of regimes (D 1.2). Machiavelli radicalizes that insight into the inadequacy of family ties as a basis for government in D 3.3–4, however, by arguing that maintaining a republic requires the killing of “the sons of Brutus,” and reminding his readers that daughters will see their fathers murdered for the sake of acquiring rule.


79 As in P 12–14, so in the Art of War Machiavelli thus argues that a prince must muster and train an army of his own subjects.


80 Machiavelli reminds his readers that Severus began his career by leading his army from Slavonia to Rome, purportedly to avenge the death of Pertinax; but once in Rome, he and his army frightened the Senate into killing Julianus and declaring Severus emperor. Recognizing that the generals of the Roman armies in the East and the West both also harbored imperial ambitions, Severus acted like a fox by sending a message to Albinus telling the general that, with the Senate’s approval, Severus wished to share the title with him. In the meantime the lion-like Severus marched against Pescennius Niger in Asia, defeated his army, and killed him. Returning to Rome, Severus then complained to the Senate that Albinus had treacherously tried to kill him, so that it was necessary for Severus to go and punish the traitor by defeating his army in France and killing him.


81 Both Garver, Machiavelli and the History of Prudence, and Kahn, Machiavellian Rhetoric, thus go too far when they argue that Machiavelli collapses the two ways of fighting that he first distinguishes as human and bestial into the two different “bestial” modes of the fox and the lion, because fox-like deception is particularly human. The human model of the “fox and the lion,” Severus, represents only half of what is necessary to gain and maintain rule. Impressed by Machiavelli’s insistence on the need for “cruelty,” these commentators do not notice Machiavelli’s emphasis on the importance of laws, especially courts.


82 Another fact that Machiavelli does not mention is that the Roman armies that elevated and unseated the emperors he names included a great many mercenaries.


83 The guards who surrounded the Turk were young men taken from their homes (often Christian) in their youth and then raised and educated as Muslims in his palace in Constantinople. They thus lacked the desire to defend their own families and property that Machiavelli has suggested a prince should enlist in making his fellow citizens, subjects, or dependents into his own “arms.” Popes had the ability to name cardinals, but since the pope changed so frequently, the college could and would contain cardinals he did not raise to that office.


84 If so, Lorenzo would not have to kill his uncle the pope in order to seize control of Italy, as argued by John T. Scott and Vickie B. Sullivan, “Patricide and the Plot of The Prince: Cesare Borgia and Machiavelli’s Italy,” American Political Science Review 88 (1994): 887–900, and Joseph M. Parent, “Machiavelli’s Missing Romulus and the Murderous Intent of The Prince,” History of Political Thought 26, no. 4 (Winter 2005): 625–45. See John Najemy, A History of Florence, 1200–1575 (Oxford: Blackwell, 2006), 426–34.


85 Machiavelli made his less than stellar evaluation of Ferdinand more explicit in an exchange of letters with Francesco Vettori in April 1513. In his letter of April 29, Machiavelli characterized the king of Spain as “more cunning and fortunate than wise.” And he explained, “This king has risen to these heights from a low and poor fortune; he has always had new states and equivocal subjects to contend with. One method for holding on to new territories and for either stabilizing equivocal minds or keeping them hanging and irresolute is to arouse great expectations of oneself, always keeping men’s minds busy with trying to figure out the aim of one’s decision and one’s new ventures. This king has recognized the need for this and has employed it to advantage; hence his attacks in Africa, the partition of the kingdom [of Naples], and all his other various campaigns. He has not tried to foresee the outcome: for his aim is not so much this, that, or the other victory, as to win prestige among his various peoples and to keep them hanging with his multifarious activities” (Machiavelli and His Friends, 232, 235).


86 Even though Machiavelli does not include prudence among the qualities people think are good or the virtues for which they are praised, he refers throughout The Prince to what a “prudent” prince would or would not do (P 3, 7, 9, 15, 16, 18, 21–25). Machiavelli does not include “prudence” among the virtues, because (as both Garver, Machiavelli and the History of Prudence, and Kahn, Machiavellian Rhetoric, point out), unlike Aristotle, he does not define prudence as a steady disposition that leads one to do what is “right” or just under the particular circumstances. He defines prudence, rather, as knowing what will be effective in acquiring and maintaining rule under any particular set of circumstances. According to both Garver and Kahn, “prudence” so understood comes very close to defining virtù and is constituted almost if not entirely by rhetoric (understanding the use of force to be a kind of persuasion). Both Garver and Kahn also argue that Machiavelli seeks to teach “prudence” through his own dialogical way of arguing rather than the imitation of ancient or modern examples per se.


87 Hörnqvist, Machiavelli and Empire, 97–102, shows how Machiavelli’s critique of neutrality could be applied not only to traditional canons of Florentine foreign policy but also to Florence’s vacillation between allying with the French and the Holy League in the period just before the fall of the republic in 1512.


88 In D 2.2 Machiavelli attributes such economic benefits, including an increase in population, particularly to a free regime. Writing to a prince, in The Prince he cannot promise, as he does in his description of the free regime in D 2.2, that a man can hope that his sons may become princes. In The Prince Machiavelli suggests that the “liberty” of both the people and the prince is a product of a balance (or “conflict”) between the humors that produces the rule of law, enforced by a court. Emphasizing the conjunction between the interest of the prince and the desires of the people allows Machiavelli to speak about “justice,” even though he does not describe it as a virtue.


89 Machiavelli’s suggestion here might be seen as praise for the policies of previous Medici rulers, especially Cosimo and Lorenzo the Magnificent, who employed many workers in building kingly palaces for themselves as well as decorating churches and honoring both artists and scholars. As Machiavelli shows in FH 7–8, the Medici acquired a great popular following by means of their liberality. However, it is not so clear that their fellow citizens or subjects felt secure from taxes (which were necessary to pay for both mercenary soldiers and Lorenzo’s private building projects). In D 2.2 Machiavelli argues that citizens feel secure in their property and thus produce and procreate more in republics than under princes, because everything done in a principality is done for the sake of the prince and does not contribute to the general prosperity.


90 TM, 21–29.

92 As Najemy, Between Friends, documents in considerable detail, Machiavelli’s friend and correspondent Francesco Vettori explicitly held such views. Although in some of his letters, Machiavelli attempted to persuade Vettori to take a more optimistic view of the possibilities of human action, there is no reason to think, as Najemy argues, that this argument was directed primarily if not solely at Vettori. Here at the beginning of chapter 25 of The Prince Machiavelli explicitly addresses a view held by “many” in the past as well as now.

97 On the basis of his saying that “fortune is a woman” and that “it is necessary . . . to beat her and strike her down” (as well as his emphasis on war, conflict, and gaining control), some feminist readers have declared Machiavelli to be a misogynist. Most famously, in Fortune Is a Woman, Hannah Fenichel Pitkin argues that Machiavelli’s works contain three distinct but interwoven and mutually contradictory understandings of masculinity, which reflect his own ambivalent sexual orientation. In “‘Fortune Is a Woman’—But So Is Prudence,” in Finding a New Feminism, ed. Pamela Jensen (Lanham, MD: Rowman & Littlefield, 1996), 23–37, I emphasize the exemplary prudence exemplified by Sofronia’s rule of her household (including a character named Nicomaco) in Clizia. When we look simply at The Prince, it is difficult to take Machiavelli’s concluding statement altogether seriously or literally in the context, as it follows his comparison of fortune to a river that needs to be guided by dikes and ditches built in advance (by a prudent, if not cautious prince, who would certainly not be acting impetuously). Benner, Prince, xlvi, makes a similar observation.


98 Several commentators have observed that Machiavelli omits Romulus, the founder whom a new unifier and liberator of Italy would seem most likely to imitate. His example would point to the need for Lorenzo to kill his uncle (the pope) as well as his brother(s)—the cardinals—in order to consolidate his power, so Machiavelli pointed to it only indirectly, by omitting Romulus where a reader would most expect to see him. TM, 69; Scott and Sullivan, “Patricide”; Parent, “Machiavelli’s Missing Romulus.”


99 This sentence, emphasizing the importance of the Medici control of the Church, would seem to undermine the contention of Miguel Vatter, “Machiavelli and the Republican Conception of Providence,” Review of Politics 75, no. 4 (2013): 605–24, pace Maurizio Viroli, Machiavelli’s God (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2010), 61. Instead of writing in a Christian republican tradition, Vatter argues, in chapter 26 Machiavelli is appealing to the medieval Arabic and Jewish political conception of God’s working to establish a republic through a philosopher-prophet-king. Acknowledging that Moses is Machiavelli’s chief example, in his discussion of “The Prince as a Redeemer,” in Redeeming “The Prince,” 23–65, Viroli does not locate him or Machiavelli’s conception in an explicitly Christian tradition.


100 The advice Machiavelli has offered in the preceding pages of The Prince thus seems to be both too specific and too general to be characterized, as by Viroli, Redeeming “The Prince,” 5, as merely an “oration” designed to provoke immediate political action or, simply, as a “political myth.” Labeling Machiavelli’s concluding call for action a “myth” would appear to give support to the argument put forward by Mary Dietz, “Trapping the Prince: Machiavelli and the Politics of Deception,” American Political Science Review 80, no. 3 (1986): 777–99. Instead of providing the Medici with advice about how to succeed in acquiring and maintaining their power, Dietz argues, Machiavelli was trying to destroy them by persuading them to undertake disastrous policies. But as Viroli, Redeeming “The Prince,” 12–14, following Hannah Arendt, On Revolution (New York: Viking, 1963), 197, points out, Machiavelli saw (correctly) that the advent of nation-states in northern Europe meant that the Italian city-states were no longer tenable. As Strauss, TM, 89, observes, the confederacy Machiavelli recommends in D 2.4 represents an alternative way of achieving the Italian unity and defensive capacity he calls for in P 26.

He wrote all his works explicitly for politically ambitious individuals who either were or hoped to become political leaders.


2


Machiavelli’s New Republic


DISCOURSES ON LIVY


In The Prince Machiavelli purports to be telling a Florentine prince what he needs to do not merely to acquire but also to extend and maintain his power, both in general and in his specific circumstances. In his Discourses on Livy Machiavelli then proposes to teach two other young Florentines, who “deserve to be” princes, what they would need to know to become founders of “new modes and orders.”


Dedication and Relation to The Prince


Recognizing that “if someone who desires or who wishes to reform a state in a city wishes it to be accepted and capable of being maintained to the satisfaction of everyone, he is under the necessity of retaining at least the shadow of its ancient modes . . . , even if in fact the new orders are altogether alien to the past ones” (D 1.25), Machiavelli presents his new “modes and orders” merely as an “imitation” of the Romans. As he observed in P 6, most people cannot even imagine the possibility of doing something that has not been done in the past. Those who do not have the ability to found something entirely new should aim at following the example of someone greater. His Florentine readers were more apt to believe that they would be able to duplicate the achievements of their Roman ancestors than that they themselves would be able to do something entirely unprecedented. (As in The Prince, so in the Discourses the suggestion that he is asking his readers merely to imitate others also enables Machiavelli to understate the difficulties they would encounter, if they actually tried to act on the basis of his advice.)

Machiavelli nevertheless seeks to arouse his young readers’ ambitions at the beginning of his Discourses by stating explicitly that he is showing them the path on which only “a short road will remain for another to bring it to the destined place” (D 1.Pref.). He thus promises them, in effect, that they will receive the “credit” or fame for achieving what he has merely sketched.


Machiavelli’s “Greetings” to His Two Young Friends


Machiavelli addresses his Discourses on Livy to two young friends, Cosimo Rucellai and Zanobi Buondelmonti. From the Art of War we learn that Cosimo was the grandson of Bernardo Rucellai, a close advisor of Lorenzo the Magnificent, who had broken with Lorenzo’s son Piero. Bernardo had been a patron of the arts and student of philosophy, but Cosimo reports that his grandfather did not think that people now could imitate the Romans. Zanobi is also said to have taken part in the conversation that took place in the Rucellai family gardens; and in introducing the participants, Machiavelli praises Cosimo for his dedication to the good of his fatherland but suggests that Zanobi was more spirited (AW 1.1, 4.3). Because Machiavelli subsequently dedicated his Life of Castruccio Castracani to Zanobi and Luigi Alamanni, the youngest participant in the conversation related in the Art of War, and both of these young Florentines took part in a failed conspiracy against the life of Cardinal Giulio de’ Medici in 1522, some scholars have speculated that Machiavelli incited them to take this action.1 What we know from the Art of War is that the two young men to whom Machiavelli dedicated the Discourses were wealthy young Florentine aristocrats who spent many of their leisure hours discussing ways in which the government of their city, if not Italy as a whole, could be improved, and whether or not it was possible for them to imitate the example of their glorious Roman predecessors.2

In the Art of War Machiavelli purports to be recalling a conversation at which he was present in 1516. Scholars thus suggest that his dedicating the Discourses to his friends from the Orti Oricellari means that he began writing the Discourses sometime before that conversation is supposed to have occurred, probably in 1515; and they conclude with more certainty that the work was completed by 1519, when Cosimo died.3 If this dating is correct, Machiavelli began writing the Discourses a mere two years after he completed his first draft of The Prince. It seems unlikely that he would have changed his mind fundamentally about the conclusions he had drawn from his own experience and much study of the character of political life in such a short time. He does not announce such a change, although he proclaims ways in which he differs from former “writers” in both of his major works.4 Differences between these two works would thus appear to reflect the differences in perspective Machiavelli explicitly adopts in writing to his purported addressees. Writing as a potential advisor to the prince, he presents his arguments in an extremely concise form entirely from the point of view of the interests of the prince. As an instructor of public-spirited young Florentine “aristocrats,” politically ambitious but skeptical about their ability to imitate the Romans, he proceeds in a more leisurely fashion, paying more attention to theory as well as to history, and appealing to the common, rather than simply to the prince’s, good.5

Because Machiavelli explicitly addresses young, politically ambitious Florentines in both The Prince and the Discourses, readers should not be surprised to find a certain number of parallels between the two dedications. In both cases the undersecretary from an old, but not very distinguished family emphasizes his poverty in explaining the character of the gift he is presenting. In both cases he explicitly claims that there is nothing greater or of more value that he could deliver than “the knowledge of the actions of great men, learned by [him] from long experience with modern things and a continuous reading of ancient ones,” as he states in The Prince, or “as much as I know and have learned through a long practice and a continual reading in worldly things,” as he says in the Discourses.6 And after emphasizing the “poverty” of his gift, in both dedications Machiavelli goes on to suggest not merely that he possesses knowledge that his readers need, but that they may not be able to understand or acquire the wisdom he possesses. He is their actual superior even though he is conventionally thought to be their inferior.

In his dedications to both of his explicitly comprehensive works, Machiavelli also stresses the unconventional character of the gift he is presenting. In The Prince that unconventionality is located in the character of the gift, the knowledge he prizes above all other things as opposed to an expensive, showy present designed to please the prince; but in the Discourses the unconventionality is associated with the recipients and Machiavelli’s intentions in presenting it. Rather than follow “the common usage of those who . . . are accustomed always to address their works to some prince and, blinded by ambition and avarice, praise him for all virtuous qualities when they should blame him for every part worthy of reproach” (which Machiavelli did in The Prince only to the extent to which he expressed his “extreme desire that [Lorenzo] arrive at the greatness that fortune and [his] other good qualities promise,” and did not blame him for anything explicitly), in the Discourses Machiavelli explains that he is writing not to “those who are princes but those who for their infinite good parts deserve to be” (3). In proposing, in effect, an exchange of his knowledge for a job from Lorenzo, Machiavelli appeared to write primarily out of his own need. But in addressing the Discourses to his young friends, Machiavelli says that he “does not know which of us has to be less obligated to the other: whether I to you, who have forced me to write what I would never have written for myself; or you to me, if in writing I have not satisfied you” (3). In other words, he claims to have written not out of his own need, but in an attempt to satisfy an expressed desire or need of theirs. Machiavelli does not specify the “infinite good parts” that make these young men “deserve to be” princes.7 However, when he explains that he has chosen to address “not those who could load me with ranks, honors, and riches but those who, though unable, would wish to do so,” because “men wishing to judge rightly have to esteem those who are liberal, not those who can be; and likewise those who know, not those who can govern a kingdom,” it looks as if the “infinite good parts” of his friends consist primarily in their desire to load him with riches and honors in exchange for the wisdom they wish to receive from him, and that it is he, who claims in his dedications to both works to possess the knowledge that would enable him (in contrast to his conventionally regarded “superiors”) to govern a kingdom, who deserves to be a prince.8

In D 1.10 Machiavelli observes that the men who have been most praised have been founders of religions, next those who have instituted republics or kingdoms, third generals who have expanded their kingdom or fatherland, and only fourth “literary men,” who are of many types. However, he concludes his dedication by reminding his readers that “writers” determine the reputation of princes by praising or blaming them.9 The examples he gives of such praise and blame seem to be designed, moreover, to arouse the ambitions of his young readers to found a new and better political order in place of the old. These examples also emphasize the importance of knowing how to use the resources one has, as opposed to merely possessing the wealth and arms generally (and conventionally) associated with rule. “Writers praise Hiero the Syracusan when he was a private individual more than Perseus the Macedonian when he was king,” Machiavelli observes, “for Hiero lacked nothing other than the principality to be a prince while the other had no part of a king other than the kingdom” (4). One of the unnamed “writers” appears to be Polybius, who emphasized Hiero’s virtues as both a private individual and a ruler.10 The other unnamed writer seems to be Plutarch, who in his “Life of Aemilius Paulus” reports that Perseus squandered the armed men and money his father had accumulated to free the Macedonians from the Romans, because he did not want to part with his treasure (and, as a result, lost it all along with his nation and his family). Insofar as they illustrate the deleterious effects of hereditary succession, both stories also point to the advantages of republican election. Machiavelli could be less reticent about the former in a work dedicated to young men who only deserved to be princes than he had been in a work dedicated to a prince who had risen to that status because of his family connections. Even so, Machiavelli could not be entirely open about his attack on hereditary “aristocracy” or his critique of traditional notions of political virtue at the beginning of a book explicitly written for young men whose wealth, leisure, and humanist education were all results of their families’ wealth and status.11


Preface to Book 1: The Discovery of New Modes and Orders in the Guise of an Imitation of the Romans


In the preface to the first book, which seems also to serve as a preface to the entire work, Machiavelli begins by stressing the difficulties he confronts in proposing “new modes and orders.” Explaining the resistance a new prince or “prophet” would have to overcome in P 6, Machiavelli emphasized the inability of his followers to believe that things could really be different. A “prophet” would have to be armed in order to succeed, because he would have to force his adherents to obey his commands after they had lost their initial enthusiasm for change in the face of armed opposition. But here Machiavelli attributes the danger confronted by an unarmed “discoverer” to the “envious nature of men,” and he tries to counter that envy, first, by emphasizing his “natural desire . . . to work, without any respect, for . . . the common benefit.” He claims to have taken “a path as yet untrodden by anyone” but not in search of recognition for himself. He admits that he may be rewarded by “those who consider humanely the end,” but he humbly professes his possible lack of talent and knowledge (as he did in his dedication), promising merely that he “will at least show the path to someone who with more virtue . . . will be able to fulfill his intention” (5).

Machiavelli almost immediately conceals the novelty of his discoveries in the second (or possibly the first) paragraph of his preface, however, by urging his contemporaries to imitate the ancients, not merely in the fine arts or civil law or medicine, but in politics.12 Despite his claim in P 26 that “in Italy matter is not lacking for introducing every form; here there is great virtue in the limbs, if it were not lacking in the heads,” at the beginning of his Discourses Machiavelli complains that “no sign of that ancient virtue remains with us” (5). He nevertheless continues to locate the reason for the absence of any sign of ancient virtue in his contemporaries’ “heads” when he observes that the cause is “not so much the weakness into which the present religion has led the world” (although in D 2.2 Machiavelli argues that this is a real factor) or “the evil that an ambitious idleness has done to many Christian provinces and cities” (that he emphasizes in D 2.2 and 3.1), but “not having a true knowledge of the histories.” Although an “infinite number” of his contemporaries take pleasure in reading ancient histories,13 they do not believe that it is possible to imitate the deeds of ancient kings, republics, legislators, or generals—“as if heaven, sun, elements, men had varied in motion, order and power from what they were in antiquity.” According to Machiavelli’s knowledge of worldly things, nature remains the same.14 Ignoring the Christian revelation that announces God’s acting in time and so altering the course of history, he proposes to show his readers “the utility for which one should seek knowledge of histories,” by writing on “all those books of Titus Livy that have not been intercepted by the malignity of the times.” He will bring out whatever he judges “necessary for their greater understanding, according to [his] knowledge of ancient and modern things” (6).15 Machiavelli’s utilizing of his knowledge of things both ancient and modern accords with his suggestion that nature does not fundamentally change. But the “utility” of the knowledge he proposes to draw out of his reading of Livy on the basis of his knowledge of things both ancient and modern cannot simply be the same as the knowledge the ancient historian intended to communicate to his readers (if only because Livy did not possess knowledge of what is distinctively modern). Even in explicitly advocating merely an imitation of the ancients, Machiavelli indicates he is doing something new.


The Organization of the Discourses


Because the things done by the Romans, and celebrated by Livy, proceeded from either public or private counsel, inside or outside the city, Machiavelli devotes the first book of his discourses to those things occurring inside as a result of public counsel. He implies (and later states) that the second book concerns things occurring outside as a result of public counsel. The third book does not have a preface, but readers can infer from the general schema that it treats things done both inside and outside the city on the basis of private counsel.16

Although Machiavelli makes the broad organization of the Discourses into these three parts explicit, readers have found it difficult to determine the internal organization of each of the three parts or his line of argument in the work as a whole.17 Sometimes the Discourses follow the order of Livy’s narrative, but often they do not. Nor is the connection between one chapter and the next always obvious. Observing that the Discourses are explicitly related only to the first ten books of Livy’s history, but that like Livy’s history as a whole, Machiavelli’s work has 142 chapters and so presumably covers the whole, Strauss contends that “Machiavelli’s use and nonuse of Livy is the key to the understanding of the work.”18 Livy was much more widely read and better known by educated readers in Machiavelli’s time than now. Nevertheless, it is difficult to believe that Machiavelli expected his readers to follow the intricate way in which he according to Strauss used (and changed) Livy’s history not merely to convey his own understanding of politics in the spaces created between the two texts, but to present a covert critique of the Bible by questioning the authority of Livy. There is no evidence, in fact, that anyone before Strauss read Machiavelli this way—brilliant as his reading is.19 As this account of the beginning of the Discourses indicates, I have learned a great deal from Strauss. In light of the evidence that Machiavelli hoped to have an effect on his immediate audience as well as possible later readers, and that his primary concern was not a critique of Christianity so much as an improved understanding and practice of politics, however, in the following account I have tried to show that Machiavelli’s Discourses constitute a coherent argument about the difficulties of establishing and maintaining a free way of life by means of a republican form of government.20 In book 1 he gradually discloses the general principles upon which the domestic order of such a government should be founded. In book 2 he then outlines a foreign policy that would preserve such a government with a particular eye to the situation of Florence. Finally, in book 3 he indicates very indirectly, because he knew from personal experience how dangerous it could be to make such recommendations, the sorts of things his young Florentine readers would need to do as private individuals in order to bring the new republican orders he is advocating into existence—and to maintain them.21

Because the order of Machiavelli’s “discourses” is so difficult to extract from the welter of historical details and observations, I begin the account of each book with an outline of the argument as I understand it.


Outline of Book 1: How to Design and Maintain the Domestic Institutions of a Free Republic


A. The Beginnings of Cities and Rome as Exemplar (D 1.1)

1. The Case for Sparta—the Traditional Exemplar (D 1.2–3)

a. The Desirability of “Tumults” (D 1.4)

b. Why the People Should Be Trusted More Than the Great (D 1.5)

c. Why Republics Have to Expand (D 1.6)

3. Lessons Derived from the Development of the Roman Republic (D 1.7–27)

a. How to Prevent “Tumults” from Becoming Civil Wars (D 1.7–8)

b. How to Found, Maintain, and Reorder a Republic (D 1.9–27)

1) The Necessity of a Single Founder (D 1.9)

2) Why a Founder Should Act for the Common Good (D 1.10)

3) Religion as a Means of Maintaining a Republican Order (D 1.11–15)

a) Elections as a Remedy for the Problems of Hereditary Succession (D 1.19–20)

b) The Difficulty of Preventing or Remedying Corruption (D 1.16–18)

2. The Need for Reforms and Popular Trials to Supplement Competitive Elections (D 1.49)

3. No One Should Be Able to Bring Government to a Standstill (D 1.50)

4. The “Great” Must Demonstrate Their Willingness to Sacrifice for the Common Good in Order to Be Elected (D 1.51)

a. The People Are Not Always Wise (D 1.53–54)

b. Nor Are the People Entirely Good (D 1.55)

c. Claims to Divinely Inspired Knowledge Are Not Necessary (D 1.56)

d. The Power of the Multitude Is Transitory and Thus Limited (D 1.57)

e. Nevertheless, the People Are Wiser and More Stable Than Princes (D 1.58)

f. Popular Governments Keep Faith Better Than Princes (D 1.59)

g. Popular Government Gives Everyone an Incentive to Work for the Benefit of All (D 1.60)


Book 1: How to Design and Maintain the Domestic Institutions of a Free Republic


A. The Beginnings of Cities and Rome as Exemplar (D 1.1)


To establish Rome as the exemplary city, Machiavelli looks back at the beginnings of cities in general; and in doing so, he dismisses several alternative accounts, either silently by omission or in passing. For example, although Machiavelli’s purported source, Livy, expresses some skepticism about the truth of the stories about the founding of Rome, he nevertheless weaves them into a continuous narrative, incorporating the claims about the divine guidance and noble blood of the founders. Machiavelli’s presentation of the beginnings is much less chronological and more schematic; and he does not mention much less credit any claims about divine guidance or interference.22 As he merely suggested in The Prince, here he states explicitly that human beings form political associations or “cities” first in order to defend themselves and, second, to increase their wealth and dominion. In opposition to Aristotle and the Christian tradition that incorporated his philosophy, Machiavelli does not think that human beings are drawn together by natural attraction or affection.23 It does not matter, therefore, whether the people of a city originate in a single tribe or gather together from disparate places. What is important is that their domestic orders enable them not merely to defend themselves but to conquer others. From the very first paragraph of the first part of his Discourses Machiavelli thus indicates that it is the close relation between their domestic orders and foreign conquests that makes the Romans exemplary.

According to Machiavelli, “all cities are built either by men native to the place . . . or by foreigners.” In the first case people who were living dispersed gather together, either on their own or directed by one of them having greater authority, to defend themselves. He cites Venice as an example of the former and Athens as an example of the latter. “The second case is that of a city built by foreign races, whether free men or those depending on others, who are sent out as colonies either by a republic or by a prince to relieve their lands of inhabitants or to secure a newly acquired country . . . without expense.” Having recommended such a policy to a prince who acquired a new territory in P 3, Machiavelli observes here that the Roman people built many such cities throughout their empire. But, he adds, “because such cities do not have a free origin, it rarely happens that they make great strides and can be numbered among the heads of kingdoms” (8). Whether one accepts the story of its founding by Sulla’s soldiers or by the inhabitants of Fiesole descending from their mountains to the plain during the peace established by Octavian, Florence was built as a colony. Setting up the contrast between his own city and its great Roman predecessor that runs throughout the Discourses, although often only implicitly, Machiavelli notes that the modern republic without free origins has proved to be weaker.24 As he states explicitly with regard to Rome later in the chapter, Machiavelli does not think that the specific (quasi-mythical) accounts of the foundings of cities are as important (or reliable) as the general reasons and causes for the differences among them that he derives from his knowledge of things both ancient and modern.

Machiavelli somewhat ironically says that peoples have free origins when they “are constrained by disease, hunger, or war to abandon their ancestral country and to seek for themselves a new seat” (emphasis added), presumably because these peoples are not, like colonists, subject to an external political authority. These peoples may either inhabit cities they find in the countries they acquire, as did Moses (according to Machiavelli), or build anew, as did Aeneas.25 In either case, Machiavelli adds, the virtue of the builder will be shown in his choice of the site and the laws he orders. It might seem better for the “builder” to choose a sterile site in which circumstances would force people to work of their own accord in order to survive (as they were constrained by natural or man-made disasters to emigrate “freely”), rather than to command them to do so directly with laws, “if men were content to live off their own and did not wish to command others.” However, he has already observed, people form cities because they perceive the need to defend themselves from those who wish not merely to seize their goods, but also to oppress them. So, Machiavelli concludes, it is necessary to choose the most fertile places, where the city can expand so as to be able to defend itself, and to counteract the idleness to which the fertility of the place might give rise by ordering laws that impose a necessity to exercise on those who have to be soldiers. As a result of this exercise, they will become better soldiers than those who live in countries that are naturally harsh and sterile.26

Machiavelli does not explicitly apply the standards he has just articulated to the two “builders” he named. Judged by such standards, however, Moses was not a virtuous “builder.” He not merely failed to reach the promised land; he relied on their experience in the sterile Sinai desert to make his people tough enough to seize Canaan, and did not give them laws that made them good enough soldiers to defend themselves in the future.27 Machiavelli observes that it does not matter whether one takes Aeneas or Romulus as the progenitor of Rome, because in either case the Romans had a free beginning. He thus discounts the importance both of his own initial distinction between cities settled by natives and those settled by foreigners (and thus similar tribal, ethnic, or racial origins), and of the noble blood as well as the divine guidance attributed to the founders of a city with “a free beginning, without depending on anyone” (including, it seems, any god).

According to Machiavelli, it was the “many necessities the laws made by Romulus, Numa, and the others imposed” that prevented “the fertility of the site, the advantages of the sea, the frequent victories, and the greatness of its empire” from corrupting Rome “for many centuries.” These laws kept Rome “full of as much virtue as has ever adorned any other city or republic” (9). He thus turns to analyzing the “necessities” imposed by these laws.


B. Why the Roman Republic Is Exemplary (D 1.2–6)


Having argued in D 1.1 that a city’s laws are more important than its location or the composition of the population in establishing and maintaining its freedom, Machiavelli turns in D 1.2 to review and contest previous accounts of the best legislation or legislator. Emphasizing the importance of the beginnings of cities, Machiavelli initially classifies republics according to their foundings: best, if they acquired all their laws and institutions all at once, as Sparta did from Lycurgus; second best, if they acquired them over time, through chance and in response to “accidents,” as did Rome; or worst, if they never succeeded in acquiring a firm basis for maintaining their freedom. “That republic can be called happy,” Machiavelli comments, “whose lot is to get one man so prudent that he gives it laws ordered so that it can live securely under them without needing to correct them” (10, emphasis added). Having lasted for eight hundred years without corruption or any dangerous tumult, Sparta appears to represent a much better example of a free republic than Rome, which became perfect only as a result of a series of accidents.28

Cities can “never re-order themselves without danger,” Machiavelli explains, “because enough men never agree to a new law that looks to a new order in a city unless they are shown by a necessity that they need to do it” (10–11). And, he indicates by pointing to the contemporary relevance of the discussion, that necessity consists in the danger of foreign conquest. Florence was reordered as a result of the “accident” in Arezzo in ’02 (a rebellion against Florentine rule that led the republic to appoint Machiavelli’s patron, Piero Soderini, gonfalonier for life), and disordered by the “accident” in Prato in ’12 (the defeat of the Florentine militia by the Spanish army, which led to the overthrow of the republic and the return of the Medici). As in his account of the beginnings of cities, so in discussing their internal order, Machiavelli points to the close connection he sees between the internal ordering of a city and the requirements of its external defense.


1. The Case for Sparta—the Traditional Exemplar (D 1.2–3)


To show that Rome is a more exemplary republic than Sparta Machiavelli has to examine and criticize the arguments raised on behalf of Sparta. The first such argument is based on the traditional division of regimes, according to the number of rulers, into monarchies, aristocracies, and democracies, and a purported cycle that occurs as a result of the degeneration of each good form into its opposite. Although we know from the first chapter of The Prince that Machiavelli does not accept the traditional tripartite division of regimes, many commentators have taken his summary account of the cycle to represent his own understanding.29 However, after summarizing the argument for the cycle, taken largely from Polybius, but adapted slightly to reflect his own understanding, Machiavelli distances himself sharply from it.30 No republic would last long enough to go through the full cycle, he protests, because “a republic always lacking in counsel and forces becomes subject to a neighboring state that is ordered better than it.” He dismisses all six of the “pure” forms of government as “pestiferous,” the three good ones, because of their brief life, along with the bad into which the good tend to degenerate. “Those who prudently order laws, having recognized this defect, avoid each of these modes by itself” and “chose one that shared in all, judging it firmer and more stable” (13), because in a city where there is simultaneously a principality, aristocracy, and popular government, each part guards the other. Machiavelli thus agrees with previous writers and legislators like Lycurgus that a mixed regime is better than any of the simple or “pure” kinds, but he does not endorse it for quite the same reasons. Whereas they praised the superior justice and stability of such mixed regimes, he characteristically relates the goodness (or badness) of the internal order to a government’s capacity (or not) to defend itself from external aggression.

Constructed as a mixed regime from the beginning, Sparta still appears to be the exemplary republic. Machiavelli contrasts the longevity of the balance of the monarchical, aristocratic, and popular elements Lycurgus established with the instability and brief life of the Athenian laws ordered by Solon, who incorporated only a popular element. Like Sparta, Rome ultimately incorporated all three elements, but Machiavelli admits that it took some time and several changes of government to achieve the perfect mixture. It was first necessary to overthrow the tyrannical kings to establish a true mixture of aristocracy with a monarchical element (in the two consuls elected from the senate to lead the armies). The Roman people did not learn that they had to demand protection against the nobles, however, until the death of the last Tarquin made the nobles lose their fear that the plebs would not take their side in a renewed dispute and they began to treat the plebs inhumanely. After much contention between the plebs and the nobility, they created tribunes with so much eminence and reputation that they could not merely serve as intermediaries between the plebs and the Senate, but counter the insolence of the nobles.


2. The Case for Rome—the New Exemplar (D 1.4–6)


The general lessons Machiavelli draws from the development of Rome explain why he ultimately considers Rome to be a “perfect republic,” even though it did not have a legislator who provided it with a mixed regime from the very beginning. His extremely selective, if not simply inaccurate use of historical examples to document that superiority shows, moreover, that he is recommending Rome not as its history was depicted by Livy, but as a model he has derived from that history on the basis of his own knowledge of things both ancient and modern.31

Machiavelli argues that Rome was superior to the apparently more stable Sparta because Rome was an expansive regime with a popular base. Beginning with his declaration in D 1.3 that “it is necessary to whoever disposes a republic and orders laws in it to presuppose that all men are bad” (15), he disagrees with the ancient advocates of “aristocratic” republics who urged the necessity of educating a small class of potential rulers to control the rest of the population with laws (e.g., Aristotle, Politics 2.1267b1–9). According to Machiavelli, the behavior of the Roman nobles after the expulsion of the Tarquins shows that one cannot rely on the apparent public-spiritedness of the persons to whom the laws grant power. To prevent them from oppressing others, laws must be designed to make those with power afraid of the consequences of abusing it. The Romans did this by creating the offices of the tribunes to keep the nobles in line.


a. The Desirability of “Tumults” (D 1.4)


Recognizing that many have faulted the government of Rome because of the constant “tumults” between the nobles and the plebs, Machiavelli insists in D 1.4 that these tumults were “the first cause of keeping Rome free.”32 As in P 9, he observes that “in every republic are two diverse humors, that of the people and that of the great, and that all the laws that are made in favor of freedom arise from their disunion” (16). Reasoning as he did in P 12 that “there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms, and where there are good arms there must be good laws,” he argues that since the Romans obviously had good arms (which enabled them to attain the empire), they must also have had good laws. Their arms were good (and numerous), because the Romans armed the plebs; and the plebs refused to enroll in the armies, upon occasion, unless they were given part of the government. “The desires of free peoples are rarely pernicious to freedom,” Machiavelli explains, “because they arise either from being oppressed or from suspicion that they may be oppressed” (17). It was good, therefore, to include them in the government. If the people are mistaken, their erroneous suspicions can be corrected by means of assemblies, in which a good orator can show them how they have been deceived.33


b. Why the People Should Be Trusted More Than the Great (D 1.5)


“Because in every republic there are great and popular men,” Machiavelli acknowledges, there is a disagreement about which should be relied on to guard the city’s freedom. Sparta and Venice put this guardianship in the hands of the nobles, whereas Rome put it in the hands of the plebs. Because Sparta and Venice lived free longer than Rome, some argue that the nobles have thus proved to be better guards. Machiavelli affirms, however, “that one should put on guard over a thing those who have less appetite for usurping it”; and, he repeats, the “nobles” have a great desire to dominate, whereas the “ignobles” (ignobili) want only to escape oppression. He admits that partisans of the nobles will point out that granting them power will satisfy their ambition more and dampen the restless spirits of the plebs that cause the confusion and scandals in republics that reduce the nobility to desperation. Roman history provides a prime example of the plebs’ not being satisfied with one plebian consul, but wishing to have all the offices, and supporting leaders like Marius, who sought to beat down the nobility entirely (and thus destroyed the mixed regime). Machiavelli concedes as much in his discussion of the attempt by the Gracchi to revive the agrarian reform in D 1.37. But he concludes that the answer to the question about which part or party best guards a city’s liberty depends not simply on reason or historical precedents, but on whether “you are reasoning about a republic that wishes to make an empire, like Rome, or about one for whom it is enough to maintain itself” (18), like Sparta or Venice. Since Machiavelli has already argued that a city is not well located unless the site allows it to expand sufficiently to defend itself from foreign aggression, readers should not be surprised by his choice of the plebs. Admitting that both the nobles and the plebs have ambitions that need to be “vented,” he nevertheless argues that those who possess the most are most apt to cause tumults and so endanger the liberty of the city. First, “it does not appear to men that they possess securely what [they] have unless [they] acquire more”; second, their wealth gives them more resources with which to work larger changes; and, third, their wealth and honors are most apt to provoke the envy and emulation of others.34

Someone might ask whether the Roman state could not have been ordered so as to remove the enmity between the people and the Senate. Machiavelli thus explains: Venice and Sparta were able to maintain their freedom as long as they did without internal dissension, because both cities kept the number of inhabitants to be ruled low and so, in effect, preempted the possibility of a successful popular rebellion.
