Venice declared all those who participated in the government of the city at a certain point to be “gentlemen,” prohibited those who came later from taking part, and by not allowing a large number of people to come into the city, prevented an inequality between rulers and ruled to develop.35 Although he praised Lycurgus (D 1.2) for creating a mixture of principality, aristocracy, and democracy, Machiavelli now maintains that Sparta was governed by a king and narrow Senate. (He thus makes early Sparta look like prerepublican Rome by ignoring the fact that Sparta had two hereditary kings and ephors [the popular element]—facts he recognizes elsewhere.)36 These few citizens could maintain control without much dissent, partly because the equality of belongings mandated by Lycurgus made the plebs less ambitious, and partly because the kings maintained their dignity against the other nobles by defending the plebs from every injury, but mostly because the Spartans did not accept foreigners, so that their population could not be corrupted.


c. Why Republics Have to Expand (D 1.6)


Machiavelli does not mention the fact that Sparta used slaves to farm and armed only her relatively few citizens. Instead he emphasizes the fact that Rome would not have been able to wage the wars it did without arming the plebs and increasing the population by accepting foreigners. At first he suggests that the resolution of the question of why a republic must expand involves a tradeoff of “inconveniences.” A city can live free and united if it is located in a strong place where it would be difficult to crush but does not pose a threat to its neighbors. “For war is made on a republic for two causes: one, to become master of it; the other, for fear lest it seize you” (22). Indeed, Machiavelli declares “that if the thing could be held balanced in this mode, it would be the true political way of life and the true quiet of a city.”37 But he quickly adds that “since things of men are in motion and cannot stay steady, they must either rise or fall.” So what reason does not dictate, “necessity” does. That “necessity” with regard to cities is that if “heaven” is so kind as to relieve them from the necessity of waging war, their people will become idle, effeminate, or divided, and thus eventually ruined internally, if not externally. “In ordering a republic,” Machiavelli thus concludes, “it is necessary to follow the Roman order and not that of the other republics . . . and to tolerate the enmities that arise between the people and the Senate . . . as an inconvenience necessary to arrive at Roman greatness” (23).


3. Lessons Derived from the Development of the Roman Republic (D 1.7–27)


a. How to Prevent “Tumults” from Becoming Civil Wars (D 1.7–8)


“Tolerating” these enmities does not mean merely letting them flare and allowing the two humors to fight their differences out. The point is, rather, to design “orders” that will not only prevent the conflict between the “humors” from degenerating into civil war but also use that conflict to support the rule of law. The first such “order” he mentions is granting “those who are posted in a city as guard of its freedom . . . authority . . . to accuse citizens to the people, or to some magistrate or council, when they sin in anything against the free state.” Such an order has “two very useful effects for a republic”: First, it deters citizens from attempting things against the state for fear of incurring such an accusation and insures that if they do attempt to overturn the state, such individuals will be “crushed instantly and without respect” (23). Second, and seemingly more important, public trials that enable the people to accuse specific individuals of attempting to overthrow the republic and that allow those individuals to present witnesses and evidence to counter the accusations provide a means of “venting those humors that grow up in cities” that produce civil wars if they are not directed and regulated by laws.

In citing the trial of Coriolanus as an example of the advantages of accusations, Machiavelli reports that Livy “says that the Roman nobility had become angered against the plebs because the plebs appeared to it to have too much authority through the creation of the tribunes.” But when the plebs heard that Coriolanus counseled the Senate to withhold the grain they had brought from Sicily to relieve the famine to “punish the plebs and take from it the authority that it had taken to the prejudice of the nobility,” they became so angry that they would have killed Coriolanus as he emerged from the Senate in a tumult, “had the tribunes not summoned him to appear to defend his cause” (24). Machiavelli does not mention the fact (to be found in Livy 2.35) that Coriolanus did not appear and was condemned in absentia. His example certainly does not support Machiavelli’s claim in the next chapter that “calumnies are detestable in free cities,” and that there is no “better order for taking them away than to open up very many places for accusations,” because “calumnies have need neither of witnesses nor of any other specific corroboration to prove them, so that everyone can be calumniated by everyone; but everyone cannot . . . be accused, since accusations have need of true corroborations and of circumstances that show the truth of the accusation” (27). Machiavelli seems to admit that Coriolanus was not treated justly when he concludes that “if a citizen is crushed ordinarily, there follows little or no disorder in the republic, even though he has been done a wrong” (24). But it is not for the sake of achieving justice that Machiavelli recommends the institution of publicly accusing individuals said to have “sinned” against the republic before a popular jury. According to Machiavelli, such public trials serve to “vent” the “ambition” (or, we might say, anger) of the public by directing it against a single individual, rather than against the city and its government as a whole, and thus preserve the rule of law. He recommends public accusations because they affect only a few individuals, however unjustly, and benefit the “generality” because trials are conducted in public according to law, and so preserve republican government, whereas the use of private forces or foreign troops to punish offenders would destroy it. In using the accusation of Coriolanus as an example of the advantages of such a process, Machiavelli suppresses the “inconvenient” fact that after he was condemned, Coriolanus defected to a foreign city, where he raised an army that threatened to destroy Rome, until his mother pleaded with him to desist.38

Although Machiavelli initially says that he is advocating the creation of an authority able to accuse citizens before “the people, or some magistrate or council,” both his ancient and his Florentine examples suggest that the jury needs to be numerous and popular if public trials are to prevent civil wars that so weaken a state that it becomes vulnerable to foreign conquest.39 Machiavelli’s first example of a Florentine who was thought by many to have ambitions to overthrow the republic is extremely ironic. Because he did not have to fear a public accusation and trial, Francesco Valori concluded that there was no way of checking his ambitions “except with a sect contrary to his.” He thus began organizing a private army of supporters to defend him”; and because “those who opposed him had no ordinary [lawful] way to repress him, they thought of extraordinary [extralegal] ways until they came to arms.” In fact, Valori was the leader of Savonarola’s party who refused to grant the appeal to the popular Council in capital cases, for which Savonarola himself had agitated, to five ottimati accused of conspiring to overthrow the republic and bring back the Medici. (Valori feared that the Council would acquit the one who only knew of the plot but did not actually participate in it.) Because the friar did not criticize members of his own party who did not enforce the law he had promoted, Savonarola lost much of his popular influence and was condemned by the Church.40 Machiavelli suggests that the same failure of the Florentine republic to establish a public mode of accusing individuals said to have an ambition to overthrow the republic before a popular jury also made it impossible for Piero Soderini to respond effectively to the accusations other ottimati made against him. “To accuse one powerful individual before eight judges in a republic is not enough,” Machiavelli comments; “the judges need to be very many because the few always behave in the mode of the few” (25). Those few presumably correspond to the “great,” who are always trying to increase their ability to oppress others, and whose exoneration of one of their own in a closed session would continue to be suspect to the people. In The Prince Machiavelli thus argued that the institution of a public court like the French parlement would enable a prince to secure himself by enabling the people to check the nobles. Had there been such a court in Florence, he suggests here, Soderini would have been condemned and his accusers (including preeminently the Medici) would have “vented their animus without having the Spanish army come.” Or if he had been shown not to be guilty as charged, “they would not have dared to work against him for fear of being accused themselves” (25).

As Machiavelli makes clear with the example of Manlius Capitolinus in D 1.8, ambitious individuals often charge those in power with misusing the public’s trust. Not merely will such individuals attract the support of other envious people if their “calumnies” are not made subject to investigation and proof in a public forum, but their supporters will end up fighting the supporters of their opponents in the streets, if not on a battlefield with foreign troops, and the republic will be destroyed.


b. How to Found, Maintain, and Reorder a Republic (D 1.9–27)


Having argued that the popularly based Roman version of the mixed regime proved to be superior to the more aristocratic Greek versions, because the latter were destroyed either by civil wars between the two “humors” or by foreign conquest, Machiavelli returns in D 1.9 to the beginning of Rome to show the way in which it developed its admirable institutions over time. He begins by excusing what many would see to be a great fault in its founder: Romulus not only killed his brother but also consented to the murder of Titus Tatius the Sabine, whom he had chosen as a partner in the kingdom (to make peace after the Romans stole the Sabine women).41


1) THE NECESSITY OF A SINGLE FOUNDER (D 1.9). Many commentators have emphasized the “general rule” Machiavelli enunciates on the basis of Romulus’s example, “that it never or rarely happens that any republic or kingdom is ordered well from the beginning or reformed altogether anew outside its old orders unless it is ordered by one individual.” Because Machiavelli argues that the “effects” excuse Romulus’s violent deeds, these readers conclude that the founding of a regime requires an “extraordinary” (immoral and illegal) act of violence or crime, and, more generally (as in P 18), that the end justifies the means.42

Such readers do not pay sufficient attention to the specific reasons why Machiavelli not merely excuses Romulus’s deeds, but also calls him “prudent” and “virtuous.” The first reason is that it is necessary for a single mind to order a city. Because people disagree about what is good, many minds will not be able to agree on what order should be instituted. Machiavelli thus excuses Romulus for killing his brother and colleague in order to obtain the necessary authority for himself. Machiavelli calls Romulus not merely prudent, but virtuous, because Romulus showed that he was acting not on his own behalf but for the sake of the common good (bene comune). He demonstrated the beneficent intention behind his seemingly criminal actions by refusing to establish a hereditary succession and by sharing his power with a senate.43 By cutting off his own family and sharing power with others Romulus not only indicated that, like the theorists of the cycle of regimes, he understood that hereditary rule tends to degenerate.44 He also understood the need to gain support for the order he had established from those who had not shared his understanding of the good at the beginning but would come to appreciate the benefits of the order once established and therefore defend it. The way people become attached to a government, he recognized, is by taking part in its decisions. By establishing a senate with which he took counsel and by whose opinion he decided, Romulus proved that he was acting not solely from his own ambition but for the common good.45

Machiavelli’s justification for Romulus’s crimes raises four questions that he pursues in greater depth and detail in the remainder of book 1. First, is it necessary for a leader who wishes to renew the orders of a republic to act outside the law and thus risk overturning the republic entirely?46 Or is it possible to design institutions that can be renewed from within? Second, what leads a prince who acquires sole authority to act for the common benefit—if only out of concern for the preservation of his own work and reputation? Third, how does this prince acquire support from those who do not understand the reasons for his initial actions? And, fourth, what can a prince who wishes to establish an enduring order do to ensure that he will have successors who understand what is needed to maintain that order?


2) WHY A FOUNDER SHOULD ACT FOR THE COMMON GOOD (D 1.10). Machiavelli addresses the question of the prince’s incentives in D 1.10. Although the most praised men are heads and orderers of religions, then the founders of republics and kingdoms, third the generals whose victories expand their kingdom or fatherland, and fourth the literary men who celebrate their deeds, he observes, most actual princes are deceived “by a false good and a false glory.” Encouraged by the obsequious flattery of their attendants to try to secure their rule by destroying anyone who threatens to oppose them, most princes become tyrants, living in unabated fear of conspiracies and blamed, rather than praised, after they die.47

Machiavelli seems to echo the classical philosophical critique of tyranny when he affirms that reading ancient history should make anyone wish to be a savior of his republic like Scipio rather than its destroyer like Caesar, or a prince like Timoleon or Dion instead of a tyrant like Nabis, Phalaris, or Dionysius. He acknowledges that the destroyer of the Roman republic, Caesar, has been more celebrated by “the writers” than any of these exemplary princes, whose good works endured only during their own lifetimes.48 But he suggests that those who praise Caesar have been “corrupted by his fortune” (that is, attributed his success to his virtue) and were “awed by the duration of the empire that, ruling under that name, did not permit writers to speak freely of him” (32). Readers impressed by the praise of Caesar should look at what writers (preeminently Cicero) say in criticizing Catiline, who wished but failed to achieve what Caesar did, and in praising his enemy, Brutus, to get a truer, more balanced view of Caesar’s achievement and “glory.”

By referring to Brutus, Machiavelli reminds his readers that the destroyer of the Roman republic died violently as a victim of a conspiracy of his former friends (members of the Senate whose power Caesar was effectively seizing).49 Caesar’s reputation or “glory” was based not so much on the happiness or security of his own life as on the empire he established in place of the republic. His name or fame was thus hostage, in effect, to the deeds of his successors. Machiavelli admits that some of Caesar’s successors were good emperors. Expanding and slightly modifying the analysis of the emperors he presented in P 19, he explains that these emperors did not depend upon the Praetorian Guard or the legions, i.e., force, to keep them in office, because “their habits, the benevolence of the people, and the love of the Senate defended them.” Both they and their people lived secure in a “world full of peace and justice,” in a version of what Machiavelli calls a well-ordered kingdom, including “the Senate with its authority, the magistrates with their honors, the rich citizens enjoying their riches, nobility and virtue exalted.” These were, indeed, “golden times when each can hold and defend the opinion he wishes” (33).50 Underlining a point he made about Romulus, Machiavelli also reminds his readers that, with the exception of Titus, these good emperors succeeded by adoption rather than by inheritance. Most of Caesar’s successors were elevated, however, by the legions or the Praetorian Guard. As Machiavelli pointed out in P 19, these emperors had to allow their soldiers to oppress the people or be killed by their own soldiers. Only a “criminal” (as he says here) like Severus was saved by his exceptionally great fortune and virtue. Considerations of his own safety as well as his future reputation should lead a prince to see the need to establish institutions that would check the power of later princes. Seeming to speak here particularly to his immediate audience of politically ambitious Florentine youths, Machiavelli concludes that a prince who “seeks the glory of the world . . . ought to desire to possess a corrupt city—not to spoil it entirely as did Caesar but to reorder it as did Romulus” (33). Those who establish institutions like the Roman Senate, which benefit later generations, rather than tyrannies which oppress them, he promises, will become venerated. (See P 6.)

A reader cannot help but ask somewhat skeptically: would it truly be more glorious for a young man to reform his own corrupt republic than to become like Caesar king, if not tyrant, of the entire world? Later in the Discourses (see especially D 2.33 and 3.34), Machiavelli will raise questions about whether glory is a reliable measure of true human greatness. Glory is after all a product of widespread popular opinion, not of knowledge; and it is often not enjoyed by the individual who acquires it posthumously, especially if he is assassinated, as Caesar was. Machiavelli will appeal instead to the desire to secure their own lives that leaders share with their people.


3) RELIGION AS A MEANS OF MAINTAINING A REPUBLICAN ORDER (D 1.11–15). After arguing that a prince should act to secure his own life and the common good rather than strive for praise and to perpetuate his name or family by establishing a hereditary monarchy, Machiavelli turns in D 1.11–14 to examine the way in which the Romans used religion to convince people who did not understand the reasons for the orders to support and obey them. Romulus did not need to appeal to the authority of God to order the Senate and make other civil and military orders, Machiavelli suggests, because Romulus could and did use extraordinary force to make himself feared and obeyed.51 To establish the religious beliefs and practices that would make a ferocious people obey the law and support the Senate along with the other civil and military orders after Romulus died, however, Numa Pompilius had to claim to have divine inspiration. He thus pretended to be intimate with a nymph who told him what to tell the people. And the people believed him—partly because of his own goodness and prudence, and partly because the men were crude.

Reminding his readers that the purpose of the Discourses is to show his contemporaries that it is possible to imitate the ancient Romans, Machiavelli concedes that “whoever wished to make a republic in the present times would find it easier among mountain men, where there is no civilization, than among those who are used to living in cities, where civilization is corrupt” (35). But he then observes that the people of Florence do not consider themselves either ignorant or coarse, yet “they were persuaded by Friar Girolamo Savonarola that he spoke with God . . . without having seen anything extraordinary to make them believe him. For his life, learning, and the subject he took up were sufficient to make them lend faith.” Machiavelli thus concludes that “no one . . . should be terrified that he cannot carry out what has been carried out by others, for as was said in our preface, men are born, live, and die always in one and the same order” (36).

The fact that all men die is, indeed, the reason those who found a kingdom or republic need to establish a religion to maintain it. So long as a virtuous prince is alive, he can enforce his laws by making people afraid to disobey. But if their fear of the prince is not extended and supplemented by a fear of the gods, the orders a prince establishes and maintains will die with him. So Machiavelli urges, “princes of a republic or of a kingdom should maintain the foundations of the religion they hold,” for “if this is done, it will be an easy thing for them to maintain their republic religious and, in consequence, good and united” (37). Prudent leaders will not merely hide their own lack of belief; they will magnify anything that favors religion, especially if they know about natural things. As Machiavelli argued in P 18, a prince must always appear to be religious, even if he himself does not and cannot believe. His people will not continue to believe if he does not act as if he does.

Roman leaders like Camillus fostered popular beliefs that the gods particularly favored their city, because these beliefs made it easier for the great men of Rome to obtain popular support for their plans and so to maintain unity, rather than division within the city. But the “princes of the Christian republic” have destroyed the religious beliefs of the people living closest to them by providing “wicked examples.” And because the Church lacks sufficient temporal power to impose its rule on the rest of Italy but is able to call upon other powers to defend it from domination by any other state, Italy remains not only disunited but also vulnerable to foreign invasions. Rather than calling for a pope-led expedition to “liberate” Italy from the barbarians, as in P 26, Machiavelli here somewhat fancifully proposes exporting “the Roman court, with all the authority it has in Italy, to inhabit the towns of the Swiss.” He thus suggests not merely that the temporal power and independence of the Church has prevented the unification and defense of Italy under a national monarchy like that of France or Spain. He also insists that “the bad customs of that court” have made it impossible for the Italians to live, like the Swiss, “according to the ancients as regards both religion and military orders” (39). To imitate the Romans, Machiavelli intimates, his contemporaries will have to destroy the Roman church.52 Alternatively, Machiavelli predicts, it may destroy itself and so create conditions under which Italy can be unified, because the loss of faith in the province caused by the corruption of the Church makes it likely that it will be either ruined or scourged in the near future. The religious difference that seems to make imitation of ancient politics impossible may not last.53

Machiavelli explicitly treats Roman religion as a means the nobles used to overcome plebian resistance to their policies and rule in D 1.13–14. And treating “religion” solely as an instrument of rule allows him to avoid commenting on the substantive differences between Christian and pagan forms (which he explicitly does later in D 2.2). In D 1.13 he gives examples of the ways in which Roman nobles used “certain prodigies,” oracles, and the Sibylline books to convince the plebs to reinstate nobles as consuls, persist in long sieges, and undertake new military expeditions. And in D 1.14 he explains how Roman generals manipulated the auguries, without revealing their own skepticism, to give their troops confidence. But in D 1.15 he shows that the threat of divine punishment and immediate death to those who refused to take an oath to fight in defense of their city was not sufficient to make the Sabines victorious in their battle against the experienced, disciplined, and hence confident troops of the Romans.54 Machiavelli thus concludes that religion is a useful supplement in maintaining orders first instituted by means of coercion, but it is no substitute for such orders.


4) THE LIMITS OF RELIGION AND THE PROBLEM OF CORRUPTION (D 1.16–20). Machiavelli gradually brings out the limited utility of “religion” in the next four chapters. He began his discussion of the religion of the Romans by praising Numa for reducing “a very ferocious people . . . to civil obedience” by means of religion, and went so far as to suggest that Rome owed even more to Numa than to Romulus. But he begins D 1.16 by observing how difficult it is “for a people used to living under a prince to preserve its freedom, if by accident it acquires it, as Rome did after the expulsion of the Tarquins.” The reason is that a “people is nothing other than a brute animal that, although of a ferocious and feral nature, has always been nourished in prison and in servitude.” So “if it is left free in a field to its fate, it becomes the prey of the first one who seeks to rechain it, not being used to feed itself and not knowing places where it may have to take refuge” (44). In other words, the same peaceful arts that civilize a people by making it willing to obey the law also make that same people too pacific to defend itself from conquest or tyranny.

Machiavelli began D 1.12 by declaring that “those princes or those republics that wish to maintain themselves uncorrupt have above everything else to maintain the ceremonies of their religion uncorrupt and hold them always in veneration,” leading a reader to think that a “corrupt” city would be irreligious. Machiavelli has subsequently shown, however, that “religion” does not suffice to maintain the republican orders established by a public-spirited founder. On the contrary, religion remains politically salutary only when nonbelieving leaders hide their own lack of belief and maintain the ceremonies to obtain the obedient cooperation of the people. In themselves, he now admits, the “civilizing” arts of peace Numa used to maintain the orders of Romulus threatened ultimately to undermine the freedom of the city, both internal and external.55 “Having considered the virtue and mode of proceeding of . . . the first three Roman kings,” he concludes in D 1.19, “one sees that Rome chanced upon very great fortune when it had the first king very fierce and bellicose, the next quiet and religious, the third similar in ferocity to Romulus and more a lover of war than of peace. For in Rome it was necessary that in its first beginnings an orderer of a civil way of life emerge, but it was indeed then necessary that the other kings take up again the virtue of Romulus; otherwise that city would have become effeminate and the prey of its neighbors” (52).56


(A) ELECTIONS AS A REMEDY FOR THE PROBLEMS OF HEREDITARY SUCCESSION (D 1.19–20) Machiavelli uses the example of early Rome to show that a succession of prudent and virtuous leaders is more necessary than religion to maintain the republican orders of a free city. That was the great innovation Lucius Junius Brutus introduced when he replaced the king, who was apparently elected for life, with two consuls annually elected by the Senate. The great advantage of republics over hereditary principalities or kingdoms, Machiavelli declares in D 1.20, is that they can solve the problem of hereditary succession that previous writers thought led to the cycle of regimes by electing an “infinite” number of virtuous princes. But, Machiavelli shows in D 1.16–18, elections are not sufficient to preserve the freedom of a republic, because elections will insure a succession of virtuous leaders only if virtuous individuals put themselves forward and the people vote for them.

Machiavelli reminds his readers that Rome solved the problem of succession by chance. Romulus’s successors were officially elected by the Senate, but a series of Tarquins threatened to make the kingship hereditary. Brutus took the opportunity afforded by the rape of Lucretia by the king’s son (an “accident” [D 3.5] that Machiavelli does not even mention here) to found or, perhaps we should say, to reorder the republic by getting the people to swear that they would never consent to the reign of a king in Rome, and assigning the king’s major function of commanding the army to two consuls elected annually by the Senate. He also eliminated the partisan enemies of the government he had newly reordered by having his own sons publicly tried, condemned, and then killed for having schemed to reinstate a hereditary monarchy. Machiavelli has already reminded his readers in D 1.3 that after much turmoil the republic had to be reordered again in order to create the tribunes.


(B) THE DIFFICULTY OF PREVENTING OR REMEDYING CORRUPTION (D 1.16–18) Machiavelli has promised to show his readers how they can “imitate,” that is, intentionally and knowingly replicate, the results of chance events in Rome in modern Europe. Perhaps he was thinking of the recent failures of two different sets of republican leaders, led first by Savonarola and later by Soderini, to maintain free institutions in Florence after the French invasion dislodged the Medici. In any case, he begins his discussion of the difficulty but need for regular reorderings of republics by emphasizing the difficulties a people used to living under a prince faces “if by some accident it becomes free.”57 “Not knowing how to reason about either public defense or public offence” (that is, how to protect themselves from external aggressors or to provide for their own needs), such a people will quickly find themselves under a heavier yoke, if they or “the matter” is corrupt. “A corrupt city that lives under a prince can never be turned into a free one, even if that prince is eliminated along with all his line,” he explains in D 1.17. “One prince must eliminate the other; and without the creation of a new lord it never settles down, unless indeed the goodness of one individual, together with virtue, keeps it free. But such freedom will last [only] as long as the life of that one, as happened in Syracuse with Dion and Timoleon” (47). In sum, when a city used to living under a prince accidentally becomes free, it faces not merely the problems Romulus confronted in founding a republic, but the additional problems posed by its “civilized,” peaceful experience. Ironically, the more successful a government is in making its people obedient to the laws, the more it makes them vulnerable to becoming subject to a tyrant or despot. A republic or a free way of life is more difficult to establish and maintain than a principality or despotism.

As in his depiction of the four founders in P 6, so Machiavelli has argued in the Discourses with regard to Romulus (D 1.9) and now Brutus (D 1.17), the founder of a republic must be a single individual or “prince” who eliminates the opposition by means of an “extraordinary” use of force. As in P 6, so Machiavelli emphasizes here, any prince who wants to establish (or reestablish) a free state will have the partisans of the old as enemies, who will need to be suppressed by force. But where the entirely new prince could count on the support, be it lukewarm, of the people who were oppressed by, and the nobles who were dissatisfied with, the previous government, Machiavelli now points out, the founder of a free government will not have any partisans. The first reason is that under a free government, honors and rewards are distributed honestly and openly for stated causes, so the individuals who receive such honors and rewards believe that they deserve them and do not feel obligated to anyone else. The second reason is that few people recognize the common utility of a free way of life, which consists in “being able to enjoy one’s things freely, without any suspicion, not fearing for the honor of wives and that of children, or being afraid for oneself” (45), until it is lost. As Machiavelli states more directly in FH 4.1, people tend to confuse liberty with license, i.e., the absence of rule altogether; but where there is no government, he shows in all of his writings, there is no security.58

Explicitly addressing princes “who have become tyrants over their fatherlands” (46), Machiavelli informs them that they must first “remedy these inconveniences” by killing “the sons of Brutus,” who now include all those who think they would benefit more from the hereditary kingdom that has been replaced than from the new order. But he then advises (as he advised all princes in The Prince) that if they wish to maintain their rule, they should seek to make the people friendly. They should “examine what the people desires,” and they “will always find that it desires two things: first, to be avenged against those who are the cause that it is servile; and second, to recover its freedom.” Using the tyrant Clearchus’s butchering of the aristocrats of Heraclea to make the same point he illustrated with Cesare’s display of the quartered body of Remirro de Orco in P 7, Machiavelli observes that the people take great satisfaction in seeing those they have feared violently eliminated. Since it is not possible for a prince entirely to satisfy the people’s desire to recover their freedom without relinquishing his own rule, Machiavelli instructs him to inquire further into the causes of that desire. These are of two distinct kinds (corresponding to the two “humors” to be found in every republic). A few (forty to fifty) will wish to command. But as Machiavelli also showed with the example of Cesare Borgia, such ambitious individuals can be either eliminated or “bought off” by “having them share in so many honors . . . that they have to be in good part content.” For most people, as Machiavelli argued in P 19, it is enough to live secure. They will be satisfied by a prince who establishes orders like those of the kingdom of France, in which the people see that the king himself is bound by “infinite laws in which the security of all its peoples is included” (46), excepting only his command of the army and public funds. Machiavelli thus indicates in passing how close the mixed republic he is advocating on the Roman model is to a “well-ordered kingdom.”59

A prudent, public-spirited prince is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the founding or reordering of a republic. The people or “matter” must not be corrupt; and they become corrupted very easily if their “heads” are. Machiavelli thus judges “that it was necessary either that the kings be extinguished in Rome or that Rome in a very short time become weak and of no value. For considering how much corruption those kings had come to, if two or three such had followed in succession, and the corruption that was in them had begun to spread through the members, as soon as the members had been corrupted it would have been impossible ever to reform it” (47).

To remind his readers that the problem is not limited to Rome, Machiavelli provides two modern examples—Milan and Naples—of cities that “no accident . . . could ever make free, because their members are all corrupt” (48). By pointing specifically to the experience of Milan after the death of Filippo Visconti, Machiavelli indicates that one sign of corruption is lack of arms among the people. After the Milanese were freed from the tyranny of Visconti, they were forced to accept the mercenary captain Francesco Sforza as duke as the price of his defending them from the Venetians with his troops.60 As Machiavelli’s preferred Roman example demonstrates, however, an armed people is not sufficient to forestall corruption. The western legions were not filled with mercenaries when Caesar crossed the Rubicon and marched on Rome in order to become king in everything but name. The people did not understand how the Senate protected their liberties but flocked instead to follow a popular leader, Marius, who promised to destroy the power of the patricians.

By observing that “orders and laws made in a republic at its birth, when men were good, are no longer to the purpose later, when they have become wicked” (49), Machiavelli indicates that the “corruption” he has in mind is not moral in the ordinary sense.61 He has already argued that Romulus demonstrated his virtù by murdering his brother in order to take sole command and impose order on the unruly Romans. He has also suggested that the civilizing arts of peace used by the “weak” prince, Numa, who made the Romans peaceful and obedient by means of religion, also created conditions under which they would have become corrupt, had their kings not become so obviously corrupt first. Corruption is something that happens to previously civilized human beings; it is not, strictly speaking, by nature, although it happens to civilized people if no steps are taken to prevent it.

Like virtù, Machiavelli gives corruption (corrozione) an unconventional, specifically political rather than moral meaning. But virtù and corruption are not simply opposites, as Machiavelli uses the terms. He describes the virtù of individuals, and attributes “goodness” (bontà) to peoples. (The use of “civic virtue” to describe the characteristics Machiavelli urges republican leaders to instill in their people is thus inaccurate and misleading.)62 By corrupt or corruption Machiavelli consistently refers to the loss of the ability and willingness of people to defend themselves from oppression, either internal or external. As he indicates here with regard to the early Roman kings, individual rulers and their government can also become corrupt. They become corrupt when they do not do what is necessary to maintain their dominion: arming their subjects to defend the province from foreign aggression, and securing the lives and property of their people, not only by enforcing the law, but also by obeying it themselves.63

Instead of explaining exactly what he means by corruption or its causes, however, in D 1.18 Machiavelli describes its results. “In Rome,” he explains, “there was the order of the government, or truly of the state, and afterward the laws, which together with the magistrates restrained the citizens. The order of the state was the authority of the people, of the Senate, of the tribunes, of the consuls” along with “the mode of soliciting and creating the magistrates; and the mode of making the laws” (49). Because these orders (of the complete or perfect republic, as Machiavelli characterized it at the end of D 1.2) were not changed as the citizens little by little became corrupt, the laws they adopted to check that corruption, e.g., prohibiting adultery or excessive displays of luxury, did not work.

“To keep men good,” Machiavelli argues, it would have been necessary to change the orders, as becomes clear if one examines the ways in which the Romans selected their magistrates and made laws. “The Roman people did not give the consulate and the other first ranks of the city except to those that asked for it.” This order was good so long as only men who would have been shamed by rejection and thus strove to be deserving of the honor put themselves forward. But “this mode later became very pernicious in the corrupt city,” because “those who had more power asked for the magistracies, and the impotent, even though virtuous, abstained from asking for them out of fear.” The Romans began to suffer this “inconvenience not at a stroke but by degrees, as happens with all other inconveniences; for after the Romans had subdued Africa and Asia and had reduced almost all Greece to obedience, they became secure in their freedom, as it did not appear to them that they had any more enemies who ought to give them fear.” When the Roman people began to feel secure and lost their fear, they no longer bestowed the consulate on men of virtue, but gave it “to those who knew better how to entertain men than those who knew better how to conquer enemies.” And later “they descended to giving it to those who had more power; so through the defect in such an order, the good remained altogether excluded.” The same degeneration was to be seen in the legislative process. Departing from actual Roman practice, Machiavelli claims that “a tribune, or any other citizen whatever, could propose a law to the people, on which every citizen was able to speak . . . before it was decided. This was a good order when the citizens were good,” because it led to a full discussion of what policy would be most in the public interest, so that the people could choose. But after the citizens had become bad, “only the powerful propose[d] laws, not for the common freedom but for their own power; and for fear of them nobody [spoke] against them. So the people came to be either deceived or forced to decide its own ruin” (50–51).64

As Machiavelli describes it, the Roman people became corrupt when they no longer feared external enemies and so no longer joined together in the common defense. They cravenly succumbed to the rule of the most powerful citizens instead of rising up to support virtuous leaders who opposed those who sought to foster their own interests rather than protecting the freedom of all. In both its corrupt and its uncorrupt condition the people were moved by fear. The difference was in what they feared and consequently how they responded to it.

The desire of the people not to be oppressed could be called a desire not to be dominated or “non-domination,” as it has been characterized by Quentin Skinner and Philip Pettit. But the liberty Machiavelli believes can be enjoyed only by a noncorrupt people is not achieved, as Skinner maintains, simply by laws that “force us out of our habitual patterns of self-interested behavior, to force us into discharging the full range of our civic duties.”65 On the contrary, Machiavelli suggests here, these laws depend for their effectiveness on the people’s perception of what is in their interest, as individuals first and then as citizens who are protected by the community.66 When the people become “corrupt,” that is, when they no longer perceive how the leadership of the best and serving in the army themselves is in their own interest, the laws that mandate service or forbid excessive luxury and other more obvious kinds of corruption no longer work. Pace Skinner, people don’t simply forget the way in which the government serves their private interests; their perception of what is in their interest depends to a great extent on the circumstances.67 The paradox and problem is that the laws intended to foster virtue and prevent corruption cease to work as a result of the success of the government or state in providing the security people seek. Once people feel secure, they want to be flattered or entertained. Powerful and wealthy individuals seek more, and they eventually terrorize those with less into complying with their desires and withdrawing from public life and service entirely.

Because the people of a republic gradually become corrupt as a result of the success of their government in securing their lives and property, measures have to be taken to counteract that corruption, either gradually as it occurs, or all at once, when the corruption becomes so obvious that it can no longer be endured. But both responses appear to be almost impossible. Individuals able to see the pernicious long-term effects of the current orders rarely arise in cities; and when they do, they find it difficult to persuade others to act on their insights, both because the problem is not yet evident, and because “men used to living in one mode do not wish to vary it.”68 However, it is equally difficult to remedy the problem when it becomes evident. “It is not enough to use ordinary modes, since the ordinary modes are bad; but it is necessary to go to the extraordinary, such as violence and arms, and before everything else become prince of that city, able to dispose it in one’s own mode.” Machiavelli sadly concludes that “because the reordering of a city for a political way of life presupposes a good man, and becoming prince of a republic by violence presupposes a bad man, one will find that it very rarely happens that someone good wishes to become prince by bad ways, even though his end be good, and that someone wicked, having become prince, wishes to work well” (51). Difficult as it is to see how and why the founder of a republic like Romulus would cut off the succession of his own family, it appears to be even more difficult to see how a republic once founded will not eventually degenerate back into a principality.69


(C) THE NEED TO ARM AND TRAIN THE PEOPLE INSTEAD OF RELYING ON THE FEW BEST (D 1.21–24) Returning to the example of Rome, Machiavelli emphasizes how fortunate that city was to have Tullus succeed Numa. “For when he succeeded to the kingdom, Tullus did not find a man who had ever been in war, since Rome had been at peace for forty years.” Because he was a prudent man, when he planned to wage war, Tullus did not recruit experienced soldiers from nearby cities, but “so much was his virtue that in a stroke . . . he was able to make very excellent soldiers” out of his own men. He thus forestalled if he did not reverse the corruption of the Roman people, for a time, by making them capable of defending themselves. In other words, Tullus showed how a corrupt people can be reformed by a good man with good intentions who trains them to fight in their own defense.

Whether a people becomes corrupt or not depends upon the virtue of their prince. “It is more true than any other truth that if where there are men there are no soldiers, it arises through a defect of the prince and not through any other defect, either of the site or of nature” (55).70

Tullus was not prudent in all respects, however. On the contrary, Machiavelli argues in D 1.22, when he agreed with Mettius, the Alban king, to let the fate of their respective peoples rest on the outcome of a battle between three champions of each, and then allowed the victorious Horatius to escape punishment for killing his sister, Tullus made three egregious errors. First, as Machiavelli explains at more length in D 1.23, Tullus risked both his own fortune as ruler and the freedom of his city by using only a small part of his forces to defend them. Second, as Machiavelli explains in D 1.24, “in a well-ordered city, faults are never paid for with merits.” Victorious young soldiers or generals should not be allowed to violate the law, because they set bad examples for others. The exoneration of Horatius provides Machiavelli with an example of the people’s too great compassion and gratitude—a tendency he tries to correct in the lessons he derives from the Roman experience in the second half of book 1. Third, “policies are never wise if one should or can doubt their observance” (56). The Alban king had agreed to become Rome’s subject, if the three Roman Horatii defeated the three Alban Curiatii; however, because he retained most of his army, Mettius used the first opportunity to try to regain his and his people’s freedom from Roman rule.

Machiavelli’s account of Tullus’s errors points to the conclusion that the early Roman republic was not well ordered, because it relied on a few aristocrats instead of the armed people as a whole to defend it. It endangered its own future freedom by allowing a victorious soldier to escape punishment for his crime under the law, and so encouraging the insolence of others, as well as by counting on the word or faith of another king. Adding that “the guarding of passes is often harmful,” because a general puts his entire army or city at risk by necessarily relying on a few men to block an advancing enemy at a mountain pass, Machiavelli ties the importance of relying on one’s full force or population (namely, the people) to the principle he announced in the first chapter. A founder should rely not on nature, whether of a site or of the human beings in question, but on laws that mandate military training—to defend his city.71


(D) WHY GRADUAL REFORM IS BETTER THAN REVOLUTION AND REDISTRIBUTION (D 1.25–27) A succession of prudent leaders who train their citizens to be soldiers is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the preservation of a republic. Because the people become corrupt as a result of their “civilization,” republics need to be reordered, either gradually or all at once. When Machiavelli returns to discuss the two basic modes of reform in D 1.25–27, however, he modifies his descriptions of the two modes in important ways.

Rather than emphasizing the difficulty a reformer faces in persuading people unable to perceive the dangers of their current practices in the long run to change, in D 1. 25 he advises a reformer who wants his innovations to be accepted and maintained by all to conceal the changes he is making in the old order by keeping offices with the same names or external trappings.72 As in P 18, Machiavelli reminds his readers that “the generality of men feed on what appears as much as on what is; indeed, many times they are moved more by things that appear than by things that are” (60). And he cautions would-be reformers that “this should be observed by all those who wish to suppress an ancient way of life in a city and to turn it to a new and free way of life.” Since, as he observed in P 2, “the new things alter the minds of men, you should contrive that those alternations retain as much of the ancient as possible,” lest the people come to expect ever new innovations that will destabilize the new order the reformer wishes to introduce.

When he concludes more generally that he “who wishes to order a political way of life by the way either of republic or of kingdom” (61) should proceed in this fashion, Machiavelli not merely addresses the ambitions of his young readers. He also reminds us readers that he, too, is presenting his “new modes and orders” in the guise of an “imitation” of ancient orders of the Romans. The version of the “mixed regime” he is advocating makes republics closer to moderate kingdoms than the Romans, who hated the name of king, would have understood.

Machiavelli contrasts this covert, gradual way of reordering a republic in order to preserve it to the way in which someone who wishes to seize and maintain the absolute power the “authors” called tyranny should proceed. By destroying all the old orders and making everything anew, such a prince makes everything—names, authorities, offices, wealth, cities, residences—depend upon him, as “did David when he became king” (61). Shockingly, the only time Machiavelli quotes from the Bible in the Discourses, he inaccurately attributes what Mary says of God in the Gospel of Luke to the king of the Jews. The point of the inaccurate attribution seems to be that any human being who seeks to exercise the omnipotence of the biblical God, even in the guise of a good shepherd who seeks to relieve the misery of the poor and establish a just regime by vanquishing the wealthy (or “great”), will become a tyrant.73 By treating his subjects, in effect, as animals—a different species to be herded (and harvested)—such a prince uses “modes” that “are very cruel, and enemies to every way of life, not only Christian but human” (61).74 Machiavelli concludes, therefore, that “any man should flee [these means], and wish to live in private [like Machiavelli himself] rather than as king.” He thus seems to be accepting a version of the Socratic argument in the Gorgias that it is better to suffer injustice than to do it and that a man who goes into politics in an effort to protect himself, his family, or his people from unjust rulers will end up becoming like them. However, when Machiavelli discusses individual decisions later in the Discourses (3.2), again in the context of a consideration of Brutus, the founder of the Roman republic, he argues that withdrawal into private life is not an option, because other people will not leave you alone. Recognizing that his young readers have political ambition, here he simply observes, “he who does not wish to take this first way of the good must enter into the evil one if he wishes to maintain himself.” The problem is that “men take certain middle ways that are very harmful, for they do not know how to be either altogether wicked, or altogether good” (62), as he will show in the next chapter. It might look as if Machiavelli is telling his readers (e.g., those to whom he dedicated his Discourses) that if they wish to take part in politics, they must avoid “middle ways” and adopt extreme measures. However, careful analysis of the examples Machiavelli gives in D 1.27 does not support that conclusion.

Machiavelli acknowledges in the title that “Men Very Rarely Know How to Be Altogether Wicked or Altogether Good.” For example, he points out that even though Giovampagolo Baglioni, the tyrant of Perugia, had slept with his own sister and killed his cousins and nephews in order to rule, he did not kill the pope when he had an opportunity to do so. Since Baglioni could not have been restrained by goodness or conscience or piety, prudent observers (who included Machiavelli himself) concluded “that it arose from men’s not knowing how to be honorably wicked or perfectly good” (62–63). To have been “honorably” (but not “altogether”) wicked, Machiavelli suggests, Baglioni should have been daring enough “to engage in an enterprise in which everyone would have admired his spirit and that would have left an eternal memory of himself as being the first who had demonstrated to the prelates how little is to be esteemed whoever lives and reigns as they do; and he would have done a thing whose greatness would have surpassed all infamy, every danger, that could have proceeded from it” (63).75

Machiavelli clearly exaggerates, however. Machiavelli’s Florentine readers would surely have remembered that Savonarola had incurred the wrath of Alexander VI by leveling just such charges against the Church. In The Prince Machiavelli argues that Savonarola failed to destroy the corruption in the Roman Church because he was an “unarmed prophet.” Baglioni had the mercenary arms of a small tyrant, but it does not seem likely that he could have destroyed the institution that Machiavelli has argued kept Italy disunited and vulnerable by, in effect, cutting off its head(s). Would “everyone have admired his spirit”? Or would the Orsini and the Colonna as well as the kings of Spain and France not have taken the opportunity to defend the sanctity of the Church by using their armies to retake the cities previously controlled by the Church, which would now be headed by a set of cardinals and a pope chosen by the victor?

Moreover, Baglioni is not Machiavelli’s only example in this chapter of a man who did not know how to be altogether wicked or altogether good. The official representative of the prince of peace on earth, Pope Julius II, led his own armies (as Machiavelli will argue in the immediate sequel, a prince should). The pope’s army might or might not be considered a wicked means of achieving good; but his use of a tyrant (Baglioni) and his mercenaries to rid another city of its tyrant certainly appears to involve a contradiction between means and ends. In D 1.27 Machiavelli suggests that the pope and his cardinals foolishly entered Perugia unarmed, because of Julius’s characteristic impetuosity (or perhaps because of his faith in a providential God who would protect him). Machiavelli does not report the fact (known to him as the diplomatic representative of the Florentine government at the time) that Julius had agreed not only to pay Baglioni and his men to serve in the pope’s campaign against Bologna, but also to protect Baglioni from the vengeance exiles from Perugia wished to take on him.76 Neither the pope nor the tyrant wanted to retire from public life, so both had to use evil means of maintaining themselves. A pope cannot exercise temporal power, Machiavelli suggests, without using evil means. If the prelates of the Church want to be entirely good, they must retire entirely into private life. A tyrant who wishes to maintain himself must use inhuman means, or if like all other human beings he cannot be entirely evil or entirely good, he should follow Machiavelli’s advice in The Prince, learn how to fight like a man with laws as well as like a beast with force and fraud, and seek popular support. The problem with the pope and the petty tyrant was not that they did not know how to be entirely good or entirely bad; neither is possible for a mere human being. The problem in the case of both Julius and Baglioni was that they took “certain middle ways that are very harmful” (62, emphasis added).77 In the succeeding chapters Machiavelli thus specifies other “middle ways” of balancing the people’s desire not to be ruled with the desire of the great to command and oppress that produce and sustain laws securing the liberty of all.78


C. Machiavelli’s New Politics of Suspicion and Competition (D 1.28–33)


As in P 15, so in D 1.27 Machiavelli suggests that a prince must learn how not to be good (which is not, however, the same as being “altogether wicked”) and use that knowledge when necessary if he wants to maintain himself. But in his Discourses Machiavelli adds that citizens of a republic must also learn not to be perfectly moral—in particular, they must learn not simply to be grateful for the services rendered by their leaders—if they want to retain their freedom.

Individuals who perform great deeds for the benefit of all deserve to be rewarded. Machiavelli thus begins D 1.29 by affirming that “when either a people or a prince has sent out one of its captains on an important expedition, from which the captain will have acquired very much glory if he should win, that prince or people is held to the bargain of rewarding him.” But then he qualifies this statement by arguing that a prince who dishonors or offends his captain out of avarice “makes an error that has no excuse” (64). However, if a prince or republic is ungrateful to a victorious captain because it suspects him of harboring ambitions to overthrow the existing regime, it acts on the basis of a political necessity.

“Because the nature of men is ambitious and suspicious and does not know how to set a limit to any fortune” (65), a victorious captain who has acquired a great reputation with his soldiers and the enemy may well conclude that he should rule instead of those who sent him to fight. “To avoid the necessity either of having to live with suspicion, or of being ungrateful,” Machiavelli urges (as he did in P 13), a prince should lead his own army. Then he will not have to worry about giving too much or too little credit to his captain or letting that captain attract his own partisans. Republics do not have the option of leading their own armies, however, and they may either offend those citizens they ought to reward or suspect those in whom they ought to have confidence. In corrupt republics, such suspicions may lead to great evils, “as happened to the Rome of Caesar, who took for himself by force what ingratitude denied him.” But “in a republic that is not corrupt [such suspicions] are the cause of great good and make it live free, since men are kept better and less ambitious longer through fear of punishment” (66).

Like the rewards (see D 1.24), however, the punishments can and should be moderate. The Romans were prudent enough not to threaten generals with terrifying punishments if they lost battles, because they might then becoming unwilling to fight. But they were punished if they sacrificed the common good (or victory) to considerations of their own glory (D 1.31).

Republics are less ungrateful than princes, because the people are less suspicious. But, Machiavelli warns, the people’s lack of suspicion may prove to be dangerous to their freedom. Indeed, Machiavelli suggests, the people’s relative lack of ingratitude is less a sign of their superior virtue or morality than a reflection of their lack of foresight. Like the Roman plebs, who celebrated the relief from the salt tax and payment for military service granted them by the Senate (D 1.32), people tend to react positively to immediate benefits and to discount or even ignore the future costs. As a result, in republics individual citizens are often allowed to gather more strength than they should. Men naturally seem to favor the beginnings of things, so when a youth of extraordinary virtue arises, citizens honor him without perceiving the potential danger. They recognize their error only after the threat has become too strong to be eliminated by means of direct opposition. The Roman republic avoided this problem as long as it did because it put the whole city to work in war. “So many virtuous men emerged . . . that the people did not have cause to fear any one of them, since they were very many and guarded one another” (D 1.30; 68).

Machiavelli shows, however, that the Roman people did not understand how competition among the great for power and influence benefited them. Nor, he suggests, did the Roman nobles always perceive that competition for office was the best way to guard themselves as well as the people from the tyranny of a popular hero like Caesar. In the remainder of book 1 he thus treats Rome not as a simply exemplary regime, but as an ongoing experiment in republican rule from which later generations can learn.


D. Successful and Unsuccessful Roman Reorderings (D 1.34–45)


Although Machiavelli initially suggests that the Roman republic was “perfect” after the tribunes were added to the consuls and Senate, he shows that all republics need to be continually reordered if they are not to become corrupt and lose their freedom. Neither “morals” legislation like sumptuary laws nor generalized suspicion (or envy) of the leaders of a republic suffices to counteract the fear of the rich and powerful that gradually develops. New “orders” or offices with the power of enforcing their decrees must continually be invented.

Machiavelli presents the creation of the “order” of the dictatorship in Rome as an example of a beneficial reordering and then uses the history of the appointment and reappointment of the Decemvirs to illustrate typical mistakes made by both the plebs and the nobles. By noting his fellow citizens’ failure to understand how to delay or prevent Cosimo de Medici’s rise to power, in D 1.33 Machiavelli indicates that his recommendations with regard to good and bad reorderings have particular relevance to Florence (and thus to the immediate concerns of his dedicatees).


1. The Advantages of the Dictatorship (D 1.34)


Machiavelli begins his analysis of the dictatorship in D 1.34 by observing that some unknown “writer” condemned the creators of the office for having caused the later rise of tyranny in Rome, because Caesar held that office. But, Machiavelli objects, neither the name ‘dictator’ nor his absolute powers were the cause of the rise of tyranny later in Rome; the real cause was the prolongation of commands that enabled individuals to acquire great wealth and partisans. “While the dictator was appointed according to public orders, and not by his own authority, he always did good to the city” (74). A citizen cannot seize extraordinary authority for himself in a noncorrupt republic in which no one is very rich and has many partisans, because such powerful individuals no longer fear the laws, and they are so formidable that people will not freely vote for them. The creation of the office of the dictator was good, because it remedied one of the fundamental defects of republics in dealing with emergencies: because many people are involved in making decisions, republics proceed slowly. The appointment of a dictator, who could act without consultation or delay and punish without appeal, enabled the Romans to respond quickly to an urgent danger. Because the grant of absolute power was limited both in its goal or extent (to respond to the specific danger) and in time (six months), it did not diminish the power of the Senate or the people, who resumed their old authority at the end of the dictator’s term of office.

Machiavelli emphasizes how important it was that the powers of the dictatorship were both provided and restrained by the laws. As a result, no one acquired the habit of acting outside them. He also praises the Roman mode of choosing the dictator by putting the decision to appoint one as well as the selection of the particular individual into the hands of those (the consuls) who were most shamed by the need to do so. “For wounds and every other ill that a man does to himself spontaneously and by choice hurt much less than those that are done to you by someone else” (75). This sentence might be taken as a condensed statement of the reason Machiavelli argues that the people, who do not want to be oppressed or commanded, should be included in government, at least to the extent of electing their leaders and trying them for malfeasance when they do not perform their duties as they should.


2. The Necessity of Maintaining Rotation in Office (D 1.35–36)


Even though the Roman people freely voted for the Decemvirs, Machiavelli observes, the ten became tyrants, because they were granted absolute power for too long a period, and because the old orders—the tribunes, consuls, and Senate—were not kept in place. Republics like Sparta and Venice that granted some officials long-term authority made sure that there were “guards posted who made them unable to use their authority badly” (77).

Before he details and explains the sources of the mistakes made by the nobles, the people, and the leader of the Decemvirs, Appius Claudius, Machiavelli makes four general observations concerning the requirements (and difficulty) of maintaining a free government. The first is that those individuals who have held the highest offices in the republic be willing to serve in lesser capacities. Machiavelli might appear to be reviving Aristotle’s notion of a truly political way of life as ruling and being ruled in turn. Unlike Aristotle (Politics 1277b25–30), however, Machiavelli does not emphasize the need to rule in order to acquire the virtue of prudence. He stresses the value of the restraint experienced politicians exercise on the ambitions of youths elected to high office. Rotation in office is necessary, if a number of virtuous men are to check the potentially tyrannical ambitions of any one. And maintaining such a check on the rise of a potential tyrant requires a certain kind of humility (or the appearance of such) on the part of those who have held the highest public offices but then demonstrate their willingness to obey the orders of others.


3. Why Republics Cannot Be Reordered Effectively by Redistributing Property (D 1.37)


In D 1.37 Machiavelli then makes it clear that in order to maintain a republic it is necessary to check the excessive ambitions of the people as well as those of the “great.” He begins by appealing to the authority of “ancient writers” who explain the variability of human affairs by observing “that men are wont to worry in evil and to become bored with good.” He nevertheless seems to be stating his own convictions about the unavoidability of continuing conflict when he explains, “whenever engaging in combat through necessity is taken from men they engage in combat through ambition, which is so powerful in human breasts that it never abandons them at whatever rank they rise to. The cause is that nature has created men so that they are able to desire everything and are unable to attain everything. So, since the desire is always greater than the power of acquiring, the result is discontent with what one possesses.” And “since some men desire to have more, and some fear to lose what has been acquired, they come to enmities and to war, from which arise the ruin of one province and the exaltation of another” (78).

Machiavelli states his general understanding of the reasons human beings live in perpetual conflict with one another in order to make a specific point: “it was not enough for the Roman plebs to secure itself against the nobles by the creation of the tribunes, to which desire it was constrained by necessity.” As soon as the plebs had secured itself, it “began at once to engage in combat through ambition, and to wish to share honors and belongings with the nobility as the thing esteemed most by men.” Machiavelli thus shows that the two opposed and apparently mutually exclusive “humors” that exist in all cities actually form a kind of continuum. So long as people do not feel secure in their lives and properties, they wish simply not to be oppressed. However, as soon as they feel secure, they begin to desire to have more—not simply goods but also offices (or political honors and power). That is, they acquire the desire of the “great” to dominate others; and, Machiavelli argues, it was this desire on the part of the Roman people that led “to contention over the Agrarian law, which in the end was the cause of the destruction of the republic” (79).

Machiavelli seems to endorse the end or purpose of the Agrarian law when he writes that “well-ordered republics have to keep the public rich and their citizens poor.” There must have been some defect in the law—its origin, the delay in enforcing it, or its corruption by its later use. However, by concluding that it turned the city upside down every time it was mentioned, he suggests that it suffered from all three defects.

The two major provisions of the law limited the amount of land any one citizen could possess and mandated that the fields taken from enemies be divided among the Roman people. Both “offended” the nobles, who possessed more than they should and were deprived of the means of becoming even richer. However, the law was not enforced, despite many attempts to do so, because the nobles had “temporized with it, by leading an army out, or by having the tribune who proposed it opposed by another tribune, or by sometimes yielding to a part of it, or indeed by sending a colony to the place that had to be distributed” (79).79 After Roman conquests extended to and beyond the borders of Italy, the plebs no longer wanted their share of public lands far from Rome and hard to cultivate. When the Gracchi tried to revive the law, they thus found the power of their adversaries redoubled; and the hatred between the plebs and the Senate became so great that it led to armed conflict. Since the public magistrates could not settle the dispute, each of the parties had recourse to private remedies. “Thinking of how to make itself a head to defend it,” the plebs first gave reputation to Marius by making him consul four times, after which he was able to make himself consul three more times. The check posed by rotation in office was destroyed. The nobility responded by favoring Sulla in a similar fashion, and he won the civil war for them. But the conflict between these “humors” was revived later by Pompey, as leader of the nobility, and Caesar, as successor to Marius. With Caesar’s victory, Rome acquired her first tyrant and was never again a free city.

Machiavelli does not blame the plebs for having resisted the “ambition” of the nobles to acquire ever more property. On the contrary, he suggests, “if the contention over the Agrarian law took three hundred years to make Rome servile, it would perhaps have been led into servitude much sooner if the plebs had not always checked the ambition of the nobles, both with this law and with its other appetites.” He observes, moreover, “one also sees through this how much more men esteem property than honors. For the Roman nobility always yielded honors to the plebs without extraordinary scandals, but when it came to property, so great was its obstinacy in defending it that the plebs had recourse to the extraordinary [means] that were discoursed of above to vent its appetite” (80).80 The Gracchi deserve praise more for their intention than for their prudence, he concludes, because one should not try to take away a disorder that has grown in a republic by reviving a law that has fallen into disuse. Just as he advised those who opposed the rise of a virtuous young man favored by the people to “temporize,” if they were not able to remedy the problem entirely, so Machiavelli now suggests that popular leaders concerned about increasing economic inequality in a republic should “temporize” with it. Outright opposition would do nothing but accelerate the downfall of the republic by arousing the nobles’ fear of loss.

In D 1.26 Machiavelli suggested that a “new prince” who wished “to make the rich poor” and “the poor rich” would have to be an inhuman tyrant like Philip of Macedon, who “transferred men from province to province as herdsmen transfer their herds” (61). Recognizing that human beings are acquisitive animals, who seek ever more possessions in order to secure themselves, he uses the commotion over the Agrarian law to show that property owners will violently resist redistributive policies. Attempts to impose large-scale redistribution will, as in Rome, lead to civil war, which will, in turn, produce chaos and then tyranny or leave the city so weakened that it falls prey to foreign conquest.81


4. Why Previous Efforts to Reorder Republics Have Generally Failed (D 1.38–39)


If it is not possible for a republic to prevent the emergence of a tyrant directly, either by opposing the rise to power of a popular leader or by seeking to avoid the corruption that follows from great economic inequality by imposing a redistribution of property, the question arises: how can a republic be reordered so as to avoid becoming corrupt? In D 1.38 Machiavelli suggests that modern republics show themselves to be weaker and more irresolute than the Romans, because they do not understand how to accept and present a “necessity” as their own choice.82 And in D 1.39 Machiavelli suggests that the “necessity” peoples both ancient and modern do not recognize is the need for government. They tend to see their government as the source of their problems and to blame the individual magistrates, because they do not understand the deeper, more general causes of their afflictions.

The people of Florence blamed the magistracy of the Ten of War for the heavy taxes incurred to support an unsuccessful attempt to regain the parts of their empire they had lost, rather than blame the “ambition” of their enemies. Likewise, Machiavelli observes, the plebs in Rome blamed the consuls and the ambition of the nobles for wars that continually arose, rather than the ambition of its neighbors. But in this case, Machiavelli suggests, his fellow citizens learned more quickly than the Romans. Seeing not merely that the war did not stop after they dissolved the Committee of Ten, but that the disorder got worse in the absence of prudent leadership, the Florentines remade the magistracy. Demonstrating the tendency of people in general to mistake names for things, the Roman plebs was not content until the consular name was eliminated and tribunes drawn from and responsible to the people were given consular powers. They did not understand that they were still granting a select group of men great power, or that it was necessary that they do so.

In D 1.40 Machiavelli explains more generally that the Roman attempt to reorder the republic by having the Decemvirs codify their laws resulted in a tyranny “for the same causes that the greater part of tyrannies in cities arises: . . . from too great a desire of the people to be free and from too great a desire of the nobles to command. When they do not agree to make a law in favor of freedom, but one of the parties jumps to favor one individual, then it is that tyranny emerges at once” (88).83


5. What Is to Be Learned from the Fall of the Decemvirs (D 1.40–45)


In showing the reasons not only why the Decemvirate became a tyranny, but also why it collapsed, in D 1.40–45 Machiavelli traces the mistakes of the people, the nobles, and the leader of the Ten, Appius Claudius, all back to their desire to acquire the power of government solely for themselves by denying any part to their opponents.84 The nobles and the people of Rome agreed to create the Ten and to grant them unlimited power because the people wanted to eliminate the consular name (and powers of the nobles holding the office), whereas the nobles wanted to eliminate the tribunate. The people erred in voting to grant the Ten absolute power without maintaining the constitutional checks on the dictatorship because they wanted to eliminate one if not both of the old orders controlled by the nobles. They did not understand that “although nobles may desire to tyrannize, that part of the nobility that finds itself outside the tyranny is always an enemy to the tyrant; nor can he ever win over all of it, because of the great ambition and great avarice that are in it” (88). The very desires that make the people fear the nobles make the nobles the best check on a popular potential tyrant.

Although they limited the term and the goal for which they granted the power, the people were fooled into voting the Ten a second year of unchecked power by the Decemvirs’ restrained use of that power during their first term and their leader Appius’s obvious attempts to seek popular favor. Deceived by his abrupt change of face from an arrogant aristocrat to a man of the people and by the good behavior of the Decemvirs during their first term of office, the people were surprised by the violence Appius and his colleagues began to use against them after the Ten were voted a second year of unchecked power. Recognizing their error, the people pleaded with the nobles to reinstate the old orders—but to no avail.

The nobles were suspicious of Appius’s changed behavior, but they did not know how to counter his ambitions any better than the plebs. Assuming that he would follow aristocratic norms that forbade a man from nominating himself for office, they gave him authority to propose names of individuals to be elected to the people; and he seized the opportunity to nominate himself first. Gratified by the oppressive measures Appius began taking against the people during the second year of the Decemvirate, the nobles did not respond to the people’s plea that they reinstitute the old orders. Nor when the Ten were forced to reconvene the Senate to order an army to defend the city did the senators take the opportunity to eliminate the Decemvirate. They hoped that if the Ten resigned voluntarily, the tribunate might not be remade. Only after the dispirited Roman armies were defeated in the field, and the plebs protested Appius’s attempt to take Virginia by force by going to the Sacred Mount outside the city, were the senators forced to see that a city without a people was no city. At that point they agreed to reinstate the older orders.

Because both the people and the nobles were blinded by their desire to eliminate the offices held by the other “humor,” Machiavelli concludes in D 1.41, Appius would have succeeded in becoming tyrant of Rome far before Caesar, if he had not revealed his animosity toward the people so soon after his reelection.
