As Machiavelli observed in P 21, “those tyrants who have the collectivity as a friend and the great as an enemy are more secure, because their violence is sustained by greater force than that of those who have the people for an enemy and the nobility for a friend” (88–89). In D 1.42 Machiavelli observes that Appius’s ability to transform his colleague Quintus Fabius from a good man into a criminal by giving him a share of the profits shows how easily human beings can be corrupted. Rather than relying on good upbringing or education, he suggests, legislators of republics and kingdoms ought to check human appetites by making it impossible for them to err with impunity. Appius was driven out by popular dissatisfaction. Although the Roman armies retained the same virtue they had before and after the Decemvirate, Machiavelli notes in D 1.43, they would not fight for a tyrant with the same spirit as when they fought as free persons. However, he also shows in D 1.44 that “a multitude without a head is useless.” Although Virginius appointed twenty military tribunes to negotiate with the Senate, the spokesmen for the plebs had to be advised by the two senators with whom they met not to state their desire for vengeance openly, but merely to request the reinstitution of the constitutional orders that would enable them to do what they wished.85 The history of the Decemvirate should have taught republican leaders the importance of maintaining legal checks on the abuse of power by officials. Yet, Machiavelli reports in D 1.45, Virginius wanted to deny Appius the right of appeal to the people that Appius had denied to others. Later in Florence, Machiavelli reminds his readers, Savonarola also lost most of his reputation when he failed to complain about the nonenforcement of a law he had made allowing citizens to appeal sentences given by the Eight and the Signoria before the people. If people see that the government is not bound by its own laws, they will not feel that their lives and property are secure, and they will become more audacious in thinking about how they can improve their condition.


E. The Lessons Machiavelli Derives from Roman History about the Best Internal Order of a Republic (D 1.46–60)


Machiavelli summarizes the lessons about the internal ordering of a republic he has derived from reading history for his young aristocratic Florentine readers at the end of book 1.


1. The Ever-Escalating Ambition of Men Cannot Entirely Be Restrained by Competitive Elections (D 1.46–48)


He begins D 1.46 by restating the source of the problem: “Men Ascend from One Ambition to Another; First One Seeks Not to Be Offended, and Then One Offends Others.” Although he has shown that such ambition animates the people as well as the “great” (and that the two “humors” thus exist along a continuous spectrum), Machiavelli reminds his readers that the rise of a virtuous young man to preeminence constitutes the greatest immediate threat to maintaining a free way of life.

To check the rise of such a potential tyrant, other politically ambitious men should compete with him for popular favor. The most obvious way to institute such competition is to select the highest officials by means of elections. In D 1.47 and 1.48 Machiavelli thus assures his aristocratic readers that the people are able to judge the character of particular individuals (even if they are often deceived about generalities like names). Members of the upper class can make it easy for the people to judge individual candidates correctly, moreover, by arranging to have a vile man run against an excellent one or vice versa.86


2. The Need for Reforms and Popular Trials to Supplement Competitive Elections (D 1.49)


Rome constitutes the exemplary republic, Machiavelli reminds his readers in D 1.49, not because Rome had a legislator like Lycurgus who provided for all its needs from the beginning, but because the Romans continually created new orders to meet pressing needs. However, as he showed in analyzing the failure of the Decemvirs, so he now observes with regard to the later creation of the censors, the Romans made mistakes. For example, they initially gave the censors too long a term of office, and when a dictator prudently corrected that error, the censors retaliated by denying him membership in the Senate. Because history does not show that the dictator was able to defend himself, Machiavelli concludes, either the history or the orders of Rome were defective. He thus reminds his readers that the recommendations he makes rest on his reasoning about what is to be found in the histories; he is not simply relating what happened or urging his readers to imitate everything the Romans did.

Machiavelli indicates the applicability of his analysis to his own city by observing that the Florentine republic freely voted to give a few citizens expansive authority to reform it many times. However, they never succeeded in creating orders for the common utility, because they (like the plebs and the nobles with the Decemvirs) always used their authority for the benefit of their party.87 In well-ordered republics, Machiavelli argues, decisions in capital trials should be given to the people (unless an emergency makes such an appeal impossible, in which case the Romans appointed a temporary dictator). The badly ordered Florentine republic initially put decisions in capital cases in the hands of a foreigner, who could easily be corrupted by powerful citizens, as could the eight citizens to whom the Florentines later transferred the power. Recognizing that ten citizens might not be enough to punish the powerful, even if they had the authority, the better-ordered Venetians made their largest council able to punish citizens who were accused.


3. No One Should Be Able to Bring Government to a Standstill (D 1.50)


If government is necessary to check the desires of both the people and the great, as Machiavelli’s history of the Decemvirate illustrates, in a well-ordered republic no official should be able to bring the government to a standstill. In D 1.50 he thus reports that in Rome, when two consuls agreed on nothing but their refusal to appoint a dictator, the Senate obtained the help of the tribunes in forcing them to do so (and so illustrated the “utility” of the plebian tribunes as checks on the aristocratic consuls). In Venice, which Machiavelli again uses as an example of a well-ordered modern republic, they passed a law that forbade an official to leave office until a substitute or successor was in place.


4. The “Great” Must Demonstrate Their Willingness to Sacrifice for the Common Good in Order to Be Elected (D 1.51)


In D 1.51 Machiavelli seems to repeat a lesson he gave in D 1.32 about the desirability of making a show of doing through liberality what a republic or prince is constrained to do by necessity; but the example of the Senate’s prudence and generosity he uses here makes an important addition to his earlier advice. When the Senate voted to pay men a stipend to serve in the army, so that they could fight longer wars further away from home, the tribunes objected that the plebs would be paying their own stipends through higher taxes. But the senators deflected the criticism by seeing that the nobility paid the heaviest and greatest taxes first. If the nobles want the people to elect them, Machiavelli reminds his aristocratic readers, they must demonstrate their own willingness to sacrifice for the sake of the common good.


5. The Education of “Aristocrats” Will Not Curb Their Ambition (D 1.52)


People tend not to recognize the threat to the state represented by popular leaders such as Cosimo de’ Medici or Caesar until they have become too powerful to eliminate. In D 1.33 Machiavelli thus suggested that it was better to “temporize” with such individuals in the hope that they would make an error or that the evil would at least be deferred. But in D 1.52 he suggests that the nobility can prevent such an individual from acquiring too much power by competing with him for popular favor. That Machiavelli is not advising his readers merely to “fight fire with fire” becomes clear from his two negative examples. He concedes that a politician like Piero Soderini, who rose to power by favoring the collectivity, could not use the tactics of his enemies against them, if like the Medici his adversaries tried to unseat him by secretly buying influence with others. If it became known that he had secretly tried to “benefit” (or buy off) his enemies, his reputation with the people would suffer. (As Machiavelli suggested in D 1.7, Soderini should have tried to institute a popular court before which he could defend himself from his calumniators or accuse them of treason.) Nor, Machiavelli urges, should the nobles count on a good upbringing or education to restrain the ambition of others. The nobles misjudged Appius when they gave him the power to nominate the Decemvirs. Likewise, Cicero misjudged Octavian when he sent him against Mark Anthony, believing that the name of Caesar would attract Anthony’s soldiers away from him. The people have a tendency to mistake names for things, but Cicero was mistaken in thinking that Octavian would adhere to the aristocrats rather than seek to increase his own power by allying with another popular figure.88 As Machiavelli pointed out in D 1.42, young nobles are easily and quickly corrupted by sharing in the “profits” of tyranny.


6. Why Popular Government Is Best (D 1.53–60)


a. The People Are Not Always Wise (D 1.53–54)


Reminding his readers of how “many times the people desires its own ruin, deceived by a false appearance of good, and that great hopes and mighty promises easily move it,” in D 1.53 Machiavelli again shows that he does not recommend referring final decisions to the people because he thinks that the people are always good or wise judges. On the contrary, he observes that the people almost always support a policy that appears to represent a gain, even though there is a loss concealed underneath, and that they will favor a spirited rather than an apparently cowardly or cautious endeavor. In D 1.4 Machiavelli quoted Cicero, who claimed that, though ignorant, the people could be persuaded of the truth by a good man. Here Machiavelli maintains merely that their respect for old and esteemed citizens can be used to persuade the people to exercise some restraint. (The modern example of the exercise of such influence he gives in D 1.54 is a bishop, suggesting that the Christian religion can be used in some of the same ways the Romans used theirs.) However, he warns leaders against arousing the people’s enthusiasm for daring but potentially ruinous enterprises by reminding them that, presupposing victory, the people will blame the leader for their losses, without taking any responsibility themselves for having elected the leader and supporting his policies. A prudent leader will recognize popular proclivities and try to enlist or withstand them when appropriate. He may be forced to let the people have their way and see the disastrous results, so long as he can avoid responsibility for the calamity.


b. Nor Are the People Entirely Good (D 1.55)


The title of D 1.55 suggests that Machiavelli thinks that things can be done easily in cities where the multitude is not corrupt, and that the extent of economic inequality determines whether a principality or a republic can be founded. But the three examples he gives of the relative “goodness” (bontà) or corruption of various nations both complicate and expand the options available to someone who knows how cities can be reordered. The first, the Senate’s decision to ask the plebs to give back a tenth of the booty they took from the Veientes to redeem Camillus’s vow to Apollo, may literally show “how much the Senate trusted in the goodness” of the plebs. However, in reporting that the plebs openly and indignantly refused, Machiavelli indicates just “how much goodness and how much religion were in that people, and how much good was to be hoped from it” (110). Their goodness was not so much as to make them give up the spoils, but only to resist openly and without fraud. (Indeed, Machiavelli indicates that the “honesty” of the people is largely a product of their number, which makes it impossible for them to act as a body in secret.)89 In his second, negative example of the corrupt provinces in his time, Machiavelli explains that there are fewer disorders in France and Spain than there are in Italy, not because the people are better, but because these nations have a king to maintain their unity. Even in his last, best example of the Germans who pay tithes without supervision, he observes that if each individual did not contribute the required amount, the fraud would be recognized and another mode of collection adopted. In all three examples, the “goodness” of the people is not spontaneous or inherent, but depends on the people’s belief (or lack thereof) that the government will force them to contribute what they do not give voluntarily.

Machiavelli furthers the impression that the goodness of a people is not an inherent quality so much as a product of its external conditions when he explains that there are two reasons that the Germans are less corrupt than the Italians, French, or Spanish. First, they do not have a lot of commerce with their neighbors and are content with home-grown goods. But second and more important, the German republics are not corrupt because they do not have any “gentlemen” who live idly on the returns from their possessions and from castles command subjects who obey them. The kind of inequality that makes it impossible to establish a republic, readers thus see, is not merely economic; it is political and military. As Machiavelli observed in P 12, there is no proportion between the armed and the unarmed. Anyone who wants to reorder such a province will have to use force to deprive the “gentlemen” of their ability to resist the prince and oppress their fellows.

External conditions might seem to determine what kind of government can be established in any given place. However, Machiavelli now affirms that “a prudent man having knowledge of the ancient civilizations” (like Machiavelli) would know what to do to make a republic from a province suited to be a kingdom or kingdom from a province suited to be a republic. Just as Machiavelli argued that it was the prince’s fault if there were no soldiers, so he now suggests that the goodness or corruption of a people depends on whether they have a man who possesses the knowledge and daring to do what is necessary to order and reorder them.


c. Claims to Divinely Inspired Knowledge Are Not Necessary (D 1.56)


In The Prince and Discourses Machiavelli claims to possess the knowledge needed to found and reorder both principalities and republics. But in D 1.56 he somewhat fancifully tells his readers he does not have the knowledge of the “signs” of future events of the kind both the ancient augurers and Friar Girolamo Savonarola claimed to possess. He is not prophesying or predicting the future; he is using his knowledge of the world to show what can and cannot be done.


d. The Power of the Multitude Is Transitory and Thus Limited (D 1.57)


Establishing the sort of republic he is recommending does not require even the pretense of supernatural knowledge. As Machiavelli indicates in D 1.57, however, it does require understanding “the nature of a multitude.” Peoples tend to become violent when they are deprived of their freedom or their (deposed) prince is still alive. But, Machiavelli observes, “when the spirits of men are cooled a little and each sees he has to return to his home, they begin to doubt themselves and to think of their safety, either by taking flight or by coming to accord” (115), unless they have a “head” or “heads” to keep them united.90 Anyone who wishes to reorder a province must prepare himself to withstand the first onslaught of popular resistance; but if he has a stronghold that enables him to escape the first thrust, he will survive it.


e. Nevertheless, the People Are Wiser and More Stable Than Princes (D 1.58)


In D 1.58 Machiavelli nevertheless announces that he disagrees with all previous writers, including his apparent authority Livy, who maintain that “nothing is more vain and inconstant than the multitude” (115). On the contrary, Machiavelli argues, a multitude unshackled by laws is no worse than a prince without legal restraint. Indeed, he proceeds to argue that a people restrained by laws rules better than a prince or king so constrained. That is, of course, the effective meaning of his preference for republics over principalities. In this chapter Machiavelli spells out his reasons.

Princes and peoples do not differ in nature; “it is in one mode in all” (117). The difference is that the people have more respect for the law (because, as Machiavelli reminded his readers in the previous chapter, they are individually weaker and more fearful). In D 1.29 he argued that peoples tend to be less ungrateful than princes, because people see outstanding generals and legislators to be public servants, rather than competitors, as does a prince. Machiavelli nevertheless suggested that popular gratitude might not be prudent, because popular leaders can become tyrants. Here he insists that the people are not only less ungrateful, but also more prudent, more stable, and have better judgment for five reasons. First he points to the effects of widespread opinion, which shapes human action and might thus be said to predict the future (better perhaps than the “signs” that appear to have done so only after the fact). Widespread opinion is so powerful, he notes, that “the voice of a people may be likened to that of God” (117). Second, Machiavelli observes that people can judge a dispute between two equally good orators as well as, if not better than, a prince. They, too, can listen to reason, and a large number of people cannot be swayed as easily by personal ties or passions as a single ruler. Third, he argues not merely (as he did in D 1.47) that the multitude can judge the character of individual candidates for office, but that they do so better than princes, because, unlike some princes, they will not select obvious scoundrels. Fourth, he observes that widespread popular opinions tend to be long-lasting and so stable. But, beyond all this, Machiavelli emphasizes, the fact that cities ruled by peoples grow more rapidly than those ruled by princes shows that governments of the people are better. Like the “vulgar” (P 18), Machiavelli judges things and people by their effects or outcomes.

Affirming that “the multitude is wiser and more constant than a prince,” Machiavelli acknowledges that the reforms or reorderings necessary to maintain a republic have to be the work of a single man or mind. But, he urges, “if princes are superior to peoples in ordering laws, forming civil lives, and ordering new statutes and orders, peoples are so much superior in maintaining things ordered that . . . they attain the glory of those who order them” (118).91 What Machiavelli seems to have in mind is that the people—be they Athenians, Romans, or French—become more famous than any of the individuals who serve or rule them (if for no other reason than that the people reproduce themselves and thus last longer).92

Machiavelli concludes this chapter by making it clear (as he did not at the beginning of the book in his initial comparison of Rome with Sparta) that he does not judge the excellence of different governments merely or even primarily by their longevity. On the contrary, he observes “that the states of princes have lasted very long, the states of republics have lasted very long, and both have had need of being regulated by the laws. For a prince who can do what he wishes is crazy; a people that can do what it wishes is not wise” (118). Nevertheless, he repeats his judgment that a people regulated by laws has more virtue than a prince so regulated, and peoples unconstrained by laws make fewer errors than unconstrained princes. Reversing the traditional view that popular rule rests ultimately on the force of the largest number, Machiavelli suggests that popular rule is superior to princely rule because popular rule is, in effect, the rule of public opinion and thus depends upon persuasion rather than force. A good man can convince a licentious and tumultuous people to return to a good way by speaking to them, but a wicked prince can be checked only by steel. What is feared in the rule of a multitude unconstrained by law is not the present instability or violence of the people ruling, but the future possibility that a tyrant will arise from it. That evil is already present in the rule of a wicked prince. Popular rule can be violent, but “the cruelties of the multitude are against whoever they fear will seize the common good; those of a prince are against whoever he fears will seize his own good” (119). The people are not less selfish by nature than their leaders; but, Machiavelli reminds his readers, there are many more of them, and the good of the multitude is thus a closer approximation of the common good than the good of any individual. The fact that all the writers before him have spoken ill of the multitude ironically provides evidence for the gentle character of their rule, based on neither fear nor force. “The opinion against peoples arises because everyone speaks ill of peoples without fear and freely, even while they reign,” but “princes are always spoken of with a thousand fears and a thousand hesitations” (119).


f. Popular Governments Keep Faith Better Than Princes (D 1.59)


In D 1.59, Machiavelli underlines the fact that the reason he is arguing in favor of popularly based rule is not that he thinks that the people are morally superior to princes. There he observes that republics and princes are apt not to abide by their agreements or keep “faith” for basically the same reasons: if the accord was coerced, or if compliance threatens the existence of the state. In other words, popular governments are not any more honest or grateful for past benefits than princes. They do not break their agreements as quickly or easily as princes, and so tend to abide by their agreements longer, because a number of people take longer to come to a decision and cannot keep that decision secret so well as a sole ruler.


g. Popular Government Gives Everyone an Incentive to Work for the Benefit of All (D 1.60)


The real advantage of a popularly based republic, Machiavelli concludes in D 1.60, is that by making all citizens eligible to be elected to the highest offices, without regard to age or “blood” (i.e., family), a republic like Rome obtains the advantage of individual virtue, wherever it is to be found. Moreover, it gives each and every citizen an incentive to work for the community in order to gain glory for himself.


Conclusion of Book 1


By the end of book 1 it should be clear that Machiavelli is not advocating the establishment of an aristocratic republic of the kind praised by Aristotle and Cicero. The education he seeks to give his two young readers, who “deserve to be princes,” does not consist in habituation or training in controlling their own fears and desires so that they will be able to control people without the benefit of such an education by means of law. He is trying to show them how to establish and maintain a new kind of republic by designing institutions and laws that will make the conflicting desires of the two humors to be found in every city work for the benefit of (almost) everyone.93

If his readers have an opportunity to reorder their city as a republic, Machiavelli urges them to allow all citizens to be eligible for the highest offices, and to have those offices filled by popular elections. Not only are the people able—at least most of the time—to distinguish good from bad candidates, especially if the politically active class takes care to make the contrast between the candidates clear.94 Such electoral laws also make individual citizens compete in order to gain glory for themselves by serving the republic.

Republican reformers should also make sure that capital crimes—especially those involving charges of treason—are tried publicly by a large jury, so that the people remain confident that individuals in high office have to obey the law or suffer punishment just the way the people do. Machiavelli thus advises “princes” to establish courts to enable the people to check the nobles (P 19) and to show that they themselves are bound by an “infinite” number of laws (D 1.16).

Despite his revolutionary declaration that “the multitude is wiser and more constant than a prince,” Machiavelli has no illusions about the ability of peoples to govern themselves directly. He is not a democrat of this kind.95 On the contrary, he declares that “a multitude without a head is useless” (D 1.44). Leaderless mobs can act spontaneously with frightful ferocity, but they cannot maintain any sustained action or policy. The people’s desire to take vengeance on those who have oppressed them also blinds them to the need to maintain legal forms and procedures. Nor can a people devise or undertake the innovations necessary to maintain republican liberty. Because there are more of them and their desire to avoid oppression approximates the general interest in maintaining liberty, Machiavelli nevertheless argues against all previous “writers” that the people are rightly the final judges of their princes and the policies they propose. The people suffer and thus know the outcomes, even if they do not always understand the causes.


Outline of Book 2: Why Modern Italians Should Learn from, but Not Simply Imitate, Ancient Rome in the Conduct of Foreign Affairs

2. Machiavelli’s Fervent Appeal to the Young to Complete His Project (D 2.Pref.)

3. The Romans Did Not Understand the Causes of Their Own Success (D 2.1)

b. The Pernicious Effects of a “Cowardly” Interpretation of Christianity

2. The “Second-Best,” Tuscan Alternative (D 2.4)

2. Acquiring “Partners” by Fraud as Well as by Force (D 2.9–15)

b. Well-Trained Men Are Needed in Addition to Artillery (D 2.17)

2. Germany Does Not Provide an Alternative Model (D 2.19)

G. On the Use of Knowledge, Discretion, and Glory (D 2.33)


Book 2: Why Modern Italians Should Learn from, but Not Simply Imitate, Ancient Rome in the Conduct of Foreign Affairs


In book 1 Machiavelli showed that the internal orders of the Roman republic were closely tied to her expansionary foreign policy. First, he argued that the Roman plebs obtained a part of their government and so “perfected” the republic by refusing to fight in the armies unless they were granted some offices and, eventually, made eligible to hold all. Then he suggested that the Roman people remained uncorrupt so long and only so long as they feared foreign attacks and were, therefore, willing to defend the republic. Both the internal and the external liberty of Rome thus required that her people remain armed. It would not be possible for his contemporaries to “imitate” the domestic orders of the Roman republic, therefore, if they did not “imitate” expansionary Roman foreign policy by mustering and training an army of local inhabitants. But as Machiavelli reminds his readers at the beginning of the Art of War when Cosimo Rucellai restates the reasons his grandfather and other aristocratic Florentines did not think it was possible (or prudent) for them to try to imitate the Romans, arming the plebs was what the ottimati most feared. (That was the reason they had opposed Machiavelli’s own attempts to form a Florentine militia.) In book 2 Machiavelli thus seeks to convince his aristocratic young readers that it will be not merely safe but absolutely necessary to arm the people, if they want to refound a free Florentine republic. At the same time he clearly indicates that the rearming and refounding he is recommending do not constitute a mere imitation.


A. How Machiavelli Gradually Departs from the Roman Model While Praising It (D 2.Pref.–2.2)


1. The Past Is Often Erroneously Praised (D 2.Pref.)


Machiavelli begins book 2 of the Discourses by criticizing the prejudice in favor of the ancients to which he appealed at the beginning of book 1. Our knowledge of ancient times is imperfect, he reminds his readers; writers about past events tend to extol the virtues of the victors and to conceal their faults. Fear and envy lead contemporary observers to criticize their peers and to elevate their predecessors. All praise of the past and criticism of the present is not invalid, however; “since human things are always in motion” (123), people in a given place are either ascending or descending. Because he deems “the world always to have been in the same mode,” Machiavelli thinks that there is always “as much good as wicked in it” (124), but the locus of each shifts from time to time and place to place. In ancient times virtue could be seen in a series of empires—first in Assyria, then in Media and Persia, and finally in Greece and Rome—but after the fall of Rome it has been scattered among “the kingdom of the Franks, the kingdom of the Turks, that of the sultan, and the peoples of Germany” (124). The peoples of these nations deserve to be praised for their virtue, but “whoever is born in Italy and in Greece and has not become either an ultramontane in Italy or a Turk in Greece has reason to blame his times and to praise the others” (124).

Even if people had complete knowledge of the past, Machiavelli acknowledges, they would still tend to blame the present and praise the past, because their judgments change as they age. “Since men when they get old lack force and grow in judgment and prudence, it is necessary that those things that appear to them endurable and good during youth turn out unendurable and bad when they get old.” More generally, he observes, “human appetites are insatiable, for since from nature they have the ability . . . to desire all things and from fortune the ability to achieve few of them, there continually results from this a discontent in human minds and a disgust with the things they possess.” As a result, they “blame the present times, praise the past, and desire the future, even if they are not moved to do this by any reasonable cause.” Nevertheless, he concludes, the difference between the virtue of the Romans and the vice now reigning in Italy is so manifest that he can continue to dramatize the contrast “so that the spirits of youths who may read these writings . . . can flee the latter and prepare themselves to imitate the former at whatever time fortune may give them opportunity” (124).


2. Machiavelli’s Fervent Appeal to the Young to Complete His Project (D 2.Pref.)


In the preface to book 2 Machiavelli thus reminds his readers, as he did in the preface to book 1, that he is addressing youths he hopes will carry out a project he himself could not, because of the “malignity” of his own fortune. The connection between Machiavelli’s advice to his young readers to “imitate the Romans” particularly with regard to their military orders in book 2 and his own political career is especially close. The policy he recommended to his oligarchic superiors when he served as secretary to the Florentine republic was that they “imitate the Romans” by mustering and training a militia (or army) composed of citizens and subjects. He gives princes similar advice about the importance of relying on one’s own arms (or people) rather than mercenaries and auxiliaries in both The Prince and the Art of War and promises that the Italian prince who organizes and leads his own army will conquer the province. In urging his young Florentine readers to imitate the expansionary policy of the Roman republic in his Discourses, however, Machiavelli emphasizes the importance of depending not solely on conquering their neighbors but on forming an alliance or league with them. And if imitating the Roman conquest of the world seems too difficult (as it might well seem to citizens of a city without its own army and in need of hiring mercenary forces), he urges them to follow the example of their Etruscan forebears who formed a defensive league of 12–14 cities. Such a league would combine sufficient territory and troops to defend Tuscany from the invasions Italy was currently suffering from the French, Spanish, and Germans.96 However, it would take such a large number of cities a good deal of time to make any decision and each member would gain little from any addition to the league beyond the number and size necessary for defending it. As a result, such a league would not have the destructive effects of Roman conquests outside of Italy, conquests that eventually led to the destruction of liberty everywhere, including Rome itself.97


3. The Romans Did Not Understand the Causes of Their Own Success (D 2.1)


As in P 25, so in the second book of the Discourses, Machiavelli urges his contemporaries to rely on their virtù by arming themselves rather than leaving their fate to fortuna (or God). In using the example of the Roman republic to support the policies he recommends, Machiavelli thus finds it necessary to disagree with the ancient historians upon whose writings he is purportedly relying. Both Plutarch and Livy show that the Romans attributed their success in acquiring empire to their good fortune as well as to their own virtue. To maintain that his contemporaries can imitate the Romans’ success, Machiavelli has to prove that both the historians’ and the Romans’ understanding of the reasons for that success is wrong. If the Romans had identified the sources of their success correctly, Machiavelli’s contemporaries could imitate Roman modes of waging war, but they could not expect necessarily or predictably to share the same “fortune,” because they, unlike the Romans, did not worship “Fortuna” as a god and consequently could not expect her to reward them. As at the beginning of book 1 he thus implicitly raises the question of whether the change from pagan to Christian religion makes the imitation of the Romans he is explicitly advocating impossible.

Machiavelli demonstrates the way in which he thinks his contemporaries can learn from reading ancient histories by disagreeing with both Plutarch and Livy about the causes of the events they relate. According to these historians, it was the Romans’ good fortune not to have to wage two major wars at one time. In fact, Machiavelli argues, it was not a matter of mere chance. There are reasons that can be recaptured by later observers. Once a people acquires a reputation by fighting and defeating its nearest neighbors, other peoples and princes become afraid to assault it. As a result, the Romans or any other people in a similar situation are able to choose which wars to fight, when, and how. Other nations remain sitting on the sidelines, partly out of respect for the aggressor’s power and partly because they are deceived by assurances they receive from the warring nation (and their own illusory hopes of avoiding conflict). Instead of helping the victims, these more distant nations conclude that the present war does not concern them. They discover their error only after the victorious power, made stronger by its conquests, attacks them.


4. Roman Expansion Destroyed Freedom Everywhere (D 2.2)


The Romans not merely failed to understand the causes of their own success. In D 2.2 Machiavelli acknowledges that Rome’s success in acquiring empire was not unambiguously good.

In the guise of praising Roman virtue for its success in overcoming the obstinate resistance of many free peoples, Machiavelli reminds his readers that Roman expansion destroyed freedom everywhere, including Rome itself. In P 5 he maintained that a people who has enjoyed freedom never forgets its ancient orders (and thus always retains a reason to rebel), unless that people is broken up and dispersed. But here he observes that at his time “there is only one province that can be said to have free cities in it” (129), although in ancient times there were many; and the cause is “that the Roman Empire, with its arms and its greatness, eliminated all republics and all civil ways of life” (132).


a. Machiavelli’s Praise of the Free Way of Life


This observation provides Machiavelli with the occasion for giving his most extensive praise of a free way of life (and the reasons he prefers republics to principalities). He observed earlier that free cities expand much more and more rapidly than principalities, but here he gives the reasons: “it is not the particular good but the common good that makes cities great. And without doubt this common good is not observed if not in republics, since everything is done for that purpose.” Equating the “common good” with the good of the greatest number, Machiavelli concedes that “it may turn out to harm this or that private individual,” but “those for whom the aforesaid does good are so many that they can go ahead with it against the disposition of the few crushed by it” (130, translation slightly altered). If a single ruler makes conquests, whether he be a prince or a tyrant, he will use them to benefit himself. He will not seek to share the power or wealth with the city as a whole, or even the nobles, because he will not want to give any, much less many, of his subjects the ability or ambition to rebel against his rule.

Perceiving the close connection between the preservation of the republic and their own lives and liberties, the people of a free city not only fight fiercely to preserve it from foreign domination. They also work to improve their own lot domestically.

All towns and provinces that live freely . . . make very great profits. For larger peoples are seen there, because marriages are freer and more desirable to men since each willingly procreates those children he believes he can nourish. He does not fear that his patrimony will be taken away, and he knows not only that they are born free and not slaves, but that they can, through their virtue, become princes. Riches are seen to multiply there in larger number, both those that come from agriculture and those that come from the arts. For each willingly multiplies that thing and seeks to acquire those goods he believes he can enjoy once acquired. From which it arises that men in rivalry think of private and public advantages, and both the one and the other come to grow marvelously (132).98


In light of the great advantages of a free way of life, readers cannot but ask why so few republics emerged in Europe after the fall of the Roman empire. In D 1.16 Machiavelli observed that the advantages of a free way of life are usually not appreciated until they are lost. But he shows here that he and others are fully aware of the advantages they have lost. The reason those advantages have been lost, he now explains, is the difference between “our education,” which is to say, “our religion,” and that of the ancients.


b. The Pernicious Effects of a “Cowardly” Interpretation of Christianity


Although Machiavelli affirms that our religion has “shown the truth and the true way,” he also observes that it has made men esteem the honor of the world less. “Ancient religion did not beatify men if they were not full of worldly glory, as were captains of armies and princes of republics. Our religion has glorified humble and contemplative more than active men. It has then placed the highest good in humility, abjectness, and contempt of things human; the other placed it in greatness of spirit, strength of body, and all other things capable of making men very strong.”99 The only form of strength encouraged by our religion is the ability to endure suffering. “This mode of life thus seems to have rendered the world weak and given it in prey to criminal men, who can manage it securely, seeing that the collectivity of men, so as to go to paradise, think more of enduring their beatings than of avenging them.” However, Machiavelli concludes, “although the world appears to be made effeminate and heaven disarmed, it arises without doubt more from the cowardice of the men who have interpreted our religion according to idleness and not according to virtue. For if they considered how it permits us the exaltation and defense of the fatherland, they would see that it wishes us to love and honor it and to prepare ourselves to be such that we can defend it” (131, emphases added).

Machiavelli thus reminds his readers of what would appear to be the chief reason his contemporaries did not think that it was possible to imitate the Romans: they are Christians, whereas the citizens of the Roman republic were pagans. But he assures such readers that the elevation of humility and contemplation in place of more worldly virtues results from a “cowardly” interpretation of their religion. In P 12 and D 1.12, he suggested that such a “cowardly” interpretation has been promoted by priests and monks because they are unarmed.100 Machiavelli does not spell out what interpretation of Christianity would permit the exaltation and defense of the fatherland, but his observation that among the places where virtue was scattered after the fall of the Roman empire are the kingdom of the Franks and Germany today supports his claim that Christian beliefs are not simply incompatible with good arms.


B. Different Modes of Republican Expansion (D 2.3–4)


Rather than seeking to spell out the new form of education that would reawaken a love of freedom as based on a new interpretation of “our religion,” Machiavelli turns to the immediate cause of the destruction of liberty in the West, Roman expansion. The question that fact raises is: how is it possible to gain the advantages of Roman foreign and military policies without destroying the liberty they were intended to secure? Machiavelli suggests that his Florentine contemporaries should seek to command a “partnership” with other Italian cities the way Rome did before it began conquering kingdoms beyond the Italian peninsula or, if that seems too difficult, to follow the example of their Etruscan ancestors and form a defensive league in Tuscany.101


1. The Roman Example (D 2.3–4)


Machiavelli first explains, “Rome became a great city through ruining the surrounding cities and easily admitting foreigners to its honors.” As in contrasting Rome with Sparta at the beginning of book 1, he emphasizes the importance of a city’s acquiring a large population if it wants to expand. But now he explains that Rome did so in two ways: It opened its gates to people fleeing from other cities (in contrast to Sparta, which tried to minimize, if not entirely forbid, any form of commerce with foreigners). It also forced the inhabitants of nearby cities it had decided to eliminate to move to Rome. In D 2.4, however, Machiavelli makes it clear that Rome did not expand its power in Italy solely or even primarily through conquest. After it fought and conquered other Italian cities, it came to terms with them. These cities agreed to provide Rome with a certain amount of land to support the colonies it established to guard its conquests and to follow its command in future wars, so that it remained the seat of the empire, but they continued to live under their own laws. This alliance or league-like arrangement persisted until the Romans “began to go out of Italy with their armies, to reduce kingdoms to provinces, and to get subjects who did not care about being subjects since they were accustomed to living under kings and who did not acknowledge a superior other than Rome since they had Roman governors and had been conquered by armies with the Roman title.” By fighting with Rome in the wars it waged outside of Italy, its partners “came to subjugate themselves by their own labors and blood without perceiving it. . . . [They] found themselves in a stroke encircled by Roman subjects and crushed by a very big city. . . . And when they perceived the deception under which they had lived, they were not in time to remedy it” (136).


2. The “Second Best,” Tuscan Alternative (D 2.4)


There are three ways for a republic to expand, Machiavelli explains. Like the twelve members of the ancient Etruscan league, a city can form a league with other cities to provide for their common defense. This kind of league is less effective as a means of expansion than the Roman mode of retaining command and deceiving its allies about their equal partnership. Only a limited number of cities can join together to make common decisions, and they are not able to move quickly or decisively because of the time it takes a number of people to agree on a common policy. The members of such a league do not have much incentive to expand beyond the number of cities needed to defend their current territory, moreover, because all gains have to be divided equally among the members, so no one city can expect to profit much from another conquest. Even though very little is known about the ancient Etruscan league, Machiavelli argues, it represents a better mode of expansion than the expensive and not very long-lasting attempts of cities like Sparta and Athens to make their allies into subjects.102 So if his Florentine readers deem it too difficult to follow the Roman model, he concludes, imitating “the ancient Tuscans should not seem so, especially to present Tuscans” (138).

As Machiavelli indicates in the remainder of book 2, the formation of a league would have represented a big improvement on Florence’s historical efforts to acquire an empire by conquering its neighbors (e.g., Pisa and Lucca) and ruling them as subjects, the way Sparta and Athens treated their “allies.” If Florence had succeeded in forming a new Tuscan league, it might have constituted a defensive union capable of withstanding the French and Spanish armies that had recently invaded Italy at the pope’s behest, even if the new Tuscan league did not extend to the entire Italian peninsula. The internally imposed limitations on the expansion of a league might be considered an advantage, moreover; so long as Rome did not conquer provinces outside of Italy, its “partners” continued to live free insofar as they continued to rule themselves according to their own laws. Rome’s expansion led to the loss of freedom for Rome as well as for her partners.103 A league or confederation thus appears to be the way republics can provide themselves with an effective defense, without falling prey to either the internal corruption that infects a people who no longer fears external aggression or conquest by a foreign power.104


C. Why Christianity May No Longer Make Imitation of the Romans Impossible (D 2.5)


Because the model of a league provided by the Etruscans was forgotten, in an apparent digression Machiavelli inquires into the reasons human memory does not extend back more than five thousand years. His discussions of the two ways in which human memories are destroyed point, however, to a way or ways to eliminate one of the major obstacles to the unification and defense of Italy.

Machiavelli observes that the diverse causes of the elimination of memories of past times are either human or from heaven (but, we should note, in neither case divine).105 The example Machiavelli gives of the first, the variation of sects and languages brought about by changes in religion, appears to be strangely inapt. Early Christian fathers like Saint Gregory did try to destroy all memories of ancient theology by “burning the works of the poets and historians, ruining images, and spoiling every other thing that might convey some sign of antiquity.” One reason Machiavelli suggests they did not succeed entirely was, ironically, that they had to retain the Latin language in order to write the law suppressing all other forms of religion. (Machiavelli thus suggests in passing that changes of “sects” or religions require political support and enforcement.) Machiavelli had to have known that the new “law” brought by Jesus was formulated in contrast to the old Hebraic law, and that the Gospel containing that law was written in Greek, not Latin. As Machiavelli also knew from reading Livy (whose history is thought to have been among the books Gregory burned), the Romans did not try to destroy the religion or the language of the Etruscans. The attempt to ban if not destroy all other religions rather than absorb their gods and worship was peculiar to Judaism and its Christian offshoot. As he reminds his readers in D 2.8, it was associated with particularly deadly wars, because one sect tried to replace the other (and the people who adhered to it) completely. The point of Machiavelli’s erroneous discussion of the human causes of the loss of memory thus seems to be his concluding observation that “these sects vary two or three times in five or six thousand years” (139). If so, Machiavelli would be suggesting, as he did in D 1.12, that the Christian religion might soon be coming to an end, because the obvious corruption of the priests was making it difficult for people to believe in them or their creed.

Causes coming from heaven that eliminate the human race and reduce the inhabitants of part of the world to a few who either do not know what has occurred before or fabricate stories they want others to believe include famines, plagues, and floods. Examples of such phenomena and their effects are to be found in the Bible, but Machiavelli treats them as natural phenomena in which he believes, because “the histories are full of them, because this effect of the oblivion of things is seen, and because it seems reasonable that it should be so” (140). Again he treats the “histories” as sources of events or effects, but relies on his own reason, rather than any authority, in determining the causes.

By suggesting that nature purges the world in these ways of excess population and the evils that go with it, Machiavelli again points to a connection between the reasons human beings do not possess complete knowledge of the past and the wars they fight. Later, in D 2.8, he reminds his readers that the most dangerous and destructive wars are not fought, like those of the Romans, primarily from ambition, intentionally or by choice. These wars are fought by peoples forced to leave their homelands because of natural disasters like famines or wars, who have to try to displace the current inhabitants of another province. And having brought the human and heavenly causes of destruction together as possible sources of the most complete destruction of earlier civilizations, he cites “Moses and the peoples who seized the Roman Empire” (144) as examples. He thus obliquely refers to the replacement of both by Christians in describing the ways in which these peoples not only displaced and destroyed all the past inhabitants, but also changed the names of places (along with the language spoken and the religion). However, such devastating wars can be avoided. At the end of the chapter Machiavelli observes that there have not been any such invasions for the last five hundred years: partly because so many people fled the cold poor regions of Scythia during the decline of the Roman Empire; partly because Germany and Hungary, from which such peoples also came, have improved their country and so do not feel the same need; and partly because very great movements by the Tartars are contained by the Hungarians and Poles, “who often glorify themselves, saying that if it were not for their arms, Italy and the church would have often felt the weight of the Tartar armies” (145). In other words, Machiavelli suggests that the human race is not doomed to live through repeated cycles of generation and destruction, as many ancient philosophers argued. Nor is our knowledge or “memory” necessarily limited to or by such inevitable cycles. On the contrary, we have more control over our fate if we understand the forces—human and natural (which are, as he indicated also partly human)—at work.

Machiavelli knew that many of his contemporaries feared an invasion by the Turks, who had fought Venetian fleets in the Mediterranean, sacked the coast of Italy, and were moving into Hungary.106 If successful, such an invasion would probably have resulted in the replacement of the Christian “sect” by another. Alternatively, as Machiavelli’s friend Vettori suggested, fear of such an invasion might provoke a reform of the Papacy and a reinterpretation of the Christian religion that would unite not merely the Italians but all the nations of Christendom in defense of the fatherland.107

Machiavelli does not claim to foresee the future, but in this “digression” he does indicate ways in which he thought the weakening effects of a lazy interpretation of Christianity might be overcome.108 So long as the Romans retained their virtue, he emphasizes, they defeated the desperate peoples who invaded their lands. As in The Prince, so in the Discourses, Machiavelli insists on the power of human “arms” or agency to meet and overcome pure “fortuna” or chance. This power rests upon the use of human reason in analyzing the experiences, both historical and present, human beings have had. It is not complete, because our knowledge of the past is not complete. What knowledge we have nevertheless leads Machiavelli to conclude that there are observed regularities in nature, including human nature, that we can use in guiding human affairs (or, as he puts it in P 25, building dykes and dams to guide the potentially destructive floods of the river of fortune).


D. Why Modern Republics Should Adopt Roman Military Orders (D 2.6–18)


Because Machiavelli attributes the loss of ancient virtue to the difference between their education or religion and “ours” (D 2.2), some readers have taken most if not all of his discussion of the advantages of Roman military policy to refer metaphorically to the “spiritual warfare” he is waging against the cause of the loss of ancient virtue (and the reason, therefore, for the fall of Rome), i.e., Christianity.109 Machiavelli’s explanations of the reasons “it is not a prudent policy to make a friendship with a prince who has more reputation than force” (D 2.11) and how “often men deceive themselves believing that through humility they will conquer pride” (D 2.14) do seem to refer to Christian dogmas. (Josef Stalin infamously asked how many legions the pope had.) However, Machiavelli’s arguments concerning the foreign and military policies his contemporaries should adopt following the Roman model can also be read simply as corrections of historical Florentine policies that he details and criticizes much more fully in his Florentine Histories.

As Machiavelli reminds his readers in D 2.2, Florence did not try to follow the example of its Etruscan ancestors by forming a defensive league of cities in northern Italy. It periodically tried and failed to conquer its closest neighbors and relied on the support of the distant French king. After the aristocratic class was destroyed in one of the battles between the Guelfs (the Church party) and the Ghibellines (the allies of the emperor), the merchants who controlled the government of Florence came to rely almost entirely on mercenary captains and armies. Especially after the Ciompi rebellion, they were afraid of arming the poorer inhabitants of the city. As a result, Machiavelli shows in repeated cases, Florence survived not because of the virtue of her citizens or leaders, but primarily by chance.

Drawing a contrast with the disastrous history of Florence’s “going it alone,” in book 2 of the Discourses Machiavelli first insists on the advantages of forming a defensive league like the ancient Etruscans, if not the superior Roman mode of unifying its Italian confederates under its command and control. Since both forms of confederation require a city to have forces sufficient to compel its neighbors to come to terms, Machiavelli then turns to a discussion of the ways in which the Romans organized themselves to fight wars in more or less explicit contrast to Florence’s reliance on mercenaries and a foreign king.


1. Training Citizen Soldiers to Fight Short Wars for Minimal Rewards (D 2.6–8)


In an extremely abbreviated and simplified account of Rome’s expansion in Italy, Machiavelli maintains that the Romans mustered and trained large armies with which they could subdue nearby cities quickly and inexpensively.110 Even after they began paying soldiers salaries, so that their armies would be able to undertake more distant campaigns, he emphasizes, the Romans limited the salaries and booty with which they rewarded their troops. They also granted colonists small tracts of land, so that they could support further conquests with the fruits of their victories and did not have to burden the people with heavy taxes. As Machiavelli describes it, Roman military policy was thus the polar opposite of the use of mercenaries by Florence (and other Italian cities like Venice). These mercenaries had to be paid from the public treasury and thus required higher taxes, which aroused the opposition of the people to the wars and the leaders who led or proposed them.


2. Acquiring “Partners” by Fraud as well as by Force (D 2.9–15)


Roman armies were able to defeat three attacks by desperate French hordes, Machiavelli emphasizes, so long as the Romans retained their virtue (i.e., fought with their own arms and not with mercenaries). However, he acknowledges in D 2.9, they did become embroiled in wars they themselves did not want to fight “by chance” or the designs of hostile peoples. Rome was drawn into such wars because of the overestimation of their own strength by some of her allies or a desire on the part of others to start a war with Rome by attacking one of its allies. Forming a confederation or league with others is not sufficient to enable a nation to defend itself.

At the same time, Machiavelli shows that a nation may find itself able to expand its jurisdiction without conquest, if another nation gives itself freely as a subject to obtain its protection. Rome’s jurisdiction expanded when the Campanians (Capuans), recognizing that they were unable to defend themselves from the Samnites, freely gave themselves to the Romans as subjects, so that the Romans would feel obliged to defend them. In contrast to the Romans, who expanded their dominion as a result of the voluntary subjection of the Capuans, Machiavelli reminds his readers, the Florentines were forced to offer themselves as subjects to King Robert of Naples to get him to defend them, because they could not defend themselves. As a result, Florence fell prey to the rapacious tyranny of the duke of Athens. (See FH 2.24–26, 2.29–30, 2.33–37).

Machiavelli’s contention in D 2.10 that “gold is not sufficient to find good soldiers, but good soldiers are quite sufficient to find gold” (148) can be read as a summary condemnation of the Florentine merchants’ attempts to buy not only captains and troops, but also allies. The Florentines looked to the king of France both to defend them and to acquire other cities for them. In D 2.11 Machiavelli uses this policy to illustrate his admonition, “leagues that are made with princes who do not have either the occasion for aiding you because of the distance of their site, or the force to do it because of his own disorder or some other cause of his own, bring more fame than aid to those who trust in them” (150). And in D 2.12 he shows that there are advantages and disadvantages to be had by attacking other countries abroad or waiting to defend one’s own at home. However, he concludes, “either I have my country armed, as the Romans had or as the Swiss have, or I have it unarmed, as the Carthaginians had or as the king of France and the Italians have. In the latter case the enemy ought to be held at a distance from home; for, since your virtue is in money and not in men, whenever your way of getting it is impeded you are done for” (153). To rely on money and trade rather than an armed people is to be unarmed at home.

As Machiavelli reminds his young Florentine republican readers in D 2.13, however, force is rarely if ever enough; as in The Prince, he insists that it is necessary to be a “fox” as well as a “lion.” Indeed, he observes, some have been able to rise from a base to an elevated condition through fraud without force; but he also shows that fraud alone will not enable them to retain what they have acquired. Once again, he praises the way in which the Romans initially deceived the Latins and other neighboring peoples by pretending to make them “partners” (compagni), but using their arms to subdue others and gain reputation for themselves. But he now acknowledges in the incidents he cites from the Roman wars with the Latins in D 2.13–15 that Rome’s “partners” did not remain deceived until it conquered provinces outside of Italy. On the contrary, seeing how the Samnites were constrained to an accord after they were twice defeated by the Romans, the Latins perceived their own servility and rebelled. Although the Latins initially attacked Rome only indirectly by attacking one of its allies, and the Romans tried to placate the Latins by not declaring war on them, neither people believed that they could hide their hostile intentions for long. Both understood that their future would be decided on the battlefield.


3. Using Roman Military Orders (D 2.16–18)


Indeed, Machiavelli declares, “the most important battle ever waged by the Roman people in any war with any nation was that which it waged with the Latin peoples in the consulate of Torquatus and Decius” (160). Since the Latins became servile after they lost, he reasons, so the Romans would have become servile if they had not won. Titus Livy agrees with this judgment, Machiavelli suggests, because he makes the two armies alike in every respect—order, virtue, obstinacy, and number—except that the heads of the Roman army were more virtuous.


a. Maintaining Reserves to Fight Anew (D 2.16)


Rather than follow Livy by emphasizing the extraordinary sacrifices of the consuls, however, Machiavelli explains the way both the Latins and the Romans ordered their troops and the reasons they did so, because this is what his contemporaries need to understand. These ancient armies had three divisions. The astati in front were placed close together so that they could stand up to the enemy; but the principi behind them were more spread out, so that the astati could withdraw, if need be, into the ranks of the principi without disordering them. With fresh reinforcements, the merged lines could then renew the fight. The triari behind the principi were spread out even more sparsely, so that they could receive the first two lines, if they had to withdraw, and then renew the fight with fresh troops once more.111

Because they have abandoned these orders, Machiavelli observes, Christian armies at his time do not have the ability to recover and force an enemy to defeat them not once, but thrice. Unable to withstand any but the first push, these armies lose easily for a variety of reasons. Because their captains do not know how to order their troops so that the back lines can absorb the front, these armies become disordered if they need to withdraw, especially if the enemy forces the cavalry back into the infantry. Machiavelli concedes that some contemporary captains maintain a tripartite organization of their armies, but he objects that they use the distinctions among the vanguard, battalion, and rearguard merely for commanding them in their quarters. They thus “imitate” the Romans in external ways without understanding how their orders worked or the reasons for them.


b. Well-Trained Men Are Needed in Addition to Artillery (D 2.17)


His contemporaries try to excuse their ignorance by arguing that the introduction of artillery has made the use of ancient military orders impossible, so in D 2.17 Machiavelli disputes that opinion. His diminishing of the importance of artillery has been much criticized, but his critics seem to have missed Machiavelli’s generally sensible main points by concentrating on the details.112 The introduction of a new weapons technology does not make offensive expansionary wars (like those the Romans fought) impossible.113 On the contrary, those who wish to wage offensive wars are more apt to invent new means of doing so than those who wish merely to defend what they now possess. It is easier to attack with weapons that fly through the air, moreover, than to defend against them. The use of firearms may appear to make it more difficult for men to show their virtue than in ancient times, because much of the fighting is done at a distance. Nevertheless, personal courage and physical training are still required, because it continues to be almost impossible to take and hold territory without hand-to-hand fighting. Neither here nor in the Art of War does Machiavelli suggest that the introduction of artillery makes no difference. He admits that artillery is useful in an army when ancient virtue is mixed with it, but he denies that artillery or any other weapons technology can simply or completely substitute for virtue—training, experience, courage, and prudent leadership. To look solely to technology to provide for the common defense or to gain new territories is to hope to achieve with little expense and effort things that require a great deal of both.


c. To Rely on the Infantry Is to Rely on the People (D 2.18)


Machiavelli’s urging his contemporaries to follow the example of the Romans in relying more on the infantry than on the cavalry should be understood in its political context. In book 1 he showed that the plebs acquired their share of the government of the Roman republic only because they were armed and could frustrate the patricians’ desire to expand their holdings by refusing to fight. And he observed that the Roman people remained uncorrupt only so long as they perceived a need to defend the fatherland. Machiavelli knew from personal experience that the oligarchs who controlled the Florentine republic were afraid of arming the people. In arguing that infantry or armed men are a more fundamental and useful element in an army than cavalry, he thus emphasizes the superior flexibility (or malleability) of men that makes them more capable of being trained and controlled, and so more useful, than horses or combinations of horses and men.114 He also cites “the authority of those who give rules for civil things, where they show that at first wars began to be made with horse,” but after they were introduced, ordered infantries were quickly seen to be more useful.115 As with the artillery, he does not deny that cavalry has its uses. On the contrary, he affirms that horse are “necessary in armies to perform reconnaissances, to raid and prey upon countries, to follow enemies when they are in flight, and to be also in part an opposition to the horse of the adversaries.”116 But he insists, “the foundation and the sinew of the army . . . should be the infantry” (169).117


E. Why Modern Italian Republics Have Failed to Realize Their Imperial Ambitions (D 2.19–26)


Machiavelli traces the disastrous results of Italian politics to the erroneous opinions of their “heads.” As in The Prince, so in the Discourses he blames “the sins of the Italian princes that have made Italy servile toward foreigners” (169).


1. Failing to Follow the Roman Example (D 2.19)


Rather than arming themselves and their peoples, these princes have transferred military affairs into the hands of “captains of fortune,” who have chosen to employ a few horsemen, because they do not have the funds to pay a large number of infantrymen or subjects they can impress into service. The success of the ultramontane troops that have invaded Italy should have convinced Italian princes and republics “that all that is narrated about infantry in the histories is true,” and that “they ought to believe all the other ancient orders to be true and useful” (172). Explicitly joining domestic and foreign policy, Machiavelli urges, “republics and princes would . . . be stronger in opposing a thrust that might come against them . . . and those who have in their hands a civil way of life would know better how to direct it,” if they read Roman history as he has recast it.

They would believe that increasing the inhabitants of one’s city, getting partners and not subjects, sending colonies to guard countries that have been acquired, making capital out of booty, subduing the enemy with raids and battles and not with sieges, keeping the public rich and the private poor, and maintaining military exercises with the highest seriousness is the true way to make a republic great and to acquire empire. (173)


They would do what the Roman republic had done in effect to conquer Italy, and not continue to employ the expansionary policies of the Florentine and Venetian republics, which had not merely failed but bankrupted these modern republics.


2. Germany Does Not Provide an Alternative Model (D 2.19)


Because Roman expansion resulted in the loss of liberty everywhere but in Germany, Machiavelli recognizes, some of his readers might conclude that they ought to adopt the defensive policies of the German cities instead of the expansionary policies he has been advocating.118 So he first reminds them of the fundamental reason he argued that Rome constitutes a better model of republican government than Sparta: in a world in which everything is always changing, a city will contract and disappear if it does not seek constantly to expand. Second, and more specifically, he explains that the conditions that allow the German cities to retain their freedom are singular and cannot be duplicated elsewhere. Those conditions include the weakness of the Roman emperor, who officially rules the region. His weakness and consequent poverty enabled the cities initially under his control to buy their liberty by agreeing to make small annual payments to him. Others like the Swiss openly rebelled, and the emperor did not have sufficient forces to restrain them. Nor did he receive much assistance from the other princes in the region, because they were poor and envied his position. The region is thus divided into free cities and small principalities. They remain within their own walls and allow the emperor to adjudicate their differences, because they fear that if they try to expand, they will encounter and be defeated by the Swiss.

Machiavelli’s readers might be tempted to ask why the pope, who, being unarmed, is even weaker than the Holy Roman Emperor, could not play a similar role in mediating the differences among Italian republics and principalities. The reason, Machiavelli suggests, is that there is no league or confederation of free republics in Italy equivalent to the Swiss in Germany, which makes other cities afraid of trying to expand their own territories. However, if the Florentines followed Machiavelli’s advice by arming their people and forming a league with other republics in Tuscany, they could play such a role. An armed northern Italian confederation could not only defend the south from the French and German armies that had invaded from the north, sometimes at the pope’s request. They could also, in effect, prevent the pope from calling in such troops or stirring up other conflicts among other Italian cities by making him depend on them to defend him, as Machiavelli indirectly suggests in the following two chapters (D 2.20 and 2.21).119


3. Not Knowing How to Make Friends or Thwart Enemies (D 2.20–21)


Arming the people is the first, necessary step toward organizing an effective republican foreign policy, but, Machiavelli reminds his readers, it is not sufficient. To follow either the Roman or Etruscan confederal model, it is also necessary to obtain allies. Rome had to defeat some of its neighbors on the battlefield before they came to terms. Like Capua, however, the weaker neighbors of a strong republic may voluntarily subject themselves to it in exchange for its protection. In other words, a republic does not—and should not—have to conquer all the cities nearby in order to expand. As the example of the Romans in Capua also shows, however, formerly free cities will remain subject to a stronger neighbor more contentedly and quietly if they are allowed to continue living under their own laws “under a dominion they do not see” (177). The leaders of the Florentine republic have not been able to realize their imperial ambitions, because they have not learned that “government is nothing other than holding subjects in such a mode that they cannot or ought not offend you. This is done either by securing oneself against them altogether, taking from them every way of hurting you, or by benefiting them in such a mode that it would not be reasonable for them to desire to change fortune” (182).120

In other words, a republic should conduct its foreign policy on the basis of the same understanding of the necessities of ruling that Machiavelli recommended to princes in D 1.16. It should protect its people or allies from those who threaten to destroy them and thus show its utility or benefits. It should eliminate the peoples or parties that threaten to destroy it. Or if and when it is not possible to eliminate the threat (as in the case of its own people), it should either destroy the “heads” of the opposition or buy them off with such great benefits that they have little reason to resist. Most important of all, it should gain the trust and support of the people by seeing that they and their property are protected from potential oppressors, domestic as well as foreign.


4. Not Having Followed Machiavelli’s Advice (D 2.22–26)


Unfortunately, Machiavelli observes, “in corrupt republics, especially in quiet times,” the “excellent men” who understand these necessities “are treated as enemies, either from envy or from some other ambitious causes.” Those chosen to lead either are selected because of a “common deception” or “put forward by men who wish for the favor rather than the good of the collectivity” (179). Machiavelli seems, indeed, to have himself and his exclusion from the government of Florence primarily in mind. Three of the modern examples he gives of important decisions made by inexperienced or imprudent leaders were made by other Florentines against his advice. Had Pope Leo studied Roman history under Machiavelli’s direction, he would not have listened to the counselors who advised him not to accept the alliance the French king offered when he planned to attack the duke of Milan, but to keep his troops on the sideline to fight the victor, believing that the victor’s power would have been weakened by the fight.121 The pope would have learned from the outcome of the battles between the Romans and the Latins that the victor seldom loses many men, and even if the battle lasts long and many die, the victor acquires a very great reputation that terrifies others. Likewise, if the Florentines had learned what Machiavelli sought to teach them from the example set by the Romans, they would have destroyed Arezzo in the wake of the rebellion of 1502 and thus made it an example that would deter others. Unfortunately, the leaders of the Florentine republic decided (again against Machiavelli’s advice) to exile and fine some of the Aretines and take away all of their honors and former ranks, but to leave the city intact (and full of people now hostile to Florence). As Machiavelli advised princes in dealing with their peoples in P 20, so he now warns potential heads of republics that in holding cities they have captured, “fortresses are generally much more harmful than useful” (184). They are harmful, because they tempt rulers to oppress the people rather than to gain their support; and they are not terribly useful, because they cannot be maintained without the help of an external army. He also warns those who would attack a city they believe is weak because it is internally divided that they are apt to unite and so strengthen it in the face of an external enemy. Better to try to make oneself the arbiter of the opposed parties, as Florence did in Pistoia, than to arouse the enmity of the city as a whole by trying to subdue and make it subject, as the Florentines did with Siena.

Machiavelli suggests that the mistaken Florentine policies all arise from a combination of weakness due to lack of arms and an arrogant desire to appear to be stronger than they actually are. Prudent leaders avoid vilifying and abusing their enemies, he reminds his readers in D 2.26, because such empty words merely serve to make enemies more obstinate by arousing their hatred. Like fortresses, “using words of little honor against the enemy arises most often from an insolence that either victory or the false hope of victory gives you” (193). Once again, Machiavelli draws an example from his own experience. “In 1512 a Spanish army came into the Florentine dominion to put the Medici back in Florence and tax the city, brought by citizens from inside who had given them hope that once they were in the Florentine dominion they would take up arms in their favor.” When the Spanish found no one there to greet or help them, and lacked provisions, they “tried for an accord, which the people of Florence, having become proud, did not accept” (194). It was not Machiavelli’s ill-trained militia that lost Prato and brought the ruin of the state; it was the bad judgment of the Florentine people (or their leader and his patron, Piero Soderini, who did not accept the overture from the Spanish) that led to the fall of the republic.


F. The Character of Machiavelli’s Advice (D 2.27–32)


As his analysis of the mistake Soderini made in not accepting the Spanish peace initiative shows, Machiavelli’s criticism of the traditional Florentine policy of taking “the middle way” does not mean that he is unalterably and absolutely opposed to all compromise. What he opposes are weak, ineffective decisions based on inaccurate estimates of one’s own forces in relation to those of the enemy. If a city does not have the power to destroy another, it must try to negotiate an agreement that will make the other city friendlier rather than more hostile and so preserve its own independence, if not its control over others.

Only as he nears the conclusion of what has been a generally unfavorable comparison of the foreign policies of the Italian republics with those of Rome does Machiavelli return to the point he made in the first two chapters of book 2: Rome does not in all ways or at all times constitute an exemplary model.

In D 2.28 he uses the Romans’ decision to send the three young Fabii as ambassadors to urge the “French” not to attack the Chiusi as an example of “how dangerous it is for a republic or a prince not to avenge an injury done against the public or against a private person.”122 Not merely were these three young soldiers inept diplomats, “more capable of doing than saying, [who] put themselves among the first to combat” the French when they came to fight with the Tuscans. Even worse, when the French complained to the Roman Senate and asked them to turn over the three offenders “against the law of nations,” the Romans did not punish the Fabii in any way, but honored them by electing them tribunes with consular powers.123 The Romans thus unnecessarily and arrogantly provoked the incensed “French” to march on Rome.124

In D 2.1 Machiavelli disputed the pious Roman belief that their military successes were due only partly to their own virtue, because they were due partly to fortune as well.
