In D 2.29, however, Machiavelli follows Livy, paraphrasing where he does not quote, in attributing Rome’s near defeat in the war that ensued to “the power of heaven over human affairs.” It was “heaven” that “first made the Fabii err.” Then it ordered the Romans not to take any of their usual precautions. They had already sent their most able leader, Camillus, into exile; and the tribunes did not levy the troops expeditiously or march out of Rome until the enemy was within ten miles. They had not set up a camp in advance, and their line of march was so thin and ill designed that the enemy was able quickly to surround it. The Roman army thus fled, most to Veii and some to Rome, where they left the gates open.

Livy’s narrative shows that the Romans were so ill prepared to meet the Gauls because after the successful siege of Veii the plebs were no longer willing to elect patrician tribunes. Their tribunes had indicted Camillus for seeking to retake some of the spoils to honor his pledge to Apollo, and when his friends informed him that they would pay the fine, but could not prevent his being convicted, he went into exile. Having lost all fear of an enemy attack, or arrogantly believing that they could deflect it with little effort, the same tribunes failed to employ the usual remedies and precautions in defending the city.

Rather than emphasizing the corrupting effects of the loss of fear of external aggressors, as he does elsewhere, Machiavelli asserts here that “Fortune” judged it was necessary to beat Rome (as he will show at the beginning of the next book) in order to make her greater. So it “had Camillus exiled, but not killed; made Rome be taken but not the Capitol; and ordered that the Romans not think of any good thing to protect Rome but later not lack any good order to defend the Capitol.” And in 2.30 he again cites Livy’s statement that Fortune had Camillus arrive with his army just in time to save Rome from using gold to buy off the French, who were like the Romans starving as a result of the siege, instead of defeating them with arms.

Machiavelli’s explicit lesson, indicated by the title of 2.30 is that “truly powerful republics and princes buy friendships not with money but with virtue and the reputation of strength.” So he again urges his contemporaries not to employ mercenary soldiers and try to buy allies, but to train and arm their own people to defend them. By reminding his readers that the Romans did not succeed merely because of such training, however, he reminds his readers that he is not urging them to imitate the Romans in all respects.


In emphasizing the importance of training and arming the citizens of a republic to fight in its defense, Machiavelli does point back to his own advocacy of such a policy in Florence and the defeat (he might say as a result of bad fortune) of the militia he trained. In light of his dismissal from the government of Florence and subsequent exile from the city, his warning his readers “How Dangerous It Is to Believe the Banished” (D 2.31; 202) has to look somewhat ironic. In contrast to other exiles, however, he assures his readers that he does not want to extend vain promises or hopes. By citing the example of Themistocles he suggests that, despite appearances to the contrary, he would not give aid to the enemies of the republic of Florence (even though his circumstances have forced him to seek employment with the Medici).

In describing the “many modes” in which the Romans seized towns in D 2.32, Machiavelli points out that “they guarded themselves from taking towns by siege, for they judged the expense and inconvenience of this mode to be so great as to overcome by far the utility that could be drawn from what it acquired” (203). He is recommending their early policy of fighting short wars nearby, establishing colonies, and then punishing cities who rebelled, by means of which they established their initial Italian federation. By acknowledging that the Romans were forced to turn to the siege (as they did at Veii, Capua, Carthage, Jerusalem, and similar towns), he reminds his readers of the corrupting effects of Rome’s more spectacular victories and unrestrained imperial expansion. His concluding account of how the Romans used glory as both an incentive and a check on their captains in D 2.33 is similarly ambiguous.


G. On the Use of Knowledge, Discretion, and Glory (D 2.33)


The example Machiavelli gives of the way in which “the Romans gave free commissions to their captains of armies” seems to undermine the general contention indicated by the title of the chapter. After Fabius defeated the Tuscans near Sutri, Machiavelli reports, he did not consult the Senate or seek their authorization to pass with his army through the Ciminian forest into Tuscany. After they heard of his victory, the Senate nevertheless sent two legates to command the consul not to pass. When they arrived and found that Fabius had already passed through the forest and won his battle with the Tuscans, the legates were wise enough to celebrate his victory and not to reprimand him for not obeying orders he had not received. The Senate had not displayed the prudence Machiavelli attributes to them, however. By sending the legates to command the consul not to pass through the forest, the senators had not shown that they recognized that they did not possess the knowledge of the particular circumstances necessary to give good counsel, even though many of them were experienced in war. Nor had the senators shown that they understood that consuls would prosecute wars more cautiously and less vigorously if they did not think that they would receive sole credit for their victories. Machiavelli seems to be attributing his own reasoning to the Senate when he concludes, “they wished the consul should act by himself and that the glory should be all his—the love of which, they judged, would be a check and a rule to make him work well.” Like “the republics of present times, such as the Venetian and the Florentine,” the Roman Senate seems in fact to have understood it “otherwise” (207) by unwisely trying to regulate their captain’s every move.


Conclusion of Book 2


At the conclusion of book 2 Machiavelli thus indicates that the Romans did not understand the reasons for the success of their external policies any more than they fully understood the excellence of their domestic modes and orders. Like the domestic institutions he recommends in book 1, so the foreign policy he advises his Florentine contemporaries to adopt in book 2 is based on his own analysis of the causes of Roman success. In order to maintain popular participation in the republic as well as to mount a successful defense, he urges his contemporaries to train an army of citizens or subjects able to mount short, intensive, repeated attacks on their neighbors—attacks that would persuade them to yield and come to terms. If Florence acquired the ability to defend itself, it could negotiate an alliance with its Tuscan neighbors that would enable them to defend themselves from the French, Spanish, and German armies that had invaded Italy. The formation of such a league, among the cities of Tuscany, if not of the Italian peninsula as a whole, would require some deceit (as did the Roman conquest). But the external power of the armies of the national monarchies along with the internal limitations of the decision-making abilities of a federation would effectively confine a Florentine league to Italy and prevent it from threatening to destroy liberty both at home and abroad the way the Roman Empire had. Confronted by such armies, the member states of the new confederation would also perceive the need to keep their people armed and ready to defend themselves.

In order to create and maintain such a league of free cities, Machiavelli has also suggested, it will be necessary to find and elevate leaders who, unlike most of his contemporaries, understand the art of government. But how can such excellent men overcome the envy or ambition of others that leads them to treat such men as enemies in corrupt republics? Didn’t Machiavelli argue in book 1 that a victorious general like Caesar who acquires a popular following poses the greatest threat to the preservation of republican government? Didn’t he urge other ambitious citizens to check the rise of any virtuous youth by vying with him for popular favor? Isn’t that competition an expression of their envy and ambition? How can a republic acquire the leadership it needs without falling prey to a tyrant? That is the problem to which Machiavelli returns in book 3.


Outline of Book 3: What the “Princes” of Machiavelli’s New Republic Need to Know


A. On Founding and Reordering (D 3.1–7)

1. Why It Is Necessary Repeatedly to Return to the Beginning (D 3.1)

2. Lucius Junius Brutus—Conspirator Par Excellence (D 3.2–5)

3. The Difficulties Confronting Would-Be Conspirators or Refounders and How Those Difficulties Can Be Overcome (D 3.6–7)

B. Why Machiavelli’s Contemporaries Find It Difficult to Imitate the Romans (D 3.8–15)

1. Changed Circumstances (D 3.8–10)

2. To Imitate Is Not Merely to Copy, but to Understand (D 3.11–15)

C. The Difficulty of Defining the Distinctive Virtue of a Republican Leader (D 3.16–23)

1. The Problem of Envy (D 3.16–17)

2. Winning Wars Is Not an Adequate Test (D 3.18–23)

a. Victory May Be a Result of Chance (D 3.18)

b. Both Harsh and Gentle Modes Work (D 3.19–23)

D. The Causes of the Fall of the Roman Republic and the Failure of Cincinnatus (D 3.24–25)

E. What Machiavelli’s Contemporaries Can Learn from the Romans (D 3.26–34)

1. The Source of Tyranny Is Competition for Economic Goods, Not Love of the Beautiful (D 3.26)

2. To End Civil Dissension, It Is Necessary to Eliminate the “Heads” (D 3.27)

3. Competition for Office Must Be through Public Rather Than Private Means (D 3.28–29)

4. How to Solve the Problem of Envy (D 3.30)

5. Military Training as a Mode of Moral Education (D 3.31–33)

6. Why Glory Is Not Always a Reward for Public Service (D 3.34)

F. The Education Machiavelli Offers Future Leaders of Republics (D 3.35–49)

1. The Danger of Putting Oneself at the Head of a New Endeavor That Concerns the Welfare of All, and the Role of an Advisor (3.35)

2. Training Is Stronger Than Nature (D 3.36)

3. How Troops Should Be Trained—or People Educated (D 3.37–38)

4. The Knowledge a “Captain” Needs to Train His Troops (D 3.39)

5. How Republican Leaders Should Keep Faith (D 3.40–42)

6. How Human Nature Is Shaped (D 3.43–44)

7. Fabius Rullianus as the Exemplary Republican Prince (D 3.45–49)


Book 3: What the “Princes” of Machiavelli’s New Republic Need to Know


In contrast to books 1 and 2, Machiavelli does not begin book 3 with a preface in which he explains what he proposes to do and why. The reason he does not introduce book 3 with such a statement becomes evident if readers consider the logic of the argument he has been presenting. Machiavelli has explained what sorts of domestic orders should be instituted in a republic that would last longer than Rome and the kind of defensive policies that would protect the liberty of that republic without destroying it everywhere the way Rome did. He could now be expected to show his readers what they as private individuals could and should do to bring such a republic into existence and preserve it. If he had offered such advice directly and unambiguously to his young Florentine readers, however, he and they both could have been accused and convicted of conspiring to overthrow the Medici. In book 3 he thus proceeds much more indirectly and ambiguously to show his young readers what they need to do by demonstrating “how much the actions of particular men made Rome great and caused many good effects in that city” (212).125


A. On Founding and Reordering (D 3.1–7)


1. Why It Is Necessary Repeatedly to Return to the Beginning126 (D 3.1)


Readers of The Prince (who, no doubt, included Machiavelli’s young friends) might have taken away the impression that it is necessary to use force and fraud to seize power, but that once order is established rulers should strive to make their people forget the base origins of the governments under which they live.127 In striving to teach his young readers what they have to do not only to found but also to maintain a republic, however, Machiavelli emphasizes the importance of having the people, who naturally do not want to be commanded or ruled, repeat the experience that led them initially to accept and obey a government. In describing the deeds of particular men that made Rome great, he thus emphasizes the effects they had on the people more than the character or lives of those individuals (as did Plutarch).

“All worldly things have a limit to their life,” but mixed bodies such as sects or republics last longest if they have orders that enable them to be often renewed by bringing them back to their beginning. In D 1.1 Machiavelli argued that the beginnings of cities are to be found in the need a group of people perceives to come together to defend themselves from others, and that a city like Rome lasted as long as it did because of the “many necessities the laws made by Romulus, Numa, and the others” (D 1.1; 9) imposed on the people to arm and defend themselves. So he observes here that when republics are brought back to their beginning, as the Romans were by the French capture of the city, people see that it is “necessary not only to maintain religion and justice, but also to esteem . . . good citizens . . . and put aside all envy” (210).

Such salutary returns to the beginning can occur either because of an “extrinsic accident” or because of the “intrinsic prudence” of individual citizens. Since “extrinsic accidents” such as the French taking of Rome threaten the future independence if not very existence of the city, renewing the republic by means of the “intrinsic” prudence of individual citizens is obviously better. The first “intrinsic” way a republic can be brought back to its beginning is by means of laws and orders such as the tribunes and censors that checked the arrogance of ambitious individuals in Rome. As the examples Machiavelli lists suggest, these checks consist primarily in public trials he calls “executions” (even though not all the trials he lists resulted in the death or even conviction of the accused).128 In D 1.7 he argued that such trials enable the people to vent their anger against individuals they think are trying to oppress them, but here he maintains that such trials remind people of the fearsome punishments they face if they dare to transgress the laws or try to innovate. In both cases he is reminding his readers that people do not want to be “dominated” or ruled and that they resent the individuals who impose order upon them. To return to the beginning or “first principle” of political order is thus to reawaken the fear that leads human beings to come together and form a government to defend them. Indeed, he warns, if the people are not reminded every five to ten years of the fearsome punishments they face if they do not obey the law, they will become corrupt (or slavish, as he suggested in 1.16). But he also claims that if such reminders had occurred that frequently in Rome, the people and their republic would never have become corrupt.

Despite his initial acknowledgment of the transitory character of all worldly things, Machiavelli seems to be suggesting that a republic can overcome the limits of the existence of all worldly things—if it has a sufficient number and sequence of virtuous individuals. For, he emphasizes, it takes a virtuous individual to set in motion the laws and orders designed to check the arrogance of others.129 He adds, moreover, that the virtue of a single man like Horatius Coclus or Regulus Attila can produce almost the same effects as the trials.130 (Awe is akin to fear.) When he first discussed the problem of corruption in D 1.16–18, Machiavelli noted that a people would not remain uncorrupt for long under a series of corrupt “heads”; but he also stated that the Roman people remained uncorrupt so long as they felt threatened by foreign aggression. Now he suggests, not only do the people need to be frequently and repeatedly reminded of the reasons they ought to fear disobeying the law by seeing their leaders accused and tried of aspiring to overthrow the republic and establish a tyranny. The people also need to be reminded of the reasons why they ought to risk their own lives and families by serving in the army by seeing the individuals elevated to high office sacrifice theirs. Such sacrifices encourage others to imitate the virtue of their leaders, and witnessing the trials and sacrifices of their leaders helps the people overcome their envy.131

The need to renew the respect people have for both the orders and the leaders of their community by returning to its beginning is not restricted to republics, moreover; it also applies to “sects” and kingdoms. By imitating the life of Christ in adopting a life of poverty, Machiavelli observes, the orders of Saint Dominick and Saint Francis prevented people from entirely losing faith in the Christian religion because of the misdeeds of the prelates.132 But the effects of this particular return to the beginning have not been unambiguously good. By convincing people that they should accept the evils they encounter on earth and leave punishment to God in the afterlife, these monkish orders have been able to do the worst they can, because their members do not fear punishment they cannot see.133 These monkish orders have preserved the Christian faith, but they have also undermined the salutary fear of punishment upon which the rule of law in both republics and kingdoms depends.

“Kingdoms also have need of renewing themselves” by bringing their laws back toward their beginnings; and Machiavelli again praises the French parlement as a means of producing such a good effect. In P 19 he argued that the court protected the monarch by enabling the people to check the nobles (with ambitions to unseat and replace him); but here he states that the court renews and revives the laws and orders of the kingdom by passing verdicts against the king as well as against the nobles.134 In D 1.16 he argued that both the king and the people of France live secure, “because of nothing other than that the kings are obligated by infinite laws in which the security of all its peoples is included” (46). Now he suggests that the king’s subordination to the rule of law has to be demonstrated to the people in public.

Machiavelli first praises the orders of the Roman republic that brought it back to its beginning by counteracting the ambition and insolence of men. Yet the common element in all three forms of “return” and “renewal” he describes here is the need for leaders to demonstrate their willingness to endure the most extreme forms of the restraints and burdens they impose upon others. By risking if not sacrificing their own lives, families, and goods, such leaders convince their followers that they are acting for the sake of the community, not merely for their own private benefit, and so overcome the envy of others. But what makes such sacrifices worthwhile for the individual? The answer Machiavelli suggested in D 2.33 was their desire to win glory. But he indicates here, as he argued in 2.2, that if it is to have beneficial political effects, glory must consist in worldly renown, not a promise of justice or life after death that eviscerates men’s interest in enforcing the law here and now.135

In the remainder of book 3 Machiavelli shows not merely that Roman commanders acquired glory in a variety of ways, but that their desire to win glory did not suffice to preserve the republic. On the contrary, as shown most dramatically by Julius Caesar, the desire of individual commanders to return to Rome in triumph culminated in the rise of a tyrant. The Romans did not understand how agitation over the Agrarian law and the prolongation of commands led to the fall of the republic. But now that these things are understood, Machiavelli promises, remedies can be found.


2. Lucius Junius Brutus—Conspirator Par Excellence (D 3.2–5)


As Machiavelli’s first example of an individual whose deeds benefited Rome shows, not only is it necessary to elect leaders on the basis of their demonstrated merit for short terms of office. It is also necessary to eliminate those whose envy and ambition lead them not merely to oppose whoever is in power, but to try to overthrow the republican order.

Machiavelli can treat Brutus as someone who renewed the republic by returning it to its beginning, rather than simply as its founder, because, as he emphasized in book 1, Romulus had established an elected rather than a hereditary monarchy whose powers were checked by a senate. In D 1.25 Machiavelli used several of Brutus’s innovations as examples of the way a reformer could obtain popular acceptance of changes by keeping the old names or appearances of offices while changing their powers. By using Brutus as his first example of a return to the beginning, Machiavelli indicates that by a “return” he does not mean simply a repeat.

Machiavelli first praises Brutus for the prudence he displayed by pretending to be a fool so long as he did not have sufficient force to act openly against Tarquin. By simulating craziness, Brutus was not merely able to protect himself and his patrimony, as Livy states. He had public or political as well as private reasons for the pretense. By simulating craziness, Brutus could safely remain a member of the king’s household and so be in a position to see and take advantage of the first opportunity to act against the tyrant. Indeed, Machiavelli argues more generally, an individual cannot act effectively in politics by trying to remain “above the fray” or seek to withdraw entirely from public life, as did both Socrates and Epicurus. A prince will suspect anyone of “quality” who does not openly declare himself to be for the prince of secretly scheming against him. So a prudent man will stay close to the prince—praising and doing things of which he does not approve—in order to remain in safety, if not to prosper along with the prince, and to be on hand to take advantage of any opportunity that arises of overthrowing him.136 It is difficult not to regard Machiavelli’s repeated protestations of his desire to serve the Medici in light of his interpretation of Brutus.

Machiavelli does not praise Brutus solely for concealing his intention to act against Tarquin until he was able to do so openly and effectively. He also extols the severity Brutus displayed in seeing that his sons were tried and executed for conspiring to overthrow the new republic. As in his initial discussion of the difficulties involved in a transition from a principality to a republic or vice versa in D 1.16 (except that he now calls the “principality” a “tyranny”), Machiavelli declares that “after a change of state, either from republic to tyranny or from tyranny to republic, a memorable execution against the enemies of present conditions is necessary” (214).

As in P 3, so Machiavelli urges here: “every prince can be warned that he never lives secure in his principality as long as those who have been despoiled of it are living.” Repeating his criticism of Cesare Borgia at the conclusion of P 7, he also reminds his readers, “old injuries are never suppressed by new benefits” (216). In the Prince Machiavelli distinguished between “the great” who do not forget old injuries and the people who judge things by their appearance or results. He develops the implications of that distinction here in pointing out the contemporary relevance of his analysis of Brutus. He not only faults Piero Soderini for believing that “he would overcome with his patience and goodness the appetite that was in the sons of Brutus [aka Medici] for returning to another government”; he also criticizes Soderini for overestimating the respect people have for the rule of law.137 Soderini feared that if he “took extraordinary authority” and broke up “civil equality together with the laws” in order to oppress his foes, the people would not allow another gonfalonier for life to be appointed, because they would conclude that the office created a tyranny. He did not understand that his works and his intention would be judged by the outcome. If he had used extralegal force to save the republic from its foes and lived long enough to manage the aftermath, he could have convinced everyone “that what he had done was for the safety of the fatherland and not for his own ambition.” Moreover, he could have managed “things so that a successor of his would not be able to do for evil what he had done for good” (215).

Machiavelli’s comments on Soderini let readers see that in praising Brutus, Machiavelli emphasizes his use of fraud and force, but does not mention the way he fought like a man, that is, with laws.138 Romulus had slain his brother, whereas Brutus “merely” presided over a court trial that culminated in the execution of his sons. But Machiavelli does not mention this difference or his contention earlier that the Florentines should have established a public court in which Soderini and his critics could have aired their charges and have them judged. In using Brutus as an example of what it means to return to the beginnings, Machiavelli emphasizes the necessity of using both fraud and force to establish and maintain any government, including one bound by laws. However, he immediately reminds his readers that the fact that a “prince” needs to use force (or be armed) does not mean that he does not need to acquire and maintain the support of his people. And to do that, he must at least appear not merely to be enforcing the law against others, but to be obeying it himself. The requirements of founding or refounding a republic thus appear to be remarkably like those Machiavelli spelled out in P 6–19 for a prince who wants not only to acquire but also to maintain his dominion.

After praising Brutus for not revealing his intentions until he was able to act on them and for his severity in executing the opponents of the government he established, Machiavelli dismisses the traditional account of the expulsion of Tarquin the Proud: because his son Sextus raped Lucretia. Brutus was able to depose the king, Machiavelli argues, because Tarquin had broken the laws of the kingdom and governed it tyrannically.139 By taking away all the authority of the Senate and forcing the people to labor on public works, the tyrant had made himself hated by the entire collectivity. “If Tarquin had lived like the other kings and Sextus his son had made that error, Brutus and Collatinus would have had recourse to Tarquin and not to the Roman people for vengeance against Sextus” (217).140 Tarquin did not fall because of a moral lapse on the part of his son; he fell because he had lost the support of both the nobles and the people by not ruling according to law.

Tarquin’s tyrannical use of his power may have created the conditions in which Brutus could depose him with the support of both the Senate and the people. But Brutus’s restoration of the liberty of the Roman people did not prevent his sons from conspiring to overthrow the republic any more than it had prevented the sons of Ancus or the daughter of Servius Tullius from trying to seize the power of a legally appointed king.141 In the longest chapter in the entire Discourses Machiavelli thus turns to discuss the reasons why human beings conspire against both princes and republics, why such attempts usually fail, but how and when they can succeed.

Brutus had traditionally been celebrated as the founder of the Roman republic, so it was appropriate for Machiavelli to begin describing the deeds of individuals that made Rome great with him. Had Machiavelli glorified Brutus as the example of the way in which an individual made Rome great, however, Machiavelli would have appeared to be encouraging his young readers to conspire against the tyrants who had overthrown the republic of Florence the way Brutus had conspired against Tarquin. Machiavelli thus blames Tarquin for losing the support of the collectivity, and states that he will discuss conspiracies “so that princes may learn to guard themselves from these dangers and private individuals may put themselves into them more timidly—indeed, that they may learn to be content to live under the empire that has been proposed for them by fate” (218). He also appeals to the authority of Tacitus, who described much worse conditions and tyranny in the Roman empire, for support.142 Only in the brief chapter that follows his discussion of conspiracies does Machiavelli point out the parallel between “the change that Rome made from kings to consuls, where none other than the Tarquins were expelled” and “the state of the Medici in Florence, in the ruin of whom later, in 1494, none other than themselves were offended” (236). But in doing so he shows he has not forgotten the contemporary relevance of his lengthy analysis of the causes and effects of conspiracies.


3. The Difficulties Confronting Would-Be Conspirators or Founders and How Those Difficulties Can Be Overcome (D 3.6–7)


Machiavelli begins by examining the causes of conspiracies against princes. As in P 19, so Machiavelli here declares that the most important cause of such a conspiracy is the prince’s having made himself hated by the collectivity, because their hatred encourages individuals who have been offended to act against him. As in P 19, Machiavelli thus warns princes against arousing the hatred of individuals by threatening them with death, dishonoring them and their families, or depriving them of an inheritance. But here he notes that another very great cause “that makes men conspire against the prince is the desire to free the fatherland that has been seized by him” (220–21). All these causes can be seen to have been operative in the case of Brutus.

Those who conspire against princes encounter dangers at all three stages: planning, execution, and aftermath. Anyone can kill a prince if he is willing to relinquish his own life, but few can be found who are willing to accept a certain death. Those who wish to live will need associates to protect them, but when conspirators inform others of their plans they give their hoped-for associates a means of ingratiating themselves with the prince by informing him of the danger and at the same time securing themselves from his wrath. All the conspiracies about which one reads in the histories have thus been undertaken by great men or those very close to the prince, because these alone have an opportunity to kill the prince, yet can hope to survive. Indeed, Machiavelli suggests, “a prince who wishes to guard himself against conspiracies should fear more those to whom he has done too many favors than those to whom he has done too many injuries. For the latter are lacking in occasion, the former abound in it; and the wish is similar because the desire to dominate is as great as or greater than is that of vengeance” (222). Although conspirators usually claim, like Brutus, to be acting on behalf of justice, Machiavelli suggests that ambition is an equal if not stronger motive. And sounding a theme he will develop further, a prince or leader should worry most about the envy of those closest to him, that is, the other members of the ruling class or elite.

Conspirators have often been exposed by report or by conjecture, because they have spoken imprudently before a household servant or acted in a way that revealed their intention. But Machiavelli points out a way to escape these dangers. If a conspirator communicates his intention to those whose help he needs only at the moment of execution (as Brutus did to Lucretia’s husband and the other soldiers), they will not have an opportunity to inform the prince or accuse the conspirator.143 Above all, and very relevant to his own case, Machiavelli warns, a conspirator should never put anything in writing that he cannot effectively deny. (The ambiguities or apparent contradictions in Machiavelli’s text would have provided him with a ready defense against the accusation that he was conspiring with his young friends against the Medici regime.)

The dangers incurred in the execution (as opposed to the planning) of a conspiracy “arise either from varying the order, or from spirit lacking in him who executes, or from an error that the executor makes through lack of prudence or through not bringing the thing to perfection by leaving alive part of those who were planned to be killed” (227). All these problems beset the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici in 1478. Yet, Machiavelli points out, although more than fifty people knew of the plans, no one exposed the conspiracy. It failed because they had to change the location at the last minute, the cardinal refused to share in a homicide in church, and an inexperienced assassin warned Lorenzo by saying “Oh, traitor,” as he approached; as a result, they succeeded in killing Giovanni de’ Medici, but not Lorenzo, who became the “Magnificent.” Even though Machiavelli concludes that “everyone ought to abstain from similar conspiracies against many heads, because one does not do good either to oneself or to the fatherland” (230), he lists several examples of successful conspiracies against more than one prince. If it took so many missteps and accidents to defeat the Pazzi, a skeptical reader might conclude, a simpler plan revealed to fewer people might succeed against the same ruling family (although conspirators against the Medici would still have to take account of the reluctance some felt to act, if not literally in a church, then against men of the Church).144

The last danger conspirators face is that someone will be left to avenge the dead prince, as Lorenzo was left to avenge the death of his brother (and Tarquin was left in exile and thus able to conspire with Brutus’s sons to overthrow the newly founded republic). The example Machiavelli uses of Madonna Caterina, who left her children as hostages in order to enter the fortress at Forlì, from which she then defied the men who had murdered her husband by showing them that she had the capacity to produce more children, reminds readers that family ties are not sufficient to overcome the desire to rule. However, Caterina did not succeed in securing her rule by sacrificing her children the way Brutus did, because she and her husband were so hated by the people. Machiavelli has repeatedly advised princes not to rely on fortresses to protect them from the hatred of their people; and here he concludes, “of all the dangers that can come after the execution, there is none more certain nor more to be feared than when the people is the friend of the prince that you have killed” (232). By using Caesar as an example, Machiavelli also reminds his young Florentine readers that the republic of Rome was not restored by the conspiracy led by a later Brutus, because Caesar was avenged by the people of Rome.145 Machiavelli does not make a point that he emphasizes in the Florentine Histories—namely, that conspirators often hope that the people will arise to join and support them, but that a corrupt people like the people of Florence will not.146

The mention of Caesar leads Machiavelli to consider the dangers faced by those who conspire against the fatherland rather than against the prince, “in a republic where there is some part of corruption, for since one not corrupt has no place for a wicked beginning, these thoughts cannot befall one of its citizens.” Yet he reminds readers two chapters later (in D 3.8) that such thoughts did occur to two leading citizens in the early “noncorrupt” Roman republic. Here he argues that conspiracies against the fatherland are less dangerous to conspirators than plans to assassinate a prince, “because republics are slower than a prince, suspect less, are thus less cautious and have more respect for their great citizens” (232, translation slightly emended). In a republic, individuals and parties are free to oppose the established government in public. The dangers arise almost entirely in the attempt to seize and overturn the government, because it is rare that an individual will have sufficient forces to subdue many citizens.

Nevertheless, Machiavelli points out, generals of armies such as Caesar, Agathocles, and Cleomenes have been able to seize their fatherland at a stroke. Others, like Pisistratus of Athens, have used fraud to obtain bodyguards to protect them; still others have used foreign armies. (That was how the Medici, in effect, used the Spanish army at the gates of Florence to seize power in 1512, although Machiavelli does not include this recent example among his illustrations—all ancient—of the way in which such attempts may or may not succeed, according to fortune).

Having warned potential conspirators about the dangers they face, and shown them how those dangers can be evaded or overcome, Machiavelli concludes by warning “that prince or that republic that might be conspired against” to learn the quality of the conspiracy and measure the conditions and abilities of the conspirators in comparison to their own before they take action against it. If the conspirators are weak, they should be crushed without hesitation; but if they are strong, the government should temporize and dissimulate until it is strong enough to destroy its opponents. Machiavelli thus presents himself as arguing from the perspective of the established government, not as someone showing potential conspirators against it how they can succeed.

Changes of government, “from freedom to servitude and from servitude to freedom,” are not always accompanied or accomplished by much bloodshed, Machiavelli points out in D 3.7. The amount of bloodshed depends upon whether “the state that is changed arises with violence or not, . . . and because when it arises with violence it must arise with the injury of many, it is necessary later, in its ruin, that the injured wish to avenge themselves” (236). Reminding his readers of the relatively bloodless changes effected by Brutus in deposing Tarquin and the Florentines in deposing Piero de’ Medici in 1494, Machiavelli assures them that when a change of government occurs with popular support, only the previous “head” need be injured. Since the Florentine republic was overturned with little bloodshed, he suggests, the Medici regime that replaced it could also be overturned with a minimum of violence.147 By emphasizing the need “to kill the sons of Brutus” Machiavelli has nevertheless insisted that not merely some violence but public executions are necessary to establish a lasting republic. By pointing out the parallel between the relatively bloodless revolutions that established the Roman and Florentine republics, he has also called attention, be it indirectly, to the glaring contrast between the results. Whereas Brutus established a republic that lasted for centuries, the Florentine republic that replaced the Medici lasted only eighteen years. The reason that republic did not last, Machiavelli has almost stated outright, was that its leader, Soderini, did not understand the need to “kill the sons of Brutus.” In the Prince Machiavelli suggested that a failure to understand the implacable hatred of their opponents was characteristic even of seemingly ruthless modern princes like Cesare Borgia. However, the more common explanation or response, especially among Florentine admirers of Rome like his dedicatees, would have been that unlike the early Romans, the people of Florence were corrupt. In the next chapter Machiavelli thus turns explicitly to the question of what an ambitious man can do with a corrupt people. And he shows in the chapters that follow that if a “prince” wishes to reestablish or reorder a republic, it will not suffice to seize control of the government. He will also have to reform the people.


B. Why Machiavelli’s Contemporaries Find It Difficult to Imitate the Romans (D 3.8–15)


1. Changed Circumstances (D 3.8–10)


The first reason his contemporaries find it difficult to imitate the Romans, Machiavelli suggests, is that circumstances have changed. Claiming merely to be repeating what he said in D 3.6, Machiavelli begins D 3.8 by proclaiming that “a wicked citizen cannot work for ill in a republic that is not corrupt” (237). In fact, he wrote, “since one not corrupt has no place for a wicked beginning, these thoughts cannot befall one of its citizens” (232). Now he acknowledges that such thoughts did occur to Spurius Cassius and Manlius Capitolinus in the early Roman republic, but he emphasizes that neither the patricians nor the plebs would allow them to acquire the tyrannical powers they desired.

The two examples are significant, because they represent two of the causes of the fall of the Roman republic. First, there was the desire of both the patricians and the plebs to increase their wealth and, consequently, an unwillingness to share the spoils of war that finally produced civil war. Second, there was the envy that led the people not to elevate the best citizens to high office and so provoked the great to seek to win the recognition they believed they deserved by overthrowing the republic. Although Machiavelli does not state so explicitly, readers of Livy would know that Spurius Cassius was one of the first proponents of the Agrarian law that Machiavelli argues led eventually to the fall of the Roman republic.148 Machiavelli does not remind his readers that Manlius Capitolinus’s attempt “to make tumults in Rome against the Senate and against the laws of the fatherland . . . because of the envy that he had for the honors that were done to Camillus” (237) failed because it occurred in the wake of the French taking of Rome. That catastrophe showed the people “that it was necessary not only to maintain religion and justice but also to esteem its good citizens” (210). In other words, the patricians and plebs of the early Roman republic were uncorrupt not because of their “intrinsic” virtue so much as of an “extrinsic accident.”

Had Spurius Cassius or Manlius Capitolinus “been born in the times of Marius and Sulla, when the matter was already corrupt and he would have been able to impress the form of his ambition,” Machiavelli concedes, “he would have had the same results and successes . . . as others later who aspired to tyranny.” Machiavelli thus warns the “potential princes” he is addressing “that one has to seek glory in a corrupt city by modes other than in one that still lives politically,” and “that men . . . should consider the times and accommodate themselves to them” (238). The implication is that his readers cannot simply follow the examples of the great “captains” of the early Roman republic, because those captains were not dealing with a corrupt people like the Florentines.

However, Machiavelli observes in D 3.9, as he did in P 25, individuals cannot simply choose the manner in which they proceed. They have different inclinations by nature, and they will not vary from modes that have succeeded for them in the past. “Hence it arises that a republic has greater life and has good fortune longer than a principality, for it can accommodate itself better than one prince can to the diversity of times through the diversity of citizens in it” (240).

Machiavelli thus reminds his readers that the actions of particular men that made Rome great were achieved under the republic primarily, if not solely, by men elected to office. Since the consulate was the highest office, and consuls served primarily as generals, he discusses their actions as “captains.” Whether as consuls or tribunes with the powers of consuls, they were elected to serve the ruling body, whether that was the Senate or the plebs. As Lefort emphasizes in his analysis of the Discourses, in discussing the role of a “captain” Machiavelli is analyzing the character of political as well as military leadership in a republic.149 Discussing the problem in explicitly military rather than political terms makes his recommendations sound more technical, less controversial, and hence safer.

In D 1.20 Machiavelli argued that republics were superior to hereditary principalities precisely because they could elect different kinds of individuals as needed under different circumstances. But here he observes that “the ruin of cities also arises through not varying the orders of republics with the times,” and that “they have trouble varying because they need times to come that move the whole republic” (240). In other words, elections are not sufficient to guarantee that republics have the leadership they need. The people have to be persuaded that they need to elect individuals able to respond to the necessities imposed by the particular circumstances; but by the time the people perceive the necessity, it is often too late.


2. To Imitate Is Not Merely to Copy, but to Understand (D 3.11–15)


The second reason his contemporaries have not been able to “imitate” the Romans, Machiavelli suggests, is that they have merely copied the externally observed behavior of the Romans without understanding the reasons for it or how it was related to the particular circumstances. As in the Prince, Machiavelli cites Fabius Maximus as a famous example of a general whose nature and experience led him to proceed cautiously. But, he now informs his readers, the example set by Fabius has been almost completely misunderstood by contemporary Italians. They have taken Fabius to represent the advantages of avoiding battle. So if Italian princes command their own troops, they do so only for show; and republics make an even worse error than the princes by entrusting their defense to others and not understanding anything that belongs to war. When “these idle princes or effeminate republics send out a captain,” they send him with orders to guard against fighting, believing “that they are imitating in this the prudence of Fabius Maximus” (242). In fact, Machiavelli protests, just as “Gnaeus Sulpitius the dictator dragged out the war against the Gauls, [because] he was unwilling to commit himself to fortune against an enemy whom time and a foreign place were daily making weaker” (243), so Fabius avoided battle in order to wear Hannibal and his troops down and make them fight him under conditions of his own choosing. A general should follow the example of Fabius and Gnaeus Sulpitius only under these conditions, Machiavelli insists. Rome would never have defeated Hannibal if Scipio had not replaced Fabius as general. And if one takes an army into a foreign country, as Scipio did, one should expect to fight, because the enemy will defend himself.

If his Florentine readers were to adopt the imperial policy Machiavelli recommended in book 2, they would have to lead an army out. Imitating the Romans means fighting offensive wars, not trying to avoid battle.

A general wins most glory if he is solely responsible for a victory. Machiavelli thus begins and ends the next section of chapters (D 3.11–15) by pointing out the advantages of unitary leadership. In urging his contemporaries to adopt the tripartite Roman order of battle in book 2, Machiavelli argued that the fate of an army would be less subject to fortune if it were organized so that it could withstand and recover from the first thrust of an enemy. Here he applies a similar argument to the conduct of both domestic and foreign policy by an individual, small group, or political association. A unitary actor may initially be overpowered by the superior numbers of his opponents, but if he is able to withstand their first thrust, he will be able to divide them. To illustrate this principle, Machiavelli points not only to the way Roman senators were able to reduce the power of the tribunes by manipulating elections so that some of the tribunes would oppose others, as he described earlier (D 1.47–48).150 He also shows how the principle applies to foreign policy when a nation finds itself isolated (as Venice did when all the other Italian powers opposed it, but was able to make special deals with individual members of the alliance and so separate them from it).

In D 3.12 Machiavelli suggests that one of the ways a “prudent captain” overcomes opposition is to make it necessary for his own soldiers to fight and easy for the enemy to surrender. What might appear to be merciful treatment, promising to spare those who put down their arms, proves to be a calculating means of achieving victory at the least price. “A prudent captain who has to go capture a city ought to measure the ease or the difficulty of capturing it from knowing and considering what necessity constrains its inhabitants to defend themselves.” As he observed in P 3, “towns are more difficult to acquire after rebellion than they were in the first acquiring, for in the beginning they surrendered easily, not having cause to fear punishment because they had not offended.” Explaining that “such obstinacy also arises from the natural hatreds that neighboring princes and neighboring republics have for one another, which proceeds from the ambition to dominate and from jealousy for their state—especially if they are republics—as happened in Tuscany,” Machiavelli again indicates the way in which his advice to an individual who wants to obtain glory for himself applies to Florentine foreign policy. “Whoever considers well the neighbors of the city of Florence and the neighbors of the city of Venice will not marvel, as many do, that Florence had more expense in wars and acquired less than Venice. For it all arises from the Venetians’ not having had neighboring towns so obstinate for defense as Florence has had, because all the cities next to Venice had been used to living under a prince, and not free” (247). Like Rome, Machiavelli suggested in book 2, Florence would have to acquire an empire of previously free cities partly by force and partly by offering them a somewhat deceptive alliance as equal partners. In order to make such alliance look more advantageous than complete independence, he also emphasized that Florence would need not only to muster and train an army composed of its own citizens, but also to allow her new “partner” to continue to live under its own laws.

In D 3.13 Machiavelli returns to the question of the relation between the one and the many by asking “which is more to be trusted, a good captain who has a weak army or a good army that has a weak captain” (249). He first cites Livy’s judgment, based on the Romans’ experience with Coriolanus, that the republic grew more by the virtue of its captains than that of the soldiers. But, Machiavelli reflects, the histories show that virtuous armies, deprived of their captains, have also won battles. Caesar thought that neither should be valued much. However, because a good captain can train a good army if given the opportunity, and “a good army without a good head usually becomes insolent and dangerous,” Machiavelli concludes, “a captain who has time to instruct men and occasion to arm them is very much more to be trusted than an insolent army without a head made tumultuous by it.” Leaving no doubt about the recommendation he is making to his politically ambitious young readers, he states that “the glory and the praise are to be doubled for those captains who have had not only to conquer the enemy but to instruct their army” (250–51). The leaders of the Florentine republic opposed and thus delayed Machiavelli’s own attempts to muster and train a local militia not only to defend the city, but also to seize nearby towns like Pisa. If his young readers wish to revive republican government in Florence, he thus suggests, they will need not merely to seize control of the government from the Medici by means of a conspiracy. They will also have to overcome the corruption of the Florentine people by training them to defend themselves. If so, the reform or reordering of the Florentine republic would surely not occur, much less be maintained, “in a day.” It was a long-term project.

Underlining his emphasis on the importance of training, in D 3.14 Machiavelli shows that promising strategies may backfire if troops are not trained to heed specific orders coming from an established line of command.151 Because “new voices” or deceptive “inventions” startle troops, they may help a captain counter or gain an advantage over his enemy, but such devices are also apt to cause panic and disorder in his own troops so that the deception is easily uncovered. As in his discussion of the use of religious rites to inspire fear of failure in D 1.15, so Machiavelli concludes here that the superior training of Roman troops enabled them to overcome the fearsome illusions fabricated by their enemies. As in his discussion of the limitations of artillery, Machiavelli also insists that there is no quick or clever substitute for a well-trained army.

In D 3.15 Machiavelli summarizes the central lesson of his discussion of “captains” by arguing that “one individual and not many should be put over an army; and that several commanders hurt” (253). When a number of captains had different opinions about how to proceed and only the virtue of the soldiers protected them, the Romans appointed a dictator. Machiavelli points out that this is another lesson his contemporaries have not learned from the histories. “If one seeks the causes of the ruin of Italian and French armies in our times, one will find the most powerful to have been . . . sending to places more than one commissioner . . . to administer them better, which produces confusion beyond reckoning” (254). Machiavelli clearly prefers what in The Prince he calls a “civic principality,” in which one individual is elected by his fellow citizens to lead the republic (when, as he emphasizes in the Discourses, different individuals are elected for limited, nonconsecutive terms) to the “aristocratic” rule of the few best, most educated, and virtuous citizens in a council or senate. Distrusting the rule of any one individual, such a body appoints multiple commissioners to execute its decisions.152


C. The Difficulty of Defining the Distinctive Virtue of a Republican Leader (D 3.16–23)


1. The Problem of Envy (D 3.16–17)


Why don’t republics elect a succession of their most virtuous citizens as “captains” and so encourage these individuals to contribute to the common good by seeking glory for themselves? They claim (as in sending more than one commissioner to lead an army or administer a province) that more minds are better—or at least safer—than one. Republics would appear to be harbor the same suspicions of the motives of their captains or generals that Machiavelli argued the people of republics should have in book 1. But Machiavelli insists here that “great and rare men are neglected in a republic in peaceful times,” because the reputation their virtue has given these individuals has aroused the envy of many citizens who wish to be seen not merely as equal but as superior to the great.

This neglect gives rise to two different problems. Not only is the republic deprived of the leadership of its most able citizens until a crisis arises (when it may be too late, because a general cannot train an army to meet a foe the moment it is needed). Angered not merely by the lack of esteem for their own virtues, but by the elevation of lesser men in their stead, worthy “citizens who see . . . that easy and not dangerous times are the cause of it strive to disturb them, starting new wars to the prejudice of the republic” (255).

At this point in the text Machiavelli claims to see only two remedies for the danger the envy of outstanding citizens poses to republics, both of which were employed by the Roman republic: “one, to maintain the citizens poor so that they cannot corrupt either themselves or others with riches and without virtue; the other, to be ordered for war so that one can always make war and always has need of reputed citizens” (255). Since the Roman armies were always kept outside the city, Machiavelli points out, promotion was based on merit (not on what was pleasing to the people or the wealth and power of the individual in question)—until, after they had conquered Carthage and Antiochus, the Romans no longer felt a pressing need to defend themselves from foreign aggressors.153 Neither of these remedies would be available to “captains” in Florence, however, unless they tried to redistribute wealth in a way Machiavelli showed in D 1.37 led to the downfall of the Roman republic, and unless the republic decided to arm its citizens. Machiavelli has shown, moreover, not merely that the first of these remedies was not simply or always available to the Romans, but that over time the second “remedy” undercut the first.154 The success of Roman armies in conquering ever more distant lands led to increasing economic inequality in the republic and so to the escalating contention about the Agrarian law that eventually brought down the republic. In the next chapter (D 3.17) Machiavelli thus acknowledges that even before they defeated Carthage, the Romans had not been able entirely to overcome the danger to the republic posed by the anger of generals who felt that they had been dishonored.

After he had been outwitted by the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal in Spain, Machiavelli claims, Claudius Nero was charged with misconduct by both the Senate and people and was greatly dishonored and angered as a result.155 Although Machiavelli praised the Romans for not punishing defeated generals harshly (e.g., by crucifying them, in D 1.31), he uses the example of Claudius to show that the anger a general feels if he is publicly dishonored by being accused of malfeasance makes it unsafe to employ him later. Concerned more about reestablishing his own reputation and glory than about the safety of the city that had dishonored him, Claudius chose to face and try to defeat Hasdrubel before he went to join the other consul in the marches to fight Hannibal. Asked why “he had adopted so dangerous a policy, whereby without an extreme necessity he had almost staked the freedom of Rome, he replied that he had done it because he knew that if he succeeded he would reacquire the glory he had lost in Spain; and if he did not . . . he would have avenged himself against the city and the citizens who had so ungratefully and indiscreetly offended him” (257). Contrary to his conclusion in D 2.33, Machiavelli now suggests that the Romans were not well advised to rely on a general’s concern for his own reputation to make him do what was best under the circumstances, because he might try to enhance or salvage his reputation at the expense of the republic. Machiavelli declared in D 3.1 that a republic would never become corrupt if it had a sufficient number of citizens of outstanding virtue. Now he concludes that because it is impossible to “give a certain remedy for such disorders that arise in republics, it follows that it is impossible to order a perpetual republic, because its ruin is caused through a thousand unexpected ways” (257).156


2. Winning Wars Is Not an Adequate Test (D 3.18–23)


a. Victory May Be a Result of Chance (D 3.18)


In D 3.18 Machiavelli shows that victory on the battlefield is not reliable evidence of a general’s virtue. He suggests that he is going to discuss the attributes or abilities of an excellent “captain” in the title of the chapter, in which he states, “nothing is more worthy of a captain than to foretell the policies of the enemy.” He immediately undercuts that observation, however, not merely by erroneously attributing the saying to Epaminondas (who is one of Machiavelli’s examples of an excellent captain, because he trained unarmed Thebans to become soldiers able to defeat the Spartans). He explicitly observes, “it is not so difficult to understand the plans of the enemy [since a general could think about what he would do if he were in the position of his enemy] as it is sometimes difficult to understand his actions, and not so much actions that are done by him at a distance as ones present and near.” In what is now called “the fog of war” it is often difficult to determine who actually won or lost a battle. The opponents of Julius Caesar did not lose to the superior forces of his supporters, Machiavelli suggests. Cassius despaired when he erroneously believed that Brutus had lost on his wing and committed suicide. Likewise, the part of the Swiss army that remained whole when they confronted the French at Santa Cecilia thought that their forces had won and so remained to fight at a disadvantage the next day rather than retiring to save themselves.157

Machiavelli then gives two examples of equally balanced armies, one ancient and one modern, both of which have withdrawn because neither believes it can win a battle against the other. In both cases the side that accidentally discovers that the other has withdrawn turns around, seizes what spoils it can from the deserted camp of the enemy, and then claims victory. Clearly these “victories” were not proof of the excellence of the captain or his troops. As Machiavelli argues explicitly in a later chapter (D 3.31), victors attribute their good fortune to their virtue and then despair when their fortune changes. But if winning a battle is not necessarily evidence of a captain’s virtue, what is? In all the examples Machiavelli gives in this chapter, the decisive factor was accurate information or knowledge about the condition of one’s own troops as well as that of the enemy. The problem, as he noted at the beginning, is acquiring such knowledge in the midst of a war.


b. Both Harsh and Gentle Modes Work (D 3.19–22)


What, then, makes a good republican “captain” or leader? By asking in the title of D 3.19 “whether to rule a multitude compliance is more necessary than punishment,” Machiavelli indicates that his examination of the characteristics of a virtuous republican “captain” does not apply merely to military organization and leadership, but extends to political leadership more generally. Contrasting the difficulty the cruel Appius had in making his men obey him with the success of the kind and humane Quintius, Machiavelli first concludes “it appears that in governing a multitude, it is better to be humane rather than proud, merciful rather than cruel.” However, he then observes that Cornelius Tacitus, along with many other writers, maintains, on the contrary, “in ruling a multitude, punishment is worth more than compliance” (260).158 In order to “save” both opinions he draws a distinction. A republican “captain” leading an army composed of his fellow citizens, who regard themselves as his equals, cannot rely entirely on punishment or fear to make his men obey. In leading armies of men entirely subject to them, the emperors of whom Tacitus wrote could be harsh. Machiavelli immediately notes an exception to the “rule” he has just announced, however; a republican captain can be harsh and cruel, if he displays the “excessive virtue” of a Manlius Torquatus. In P 19 Machiavelli argued that an emperor like Severus also needed such “excessive virtue” to control both his troops and his people. But he repeats here what he argued in P 19, that even an emperor ought to moderate the cruelty with which he treats his subjects if he is not to become hated, and that he will most effectively avoid becoming hated if he refrains from taking any and every opportunity to seize their property. Readers see that in this section of the Discourses Machiavelli is reexamining in a republican context the question he raised in P 17 of whether it is better for a prince to be loved or feared.

In D 3.20 Machiavelli seems to tip the balance toward humanity or even charity. He reminds his readers how Camillus persuaded the Falisci, who had previously resisted the Romans stubbornly and fiercely, to surrender their town voluntarily by returning—stripped and beaten by his victims—the schoolmaster who had tried to give their children as hostages to the Romans. He then lists other examples of “how much more a humane act full of charity is sometimes able to do . . . than a ferocious and violent act” (261), including the way the liberality of Fabricius expelled Pyrrhus from Italy when Roman arms could not, and Scipio acquired more reputation in Spain from returning a wife to her husband unblemished than from capturing New Carthage. Such acts of humanity are “desired in great men by peoples,” Machiavelli observes; they have been “praised by writers, and by those who describe the life of princes, . . . how they ought to live.” Xenophon, for example, “toils very much to demonstrate how many honors, how many victories, how much good fame being humane and affable brought to Cyrus, and not giving any example of himself either as proud or as cruel, or as lustful, or as having any other vice that stains the life of men” (262).159

In P 14 Machiavelli observed that the Roman republican “captain” Scipio had looked to Xenophon’s depiction of Cyrus as a model. However, in P 17 he argued that Scipio’s charity would have sullied his “fame and glory if he had continued with it in the empire; but while he lived under the government of the Senate, this damaging quality of his not only was hidden, but made for his glory” (68). Perhaps strangely in what would seem to be the republican context of the discussion, Machiavelli does not mention the subordination of the republican captain Scipio to direction and correction by the Senate as a reason he could be kind. As in P 17, so in D 3.21, Machiavelli uses Hannibal’s success in using “cruelty, violence, robbery, and every type of faithlessness” in Italy to “produce the same effect that Scipio had produced in Spain” with his charity to challenge the traditional teaching of “the writers” about what sort of conduct and character is desirable in a “captain” or “prince.”

The first reason the people in both conquered provinces flocked to the conquering general, despite the differences in their modes of proceeding, Machiavelli explains, is that “men are desirous of new things, . . . for [as he observed in D 1.37] . . . men get bored with the good and grieve in the ill.” As he observed in P 3, “this desire makes the doors open to everyone who makes himself head of an innovation in a province” (263).

The second and most fundamental reason is that “men are driven by two principal things, either by love or by fear.” And as Machiavelli had also argued in P 17, “most often whoever makes himself feared is more followed and more obeyed than whoever makes himself loved” (263). Instead of the humanity desired in great men by the people and endorsed by many writers, Machiavelli thus seems to agree with the opinion he attributes to Tacitus and other writers.

Machiavelli first appears to explain the successes Hannibal and Scipio had despite proceeding in opposite ways by the virtue that made them reputed. However, he then concedes that after “his soldiers in Spain rebelled against him, together with part of his friends,” because they did not fear him, “Scipio was constrained to use part of the cruelty he had fled from” (263–64). Machiavelli does not know of any particular incident in which Hannibal’s cruelty and lack of faith hurt him, but he suggests that the Romans insisted on killing him, even after he was unarmed and his army dispersed, because he had been so hateful. Despite this disadvantage, Machiavelli points out, as he did in P 17, that Hannibal’s extraordinary cruelty produced a great advantage, “which is admired by all the writers: that although his army was composed of various kinds of men, no dissension ever arose in it” (264).

Because the successes Hannibal and Scipio enjoyed by employing opposite means might be attributed to their different circumstances—Hannibal was commanding an army composed of many different peoples speaking different languages in a foreign land, whereas Scipio commanded an army composed of his fellow citizens—in D 3.22 Machiavelli takes up a better test case. Manlius Torquatus and Valerius Corvinus both lived in Rome at the same time, displayed equal virtue, and received similar triumphs and glory. In leading their armies, they nevertheless proceeded very differently.

Machiavelli first suggests that neither Manlius nor Valerius should be praised for his virtue, because neither chose to proceed as he did. Manlius was harsh by nature; because only a harsh man can command harsh things, a captain like Valerius, who did not have such a nature, could not imitate Manlius. Valerius could proceed humanely, Machiavelli explains, because the Romans he commanded were still a law-abiding people. Any punishments he inflicted on his men were imputed not to him but to the laws. However, since the willingness of the people in a republic to obey the law depends upon the ability of men like Manlius to return its orders to their beginning by making the people fear punishment, Valerius’s ability to make himself extremely popular with his men by treating them familiarly as equals depended upon conditions established by men like Manlius. Machiavelli declares, “a republic so happy that it often had one who with his example might renew the laws . . . would be perpetual” (266).

Unfortunately, Machiavelli has shown that Manlius could not be imitated by someone who did not share his nature. The emergence of a line of such leaders would thus be a product of unlikely chance.160 Nevertheless he states his belief that “in a citizen who lives under the laws of a republic, the proceeding of Manlius is more praiseworthy and less dangerous, because this mode is wholly in favor of the public and does not in any part have regard for private ambition. For by . . . showing oneself always harsh to everyone and loving only the common good, one . . . does not acquire particular friends for himself, which we call . . . partisans” (267).

Machiavelli acknowledges that Valerius’s mode of proceeding did not hurt the public, but he warns, “because of the particular goodwill that [such a captain] acquires with the soldiers, many doubts resurge as to the bad effects on freedom of a long command” (267). Drawing once again on Xenophon’s description of Cyrus, Machiavelli observes that seeking obedience and love from his soldiers and subjects is an appropriate mode of proceeding for a prince. Contrary to the first impressions of advocates of republican or democratic rule, he thus concludes that Valerius’s mode of treating his men as free and equal is useful in a prince but pernicious in a citizen. It is injurious not only to the fatherland but also to the captain “because those modes prepare the way for tyranny . . . , [and] in suspecting his mode of proceeding, his city is constrained to secure itself against him” (268).

The harsh modes of Manlius may be better for the republic, but, Machiavelli concedes in 3.23, they can hurt the captain. As demonstrated by the Romans’ decision to exile Camillus after he won a great victory over Veii, the people may recognize the virtue of a captain but still hate his severity. Livy reveals three causes for the people’s hatred of Camillus: first, his depositing the money from the sale of the goods of the Veientes in the public treasury rather than distributing it among the soldiers as booty (a policy Machiavelli has praised); second, his having his chariot pulled by four white horses in his triumph, as if he were equal to the sun (for the Romans, a god); and, third, his attempting to take back booty the soldiers had already seized to satisfy a vow he had made to Apollo. In the Prince Machiavelli advised rulers to make themselves feared but not hated and warned them that nothing led people to hate a prince more than his seizing their property. Here he adds a particular warning to republican leaders: free peoples resent signs that their leaders believe that they are better than their fellow citizens, even though such displays of pride and pomp do not cause the people any material harm.161

Machiavelli’s account of the different modes of leadership in a republic thus culminates in a problem. Harsh modes like those of Manlius may be best for a republic, because they make people and soldiers fear to disobey their commanders and the laws. Such harshness is not popular, however; both people and soldiers respond better to humane leadership. The people will come to hate even an admittedly virtuous “captain” like Camillus, not only if he tries to devote property they want to public or pious purposes (and thus keeps them poor), but also if he claims any visible recognition of his superiority or “glory” that does not come from the people. Machiavelli’s lengthy discussion of the best way to rule a multitude thus seems to point toward his praise of “the poverty of Cincinnatus”; he was willing to use harsh means of conquering others, rewarded or punished his inferiors on the basis of their demonstrated merits, and did not seek either to enrich or to glorify himself. However, as Machiavelli announces in the next chapter, the admirable example set by Cincinnatus was not enough to save the Roman republic from eventual destruction. Readers are thus led to ask what policies Machiavelli thinks modern republicans could adopt to prolong the life of such a regime.


D. The Causes of the Fall of the Roman Republic and the Failure of Cincinnatus (D 3.24–25)


The prolongation of commands was, according to Machiavelli, one of the two causes of the dissolution of the Roman republic, along with the Agrarian law. The contention that arose over the Agrarian law was visible to everyone; it culminated in civil war, however, because of the prolongation of commands.162 And, Machiavelli suggests, the importance of this seemingly minor institutional change was not understood by the Romans and has not been appreciated by readers of the histories ever since.

If the Roman patricians had shared the goodness and prudence of Lucius Quintius, who urged the Senate not to follow the bad example set by the plebs in prolonging the commands of the tribunes for a year to enable them better to resist the ambition of the nobles, Machiavelli observes, Rome would have been spared this “inconvenience.”163 When the Senate later agreed to prolong the commands of the consuls, in order to enable them to win victories in distant lands and then return to celebrate their triumph in Rome, he concedes, it was acting for the public utility. But its decision had unanticipated consequences: fewer men had an opportunity to exercise command and so gain a reputation; and the soldiers who served under them gradually became more attached to their commander than to the Senate. As a result, Marius and Sulla could form partisan armies, and Caesar was able to seize the fatherland. As Machiavelli emphasizes in the last chapter of his Discourses, small changes in electoral laws can either preserve or destroy a republic.

Machiavelli argued earlier (D 3.16) that he saw only two remedies for the envy that makes the citizens of republics not recognize their most outstanding citizens in times of peace: keeping everyone poor and constantly preparing for war. And in the central chapter of book 3—arguably the climax—he presents Cincinnatus as an embodiment of the excellence of these policies. Cincinnatus was plowing the fields of his small farm when the legates came to inform him that he had been elected dictator. Showing that he was not able to support himself and his family without working, but that he was still willing to subordinate his private concerns to public needs, he put on his toga and went to lead an army to relieve the beleaguered consul Minucius. After defeating the enemy, Cincinnatus demoted the failed general to a legate and made a man who had been serving on foot because of his poverty master of the horse, on the basis of his demonstrated ability.

Machiavelli thus takes Cincinnatus to exemplify the Romans’ policy of not encouraging the search for wealth by honoring virtue wherever they found it. Generalizing on the basis of the example set by Cincinnatus (and Marcus Regulus, who asked leave from the army to return to look after his own small property), he concludes that “it was enough to those citizens to get honor from war, and everything useful they left to the public.” He goes even further by praising “the greatness of their spirit [that] lifted them above every prince. They did not esteem kings, or republics; northing terrified or frightened them.” Yet “when they later returned to private status, they became frugal, humble, careful of their small competencies, obedient to the magistrates, reverent to their superiors” (272). In addition to the principle of rewarding virtue without regard to wealth, Cincinnatus thus represents the importance of rotation in office, accepting public duties when elected, but relinquishing power when he had accomplished his task.

As Machiavelli has already indicated, however, the virtuous example set by Cincinnatus was not enough to preserve the republic.164 His unwillingness to follow the “bad example” set by the plebs reflected the old aristocratic understanding of the rule of the nobles as based on their superior character. It also reflected the traditional notion that virtuous rulers are educated primarily by means of the virtuous examples set by others. Yet from the beginning of book 3 Machiavelli has been suggesting that this old understanding of the education of leaders primarily through the imitation of virtuous examples (which he himself recommended at the conclusion of P 14) should be replaced by the analysis and understanding of the effects of their deeds (i.e., the “effectual truth” he began presenting in P 15). According to Machiavelli, Cincinnatus was right to object to the prolongation of the commands of the consuls in response to the plebs’ prolongation of the commands of the tribunes. However, he objected for the wrong reasons. He persisted in expressing the arrogance of the nobility; he failed to take account of the need to counter innovations introduced by the opposing humor and did not understand the way in which institutions mold the behavior of the individuals who occupy them, because he found such calculations or “power-grabbing” schemes base. Neither Cincinnatus nor the senators who later prolonged the consuls’ commands understood the effect that prolongation would have on the loyalties of their men and the way these partisan armies would be used in a civil war motivated primarily by economic interests. But now that Machiavelli has explained these things to his readers, new remedies can be devised for the ambition and envy that resulted in the fall of the Roman republic. Those “remedies” consist, first and foremost, in a new kind of education for the politically ambitious.


E. What Machiavelli’s Contemporaries Can Learn from the Romans (D 3.26–34)


As Machiavelli argues explicitly in The Prince with regard to leaders who want to acquire and maintain a principality, so he suggests in the Discourses somewhat more indirectly, leaders who wish to found or reorder a republic need a new kind of education. Praise and blame are not reliable indications of virtue and vice, because people praise what succeeds and blame what fails (P 3). And as he observed in both P 25 and D 3.8, 3.19–22, individuals with opposite characters succeed under different circumstances. Their characters differ, moreover, as a result of their natural inclinations and later experiences.
