It does not make sense, therefore, to try to educate or inculcate those who wish to rule with a given set of virtues—whether those are the classical “cardinal” virtues of courage, moderation, justice, and wisdom or the “theological” virtues of hope, faith, and charity. What those who want to become leaders need to learn are the passions that move human beings and how to direct them.


1. The Source of Tyranny Is Competition for Economic Goods, Not Love of the Beautiful (D 3.26)


Caesar may have grasped the honor he thought that he deserved by force, when neither the Senate nor the people bestowed it upon him voluntarily, as Machiavelli observes in D 1. But, Machiavelli has also argued, Caesar would not have been able to do so if a civil war had not erupted as a result of the contentions over the Agrarian law and the prolongation of commands had not enabled him to form and lead a partisan army.

In the chapter that follows his praise of Cincinnatus, Machiavelli thus reminds his readers that concern about honor (or eros for the noble, to put it in Greek philosophical terms) does not move men in politics as much or as fundamentally as the desire to acquire.165 That was the reason the extraordinary examples set by individual nobles such as Cincinnatus or Regulus could not and did not preserve the Roman republic in the long run. (The deeds of these individuals were honored because they were extraordinary; but precisely because such men and deeds were extraordinary, they were not ordinary or usual on the part of men of their class.)

Earlier in the Discourses Machiavelli minimized, if not simply dismissed, the importance of the rape of Lucretia and the death of Virginia as causes of the deposing of Tarquin and the Decemvirs.166 But in D 3.26 he cites these incidents along with Aristotle’s warning to tyrants against injuring someone on account of women and his own warning to princes not to arouse the antagonism of individuals by taking their women or property (in P 19 and D 3.6) to show how states can be ruined “because of women.” As Machiavelli’s sole reference to Aristotle should remind his readers, the traditional philosophical explanation of the origin of divisions within cities in general, and tyranny in particular, was the excessive and intense desire or eros of human beings.167

Machiavelli challenges the ancient understanding of the source of tyranny, as well as the relative importance of honor and property, in his retelling of the story of the dispute that arose in Ardea concerning the marriage of a rich woman with which he begins both this and the succeeding chapter. In Livy’s version of the story the woman was beautiful and so an erotic object; in Machiavelli’s version it was her inheritance that caused the dissension between her tutors, who wanted her to marry a plebian, and her mother, who wanted a noble alliance. When the entire nobility took up arms in support of the noble, the plebs responded in kind; and after the plebs were defeated, they looked to the Volsci for aid, so the nobles sought assistance from the Romans. The Romans then vanquished the Volsci and restored unity to Ardea by killing all the heads of the sedition.


2. To End Civil Dissension, It Is Necessary to Eliminate the “Heads” (D 3.27)


The conflict that arose in Ardea constitutes an example of the division between the two humors Machiavelli observes in all cities: the opposition between the desire of the grandi or nobili to command and oppress and the desire of the people not to be commanded and oppressed. These humors exist in cities and not simply by nature, because they concern rule. Since those who rule can also seize the property of those they rule, the two humors also correspond loosely to the rich and the poor. However, Machiavelli regards the leaders of the poor who share a desire to command as grandi in aspiration, if not in economic class or explicit political allegiance.168 The “lessons” he presents in how to establish and maintain a free government are thus addressed to such leaders of the people as well as to the nobili as conventionally understood.

Machiavelli’s stated purpose at the beginning of the Discourses is to show his readers what they can learn from reading Livy’s history that will be useful in their own changed circumstances. In book 1 he gradually showed them how the history of the Roman republic illustrated the ways in which institutions and laws could be designed to direct the conflict between the two humors so that it preserved the liberty of all. Because the cooperation between the Roman plebs and patricians was made possible by their joint participation in an imperial policy that culminated in the destruction of liberty everywhere, in book 2 Machiavelli advocated a new kind of expansive foreign policy that would enable republics to preserve their liberty, both internally and externally, by forming a league. In book 3 he is explicitly concentrating on the deeds of individuals and their effects. He suggests that he and his readers can understand the effects of the individual deeds and public policies of both the Romans and his contemporaries better than they did or do themselves, because he and his readers are able to compare past and present.

In D 3.27 Machiavelli thus contrasts the effectiveness of the Roman policy in Ardea with the Florentine belief “that one needed to hold Pistoia with parties and Pisa with fortresses” (275). Machiavelli criticized the use of fortresses to hold cities in both P 20 and D 2.24, because such fortifications led rulers to think that they could oppress the people without worrying about arousing their hatred. In D 2.21 and 2.25, Machiavelli thus praised the Florentines for entering and acquiring control of Pistoia by means of the warring factions. Like the Romans in Capua, the Florentines had not had to conquer Pistoia with force in order to make the city subject to them. When the Florentines tried to rule Pistoia by forcing the two factions there to agree to a peace, however, they discovered that such an externally imposed agreement will not hold where there has been much bloodshed (cf. D 3.7). So the Florentines began removing the heads of the parties, either to prison or to some other place. Eliminating the heads permanently, as the Romans did, “would have been most secure.” But, Machiavelli concludes, “because such executions have in them something of the great and the generous, a weak republic does not know how to do them” (274).

In D 2.23 Machiavelli criticized the traditional Florentine policy of taking “the middle way” by showing the superiority of the Roman policy of either eliminating or embracing subjects they had conquered. His emphasis here is not so much on the problematic results of “certain middle ways” as on the reason his contemporaries adopt such ineffective policies. When “princes of our times . . . have to judge great things,” he concludes, “they ought to wish to hear how those who have had to judge such cases in antiquity governed themselves, but the weakness of men at present, caused by their weak education . . . makes them judge ancient judgments in part inhuman, in part impossible” (274–75). In his Discourses Machiavelli is trying to provide republican leaders of his time with a “strong” education to replace the “weak education” they have received by showing them it is possible not merely to imitate the ancients, but even to surpass them. And, we see, many of the “lessons” he delivers to aspiring republican “princes” in the second half of book 3 of the Discourses have a great deal in common with those he presented to “princes” in The Prince. Here, for example, the reasons he suggests that it is best to eliminate the leaders of the factions of a city that has been torn apart by a civil war parallel those he gave to a prince who has conquered a new territory to eliminate the bloodline of the old prince (P 3) and to use “cruelty” well (P 8) by using it all at once to establish order and not continuing to use it to oppress the people.


3. Competition for Office Must Be through Public Rather Than Private Means (D 3.28–29)


In D 3.28 Machiavelli suggests that his contemporaries could learn from the Romans how to deal with class conflict not only in cities they acquire but also in Florence itself. He reminds them that “when the city of Rome was overburdened with hunger, and public provisions were not enough to stop it, one Spurius Maelius, who was very rich” (276), sought to buy the favor of the plebs by providing them with grain privately. But seeing the “inconvenience” that could arise from his liberality, the Senate appointed a dictator (Cincinnatus, although Machiavelli does not name him) who had Spurius killed. As in foreign policy, so in governing their own city, a prince or political class who understands the art of government should know how to deal with ambitious men who seek to lead a popular insurrection. As Machiavelli observed in D 1.44, “a multitude without a head is useless.”

In D 3.8 Machiavelli stated that, like Manlius Capitolinus, Spurius failed to overthrow the republic because the Roman people were not yet corrupt. But here and in the following chapter Machiavelli maintains that Spurius failed because the leaders of the republic then understood how to counter such a threat. Just as he observed in D 1.21 that “if where there are men there are no soldiers, it arises through a defect of the prince,” so he argues more generally in D 3.29 that “the sins of peoples arise from princes,” through their negligence or errors. In other words, the corruption or incorruption of a people depends upon whether their leaders see what is needed to order (or organize) them.

As Machiavelli suggested in his account of the fall of the Decemvirs in D 1.40–45, the preservation of a republic depends upon its having a political class or elite who know how to rule by sharing honors or offices with the plebs and checking the ambition of anyone who seeks to become a tyrant by flattering or otherwise acquiring popular favor. So he declares here, “A republic without reputed citizens cannot stand, nor can it be governed well in any mode.” But “the reputation of citizens” or the ambition of these “reputed citizens” to become first among their peers, as he argued in D 1.46, is also the cause of the tyranny of republics. To “regulate this thing,” he now explains, a city needs to be ordered so that citizens are reputed for acts that help and do not hurt the city and its freedom. And to institute and maintain such an order, it is necessary to distinguish the two ways in which citizens gain reputation: public and private. A city that wants to retain a republican form of government should make it possible for individuals to gain reputation only by giving good counsel and working for the common benefit. Private ways of benefiting this or that private individual “by lending him money, marrying his daughters for him, defending him from the magistrates, and doing for him similar favors that make men partisans to oneself and encourage whoever is so favored to corrupt the public and to breach the laws” should be closed. Rome rewarded public ways of acquiring a reputation by honoring individuals who worked for the common good and closed the private ways of acquiring a reputation by means of public accusations. “And if these were not enough, because the people was blinded by a species of false good, it ordered [the creation] of a dictator,” as it did to counter the danger posed by Spurius Maelius.

Although Machiavelli does not mention it here, these were the measures he criticized Soderini for not taking against the Medici in D 3.4. Nor does Machiavelli explain, as he does later in his Florentine Histories, that both Cosimo de’ Medici and his grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent used the “private modes” of “acquiring a reputation” he lists to acquire tyrannical power in what was nominally a republic in Florence.169 But his immediate audience would surely recognize the implicit references.

To force ambitious “princes” to compete for office through public means is, in effect, to force them to serve the interests of their people in general. Those interests, Machiavelli reminds his young readers in D 3.29, are in securing their individual lives, families, and properties from those who would illegally seize them for their own benefit. The weakness of modern Italian governments is not the fault of the people, Machiavelli insists. It flows from the failure of Italian “princes” to understand the “art of government,” which consists in eliminating those who would undermine the legal order and benefiting those whose support it needs.

Machiavelli indicates that some of the weakness of modern Italian governments can be attributed to their “weak” Christian education (as he characterized it in D 2.2) by writing about “the sins” of princes and peoples. But in D 3.29 he insists that the slaughter and pillage that occurred in provinces like the Romagna before Pope Alexander VI eliminated the lords who commanded there arose “not from the wicked nature of men, as they used to say” (presumably when “they” talked about “original sin”), but from the “sins” of princes.170 Because these princes wanted to live like the rich, they made laws they themselves did not obey or enforce, except to collect penalties from other nonobservers. In P 7 Machiavelli explained that Alexander VI’s illegitimate son Cesare Borgia brought good government to the Romagna by giving a cruel man, Remirro de Orco, full power to pacify and unite the province, in effect, by eliminating the impotent lords. But judging that such excessive authority was not necessary and might become hateful, after his competitors were eliminated Cesare set up a civil court and made the execution of Remirro a ferocious spectacle that left the people both satisfied and stupefied. Here he concludes by citing the behavior of a pirate who piously allowed the Romans to deliver the booty of the Veientes to Apollo as an example of Lorenzo de’ Medici’s restatement of the traditional idea “that which the lord does, many do later.” By piously building churches, Machiavelli slyly suggests, the last great Medici lord not merely sought to justify his family’s proclivity to seek wealth for themselves and impoverish the public. He and his family also encouraged others to put a pious cover on their own attempts to enrich themselves.


4. How to Solve the Problem of Envy (D 3.30)


In D 3.30 Machiavelli returns to the problem of envy, which he now makes clear is characteristic not of the people as a whole, but particularly of those who compete with a leader for reputation and position. As in D 3.1 he uses the elevation of Camillus after the French seizure of Rome to show how that envy is eliminated “through some strong and difficult accident in which each, seeing himself perishing, puts aside every ambition and runs voluntarily to obey him who he believes can free him with his virtue.” But here (in contrast to his account of the problem of envy and the only possible responses to it in D 3.16) Machiavelli explains the willingness of other tribunes to subordinate themselves to Camillus not simply by the external danger, but by his having demonstrated his willingness to administer the office of dictator “for public usefulness and not for his own utility” (279) three times before. Because they had seen him relinquish power repeatedly, as required by law, Camillus’s colleagues did not fear his greatness or feel it shameful to be his inferior. Such willingness on the part of exceptionally talented leaders to cede power, often to their opponents, at the conclusion of their term of office is absolutely essential, if a republican form of government is to be maintained. And, Machiavelli suggests, the only way to achieve the necessary rotations in office is by repeated examples of it that shape the expectations of both leading politicians and their people.

The other way to overcome envy is when “those who have been your competitors in coming to some reputation die” either by violence or natural causes. In a virtuous city organized as Machiavelli recommended in book 1, these competitors would vie with the popular favorite to show that they can better serve the public. But “men used to living in a corrupt city [like Florence], where the education has not produced any goodness in them,” compete for office more through private than through public means, and the opponents of those in power “would be content to see the ruin of their fatherland” rather than allow another citizen to rise above them. “To conquer this envy there is no remedy other than the death of those who have it.”171

So if a virtuous leader is not fortunate enough to see his competitors die naturally, he will be forced, as “whoever reads the Bible judiciously” sees that Moses was, “to kill infinite men who, moved by nothing other than envy, were opposed to his plans” (280).172 By contrasting Friar Girolamo Savonarola and Piero Soderini with Moses, Machiavelli points to the way in which Christianity makes modern leaders weak, not so much the priests themselves, who he has already claimed do not believe their own doctrines (D 3.1), as the laymen who adhere to the faith. Both Savonarola and Soderini recognized the necessity of eliminating their competitors. However, as a priest and not officially a prince with the power of the sword, the first did not have the authority to enable him to do it. And he was not understood by those who followed him, even though he railed against the “wise of the world” in his sermons.173 The second “believed that he could overcome as many as were opposed to him through envy without any scandal, violence, and tumult. He did not know that . . . goodness is not enough.” Machiavelli does not repeat the suggestion he made in D 1.49 that Savonarola and Soderini should both have used popular courts to accuse their enemies and defend themselves. (His reason may be that in citing the way the Romans dealt with the threat posed by Spurius, he has suggested that a popular court might not have been sufficient; it would have been necessary to appoint a dictator.) He concludes simply that both of them “were ruined, and their ruin was caused by not having known how or having been able to conquer this envy” (280).

By returning to the example of Camillus, who “never permitted a multitude to take up arms except with a certain order” (281), Machiavelli suggests that Savonarola and Soderini both failed to overcome the problem of envy because they did not select and train a group of armed men to enforce their decrees on those who opposed them. Both counted on the support of the people but allowed the people to remain a disorderly mob they could not reliably control. Savonarola did not remain in power long enough for his subordinate to organize the militia as he intended; and Soderini faced the opposition of many of the other ottimati when Machiavelli tried to convince him to sponsor the organization of a militia.


5. Military Training as a Mode of Moral Education (D 3.31–33)


In D 3.31 Machiavelli observes that not merely virtuous captains like Camillus but the Roman people as a whole were able to maintain their courage and dignity in defeat as well as in victory because they were well trained and educated. He contrasts them with the modern Venetians, who became so insolent in good fortune that they imagined themselves superior to the king of France and the Church, but then became so cowardly and abject after their luck deserted them that “they not only lost all their state by rebellion but gave a good part of it to the pope and to the king of Spain” (282). Pointing back to The Prince, he states, “although it was said another time that the foundation of all states is a good military, and that where this does not exist there can be neither good laws nor any other good thing, it does not appear to me superfluous to repeat it.” Once again he emphasizes the dependency of the rule of law on the ability to enforce it. At every point Roman history demonstrates this necessity, “and one sees that the military cannot be good unless it is trained, and that it cannot be trained unless it is composed of your subjects.” Money or “private means” alone will not suffice to obtain the loyalty and service of armed men; as Machiavelli urged in P 9, the people must be made to see that they need the government of the prince to secure themselves from oppression.

Machiavelli again uses Camillus as his example of a prince who understood the importance of training men he selected to bear arms. He was able to encourage troops dismayed by the superior numbers of the enemy by reminding them of their past victories and observing that “what anyone has learned or is accustomed to, he will do” (283). As Machiavelli repeatedly observes, most people have difficulty imagining that things can be different from what they see around them; they are persuaded primarily by what they have experienced.

By the weak education of modern republicans, Machiavelli also indicates, he refers to more than their lack of military training. Because anyone “who governs himself like” the Venetians will become insolent in good fortune and abject in bad, a good education will not merely enable a people to govern itself better; it will also make an individual “a better knower of the world” (like the author of the Discourses) who will “rejoice less in the good and be less aggrieved with the bad” (283).

Machiavelli recognizes that leaders like Moses, Savonarola, and Soderini, who wish to bring new laws and thus found a new regime, do not need merely to eliminate the opposition. They must also obtain and maintain popular support. Training a militia is one but not the only way to do so. Another way, Machiavelli suggests in D 3.32, is to implicate a large number of people in the “crime” of rebellion so that they will resist any attempt to restore the old order from fear of punishment. This policy is the flip side of Machiavelli’s earlier advice to a captain to do whatever he can to make it necessary for his troops to fight but easy for the enemy to surrender. It is nevertheless a policy of desperation.174 Much better to follow the example of Camillus by showing oneself to be virtuous—ordered, solicitous, and spirited, upholding the majesty of his rank, punishing errors and upholding his promises to the people—and giving one’s followers confidence by showing them an easy way to victory and making light of possible obstacles.

Having suggested that the weakness of modern republics can be attributed in part to the Christian education of their leaders (as he did in 2.2), in D 3.33 Machiavelli acknowledges that the Romans used religion to give their armies confidence. However, as in his first comparison of the political use and consequences of ancient and modern religion in D 1.11–15, Machiavelli again argues that the Romans relied more on the quality of their generals and the training of the men than on such “little things” as auguries. With a history of success a leader like Fabius (who was able to lead the Romans through the previously impenetrable Ciminian forest, according to Livy 9.36, partly because his brother knew the local dialect and could learn the way without alerting the locals, D 2.33) could simply claim to have secret (but not necessarily supernatural) knowledge. As in his discussion of the effects of the governments of the first three Roman kings, Machiavelli concludes that whether citizens are trained to be soldiers who have confidence (or faith) in themselves and their captain depends much more on the prince and his knowledge of the art of government than on their religious beliefs.


6. Why Glory Is Not Always a Reward for Public Service (D 3.34)


The best way to acquire and maintain popular support, however, is through elections. In D 3.34 Machiavelli thus returns to a question he explicitly sidestepped in D 1.60 when he acknowledged that Valerius Corvinus’s claim that the Romans made the consulate “the ward of virtue, not of blood” would be very much disputed. The people may be able to distinguish good from vile individual candidates, as he maintained in D 1.47, and be less variable, imprudent, and ungrateful than a prince in distributing offices, as he argued in D 1.58; but this does not mean that the people recognize or reward true virtue. Like princes, Machiavelli observes, the people award offices to young men because of their family and friends, when they do not have actual deeds with which to judge an individual. Although deeds of extraordinary virtue (or difficulty) provide a better basis of judgment than family, and people can be as well advised as princes are about the relative merits and faults of individual candidates, Machiavelli also shows that the deeds that most impress people are more excessive and extraordinary than truly virtuous or beneficial to the republic.

Machiavelli uses the examples of the alternative modes of ruling harshly or humanely he described earlier to make his point without stating it directly. Although he has declared his belief that Manlius’s harsh modes were more praiseworthy and less dangerous for a republic than the humane modes of Valerius, he now reminds his readers that Manlius first acquired reputation and office by threatening a tribune with death unless he withdrew the accusation he had lodged against Manlius’s father. Manlius may thus have demonstrated his filial piety, but his act also constituted a challenge to the public accusations of leading figures that Machiavelli has argued serve to maintain the liberty of the republic, if not an outright violation of the law. Likewise, in the battle with the Frenchman from whom he took the collar of gold and thus acquired the name of Torquatus, Manlius risked the entire fortune of the Roman army on less than its whole force, “a thing altogether rash” (294) and a policy Machiavelli argued was unwise in D 1.23. Finally, although his killing of his son for fighting and winning a battle contrary to his orders may have made the Roman troops more obstinate, both Livy and Machiavelli attribute the victory Manlius won against the Latins as much if not more to his prudence in keeping his triari in reserve until the troops of the enemy were tired. Machiavelli observes, however, that “these three actions gave him more name and made him more celebrated for all centuries than did any triumph and any other victory, . . . [because] in those victories Manlius had very many like him [and] in these particular actions he had either very few or no one” (288).175 In other words, Machiavelli shows, the people do not reward individual leaders with reputation or “glory” so much for their public service as for their extraordinary deeds. Likewise, he points out, all his triumphs did not bring Scipio the Elder “so much glory as having defended his father on the Ticino while still a boy, and after the defeat at Cannae, when with drawn sword he spiritedly made many young Romans swear that they would not abandon Italy.” And “that opinion of him was further increased when he sent back the daughter to her father and the wife to her husband in Spain [with her chastity intact]” (289). Finally, admitting that the people might be tempted to elect someone inadequate, Machiavelli emphasizes the ability of any citizen to bring out the candidate’s defects in a public council and win glory by doing so, as Fabius Maximus did when the people were moving toward making Titus Ottacilius consul. He does not remind his readers that in D 1.53 he argued that “many times the people desires its own ruin, deceived by a false appearance of the good,” and that Fabius was unable “to persuade the Roman people that it would be useful . . . to proceed slowly in that war” (106). Because the people prefer spirited to cautious policies, the Romans did not follow Fabius’s sage advice, but made Varro consul “through no merits of his other than to have promised . . . to break Hannibal” (107); and he lost the battle of Cannae, which might have resulted in the destruction of Rome.

Machiavelli contends that the people should be the final judge of both laws and individuals, because they seek outcomes that benefit most people most of the time. The people do not understand the causes of the effects they desire, however, and they confuse the rare with the excellent. Individuals who wish to establish new republican modes and orders need to understand not only what impresses the people and gets their support, but also that popular judgments of both individuals and policies tend to be erroneous in predictable ways. Those who share such an understanding will not be surprised to see the people make bad choices; they will try to devise strategies and design institutions to counteract dangerous popular tendencies. They will establish laws that allow them to live secure rather than seek reputation or glory from their contemporaries, who are apt to envy them (see D 2.Pref.), and hope that their achievements will be appreciated by later writers (D 1.10) who will celebrate the effects of their deeds.


F. The Education Machiavelli Offers Future Leaders of Republics (D 3.35–49)


1. The Danger of Putting Oneself at the Head of a New Endeavor That Concerns the Welfare of All, and the Role of an Advisor (D 3.35)


Machiavelli calls attention to the dangerous character of his own enterprise (as described in the prefaces to books 1 and 2) in D 3.35 when he discusses “what dangers are borne in making oneself head in counseling a thing.” Like Fabius, he begins by claiming to have knowledge he cannot communicate: “How dangerous a thing it is to make oneself head of a new thing that pertains to many, and how difficult it is to treat it and to lead it, and when led, to maintain it, would be too long and too high a matter to discourse of.” Machiavelli has been discussing just this matter since the beginning of book 3 when he introduced the example of Brutus, if not for the entire Discourses; but he has been doing so indirectly rather than directly. Instead of detailing the dangers his young readers will encounter should they try to act on his advice (which would clearly discourage them from doing so), he limits himself to explaining the dangers a counselor faces when he makes himself head of a grave and important decision in advising a prince (and so highlights his own role as “head”). As at the beginning of the Discourses, he acknowledges that an advisor will never receive all the honor for a great achievement. But, he now warns, “since men judge things by the end,” the advisor will be blamed if not killed should the policy he recommends fail.176 However, an advisor who does not tell a prince or republic what he thinks would be useful fails to perform his office. Nor can he secure his safety by remaining silent, because, as Machiavelli urged in D 3.2, in a short time he will become suspect. Out of a concern for his own and his readers’ safety, Machiavelli explicitly recommends moderation, for the only time in either The Prince or the Discourses. He advises a counselor to state his “opinion and defend it without passion, . . . so that if the city or the prince follows it, it follows voluntarily, and it does not appear to enter upon it drawn by your importunity” (291). The advisor may thus avoid blame. He will not acquire all the glory of a success, in any case, because he will not be the one who carries out his suggestion; but he may attain a certain kind of glory, if those who act contrary to his advice fail. Machiavelli’s advocacy of moderation here would appear to contradict what he said at the conclusion of the preface to book 2 about his being spirited in pointing out the vices of his contemporaries and recommending imitation of the virtue of the Romans to inspire his young readers. What he indicates at the end of his Discourses is that he has combined a certain kind of audacity (D 3.44) with a certain amount of reserve (D 3.45) in presenting a new understanding of republican politics merely as an “imitation” of the Romans, whom he not only praises but also criticizes.


2. Training Is Stronger Than Nature (D 3.36)


Reiterating some of the most fundamental principles he announced earlier in the Discourses, Machiavelli points to the thoroughly untraditional character of the education he is offering those who deserve to be princes in the last fourteen chapters. He begins in D 3.36 by asserting that training is more powerful than nature (cf. D 1.1, 1.21; also AW 2.167, 6.12–18, 7.1–3). Contrasting the French, who enter battle furiously but fade because of their lack of order, with the ordered virtue of the Romans and the complete lack of either spirit or order among contemporary Italians, he observes that many believe that the French are this way by nature. He does as well, but he asserts that does not mean that their nature “cannot be ordered with art so that it maintains them ferocious to the last” (292).

Claiming “everyone understands with the testimony of Titus Livy how a good military ought to be made,” Machiavelli quotes “the words of Papirius Cursor, when he wanted to punish Fabius, master of the horse” (293). Papirius contended that not merely all military discipline but all reverence for the gods would be lost if a soldier who disobeyed an order from his commander were not summarily executed. Contrasting this harsh message with the practices of contemporary Italians, Machiavelli does not remind his readers that Livy also shows (8.31–36) that Papirius did not persuade either his soldiers or the Roman people—even though Papirius appealed to the precedents established by Brutus and Manlius Torquatus in killing their own sons, precedents Machiavelli also seems at times to valorize. Indeed, Livy shows that Papirius came close to provoking a mutiny among his soldiers and popular rebellion in Rome, and that he was able to resume successful command of the army only after he resorted to a more humane policy.

In D 3.1 Machiavelli included “the execution of Papirius Cursor against his master of the cavalrymen Fabius” along with the deaths of the sons of Brutus and Manlius Torquatus among the “executions” that brought the Roman republic back to its beginnings by arousing fear of disobeying the law along with respect for religion and its esteemed citizens. However, he has subsequently shown that humane policies can win a “captain” as much glory as the excessively harsh measures used by Manlius Torquatus (D 3.22). Such excessive punishments and individual sacrifices do not always constitute the best policies for a republic (D 3.33–34), even though they impress the people more than a string of victories and so make the individuals famous. He concluded his discussion of the ways “to make the army confident both among themselves and in the captain,” moreover, by recommending a means used by Fabius. In three of the last five chapters in the Discourses, he again explicitly argues that policies later adopted by the rebellious master of the horse should be emulated.

Machiavelli recommends the harsh discipline and orders of the Romans in contrast to the weak and vacillating policies characteristic of his Christian contemporaries, but he does not recommend Roman policies unambiguously or without qualification. On the contrary, with his praise of Fabius in the concluding chapters of both books 2 and 3, he points to the importance of doing what no one previously thought was possible and, more specifically, of recognizing the effects small changes in the law can have.


3. How Troops Should Be Trained—or People Educated (D 3.37–38)


Taking up the question of how troops should be trained, especially to face a new enemy, in D 3.37 Machiavelli shows that he is not simply recommending the policies of either Manlius Torquatus or Valerius Corvinus. Machiavelli has already repeatedly declared that it is foolish to risk the fate of an entire army or city by using less than one’s entire force, the way Manlius gained his name by deciding a battle through single combat with a Frenchman. Now he explains that Valerius’s attempt to make his troops confident by fighting small battles could have backfired by discouraging them had they lost. By praising Marius, the partisan captain of the plebs, for encouraging his troops by letting them see their fearsome enemies in disarray, Machiavelli reminds his young readers that he has also shown them that the forces they will have to fight (the Church and the Medici) are disunited and weak. By arguing in D 3.38 that “a captain in whom his army can have confidence” is one who, like Gracchus the Roman and Epaminondas the Theban, trains slaves to become soldiers capable of winning their own freedom, by accustoming them to obedience and order in mock battles (which they cannot lose and so become discouraged) so that he can “put them to work with the greatest confidence in true fighting” (297), Machiavelli also points to the way he has been “training” his readers in the Discourses. He teaches us the causes of military and political successes and failures by leading us through “mock battles” (without risk of failing) about the reasons why the Romans generally won and his contemporaries have so often failed.


4. The Knowledge a “Captain” Needs to Train His Troops (D 3.39)


When Machiavelli turns in D 3.39 to discuss the kind of knowledge a “captain” needs in order to train or educate others to win their own freedom, he seems to duplicate part of a similar discussion in P 14. There he declared that “a prince should have no other object, nor any other thought, nor take anything else as his art but that of war,” and explained that this art is learned in two modes: with deeds and with the mind. Hunting was the way in which a prince would not only keep himself and his men fit, but also enable them to learn the countryside. They would exercise their minds by reading about the actions of excellent men in the histories. Here he states more modestly that “among the other things that are necessary to a captain of armies is the knowledge of sites and of countries, for without this general and particular knowledge a captain of armies cannot work anything well. Because all the sciences demand practice if one wishes to possess them perfectly” (297–98), both a captain and his troops need practice, and the practice through which this particular knowledge is acquired is hunting. However, both the examples he gives of what can be learned in this way come from (and thus presuppose) a reading of the histories (under Machiavelli’s direction); and both emphasize the way in which a “captain” can use his knowledge to deceive his enemies.177

In The Prince Machiavelli emphasized the good or bad use of force or “cruelty,” because he was urging his immediate addressee to organize an army to seize Italy and free it from the barbarians. In the Discourses he is addressing young Florentines who will have to conspire against the ruling powers, not only the Medici in Florence but also the Church in Rome, if they want to revive republican government. So in D 3.40 he generalizes his discussion of the benefits of learning the countryside by hunting by maintaining “that to use fraud in managing war is a glorious thing” (299). His extension of that argument to the reasons why neither a prince nor a citizen of a republic needs to abide by his promises or keep faith in D 3.41 and 3.42 thus has a double reference.


5. How Republican Leaders Should Keep Faith (D 3.40–42)


Machiavelli begins D 3.40 by voicing the noble opinion that “the use of fraud in every action is detestable.” But Machiavelli’s advice to princes, whether actual or potential, does not conform to traditional understandings of “nobility.” He admits that breaking faith may enable someone to acquire a state or kingdom: in D 2.13 he argued that it is necessary and sometimes sufficient to use fraud for that purpose, but here he insists that it will never acquire glory for you, unless you use it against an enemy for the purpose of waging war. He cites the example of the Samnite captain who led the Romans into an ambush at the Caudine Forks by hiding his troops in the mountains and then sending some of his soldiers dressed as shepherds with a large herd into the plain to tell the Romans, when asked, that the Samnite army was occupied with a siege elsewhere. The Samnite victory over the Romans would have been glorious, he explains, if the captain had followed his father’s advice either to let the Romans save themselves freely or to kill them all. However, he took the middle way, “which neither wins friends nor removes enemies” (Livy, 9.3), by forcing the Romans to make peace on dishonorable terms or be massacred, and lost all of the advantages that he might have gained.178

In D 3.41 Machiavelli reports that a legate convinced the Romans to save the army and accept the dishonorable terms by pointing out that the army could remove the ignominy by fighting another day, but if the army were destroyed, Rome and its freedom would be lost, even if the men died gloriously. This advice should be “noted and observed by any citizen who finds himself counseling his fatherland,” Machiavelli emphasizes. “For where one deliberates entirely on the safety of his fatherland, there ought not to enter any consideration of either just or unjust, merciful or cruel, praiseworthy or ignominious, indeed every other concern put aside . . . to follow the policy that saves its life and maintains its liberty” (301).179 There will be no justice, mercy, or glory for any citizen if the polity is destroyed.

Despite what he said about its not being glorious to “break faith given and pacts made” in D 3.40, Machiavelli makes it clear in D 3.42 that he does not think that individuals should worry about not keeping their word or abiding by their oaths. Initially he argues that “promises made through force ought not to be observed,” because “when the force is lacking, forced promises that regard the public will always be broken and it will be without shame for whoever breaks them” (302).180 But then he extends his observation to all promises “among princes, . . . when the causes that made them promise are lacking” (302). To discover whether such behavior is praiseworthy, he refers his readers to P 18, where he suggested that a prince can always find a reason not to keep his word. In D 1.59 he observed that republics do not keep faith with others any more or better than princes; they simply act more slowly.

In D 3.43 Machiavelli underlines the relevance of this advice to his dedicatees by pointing out, in the guise of blaming the French for their faithlessness, that the Florentines have repeatedly proved themselves to be too credulous. As a result, they have repeatedly been disappointed in their attempts to buy arms from the French. Machiavelli has just reminded his readers that “princes” can always find a reason not to abide by their agreements—unless they are forced to do so. Without their own arms, the Florentines have not been able to force the French (or the German emperor) to deliver the services or cities they promised.


6. How Human Nature Is Shaped (D 3.43–45)


At the beginning of D 3.43 Machiavelli seems to be emphasizing not only the constancy of human nature but also the utility of studying ancient history when he observes:. “Prudent men are accustomed to say, and not by chance or without merit, that whoever wishes to see what has to be considers what has been; for all worldly things in every time have their own counterpart in ancient times, . . . because these are the work of men, who have and always had the same passions, and they must of necessity result in the same effect” (302). As he noted in the preface to book 2, these “works are more virtuous now in this province than in that,” and he now explains that they vary according to the form of education the people in question have adopted. The Florentines have suffered because they have been badly educated. The problem with their education is not simply that it is Christian, however; the French are Christians as well. The problem, as Machiavelli emphasizes in The Prince, is that the Florentines have not known how to fight—either by using bestial modes of force and fraud or by using the more human means, laws. He is trying to teach his young readers how to employ all three.

As in his account of the way in which a conspirator can obtain the cooperation of others by forcing them to decide to act with or against him on the spot, without time for deliberation, so Machiavelli argues in D 3.44 that “one often obtains with impetuosity and audacity what one would never have obtained through ordinary modes” (304). Julius II again provides him with his central example. But in D 3.45 Machiavelli reasserts (as he did in D 2.16 and 3.11) that it is a better policy to be able “to resist the thrust of enemies and, having resisted it, to charge them.” In particular, Machiavelli points out that by resisting the enemy but reserving his strength until the enemy had lost its first ardor for combat, Fabius fared much better than did his fellow consul. Decius “exhausted himself in his first thrusts, so that seeing his band of men turned around, . . . he sacrificed himself to the Roman legions in imitation of his father, so as to acquire with death, the glory he had been unable to attain with victory” (305–6).

The contrast Machiavelli draws here between Fabius and Decius is the same as that he and Livy both drew between Manlius Torquatus and the elder Decius in the decisive battle with the Latins (cf. D 2.16, Livy 8.6–11). The difference is that in this case the more prudent policy is not associated with a harsh punishment. Machiavelli uses the difference in this context to indicate that true virtue consists not in pious self-sacrifice of the kind that won individual Romans much glory, but in devising prudent policies that serve to preserve a republic without risking one’s own life.

In imitating his father, Decius provides Machiavelli with an example of the way not merely cities but specific families within cities inculcate certain traits by forming the opinions and habits of their young at an early age. “These things cannot arise solely from the bloodline,” Machiavelli points out in D 3.46, “because that must vary through the diversity of marriages” (306). In other words, the “nobility” of the families who ruled Florence (like that of the patrician families who ruled Rome) was not inherent or a product of their nature. The dominant traits of the noble families were passed on by means of a certain kind of training or education; and by emphasizing the example of the Appii, Machiavelli suggests that the dominant characteristic produced by their “noble” education was arrogance. The source of that arrogance was the claim to have a better origin or beginning that not merely entitled the “nobles” to rule, but made them unwilling to submit to the will of the people, despite the goodness and humanity an “infinite” number of ordinary citizens had acquired by obeying the laws and respecting the auspices.


7. Fabius Rullianus as the Exemplary Republican Prince (D 3.45–49)


To be sure, the two Decii represent better examples of nobility than the Appii; in D 3.1 Machiavelli included them among the “rare and virtuous examples” that had produced almost the same effect as public executions in returning the republic to its beginnings. Yet in D 3.45 Machiavelli argues that Fabius, the master of the horse who defied Papirius Cursor’s command not to fight while he traveled to Rome to check the auspices, and later won another great victory by marching through the Ciminian forest, contrary to the Senate’s command (D 2.33), represents a better because more prudent form of republican leadership.

And in D 3.47 Machiavelli puts Fabius forward again as an example for all those who seek to be held good citizens, because he agreed, when consul, to allow the Senate to send Papirius Cursor as dictator against the Samnites. In D 1.34 Machiavelli praised the Roman policy of requiring the consuls to approve the appointment of a dictator, because the consuls were the officials particularly shamed by the need to create a superior commanding officer. But in this case, Fabius was agreeing not merely to the Senate’s determination that it was necessary to appoint a superior, but to the appointment of the individual who had tried to execute Fabius the last time he served under him as dictator (and who would now be in a position to order such an execution again, if he chose). Machiavelli indicates, however, that Fabius did not merely “turn the other cheek.” On the contrary, “by being silent and in many other modes he gave sign that such a nomination grieved him” (307). The kind of republican virtue Machiavelli is advocating is no more Christian than it is classically Roman. Fabius did not forgive or forget the wrong Papirius would have done him, but his “charity” for his fatherland was stronger than his own desire for personal revenge or his fear that his old enemy would act on the basis of that same desire. He understood that, as Machiavelli announced in D 3.42, “where one deliberates entirely on the safety of his fatherland, there ought not to enter any consideration of just or unjust, merciful or cruel, praiseworthy or ignominious,” because one’s own life and honor depend above all on the preservation of the polity.

Fabius did not disguise his unhappiness at the appointment of Papirius Cursor as dictator. But, Machiavelli has made it clear, his understanding of republican virtue does not preclude the use of fraud. Indeed, he declared in D 3.40, “to use fraud in managing war is a glorious thing.” That is why he warns his readers in D 3.48, “when one sees a great error made by an enemy, one ought to believe that there is a deception underneath” (307). In the first of his three examples Machiavelli explains that an unnamed Roman legate correctly suspected a trap when some Tuscan shepherds approached their camp. He does not explicitly contrast this legate’s reasonable doubt with the way in which Spurius Postumius let himself be deceived by the Samnites at the Caudine Forks (a use of fraud for which Machiavelli praised the Samnite captain). Nor does Machiavelli explain that the legate uncovered the deception on the basis of his knowledge of the Tuscan language, the same kind of knowledge that enabled Fabius to march through the Ciminian forest. Instead, as Strauss points out, Machiavelli restates his reasonable warning as an absolute rule, “that a captain of armies ought not to put faith in an error that the enemy is evidently seen to make, for fraud will always be underneath it, as it is not reasonable that men be so incautious” (308, emphasis added). Then he gives an example, the central example, which belies the absolute rule. As the “French” who had defeated the Romans at Allia learned when they found the gates of Rome open and the city undefended, the enemy sometimes makes errors because he panics (or, as Machiavelli showed in D 3.18, is misinformed). As Strauss points out, Machiavelli often overstates or exaggerates a point, only to qualify the same point later. That is, he argues dialectically. So Machiavelli shows here in his third example that it is reasonable to suspect double-dealing on the part of an enemy who openly consorts with both sides.181

More important, we see the way in which Machiavelli qualifies his own earlier statements in the final chapter of the book. In D 3.1 Machiavelli argued that public trials or “executions” of individuals suspected of trying to overthrow the republic are necessary every five to ten years in order to renew the fear people have of disobeying the law. But in the final chapter of his book Machiavelli declares that “a republic has need of new acts of foresight every day if one wishes to maintain it free” (308).

Those “acts of foresight” first appear to be public trials and punishments of multitudes rather than a few outstanding individuals. Machiavelli begins by reminding his readers that, as he argued earlier (D 1.6, 3.1), every city or mixed body tends to become corrupt. So he states here, “it is of necessity . . . that in a great city accidents arise every day that have need of a physician” to devise a “remedy” or “cure” for the disease. The examples he gives of such corruption in Rome were the conspiracy of Roman women to poison their husbands and the conspiracy of the Bacchanals during the Macedonian war in which thousands of men and women were involved.182 Both of these examples involved private crimes instigated by women that the authorities believed would undermine public order. Machiavelli does not note the sexual origin, however; instead he emphasizes the number of people the Romans were willing and able to punish. “For if the greatness of that republic and the power of its executions had not been seen by infinite other signs, it is seen through the kinds of penalty that it imposed on whoever erred.” Not limiting itself to private crimes, the Roman republic did not “hesitate to have killed by way of justice an entire legion at once, and a city, and to banish eight or ten thousand” (309) soldiers defeated at Cannae to Sicily where they were not allowed to reside in town or eat sitting down.

Of all the executions, the Roman policy of decimating the armies was most terrible (and, therefore, most effective). When a multitude errs and it is not evident which particular individuals are responsible (for if it were, they would simply eliminate the heads), it is not possible to punish them all and it would be wrong to punish a part and leave the others (possibly guilty) unpunished. To choose to punish a tenth of them by lot when all deserve it makes those who are killed regret their fate and the others fear that they will be punished if they err again.183

But at this point in the final chapter Machiavelli’s argument takes a surprising turn. He concludes that the poisoners and Bacchanals were punished “as their sins deserved.” However, he points out, “although these diseases produce bad effects in a republic, they are not fatal because there is almost always time to correct them, but there is actually no time in those that regard the state, which ruin the city if they are not corrected by a prudent individual” (309).

Machiavelli has argued in both The Prince and Discourses that government arises from and is based ultimately on fear; hence his emphasis on the importance of regular spectacular punishments. However, he has also insisted that government cannot be maintained solely on the basis of fear. Unalleviated fear gives rise to hatred, and the hatred of many encourages some to conspire against the government. The people are reassured that their leaders are not in danger of becoming tyrants if they see those leaders subjected to accusations and public trials.

The danger to the republic Machiavelli has emphasized most frequently has been that, like Caesar, a popular leader will seize power beyond constitutional restraints. Yet Machiavelli also argued that Caesar was able to do so as a result of a minor change made in the law for the sake of public utility, i.e., the prolongation of commands. Because the threat to the republic posed by a virtuous young leader is not always evident, republics need virtuous individuals like Cato to accuse citizens like Scipio—even unjustly—of arrogantly seeking to overthrow the republic. He now acknowledges, such accusations and trials are not enough to preserve a republic. It is necessary to have prudent individuals who not merely perceive the danger of corruption inherent in current practices, but are able to devise remedies for them—without changing the state. His example of such an individual is, again, Fabius Maximus Rullianus.

“In the actions of men one finds that close to the good there is always some evil that arises with it” (D 3.37; 294). So in the last lines of his Discourses Machiavelli reports that the Romans’ policy of increasing their own population by granting citizenship to peoples they conquered (which he praised earlier [D 1.6, 2.3]) led to such a large number of “new men” in Rome that they began to control the government. Perceiving the problem, Fabius arranged to have all the new men enrolled in four tribes, so that they could not corrupt all of Rome by ceasing to elect the most virtuous citizens to the highest offices (D 1.18). Since this “remedy” did not require a change in the government, it was “so well received by the citizenry that he deserved to be called Maximus” (310).

Machiavelli chooses his words carefully. By stating that Fabius “deserved” to be called “Maximus,” because his reform was “so well received,” Machiavelli reminds his readers that Fabius did not receive the honorific title for this particular achievement. He did not, because his fellow citizens did not perceive the threat of corruption posed by the incorporation of the new men with their varying mores into the citizen body (see D 1.18). They did not understand the crucial importance, therefore, of an apparently minor, perhaps even unjust modification of the law that deprived the new men of most of their influence on the outcomes of elections.

In the last sentence of book 3 Machiavelli thus underlines one of the central points he has been making in his education of those who “deserve” to be princes. The people are the source and repository of glory, but they do not understand or recognize true political virtue or wisdom. They prefer spirited, bold policies to gradual, cautious measures (D 1.53); and they remember rare and difficult individual sacrifices of the goods most human beings hold dear more than the victories or legislative reforms that actually serve long-term public interests, because these occur more frequently (D 3.34). Fabius Rucillanus’s great-grandson Fabius Cunctator (the delayer) also received the honorific “Maximus,” but he never received the popular or historical recognition for defending the Italian mainland from the foreign invader that Scipio did for conquering the enemy abroad. Moreover, the savior of the Roman republic did not become as famous—or as celebrated by later writers (who have even more influence than the people per se on the reputation of political actors)—as the man who destroyed it, Caesar (D 1.10).

Contrary to the suggestion he made at the conclusion of book 2, Machiavelli has shown that seeking glory may have made Roman generals great military captains, but it did not make them great legislators or founders. What republics need are leaders who understand the threats to the preservation of the republic—both internal (corruption) and external (aggression)—and are able to devise remedies for them. As Machiavelli indicates by concluding the Discourses with praise for Fabius Rullianus, these remedies involve changes not merely in the laws, but also in the “orders,” i.e., the ways in which the citizen body is organized and offices or powers are allocated to different parts in order to preserve the liberty of all. As Machiavelli indicated in his praise of Brutus in D 1.25 for using old names or titles for new institutions, it is better to make such changes gradually than to destroy everything the way a tyrannical new prince must in order to create everything anew. Patrick Coby correctly observes, “it is a large and glaring fact that Machiavelli decides to close his Discourses with homage to the lawful incrementalism of the ‘little by little’ reformer.”184 But it is also important to note that Machiavelli does not praise Fabius Rullianus simply or primarily for proceeding gradually in a way that enables him to obtain widespread consent for his reforms. He shows that Fabius consistently acted on the basis of his own judgment of what would succeed. He defied the order of the dictator in order to win a battle, because he was confident that the soldiers and people would exonerate him. He overcame superstitious fears of entering the Ciminian forest by using knowledge he had acquired in order to execute a surprise attack. He increased the confidence of his own troops by claiming that he had secret knowledge instead of appealing to their religious beliefs, which were both more difficult to control and less firm than organization and training. He relied on reserves he had created by organizing and training his own troops rather than sacrificing himself like the Decii. Finally, in contrast to Claudius Nero (D 3.17), he demonstrated his own willingness to do what was necessary to preserve the republic rather than indulge his own desire for vengeance by allowing Papirius to be appointed dictator. Even more than Camillus, Fabius Rullianus embodies Machiavelli’s conviction that a great republican prince will not seek his own glory at the expense of the republic the way Caesar finally did. Because he recognizes the need for initiative and innovation, such a leader does not always obey the commands of his superiors. Confident in his own judgment of what is necessary and of what will work under the circumstances, he allows himself to be judged by the public on the basis of the results. But he does not risk his own life unnecessarily. Like Camillus, he recognizes the need to overcome the envy of others by not seeking glory (or vengeance on those who question his loyalty and leadership) above all but rather agreeing to rotate or share command with others. Most important of all, perhaps, he recognizes the need to maintain popular opinions and customs that support a free way of life and knows how to create orders that preserve them.185


Conclusion of Book 3


In examining how the “actions of particular men made Rome great and caused many good effects” (212), Machiavelli implicitly urges his young Florentine readers to follow the example of Brutus. They should not reveal their intention of overthrowing the established regime until they are able to act effectively on it; and they should also recognize the need to eliminate the enemies of the republic once refounded, even if they are relatives. He does not encourage his readers to follow the model set by Brutus as a legislator, however, because the founder of the Roman republic resuscitated the ancient Spartan model of dual leadership checked by a senate rather than instituting a single executive. Nor does he present the “rare and virtuous examples” of the actions of later Roman republican heroes as models for his readers literally to imitate. On the contrary, he warns them against current misunderstandings of those examples (e.g., Fabius Maximus) and reminds them that the Roman republic fell because of the agitation caused by two well-intentioned but misguided laws—one requiring the redistribution of property and the other prolonging military commands. Through his analysis of the conflict over the Agrarian law, Machiavelli shows that republican government will not last if it depends upon insuring the economic equality of all citizens. In a city that enjoys a free way of life some will eventually accumulate more than others, and attempts to redistribute property require a tyrannical government, because they will provoke such fierce opposition on the part of property owners. What is needed, Machiavelli suggests in book 1 of the Discourses, is a new understanding of the requirements of a “political way of life” on the part of both the people and the elite. The people need to learn (or be persuaded to see) that any popular “savior” poses a threat of tyranny and that the best way of curtailing such a threat is through competitive elections in which most of the candidates will come from the elite. Public accusations and trials of possible tyrants serve to “vent” popular anger not merely at this or that particular leader, but at the need for government or control more generally. But members of the politically ambitious “elite” also need to learn that they will secure their own influence and wealth most reliably by competing with each other for popular favor so that no one individual becomes preeminent, rather than trying to form an “aristocratic” or “oligarchic” party that opposes all popular leaders or measures. Since “all things of men are in motion,” republics can obtain more effective leadership than principalities, because they can elect different individuals whose characteristic modes suit different sets of circumstances. Yet, Machiavelli also warns his readers, they cannot count on any specific set of laws to continue to produce the outcomes they desire, because people change along with their circumstances. (Indeed, the more successful the laws are, the more apt the people are to become corrupt.) If a republic once established is to be maintained, there must be prudent individual citizens who understand the reasons the laws work, when they work, and who can therefore, like Fabius, adjust or “remedy” the laws when they cease working effectively without entirely changing or overthrowing the state. That is the kind of education Machiavelli seeks to offer his readers.

As I have argued, Machiavelli seeks first to educate the two young men to whom he dedicates the Discourses, and the analysis contained therein has immediate relevance to their particular situation. In the Art of War Machiavelli expresses some doubt about the ability of these individuals to understand what he has written. But at the beginning of book 2 he addresses “the spirits of youths who may read these writings of mine” more generally; and, as we have seen, the political analysis and recommendations he makes have much broader relevance and application. His writings were not addressed simply or solely to the individuals to whom he dedicated them and their immediate concerns.


The Prince and the Discourses: Machiavelli’s New Education of Princes—Actual and Potential


In the Discourses Machiavelli argues that the test of political excellence is—and ought to be—what serves the common good (or the closest approximation in the good of the greatest number [D 2.2]). And since the good of the people comes closest to being the good of the community, the people are—and ought to be—the judges. The people judge—as they should—on the basis of outcomes; the intentions of political actors are difficult if not impossible to know (P 18). Yet, Machiavelli also shows, the people do not understand the causes of the outcomes they desire or how to replicate them. In order to achieve the results people want, Machiavelli thus contends in both The Prince and the Discourses, their leaders need a new form of political education. Rather than describing the formation of the character of exemplary individuals in the past, as writers like Xenophon and Plutarch did, Machiavelli seeks to disclose the causes and effects of their deeds. That is the first reason he, in contrast to many of his predecessors, concentrates on history rather than philosophy. The second and more fundamental reason is his observation that “all things of men are in motion and cannot stay steady” (D 1.6) and that all “worldly things have a limit to their life” (D 3.1). The knowledge he promises to convey in his dedications to The Prince and the Discourses explicitly concerns “the actions of great men” gleaned from his practical experience and “continual reading in worldly things.” Machiavelli indicates that he does not think that there are eternal truths available to mortal human beings through which we can bring order to our souls and thus achieve happiness.186 He sometimes suggests that it might be possible to establish and maintain a perpetual republic (D 3.1, 3.22), although he denies it in D 3.17; but he does not in fact think that anything can last forever in a world in which everything is continually coming into being and perishing. On the contrary, since both human beings and the world in which we find ourselves are constantly changing, adjustments and adaptations are continually necessary.

As the frequent repetition of arguments he made in The Prince in book 3 of the Discourses should remind readers, both works reflect the same basic understanding. They were written in close conjunction with one another, but directed to somewhat different audiences. In both works Machiavelli indicates from the beginning that he disagrees fundamentally with the classical Aristotelian understanding of political associations as developing naturally and peacefully out of more basic procreative and economic groups, families and tribes. Human beings are driven to form political associations to protect themselves from external aggressors; such associations are not formed or maintained by natural affection or friendship. There will always be aggressors—at least as long as there are human beings—because, as he states in D 1.37, “nature has created men so that they are able to desire everything and are unable to attain everything. So, since the desire is always greater than the power of acquiring, the result is discontent with what one possesses. . . . From this arises the variability of their fortune; for since some men desire to have more, and some fear to lose what has been acquired, they come to enmities and to war, from which arise the ruin of one province and the exaltation of another” (78).187 In opposition to the Christian doctrine of original sin, Machiavelli insists that human beings do not come into conflict and fight wars because they are evil.188 On the contrary, they become evil when and where no effective government has been established to punish and deter them from seizing the property and taking the lives of others with force.

Since political associations do not arise naturally but are formed only as a result of “extrinsic accidents” or threats, the institution of government has to be the product of intentional action on the part of one “mind.” If more than one person tries to determine the group’s course of action, Machiavelli observes in his praise of Romulus (D 1.9), the result will be delay, division, and inaction. In order to maintain his or her government once established, however, a founder must find a way of persuading people that it benefits them as well.189 The first way a ruler can acquire popular support, Machiavelli suggests, is by propagating a set of religious beliefs the way Numa did in Rome. However, Machiavelli also indicates, such beliefs do not lead people to obey the laws and defend the regime nearly as well or as reliably as a powerful prince or military training (partly because the efficacy of religion depends upon the rulers’ acting as if they, too, believe it). A better, more effective way of enlisting popular support for a government is to muster and train an army of one’s own subjects or fellow citizens to defend their own lives, families, and property.190

Machiavelli’s emphasis on the importance of training and maintaining an army—for principalities and republics alike—may offend some contemporary readers. He does not seek to glorify the use of force, militarism, or conquest per se, however. Indeed, he points out that the Romans’ demonstrated ability to conquer the world destroyed liberty everywhere. (He is not, as some commentators have claimed, an unabashed imperialist.) He sees military service as one of the most effective ways of enlisting people in the preservation of government in order to protect their own lives, families, and possessions. In armies, as opposed to corrupt polities, individuals are promoted because of their demonstrated abilities rather than their family connections or ability to please the people. Most important of all, however: training people to serve in an army transforms the unstable fury of a mob, which is easily dispersed, into an ordered, effective political force that can be used to preserve a prince or a republican government from its enemies, internal as well as external.

“Training,” especially the training of soldiers to follow commands immediately and without question, might seem to be opposed to liberty. But, Machiavelli argues, liberty does not consist in the absence of external restraint, as people tend to believe. Liberty is the result of a balance created and maintained between the two “humors” that exist in every “city”: the “grandi,” who want to dominate and oppress, and the people, who do not wish to be dominated and oppressed. Although he argues that the class conflict in every city, which threatens to erupt into civil war, is fundamentally over economic goods, Machiavelli insists that the division itself is political. It is not simply or primarily economic, because it concerns who will be in command or control, and both parties understand (or ought to understand) that the party in control will acquire wealth. There can be no purely economic resolution to political conflict, because all parties will always want to acquire more and be willing to use force, if they can, to get more. However, there is a political solution to the conflict over economic goods; that consists, not in periodic redistributions as classical political philosophers suggested, but in the institution of a “free way of life” that enables all individuals to keep the fruits of their labor and hope that their progeny will fare even better than they have.

Because “truly it is a very natural and ordinary thing to desire to acquire,” Machiavelli observes (again, contrary to classical political philosophers such as Plato and Aristotle), neither individuals nor groups seek to rule primarily as a matter of justice. On the contrary, he observes (D 3.6), the desire for domination is as strong as if not stronger than the desire for vengeance (which is perhaps the most primitive form of the desire for justice in an “an eye for an eye”). Ordinary people seek and accept rule by a prince to protect them against pillaging and murder by others (as in the Romagna). They will accept government if they see that it secures their lives, families, and property; but they will feel more secure if they see that the prince and nobles are also subject to rule of law. In both The Prince and Discourses Machiavelli thus urges monarchs to share rule with a senate and to subject themselves as well as their nobles to a popular court. Such a law-bound (or we might say “constitutional”) monarchy is not as good or effective a form of government as a republic that elects its “princes,” because elections allow republics to adapt to changing circumstances by employing different kinds of leaders. But, Machiavelli argues, such a law-bound monarchy will be better, more lasting, and provide more security for rulers and ruled alike than a military dictatorship or tyranny.

Elections are not sufficient to maintain a free republic, however, because the people can and will become corrupt, if nothing is done to prevent it. Ironically, the more secure the people feel, the less vigilant they are apt to be about preserving their liberty. They must, therefore, be made to feel the need to guard themselves—their lives, families, and property—from both external and internal threats. Military training along with a confederal arrangement with other republics serves the first purpose. Public trials of individuals accused of trying to overthrow the republic are also necessary to make ordinary citizens not only afraid of disobeying the law but also aware of the internal threat.

Ordinary people are not apt to perceive the threat represented by a victorious general such as Julius Caesar, especially when he shares the spoils of his victories with them. In The Prince Machiavelli thus seeks to persuade future “princes” that this old model of “liberality” is not tenable over the long run. It should be replaced by a more calculating understanding of virtù that leads a “prince” to spare his people from the heavy taxation needed to sustain distant military campaigns, lavish building projects, and gifts to his “friends.” That argument is part of Machiavelli’s broader contention that, however a prince comes to power, once in power he should seek the support of the people in order to maintain himself. The “great” are those individuals living under any regime who join with a “new prince” in the hope of improving their situation, but whose ambitions will never be satisfied and who will, therefore, eventually need to be put down with force. Whether his subordinates are mercenary captains of armies or cruel officials who enforce the law harshly, a prince who wants to establish a government that will last beyond his own lifetime must arrange to disassociate himself from the harsh means by which he acquired power. A prince needs to have help in governing, but Machiavelli reminds princes that they can “make” and “unmake” the “great” by granting some people offices and privileges or by taking those offices away along with their lives. In The Prince Machiavelli thus seeks to persuade his most ambitious readers that they do not constitute an “aristocratic” class that is better, by nature or by virtue of their education, than the people they rule. Rather than natural friends, the “great” by virtue of their shared ambition are natural enemies. Instead of rewarding his noble “friends” with offices and separate dominions, a calculating prince should learn how to use them and their armies as tools, but then see that they are destroyed. As Machiavelli points out in D 1.16, such a prince will acquire some of the popular support he needs to maintain his rule by allowing the people to take vengeance on those who have oppressed them.

In the Discourses Machiavelli nevertheless appears to take a somewhat more positive view of the “nobility” when he argues that the people need to be brought to see that the envy other nobles feel for a young virtuous “prince” is their best protection from future tyranny. And he tries to persuade the nobles that the best way of preventing the rise of a potential tyrant is to compete with him for popular favor. Furthermore, this competition needs to be institutionalized by making every citizen eligible to be elected to high office, by setting strict term limits on those offices and requiring the current occupants to step down, and by instituting trials of prominent citizens before popular juries.

The difference with regard to the potential “nobility” of the “great” is perhaps the most important difference between Machiavelli’s arguments in The Prince and Discourses. It can and should be attributed, in the first instance, to the difference in the immediate audiences of the two works. In The Prince Machiavelli explicitly addresses a prince and tries to show him what is truly in his interest as a prince. In the Discourses Machiavelli is explicitly addressing two young men from noble families who are attached to the republican government of their city and wish to restore its greatness. He thus tries to show them, most immediately, what they can and should do to restore republican government in what had, in effect, become a principality controlled by one family (the Medici). In the first two books he thus emphasizes the ways in which they should imitate their Roman ancestors. In contrast to the Florentine institutions that Machiavelli later describes in some detail in his Florentine Histories, they should not merely make all citizens eligible for high office, elect the most virtuous, and subject those suspected of subverting the law to public trials. Contrary to the “received wisdom” of the Florentine ottimati, they should train an army composed of Florentine citizens.
