Only in the second half of the Discourses does Machiavelli admit that the envy of other ambitious citizens may prevent them from electing the best to high office or allowing a virtuous captain to do what is necessary for the public good. He reminds his readers that this envy cannot be overcome by trying to revive the two Roman “remedies”—keeping the public poor and always in the field on a military expedition—because the history of the Roman republic itself shows that they were not tenable in the long run. He uses the example of Camillus to show how the envy of other ambitious individuals in a republic can be overcome. A preeminent leader must not insist on his absolute superiority to all others but show himself willing to share his power and responsibility with others by assigning them specific offices. He must also demonstrate his own willingness to obey the law like everyone else by voluntarily relinquishing the absolute power of a dictator at the end of his term.

As Harvey Mansfield has pointed out, Machiavelli breaks most clearly with the aristocratic republican tradition in emphasizing the need to have one “head.” A single “head” is necessary, not only for a republic to take expeditious action in an emergency, but also for that individual to get credit (or glory) and thus have an incentive to do what is necessary, particularly when it is dangerous. It is Machiavelli’s recognition of the advantages, if not absolute necessity, of a single leader that makes his republic look almost identical to what he calls a “civil principality” in P 9. The crucial difference lies in the republican election of a series of “civil” princes for set terms of office.

Machiavelli also uses the example of Camillus to state another principle or requirement of maintaining republican rule at which he only gestures in The Prince. Having urged the prince to seek popular support, at the conclusion of P 9 Machiavelli warns him not “to think that the people will liberate him if he is oppressed by enemies or by the magistrates.” But if he “knows how to command . . . and does not fail to make other preparations” (41), he will not find himself deceived by the people and will have laid his foundations well. Those foundations, Machiavelli explains in D 3.30, consist first and foremost in selecting which men to arm and training them, so that a prince has the force to eliminate the envious, if they seek to prevent him from doing what is necessary to preserve the republic. Toward the end of book 3 he goes even further when he argues that the distinctive characteristics not merely of various nations but of aristocratic families are products not of nature or heredity, but of education, acculturation, or “training.” The differences between peoples and princes do not arise “from a diverse nature—because it is in one mode in all” (D 1.58; 117). Individuals and various peoples may have different natural inclinations, but their distinctive characteristics are decisively shaped by their experience. A prince who knows how to do it can make soldiers out of peasants.

The person who knows how to order human beings in order to achieve the desired results is clearly in some ways superior to the one who does the ordering. Machiavelli thus begins his Discourses by observing, “the envious nature of men has always made it no less dangerous to find new modes and orders than to seek unknown waters and lands.” Desiring to achieve a “common benefit to everyone,” he nevertheless claims that he has laid out “a path as yet untrodden by anyone” that others “with more virtue, more discourse and judgment” will be able to follow to its end. Without connecting the danger explicitly to envy, much later in the Discourses Machiavelli comments on “what dangers are borne in making oneself head in counseling a thing” (D 3.35; 290). A person who merely advises a prince will get incomplete if any credit for the results. If he withholds knowledge or advice that would have prevented a disaster, however, he will be blamed—and justly so. An advisor of a prince (which Machiavelli explicitly aspired to become) should, therefore, “take things moderately.” He should not seize upon any option as his “own enterprise,” but give his “opinion without passion and defend it without passion, with modesty, so that if the city or the prince follows it, it follows voluntarily, and it does not appear to enter upon it drawn by your importunity.” Admitting that “one lacks the glory that is acquired in being alone against many to counsel a thing when it has a good end,” he notes, there are two compensations for exercising such self-restraint: “first, in the lack of danger; second, that if you counsel a thing modestly, and . . . your counsel is not taken, and by the counsel of someone else some ruin follows, very great glory redounds to you” (291).

Machiavelli thus makes himself and his own work the primary example of the reasons why someone who wishes to work for the common benefit should try to overcome the envy of others and how this can be achieved. Like Camillus, such a leader must assign others parts to play in the achievement and share credit with them. Since, Machiavelli has observed, people of “quality” become suspect when they try to withdraw entirely from public life, those who possess wisdom should not try to do so. They should offer to share their wisdom “modestly” (or, one might say, ironically) for the sake of benefiting others and not of winning reputation for themselves. They should learn from the example of Camillus that public claims to godlike superiority on account of their wisdom (of the kind ancient philosophers more or less explicitly made) are certain to arouse popular resentment and anger. Those who are truly wise will merely offer their advice to those willing to listen and able to implement it, understanding that those who have power and do not share their wisdom are not apt to listen, but that in the long run, the unwise and ignorant are apt to be proven wrong. By seeking to help others while at the same time recognizing that they themselves are in many respects subject to the power of others, the wise who follow Machiavelli’s advice will not merely secure their own safety; like Machiavelli they will lay the philosophical foundations for the future reordering of corrupt cities for the benefit of all. They will seek to persuade their readers not to seek happiness or justice as a transcendent Good or from an unknown and unknowable God. In an ever-changing world, they will try to show their readers that they must constantly invent new “remedies” or ways of redirecting human passions so that they culminate not in destructive wars but in the preservation of the lives, liberty, and prosperity of the greatest number.

In both The Prince and the Discourses Machiavelli rather explicitly sets out to debunk traditional aristocratic pretensions. He is not, however, a democrat of the ordinary kind. He acknowledges, “princes are superior to peoples in ordering laws, forming civil lives, and ordering new statutes and orders” (D 1.58; 118); and he goes so far as to declare that “a multitude without a head is useless” (D 1.44). He insists merely that, in order to last, both princely and republican governments need to serve the desires of the people. Not merely are the desires of the people more “decent” than those of the “great”; there are many more people than there are “great,” so that the satisfaction of their desires comes as close as possible in a world characterized by competition and conflict to realizing the common good. Even more, he reminds his readers ambitious to show their “nobility,” the glory ancient captains sought by risking their lives in order to save their peoples is and was awarded by the people. It tends to be awarded posthumously to those individuals whose works are deemed to have benefited those who come after them. Because “glory” or “virtue” as traditionally defined by what is praised is ultimately a matter of popular opinion, moreover, it is not always well or accurately bestowed. “Glory” is not and will not be the goal of a person who truly understands the world. He will not be allowed to retire safely into private life, however, once his prudence is recognized by others. He should thus try to help others establish and maintain a government that secures their lives, families, property—and, where possible, their liberty—as well as his own.

Many commentators seem to have missed the intimate connection between Machiavelli’s “moral revolution” or debunking of traditional notions of virtue in The Prince and his advocacy of republican institutions that secure the lives, liberties, and property of most citizens in the Discourses, especially since he insists that these institutions will work only so long as the people remain “uncorrupt.” He gives his readers much occasion to be confused about his understanding of what is truly good and virtuous by his ambiguous use of the word virtù in both works. Readers impressed by Machiavelli’s advocacy of republican institutions in the Discourses (and his own service to the republic of Florence) tend to dismiss The Prince as a transitory work, if not a satire. The great majority of readers attracted by the short and very punchy account of everything he has learned in The Prince tend to see him, on the other hand, as an advocate of cold-blooded amoral political analysis, if not of tyranny per se. These readers have not appreciated the extent to which Machiavelli’s arguments in both books are designed to persuade those who possess or seek to possess political power that the first and foremost goal of government is and must remain the security of the people. So long as people thought that some persons could be educated to be better or more virtuous than others, the first requirement of government was seen to be the education of such future rulers—for the sake of all. Observing that the proposed educations of virtuous leaders culminated in “imagined republics and principalities” that have never existed on earth, Machiavelli suggested that rule should be devoted instead to securing the good of those who were ruled. He did not think that it would be efficacious to appeal to the “charity” of those in power. Rulers who had tried to win the love of their people by being merciful had proved to be weak. He thus appealed to the desire of the “great” to command and oppress. “If all men were good,” Machiavelli acknowledged, “this teaching would not be good” (P 18; 69). However, he observed, although human beings are not wicked by nature (D 3.29), they are not all or always good—partly because they are weak and insecure. Like Aristotle (Politics 1263a41–42), Machiavelli thought that self-love was natural. But where Aristotle suggested that “excessive” self-love could be either checked by an education that made some men moderate so that they could control the rest with laws or satisfied in rare cases by the pleasures of philosophy, Machiavelli concluded that one’s own safety was a more fundamental concern for the few and the many alike. To live well, one must first be able to live.

Nor does Machiavelli praise Hiero, as does Polybius, for “during a reign of fifty-four years [having] kept his country at peace and his own power undisturbed by plots, . . . clear of that envy which is wont to wait on superiority” or for his virtue as an individual. “Although he lived constantly in the midst of affluence, luxury, and most lavish expenditure,” according to Polybius, Hiero “survived till over ninety, and retained all his faculties, as well as keeping every part of his body sound, which seems to me to testify in no slight measure, indeed very strongly, to his having led a temperate life” (The Histories of Polybius, Loeb ed. [Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press], 3.8.1–5). Machiavelli would have attributed Hiero’s longevity both as a person and as a ruler to his knowledge of the princely “art of war.” In his History of Rome Titus Livy does not describe Hiero as a private individual or his rise to power. But, as Machiavelli knew, Livy did emphasize Hiero’s wisdom, first in advising the Romans to attack Carthage and thus draw Hannibal back home (which Scipio Africanus, youngest son of Aemilius Paulus, eventually did and so defeated the Carthaginians, but not until Varro had lost the battle of Cannae and endangered the existence of Rome itself). Livy also reports that the Romans merely accepted the gold and troops Hiero brought his Roman allies, but did not heed his wise advice (22.7); and that Hiero was not able to realize his desire to leave Syracuse a free regime (24.4–5). Whereas Polybius (7.8.9) reports that his son Gelo did nothing but obey Hiero for his entire fifty years, Livy says (23.30) that only his good fortune enabled Hiero to forestall the rebellion of his son, and (24.5) that Hiero was not able to prevent his daughters from making his kingship hereditary or educate his grandson to become a virtuous prince.

If Machiavelli had, in fact, decided that emphasizing the novelty of his “discovery” at the beginning of the work was too dangerous, and so deleted the paragraph, he would have acted on the belief explicitly expressed there and more indirectly echoed in the published paragraphs that follow. Here he emphasizes the necessity of reading ancient histories in general, and that of Livy in particular, in a new way, drawing from modern as well as ancient political experience, in order to make this knowledge useful and to carry a difficult enterprise along far enough so that others could complete it. If, as Clough, “‘The Discourses,’ and Machiavelli’s Last Days,” argues, the handwritten preface was intended to be a substitute for the letter of dedication and existing preface, it points to the broader future audience Machiavelli hoped to address.


13 It thus begins to look as if Machiavelli uses “infinite” not only ironically with exaggeration, but also literally to mean undefined.


14 The attempt by Vatter, Between Form and Event, 30, to distinguish the view Machiavelli expresses here from the ancient cyclical view of nature is unpersuasive, partly because Vatter ignores Machiavelli’s reference to the difference between an ancient or pagan view and Christianity immediately before his emphasis on the continuity of nature.


15 By discoursing on an explicitly incomplete history, Machiavelli indicates his understanding that our knowledge of the past is incomplete, as he explicitly argues in the preface to book 2. Machiavelli shows that we learn from the histories, not by accepting the word of ancient authors like Plutarch on authority, but by observing regularities of human behavior in both modern and ancient times and then seeking the reasons or causes of the observed effects.


16 TM, 97. However, at TM, 103, Strauss notes that Machiavelli’s statement of the contents at the beginning of book 3 does not actually mention counsel, but only “private benefits.” Book 3 would thus appear to concern the reasons or causes the individuals whose deeds benefited the Roman republic did what they did.


17 E.g., Skinner, Machiavelli, 56–57; Michael Sherberg, “The Problematics of Reading in Machiavelli’s Discourses,” Modern Philology 89, no. 2 (1991): 175–95; Ardito, Machiavelli and the Modern State, 78.


18 Leo Strauss, “Niccolò Machiavelli,” in History of Political Philosophy, ed. Leo Strauss and Joseph Cropsey, 3rd ed. (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1987), 305. Clough, “‘The Discourses,’ and Machiavelli’s Last Days,” observes that Machiavelli’s statement that he is writing on the first ten books of Livy has led some commentators to believe that he was writing a commentary. “One consequence of this conviction has been an attempt on the part of Professor Felix Gilbert to provide a table of concordance between Machiavelli’s Discourses and Livy [in “Review: The Composition and Structure of the Discorsi,” Journal of the History of Ideas 14, no. 1 (January 1953): 142–43]. . . . This table, though, is particularly misleading, since, in Whitfield’s words, ‘Machiavelli did not always chastely quote one Livy passage to a chapter as the table shows him doing’” (81–82, quoting J. H. Whitfield, Discourses on Machiavelli [Cambridge: W. Heffer & Sons, 1969], 183). In fact, as Whitfield shows, Machiavelli often refers to several places or incidents in Livy in a single chapter. Clough suggests that “a table showing all Machiavelli’s references to Livy, and to other authorities, would be of inestimable value” (82). But having given a more complicated account of Machiavelli’s references to Livy, Strauss concludes, “the common way of studying the relation of the Discourses to Livy is defective because it disregards that Machiavellian use of Livy which reveals itself only through the suppression of Livian stories. This was the reason why, in considering the relation between Machiavelli’s plan and the Livian order, we limited ourselves so strictly to the references to Livy as distinguished from the mere use of Livian passages: whether Machiavelli refers or does not refer to Livy in a given place can easily be seen, and the collection of his references to Livy is a finite piece of work; but to achieve clarity about his use of Livy is an infinite task: its completion would require complete understanding of every sentence of the Discourses and of Livy” (TM, 104). Strauss either follows Machiavelli in using “infinite” ironically or admits that his own reading is partial.


19 In “Die Erneuerung der Philosophie,” Meier writes, “Tatsächlich läßt er sich in Thoughts on Machiavelli auf das Denken von Machiavelli ein, wie keiner, der vor ihm über Machiavelli schrieb, sich auf dessen Denken einließ” (42). Meier attributes the singularity of Strauss’s reading to his treatment of Machiavelli as a philosopher. But acknowledged philosophers such as Spinoza and Hobbes clearly read Machiavelli and took him seriously. They do not appear to have thought that Machiavelli was using Livy as a substitute for the Bible, however, or indicating his meaning through his use of numbers. Strauss emphasizes the importance of the number 26: there are 26 chapters in The Prince, he points out, and Machiavelli utters his greatest blasphemy in D 1.26. Meier notes that in his article “Niccolò Machiavelli” in History of Political Philosophy, Strauss points out that “twenty-six is the numerical value of the sacred name of God in Hebrew. . . . But did Machiavelli know of this? I do not know” (27). More generally, Meier argues that “what Strauss said about Alfarabi holds for the author of Thoughts on Machiavelli: He exploits the specific immunity of the commentator or the historian in order to express in an historical work what he thinks about a serious matter” (69). That matter is biblical religion and the way its central command for obedience to God rests on faith and thus is fundamentally inimical to philosophy.


20 In doing so, somewhat ironically, I am heeding Strauss’s admonition in Persecution and the Art of Writing (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1952): “Reading between the lines is strictly prohibited in all cases where it would be less exact than not doing so. Only such reading between the lines as starts from an exact consideration of the explicit statements of the author is legitimate. The context in which a statement occurs, and the literary character of the whole work as well as its plan, must be perfectly understood before an interpretation of the statement can reasonably claim to be adequate or even correct. One is not entitled to delete a passage, nor to emend its text, before one has fully considered all reasonable possibilities of understanding the passage as it stands—one of these possibilities being that the passage may be ironic” (30). I am arguing that Machiavelli was not merely an artful but an ironic writer. He was addressing more than one audience—not only his immediate but also future readers—and he had reasons to be less than perfectly open about the revolutionary character of his praise of the Roman republic and its institutions. I do not deny that he was critical not merely of the Church but of the effects of Christian teachings more generally (as in D 3.1). However, I am arguing that these criticisms were for the sake of introducing a better political order that would benefit most people (including rare individuals like Machiavelli himself), not for the sake, first and foremost, of protecting such freethinking and innovative individuals from persecution. Like Meier, I think that Strauss was trying to revive philosophy. Machiavelli, however, was trying to improve politics. For Machiavelli, religion (including Christianity) is and ought to be a political tool. Like Strauss I seek to show that Machiavelli develops his argument dialectically; he does not merely formulate generalizations and present historical examples as evidence to back them up.


21 Lefort, Le travail de l’oeuvre Machiavel, 584–690 (Smith trans., 328–425), shows how Machiavelli’s argument in book 3 can be specifically related to, and understood as a critique of, the Florentine politics that led to the demise of the republic (and Machiavelli’s own ouster from office) in 1512. Lefort admits that Machiavelli’s argument has a broader meaning and resonance, but he insists (and I agree) that it is necessary to see the immediate relevance and references in order to get to that broader meaning.


22 Mansfield, “Necessity in the Beginning of Cities,” in Machiavelli’s Virtue, 66.


23 Pace Pocock, Machiavellian Moment, 75–76, who claims that Machiavelli writes in an Aristotelian tradition. We see here that Machiavelli does not perpetuate an Aristotelian understanding of politics in this very fundamental respect.


24 He describes the weakness to which Florence’s origins as a colony gave rise more fully in FH 2.


25 Readers ought to observe that both examples, in fact, involved wars of conquest, and that Machiavelli characterizes them as examples of wars fought by necessity rather than by choice in D 2.8. In the Bible Moses famously did not reach or inhabit “the land of milk and honey,” and, as Machiavelli will remind his readers in D 2.3, the city Aeneas founded was conquered and absorbed by the city founded by Romulus. As Machiavelli indicates at the end of this chapter and argues in more detail in D 9–20, a city is not founded “in a day” or by one man alone, because he needs successors to maintain and extend what he started.


26 In the Art of War Fabrizio thus instructs Cosimo and Zanobi that in mustering an army they should rely more on training than on the natural spirit of some (AW 1.121–24) and that in deploying or camping they should rely more on discipline and organization than on the natural advantages of certain sites the way the Greeks did (AW 6.12–18).


27 The same might be said about Theseus who gathered together people who had sought refuge in the unsettled because barren land of Attica (Thucydides 1.2) and Cyrus, whose soldiers were tough because they had been shepherds, according to Plato, Laws 3.694a–695a, and whose empire did not last beyond his own life, according to Xenophon, The Education of Cyrus 8.7.2. The successes of these founders depended too much on the circumstances and not enough on the laws they established. In D 1.1 Machiavelli thus points to the reasons he takes the founding of Rome, in particular, to be exemplary.


28 In D 1.9 Machiavelli recognizes that Sparta did not, in fact, last without corruption or serious tumult. D 1.2 is thus an opening, provisional statement.


29 One of those commentators, Wolfgang Kersting, Niccolò Machiavelli (Munich: C. H. Beck, 1988), 62–73, observes that Machiavelli’s understanding of the cycles, unlike that of ancient philosophers, is not based on a conception of a cosmological order; it is rather based on his understanding of human passions, both the need for political order and the limits of that order those passions impose.


30 Gennaro Sasso, Studi su Machiavelli (Naples: Morano, 1967), chaps. 4 and 5, details the similarities and differences between Polybius and Machiavelli. One of the most important differences, pointed out by Harvey C. Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders: A Study of the “Discourses on Livy” (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1979), 35, is that Polybius attributes the cycle to nature, whereas Machiavelli attributes it to chance. In D 1.1 Machiavelli argues that the effects of “nature” or natural “accidents” can be duplicated, overcome, and improved upon by means of law; and if that is the case, the corruption that seems to occur regularly and thus “naturally” in each of the three basic regimes does not happen necessarily. The corruption occurs because legislators either do not know or do not choose to enact the laws necessary to forestall it. “Since inhabitants were sparse in the beginning of the world,” Machiavelli explains, “they lived dispersed for a time like beasts” (instead of “together like beasts,” as Polybius wrote, and Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders, 36, notes). When population increased and people gathered together to defend themselves, they first made the one who was most robust and courageous the captain and obeyed him. But they soon discovered that ordering a city involves more than a strong defense. It was necessary also to pass laws. Whereas Polybius emphasized the role of reason in the development of an understanding and institutions of justice, Michael Zuckert argues in an unpublished paper “Rome: Machiavelli’s New Constitutionalism,” Machiavelli emphasizes the root of this “knowledge” in empathy, the sympathy onlookers have for the pain of a beneficiary who is not repaid. Their calculations of their own self-interest under similar circumstances led such sympathetic onlookers to see the need for mechanisms to enforce contracts. And their discovery of the need for laws and punishments for those who disobeyed them led people to select not the most hardy, but one more prudent and just to be their prince. (See also Sullivan, Machiavelli’s Three Romes, 89–95.) As soon as rule became hereditary, however, the monarchy began to degenerate. The prince began to be hated and, because he was hated, to fear his opponents and thus to try to destroy them. Plots and conspiracies against the tyrant arose in response to his violence, not among the weak, but among the more generous and great spirited. Following the example of the powerful, the multitude took up arms and obeyed the aristocrats as their liberators after the prince was eliminated. Because they had come to hate the name of a sole ruler, these aristocrats constituted a government of themselves, which began by following the laws and acting for the common utility rather than its own advantage. But when their sons came into office, not having experienced the ill effects of tyranny, they became avaricious and ambitious. Someone quickly rose up to eliminate them with the help of the multitude; and they, remembering the evils of princely as well as of oligarchic rule, instituted a popular state, which lasted for a time, but eventually became so licentious that no one could count on the protection of the law. “So, constrained by necessity, or by the suggestion of some good man, or to escape such license,” the writers who traced such a cycle concluded, the people “returned anew to the principality” (13).


31 J. Patrick Coby, Machiavelli’s Romans (Lanham, MD: Rowman & Littlefield, 1999), documents many ways in which Machiavelli departs from Roman history, but he nevertheless concludes that Machiavelli is recommending the ancient republic as a model, i.e., that he is not describing a new or modern form of republicanism in the guise of ancient Rome. Fischer, Well-Ordered License, comes to a similar conclusion by arguing that Machiavelli “intended to return his contemporaries to the political ideas and practices of the ancients” (185). However, Fischer maintains that Machiavelli misunderstood the ancients, and so propelled the West toward modernity.


32 Among the ancient authors who condemned the tumults, Mansfield and Tarcov note (16n2), were Sallust, Bellum Catilinae, Bellum Jugurthinum, and Histories; Cicero, Republic 2.33 and In Catilinam; and Augustine, City of God 3.16–17.


33 Machiavelli ironically cites the authority of “Tully” (Cicero), who observed in a book entitled De amicitia (On friendship) that although people are ignorant, “they are capable of truth and easily yield when the truth is told them by a man worthy of faith” (17), to justify institutions that not only were adopted as a result of “tumults” or enmities between the nobles and people, but also gave final decisions to the people.


34 In admitting his inability to understand what Machiavelli means by the need for a “guard of a city’s freedom,” Francesco Guicciardini, Considerations of the “Discourses” of Niccolò Machiavelli, trans. James B. Atkinson and David Sices (DeKalb: Northern Illinois University Press, 2002), 1.5; 394–95, indicates the difference between his more traditional aristocratic understanding of republican government and Machiavelli’s new, more democratic analysis. On the differences between Guicciardini and Machiavelli, see Jürgen Huber, Guicciardinis Kritik an Machiavelli (Wiesbaden: Springer, 2004).


35 Venice was a particularly relevant modern instance of the model of the noble or aristocratic republic for Machiavelli and his immediate audience. Savonarola had modeled his reform of the Florentine republic, in part, on Venice (by incorporating a “Great Council”), and the ottimati families to whom both Cosimo and Zanobi belonged generally opposed the inclusion of such popular institutions (as well as the arming of the plebs).


36 As Coby, Machiavelli’s Romans, 39, points out. However, as Coby later observes (46), according to Plutarch, the ephorate was not the creation of Lycurgus, but added 130 years later. Machiavelli fails to take account of the actual historical development of Spartan institutions, the way in which it acquired dominion over neighboring Messenia, and the slave (helot) population upon which the operation of the republic depended. He thus indicates that he is more interested in combating the model of a good republic (to be found in Plato’s Laws, for example), in which a wise legislator establishes institutions and laws that are maintained, basically unchanged, than he is in Sparta. In fact, Sparta’s development followed some of the course Machiavelli attributes to Rome, i.e., a combination of expansion and institutional reform.


37 Such a balance between difficulty of conquest and the absence of imperial ambitions of its own (although the ability perhaps to aid others), along with a restricted population, was proposed as a means of preserving both the city’s freedom and its unity in Plato’s Republic 4.420b–423b.


38 Machiavelli characteristically does not credit family ties or loyalties as a basis of a free or republican way of life. On the contrary, he regularly suggests that the desire politically powerful men often demonstrate to pass their positions on to their sons is a major source of the corruption, if not of the sheer destruction, of a republic. One reason Machiavelli favors the people over the Senate as the “guardian of liberty” is that the “fathers” held their seats on the basis of heredity. Machiavelli underlines his inaccurate use of Coriolanus as a positive example of the utility of accusations, moreover, by using another slightly erroneous account of an incident at Chiusi where a man called in the “French” to punish the violator of his sister, according to Machiavelli, but in Livy 5.33, his wife (and so the potential mother of his heirs). In Livy’s history, the Chiusi incident which brings the Gauls to Italy leads to their attack on Rome and Manlius’s later “calumnies” (in Livy, an organized rebellion), because he felt slighted by the greater glory awarded to Camillus for defeating the Gauls than to him for saving the Capitol from their secret attack.


39 As in P 3, where Machiavelli first says that a prince who adds a province with the same language and customs need only eliminate the bloodline of the previous prince, but then adds that the prince should also not change any of the laws or taxes, so here he clarifies his proposal and modifies its requirements when he restates it.


40 Francesco Guicciardini, History of Florence, trans. M. Domandi (New York: Harper Torchbooks, 1970), 103–6, 116, 125, 131–35, 141; McCormick, Machiavellian Democracy, 129–33. Later in the Discourses (3.30), Machiavelli claims that Savonarola saw the need to kill those who opposed his plans because of envy, but that he was not able to convince his followers to do so. They seem to have understood the need to kill the opposition well enough, but not the need to maintain popular approval.


41 As Sullivan, Machiavelli’s Three Romes, 127, points out, Machiavelli exaggerates Romulus’s crime by saying that he consented to the killing of his ally and fellow ruler Tatius the Sabine. According to Livy 1.14, Romulus simply refused to go to war to avenge the murder of Tatius by a Laurentian mob, who were taking their revenge for his having failed to punish some of his relatives for mistreating some Laurentian ambassadors. She suggests that Machiavelli did so to show that Romulus slew his brother not merely in an act of self-defense or as a response to Remus’s challenge to his authority, but as a matter of policy and by choice. I think Machiavelli wanted to downplay the importance of Romulus’s crime against family as such and to emphasize the importance of a founder’s acting alone, because a divided authority makes it difficult to act expeditiously or effectively.


42 E.g., Coby, Machiavelli’s Romans, 42, although Coby also considers the reasoning in some detail.


43 Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders, 63, cites Augustine, City of God 15.5, who points out that the founder of the first city in the Bible, Cain, also slew his brother. Cain did not, however, share his power with a senate, and so replace personal or hereditary rule with shared power and legal restraints on its use.


44 According to the traditional story reported by Livy, Romulus acquired such an understanding from his own experience. He and his brother Remus were descendants of Aeneas. Their grandfather, Numitor, as the eldest son, was supposed to inherit the kingdom, but he was driven out by his brother Amulius, who proceeded to murder Numitor’s male children and made his niece, Rhea Silvia, a Vestal Virgin, ostensibly to honor her, but actually to condemn her to perpetual virginity to preclude the possibility of issue. She claimed that she was raped by Mars and gave birth to twin boys. The king threw her into prison and ordered her sons to be drowned. Because the Tiber had flooded, his servants left the babies on the shore, where a she-wolf heard them crying and suckled them until Faustulus, the king’s herdsman, found them and took them into his hut. When they grew up, the twins formed a gang of robbers. After the king caught Remus and was about to put him on trial, Romulus conspired with some of his fellows to kill the king. He and Remus then claimed to be the legitimate rulers on the basis of their lineage. But according to Livy (1.6), the brothers’ plans for the future were marred by the same jealousy and ambition that had divided their grandfather and Amulius. Accounts differ as to the specific occasion for their quarrel, but the brothers fought, Remus was killed, and Romulus assumed sole authority.


45 Machiavelli observes that Romulus reserved the authority of convoking the Senate and commanding the armies after war was decided upon for himself. The monarchy he established is thus rather like that Machiavelli attributes in D 1.16 to the king of France, in what Machiavelli calls one of “the well-ordered and governed kingdoms in our times” (P 19), except that the French king reserved power over finances as well as over the army to himself. Romulus did not need to do the former, because Rome’s public resources came largely from conquest. John M. Warner and John T. Scott, “Sin City: Augustine and Machiavelli’s Reordering of Rome,” Journal of Politics 73, no. 3 (2011): 865, dismiss Machiavelli’s contention here that Romulus acted for the common good on the basis of his earlier statement (D 1.2) that Romulus intended to found a kingdom and of his sources (from which Machiavelli clearly departs). The kingdom he founded was elective, however; and Machiavelli suggests that Brutus’s replacement of one elected king by two elected consuls (returning to the Spartan model of two kings) was a mistake. Restricted to the Senate and the consuls, people and tribunes, the “orders” of Rome were defective (D 1.18), because they did not include a truly monarchical or single executive power (except in the temporary dictatorship, which he praises).


46 Machiavelli raises this question both in the title of the chapter and in the examples of the Spartan kings Agis and Cleomenes, who were not founding anew, as was Romulus, but wanted to reform Sparta. Seeing that Agis had been murdered by the ephors who wanted to prevent him from taking away their power, Cleomenes saw that they were destroyed. However, weakened as Machiavelli would have predicted by its internal corruption and dissension, Sparta was then conquered by Macedonia. As Machiavelli emphasized in D 1.2, any radical reordering is dangerous (because it often involves the threat of foreign conquest).


47 Cf. Plato, Republic 9.571a–580a.


48 Timoleon and Dion are celebrated in Plutarch’s Lives.


49 Machiavelli’s oblique reference to the death of Julius Caesar might remind readers familiar with Livy of his account of the death of Romulus. “One day while he was reviewing his troops . . . a storm burst . . . [and] a cloud enveloped him, so that it hid him from the eyes of everyone present. . . . The troops, who had been alarmed by the sudden storm, recovered when it passed over. . . . Then they saw that the throne was empty, and [were] ready . . . to believe the senators, who had been standing at the king’s side and now declared that he had been carried up on high by a whirlwind. . . . A few voices began to proclaim Romulus’s divinity; . . . and at last every man present hailed him as a god and son of a god. . . . However, a few dissentients secretly maintained that the king had been torn to pieces by the senators” (1.16).


50 Strauss, TM, 33, comments that Machiavelli might thus be suggesting that there can be more freedom (intellectual, if not political) under a prince than in a republic. However, Strauss also observes that Machiavelli has just reminded his readers of the way in which criticism of Caesar was muted, i.e., that speech under the empire was not so free as he had just claimed.


51 Machiavelli thus departs, once again, from Livy (1.6–7), who reports that Romulus fortified the Palatine hill, performed religious rites taken from the Albans and the Greeks, and then gave his people their laws. He wishes to distinguish clearly between the single mind, intelligence, or wisdom needed to establish a political order and the claim that it has been sanctioned if not proposed by a divinity used to persuade the people to accept and maintain that order. Traditional stories about Minos’s having been instructed by Zeus and Lycurgus’s having been instructed by Apollo merged the origin and intelligence needed to found a lasting regime with the beliefs necessary to maintain it. (See Plato, Laws 624a–625b.)


52 See Scott and Sullivan, “Patricide,” and Parent, “Machiavelli’s Missing Romulus,” who argue that Machiavelli makes a similar suggestion in The Prince.


53 Machiavelli takes up this possibility again in D 2.5.


54 Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders, 78, observes that one could easily read through D 1.15 without realizing that the battle in which the consul Papirius defeated the Samnites, despite their using religion well, was the same battle in which he arranged for the death of the “prince” of the chicken men, to show that the “prince” had lied when he contradicted the consul’s claim that the auspices had gone well (even though they had not). Thinking that his troops would win the battle, Papirius did not simply trust the auguries, but he also did not want his troops to fear that the gods were against them.


55 When Skinner, “Republican Ideal of Political Liberty,” 306, asks “how the Romans induced their citizen-armies to fight so bravely against enslavement by invading enemies,” and responds that “he finds the key in their religious laws,” which made them fear to break their oaths, he ignores the tension Machiavelli emphasizes here between the laws which civilize a people and the training they need to become soldiers.


56 Machiavelli generalizes the lesson by showing how it applies to the successors of King David in the Bible (Solomon and Rehoboam) as well as to those of Mahomet. If Selim, the current sultan of the Turks, had loved peace more than war, like his father, Bajazet, the kingdom would have been ruined. “After an excellent prince, a weak prince can maintain himself; but after a weak one, no kingdom can be maintained with another weak one, unless indeed it is like that of France, which its ancient orders maintain. Those princes are weak who do not rely on war” (53).


57 As Machiavelli reminded his readers in D 1.12, Savonarola was able to convince the Florentines that he had spoken to God; but, as Machiavelli observed in P 6, the priest was not able to force his followers to continue to believe in him and fight for his reforms in the face of armed opposition.


58 In associating liberty so closely with security, Machiavelli sets a precedent for Montesquieu’s definition of “political liberty in relation to the citizen” as “security . . . in one’s opinion of one’s security.” Montesquieu, Spirit of the Laws, 12.1; 187.


59 Nederman and Gómez, “Between Republic and Monarchy?,” 88, note the increased emphasis Machiavelli puts on the king’s obeying his own laws in his Discourses, but they argue that such a monarchy still falls short of the vivere libero described in D 2.2, because the king cannot satisfy the people’s desire to recover their freedom without relinquishing his own rule. He can, however, make them feel secure. Marcia Colish, “The Idea of Liberty in Machiavelli,” Journal of the History of Ideas 32, no. 3 (1971): 335–37, observes that Machiavelli sometimes treats princely and monarchical rule as clear antitheses to liberty, but that he by no means does so consistently. In D 1.2, 1.16, 1.23, and D 3.5, he suggests that early Roman kings issued ordinances conformable to a free government (conformi ancora al vivere libero). And in D 1.25 he advises “those who want to set up a new and free polity [uno vivere nuovo e libero], whether it be a republic or a monarchy [o per via di republica o di regno]” to preserve its ancient customs. “Since most people want freedom in order to live securely [desiderando la libertà per vivere sicuri], a prince can satisfy their desires by ruling according to laws that guarantee security” (337).


60 FH 6.13, 6.20–24.


61 He does not, therefore, accept the Christian doctrine of original sin.


62 E.g., Wolin, Politics and Vision, 2nd ed., 212. Machiavelli does occasionally write about the “virtue” of the Roman army (e.g., D 1.43, 3.13), but the virtue of an armed force in keeping discipline and facing death is not quite the same as “civic virtue,” and, Machiavelli observes in D 3.13, it does not last long in the absence of good leadership.


63 It is also inaccurate and misleading to write as Quentin Skinner, Visions of Politics, vol. 2, Renaissance Virtues (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2002), 165, does, of the need to devise “some mechanism for preventing [human beings’] inescapably corrupt motives from having their natural but self-destructive effects.” Such a characterization of the self-regarding passions that lead human beings naturally to desire to acquire is too moralistic. These passions are not bad or “corrupt” in themselves, according to Machiavelli. The failure to do what is necessary to preserve liberty once attained is.


64 McCormick, Machiavellian Democracy, 98–99, takes this discussion to show that Machiavelli favored democratic political processes. Machiavelli’s point, however, is that procedures alone do not guarantee good results. The “corruption” or not of the people depends not on the laws or procedures, but rather on what they fear—here, foreign enemies or individuals so powerful that they are able to evade the laws; in D 3.1, the consequences of not obeying the law.


65 Skinner, “Republican Ideal of Political Liberty,” 305.


66 Pettit, Republicanism, 1–79, does not give quite the same account of liberty as “non-domination” (in contrast to what Isaiah Berlin called both “negative” and “positive” liberty) as Skinner does, but, if possible, puts even more emphasis on the role of law. He argues that “non-domination” consists in freedom from arbitrary interferences in making the choices that shape one’s life, and considers nonarbitrary interferences, such as those imposed by law, those interferences about which one has had an opportunity to join in a public debate. Both Skinner and Pettit write about a republican “tradition” that includes but is not restricted to Machiavelli. But we see in this chapter that, according to Machiavelli, the operation of laws always depends upon the “modes” and “orders.” He does not define these precisely, although he indicates at the beginning of D 1.18 that the “orders” consist in the divisions of the population with the power to elect the leading officials (consuls by the Senate and tribunes by the plebs) and the “modes” consist in the ways in which magistrates are selected and the way laws are made. The laws per se do not, therefore, determine whether a people is corrupt or uncorrupt, free or unfree.


67 Machiavelli might agree with the understanding of ‘corruption’ Skinner attributes to him along with previous republican thinkers such as Sallust and Cicero as “a term of art the republican theorists habitually use to denote our natural tendency to ignore the claims of our community as soon as they seem to conflict with the pursuit of our own immediate advantage.” However, Machiavelli would not agree that “to be corrupt . . . is to forget . . . that if we wish to enjoy as much freedom as we can hope to attain within political society, there is good reason for us to act in the first instance as virtuous citizens, placing the common good above the pursuit of any individual or factional ends. Corruption, in short, is simply a failure of rationality” (“Republican Ideal of Political Liberty,” 304). According to Machiavelli, there are always two “humors” that divide every city, and these two humors have opposed notions of the “good.” As he argued in The Prince in redefining the virtues, the prince should see the way in which his own good or desire to dominate may be made consonant with the desire or “interest” of the “people” not to be dominated. However, as Machiavelli will show again in D 2.2, the good or interest of the prince is never the same as the good of the people. There is, strictly speaking, no “common” or shared “good.” In the best cases, i.e., well-ordered republics or kingdoms, there is only an aggregation of the good of those who want to dominate with the good of those who wish not to be dominated. (See David N. Levy, Wily Elites and Spirited Peoples in Machiavelli’s Republicanism [Lanham, MD: Lexington Books, 2014], 8–9.) In both The Prince and Discourses Machiavelli seeks to show the politically ambitious grandi how to calculate the means best suited to realizing their desires, but as we have seen in his account of the way in which the Romans used religion, he does not appeal to the “rationality” of the people. It is safer, he insists in both The Prince and Discourses, to rely on their fear of punishment.


68 As Machiavelli also observed in P 25.


69 Montesquieu generalizes Machiavelli’s point here when in the Spirit of the Laws he argues that governments are based originally on fear and that the most common form to which they all tend to revert is despotism.


70 Machiavelli greatly expands his argument to this effect in AW.


71 Machiavelli reinforces the emphasis on the importance of training the people rather than relying on a few noble defenders by pointing out that local peasants can always find an alternative way around the pass, i.e., they have useful knowledge of or on the ground that the “higher-ups” lack.


72 Although Machiavelli does not say so explicitly, both his examples of keeping a “king” who continued to offer the public sacrifices in the republic and having one and only one of the consuls accompanied by the twelve lictors who had previously accompanied the king refer to actions taken by Lucius Junius Brutus in founding the Roman republic.


73 Using Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander, as an example of a small king who became prince of Greece by using such modes, Machiavelli says that “he transferred men from province to province as herdsmen transfer their herds” (61). Strauss, TM, 49, and Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders, 99–100, infer that Machiavelli is implying that God is a tyrant. His omnipotence (and omniscience) would not leave any room for human freedom, if He did not choose to do so (as Augustine argued that He did [City of God 22.1]). Machiavelli’s “mistaken” attribution of this mode of proceeding to David makes it apply to a human king, however, rather than to God. In aspiring to be not merely emperors of the world but gods, ancient politicians like Alcibiades and Caesar failed to recognize the difference between mortal humans and immortal divinities.


74 Centuries after Machiavelli wrote, we have experienced a series of such “totalitarian” revolutions, led by new princes such as Lenin, Hitler, Stalin, Mao, and Pol Pot. This chapter indicates that Machiavelli foresaw the possibility of such attempts as secularized versions of Christianity, but did not advocate them.


75 Coby, Machiavelli’s Romans, thus argues that “Baglioni’s hesitation originated not in conscience but in smallness of mind” (231).


76 Letters from Niccolò Machiavelli to the Florentine Signori, September 5–13, 1506, in The Historical, Political, and Diplomatic Writings of Niccolò Machiavelli, trans. Christian Detmold, vol. 4, available from the Online Library of Liberty (http://oll.libertyfund.org).


77 See TM, 276.


78 Cf. TM, 240, and Coby, Machiavelli’s Romans, 228–48, who also argue that Machiavelli rejects “certain” middle ways, not all. Coby’s account of the middle ways Machiavelli recommends applies particularly to princes, however, as in his recommendation of Agathocles in The Prince as an example of “cruelty well-used,” not to the design of institutions to direct and balance the two humors. Strauss, TM, 262–67, argues that Machiavelli himself advocates the middle way between virtue and vice (selfishness) that constitutes “republican virtue,” i.e., collective selfishness.


79 Livy, 2.41–43, explains that the patricians also accused the politicians arguing for renewed enforcement of the Agrarian law of trying to establish a tyranny by buying the support of the plebs.


80 In a footnote Mansfield and Tarcov suggest that Machiavelli is referring to the “tumults” he described in 1.4, but those were the tumults that preserved Roman freedom. Here I believe he is referring to the plebs’ elevation and repeated reelections of Marius as consul. McCormick, Machiavellian Democracy, 89–90, takes this statement to show that Machiavelli believes that “the great” are always greedy oligarchs who are rightly opposed by the people. Machiavelli thinks that the desire to acquire is natural to all human beings, however; he does not praise or blame one group for displaying it so much as he tries to show how this desire can be channeled in a way that benefits the largest number.


81 Machiavelli would have known that in depicting the lives of “parallel” Greek and Roman statesmen, Plutarch “pairs” Tiberius Gracchus with Cleomenes. At the conclusion of D 1.9 Machiavelli observed that by killing the ephors and anyone else who might have been able to oppose him, Cleomenes had more success in returning his city to its ancient orders (including equal property holding) than his predecessor, King Agis. McCormick thus concludes that Machiavelli favored violent means of redistribution. However, Machiavelli observes that Cleomenes’ attempted reordering was defeated by the power of the Macedonians and the inability of Sparta along with the other Greek republics to resist it, because of their internal divisions or “corruption.”


82 The example Machiavelli gives of the “generosity and prudence” of the Roman Senate is that, unable to defend their allies because of a pestilence, the Senate declared, contrary to their previously stated policy, that their allies should defend themselves, because the Romans were unable to do so. The Florentines, on the other hand, were not able to decide to grant Duke Valentino the right to march through their territory, even though they were not able to prevent him from doing so. Moreover, they proved themselves unable to trust the French king to hand over Pisa and Arezzo to them, as agreed, if he came to occupy these cities by negotiation rather than by force, even though he clearly could not hand over the cities to the Florentines if he did not possess them.


83 Machiavelli does not make the difference between his account of tyranny and that to be found in ancient authors explicit until D 3.26. However, by discounting the importance of the attempted rapes of Lucretia and Virginia in the fall of the tyrants Tarquin Superbus and Appius Claudius, in contrast to Livy, Machiavelli indicates that unlike like Plato, Republic 9.571a–580b, he does not regard the tyrant as Eros incarnate, even though in P 19 and D 3.6 he like Aristotle warns “princes” against violating the wives, daughters, and relatives of their close associates. Like the grandi or nobili, he suggests, tyrants act out of a desire to dominate more than a desire for glory, which he argued in D 1.10 would lead them to try to benefit their people.


84 In the Florentine Histories Machiavelli shows that this same desire in all parties produced the constant changes, instability, and ultimate ineffectiveness of that city’s republic.


85 McCormick, Machiavellian Democracy, 86, takes this incident to show that the people were not as passive as they might seem to be in much of The Prince and Discourses. He does not appear to recognize Machiavelli’s criticism of their failure to understand what should—and should not—be said in public (or the need to use fraud as well as force in effective politics).


86 Vickie B. Sullivan, Machiavelli, Hobbes, and the Formation of a Liberal Republicanism in England (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2004), 52–55, and McCormick, Machiavellian Democracy, 70–76, debate the extent to which Machiavelli advocates manipulation of popular opinion by the nobles through the example of Pacuvius. Desiring to reconcile the nobles and plebs in Capua, Machiavelli reports, Pacuvius first persuaded all the senators to resign their seats by telling them that the people threatened to kill them if they did not. He then gave the people the power to kill the senators—as soon as they found replacements. By proposing that the people proceed to elect replacements one by one, he made them see that they did not want to choose any of their peers, because none of them was worthy of senatorial rank. So he finally suggested that they reinstate the old Senate, “for the fear that the senators have been in will have made them so humble that the humanity that you are seeking elsewhere you will find in them” (98). Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders, 145–47, treats the incident as an example of the way nobles can be taught the dangers of arrogance, by giving the people the power to punish them, and of a noble’s indirectly instructing the people in the need for government.


87 Machiavelli gives a detailed history of the many instances of this invidious tendency in his Florentine Histories.


88 For a fuller account of Machiavelli’s critique of Cicero, see Alexander Duff, “Republicanism and the Problem of Ambition: The Critique of Cicero,” Journal of Politics 73, no. 4 (October 2011): 980–92.


89 As Sullivan, Machiavelli, Hobbes, and the Formation of a Liberal Republicanism in England, 47, also points out.


90 According to Machiavelli, therefore, the people or “multitude” are not and cannot be the “revolutionary” force Vatter argues they are in Between Form and Event. The multitude can be destructive, but they need leaders (i.e., “princes”) in order to create and maintain a new civil order.


91 In arguing that Machiavelli thinks that the people not only are more “decent,” moral, and just, but also have better judgment, in Machiavellian Democracy McCormick relies greatly on this chapter. But he never quotes the first part of this sentence in which Machiavelli explicitly recognizes the necessary role and excellences of princes. See Ryan Balot and Stephen Trochimchuk, “The Many and the Few: On Machiavelli’s ‘Democratic Moment’” Review of Politics 74, no. 4 (2012): 559–88, for a thorough critique of McCormick’s argument.


92 Alessandro Pinzani, “Doch ein Republikaner? Ein Blick in die anderen politische Schriften Machiavellis,” in Höffe, Niccolò Machiavelli “Der Fürst,” observes that “Der Ruhm von Rom ist größer also der seiner Gründers Romulus und all seiner Generäle, Tribunen, Konsulen jeweils individuell betrachtet” (176).


93 See Paul Rahe, Against Throne and Altar: Machiavelli and Political Theory under the English Republic (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2008), 22–55; Fischer, Well-Ordered License, 124–25.


94 As McCormick, Machiavellian Democracy, 98–99, observes, Machiavelli is remarkably imprecise about the composition of the electorate. In contrast to Rousseau, Social Contract 4.2–4, he never recognizes the way in which Roman votes were weighted in favor of propertied people. (In D 3.49 he does, however, praise Fabius Rullianus for creating new voting “orders” that made the votes of the “new men” weigh less. That praise alone would appear to prove that Machiavelli was no democrat in the sense of giving each and every citizen an equal vote or voice in the determination of public policy.) In contrast to McCormick, Rousseau, Social Contract 4.5, notes that the senators were not allowed to participate in the election of tribunes, but were nonetheless subject to decisions made by the tribunes that had the force of law. Rousseau’s description of the fundamental laws of the Roman republic in Social Contract 4.2–7 is generally more specific than Machiavelli’s. Machiavelli wants his readers to understand why Roman institutions worked or did not work, not literally to copy them. As he suggests in the concluding chapter of the Discourses (3.49), voting regulations continually have to be modified in response to changes in the composition and character of the people to prevent them from becoming corrupt.


95 On the basis of Machiavelli’s statement in D 1.18 (and nowhere else) that every citizen of Rome had a right to propose laws and to discuss them, in his analysis in Machiavellian Democracy McCormick vastly overstates the “participatory” character of the Roman republic. In fact, it is not clear that a plebian could propose a law, except by persuading an elected tribune to do so. Discussions were held in contiones (short for conventions) called by a consul, praetor, or tribune of the plebs—and the presiding officer decided who could speak. In “Tempering the Grandi’s Appetite to Oppress,” 13, McCormick admits that Machiavelli’s statement “that ‘any citizen at all’ could speak in a concione” (3.34) was “perhaps against actual Roman practice.” In sum, it is not at all clear that the plebs had a “voice” in the sense of an actual vote in deciding what policies became law.


96 Maurizio Viroli, From Politics to Reason of State: The Acquisition and Transformation of the Language of Politics, 1250–1600 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1992), 162, also argues that Machiavelli urges the Florentines to follow the ancient Tuscan model.


97 Strauss, TM, 89, also observes that the “confederacy” Machiavelli recommends here constitutes an alternative to the conquest for which he calls in P 26. As Machiavelli indicates, but only indicates, in D 2.19, the expansionary policies he recommends here would entail as severe a diminishment, if not the complete destruction, of the political independence of the Vatican, as would the conquest of Italy for which he calls at the conclusion of The Prince.


98 In this passage, Machiavelli may sound like a liberal political economist. However, despite his urging a prince to show himself to be a lover of the virtues by giving recognition to virtuous men, honoring excellence in any art, and inspiriting his citizens to follow their pursuits quietly, in trade and in agriculture, so that they are not reluctant to adorn their possessions for fear of their being taken away or to open up a trade for fear of taxes in P 21, Machiavelli does not argue, as does John Locke, Second Treatise 5.36, that a “wise prince” will foster the industry of his subjects rather than seek to expand his republic or principality by means of conquest. The truth of the matter lies somewhere in between. Machiavelli consistently argues in favor of training and arming the people, but he also advises princes to see that the lives and property of their subjects are secure and to foster the arts. The difference (and superiority of republics) lies in the hope citizens of a free regime have that they or their children may attain high office. This hope makes them strive harder not merely to protect themselves and their own, but to win glory by serving the republic as a whole (D 1.60). They come to see the government of the republic not merely as an external source of protection, but as something in which they themselves have a part that they wish to increase. Once they feel that their lives, families, and properties are secure, the multitude have an incentive to serve the republic, because they are moved by the same desire to command that animates the grandi. Their “humor” or “ambition” also needs to be recognized and channeled to produce publicly beneficial results. If it is not, it will produce a series of attempted “conspiracies” against the republic or, in our terms, revolutions.


99 The contrast Machiavelli draws here between ancient and modern education and religion almost exactly parallels that Augustine draws between the pagan Romans and Christians in his City of God, books 2 and 3, with the very important difference, of course, that Machiavelli’s entirely reverses Augustine’s evaluation of the relative merits of the two. Although there is no direct evidence that Machiavelli knew the City of God, Gennaro Sasso, Machiavelli e gli antichi e altri saggi (Milan: R. Ricciardi, 1987), 157–58, assures us that he did. The echoes of Augustine’s account of the fall of Rome in Machiavelli’s celebration of Roman greatness make it difficult to believe that he did not know and have Augustine’s contrasting account of Rome in mind. See Warner and Scott, “Sin City.”


100 By describing this interpretation of “our religion” as “according to idleness” (ozio), which can also be translated ‘leisure,’ Machiavelli appears to be contesting the necessity of the combination of Christian beliefs with ancient philosophical ideas, especially those associated with contemplation, that occurred in the works of Thomas Aquinas, who synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with scriptural faith.


101 In D 1.12 he suggested that the problem is the Church, especially its effect on the politics of Italy, and not Christianity per se, when he observed that the Swiss “are today the only peoples who live according to the ancients as regards both religion and military orders” (39).


102 Machiavelli may have learned what he says here about the Tuscan league from Leonardo Bruni, History of the Florentine People. See the edition by James Hankins (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2001), 1.12–13.


103 Connell, “Machiavelli on Growth as an End,” argues that “throughout his writings, the Florentine argued against the territorial state and in favor of an expansionist republican empire” (261). Misunderstanding the emphasis Machiavelli puts on the need for expansion in D 1.6, commentators have not observed the advantages Machiavelli saw in acquiring “friends” rather than simply conquering. Not observing the way in which Machiavelli saw that the development of the national monarchies in Europe could balance or check the expansion of a Florentine or Tuscan republic, Connell concludes that the expansion by means of federation that Machiavelli recommends would have led to the establishment of an empire like that Rome had exercised earlier, just more slowly.


104 As Levy, Wily Elites, 44, argues, one cannot agree with Maurizio Viroli, Machiavelli, “that for Machiavelli ‘territorial aggrandizement does not mean conquest and predatory expansionism’” or with Mark Hulliung, Citizen Machiavelli, 56, “according to whom Machiavelli admires Rome precisely because of its predatory imperialism.” Although Hulliung denies it, Machiavelli clearly saw the connection between Roman imperialism and the downfall of the republic.


105 In responding to critics of the philosophers (like Aristotle) who maintain (contrary to the Bible) that the world is eternal by observing that human memories are relatively short for two reasons, Machiavelli responds to some but not all of the arguments Lucretius gives in De rerum natura 5.324 ff. for not thinking the world eternal. By not deciding the question, Machiavelli maintains his claim to possess knowledge only of worldly things. The fact that Lucretius uses the term ‘confess’ (confiteare) to refer to what the proponents of the eternity of the world must admit (line 376) does suggest that Machiavelli’s use of ‘confess’ (confessare) in the Discourses (e.g., 2.1) does not necessarily have an explicitly Christian reference or overtone.


106 Letters to Machiavelli expressing such fears, both while he was secretary of the Florentine republic and afterward, can be found in Machiavelli and His Friends, 13–15, 19, 21, 240–41. In Mandragola 3.3, Machiavelli has a nameless Florentine woman voice such a fear. The expansion of the Ottoman Empire into the west was turned back after Machiavelli’s death at the battle of Vienna in 1529.


107 On August 5, 1513, Vettori wrote Machiavelli: “I am afraid that God wants to punish us poor Christians, and while our princes are all irritated against each other and no way can be seen to bring them together, that this new Turkish ruler will attack us by land and by sea and make these priests give up their simpering and the other men their pleasures. The sooner it happens the better” (Machiavelli and His Friends, 240). But in his FH 1.17 and 6.32 Machiavelli observes that previous attempts by popes to unite Christendom against the infidel failed, not because of the prelates’ corruption, but because of lack of faith and virtue on the part of Christian princes.


108 In fact, we know that the Christian religion was revived (and caused a great many wars as a result) by the demands for reform made by a young monk in Germany in 1517, i.e., at the time Machiavelli was writing.


109 TM; Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders; Sullivan, Machiavelli’s Three Romes.


110 Although Machiavelli observes that the Romans began paying their soldiers after the conquest of Veii, he does not remind his readers that it took the Romans ten years to conquer Veii or that the Roman soldiers refused to give the booty they had collected to the public treasury and that the people wanted to divide themselves between the two cities.


111 Insofar as Livy shows that the Romans won the battle, because Torquatus kept his triari in reserve until the Latin troops were exhausted and then attacked, the “lesson” Machiavelli extracts from the history does not differ much from that Livy conveys about the character of the virtue of the Roman captains. Machiavelli notes the “two accidents [which] arose in the managing of this battle that had not arisen before of which there have been rare examples since” (160). But he does not urge his readers to duplicate the “extraordinary” acts of the consuls who made their troops obstinate by visibly sacrificing their own lives, as Decius did when he dressed in regal attire and plunged into the middle of the battle to remove any fears his soldiers might have retained because of the defective liver of the animal sacrifice on his side, or by immediately dispatching his son for disobeying his order not to attack the enemy (even though his attack was successful), as did Torquatus. Machiavelli does emphasize the importance of maintaining reserves, and it was his use of the reserves that enabled Torquatus to win the battle.


112 Such critics include Azar Gat, “Machiavelli and the Decline of the Classical Notion of the Lessons of History in the Study of War,” Military Affairs 52 (1988): 203–5. Coby, Machiavelli’s Romans, 132, points out that using the deep, tripartite orders of the Romans would make modern armies more vulnerable to attack by artillery. But such an observation does not invalidate Machiavelli’s general point about the importance of being able to withstand an initial thrust. In the Art of War Machiavelli argues that the order of march (or attack) has to be adapted to the terrain and circumstances, and he explicitly incorporates the use of artillery.


113 Indeed, Felix Gilbert, “Machiavelli: The Renaissance of the Art of War,” in Makers of Modern Strategy from Machiavelli to the Nuclear Age, ed. Peter Paret (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1986), 15, observes that the military balance became heavily weighted in favor of the offensive, because medieval fortifications were vulnerable to artillery fire.


114 He makes similar arguments in AW 2.86–95.


115 E.g., Aristotle, Politics 4.1297b17–22, although Machiavelli characteristically does not name Aristotle.


116 Observing that several of the examples Machiavelli gives of Roman reliance on the infantry either were undertaken for nonmilitary reasons (the dismounting of the cavalry at Lake Regillus so the patrician equestrians would share the same dangers as the plebian foot soldiers, and again at Sora, according to Livy, to defend the bodies of their fallen commanders) or were defeats as of the armies of both Crassus and Mark Anthony on the plains of Parthia, where horse would have fared better than infantry, Coby, Machiavelli’s Romans, concludes that Machiavelli has “at least exaggerated if not falsified . . . infantry’s superior fighting qualities” (135). Indeed, Coby goes so far as to argue that Machiavelli’s emphasis on the excellence of Roman means of expansion in general, as well as the role of the infantry is particular, is a “noble lie” (136–47). Machiavelli attributes to the Romans a degree of “civic virtue,” i.e., the subordination of the interests and desires of individuals to those of the community, that they really did not have. In fact, however, Machiavelli admits that the Romans were defeated in Parthia. He does not argue that their reliance on the infantry (or any other tactic, military or otherwise) always produced victory. What he explicitly writes is that the authority of the Romans justifies “esteeming” or valuing the infantry more than the cavalry, and he uses his examples to show that the Roman captains trusted their armed plebian foot soldiers. It is precisely this trust that his Florentine (or, more generally, Italian) contemporaries lacked and that Machiavelli seeks to persuade them to acquire.


117 As Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders, observes: “Of the many examples ‘one sees,’ the first is the dismounting of the Roman cavalry in a battle against the Latins to come on foot to the aid of the hard-pressed infantry. . . . There are several instances of ‘dismounting’ in this chapter, which Machiavelli says the Romans always found the best remedy in their dangers. Livy says in this case that the spirit of the foot soldiers was restored when they saw the young nobles on equal terms with them (2.20.11); and beginning from this report we might imagine that for Machiavelli, ‘dismounting’ means laying aside authority and putting one’s feet on the ground. It also suggests a way of ‘going to the people,’ and we should not overlook the obvious fact that infantry is the popular and the republican branch of militia, while the cavalry are distinguished by wealth” (243).


118 Machiavelli might even seem to have been advocating such policies himself in P 10 and D 1.55.


119 Like the Capuans, the popes might be persuaded to ask for the protection of an armed republican league without literally being forced to do so.


120 As Ardito, Machiavelli and the Modern State, observes: “Tuscany was Florence’s manifest destiny, according to a gallery of Florentine civic humanists—Leonardo Bruni, Coluccio Salutati, Giorgio Dati, and Matteo Palmieri—all of whom would have agreed with Machiavelli when he wrote, ‘A city that lives free has two ends—one to acquire, the other to maintain itself free’” (102). However, she also points out, “Machiavelli’s critique of Florentine expansionism has been neglected by interpreters who view him as remaining within the civic republican tradition and Florentine imperialism. Such a view misses an important aspect of Machiavelli’s thought that is novel, innovative, and creative. There was also . . . an aspect of the civic republic tradition that aspired to Tuscan hegemony. . . . It is with this tradition . . . that Machiavelli takes issue. . . . His awareness of new political realities, of the rise of monarchical states, and his direct experience in the Florentine territory enabled him to discern the weaknesses in received ideas and practices of territorial government. [He] found the traditional republican policies of subordinating subject cities dangerously outmoded” (104).


121 Machiavelli argued that the pope ought to accept the alliance in two letters on December 20, 1514, to the Florentine representative at the papal court, his friend Francesco Vettori.


122 Machiavelli enunciated the same principle with regard to domestic policy in D 1.22 in criticizing the Romans’ failure to punish Horatio for the murder of his sister, who wept for the death of her betrothed, partly because of his father’s plea that he had saved the city.


123 D 2.28; 196. Machiavelli does not report, as Livy (5.36) does, “The Senate . . . by no means approved the conduct of their own envoys; but though they admitted to themselves that the [Gauls’] demand was a fair one, they refused, where three men of such rank were concerned, to take what they really knew to be the proper action. . . . Accordingly, to avoid the responsibility for any losses which might result from a clash with the Gauls they referred the envoys’ demands to the people for decision, with the result that the three guilty men, whose punishment was supposed to be under discussion, were elected as military tribunes” (The Early History of Rome: Books I–V of “The History of Rome from Its Foundations,” trans. Aubrey de Sélincourt [New York: Penguin Books, 1960], 382).


124 Machiavelli’s use of “French” to describe the people then known as the “Gauls” (in contrast to Livy) reflects his contention later in D 3.43, “That Men Who Are Born in One Province Observe Almost the Same Nature for All Times,” which he applies specifically to the French in D 3.26. Because they have not been well ordered or trained, like the Romans, he contends, the French continue to come into battles furiously, and then to retreat if they do not succeed with their first thrust. They could, however, be trained to keep some of their troops in reserve and thus to persist.


125 He again suggests that he will confine this discussion to the first decade of Livy’s history, upon which he has supposedly been discoursing in the entire work, but he does not so confine his study in book 3 any more than he did in the preceding two books.


126 Like archê in Greek and principium in Latin, principio in Italian can mean either beginning or principle. Obviously it is also closely related to principe (prince).


127 A reader much later, Wolin, Politics and Vision, 2nd ed., 207, did.


128 By dividing the “executions” between those that occurred before the French took Rome and after, Machiavelli underlines his contention that the effects of both internally and externally caused returns to the beginning do not last. Perhaps to emphasize the fearsome character of these “executions,” he also exaggerates the number of deaths. Not all of the ten citizens were put to death, according not only to Livy (3.65–58) but also to Machiavelli himself (who reported in D 1.45 that Appius Claudius was not granted a right to appeal to the people and committed suicide the day before he was judged, and that the others were “condemned” and “punished,” but not necessarily killed). Maelius the grain dealer, Manlius Capitolinus, and the son of Manlius Torquatus were publicly condemned and slain, but Fabius, the master of the cavalry, whom Papirius Cursor wished to slay, was saved by his father’s appeal to the people. Machiavelli states merely that the Scipios were “accused.” Scipio Africanus retired to the country and was excused from his trial by illness. His brother Lucius Scipio was later convicted of having taken money from King Antiochus that he did not turn over to the treasury, but they could not find evidence of the gold among his possessions, so Tiberius Gracchus released him from prison. Livy 38.50–60 reports that Marcus Cato sponsored the accusations. Machiavelli praises Cato for having brought what appears to be an unjust accusation. According to Machiavelli, such accusations were not brought against reputed citizens in Rome with sufficient frequency.


129 In D 1.30, 1.40, and 1.52 Machiavelli argued that the nobles constitute the best check on the ambitions of a potential tyrant, even though the people often do not see it.


130 The individuals Machiavelli names as “rare and virtuous examples . . . that good men desire to imitate . . . and the wicked are ashamed” to contradict are Horatius Coclus, who famously died holding a bridge until the Romans retreated to safety behind him; Scaevola, who thrust his hand into the fire to show Porcena how much pain and self-sacrifice Romans would endure; Fabricius, who convinced Pyrrhus to withdraw his army from Italy by revealing a plot to poison him, but would not accept a position of great honor outside of Rome as compensation; the two Decii, generals who sacrificed their own lives in battle so that their legions would be victorious; and Regulus Attilius, who kept his promise to return to Carthage and suffered a horrible death there, after he advised the Romans not to return the Carthaginian hostages.
