131 In D 1.51, the example Machiavelli used to show that “a republic or a prince should make a show of doing through liberality what necessity constrains him to do” was the Senate’s not only offering to pay soldiers in order to wage longer wars, but also levying the heaviest taxes on themselves (and so overcoming the opposition of the tribunes, who argued that the people would, in effect, pay for the wages they earned as soldiers with higher taxes).


132 Like republican “princes,” Machiavelli suggests, religious leaders persuade their followers that they are acting on the basis of their publicly proclaimed beliefs, and not for their own private benefit, by forgoing the advantages of wealth and position by living in utter poverty.


133 Machiavelli clearly indicated in D 1.11–15 that religious leaders do not—and cannot—believe what they preach, although they have to act as if they do.


134 In D 1.16 Machiavelli used the kingdom of France as an example to support his contention that if a prince makes orders and laws that guarantee the security of all as well as his own power, and “the people see that he does not break such laws because of any accident, in a short time he will begin to live secure and content” (46).


135 Wolin, Politics and Vision, 2nd ed., 184, notes Machiavelli’s insistence on the need for both political and religious bodies to return to their “archê or fundamental principle,” but by failing to notice the difference in the effects of such a return in the two cases, he reduces both to mere rituals of renewal. As a result, Wolin also misses Machiavelli’s insistence on the need for individual action to revive the fear that leads human beings to obey the law and suggests (211) that Machiavelli thinks that republican institutions make “princes” obsolete.


136 Machiavelli thus disputes Socrates’ contention in the Gorgias 510b–511c that a good and just man would not try to preserve his own life by associating with a tyrant, because the association will require the just man to do unjust things and so become no better than the tyrant he serves. Machiavelli typically recognizes no such moral concerns for purity of character or intention; the relevant considerations are the safety of the individual and the possible public effect. He would, no doubt, remind admirers of Socrates that the philosopher who stayed away from the assembly was not merely accused but convicted of a capital crime.


137 In D 3.4 Machiavelli makes the same criticism of Tarquin Priscus, who believed that his obtaining the monarchy lawfully from the people with the consent of the Senate would stifle the anger of the sons of Ancus from whom he had seized the kingship by means of fraud. In arguing that “a prince does not live secure in a principality while those who have been despoiled of it are living,” Machiavelli seems to be making the same point he made in the previous chapter (as well as P 3). But stressing the overwhelming power of the desire for domination (and not mere safety or security), he adds, the “appetite for reigning is so great that it enters the breasts not only of those who expect the kingdom but also those who do not expect it. . . . Moved by this rage, against all paternal piety, the wife of young Tarquin, the daughter of Servius, . . . moved her husband against her father to take away from him his life and the kingdom—so much more did she esteem it to be queen than daughter of a king” (216). As Machiavelli showed earlier, the desire for domination is much stronger than family ties or affection (as ancient tragedies such as the Oresteia and Oedipus trilogy also demonstrate). And, he indicates here, it moves women as well as men. Making succession to the kingship hereditary does not make it smooth or noncontested any more than it guarantees good successors.


138 See P 18. Machiavelli’s silence on Brutus’s major institutional innovation, the annual election of two consuls by the Senate in place of the elected king, is not surprising, since he has already argued that the constitution of the Roman republic was incomplete or imperfect before the introduction of the tribunes. Machiavelli’s emphasis on the importance of a single leader or “mind” in the original founding or “ordering” of Rome (D 1.9) as well as his emphasis on the importance of having a single commander in D 3.15 suggests that he did not think having two consuls was a good idea. That institution was based on the old Spartan model of having two kings (or generals), each of which could check the other.


139 Machiavelli thus suggests, as Locke argues later in his Second Treatise, chap. 19, paras. 218–20, that it is the prince who rebels against the government, not the people.


140 As Machiavelli observes both in P 19 and D 1.16, most people will be content with the government if it secures their lives and property. He does not admit here, as he does there, that this conclusion does not apply to “the great” (among whom we would probably include Brutus, if not Collatinus), some of whom will always be dissatisfied with the government in power and seek to overturn it in order to establish one in which they have more power and influence.


141 Like Soderini, Machiavelli points out in D 3.4, both Tarquin Priscus and Servius Tullius believed that their positions were secure, because they were legally appointed and had the consent of the people. They also believed that they could overcome their opponents with new benefits or “kindness.” Like Soderini, they were mistaken.


142 By referring repeatedly to the authority of Tacitus, however, Machiavelli does remind his readers of the terrible consequences of Caesar’s seizing power. If they want to attain earthly glory, he urges them to take the opportunity of living in a corrupt city like Florence, “not to spoil it entirely as did Caesar but to reorder it as did Romulus” (D 1.10; 33).


143 To support his claim, Machiavelli uses the examples of Nelematus, an enemy of the tyrant Aristotimus; Darius in getting the other six princes to kill the Magian; and Piso, a friend of Nero.


144 In D 1.27 Machiavelli noted an (in)famous example of that reluctance in Baglioni’s failure to kill Pope Julius when the tyrant had an opportunity to do so.


145 In D 3.18 Machiavelli nevertheless suggests that misinformation and chance had much to do with the defeat of this particular effort to revive the republic.


146 See FH 7.33–34, 8.8.


147 Those “heads” in Florence would, however, include a cardinal and a pope and thus involve one of the difficulties encountered by the Pazzi conspiracy. In his “Discourse on Remodeling the Government of Florence,” written at the request of Pope Leo X in 1520 approximately one year after he finished writing his Discourses on Livy, Machiavelli proposed to deal with this problem by granting the pope (Giovanni de’ Medici) and the Cardinal Giulio de’ Medici “as much authority during the lives of both as is held by the entire people of Florence” (Machiavelli: The Chief Works and Others, trans. Allan Gilbert [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1958], 1: 110), but creating a set of three councils, elected respectively from and by the most important, middle, and general bodies of citizens, to whom authority would devolve after the deaths of the Medici princes. As men of the church, neither the pope nor the cardinal could have a legal heir (although Machiavelli knew that popes like Alexander VI had tried to make their illegitimate sons princes of some of the papal cities they controlled). However, Machiavelli never seems to have received a response to his proposal.


148 According to Livy 2.41, the plebs did not accept the lands Rome had taken from the Hernici when Spurius offered them, because he also wanted to share those lands with Rome’s allies. And “the fathers” defeated his attempt to win the plebs over by distributing grain brought from Sicily by convincing them that he was trying to become a king.


149 Lefort, Le travail de l’oeuvre Machiavel, 628, 638, 642 (Smith trans., 368, 377, 381).


150 In using the way in which the Senate manipulated elections of the tribunes by finding either extremely contemptible or virtuous candidates (cf. D 1.48) as an example of the way to deal with “very many,” Machiavelli suggests for the first time that the senators learned this stratagem from Appius Claudius, the tyrant, who had shown (D 1.42) how easily men can be corrupted. Machiavelli thus concludes the chapter by emphasizing that “any prince . . . who is assaulted by many will have a remedy whenever he knows how to use with prudence suitable means to disunite them” (246). This principle would apply to a prince facing opposition from an aristocratic body as well as if not better than to that body facing the power of representatives of the people.


151 A point he emphasizes in AW 3.198–207, as well.


152 Once again Machiavelli thus explicitly rejects the Spartan model of the mixed regime. According to the Athenian Stranger in Plato, Laws 3.691e, a god must have blessed Sparta by having twin kings born from a single line, so that the Spartans continued to appoint two, each of whom served to check potential abuses by the other.


153 Machiavelli made a similar observation in D 1.18, but did not emphasize the role of envy in producing the corruption of the republic. At the end of D 3.16 he cites an example of the same corrupting tendency in the republic of Florence (after 1494, so under the effective leadership of Savonarola) to prefer using money to buy Pisa rather than recognize the outstanding virtue of an individual captain, Antonio Giacomini, who could have taken Pisa much more cheaply by force. The great example of a Roman “captain” who did not feel that he received the honor he deserved, sought to take it by force, and brought the republic down as a result was, of course, Caesar.


154 Indeed, Machiavelli has reminded his readers, both of these “remedies” had failed before the “French” invasion of Rome. Camillus, the only general capable of saving the city, had been exiled, because he had sought to deposit the spoils of his victory in Veii in the public treasury rather than divide them among the soldiers. However, Machiavelli argues, the Roman republic was reordered and revived as a result of that “extrinsic accident.”


155 Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders, 368–69, shows that Machiavelli, in effect, manufactured the incident (and then only in one extant manuscript of the Discourses) in order to make his point. According to Livy, Claudius had not been dishonored. Instead of giving the explanation Livy (27.40.9) attributes to another consul who had been dishonored, Claudius tried to encourage his troops by telling them that arriving last on the battlefield, they would have almost all the glory.


156 In D 3.22 Machiavelli concludes that “if a republic were so happy that it often had one [such as Manlius Torquatus] who with his example might renew the laws, and not only restrain it from running to ruin but pull it back, it would be perpetual” (266). However, in that chapter he also argues that Manlius was harsh by nature and that only one who was like him could issue such harsh commands. Machiavelli does not think that such natural traits are passed on by heredity; in D 3.46 he observes that family traits are passed on by education more than nature, because heredity is mixed as a result of marriages. And in The Prince he argued that the classical attempt to educate a ruling class with the necessary virtues had failed. Ambitious leaders, he suggests in D 3.22, would try to attract partisans by ruling gently, at least initially, and thus constitute a threat to the perpetuation of the republic. In sum, there is no way of guaranteeing an unending line or succession of virtuous leaders. The most one can do is to institute and maintain laws that force ambitious men to compete and thus check each other.


157 Following Strauss, TM, 38–39; 303n48, Mansfield, Machiavelli’s New Modes and Orders, 368–69, argues that the point of the comparison is to show that, believing in the power of fate, the ancients despaired too quickly, whereas modern soldiers, believing that there is a providence and that they will be saved, are too optimistic. However, in this section of the text Machiavelli appears to be discussing the difficulty of determining the distinctive virtue characteristic of republican leadership, not religion.


158 Although Machiavelli presents the opinion he attributes to Tacitus along with other writers as a quotation, Strauss, TM, 160, notes that no such statement appears in the works of that Roman historian. Like the egregious change he makes in Livy’s account of Claudius Nero, Machiavelli’s false attribution of this statement to other past writers indicates his judgment that they have not presented the problems of republican leadership accurately.


159 Machiavelli fails to note, however, that Xenophon shows that Cyrus began his career by corrupting the citizen soldiers of the republic of Persia by promising them a share in the wealth and power of the empire he proposed to conquer.


160 In D 3.46 Machiavelli argues that the tendency within families to cultivate certain traits cannot be a matter of heredity (or nature), strictly speaking, because of intermarriage. And he mentions the Manlii as an example of a family whose members shared a characteristic harshness. But he also recognizes that there were other families in Rome who cultivated other traits. He does not suggest that this private education would be sufficient to guarantee a line of republican leaders able to renew the laws.


161 In FH 6.5 Machiavelli thus praises Cosimo de’ Medici for the prudence that led him never to overstep “civil modesty. For in his conversations, in his servants, in riding on horse, in his whole mode of living, and in his marriage alliances, he was always like any modest citizen. For he knew how extraordinary things that are seen . . . make men much more envied than those that are . . . covered over with decency” (282–83).


162 Indicating just how distinctive Machiavelli’s analysis of the fall of the republic is, Guicciardini, Considerations, concedes, “extending the term of military commands was unquestionably a great opportunity for anyone who wanted to seize control of the republic.” But he reasserts the traditional understanding of the reason for the fall of the republic, as it was articulated by Cicero and Sallust, when he insists that “the principal basis for the city’s ills was its corruption: devoting itself to greed and to pleasure, it had so degenerated from its ancient customs that the city’s bloody divisions were the result; among a free people tyranny always arises from these. That is why it was easy to corrupt citizens and soldiers, and someone like Catiline, without military authority and without troops, might hope to seize control of the republic; from this arose a conspiracy of the more powerful men to divide up the military commands and the armies among themselves and with these forces to keep the others down. Hence the extraordinary extensions of military commands like that of Caesar, who was given a ten-year command not because of some advantage to the republic or the needs of war or admiration for his virtù but because of his conspiracy with Crassus and Pompey to seize control of the republic” (3.24.1–3).


163 Machiavelli does not indicate in D 3.24 that this Lucius Quintius was known as Cincinnatus, because of his curly hair, and that he is, therefore, the exemplary leader celebrated for leaving his farm to serve the republic whom Machiavelli praises in D 3.25. Perhaps he expected his readers to know this.


164 Readers of Livy (3.13.10) would know that Cincinnatus failed to pass on his own virtue by example closer to home. The patrician Cincinnatus was poor because of a heavy fine exacted from him to pay for the misdeeds of his son. He was not at home plowing his own fields entirely as a product of his own choice.


165 He explicitly argued as much both in P 17 and 19 and in D 1.37 and 3.6 when he observed that individuals come to hate princes who dishonor them or their women and seize their property, but that the latter is a stronger and more frequent cause.


166 D 1.17, 3.5, 1.40, 1.44, 1.57.


167 Plato, Republic 9.572d–573c; Xenophon, Hiero.


168 As Machiavelli’s Florentine contemporaries and all later readers of his Florentine Histories would know, the Medici defined themselves as leaders of the people (popolari).


169 See FH 7.5, 8.36.


170 Machiavelli also reminds his readers that there was at least one prince of the Church who not only recognized the necessity of eliminating his competitors, but also (in contrast to Savonarola in the following chapter) persuaded his natural son to eliminate them.


171 Later American readers of Machiavelli’s description of the ways in which “envy” can be overcome might think of George Washington, who, rather than become a monarch, decided to establish and maintain a republic by voluntarily relinquishing office after two terms, and of his secretary Alexander Hamilton, who seems voluntarily to have sought his own death by fighting a duel with the ambitious traitor Aaron Burr. For somewhat contrasting views of the relation between Machiavelli and these American founders see Matthew Spalding, “The American Prince? George Washington’s Anti-Machiavellian Moment,” and Karl-Friedrich Walling, “Was Alexander Hamilton a Machiavellian Statesman?,” in Machiavelli’s Liberal Republican Legacy, ed. Paul Rahe (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006), 167–88, 254–78.


172 A skeptical reader might observe that just as Cesare Borgia was able to blame the severe measures he used to establish “good government” in the Romagna on the harsh nature of his minister, so Moses was able to blame the deaths of those who opposed him like Korah (Numbers 16) on God.


173 In his letter to Ricciardo Becchi, the Florentine ambassador to the Holy See, on March 9, 1498 (Machiavelli and His Friends, 9–10), Machiavelli pointed out that Savonarola vacillated about the need to use violence in opposing his enemies. Fearing that the newly elected Signoria would be hostile to his party, in his sermon on March 2 the friar urged the congregation to do as Christ and Saint Paul had: “whenever the times call upon us to imperil our lives for Him, to do so; and whenever it is time for a man to go into hiding, to do so.” Then he informed his audience that the time and God now require that the people rise up against violence, and “soldier” under God against their adversaries, who are the wicked and obstinate people who do not follow God. And explicating the same passage from Exodus in his sermon the next day, he urged his followers to behave like Moses when he slew the Egyptian. But after the newly elected Signoria sent a letter to the pope urging him not to excommunicate the friar, Savonarola concluded that he and his followers no longer needed to fear his adversaries in Florence. He no longer called for violent rebellion, therefore, but sought merely to set his followers at odds with the Supreme Pontiff as the wickedest man alive. Savonarola “acts in accordance with the times and colors his lies accordingly” (10), Machiavelli concluded. But the friar’s followers might well have been confused by his vacillations.


174 In FH 3.13, he reports the speech of a leader of the Ciompi who urged them to such an explicitly desperate policy.


175 Michelle Tolman Clarke, “The Virtues of Republican Citizenship in Machiavelli’s Discourses on Livy,” Journal of Politics 75, no. 2 (2013): 322–27, shows that Livy treats Manlius much less positively than Machiavelli does in D 3.22.


176 Machiavelli’s first example is the Grand Turk, who made an expedition to Syria and Egypt on the advice of one of his bashaws, whom he killed after his troops were destroyed by “those difficulties that had already brought many Roman armies to ruin” (290). A prince who had read the histories (as Machiavelli urges) would have avoided taking such bad advice, and thus he was to be faulted for his ignorance as much as his advisor. Cf. P 22.


177 In the first example Machiavelli explains how Xenophon shows that Cyrus used the experience his men had in hunting to explain the roles both divisions of his troops were to play in ambushing the king of Armenia. Machiavelli does not mention the order Cyrus gave his captain not to risk his own energy and life, or those of his men, the way the captain habitually did in hunting, i.e., that the practice was not a perfect model for the real battle. Nor does Machiavelli explain that the captain was willing to obey because Cyrus had honored him by granting him command of half of the troops. Xenophon, Education of Cyrus 2.4.22–29. In his second example Machiavelli refers to Livy’s account of the way in which Publius Decius used his knowledge of countries (without any account of how he had acquired it or reference to hunting) first to enable the Romans to escape a possible ambush by the Samnites by occupying a hill above the valley and then to find a way for his men to rejoin the army without the enemy’s discovering them. Lefort contends that Machiavelli is showing that the methods of Epaminondas, who Plutarch says stayed home to train his fellow Thebans and preferred to study philosophy, were superior to the modes of his colleague Pelopidas, who sought fellow conspirators outside of Thebes and preferred hunting. However, hunting here, as in The Prince, is associated with learning the kinds of things Machiavelli himself teaches. Lefort, Le travail de l’oeuvre Machiavel, 670–76 (Smith trans., 407–12).


178 Livy, Rome and Italy: Books VI–X of “The History of Rome from Its Foundation,” trans. Betty Radice (New York: Penguin, 1982), 219.


179 To say that an advisor should not have any other concern does not, however, justify Viroli’s conclusion that Machiavelli regarded his “fatherland” as a god.


180 Augustine praised Regulus Attilius for keeping his word or faith with the Carthaginians when he returned to Carthage from Rome, where he would have been safe, and suffered a horrible death because he had advised the Romans not to return the Carthaginian hostages they had taken in exchange for his life. In D 3.1 Machiavelli lists Regulus among the individuals whose virtue had almost the same effect on his fellow citizens as a public execution. However, the only specific action of Regulus to which Machiavelli explicitly refers is his asking permission to return home to take care of his villa, showing that he like Cincinnatus had not become wealthy as a result of his leading victorious Roman armies. Clarke, “Virtues of Republican Citizenship,” 317–28, shows that Machiavelli departed markedly from the premium that Romans such as Cicero put on keeping faith and showing gratitude.


181 TM, 35. Strauss takes Machiavelli’s overstatement to indicate that when he makes errors, there is fraud underlying them. I have argued that rather than making intentional “errors,” Machiavelli exaggerates both to shock and to entertain his readers, and that he modifies or adapts historical incidents to illustrate his points. As Strauss shows, some of those points come out only when one compares Machiavelli’s account with his source.


182 In a characteristic overstatement, Machiavelli asserts, “all Roman women had conspired against their husbands to kill them.” Livy 8.18 shows that an informant revealed that twenty were involved in preparing the poison and one hundred seventy (a large number, but hardly all the wives in Rome) were convicted.


183 Machiavelli repeats this praise of the Roman policy of decimation and the rationale for it in AW 6.114–15.


184 Coby, Machiavelli’s Romans, 190.


185 Taking Fabius as exemplifying the character of Machiavelli’s own enterprise rather than the sort of education he hopes to provide his readers, Strauss, TM, first suggests that “Machiavelli is another Fabius; it is the incredibility of his enterprise which secures him against detection” (17). Strauss then observes that “Rome was enabled to destroy freedom in the West . . . because she liberally admitted foreigners to citizenship. . . . Rome was then enabled to destroy freedom in the Western world because she was excessively cosmopolitan or constitutionally exposed to corruption. No wonder that Machiavelli takes leave of the reader of the Discourses with the praise of that Fabius who was deservedly called Maximus for having practically disfranchised ‘the new people.’” But, Strauss notes, “Fabius’ measure did not stem the tide forever. Hence it remains true that the Roman republic, the greatest republic . . . that ever was, prepared the Western world for Asiatic obedience. The Roman republic is on the one hand the direct opposite of the Christian republic, and on the other hand a cause of the latter, or even the model for it” (118). Strauss thus concludes his account of “Machiavelli’s Intention: The Discourses” by arguing that “Machiavelli combines the imitation of Jesus with the imitation of Fabius. Fabius, in contradistinction to Decius, judged the low assault to be preferable and . . . choosing the safer way, he gained a more gladdening victory, remaining alive, than the victory which Decius gained by his death. For Decius, imitating his father, sacrificed himself for the expiation of the Romans. . . . Classical political philosophy had taught that the salvation of the cities depends on the coincidence of philosophy and political power . . . for which one can wish or hope but which one cannot bring about. Machiavelli is the first philosopher who believes that the coincidence of philosophy and political power can be brought about by propaganda which wins over ever larger multitudes to the new modes and orders and thus transforms the thought of one or a few into the opinion of the public and therewith into public power” (173).


186 He does not, therefore, advocate the Socratic “ethics” that Benner, Machiavelli’s Ethics, attributes to him.


187 In P 3 he declares simply that “truly it is a very natural and ordinary thing to desire to acquire, and always, when men do it who can, they will be praised or not blamed” (14).


188 D 3.29; cf. Hobbes, Leviathan 6, definition of ‘good.’


189 Machiavelli’s emphasis on force might lead a reader to believe that he thinks only men can found a state; certainly they provide most of the historical examples. Machiavelli recognizes, however, again by giving historical examples, that women such as Caterina Sforza (3.6) or the daughter of Servius Tullius (3.4) are just as willing to sacrifice members of their family to their political ambitions as men like Romulus and Brutus.


190 Machiavelli’s reiterated insistence on the superiority of training to religion as a force in maintaining popular obedience speaks against the emphasis put on his admittedly unconventional understanding of the role of God in politics by Viroli, Machiavelli’s God, and Vatter, “Machiavelli and the Republican Conception of Providence.”


Part II


Later Developments


INTRODUCTION


Machiavelli claimed to have written down everything he knew about worldly affairs in the two works he composed after the Florentine republic fell in 1512 and he was dismissed from office. He did not publish either of his two comprehensive works during his lifetime, yet he kept writing. We are led, therefore, to ask how these later writings are related to the comprehensive understanding of the world he put forward in The Prince and Discourses on Livy.

The Prince seems to have circulated widely in manuscript form, first in Florence and then in northern Europe. But Machiavelli had reason to think he had not been understood. He was not appointed to a political office by either of the Medici princes to whom he had dedicated The Prince. Nor did he have the satisfaction of seeing Lorenzo and Leo act on the basis of his advice to seize Italy. Even worse, the young Florentine aristocrats to whom Machiavelli dedicated the Discourses did not seem to understand what he wished to teach them any better than the Medici princes. As he indicates in the setting and characters of the dialogue on the art of war he published in 1521, they enjoyed talking about what it would mean to imitate the Romans, but they had obviously not learned, much less undertaken, what Machiavelli had insisted was the necessary first step: organizing and training a group of supporters to use arms to seize power and then defend the new regime against its opponents.

In his later works Machiavelli showed more specifically how his broad analysis applied to the lives of his contemporaries, in private as well as in public. At the same time he also made the philosophical foundations of his political project clearer. Instead of trying to present his complete understanding of politics in more or less extensive form, in each of his subsequent works Machiavelli emphasized a particular theme or partial application of his more comprehensive understanding—to make it both more palatable and more easily understood. By writing in a variety of genres—two comedies, a dialogue, and two histories—Machiavelli was able to put some of his most controversial thoughts into the mouths of others. As a result, he was able to put those thoughts forward more publicly, if still somewhat indirectly and ironically.

In a comedy he seems to have completed and produced in 1518 Machiavelli demonstrated how his teaching a prince how not to be good and to use that knowledge according to necessity could and should also be applied to the lives of private individuals.1 Contrary to the claims of some of his most highly regarded interpreters, in Mandragola Machiavelli thus showed that politics is not an entirely “autonomous” sphere. The lack of pure morality and conscience that he insisted a successful prince must demonstrate can and should be found in the lives of ordinary human beings as well, if they would live happily. In contrast to his more comprehensive treatises, he could not merely publish but produce Mandragola safely, because in a play, the playwright merely presents the speeches and deeds of others. None of the truly scandalous statements made by his characters could legitimately be said to represent the playwright’s own opinions. He could (and did) say that he was simply trying to entertain.

Turning back to consider a deadly serious public topic, in The Art of War he published in 1521 Machiavelli presented his young Florentine friends with a lesson about how to imitate the Romans specifically with regard to military organization and tactics. He instructed them to use this knowledge in advising their prince, because a prince who adopted the military organization and tactics he recommended would be able, as he had urged at the end of The Prince, to seize Italy and free it from the barbarians. By writing those instructions in the form of a dialogue, in which the author simply explained in the preface how he came to know about the conversation he relates, he presented the speeches and deeds of others as in Mandragola, rather than stating his own opinions and arguments to support them. The irony of Machiavelli’s presenting a mercenary captain (of the kind he so harshly criticized in both The Prince and Discourses) as the teacher of an art he emphasizes can be learned only by means of practice to a group of young aristocrats lounging at their ease in a garden has not been lost on commentators (although they have not agreed about its significance). However, because Fabrizio Colonna’s lecture contains a great many details drawn from classical works on military strategy, many readers have understood (and criticized) the dialogue as a technical treatise. They have not picked up the political implications of the military organization and tactics Machiavelli had also recommended, although much more briefly, in his Discourses.

Machiavelli might have appeared to be presenting a historical model of an Italian prince who understood the art of war in the highly fictionalized account of the life of Castruccio Castracani he wrote during the summer of 1520. However, in his Life Machiavelli showed that the young tyrant of Lucca knew how to seize power but not how to maintain it or pass it on to his heirs. By attributing a list of updated “sayings” of the philosophers drawn from Diogenes Laertius to Castruccio at the end of his Life, Machiavelli also indicated something about the philosophical background and basis of his own thought. In composing what first appears to be a praising account of the life of a tyrant, moreover, Machiavelli provided his young friends, Zanobi Buondelmonti and Luigi Alamanni, with an example of the kind of historical writing he could produce. They may or may not have used it in their attempts to persuade the Medici to hire him to write a history of Florence; but, in any case, they succeeded. In November 1520 then cardinal Giulio de’ Medici commissioned Machiavelli to write the Florentine Histories.

Just before he finished writing his history, Machiavelli wrote and produced a second comedy in which he seemed to mock himself by presenting an old man named Nicomaco making a fool of himself by falling in love with a young girl. In Clizia, Machiavelli explicitly re-presented an ancient Greek story that had been made into a Roman comedy by Plautus. By means of the changes he made in “updating” that story so that it could take place in Florence, Machiavelli nevertheless showed why it was necessary to maintain the appearance of conventional morality, especially concerning the family, if human beings were to survive and prosper. Some commentators have taken the title character, Clizia, who never appears onstage, to represent his dream of a reunited Italy. But, I shall argue, Machiavelli’s depiction of the destructive effect of Nicomaco’s erotic desire for eternal youth and beauty on his family dramatizes the impossibility of realizing “fantastical” desires for immortality and the necessity, therefore, of disciplining and redirecting those desires to more worldly goods like wealth and reputation.

Finally, in his Florentine Histories Machiavelli showed how his native city had gone awry. In the preface he explains why he found it necessary to cover the same ground and so, in effect, to correct the more clearly celebratory histories of the republic written by his predecessors. He apologizes for appearing to have flattered the family of his Medici sponsors, but he protests that he has simply described their achievements: the way they seized control of the Florentine republic and maintained that control by means of their liberality. Presenting a mass of “facts” and making very few judgments explicitly in his own name, he nevertheless shows that the foreign policies praised by previous historians for maintaining Florentine independence were disastrous, internally as well as externally, and that the political tactics that enabled Cosimo de’ Medici to seize and maintain control of the state destroyed the liberty of the republic. As in his Discourses, so in the Florentine Histories, Machiavelli generally contrasts the weak, ineffective policies of his native city (which he describes in much greater detail) with the admirable institutions and policies of the Roman republic (to which he alludes only briefly). However, he concludes, whereas the civil war that erupted between the two humors in Rome made the rise of a tyrant there inevitable, the equality in Florence became so great that a better republic could easily have been founded there—if only there had been a legislator who knew how. Machiavelli had been trying to teach his readers how and why they should introduce such “new modes and orders” in all of his works.


Footnotes


1 There is some debate about exactly when Machiavelli wrote Mandragola. There is evidence that he had begun writing comedies while he was serving the republic. For example, he had reputedly written a new version of Aristophanes’ Clouds, but the manuscript was destroyed by his grandson and literary executor, Giuliano de’ Ricci, because it contained so many slanderous remarks about Florentine politicians. The plot of Mandragola is set in 1504; and at one point a character refers to a fortress near Pisa that the Florentines took in June 1503. Sergio Bertelli, “When Did Machiavelli Write Mandragola?,” Renaissance Quarterly 24 (1980): 317–26, thus believes that Machiavelli began composing the comedy, but may not have finished it, while he was still a secretary of the republic. However, there is no evidence of a completed manuscript or a production before 1518.


3


In What Mode Private Individuals Should Keep Faith


MANDRAGOLA


In the prologue to Mandragola Machiavelli explains his turn to comedy in terms of the disappointing reception of his previous work: “If this material is not worthy—on account of its being so light—of a man who wishes to seem wise and grave,” he should be excused for “trying with these vain thoughts to make his wretched time more pleasant, because he has nowhere else to turn his face, for he has been cut off from showing with other undertakings other virtù” (11). Some commentators have thus argued that in Mandragola he was merely trying to entertain himself along with his audience.1 He does not appear to have thought comedies were merely a form of diversion or entertainment, however. In the prologue to Clizia, he declares that “comedies were discovered in order to benefit” as well as “to delight the spectators” (5). Even more pointedly, in his Dialogue on Language he writes: “Though the aim of comedy is to hold up a mirror to domestic life, the way it does this . . . [allows] . . . the men who come eagerly to enjoy themselves, [to] taste afterwards the useful lesson that lay underneath.”2

As in the dedications to his major prose works, so in the prologue to Mandragola, Machiavelli suggests that he is presenting his audience with something of value. On the basis of his past experience, however, he does not expect to receive any reward for his labor but sneers and other insults. His contemporaries’ unwillingness to recognize the excellence of the works of others is the reason “why, in all things, the present age falls off from ancient virtù.” Most people are not willing to labor and strain on what must by nature be transitory achievements without the promise of some form of remuneration. But he will not be discouraged, because he knows how to trade insult for insult and “doesn’t stand in awe of anyone, even though he might play the servant to one who can wear a better coat than he can” (11). More clearly than in the dedications to his prose works, Machiavelli expresses not only resentment of the envious pretensions of the wealthy and powerful to be better men than he but also his conviction that one who works for the common benefit should not expect gratitude or glory as a reward.

What, then, is the “useful lesson” lying underneath the comic plot of Mandragola? In this comedy Machiavelli explicitly writes as a private individual about private domestic life. Since he is a famous political theorist, however, many commentators have tried to show the relevance of the play to public affairs. Some have read it as a satirical allegory in which the fictional characters are identified with specific Florentine politicians (or, in the case of Lucrezia, with the Florentine people).3 The problem with such allegorical readings is, first, that the allegorists do not agree either on the specific correspondences—e.g., whether Callimaco represents a generic “prince” or Lorenzo de’ Medici, or whether the childless Nicia should be taken as the childless Piero Soderini—or on the point of the satire, whether it looks forward to the rise or to the fall of the Medici.4 Second, if Machiavelli had written a satire with such a one-to-one correspondence between the characters and plot of the comedy and contemporary Florentine politics, he would have been departing markedly from his usual practice in his explicitly political works. In both The Prince and the Discourses he criticizes his contemporaries, but he does not restrict the compass of his analysis simply to contemporary much less simply Florentine events. Third, while he was serving the Florentine republic Machiavelli apparently wrote a satirical comedy based on Aristophanes’ Clouds that (like its Greek model) contained explicit references to contemporary political figures; but he chose not to complete or produce it. Whether he had concluded that that kind of political commentary was imprudent or that it did not accomplish what he wished is not clear. What does seem evident is that he had come to such a determination before he wrote Mandragola.

Recognizing the problems with the allegorical readings of Mandragola, other commentators have contented themselves simply with pointing out the themes from his political works that can be found in the comedy as well. But there are also difficulties with such “thematic” readings, because the differences between the comedy and the prose works in the treatments of the loss of ancient virtue in contemporary Florence, conspiracies, and the new founding or refounding of existing institutions seem to be as great as the similarities.

Virtually all commentators agree that Mandragola constitutes a retelling of the ancient story of the rape of Lucretia.5 To see what is truly “new” in the “new case” (caso—cause, chance, or incident) that Machiavelli tells his audience in the prologue has been “born” (nato) in this land of Florence (but will be seen at other times in Rome or Pisa),6 we need to look in more detail at what he retained and what he changed from the old story.7

In Livy’s history (1.57–59), the rape of Lucretia had great political significance, because it provided the occasion if not the cause for Lucius Junius Brutus’s founding of the Roman republic.8 King Tarquin had attacked the wealthy neighboring city of Ardea to replenish his own treasury, which had been depleted by the splendor of his public works. By distributing some of the booty, he also hoped to appease the common people, who resented their impressed labor on those works. Unable to take the city by storm, the Romans had begun a long siege. Passing their idle hours dining and drinking, a group of young princes began bragging about their virtuous wives. Insisting that his wife, Lucretia, was the best, Tarquinius Collatinus urged them to ride back to Rome to see. There they found all the other wives dining together luxuriously; Lucretia alone was at home weaving by candlelight with her maids. His desire to conquer and possess aroused by her virtue as well as her beauty, the king’s son Sextus resolved to return the next day to ravish her. When she refused to accede to his wishes at sword point, he threatened her with disgrace. If she did not gratify him, he would kill both her and his manservant, place their bodies side by side in her bed, and tell others that he had found them in illicit embrace. To avoid dishonor, Lucretia submitted; but she sent for her husband immediately after Sextus left. After hearing her tale, Collatinus tried to convince her that she was free of shame because she had not willingly submitted. But having obtained her husband’s pledge to punish the man who had raped her, Lucretia plunged a dagger into her heart to prove that she had not submitted to the disgrace voluntarily. Drawing the bloody dagger from her wound and displaying it along with her body, Brutus aroused enough public outrage to exile the king and establish a republic in place of the monarchy.

In Mandragola a handsome wealthy young Florentine named Callimaco Guadagni hears of the extraordinary beauty of a woman named Lucrezia from one of her in-laws, who has come to Paris and engaged him in a debate about the relative beauty of French and Italian women.9 Like the Roman princes, Callimaco decides to return home to see for himself. The provocation and action in the new “case” are thus similar to those of the old, but the setting and circumstances are importantly different. Whereas the Roman princes took a brief leave from a military camp, Callimaco returns to Florence from a voluntary exile undertaken to avoid war. He is young, noble, and wealthy, but he is no soldier or patriot. On the contrary, after his parents died, his guardians had sent him at age ten to Paris, and he had remained there for another ten years to escape the wars in Italy that began with the French invasion in 1494.10 At the very beginning of the play the audience thus sees one reason for Machiavelli’s conclusion that the present age has fallen off from ancient virtù.

Callimaco proves not only to be less forceful but also to be less resourceful than his Roman predecessor. Having arrived in Florence, he tells his servant Siro he has done nothing for an entire month, because he does not know how to overcome the three obstacles to the satisfaction of his desire: the chaste nature of Lucrezia, “which is extremely honest and in all ways alien to the things of love,” her rich husband Nicia who “lets himself be governed by her,” and the absence of any opportunity or occasion to approach her in private.11 Unable to devise a “remedy” on his own, Callimaco has sought the assistance of a “parasite” and former marriage broker named Ligurio.12 Siro warns his master to “watch out that he doesn’t trick you; these spongers aren’t usually very faithful.” Like his creator, however, Callimaco believes that human beings will work, if and when they see the promise of a reward. Reflecting the commercial spirit and habits of his native city, he assures Siro that Ligurio will serve him faithfully, because he has promised that “if he succeeds, to give him a good sum of money.” And “if he doesn’t succeed,” trying to obtain his assistance won’t have cost much. Ligurio will merely have “pick[ed] up a lunch and supper out of it, which I wouldn’t have eaten alone anyway” (1.1).

Having become familiar with Nicia, Ligurio has persuaded him to take his wife to the baths (where Callimaco can approach her). Nicia does not want to go to the trouble of moving his entire household, knows that his wife will object, and is frustrated by the disagreement among the doctors about which baths would best cure her sterility. But he and his wife are so desperate to have a child, he tells Ligurio that he is willing to do anything. So he asks the parasite to talk to the doctors and find out which baths would be best.

In the meantime Ligurio warns Callimaco that he may not succeed in seducing Lucrezia at the baths; another young man may prove to be more attractive. (Callimaco apparently is no more handsome than he is courageous or resourceful.) And Ligurio devises another plan. Because Callimaco is educated and can impress the lawyer with his use of Latin, Ligurio introduces him to Nicia as a doctor.13 And in that role Callimaco prescribes a potion containing the mandrake which will make any woman who drinks it pregnant. The problem is that the first man who lies with her will die within eight days. Nicia does not want to die, but Callimaco assures him that there is a remedy: “make another man sleep with her . . . one night . . . and draw off all that infection of the mandragola to himself” (2.6). Nicia again protests that he does not want to make his wife a whore and himself a cuckold. But after Callimaco informs him that the king of France and many lords there have done it, and assures him that he will not end up before the Florentine criminal tribunal, Nicia agrees to go in disguise with Ligurio, Siro, and Callimaco to seize the first young man they encounter in the street, put a bag over his head, and lead him into the bedroom with instructions about what he has to do (but no warning about the consequences). In the morning Nicia will send him away before daybreak, so he won’t have seen anyone. Then Nicia can ask his wife to bathe and be with her at his pleasure.

Nicia is older than Callimaco, but he does not seem to be any braver, wiser, or more resourceful. Like Callimaco, he is rich, but he complains that he does not have much status in the city. Although he studied hard for two years to earn his law degree, he admits that he would not be able to support himself by practicing his profession. Like the author of the play, he complains about the unwillingness of his fellow citizens to recognize and appreciate any virtù (2.3). In contrast to the author of the comedy, Nicia clearly cares about his and thus his wife’s reputation. But he is not concerned about committing murder, so long as he is not apprehended and punished for it. Nor does he care about putting his wife’s immortal soul in danger of damnation by having her commit adultery. He is obviously not a good Christian. She says prayers for hours before going to bed (perhaps to postpone her wifely duty as long as possible, perhaps to shore up her own resolution), but he has not seen Frate Timoteo for ten years. It does not appear that he, in contrast to his wife, has ever gone to church regularly.

Although his wife also wants a child, Nicia does not believe that she will cooperate with their scheme. It is in the obtaining of Lucrezia’s cooperation, as well as the specific way in which that is achieved, that Machiavelli’s comedy differs most from its ancient Roman source.

First, most obviously and most importantly, in Machiavelli’s comedy, in glaring contrast to the original story, there is no threat or use of force—by the lover, husband, woman, or man who seeks to reestablish order. All the characters who participate in the “plot” agree to do what they are asked, even if they do not always understand why. (Following Machiavelli’s rules for an effective conspirator [D 3.6], Ligurio does not tell any of his partners anything they need to know before they need to know it.) It is the absence of even the threat of coercion that fundamentally distinguishes the machinations to establish a new order in Nicia’s household from a political refounding. Machiavelli recognizes that it is possible to seize control of a government by means of fraud (D 2.13), but he does not think that an unarmed prophet can maintain control of his people (P 6). Some commentators have suggested that Ligurio plays the role of a Machiavellian political leader, because he says as they set off to seize the disguised Callimaco, “I’ll be the captain, and get the army in order for the battle” (4.9).14 But Ligurio is leading an “army” of three, and he has no way to punish a deserter or rebel. (Machiavelli emphasizes that public punishments are necessary means not merely of maintaining but of restoring governments by returning them to their beginning [D 3.1, 3.49].) The conspirators are only pretending to use force when they seize the disguised Callimaco and take him to Lucrezia’s bed. The individuals who take part in the charade Ligurio has orchestrated do so because it enables each of them to satisfy his or her own strongest desire. But that satisfaction in all cases depends on the plot’s being kept secret. As a result, the man who devised it does not receive public credit or recognition for his work for “the common benefit of each” (D 1.Pref.).15

The second evident difference between Machiavelli’s comedy and the original tragedy is that in place of a threat of force or loss of honor, the conspiracy against Lucrezia’s virtue succeeds by means of an appeal to her Christian beliefs. That resolution is paradoxical (and comic) because those same Christian beliefs appear to be the primary obstacle to her cooperating and so producing an heir for Nicia.

In order to obtain Lucrezia’s cooperation, Ligurio informs his collaborators, they will need to enlist the help of both her confessor and her mother. Gaining the cooperation of the frate alone will not suffice. Lucrezia has come to suspect the honesty of all prelates, because one of the frati approached her inappropriately when she went to church to pray for a child. She will not go to see her confessor, much less listen to him, unless her mother brings her. Lucrezia believes—and for good reason—that her mother is genuinely concerned about maintaining her daughter’s honor (3.10). Sostrata understands that her own support depends upon the solidity of her daughter’s domestic arrangements. She thus urges her daughter to obey her husband’s desire that she comply with the strange plan, because “a woman who has no children has no home. Her husband dies, she’s left like a beast, abandoned by everyone.” (Indeed, the frate, who should be a man of compassion, describes the mother as “beast” [3.9].) In contrast to Nicia, Sostrata sympathizes with her daughter’s fear of committing a sin and being eternally punished for it. However, since her confessor has removed any questions of “conscience,” Sostrata asks her daughter, “What are you afraid of? There are fifty women in this city who would raise up their hands to heaven for it” (3.11).

Ligurio believes that he will be able to obtain the help of Frate Timoteo by offering him a bribe. He observes that “these frati are cunning, astute; and it stands to reason, because they know our sins and their own” (3.2). They know the sins of others, Machiavelli reminds his audience in the next scene, because they hear confessions. Those confessions appear to come, moreover, particularly from women who are ashamed of their sexual activities, even in marriage, and are willing to compensate men of the Church handsomely for relieving their consciences. Timoteo has concluded that women are both “the most charitable people” and “the most annoying.” But “there’s no honey without flies” (4.4). When Ligurio asks him to persuade an abbess to give a pregnant girl in her care a potion to make her miscarry in exchange for a gift of three hundred ducats for him to distribute as alms, the frate thus agrees. Timoteo seems to concur with Ligurio’s contention that many goods will result—the honor of the convent, the girl, and her relatives will be maintained and the frate will receive 300 ducats from Messer Nicia for charity—whereas nothing will be harmed “but a piece of unborn flesh, without sense.” He seems, indeed, to agree with Ligurio’s general contention “that good is that which does good for the most, and that by which the most are contented,” so long as it be “in the name of God” and for charity. We know from D 2.2 that Machiavelli shares Ligurio’s “utilitarian” understanding of the common good.

Having tested Timoteo’s corruptibility with the story about the pregnant girl, Ligurio explains what he really wants. Timoteo recognizes that he has been duped, but he expects to profit by the trick. “Messer Nicia and Callimaco are rich,” and he thinks that he will get a lot from each of them. Both will, for different reasons, continue to pay him to keep the affair secret, and he won’t have to worry that either of them will expose his role. He does not, therefore, repent his decision, but he does recognize that it will be difficult to persuade Lucrezia, who is “wise and good.” He thinks, however, that he will be able to “dupe her by her goodness” (3.9).

When he meets with Lucrezia and her mother, the frate presents three reasons why she should submit her body to this disgrace and be the cause of a man’s dying for disgracing her. The first is that “where there is a certain good and an uncertain evil, one should never leave that good for fear of that evil.” In this case, Timoteo claims that the “certain good” is that she will become pregnant (which is by no means certain as a result of a “one-night stand,” unless one believes in the potency of Callimaco’s concoction), and that it is uncertain that the one who will lie with her will die (although Timoteo knows much more certainly that Callimaco will not die for this reason). The frate tells the women that he has been consulting his books, and the second reason he gives is taken from the comfort Saint Augustine offers the Christian women who were raped in the fall of Rome: “the will is what sins, not the body.”16 And asserting his authority over her in interpreting the teaching of the saint as it applies to her case, he adds: “What causes it to be a sin is displeasing your husband—but you please him; [and] taking pleasure in it—but you have no pleasure from it.” Finally, he enunciates the Machiavellian principle that “the end has to be looked to in all things.” Her end is “to fill a seat in paradise,” and the means is “to make your husband happy” (3.11).

Utterly unconvinced by the arguments of her confessor and mother, Lucrezia declares that she does not believe that she will be alive the next morning. However, that night she experiences the difference between the kisses of a young lover and her old husband. Moreover, her lover not only explains “how easily, on account of her husband’s simplicity, [they] could live happily without any scandal” but also promises upon Nicia’s death to take her as his wife. She thus concludes: “Since your astuteness, my husband’s stupidity, my mother’s simplicity, and my confessor’s wickedness have led me to do what I never would have done by myself, I’m determined to judge that it comes from a heavenly disposition which has so willed” (5.4). Although she piously states that she does not have it in her to reject what Heaven wills her to accept, she somewhat impiously declares that she now takes Callimaco to be her “lord, master, and guide,” her father, defender, and her every good. And instead of forgiving her husband for the wrong he has done her, she states her desire to punish him by giving him always what he wanted to have for one evening. So she instructs or even orders Callimaco to become her husband’s close friend, so that he can come and go as he pleases in their house, allowing her to be together with him at any time without suspicion. In declaring her obedience to the will of God and taking her lover as her master, she thus effectively takes control of Nicia’s reorganized household.

Nicia notices the change in his wife’s bearing immediately. She’s become very bold. But he nevertheless retains apparent control. He brings Lucrezia to the church to be blessed by the frate and introduces her to Maestro Callimaco, “who will have been the cause of our having a staff to sustain our old age.” Lucrezia tells her husband that she wants Callimaco to be their “close friend” or the baby’s “godfather” (5.6), and Nicia complies by inviting Callimaco and Ligurio to dinner and giving them a key to the house so that they can return at their convenience. Timoteo asks whether he will receive the money for alms, and Ligurio asks that Siro be remembered as well.

In sum, all participants in the conspiracy benefit. But the benefits—including the satisfaction of Nicia’s desire for an heir, Callimaco’s desire for the love of an extraordinarily beautiful and virtuous woman, Ligurio’s desire to have a regular source of meals, Siro’s desire to see Callimaco’s desire satisfied and the pretentions of the stupid lawyer deflated, so long as he does not risk punishment, Timoteo’s desire for funds with which to rebuild the “reputation” of the Church, Sostrata’s desire to have a secure support in her old age, and Lucrezia’s newly discovered desire for a young lover as well as a baby and future support from her husband(s)—all depend upon maintaining the appearance of a conventional marriage sanctified by the Church.

How exactly does the introduction of Christian beliefs and institutions enable Machiavelli to transform the tragic story of the rape of Lucretia into a modern comedy? It isn’t just a matter of the frate’s convincing Lucrezia to allow herself to be raped. Lucretia agreed to lie with Sextus because she did not want him to sully her honor by killing her and putting a dead slave in bed next to her; she killed herself later to show not merely her husband but all other Romans that she had not consented or taken pleasure in the act. Lucrezia is not persuaded by her confessor, but she does not propose to kill herself. She does not, because with the introduction of Christian beliefs the standard and judge of a person’s honor has changed. Lucretia was worried about what her husband and the other Romans would think of her; and it is for this prideful concern about her reputation or honor in the eyes of others that Saint Augustine condemns her (as well as her fellow citizens).17 According to Christian doctrine, it is a sin to commit suicide, because we are God’s creations and not our own. As Timoteo reminds Lucrezia, the sinful character of her act depends upon her intention; and the purity of her intention can be judged only by God—or, perhaps, by his earthly representative. Sostrata is convinced of the latter, and concludes that her daughter has nothing to fear. Perceiving the corruption of God’s representatives on earth, Lucrezia expects judgment from God himself.

In his Discourses (1.11–15) Machiavelli praises the way in which the Roman senators manipulated the religious beliefs of the plebs in getting them to fight for the city. The role he indicates for the Church and its representatives in Mandragola is, however, importantly different. Timoteo does not persuade Lucrezia to obey him or her husband. But he does provide a public cover for the ongoing adultery by blessing the progeny of the marriage. In his political works Machiavelli argues that the Church has played a disastrous role in Italian politics, because it has no arms of its own and, therefore, has to use foreign auxiliaries or mercenaries to defend itself and its interests. But in his comedy Machiavelli suggests that the Church might play a positively beneficial role in the private lives of its parishioners, where it does not need to use force in order to have an effect on their opinions by appealing to their hopes and fears. If it confines its public role to the sanctification and support of marriage, the Church will become an important means of containing a very strong human passion and directing it to a productive, procreative end. To perform such a role, the prelates will not only have to stop interfering in political affairs; they will also have to hide if not contain their own sexual indiscretions, so that they will, as Nicia comments (3.2), be providing good examples rather than bad. They can and should be corrupt in the way Timoteo is, however, by seeking to acquire funds to build and maintain the reputation of the Church. Understanding that all human beings sin, prelates should continue to give those with a guilty conscience relief by taking their confessions and extending God’s forgiveness. They should take the expressions of their parishioners’ gratitude to enhance the reputation of the Church, not only by providing alms for the poor, but also by building and maintaining splendid edifices and conducting magnificent holiday processions.18 God will thus appear to rule on earth as in heaven, “for,” as Machiavelli observes in concluding P 18, “the vulgar are taken in by the appearance and the outcome of a thing, and in the world there is no one but the vulgar” (71).

The change Machiavelli suggests in the role of the Church is, however, only a part of a much larger change he dramatizes. If they are to satisfy their desires and live in peace, he shows, “Christians” like Lucrezia must learn that the locus of their happiness is here on earth and not in the afterlife. They must take the direction of their own lives into their own hands, and not leave it to the will of heaven. No one can satisfy his or her own desires without the help of others. But as Ligurio observes early in the play, “the proverb on marriages which says ‘God makes men and they pair themselves off’ is rarely proven true.” As in the case of Nicia and his wife, “one often sees that it’s the lot of a well-qualified man to end up with a beast, and vice-versa, of a prudent woman to have a madman.” A former marriage broker, Ligurio has come to understand both the passions that move human beings and the need for human intervention in order to satisfy them. He desires to see Callimaco’s desire satisfied, it seems, because he wants to right the vagaries of fortune that give a stupid man like Nicia “a beautiful wife, wise, well-mannered, and fit to govern a kingdom” (1.3). At the end of the play, she takes charge of Nicia’s newly reorganized household, in fact but not openly. Like Ligurio, who devises the plot that enables everyone to obtain what he or she desires, this wise woman understands that she cannot rule or control others by force, nor should she try to obtain public recognition or glory in doing so.

Although Machiavelli complains in the prologue that “in all things, the present age falls off from ancient virtù,” in his comedy he does not show his characters trying to imitate the ancients, nor does he urge his audience to do so, as he does in both The Prince and Discourses. Quite the contrary. In Mandragola Machiavelli not only shows his characters violating both pagan and Christian notions of virtue but also celebrates the results. In the prologue Machiavelli announces that he is dramatizing a “new case” that has arisen in Florence. As in his teaching of princes how not to be good in The Prince, so we see in the course of the play that the “useful lesson” underlying the comical “case” that has arisen in Florence concerns morality. In Mandragola we learn that it is not solely the prince who should “keep faith” by always seeming to be “merciful, faithful, humane, honest, and religious” (P 18), even though he cannot and should not always be so in fact. Private individuals are not able to satisfy their desires unless they conceal their true motives and pretend to be serving others.19 They must appear to act according to conventional religious and moral beliefs they do not actually share, because these conventional beliefs support socially useful institutions like the family and the Church. These institutions are useful, furthermore, because like all well-conceived laws they direct or redirect human passions away from potentially destructive conflict so that they have not merely productive and stabilizing but even liberating results.20

In Mandragola Machiavelli thus shows that a crucial part of the new moral teaching he presented in The Prince applies to private life as well, but he does not suggest that there is no difference between public and private. There are few individuals as clever in helping others satisfy their own desires as Ligurio and few women as wise as Lucrezia about the way in which they can rule without seeming to do so.21 In most cities, Machiavelli shows in his political works, the passions of men may be aroused by women, but they fight, in fact, primarily over economic goods.22 Despite the introductory song he appended to the comedy in which the nymphs and shepherds urge the audience to follow their desires, “because life is brief and many are the pains which, living and struggling, everyone sustains,” Machiavelli is not an epicurean or hedonist. In contrast to his nymphs and shepherds, he clearly states in the prologue, he has not withdrawn from the world and chosen the solitary life voluntarily. He would participate in public, political life, if he could. And in public life, where individuals strive for recognition despite the envy of others, there is conflict, conflict that can at best be controlled but never entirely obliterated by laws backed with force. If we look back at his praise of the advantages of a free way of life in D 2.2, we will discover that most of them are private. And in private life, as he shows in his comedy, where associations are voluntary, love can be stronger than fear. Because of the need to maintain appearances, fear of scandal does not disappear. But in the wooing of Lucrezia, Machiavelli shows, Callimaco makes a crucial change in Ligurio’s advice. Whereas Ligurio instructed Callimaco to tell Lucrezia how they could continue to take pleasure in each other without scandal, and to threaten her with scandal if she did not agree (4.2), Callimaco promises to marry her when Nicia dies (5.4), because he wants her to love, not to fear him.23 The one exception with regard to the essentially private advantages of a free way of life that Machiavelli extols consists in the hope every man can have that his son will be elected to high office. Human ambition, which extends beyond pleasure, makes it impossible for the most talented to be satisfied, as Callimaco, Nicia, Lucrezia, and Ligurio apparently are, with the pleasures they enjoy in private. As Machiavelli observes in D 1.37, when human beings no longer contend from necessity, they do so from ambition.

Machiavelli’s immediate audience was composed primarily of young ambitious Florentines who might enjoy their amorous affairs, but who also hoped to occupy high office. In his subsequent works he thus tried to correct some misapprehensions they seem to have held or acquired about the means needed to realize those ambitions.

4


Machiavelli’s Defense


THE ART OF WAR


In writing a dialogue on the “art of war,” Machiavelli turned back from comedy to the most deadly serious public matter. It was, moreover, a subject that had been at the center of Machiavelli’s own public career as well as his previous prose writings. The policy he had urged his patron Piero Soderini to adopt in the face of strenuous opposition from other ottimati was the formation and training of a Florentine militia. It was the policy he did not have time or opportunity to bring to fruition before his ill-trained peasant militia was massacred by the Spanish at Prato and his efforts to marshal and train an effective native defense force were declared to have been in vain, if not ill advised. In The Prince Machiavelli wrote that “a prince should have no other object, nor any other thought, nor take anything else as his art but that of war and its orders and discipline; for that is the only art which is of concern to one who commands” (53). And in both The Prince and Discourses, he traced the failure of Florence to secure the liberty of the city, both domestically and from foreign aggressors, to its reliance on mercenary arms. Yet by relating lectures delivered in a garden after dinner by a mercenary captain to the young friends to whom he dedicated his Discourses, Machiavelli suggests, rather ironically, that even his most enthusiastic admirers seemed not to have absorbed the first and most obvious lesson he had to teach. Rather than seeking to learn how to acquire their own arms by practicing in the field, they preferred to discuss the merits of various forms of republican government at their leisure or to watch comedies at court.

After the militia he had trained was so badly defeated at Prato, Machiavelli recognized that he would not be regarded as an expert on the means of ordering an effective military force. In writing about the “art of war” he did not, therefore, put the substance of his recommendations forward in his own name. As in the comedies he wrote and produced during his lifetime, so in the dialogue he composed and published, he began with a short preface in which he explained his writing as a result of his forced retirement from active public service, and put the body of his controversial opinions into the mouths of others. Indeed, by attributing the lessons his young friends received about the art of war to Fabrizio Colonna, the mercenary captain who led the Spanish forces that forced Piero Soderini to capitulate, Machiavelli kept himself in the background and made the technical, apparently nonpartisan character of those lessons stand out and so concealed their revolutionary political implications. His attribution of these most necessary lessons to an enemy of the Florentine republic and his showing that young Florentine friends still needed to learn what he had tried to teach them in writings that had circulated only in private nevertheless prove, upon examination, to be thoroughly ironic. In fact, the dialogue constitutes a defense of the policies Machiavelli advocated both as a practical politician and as a political theorist.


Machiavelli’s “Apology”


By signing the book as Niccolò Machiavegli, Florentine Citizen and Secretary, and dedicating it to Lorenzo di Filippo Strozzi, Florentine Patrician, the author reminds his readers not only of the office he once held and the services he rendered to the republic, but also of his frustrated desire to regain public employment. Lorenzo Strozzi was a wealthy banker and member of an influential family who had facilitated contact between Machiavelli and the Medici in 1520, a year before the Art of War was published. A son-in-law of Bernardo Rucellai, who had occasionally visited the Orti Oricellari where the dialogue is set, Lorenzo was an ideal “go between.”1 As in The Prince, so in the Art of War, Machiavelli thus addresses a ‘Lorenzo’ in hope of gaining future employment and apologizes for his presumption for writing about an activity of which he “has not made a profession.” As Machiavelli implied in his letter of dedication to The Prince, so he suggests even more openly here: those who have been charged with the responsibility have not known what they were doing. Any errors he might have made in writing could not have the harmful effects made by those who had ruined empires with their deeds. Leaving his patron to judge the quality of his work, Machiavelli explains that he has dedicated the work to Lorenzo in gratitude for the benefits the author has received and because “it is customary to honor . . . those who are resplendent in nobility, wealth, talent, and liberality” (5). To anyone who had read a manuscript copy of The Prince or Discourses (and all later readers of his works), Machiavelli thus indicated that the Art of War has a more conventional form or exterior than the two works he had explicitly acknowledged were not written or presented as was “customary.”

In calling attention to his forced retirement from public life, Machiavelli also reminds readers of the reasons he did not feel entirely free to say everything that he thought openly, fully, or explicitly. In his preface, he acknowledges the controversial character of his subject. “Many have held . . . that there are no things less in agreement with one another or so dissimilar as the civilian and military lives.” They observe that “if someone plans to succeed in the soldier’s career, he not only changes dress immediately, but also departs from every civilian practice in his customs, usages, voice, and bearing.” Because a soldier must be ready to use violence and frighten others, he cannot adopt civilian customs, dress, or speech, all of which seem effeminate and thus contrary to the requirements of his profession. In our time, Machiavelli acknowledges, military and civilian life are opposed. However, he reminds his classically educated readers, this was not always the case. On the contrary, “if ancient orders were considered, nothing would be found more united and in conformity” than military and civilian life. Recurring to antiquity enables Machiavelli, first, to emphasize the fundamental importance of defense by reminding his readers that no laws, religion, or arts will survive where people are not protected from foreign aggressors. Indeed, he comes close to restating his famous claim in P 12 that “there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms and where there are good arms there must be good laws” in more moderate language by observing that “good orders without military help are disordered.” Then he claims that soldiers make exemplary citizens, not merely because they are willing to risk their lives in defending the fatherland, but because they must love peace (since they have reason to fear harm in war), and they must both love and fear God most of all, since they beyond all others need His support. “This necessity,” Machiavelli explains, “made the soldiers’ life praised by other men and followed and imitated with utmost attention.” The “sinister opinions” about the incompatibility of military and civilian life have arisen only in modern times, when “military orders are altogether corrupt and separated by great lengths from ancient modes” (AW Pref., 3–4).

In his “preface” Machiavelli does not explain how or why military orders in his time have become corrupt (although he does in both The Prince and Discourses). That corruption cannot simply be a product of the observed difference in manners between civilians and soldiers he mentions here, since ancient soldiers also wore uniforms and were harsh in both speech and deed. Nor were ancient soldiers the most god-fearing and peace-loving parts of the population, (even though in D 1.11 Machiavelli praises Numa for making the Roman people more pacific by inculcating a set of religious beliefs that the senators later used to get the plebs to fight). As in D 1.12, 2.2, so in the Art of War (2.305–7), Machiavelli suggests that the Christian religion is the origin of the “sinister opinions . . . that have arisen that make [men] hate the military and flee association with those who practice it” (AW Pref., 4) only after he is well into the book. Christianity may have been the origin of “sinister opinions” concerning the incompatibility of military and civilian life; but, we learn early in the dialogue, the wealthy merchants who ruled Florence constituted a more immediate source of the opinion that it was not desirable to resuscitate the harsh military modes of the ancients. The ottimati did not merely consider the harsh modes of the ancients contrary to the “civilized” life of gentlemen; they also feared that arming the plebs, i.e., the lower classes of laborers and peasants, would threaten their control of the republic.2 In trying not merely to revive study of the art of war, but to establish a Florentine militia, Machiavelli was challenging both the firm convictions and considered interests of the ruling class. No wonder he approached his subject somewhat indirectly.

Drawing, as in The Prince and Discourses, on “what he has seen and read,” in the preface Machiavelli states simply that he has concluded that it is possible to revive ancient modes—presumably by changing the corrupt modern orders and the “sinister opinions” that have arisen about them, although Machiavelli does not say so explicitly. He merely proposes to use his “idle time” to write what he understands about the art of war for the satisfaction of those who are lovers of ancient actions. But he thus indicates the character of the audience he addresses most immediately. Like Cosimo Rucellai, whose grandfather Bernardo planted the garden in which the dialogue is supposed to have taken place, they are heirs of the “civic humanists” who share some of their forefathers’ tastes and opinions. They may admire ancient actions, but, we learn early in the dialogue, they do not want to adopt the harsh morality of the ancients; they would be defamed and vilified by their contemporaries if they did. These young men are public-spirited, but unlike their ancestors, they do not hold office and perhaps will not be able to so long as the Medici control the government. Machiavelli may be appealing to their revolutionary desires, but he cannot do so openly.

Admitting that he is not a professional soldier, Machiavelli suggests that he shares the liability of the young men he depicts listening to the mercenary captain who speaks to them about “the art of war.” In relating the dialogue Machiavelli never explicitly connects Fabrizio’s insistence that “one cannot make a foundation on other arms than one’s own [cf.
