P 6–9, 12–14, 24, 26; D 2.20] and one cannot order one’s own arms otherwise than as a militia” (AW 1.189) with his own persistent attempt to form such a militia as “Florentine Citizen and Secretary” (as he repeatedly describes himself at the beginning and end not only of the dialogue but also of the particular books in it). Once we recognize the connection, however, we realize that the knowledge Machiavelli attributes to Fabrizio belongs to the author of the dialogue (which probably did not actually take place). Fabrizio’s self-justifying claim that he has obviously spent a great deal of time and effort acquiring this knowledge, but did not have an opportunity to put it into practice because he did not have the requisite political authority (AW 7.194–97), applies much more clearly to Machiavelli than to the historical mercenary captain (who was duke of Palliano and Marsi as well as count of Tagliazozzo and Celano). The Art of War thus constitutes a defense of Machiavelli’s practice as secretary of the republic of Florence, where he advocated and initiated the formation of a militia, as well as a statement of his “theory.”3


The Dialogue


A. Occasion, Setting, and Dramatis Personae


Machiavelli explains that he is relating the conversation to celebrate and perpetuate the memory of his young friend, Cosimo Rucellai, who has recently died (1519). He begins by praising Cosimo both as a friend and as a patriot. Cosimo demonstrated his liberality by inviting his friends to partake not merely in sumptuous dinners, but also in the conversations that followed in the Orti Oricellari planted by his grandfather. But unfortunately he did not live long enough to perform any great and magnificent deeds on behalf of his fatherland. Since Cosimo was preparing himself for such public service by discussions of the kind he once had with Fabrizio Colonna, Machiavelli suggests that recalling that conversation might not only serve as a fitting memorial to his young friend, but also enable others to “learn many things useful not only for military but also civil life, wisely disputed by a very knowledgeable man” (1.8). Machiavelli’s stated intention in relating the conversation is thus quickly shown not simply or even primarily to be honoring Cosimo or conveying technical knowledge about military organization, so much as enabling his readers to learn many things useful for civil as well as for military life. In other words, his discussion of the “art of war” has a much greater import and range than first appear.

Many readers of the Art of War have noted the apparent irony of Machiavelli’s choice of Fabrizio Colonna as his spokesman. Why would Machiavelli choose a mercenary captain of the kind he criticized so vehemently in both The Prince and Discourses to deliver his useful lesson? Why, indeed, would he choose the mercenary captain who led the Spanish troops responsible for the fall of the Florentine republic in 1512 (and so indirectly for Machiavelli’s own dismissal from its government)?

Mansfield explains Machiavelli’s choice by pointing out that Fabrizio possessed the practical knowledge of the art of war that Machiavelli admitted he lacked and could thus speak with more authority. By using such a historical figure, Machiavelli also distanced himself from what might be taken to be the anti-Medician implications of the argument.4 Marcia Colish, on the other hand, thinks that Machiavelli chose Fabrizio because of the conjunction between Machiavelli’s opposition to the Medici and the known enmity of the Colonna to the Medici, who had allied themselves by marriage with the Orsini, the opponents of the Colonna in Rome. Choosing a spokesman to reflect his own opposition to the Medici would, however, undermine Machiavelli’s ongoing attempt to obtain employment from the Medici, of which he reminds readers in the dedication.5 Colish also and more convincingly points out that authors of dialogues in the Renaissance liked to use figures whose lives and opinions were familiar to their audience, and that Machiavelli’s predecessors in the writing of dialogues as well as histories, Leonardo Bruni and Poggio Bracciolini, intentionally had such figures argue for positions contrary to those they were known to hold to add irony and entertainment to their work.6

Fabrizio provided a safe cover for Machiavelli, because he was a friend of the Medici. He had been captain of the Spanish armies that forced Piero Soderini to capitulate and enabled the Medici to recapture control of the Florentine republic. According to Machiavelli, Fabrizio was in Florence and thus able to converse with Cosimo and his friends, because he was visiting Lorenzo de’ Medici.

Machiavelli ironically uses Fabrizio to conceal not only the revolutionary potential of the knowledge he is disseminating but also the republican bias of the priority Fabrizio gives the infantry, even though he treats the recruiting, training, arming, and deploying of the army as an “art” that can be practiced equally well by a republic or a principality.7 In arguing that knowledge of the art of war is essential for the leaders of both republics and principalities, Fabrizio takes the same position Machiavelli did in P 12–14.

Although Machiavelli clearly distinguishes himself as narrator from the major speaker in the dialogue at the beginning, he indicates later that it is he who is speaking in the name of Fabrizio. When talking to Zanobi, “Fabrizio” says twice (AW 4.118, 5.92) that he has reasoned with him and his friends another time about the subject in question (in D 3.10 and 2.6). Fabrizio had been fighting wars most of the time these young men were growing up in Florence, and so was not likely to have “reasoned” with them there, while Machiavelli was known to have been talking and writing to them.

In The Prince Machiavelli argued that the art of war “is of such virtue that it not only maintains those who have been born princes but many times it enables men of private fortune to rise to that rank” (P 14, 58, slightly adapted). In the Art of War Machiavelli thus implicitly presents himself (or his spokesman) as teaching young Florentine aristocrats what they need to know to become prince of Italy (see AW 7.243). The question Fabrizio leaves open at the end is whether the young Florentines will have a better opportunity than he to put what they have learned into practice (and if they have such an opportunity, whether they will, in fact, be able to take advantage of it).

By depicting Fabrizio in conversation with his young friends, Machiavelli also lets his readers see the character of the audience he addressed most immediately, and the kinds of difficulties he encountered in trying to persuade them to undertake his revolutionary project. The host of the meeting described in the Art of War is Cosimo Rucellai, one of the two young men to whom Machiavelli had dedicated his Discourses on Livy. The other dedicatee of the Discourses, Zanobi Buondelmonti, also takes part in the conversation, as does Luigi Alamanni (to whom Machiavelli dedicated his Life of Castruccio Castracani along with Zanobi in 1520) and Battista della Palla.8 All four were young friends of Machiavelli who had been pressing the Medici to grant Machiavelli a commission to write the Florentine Histories. (Cardinal Giulio de’ Medici, later Pope Clement VII, finally did this in 1520. It was not, however, the political office or responsibility that Machiavelli had been seeking.) Cosimo died in 1519, but Zanobi, Luigi, and Battista all played leading roles in a conspiracy in 1522 to assassinate Giulio and reinstate Machiavelli’s former patron, Piero Soderini, as head of a Florentine republic.

The young men whom Machiavelli shows Fabrizio instructing in the art of war were thus not only the same young men to whom he addressed his own Discourses, but also among those who actively sought to reintroduce republican government in Florence. As readers hear each of these young men interrogate Fabrizio, we learn something about their individual characters and Machiavelli’s view of them. Machiavelli praises Cosimo for his generosity to his friends and his noble public ambitions, but he also shows that Cosimo was physically weak and politically conservative. Luigi is said to be young and impetuous, whereas Zanobi is “spirited,” and Battista “prudent.” But it is far from clear that in organizing a conspiracy in 1522 to assassinate Giulio de’ Medici and reinstate Piero Soderini as head of a Florentine republic, Luigi, Zanobi, and Battista were following Machiavelli’s advice.9 The severity of Machiavelli’s criticism of Soderini in D 3.3 and 3.30 makes one wonder whether Machiavelli would have greeted the reinstatement of his former patron with great enthusiasm. Writing at the invitation of Leo X in “Discourse on Remodeling the Government of Florence,” in 1520 Machiavelli had proposed a peaceful transition from the rule of the Medici princes, who as men of the Church were without heirs, to a republic to be established when they died.10 (To be sure, the Medici princes do not seem to have heeded his advice, if they read it.) The conspiracy organized by Machiavelli’s young friends looks very much like the conspiracies he repeatedly shows in the Florentine Histories failed to establish a stable, much less a free government, because the people were corrupt. As he observes in both D 3.6 and FH 7.33, those who conspire to assassinate the current prince hope that the people will rise and join them in a rebellion. But where the people no longer understand the advantages of a free government or are too afraid to fight for it, they will not support the rebels. Conspirators at the head of men they have selected and trained to bear arms have a much better chance of actually taking control and establishing a new regime.11 In all three of his major prose works, Machiavelli thus emphasizes the importance of training and leading one’s own troops. The young men who listened to a lecture on the art of war while sitting in a garden without ever trying to practice it the way Machiavelli himself did—both in the field drilling raw recruits and in his study—do not seem to have absorbed what he described as his first and most important lesson. He was evidently pleased by their willingness to listen and read what he wrote, as well as by their attempts to obtain employment for him from the Medici, but he must have viewed their professed admiration with some irony.

The setting of the conversation also points to the circumstances in which Machiavelli was writing and the obstacles these circumstances represented to the achievement of his political goals. As Cosimo reminds his guests, the gardens in which they are seeking shade after they have dined were planted by his grandfather, Bernardo Rucellai. Like Machiavelli and many other Florentines, Bernardo was an admirer of ancient Rome; but as the initial exchange between Cosimo and Fabrizio indicates, Bernardo did not admire or seek to imitate the same aspects of the ancient republic that Machiavelli did. (Among other things, the conversation related in the Art of War thus shows readers that in both his Discourses and Art of War, Machiavelli was trying to wean Cosimo away from opinions he had acquired from his grandfather.) Bernardo had been a close friend and advisor of Lorenzo the Magnificent. (They were, indeed, related by marriage; Nannina de’ Medici, Lorenzo il Magnifico’s sister, was Bernardo’s wife.) But when Lorenzo began to rule more autocratically, Bernardo distanced himself. He urged Lorenzo’s son to exercise his power with more restraint and to concede more influence to the Florentine aristocracy, and when Piero refused, Bernardo openly opposed him. He was appointed to the commission assigned to give Florence a new constitution in 1494, but he opposed the popular elements, especially the Grand Council, that were added under the influence of Savonarola, and went into voluntary exile. He supported the creation of a gonfalonier for life in 1502 but vehemently opposed both the appointment of Piero Soderini to the office and the failure to abolish the Grand Council. The Orti Oricellari he then planted became home not only to his collections of ancient plants and statues of classical heroes, but also to meetings of admirers of Marsilio Ficino’s Platonism, which emphasized the importance of orienting one’s life by a transcendent standard of beauty (or nobility). Summarizing Bernardo’s career, Felix Gilbert concludes that “Rucellai’s political aim was the establishment of a restricted government, over which the aristocrats would have full control. He was an enemy of the absolutist rule of one man, but he was an equally decided opponent of any popular form of government. . . . In his book on the classical antiquities of Rome, . . . Rucellai states quite explicitly that he considers popular rule fatal for Florence and that . . . he concentrated all his energies on purging the city from the weight of this dross.”12

Machiavelli may have chosen the form of a dialogue to counter some of the influence Ficino and his students continued to exercise on humanistically educated Florentine aristocrats. But he reverses and so undermines some of the dominant features of the Platonic dialogues by showing a military captain rather than a philosopher teaching politically ambitious youths what they need to know in order to become great statesmen. Rather than urging them to become moderate and just, he instructs them about the best means of acquiring the lands, people, and goods belonging to others. It is probably no accident that Machiavelli informs his readers that the participants in the conversation he relates moved into the shade to avoid the sun after they had eaten a sumptuous dinner—in contrast to the conversation Plato relates in the Republic among people who never receive the dinner they are promised and stay instead to discuss the design and establishment of a revolutionary regime in the middle of the night. It is clear that Machiavelli is trying to wean his young friends away from the aristocratic prejudices and more classically republican views of their fathers. Bernardo died in 1514, only a year or two before the conversation related in the Art of War is supposed to have taken place. As Machiavelli shows at the beginning of the conversation, Bernardo’s views continued to shape the opinions and habits of his grandson Cosimo.


B. Sources of Resistance to “Imitating the Ancients” with Regard to the Military, and Machiavelli’s Response to Them


As the questions Cosimo Rucellai first puts to Fabrizio demonstrate, the resistance to Machiavelli’s call in the Discourses to imitate the ancients was not limited to older, more conservative Florentines. The young men to whom he had dedicated the Discourses shared some of their elders’ objections to Machiavelli’s project. Indeed, in the initial exchange between Cosimo and Fabrizio, Machiavelli points to four different sources of resistance to the imitation of ancient military modes.

The first source of resistance arose from a perceived change in manners or mores, particularly with regard to education. Suspecting that his guests might not recognize the plants they see around them, Cosimo explains that his grandfather collected specimens of ancient varieties. Fabrizio somewhat impolitely responds that it would have been better if admirers of the ancient had sought to be like them “in the strong and harsh things, not in the delicate soft ones . . . , and to take up the modes of the true and perfect antiquity, not the false and corrupt one. For after those studies pleased my Romans, my fatherland went to ruin” (1.17). By the false mode and studies, Fabrizio seems to be referring to imitations of the ancients in the fine arts and the revival of Platonic philosophy supported by Lorenzo the Magnificent and his “right-hand man,” Bernardo Rucellai. Cosimo thus jumps to defend his grandfather by claiming that no one despised softness and loved the harshness of the ancients more, but that living in a corrupt time, Bernardo recognized that without being universally defamed, neither he nor his children could imitate Diogenes by going naked in all seasons, forcing their children to sleep in the open and endure all sorts of deprivations like the Spartans, or despising gold and eating only vegetables like Fabricius. The Rucellai are gentlemen, and they care about their reputation.13

Although he says that he is relating the dialogue in honor of Cosimo’s memory, to show how the young man prepared himself for public service by hosting such conversations, Machiavelli intimates here that Cosimo may not have been able to realize his noble ambitions, because his family refused to follow ancient modes of education they deemed too harsh. As a consequence, Cosimo remained weak and sickly. He did not have the physical stamina needed to become a general-statesman in the Roman mode.

Recognizing that Cosimo shares his grandfather’s concern for what is praised and blamed by his contemporaries, Fabrizio quickly retreats. He “was not speaking so much of those hard modes of living, as of other more humane modes . . . that have more conformity with life today” and that would not be difficult for a prince of a city to introduce. The examples he gives of honoring and rewarding the virtues, not despising poverty, esteeming the modes and orders of military discipline, constraining citizens to love one another, living without sects, and esteeming the private less than the public (AW 1.33, emphasis added) seem to describe older aristocratic practices. However, by promising that if such orders are entered into by degrees, it will not be difficult to persuade people who think about them much, “for in them truth appears so much that every common talent can be capable of it” (AW 1.34), Fabrizio does not appear to be asking for extraordinary self-sacrifice or virtue. He is either adapting his speech to the taste of his audience and their corrupt times or proposing a less harsh notion of the education necessary to produce good citizens and soldiers than the ancient beliefs and practices to which Cosimo objects—both philosophical (Diogenes) and political (Sparta and Fabricius).

Changes in taste or styles and goals of education were not the only source of resistance to the imitation of ancient military practices Fabrizio is advocating. Machiavelli’s young friends also perceive the morally dubious character of an autonomous “art of war.” After he defends his grandfather from Fabrizio’s critique on the basis of considerations of reputation, Cosimo attacks his critic by suggesting that Fabrizio is behaving hypocritically in urging others to imitate the ancients, since he has not done so himself. The ancients were citizen soldiers who patriotically fought for their country; he is a mercenary, willing to serve whoever will pay him.

“Fabrizio” responds to Cosimo’s observation about his own failure to imitate the ancients by explaining that men who wish to do something must first prepare themselves to do it. (He thus becomes an example of the effort for which Machiavelli initially praised his host as well as the source of instruction.) But, Fabrizio warns Cosimo and his fellows, the character and extent of their preparations will not be externally visible, so long as they do not have an opportunity to act on them. He thus proposes to demonstrate the truth of his claim to have prepared himself by discoursing “at length . . . on what preparations are necessary to make before, what opportunity must arise, what difficulty impedes” (AW 1.44).

Fabrizio suggests that the members of his audience will be more willing to listen to his proposals than their elders, because their youth makes them “more friendly to military things and more ready to believe” than those “already having white heads and ice in their veins.” But, he insists, opposition to the imitation of ancient military orders is not merely a matter of age or of changed, gentler mores. His contemporaries rightly see that the acquisition and exercise of an autonomous “art of war” is morally repulsive. Machiavelli thus highlights the ironical character of his choice of a spokesman by having “Fabrizio” condemn his own actual practice as a mercenary captain by declaring that the “art of war” is “an art by means of which men cannot live honestly in any time.” No one can support himself by means of war without becoming “rapacious, fraudulent, violent” and having “many of the qualities that make him not good,” because he must always seek to undermine the peace in order to nourish himself (AW 1.47–51).

Echoing his grandfather’s appreciation of the need for noble leadership (and perhaps referring to the statues surrounding them in the garden), Cosimo objects: Fabrizio is ignoring “the glory of Caesar, Pompey, Scipio, Marcellus, and so many Roman captains who are famously celebrated as gods” (AW 1.63). Caesar and Pompey were able, but not good men, Fabrizio retorts, because they sought their own profit and advancement at the expense of the republic; and the exchange serves to remind Machiavelli’s readers of two of the reasons some older and more experienced men objected to the imitation of the ancient modes of warfare. Those modes had led to the fall of the Roman republic and the elevation of individual generals into emperors whose successors became tyrants. Why then should those who wish to see republican government revived want to reinstitute these ancient modes?

The third source of resistance to the revival of ancient military orders that emerges in the exchange between Cosimo and Fabrizio thus consists in fear of the political consequences. By stating that no republic or principality, if well ordered, will allow any of its citizens or subjects to practice the art for his own private benefit, Fabrizio shows that the imitation of the ancients he is advocating is and must be a matter of public policy. It can be neither justified nor achieved merely through the action or education of individuals. (The conversation he is having with these young men, and the dialogue Machiavelli is writing, can therefore only be preparatory.) As Fabrizio admitted in condemning the practice of mercenaries, there is a potential tension between the interests of individual soldiers and the governments they purportedly serve. The question thus becomes whether or how this conflict of interest can be overcome.

Granting a possible antagonism between republican government and the practice of the art of war by talented and ambitious generals, Cosimo suggests that a king might nevertheless want to employ an individual who practices that art (as the king of Spain did, in fact, employ Fabrizio); but Fabrizio denies it.14 Restating a position Machiavelli affirms in both P 19 and D 1.16, Fabrizio states that “kingdoms that have good orders do not give absolute rule to their kings except in the armies; for in this place alone is a sudden decision necessary, and for this there must be one unified power. In other things he cannot do anything without counsel; and those who give him counsel have to fear that he may have someone near who in times of peace desires war because he cannot live without it” (AW, 1.80–81, translation slightly modified). Explicitly choosing to dwell longer on this subject, as it applies to kingdoms that exist at his time, Fabrizio explains (in terms that resemble the argument Machiavelli gives about the true meaning of “liberality” in P 16), a king cannot keep a paid army without having it constantly fight and take spoils, which is impossible, so he will have to pay the soldiers from his own resources, which will bankrupt him, and thus eventually cause him to lose not merely esteem, but his state. Fabrizio admits that the Roman republic maintained an army constantly in the field, but he argues that they avoided the dangerous consequences by varying the men serving in it. Emphasizing the dangers involved in a king’s relying on a nonnative army, Fabrizio reminds Cosimo that the emperors Octavius and Tiberius began to disarm the Roman people in order to rule them more easily and created an army called the Praetorian Guard to defend them from the people and the Senate, but (as Machiavelli also reminds his readers in P 19) that guard eventually came to control and choose the emperors.

Cosimo objects to Fabrizio’s contention that it is impossible to support an army in peacetime by observing that “many lords and gentlemen nourish themselves in time of peace by means of the studies of war” (as do Fabrizio and his peers), and that “many infantrymen are now employed in guarding cities and fortresses” (AW 1.94–95); but Fabrizio points out that these lords and men are neither numerous nor good enough to fight a war effectively. Pope Julius II’s decision to use a Swiss guard, “born and raised under the laws and selected by the community,” instead of native Italians shows that current modes of waging war in Italy are corrupt. Fabrizio thus reiterates: “a wise republic . . . ought to use its citizens as heads in war, and in time of peace want them to return to their art” (as did Cincinnatus whom Machiavelli praises in D 3.25), and “a wise king ought not to employ foreigners except as a reward for some outstanding deed or because he wants to avail himself of one man in peace as well as in war” (AW 1.106–8). Fabrizio then goes so far as to claim that he has “never used war as an art” (AW 1.09), and that the king of Spain rewards and esteems him not so much because he understands how to make war as for the counsel he provides in peace.

The description of “Fabrizio” as someone able to advise a king in peace as well as war clearly fits the author of The Prince much better than the historical mercenary captain. (If the king of Spain valued Fabrizio’s advice in peace as well as war, wouldn’t the king be taking the captain back to Spain rather than letting him return to Rome?) It was Machiavelli, of course, who had been advisor to the head of the Florentine republic and had not been able to overcome the objections of the Florentine nobility in time to train a citizen militia capable of defending it.

Cosimo voices the traditional aristocratic Florentine objections to the formation of a militia when he reminds Fabrizio that “many wise men” have said: “either it is useless, and entrusting ourselves to it will make us lose our state; or it is virtuous, and by its means whoever governs it will easily be able to take [our state]” (AW 1.157).15 Fabrizio responds to the first part of the objection by observing that the “poor showing” of the militia was a result of its inexperience and forced service, but that inexperience can be overcome by proper modes of recruitment, training, and ordering.16 By arguing that soldiers should neither be selected solely from volunteers, in which case they will serve themselves and not their superiors, nor simply be coerced, because that leads to discontent, but that they should be impressed into service by the respect they have for the prince and fear of disobeying the law, Fabrizio at the conclusion of his discourse also points to the exact character of the “opportunity” he explicitly says he has not had (AW 7.210–28): he has never had the political authority to muster and train his own army. He does not respond to the second part of the traditional objection to the formation of a native militia, that an able captain always constitutes a threat to the existing government, because, as Machiavelli shows in D 1.28–32, he cannot. To overcome the potential threat, Machiavelli argues in both his Prince and Discourses, a prince must lead his own army and a republic must try to keep its generals within bounds by means of laws (e.g., competitive elections and public trials). Neither a prince nor a republic will be able to maintain itself, as Machiavelli insisted in his own name in the preface, if it is not able to field an adequate defense.

Fabrizio does not point to the fourth and most fundamental reason neither princes nor republics have sought to imitate the ancients, particularly with respect to waging war (as Machiavelli urged both in The Prince and Discourses) until almost the end of his exchange with Cosimo.17 After Fabrizio begins discussing the way in which a militia should be selected, armed, and trained, Cosimo asks what is responsible for the vileness, disorder, and neglect of training now; and Fabrizio responds with an explanation like but not identical to that Machiavelli gives in his Discourses 2.2. Fabrizio blames, first, the destruction of all other regimes by the Roman Empire and, second, the failure to revive many republics after the fall of the empire as a result of the Christian religion. However, where Machiavelli emphasizes the loss of freedom, Fabrizio attributes the failure of later Europeans to adopt ancient modes of warfare to their lack of fear. Many more excellent and virtuous men have arisen in Europe than in Asia and Africa, because there have been many more republics and principalities in Europe than on the other two continents; and where there are many powers, all are “constrained to keep military orders alive and to honor those who most prevail in them” (AW 2.294), from fear of the others. That salutary fear has been undermined in contemporary Europe, not only by a diminution of the number of powers, but also “on account of the Christian religion, [which] does not impose that necessity to defend oneself that there was in antiquity” (AW 2.305). Ancient peoples “kept military training alive and honored whoever was excellent in it” (AW 2.307), because they feared losing their lives, their freedom, and their property if defeated in war. Today cities are not destroyed, even if they have rebelled a thousand times, few men are killed, and most are left with their goods; the worst evil one has to fear is paying ransom.

Unlike D 2.2, where Machiavelli explicitly contrasts the ferocity of ancient religious rites and the earthly glory awarded to men of action with the elevation of humble and contemplative men by Christians, Fabrizio does not explain how or why Christianity leads to a much more restrained form of warfare. Instead he reiterates his contention that the lack of military training can be traced to the fact that there are now relatively few powers that threaten each other in Europe. Yet as Fabrizio admits at the conclusion of his discourse (AW 7.230–38), the number of independent states does not explain the absence of military valor in Italy, where there are many states and there have been many wars. He seems to agree with the analysis Machiavelli offers in P 12, in which he suggests that priests and citizens of republics who were inexperienced in war gave the practice over to mercenaries who did not want to risk their own lives any more than necessary and who valued the money they could make from ransoming prisoners more than conquering territories to be ruled by others.

Ignoring Fabrizio’s suggestion about the deleterious influence of the Christian religion on the ability of Italians to wage war, Cosimo objects to Fabrizio’s factual claim about the mildness of contemporary warfare by observing (as Machiavelli himself did in his First Decennial) that in the last twenty-five years a great many towns in Italy were sacked and a great many princes lost their kingdoms). Granting that the people have suffered a great deal, Fabrizio nevertheless insists that so long as the “heads of states” retain the belief that they will be able “to buy themselves back with ransoms,” they will not “want to undergo the exertions of training for war” (AW 2.311–12), both because they do not think that it is necessary and because they do not know how. Like Machiavelli in both The Prince and Discourses, Fabrizio thus suggests that the first and most urgent reform needs to be in the education of future leaders.

Since Fabrizio has located the difficulty in the opinions of the “heads,” Cosimo returns to their “principal matter” by asking how he would order the cavalry. The young Florentine may thus betray an aristocratic bias, but his question definitely reflects the tendency we will see among Fabrizio’s other interlocutors as well as later commentators to focus on his specific recommendations with regard to the ordering and arming of the troops, rather than his general reasoning. Fabrizio has already admitted that the cavalry would be constituted, as in both antiquity and the present, by members of the wealthiest class. He refuses to say much about it, because he contends that modern cavalry is as good as if not better than its ancient equivalent. But as a result of Cosimo’s specific query, the question of the effect of the Christian religion and the way in which it makes it difficult to revive ancient military orders is left hanging. Neither Zanobi nor Battista picks up the question of the difference the change in religion makes when Fabrizio briefly alludes to it later (AW 4.141, 6.208).

However, later in the dialogue in describing the way in which a captain “persuades” his troops to fight when he thinks best (AW 4.126–34, 4.148–52, 5.98, 6.205), Fabrizio explicitly argues that he needs to arouse the fear of losing their lives and goods and traces the excellence of ancient military modes to maintaining that fear. To the extent to which Fabrizio (or Machiavelli) convinces his young audience to institute the military practices he recommends, readers thus see, he will have persuaded them to institute practices (such as arousing the “obstinacy” of their troops by putting them in positions in which they have to win or die) and policies (such as making it impossible for them to send home payments or other rewards of service until or unless they have fought successfully) that undo the effects of the Christian religion. Rather than attacking or critiquing Christianity directly, especially in light of the apparent resistance to such by his younger interlocutors (to say nothing of his broader audience), Fabrizio (or Machiavelli) seeks to overcome “the difficulty in removing from the multitude a sinister opinion that is contrary to the common good” (AW 4.137) indirectly by persuading a few to embrace the art of war as he understands it and so gradually to change the opinions of most by changing their practice.


C. What Imitating Ancient Military Orders Entails


1. Ancient Orders Have to Be Adapted for Modern Arms


As in the Discourses, so in the Art of War the discussion loosely follows that of an ancient text, even though in the Art of War Machiavelli does not name the author or text as he does in the Discourses or comment on specific quotations or chapters. One look at the table of contents of Vegetius’s Epitome of Military Science, to say nothing of L. Arthur Burd’s compilation of “le fonti letterarie di Machiavelli nell’ Arte della Guerra,” nevertheless reveals the extent to which Fabrizio follows the order and topics discussed by this ancient source, supplemented by references to Frontinus, Polybius, Caesar’s Gallic Wars, and Josephus.18 In failing to make the source of many of his recommendations clear, Fabrizio somewhat ironically also imitates the work of Vegetius, who is thought to have incorporated a great deal of the work of Frontinus, a book entitled the Art of War, which we no longer possesses, as well as the Stratagems, which we do, without acknowledgment.

Fabrizio nevertheless explicitly breaks with the ancient writers in certain important respects from the very beginning of his discourse.19 With regard to the selection of men, he observes that “those who have given rules for war want men to be selected from the temperate countries, so that they have spirit and prudence. For a warm country generates prudent and not spirited [men], a cold one spirited and not prudent ones” (AW 1.212). Such a rule would be good for a prince of the whole world who could draw men from wherever he wished; but Fabrizio wants to give a rule everyone can use, and that is, all republics and all princes should choose their soldiers from their own country. One should not try to select soldiers on the basis of specific traits they may possess, whether physical or moral, he urges, because one can see from ancient examples, “how with training good soldiers are made in every country” (AW 1.124).20 A captain should not try to find men suited to warfare by nature or rely on their virtue, because “a spirited army is not made so by having spirited men in it but by having them well-ordered” (AW 2.167). Fabrizio thus introduces what might be called the cardinal principle of his “art of war” and Machiavelli’s “art of politics”: a leader should rely on his own ability to order things to achieve the desired effect rather than depend upon what is given by nature.

Fabrizio would imitate the ancients by requiring recruits to do “basic training”: athletic exercises like running, wrestling, throwing and lifting weights, swimming, and horseback riding to increase their strength, dexterity, flexibility, and endurance. They should also be required to practice using their arms, obeying signals, and marching in order. As in the Roman army, they should be divided into small units of ten, each with its own head, who follows the commands of a superior in a strict hierarchy of command that culminates in one general.21

Observing that his young auditors can read the ancient writers for themselves (AW 3.10), Fabrizio says that he will not dwell on the particulars of how the Greeks and Romans arranged the lines in their armies to do battle. He is reasoning about the way in which an army should be ordered and led, not recommending specific tactics or techniques (the utility of which depends on the particular circumstances). Like Machiavelli in D 2.16, he praises the Roman mode of dividing their forces into three parts—hastati, principes, and triarii—and ordering them so that, if it is hard pressed, the first line can withdraw into the second, and likewise the second into the third, which also constitutes a fresh reinforcement. By giving an army only one front line, he explains, a captain risks letting it fall into great disorder. If the front line is not able to withstand the first thrust of the enemy, he is not able to bring up the reserves. The army thus has one and only one chance of winning a battle. All armies lose some battles, of course; but if they are ordered so that they can fight again, they can nevertheless win the war.

Unlike Machiavelli in the Discourses, however, Fabrizio discusses the ways in which both the arms and the order of a modern army have to be adapted to fit changed circumstances in some detail. Instead of slings and darters, he would use arquebuses (predecessors of muskets) with light cavalry in front and on the flanks to harry the enemy and, if possible, seize their artillery. He would also incorporate pikes on all four sides, to guard against attacks by heavily armed cavalry; and these pikes should be ordered according to the Macedonian rather than Roman model. The Germans learned to revive this ancient order, he explains, as a result of the necessity they felt in defending themselves and their liberty from the armed cavalry of nearby princes. This German order should not be allowed to replace Roman orders entirely, however, because it is primarily defensive.22 The important point, he reiterates, is that people learn to adopt good military orders from the necessity of defending themselves.


2. Youthful Impetuosity Will Not Suffice


As the discussion turns from the arming to the ordering of troops, Cosimo asks to be relieved of his office as “dictator.” (Their young host does not appear to understand the difference between a public office whose holder has the power to issue commands that must be obeyed and a private conversation in which the participants engage voluntarily.) Invited to choose a new interlocutor, Fabrizio selects the youngest member of the group, Luigi Alamanni, not only because this is the Venetian (i.e., a republican) way, but also because this training is for the young and the young are, therefore, more fit to reason about as well as to execute it. The course of the conversation nevertheless serves to correct the impression Machiavelli may have left with his famous statement in P 25 about fortune’s favoring the young. A seasoned captain will not rely solely on good luck or the youthful enthusiasm of his troops, if he is not forced to do so.

Acting in character, the impetuous and impatient Luigi urges Fabrizio to describe how an army ordered in the Roman manner he has recommended would win a battle; and in an imaginary encounter that takes no account of the character of the enemy or the site, Fabrizio shows their army winning easily. Rather than inquire, as does the apparently more sensible Zanobi, who follows him, how the battle order should be adapted to the character of the enemy and the site, Luigi merely asks Fabrizio why he has the artillery fire only once. He, too, thus exhibits the tendency of Fabrizio’s young interlocutors to ask about concrete details, tactics, or arms, rather than to challenge the reasoning. Fabrizio repeats many of the arguments Machiavelli employs in D 2.17 to show that the invention of artillery has not made ancient military orders obsolete; but Fabrizio does not go so far as to claim that “if one founds oneself on infantrymen and the modes specified before, artillery becomes altogether useless.”23 He merely asserts that “it would be impossible for an army ordered and armed [as he has specified] not to overcome in the first encounter every other army ordered as modern armies are” (AW 3.161). He concedes that an army in the field has no defense against enemy artillery and must, therefore, try to seize it, because an army cannot attack if it tries to stay out of reach or behind a wall of embankment (as Machiavelli notes in D 2.17 the Spanish forces led by the historical Fabrizio attempted to do at the battle of Ravenna, but the “Fabrizio” who speaks in this dialogue is not the historical mercenary captain).


3. The Need for Prudent Leadership


Knowing how to train and order an army will not suffice to enable a captain to win a battle, Fabrizio tells the “naturally more spirited” Zanobi (AW 4.3), who takes on the role of interlocutor when Luigi quickly retires after his imaginary victory. Like Machiavelli in P 14 and D 3.39, Fabrizio insists that a captain must also know how to change the order of his troops according to the site and the character of his enemy. For examples of ways in which to respond to both, Fabrizio (again like Machiavelli) suggests that a captain should not merely observe and reason about the various possible characteristics of the terrain and the forces confronting one another; he should also read the histories and learn about what works and what does not from the actions of excellent generals.24

Showing that he has read the histories (but not in the way Machiavelli would have him read them), Zanobi asks to be reminded of the specific reasons “Scipio did not have his hastati withdraw into the order of the principes, but divided them and had them withdraw to the horns of the army” (AW 4.42). Fabrizio explains that Scipio altered the order of his troops in order to meet the order he knew Hannibal was using (and thus gives an example of the importance of knowing the enemy); but he adds, “one cannot use this mode of opening the first line so as to give place to the second except when one is otherwise superior,” and suggests that they ought to “return to our reasoning” (AW 4.46–48). Giving many examples of different ways in which a captain might respond to a variety of arms and orders employed by his enemy that overlap to a considerable extent with the advice Machiavelli offers in his own name in D 3.10–14, Fabrizio concludes that “the greatest remedy that is used against a plan of the enemy is to do voluntarily what he plans that you do by force” (AW 4.87) and so surprise him. That was the reason Scipio changed his orders in different battles so that he was able to defeat both Hasdrubal and Hannibal.

Implicitly criticizing Luigi’s desire to wage war before he has learned about the conditions or his enemy, Fabrizio warns Zanobi that “a captain is never to do battle unless he has the advantage” or he is forced to do so by necessity. Whether a captain has an advantage or not does not depend merely on the respective numbers and characters of his troops and those of the enemy or the site (as they saw in the case of Scipio). It also depends upon his prudence and knowledge of the enemy captain. “Necessity arises when you see that by not fighting you must lose . . . ; as when you are lacking money and your army has to be dissolved; through hunger assaulting you; [or] when the enemy waits to be enlarged by new troops.” Then a captain should always fight, even at a disadvantage, “for it is much better to tempt fortune where it can favor you than to see your certain ruin by not tempting it” (AW 4.95–98).

“Above all,” Fabrizio counsels, “you ought to guard against leading an army to fight that is afraid or that is not confident of victory” (AW 4.115; cf. D 3.33). A captain thus needs to learn how to speak and act in a way that gives his men confidence. Because ordinary soldiers do not possess the same understanding of the conditions and the enemy, captains have to know how to dissuade soldiers who want to fight under disadvantageous circumstances, as well as how to persuade those who lack confidence and are not disposed to fight when necessity or opportunity makes it desirable. “That prince or republic which designs to make a new military and give reputation to this training ought [therefore] to accustom its own soldiers to hear the captain speaking and the captain to know how to speak to them” (AW 4.140). A captain does not speak to his men in order to explain his strategy, however; on the contrary, he should keep both his feelings and his plans secret. As Machiavelli argues in D 3.48, a captain must never believe that the enemy does not know how to conduct his own affairs; on the contrary, a captain must always fear that his enemy is deceiving him. But a captain has to act and talk to his men as if he despises the enemy, in order to increase their confidence.25

Rather than appeal to their reason or try to teach them, a captain needs to be able to arouse or extinguish his men’s passions. He can do so in a variety of ways. Like Machiavelli in D 1.13–15, Fabrizio observes that captains can assuage the fears, inflame the spirits, increase their men’s obstinacy, and fill them with hope by appealing to their religious beliefs. Some captains have forced their men to take an oath to fight and die rather than flee; others have claimed to have spoken with representatives of the gods, who promised them victory, or had visions of such in dreams. It is also possible to appeal to the love human beings naturally have for their own country or the esteem men feel for the virtue of their captain. He can make his men angry by repeating insults hurled at them by an enemy. But “persuasion” is not simply or solely effected by speech. Like Machiavelli (writing about Marius in D 3.37), Fabrizio observes that a captain can make his men more confident by letting them see enemy soldiers in a weakened or vulnerable condition. And when a captain cannot convince his men to fight with words, “there is no better mode [of doing so] than giving a part of them as prey to the enemy, so that those who have fought and those who have not believe you” (AW 4.128). “Above all,” he warns, a captain should “take this precaution in wanting to make his soldiers obstinate in the fight: do not permit them to send any of their property home or to put it in some place until the war has ended, so that they understand that if in fleeing they save their lives, they do not save their possessions, the love of which is no less a ground for rendering men obstinate in defense” (AW 4.134). Men can be made obstinate by necessity, as well as by persuasion, e.g., by putting the army in a position in which they have no alternative but to win or die. Indeed, Fabrizio concludes, “That is the most hardy and the best provision that one, wanting to make his own soldiery obstinate, can make” (AW 4.148; cf. D 1.15). Although Fabrizio acknowledges the power of the love human beings naturally have for their own country, he does not urge a captain to rely on the patriotism of his men. On the contrary, like Machiavelli in P 17, Fabrizio tells his young auditors that it is safer to rely on fear than love. So he concludes, if a captain wants to make his soldiers obstinate, he should arrange the circumstances so that his men will be forced to fight—or die.


D. Why the Art of War Entails the Art of Governing


Although a captain needs to know his enemy, Fabrizio admits that is not always possible. When marching through hostile territory or facing an unseen enemy, a captain must order his troops so that he can defend himself on all sides and be on the lookout for an ambush or other form of deception. The discussion thus turns to questions of defense, without Fabrizio’s specifying the shift. He has not told his interlocutors (nor has Machiavelli reminded his readers) that the Roman modes of warfare they have been urged to imitate are essentially offensive. Yet Machiavelli told his readers in the preface that the need for defense is the reason civil and military ways of life must necessarily be combined. In the last part of his discourse we see Fabrizio gradually bring civil and military life closer together.

The need to secure supplies of food and water as well as to build and defend a camp where the army can rest and refresh itself makes military organization look increasingly like civil. Unlike a city, however, an army has to move. With regard to supplies, Fabrizio thus formulates the following general rule: “A prince should order his army to be as unencumbered as possible, taking away everything that burdens it” (AW 5.83). In contrast to modern armies that demand wine and cooked bread, ancient armies provided their men with flour and a bit of fat and had them drink water.

Since they have “conquered the enemy in the field and marched upon his country,” Zanobi counters, “it is reasonable that spoils be had, towns made to pay tribute, and prisoners taken.” Implying that the soldiers should receive something more than flour and water for their efforts, he thus asks “how the ancients governed themselves in these things” (emphasis added). Fabrizio explains that the Romans enriched rather than impoverished themselves by fighting wars, because they gave all the spoils to the public, although the official in charge often distributed the spoils equitably to the soldiers to make them want to win rather than to rob. The Romans also required the soldiers to deposit one-third of their pay with the person who carried the flag of his battalion, both to prevent young men from squandering all of their pay and to give them an incentive to defend the flag. By leaving the distribution of spoils to the discretion of the soldiers, modern armies have made them insolent and undisciplined.

When Fabrizio indicates that he is ready to pass on from the manner in which an army should be supplied to the location and order of its camp, Zanobi passes on the “office” of interlocutor to Battista. Just as they have put the best soldiers ahead and behind the army, Zanobi comments, the two most prudent members of the company will have begun and concluded this reasoning. Because Zanobi apparently retains the ancient view that individuals should be assigned tasks according to their disparate natural talents, despite what has been said about the selection and training of soldiers, Fabrizio begins his discussion of the way in which a camp should be built and organized by endorsing the Roman practice of choosing a site where they can establish their accustomed order, and so rely on art, rather than the Greek practice of choosing a site for its natural advantages and adapting their order to it. Where possible, he reiterates, one should rely on training or art rather than nature.

Although he has been urging them to imitate the Romans, Fabrizio reminds his interlocutors that he does not observe their orders in everything, but takes that part that suits the present times. He worried that they would want him to specify how the army should be encamped before he showed how it should march and fight. He has not presented these topics in the same order as his ancient source or proceeded the way someone actually mustering an army would, because he is not attempting to provide his audience with a “how to” manual. He discussed the order in which the army ought to fight first, even though an army has to march and camp before it fights, because the order in which they will fight ought to determine the order in which they march and camp. He wants his auditors to understand the reasons they should imitate the ancient military orders he recommends as well as the ways in which those orders can and should be adapted for modern circumstances.

The plan Fabrizio suggests for the camp of an army of 24,000 or 50,000 men follows the square order of the troops he suggested for marching; it, too, is adapted for modern artillery and the use of pikes. Organized as a grid around roads wide enough to allow a battalion of infantry to march down them, his plan also shows how much a camp resembles a city that needs to be defended and supplied.26

The need to establish and maintain order within a camp as well as to defend it makes the army camp look even more like a city. In arranging for the defense of the camp, Fabrizio says that he would modify ancient modes of fortifying the camp by using ditches and walls, but not ramparts. He also recommends following the ancient practice of not using guards outside the ditches, because they are easy for an enemy to capture and turn. One reason to maintain a strict, uniform order of the men in camp is that such an order makes it easy to determine whether anyone is missing—or has entered. A captain does not want any of his “heads” to be doing business with the enemy or the enemy to learn his plans. He should, therefore, follow the Roman example not merely of severely punishing anyone who fails to do what he is commanded, or who secretly takes anything out of camp, or lies about what he has done. A captain should also adopt the Roman mode of dealing with whole cohorts or legions, too large to be punished individually, by putting all their names in a bag, drawing one out of ten, and killing the men whose names have been drawn. All will fear the punishment, even if they do not feel it. (Cf. D 3.49.)

Fabrizio reminds his auditors that the Romans acquired their great empire by publicly rewarding all virtuous deeds and punishing crimes, but he particularly recommends their mode of punishment. After a public trial (cf. D 1.7), he explains, the presiding tribune or consul would hit the condemned man lightly, but then allow him to flee and all the other soldiers to kill him. As a result of this particular mode of inflicting the punishment, not merely do other soldiers see that those who commit crimes lose their lives, but the soldiers identify with the judicial officers who order it rather than with the victim, because they themselves inflict the punishment. Fabrizio recognizes that publicly awarded honors like triumphal processions give individuals an incentive to perform virtuous acts. Competition for such honors may also divide soldiers, however, by setting them in competition with one another. The Roman mode of punishment not only makes prospective criminals fear for their lives but also serves to unify officers and men in a common endeavor. By giving the condemnation of Manlius Capitolinus as an example of the advantages of involving the people in the punishment of criminals, so that they will not be tempted to sympathize with the “victim” oppressed by the authorities, Fabrizio indicates that the principle or insight involved in this form of punishment “that takes away tumults and makes justice be observed” (AW 6.125) applies to civil as well as to military life.

Underlining the compatibility between civil and military life that Machiavelli stressed in his preface, Fabrizio adds that “because neither the fear of the laws nor of men is enough to check armed men, the ancients added the authority of God. With very great ceremony they made their soldiers swear to the observance of military discipline . . . and used every industry to rule them with religion” (AW 6.124–26). Like the cautious Cosimo, however, the prudent Battista also fails to take up the question of the role of religion or relevant differences in that respect between the ancients and the moderns.

By asking whether Fabrizio would allow women or idle games in the camp, Battista points, instead, to one of the major differences between a camp and a city. The presence of women corrupts the order of the former, but is essential in the latter. By asking whether there are other factors a captain should take into account in selecting a place to camp, Battista also lets Fabrizio acknowledge the importance of specific characteristics of a site—whether it is healthy (as one can tell from the faces of the inhabitants) and whether or not an enemy can cut off the army’s supply of food or water—that he might have appeared to slight in recommending the Roman policy of relying on art rather than following nature as the Greeks had. Fabrizio nevertheless underlines his central contention that a captain should rely more on art (knowledge and training) than on mere nature, first, by adding that daily exercise is the best way to keep an army healthy and that supplies must be dispensed, i.e., that the internal order imposed by the captain is at least as important as the natural characteristics of any site; and, second, by contrasting the practice of the Romans and Greeks, who limited their armies to a maximum of fifty thousand men so that they could control them by means of their art, rather than relying, like the “occidentals,” on the natural fury of their hordes or, like the orientals, on their “natural obedience” to the king.

In the midst of the discussion of encampments Fabrizio enlarges the scope of their inquiry. At the beginning of his discourse he stated that “the purpose of whoever wants to make war is to be able to fight with any enemy in the field and to be able to win a battle” (AW 1.116). But having “had this army of ours win a battle, . . . march, and [taking account of] those impediments by which it can be surrounded while marching, . . . encamped it where it must not only take a little rest,” he now says that they must “also think of how it must finish the war” (AW 6.166). To end the war a captain not only has to manage his own troops but also has to affect the decisions and behavior of the enemy. Internal and external orders (or “domestic” and “foreign” policy) are necessarily connected.

Just as a captain should do everything in his power to unite his army, so Fabrizio gives many examples to show that “a captain ought with every art to contrive to divide the forces of his enemy, either by making him suspect his own men . . . or by giving him cause to separate his own troops and, through this, become weaker.” If you want “many men or many people to do a thing that would be useful to you and of great harm to them (for instance, either undoing the walls of their city or sending many of them into exile)” (AW 6.168), you should try to deal with them in isolation from one another, so that they do not think of getting together to resist you, but only of obeying. Likewise, “if sedition or discord arises among his soldiers, it is important for a captain to know how to extinguish them with art.” Having observed earlier that men cannot rebel if their “heads” do not give them cause (AW 1.246), Fabrizio states here that “the best mode is to punish the heads of the errors” (AW 6.199; cf. D 3.27). But to do so effectively, one must take them by surprise, if they are distant, by calling everyone together so that they will not know that the purpose of the assembly is to punish them, or, if they are present, by making sure that that those who are not culpable are there to help you punish the guilty.

For a third time Fabrizio adds considerations of the rewards and punishments soldiers have to fear from the gods as well as from their captain, but this time he emphasizes the advantage modern captains have in comparison to the ancients by observing that they no longer have to deal with the “vexation” of inauspicious auguries. Unlike Machiavelli in D 1.56, Fabrizio does not observe that modern peoples also take certain natural events, such as lightning striking a cathedral, as divine signs predicting future events. He merely suggests that if modern captains experience such difficulties, they should either explain the natural causes of the phenomenon or interpret it in a way favorable to their own endeavors. Fabrizio thus intimates that the modern distinction between sword and scepter not only gives secular leaders an opportunity to interpret events in a more politically useful manner by appealing to the natural fears and desires of their people; it also protects political and military “captains” from direct interference with their decisions or challenges to their authority by priests.

Fabrizio brings civil and military orders even closer together when he proceeds to discuss the best ways of besieging or defending towns and citadels. Not surprisingly in light of the similarity between camps and towns, the recommendations he makes for defending or attacking towns correspond to many of his recommendations concerning the best modes of ordering armies in the field and their camps. Like camps, he observes, towns can be strong by nature or industry. They are strong by nature if they are surrounded by rivers and swamps or built on high cliffs and mountains. However, because towns built on mountains that are not too steep to climb easily are vulnerable to artillery, they should be located today on plains and made strong by industry, by making the walls twist so that the defenders can attack the enemy on his flanks as well as front, and digging a deep ditch inside. Like a camp, a town should have a supply of food and water and try to deny the same to the enemy. As in an army, so in defending a town everyone should know what to do to preserve order and avoid tumults. Like an army in the field, its defenders should also do everything in their power to withstand the enemy’s first thrust. As in leading an army through hostile territory, so the captain defending a town has to look out for attacks on all sides. Just as Fabrizio urged captains to separate the unarmed supply wagons from the armed men in camps, so he tells defenders of towns to send the elderly, women, and children away, and rely on experienced soldiers, because weak and inexperienced people are easily frightened by the prospect of war. Since the inhabitants of a town can continue to defend it after its walls are breached (as Fabrizio admits they inevitably will be by enemy artillery), those who attack should encourage the people to surrender by allowing them to go into exile or promising to harm only those who refuse to put down their arms. (Cf. D 3.12.) Both sides have to beware of being deceived by the other.

Bringing the discussion explicitly into the present, Fabrizio says (AW 7.94) that he reasons unwillingly about things that have happened in their own times, especially those involving him. By contrasting the ease with which Cesare Borgia took Urbino in a day by means of deception (in 1502) with the time and expense it took “others” (Lorenzo de’ Medici in 1516), Fabrizio nevertheless reminds his listeners of the difficulties Florence experienced as a result of the city’s failure to train its own militia and captains and the importance, therefore, of preparing the way he has suggested.

Politely suggesting that he has told them many things they must have considered and understood by themselves (7.152), Fabrizio concludes his account of the studies necessary to imitate ancient military orders by repeating most but not all of the general rules given by Vegetius (Epitome 3.26).27 Concerned not so much about imitating the ancients per se as about improving modern Italy, he has not tried to show them “exactly how the ancient military was made, but how in these times one might order a military that would have more virtue than the one that is used” (AW 7.181).


E. The Ironic Conclusion


Fabrizio appears to undermine the utility of the whole dialogue when, turning from his description of ancient military orders to the “parts” that would qualify an individual to become a captain, he states: “I would not know how to select another man than him who knows how to do all those things that have been reasoned about today. Even that would not be enough, if he did not know how to find them by himself. For without invention no one was ever a great man in his own trade; and if invention brings honor in other things, in this above all it honors you” (AW 7.191). Fabrizio thus not merely underlines the difference between himself and his young audience (who clearly have not learned these things for themselves). He also points to the difference between imitating great ancient predecessors (which Machiavelli recommended to Lorenzo in P 6 as well as to Cosimo and Zanobi in D 3) and Machiavelli’s own explicit innovations in his two major prose works. By not advocating in the name of Fabrizio either the new moral teaching of how not to be good that he puts forward in P 15–19 or the new, more popularly based republican “modes and orders” that he proposes in the Discourses, Machiavelli in the Art of War ironically reserves the honor of the innovator for himself.

Coming to the end of the dialogue Fabrizio brings out the problematic character of his own endeavor. Reminding his interlocutors that Cosimo asked at the beginning why he had not imitated the ancient military orders he advocates, Fabrizio suggests that in this discourse he has demonstrated how much time and effort he has put into learning how to imitate those orders. But, he now openly states, only the prince of a state large enough to muster an army of 15,000–20,000 of his own subjects could do that easily. (Having raised armies of 20,000 men on more than one occasion [FH 2.26, 2.29], Florence was such a state.) Fabrizio has never commanded any but foreign armies and men obligated to others. How could he force them to drill, to carry more arms than they are accustomed to bear as individuals along with supplies for more than several days, and to dig roads? How could he get them to abstain from games, acts of lasciviousness, curses, and other acts of insolence? By what God or saints would he make them swear?

By asking such rhetorical questions, Fabrizio makes the character of the difficulties he confronted less than crystal clear. He seems, for example, to ignore the differences between mercenary and auxiliary soldiers that Machiavelli brings out in P 12–13. It might not be possible to force mercenaries to practice, bear burdens, or live austerely, because, as Fabrizio explained earlier, they serve at their own will rather than at the prince’s. He himself was a mercenary captain, but the troops he led were answerable to the Spanish king. As Machiavelli observes in P 13, such troops can be good, disciplined, and God-fearing; they are, indeed, more dangerous to the prince who wants to use them when they are. Fabrizio admits that Spanish troops are better than Italian. He speaks here as an Italian who recognizes that “knowing how to govern an army [already] made is not enough in Italy; rather, it is first necessary to know how to make it and then know how to command it” (AW 7.208). The problem with using auxiliary troops, according to Machiavelli, is that they obey another authority. Fabrizio claims, however, to have been a trusted advisor of the Spanish king about domestic as well as military affairs. In explaining how a captain gives his troops confidence and keeps them united, Fabrizio observed that “that which above every other thing keeps the army united is the reputation of the captain, which arises through his virtue alone. For neither blood nor authority ever gave it without virtue. And the first thing that a captain is expected to do is to keep his soldiers punished and paid” (AW 6.204–5). Did the Spanish king not give his captain enough money to pay the troops? (The fact that the Spanish troops that besieged Florence were starving suggests that he may not have.) Did the king not allow his captain to establish a way of punishing those who refused to obey his commands like that of the Romans so that the other soldiers enforced the penalty and did not sympathize with the rebel? Like Machiavelli in Florence, Fabrizio seems to have failed not so much in training his troops as in persuading his king and employer to do what was necessary to make them good. In P 12 Machiavelli (in)famously declared that “because there cannot be good laws where there are not good arms, and where there are good arms there must be good laws,” he will leave out the reasoning on laws and speak of arms. In the Art of War his spokesman Fabrizio acknowledges, somewhat surreptitiously, that the reverse is also true, i.e., that there cannot be good arms where there are not good laws. And contrary to the beliefs of Florentine aristocrats like Cosimo’s grandfather Bernardo, like the Roman mode of punishment, such laws are good because they involve the people in administering them and so let the people see the necessity of obeying them.

Explaining why the Swiss are better soldiers than the Italians, Fabrizio first refers back to the observation he made earlier that the Swiss were “made good by one usage natural to them” (AW 7.225), “that they were born and raised under the laws and selected by the community” (AW 1.98).28 But silently referring to the fact that the Swiss have also become mercenaries, he adds that they have also been made or kept good by the necessity imposed on them as foreigners of fighting or dying, because they believe they have nowhere to flee. Fabrizio observed earlier that such a “necessity” is stronger in uniting soldiers and motivating them to fight than either a natural love of country or esteem for their captain. Here he concludes that the goodness of the Swiss is limited to their being accustomed to await the enemy with pike and sword, and that no one would be able to teach them what they lack, especially someone who does not speak their language. Although he used Hannibal as an example of many strategies, Fabrizio does not recommend the “inhuman cruelty” that Machiavelli says enabled Hannibal to unite a mercenary army composed of “infinite kinds of men” without dissension (P 17, D 3.21). It was possible, in other words, for an ancient captain to train and unite an army composed of soldiers speaking different languages, but Fabrizio apparently does not think that it would be possible for a modern captain to do so. Early in the dialogue Fabrizio conceded to Cosimo that it would not be possible for people at their time to adopt the harsh ways of some ancients without being defamed and vilified. Perhaps for that reason Fabrizio does not name the “necessity” that enabled the Spaniards, but not the Italians, to adopt a good order. But that “necessity” would appear to be connected with the “pious cruelty” Ferdinand used (P 21) in uniting the Spanish to free their land from the Moors. In Spain an appeal to the Church served to unite forces against the infidel. In Italy, as Fabrizio would know from his own experience, the Church allied with some cities and nations against others.29

Like Machiavelli in The Prince, Fabrizio concludes his discourse by exonerating the people and blaming princes for the disorder, both civil and military, in Italy. Since peoples of all kinds in any place can be made soldiers with the right kind of training, both Machiavelli and Fabrizio agree that where there are not good soldiers, it is the fault of the prince. (Cf. D 1.21.) Conceding that the incidence of virtue is not a function merely of the number of powers and fear of servitude resulting from the loss of one’s own state, as he suggested earlier, Fabrizio observes that Italian princes have been punished for retaining bad orders and not instituting good ones by ignominiously losing their states. There have been many wars in Italy since the invasion by Charles VIII in 1494; but although “wars usually make men bellicose and reputed,” these wars have made Italians lose reputation, because the existing orders were not good. “Before they tasted the blows of the ultramontane wars,” Fabrizio explains, “our Italian princes used to believe that it was enough for a prince to know how to think of a sharp response in his studies, to write a beautiful letter, to show wit and quickness in his deeds and words, to know how to weave a fraud, to be ornamented by gems and gold, to sleep and eat with greater splendor than others, to keep many lascivious ones around, to govern subjects avariciously and proudly, to rot in idleness, to give promotions in the military by favor, to despise anyone who may have shown them any praiseworthy way, to want their speeches to be responses of oracles.” What is worse is that “those who are left persist in the same error and the same disorder” (AW 7.236–80). They do not follow the example set by the ancient princes who wanted to keep their states and so did all the things he has reasoned about, preparing their bodies for hardships and their spirits not to fear dangers. Wanting to live the pleasant, leisured life of a gentleman, they have not been willing to risk their lives in order to preserve their states. Caesar, Alexander, and their like might be faulted for having too much ambition to rule, but they could not be blamed for any softness that makes men delicate and unwarlike.

A reader of Machiavelli’s Prince might summarize Fabrizio’s concluding complaint by saying that Italian princes did not heed the advice Machiavelli gave them about the virtues and vices they need to maintain their states. Like Machiavelli in the Prince, Fabrizio concludes by promising that “if these things were read and believed by these princes, it would be impossible that they not change their form of living and their provinces not change their fortune” (AW 7.240). He emphasizes the need not merely to acquire “one’s own arms” but, more specifically, to train and deploy an army composed of one’s countrymen. Again like Machiavelli in the Prince, Fabrizio promises that “whichever of those who today keep states in Italy first enters by this way, he will be lord of this province before anyone else” (AW 7.242). Indeed, he goes even further by suggesting that a prince who follows his recommendations will, like Philip of Macedon, who learned how to order an army from the Theban Epaminondas and found the rest of Greece in idleness (attending performances of comedies!), be able to occupy the whole country and leave his son a foundation upon which he could conquer the world.

Fabrizio ends by complaining against nature, which either should not have allowed him to know this or should have given him the ability to execute it. He has been as liberal as he has with his advice and learning to his listeners, because they are young and “qualified,” i.e., socially well situated and sufficiently wealthy, to help their princes do so. Unfortunately, from what Machiavelli has indicated about the temperaments, habits, and knowledge of his young Florentine friends, Fabrizio’s hope appears to be somewhat futile. Although he shows himself most willing to press Fabrizio with questions, Cosimo retains many of the opinions of his ancestors. The young Luigi is impetuous, lacking in confidence, and self-professedly imprudent. Zanobi may be more spirited, but he focuses on specific strategies or techniques rather than the reasons for using them. And the more prudent Battista admits that he does not understand what Fabrizio tells him about ordering a camp (AW 6.76), because he does not have the requisite training. He is more used to living at the papal court (and watching comedies) than to drilling or ordering armed men. These young Florentine aristocrats seem to have been friendly to Machiavelli and his projects, but he does not depict them as any more willing (or able in the case of the sickly Cosimo) to undertake the arduous physical exercise and risks involved in actually training and leading an army than the princes Fabrizio condemns. They might, of course, recommend this course of action to others. The dissimulation or irony with which Machiavelli presents his argument in the Art of War nevertheless seems to extend beyond his using a mercenary captain as his spokesman to the suggestion that his young Florentine friends could learn how to train and order an army sitting in a garden, relaxing in the shade after they had dined. They have been miseducated in the “ambitious idleness” Machiavelli thought would prevent his contemporaries from regaining their freedom (D 2.2.). They loved to contemplate ancient greatness and talk about the ways in which it could be revived, but they were not willing to engage in the physically and mentally arduous practices necessary to achieve their ambitions.

In the Art of War we see that Machiavelli had not jettisoned his conviction that strong military leadership would be necessary to liberate Italy from the barbarians by conquering and so uniting the province or his suggestion that the domestic political arrangements of both the Italian principalities and republics would have to be radically altered in order to secure the lives and liberties of the people. On the contrary, in the Art of War Machiavelli shows that the apparently disparate projects announced in The Prince and the Discourses are inextricably interconnected. As he declares in Discourses 1.9, 1.18, a strong prince is necessary to found or to reestablish a republic. But as he argues in The Prince 9, 16–19, such a prince will not be able to institute a lasting regime if he does not obtain the support of his people and protect them from abuse by a mercenary army. The best way to do both is to train a citizen army and to involve the people in the prosecution of criminals. In the Art of War we also see that Machiavelli did not harbor any more illusions about his young Florentine friends’ carrying out the recommendations he put forward in his Discourses than he had about Lorenzo de’ Medici’s following his advice in The Prince. His was a long-term project that would have to be carried to its completion by readers in the future. In all three works he nevertheless made it clear that the formation and training of an army composed of the inhabitants of the country to defend it from the incursions it had suffered from the national armies of France and Spain was the first, most immediate step to be taken in transforming the political life not merely of the Florentine republic, but of Italy, if not of the world.
