7 In telling Cosimo the reasons why he thinks that infantry constitute a better foundation for an army than cavalry (although he admits that cavalry are necessary and useful) in AW 2.86–95, Fabrizio repeats the tactical advantages Machiavelli describes in his own name in D 2.18: foot soldiers can go where horses cannot, or more easily, through woods and swamps; they are less easily disordered and can more easily reorder themselves than horses can; there is no potential division in inclination or spirit in a foot soldier as there is between a horse and its rider; and, finally, men can be ordered to march ahead where horses will refuse to go. Fabrizio does not add, as Machiavelli does, speaking in his own name, “if this were believed, republics and princes would err less . . . and those who have in their hands a civil way of life would know better how to direct it, either by way of expanding it or by way of maintaining it. And they would believe that increasing the inhabitants of one’s city, getting partners and not subjects, sending colonies to guard countries that have been acquired [as well as the Roman policies Fabrizio will recommend to ‘captains’ of armies below], making capital out of booty, subduing the enemy with raids and battles and not with sieges, keeping the public rich and the private poor, and maintaining military exercises with the highest seriousness is the true way to make a republic great and to acquire empire” (emphasis added). On the class basis of Machiavelli’s preference for the infantry over the cavalry, see Timothy J. Lukes, “Martialing Machiavelli: Reassessing the Military Reflections,” Journal of Politics 66, no. 4 (2004): 1099–1102.

Battista had “told the Pope, who is very fond of such things, about their meetings in the Orti, and how much they all value Machiavelli’s intellect. He has spoken warmly of the Mandragola which was ready to be acted in His Holiness’s presence.” And he suggested that “Leo was the sort of man who might more easily be won by a coarse comedy than by a Prince: he would have enjoyed the jokes and rejected what was bitter. Having thus first got him in a good mood, the clever courtier induced the Pope to give him a message for Cardinal de’ Medici telling him to give effect to his goodwill toward Machiavelli with a ‘commission to write, or something similar’” (179).


9 Viroli, Niccolò’s Smile, 210, suggests that Machiavelli instigated the plot. See J. N. Stephens, The Fall of the Florentine Republic 1512–1530 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1983), 117–23, for a fuller account of the history.

He drafted another plan for constitutional reform in April 1522 (Niccolò Machiavelli, L’arte della Guerra. Scritti politici minori, ed. Jean-Jacques Marchand, Denis Fachard, and Giorgio Masi [Rome: Salerno Editrice, 2001], 645–54). But as Ann Maria Cabrini, “Machiavelli’s Florentine Histories,” in Najemy, Cambridge Companion to Machiavelli, 133, notes, the discovery of the conspiracy in June put an end to all such discussions of constitutional reform. 13 The Rucellai were, as a result, more sensitive to the views of others than Machiavelli shows in his Life of Castruccio Castracani the mercenary captain who succeeded in seizing control of his city was; and even he found it necessary to alter the maxims he stole from the ancient cynic to fit modern circumstances. See chapter 5 for a fuller discussion.


14 Like his grandfather, Cosimo is willing to embrace the rule of one man so long as he employs and depends upon other aristocrats.

16 “Fabrizio” thus, in effect, explains the defeat of the militia Machiavelli did not have sufficient time to train adequately at Prato.

19 It cannot, therefore, be the case that Machiavelli did not foresee the importance of artillery and professional armies because he was so intent upon imitating the ancients, as Gat, “Machiavelli and the Decline of the Classical Notion of the Lessons of History in the Study of War,” contends.


20 Cf. D 1.21, 3.30–31, 3.33, 3.36–39. We see Machiavelli here, as in D 2.1, resting his recommendations on ancient practices or history, rather than on ancient arguments or theories about those practices. Fabrizio also observes that “these writers” want to take not “anyone who makes an art of amusement” (AW 1.194–96), but those who work the land, because they are hardy, and those who practice arts needed to wage war like blacksmiths and carpenters. He agrees about the desirability of taking hardy men who practice useful arts, but, in contrast to the ancient authors, he would not draw any conclusions about the character of the men from their arts. Buck, Erträge der Forschung, 102, observes that with regard to the character of desirable recruits, Machiavelli departs from his source, Vegetius.

C. Oman, The Art of War in the Sixteenth Century (London: Methuen, 1937), 93–94; Azar Gat, The Origins of Military Thought: From the Enlightenment to Clausewitz (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1989), 4–7; F. L. Taylor, The Art of War in Italy: 1494–1529 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1921), 170; and Piero Pieri, Il Rinascimento e la crisi militare italiana (Turin: Giulio Einaudi, 1952), 535–36, Machiavelli did not reject the use of gunpowder weapons. He did assign them a secondary role—partly because the weapons were not very accurate or easy to use at the time, partly because their future role could not have been deduced from the results of battles Machiavelli knew about, and partly because, in Machiavelli’s time, reliance on gunpowder weapons necessitated defensive tactics. Cassidy does not see that Machiavelli’s concentration on the offense does not merely reflect a personal preference or military judgment, but is directly related to the purpose and outcome of the organization of an Italian army Machiavelli cum Fabrizio is advocating—the conquest of Italy.

5


Why Machiavelli’s Prince Is neither a Soldier of Fortune nor a Socratic Philosopher


THE LIFE OF CASTRUCCIO CASTRACANI


Unable to obtain a regular job in the Florentine government, Machiavelli accepted what work he could. In the summer of 1520 he thus found himself in Lucca awaiting the resolution of a bankruptcy case in which he was representing some Florentine merchants. To divert himself he composed a highly fictionalized account of the life of Castruccio Castracani, the fourteenth-century condottiere who became tyrant of Lucca, and sent it to his young Florentine friends, Zanobi Buondelmonti and Luigi Alammani.1 The Life was designed to serve two different purposes. First, it gave his young friends an example of the kind of history he could write that they could use in urging the Medici to employ him in writing a history of Florence (which they eventually did). Second, it enabled Machiavelli to correct an enduring misunderstanding of the argument of the Prince. Rather than suggesting that a soldier of fortune like Cesare Borgia or Castruccio Castracani was the example he wanted his young readers to follow, Machiavelli again showed that these self-made tyrants were not able to establish lasting regimes for themselves or others, because they did not understand the “arts of peace” Numa Pompilius had used to preserve the founding of the Roman republic by Romulus. In other words, they did not appreciate the political utility of respecting the conventional moral and religious beliefs of their people that Machiavelli had dramatized in Mandragola.

Machiavelli begins by stating that he “thought it worthwhile to recall [Castruccio’s] career to the memory of men, because it seemed to him that he had found the greatest example of many things, so much virtue and so much fortune, in it” (83). Many scholars have thus taken the Life of Castruccio Castracani to exemplify his understanding of the role of both fortune and virtue in acquiring political power.2 The problem with this straightforward reading is that the good fortune and virtue Machiavelli attributes to Castruccio are largely products of Machiavelli’s own imagination and consequent alterations of the historical record, which undercut his exaggerated praise of the petty tyrant.3 The foundling birth and nurture Machiavelli attributes to Castruccio to make him look like one of the legendary founders prove upon examination not to be nearly as extraordinary or useful as Machiavelli first suggests. Likewise, in showing how Castruccio demonstrated his virtù by using both force and fraud to seize power in Lucca and the surrounding area, Machiavelli changes the strategies Castruccio employed and makes him into an imitator of ancient generals (as Machiavelli urged readers of both The Prince and the Art of War they should be, but Castruccio was not). Finally and perhaps most surprisingly, Machiavelli concludes by indicating that Castruccio did not have the wisdom, either as an educator of his adopted son or as a philosopher, that the tyrant pretended to possess. In sum, Machiavelli does not present Castruccio as a model of virtù who lost his principality merely as a result of bad luck.

Machiavelli’s young Florentine friends seem to have seen the point of his historical inventions. Zanobi wrote Machiavelli that they had read the Life as a “model” for the history of Florence they had been lobbying Cardinal Giulio de’ Medici to commission Machiavelli to write. The republican sympathies and family connections of Machiavelli’s young Florentine readers make it unlikely that they would have taken a mercenary captain who not only made himself tyrant of his own city but also tried to deprive Florence of her freedom as an exemplar of political virtue. But Machiavelli’s young friends do not seem to have had either the Lucchan’s exemplary character or the historical accuracy of Machiavelli’s account primarily in mind.4 By demonstrating the way in which he could critique while seeming to praise, in his Life Machiavelli had shown his young friends how he could write a history of Florence that would appear to celebrate Medici achievements but would reveal the defective, if not pernicious character of their rule.5 By contrasting the qualities and deeds for which Machiavelli praises Castruccio with what he or the historical record shows that Castruccio actually did, later readers can see the difference between what Machiavelli thought a truly fortunate and virtuous prince would do and a petty tyrant.6

Machiavelli concludes his account of the role of fortune and virtue in Castruccio’s career with his legacy, the education he sought to give his adopted heir and the sayings he adopted from ancient philosophers. Most commentators have ignored the long list of sayings drawn from Diogenes Laertius’s Lives and Opinions of the Philosophers that Machiavelli attributes to Castruccio (altered, to be sure, in light of the change in circumstances) at the end of his Life. But careful examination of these “maxims” not merely shows that Castruccio did not understand “the mode in which a prince should keep faith”; it also indicates some of the reasons Machiavelli did not state the philosophical basis of his political recommendations clearly or fully.


Earlier Accounts of the Life of Castruccio Castracani


The distinctive character of Machiavelli’s account of the life of the young tyrant of Lucca becomes clearer if we contrast it with earlier versions. As in so many of his earlier works, Machiavelli was transforming an existing story to make his own points. Previous authors differed in their evaluations of the Lucchan’s career and achievements. His contemporaries, the Florentine chronicler Giovanni Villani and the Pisan Dominican poet Raniero Granchi, presented Castruccio as an embodiment of the vigor, skill, and valor they found lacking in their own cities; they also found the power of providence reflected in his career.7 He was described as a shrewd but just ruler in tales by Francesco Petrarch, Franco Sacchetti, and Giovanni Cavalcanti. However, his fellow Lucchans tended to view him as a tyrant of whom they were glad to be rid.8

The late-fifteenth-century Lucchan novelist Nicolao Tegrimi was a notable exception. In Castruccii Antelminelli Lucensis Ducis Vita he presented his city’s most famous prince as a model of ancient virtue or nobility.9 In order to do so, however, he had to embroider or even alter the facts in his depiction of the three basic aspects of Castruccio’s life.

First, Tegrimi made a great deal of Castruccio’s family. To emphasize his hero’s noble ancestry, Tegrimi followed the example of the historical character, who added degli Antelminelli to his name after his ascension to power.10 To explain how the son of a merchant became a successful mercenary captain, Tegrimi created the character of Alderigo Antelminelli (whose name was taken from a Lucchan financier active in northern Europe later in the fourteen century) as a mentor. And to make his hero more like the great figures of antiquity, Tegrimi invented a story about his miraculous birth. Having fallen asleep, exhausted by her labor, Castruccio’s mother dreamed that a great fire blazed up from within her body that consumed her and everything around her. Awakened by her fright, she gave birth; and the injuries she suffered in giving birth to so large an infant made her unable to bear any more children. But, Tegrimi emphasized, Castruccio himself fathered a large family, including nine legitimate and two “natural” children. And the novelist extolled the way in which Castruccio educated them, by example as well as by precept. Castruccio was sober and continent, displaying a particular devotion to Saint Francis and inculcating the stoical habits of a soldier in his sons.11

Second, in tracing his hero’s rise to power, Tegrimi claimed that Castruccio led the troops in the battle at Montecatini to victory in the absence of their captain, Uguccione della Faggiuola.12 He particularly praised his hero’s ability to inspire his troops by speaking to them as well as his strategic intelligence and organizational skill. In general, Tegrimi showed Castruccio to be a ruler concerned about the welfare of his people. He regularly sought the advice of wise and learned men and hated flatterers.13 Although or perhaps because he himself was unlearned, he would from time to time utter a maxim he invented or took from classical sources.14

Finally, in depicting Castruccio’s legacy, Tegrimi has Castruccio give a deathbed speech in which he says that he is dying poor in possessions but rich in glory, and he reminds his sons that the aim of a ruler should be the welfare and security of his subjects. It does not seem to matter to the novelist’s evaluation of the life and deeds of his hero that Castruccio’s empire did not last. On the contrary, Tegrimi suggests (in terms reminiscent of Diotima’s delineation of the different forms of human striving for immortality in Plato’s Symposium [207a–212a]), those who sire large families cannot attain the perpetual glory of childless individuals like Moses, Romulus, Numa, Caesar, and Homer. It is, moreover, necessary to take account of the power of fortune as well as an individual’s virtue in evaluating his achievements. Tegrimi reports that Castruccio understood himself to be inferior to Caesar only in the time and place of his birth. His intentions and spirit (animo) were as great, but Lucca was not Rome.15

Machiavelli seems to have relied on Tegrimi’s Vita in constructing his own version of the life. He organized his Life into the same three stages or aspects and fictionalized his account in a similar way. However, although he incorporated many of his predecessor’s inventions, Machiavelli used them to show that Castruccio was not the exemplar of the rather traditional set of princely virtues Tegrimi had depicted.


The Good Fortune of the Foundling


Rather than emphasizing Castruccio’s noble lineage like Tegrimi, Machiavelli presents his hero as a foundling who is educated by two sets of adoptive parents. By altering the historical record in this way, Machiavelli seems to be trying to give his protagonist the characteristics if not status of an ancient hero.16 He begins by observing that

to anyone who considers the matter, it appears quite amazing that all of those (or at least the greater part of them) who have achieved outstanding things in this world . . . have . . . suffered to an unusual degree from the travails of fortune. . . . [They] have been exposed to wild beasts, or have had such humble fathers that, feeling ashamed of them, they have made themselves out to be sons of Jupiter or some other god. (3)


Machiavelli refrains from giving examples: “since their names are familiar to everyone, to list them would be tedious and undesirable to the reader” (3). But the story he proceeds to tell of Dianora’s finding the babe wrapped in grape leaves in her brother’s vineyard and his subsequent adoption by Francesco Guinigi cannot help but remind readers of the account of Pharaoh’s daughter finding Moses in the bulrushes, and King Astyages’ identification of his son Cyrus on the basis of his regal bearing.17

Although the stories of his birth and nurture make Castruccio resemble two of the ancient founders of kingdoms and empires that Machiavelli celebrates in P 6, he does not present Castruccio as their equal.18 In The Prince Machiavelli declares that the virtue of those who rise to power on the basis of their own abilities is so great that fortune gives them only the “opportunity,” that is, “the matter enabling them to introduce any form they pleased. Without that opportunity their virtue of spirit would have been eliminated, and without that virtue the opportunity would have been in vain” (P 6; 23). The opportunities he describes in the case of Moses and Cyrus consist, moreover, in the enslavement or oppression of their peoples from which the founder-heroes freed them. Machiavelli never suggests that Castruccio “liberated” Lucca or the other Tuscan cities he ruled as a tyrant (whereas he does say that the Pistoians who drove out Castruccio’s lieutenants restored “liberty to the city” [95]). Nor does he suggest, as did Tegrimi (or Herodotus before him with regard to Cyrus) that his hero’s future achievements were presaged by a dream in which a flame, flood, or vine that encompassed the earth burst out of his mother’s womb.

Machiavelli explicitly presents Castruccio’s humble birth and adoption as illustrations of the power of Fortune, who “wishing to demonstrate to the world that it is she who makes men great, and not Prudence, begins to show her powers at a time when prudence can play no part at all, so that Fortune can take the credit for everything.” However, Machiavelli also indicates the limits of the power of Fortune to make an individual great—and the extent of his own praise of Castruccio—when he adds that Castruccio’s achievements were “outstanding” for “the times in which he lived and the city in which he was born” (3), but not in themselves.

According to Machiavelli (and in marked contrast to the historical record), Castruccio had the good fortune to be found by a childless widow who was living with her childless brother, a priest named Antonio Castracani (which means castrated dog). Lacking progeny of their own, they decided to adopt and educate the baby boy. But Messer Antonio’s attempts to train the boy to become a priest like him were foiled by Castruccio’s strong natural inclinations toward war. When he was fourteen years old and no longer feared the chastisement of his parents, he put aside his books about churchly matters and dedicated himself entirely to learning how to handle weapons and win athletic contests. A nobleman named Francesco Guinigi saw how Castruccio excelled the other boys and offered to instruct him in “all the virtue and habits of a true gentleman [uno vero gentile uomo]” (86).19

In sum, Machiavelli shows that Castruccio’s good fortune was to be born with a nature especially suited to waging war and to be adopted, eventually, by a man able to teach him how to do so successfully. In contrast to the great founders with whom Machiavelli first associated him, there was nothing miraculous or mythical about Castruccio’s birth, adoption, or education.


Castruccio’s Military and Political Virtù


Just as he began by presenting Castruccio’s birth in the guise of that of a legendary founder, but then indicated that neither his nurture nor his achievements were that extraordinary, so in the second major part of the Life, Machiavelli presents an improved and enhanced picture of Castruccio’s rise to power, only to undercut his exemplary status in the end. Once again Machiavelli departs in significant ways from the historical record in relating the way in which Castruccio came to power in Lucca and was on the brink of establishing a broader Tuscan empire when he suffered an untimely death. By showing that Castruccio imitated a series of ancient generals in seeking to enlarge his dominion by means of fraud as well as force, Machiavelli suggests that the Lucchan tyrant understood very well what a private man has to do in order to become a prince. (Cf. P 18–19; D 2.13.) However, Machiavelli also shows his readers that each of Castruccio’s successes provoked a domestic reaction. Although he forcefully quashed the opposition, and organized his own people into an army (instead of relying on the mercenary forces with which he began), Castruccio was never able to gather and maintain popular support. He made his own imperial ambitions too evident without convincing his allies or his people that he was acting in their interest.20


A. Castruccio’s Rise to Power in Lucca


According to Machiavelli, Castruccio first demonstrated his military prowess when Messer Francesco put Castruccio in charge of the company he sent to aid the Visconti of Milan. Castruccio displayed so much prudence and courage in the campaign that he returned with a reputation in all of Lombardy. What aroused the envy and opposition of his fellow citizens, however, was not his ability to fight foreign wars; it was the favor Messer Francesco showed Castruccio by choosing him to be the tutor of his thirteen-year-old son Pagolo and to administer his estate after he died. The head of the Guelph party, Messer Giorgio degli Opizi, had hoped to assume power in Lucca after Messer Francesco’s death. To discredit his new Ghibelline competitor, Opizi began spreading rumors about Castruccio’s intentions of establishing a tyranny.

Rather than immediately seeking to become a tyrant himself, as Opizi charged, Castruccio became a lieutenant of the mercenary captain Uguccione della Faggiuola, who had made himself captain and then lord of Pisa. Uguccione was allied with the Ghibellines, so Castruccio conspired with friends in Lucca not merely to bring back Ghibelline exiles in Pisa, but to make Uguccione lord of Lucca. Having provided himself with the weapons and other supplies necessary to hold out for several days in the Onesti tower, at a prearranged signal Castruccio called the citizens to arms and opened the gates of the city to Uguccione and his troops. The mercenary captain killed Giorgio degli Opizi, his friends, and family, and reorganized the government to suit himself, with much injury to other Lucchans.

Exaggerating the role Castruccio played in establishing Uguccione as tyrant of Lucca, Machiavelli adopts Tegrimi’s alteration of the historical record by making Castruccio lead Uguccione’s troops to victory when they meet the Florentine army amassed to put down the rising Ghibelline power.21 He also changes the location of the battle and the strategy used to win it.22 Machiavelli does not make the actual source of the strategy he attributes to Castruccio explicit. He may have been testing his young Florentine friends’ memories of the lessons they supposedly learned from the conversation related in the Art of War.23 But readers see that in order to make Castruccio an exemplary captain, Machiavelli has attributed knowledge of ancient examples or the prudence to replicate them to his protagonist. (There is no evidence that the historical Castruccio possessed such knowledge or put it into practice.)

Machiavelli then shows that Castruccio’s military success led Uguccione to become jealous and suspicious. (In D 1.29–30, Machiavelli argues that a prince will necessarily regard a victorious captain as a potential rival.) When Castruccio resisted the arrest of a murderer who had sought refuge with him, Uguccione had the pretext he desired to act against his captain.24 He ordered his son Neri, whom he had left in charge of Lucca, to invite Castruccio to dinner and then to seize and imprison him. Afraid that the people would rebel if he killed such a popular hero without a trial, Neri sent to his father for further advice. Exasperated by his son’s ineptitude, Uguccione left Pisa for Lucca with four hundred cavalry, whereupon the Pisans rebelled. Hearing about the rebellion in Pisa, the Lucchans also rebelled. They freed Castruccio, and he and his friends then attacked Uguccione, who fled to Lombardy.

From a traitor, Machiavelli shows, Castruccio thus transformed himself into the liberator of Lucca. With the help of his friends and his newly won popular favor, he was first made general for a year. Castruccio did not take advantage of the opportunity, however, to solidify the support of his people. Anxious to obtain the title as well as control of the city, he bribed several members of outstanding families like the Pogginghi to make him lord, and they arranged for him to be proclaimed prince for life by a solemn decree of the people.25


B. Castruccio’s Campaign to Acquire a Tuscan Empire


After he was proclaimed lord of Lucca, Machiavelli shows, Castruccio set out immediately to extend his dominion. He first sought to enhance his reputation by making the Holy Roman Emperor his friend. He took five hundred cavalry to meet “Frederick of Bavaria” as he traveled to Rome to be crowned, and the gesture redounded immediately to Castruccio’s benefit.26 Having driven their lord out, the Pisans had asked the emperor for assistance; but, since he intended to return to Germany, the emperor made Castruccio lord of Pisa.

After the emperor returned to Germany, Machiavelli reports, all the Tuscan and Lombard Ghibellines turned to Castruccio for assistance, promising him rule of their states if he managed to return their states to them. His ambition thus excited and expanded, Castruccio decided to try to become lord of all Tuscany with the help of his Ghibelline allies—and his own arms.

Castruccio first organized his own army by dividing Lucca and its territory into five parts, providing the inhabitants with weapons, and putting them under captains and ensigns. Machiavelli does not explicitly say that Castruccio was following an ancient model he had recommended in D 3.30 where he observes that “Camillus never permitted a multitude to take up arms except in a certain order and mode. So following his example, an individual put in charge of the guard of a city ought never arm the men tumultuously, but first have those enrolled and selected whom he wishes to be armed and whom they have to obey” (D 3.30, 281, translation slightly modified). Machiavelli simply shows Castruccio doing what he recommended not only in the Discourses but also in The Prince, where Machiavelli praises Cesare Borgia for shifting from the unreliable auxiliary and mercenary troops he first used to seize power to organizing his own arms.27

Although he organized and armed his people, Machiavelli also shows that Castruccio did not seek their support—or that of the nobles. As he admits in his deathbed speech, he did not try to consolidate his power at home before he sought additional foreign acquisitions. On the contrary, following the model of his acquisition of Pisa, Castruccio again tried to enhance his reputation and so further his imperial ambitions by allying with a powerful foreign Ghibelline—Messer Matteo Visconti, prince of Milan. When Matteo asked him to attack Florence, so that the Florentines would have to bring their troops back from Lombardy to Tuscany, Castruccio gladly complied.

Castruccio soon had to withdraw his troops, however, in order to put down a conspiracy at home. Just as Castruccio’s rising reputation in Lucca had aroused the envy of the Opizi family, so his imperial connections and ambitions aroused the envy of his former allies, the Poggio family. Thinking that he had not given them their fair share of the rewards, they conspired against him. Although a peace-loving member of the family who had not participated in the conspiracy tried to mediate, Castruccio did not spare him when, following the example of Uguccione and his son Neri (as well as that of Cesare Borgia, P 7), he invited the whole family to dinner and executed or imprisoned them all.28 Castruccio then sought to eliminate any individual who might harbor an ambition to become prince in his stead. Like Agathocles the Sicilian (P 8), Castruccio thus demonstrated his ability to use both force and fraud to seize and maintain control of his city for the duration of his life. But, Machiavelli proceeds to show, that ‘virtù’ was not sufficient to enable him to found a lasting empire or to win glory.

While he was seeking to eliminate any opposition at home and building a huge fortress to protect himself (contrary to Machiavelli’s advice in both P 20 and D 2.24), Castruccio continued to pursue his imperial ambitions by conspiring with the leaders of the major factions in Pistoia to obtain control of that city. Promising the leaders of both the white and the black Guelphs that he would assist them in putting down the opposition, once he and his troops were let into the city he killed the heads, captured the supporters of both factions, and persuaded the populace to surrender, partly by promising to cancel some old debts. Here, too, Machiavelli attributes a strategy employed by an ancient captain—in this case, the strategy used by Cyrus’s lieutenant Adusius in making peace in Caria—to Castruccio.29 As in D 3.27, however, Machiavelli modifies the strategy to have his captain follow the Roman example of killing (instead of trying to reconcile) the heads of the conspiring factions.30

After he seized Pistoia, Machiavelli shows, Castruccio again sought to increase his international reputation rather than solidify support for his rule among his fellow citizens—this time by responding to a plea from a lieutenant of the Holy Roman Emperor named “Henry” to help put down a rebellion in Rome.31 Castruccio did so primarily by having grain shipped in from Sicily and so removing the major cause of popular unrest; but he also threatened or punished the leaders until they accepted Henry’s rule.

Castruccio thus appeared to have understood the importance of gaining the people’s support by preserving their lives and property while restraining “the great” (P 9). However, just as Castruccio squandered his opportunity to build a reputation as the liberator and savior of the people of Lucca in order to obtain the title of prince as quickly as possible, so in Rome Castruccio immediately began to flaunt his imperial ambitions. After he had been made a senator, he celebrated his new office with great pomp. He had a toga embroidered with “God wills it” on the front and “What God wills shall be” on the back. Again, Machiavelli does not explicitly draw the comparison with Camillus and the four white horses he used to draw his chariot in his triumph (D 3.23), but by wearing this toga in a celebration of his new office, Castruccio could be seen to be claiming to rule on the basis of divine support, if not of his own divinity, and thus displaying a kind of hubris that would arouse the ire of the people (to say nothing of the suspicions of God’s two other purported representatives on earth, the Holy Roman Emperor and the pope).

Although he successfully expanded his dominion by means of both force and fraud, Machiavelli shows, Castruccio’s flaunting of his imperial ambitions aroused opposition to his rule in all the cities he acquired. His expansionary policies also aroused the suspicions and hostility of a more powerful neighbor—the republic of Florence. The Florentines first conspired with some exiles to retake Pistoia. Seeking to preempt a response from Castruccio, they then assembled a great army and marched to the Nievole valley where they could cut off his route to Pistoia. (As Machiavelli shows, but does not explicitly say, a republic can use force and fraud as well as a prince.) However, Castruccio marched back post haste from Rome and defeated the Florentines at Serravalle by employing another strategy Machiavelli recommends in the Art of War (4.16–17): he used the peculiarities of the site (a fortress located on a hill) to disguise the superior number of the foe from his own soldiers and to force the enemy to retreat in confusion. In the wake of Castruccio’s victory, the Pistoians drove out the Guelphs and surrendered to him. But he, not content with merely returning to the status quo, occupied Prato and camped within two miles of the gates of Florence. Once there, he conspired with two nobles to open the gates, but the plot was discovered and the nobles killed.

In both his Florentine Histories and Life of Castruccio Castracani Machiavelli reports that Castruccio’s attack made the Florentines fear the loss of their own liberty. They thus offered to make Robert, king of Naples, lord of the city, if he would defend them. He agreed to send his son, Charles of Calabria, for a fee of 200,000 florins per year. However, it took Charles some time to arrive. In the Life, Machiavelli explains that the Florentines were able to assemble another huge army to oppose Castruccio, because he was forced to withdraw his troops from their territory in order to put down a conspiracy against him in Pisa. Once again, Castruccio lost the advantage he had won on the battlefield because of opposition inside a city he had previously conquered.

Like the battle at Serravalle, the battle Machiavelli describes between Castruccio and the Florentines at Fucecchio in his Life is a fabrication. In fact, Castruccio’s army camped within two miles of the walls of Florence and ravaged the countryside after he defeated the Florentines at Altopascio; and he later defeated them again along with the rebellious Pistoians with a siege. In his Florentine Histories (2.29) Machiavelli attributes the Florentine losses to the dilatory tactics employed by their hired commander, Ramondo di Cardona, and the political divisions within the city.32 He concludes that account, moreover, by observing that Florence was saved only by good fortune, when both Castruccio and Charles died. In the Life Machiavelli presents the Lucchan captain as a better military leader than he actually was and attributes his death to a certain lack of foresight rather than sheer bad lack.

To make Castruccio look like an exemplary captain, in his Life Machiavelli not only changes the location and reason for Castruccio’s last victory—from a rebellion in Pistoia to a rebellion in Pisa and from a siege (which, Machiavelli pointed out in D 2.32 the Romans sought to avoid, because they were long and expensive) to a pitched battle.33 He also attributes Castruccio’s victory in this last battle to his employing a combination of ancient strategies—one Hannibal used at the River Tagus (Livy 21.5) and one Scipio used at Zama (Livy 30.34)—that Machiavelli (or his spokesman Fabrizio Colonna) recommended to his young Florentine readers in the Art of War (4.40–41).

In relating the way in which Castruccio’s career came to an abrupt end at the conclusion of this battle, Machiavelli seems to attribute Castruccio’s failure to realize his imperial ambitions to bad luck and thus to return to what appeared to be the primary theme of the Life at the beginning, i.e., the power of fortuna. Because he believed that a captain should be first to mount and last to dismount, Machiavelli reports, Castruccio stood bareheaded in a wind, exhausted and drenched in perspiration, to greet his victorious troops on their return (as well as to look and see whether the enemy had regrouped and would attack). As a result, he came down with a fever and died.

Readers are led to ask, however, whether Castruccio’s end was simply a matter of bad luck. As with Cesare Borgia, with whom Castruccio has often been compared, Machiavelli first attributes his inability to establish a lasting regime to his own untimely death. But as Machiavelli states explicitly in the case of Cesare, so he implicitly suggests in the case of Castruccio, his failure to establish a lasting regime was also a result of bad judgment.34 That bad judgment is revealed in the two parts of his ‘legacy’: the deathbed speech Machiavelli invents for him to give to his imaginary adopted heir and the thirty-four sayings that Machiavelli attributes to him.


Castruccio’s Lack of Practical Wisdom


A. Castruccio’s Failure as a Teacher


As he lay dying, Castruccio purportedly told Pagolo that if he had thought that Fortune would want to cut him off in the midst of the path toward the glory promised by his many successes he would have tried to do less. Content to rule Lucca and Pisa, he would not have conquered Pistoia and angered the Florentines. He would thus have left Pagolo a smaller, but more secure state, with fewer enemies and envy.

J. H. Whitfield takes Castruccio’s deathbed disavowal of his imperial ambitions as a late endorsement by Machiavelli of moderation or “the middle way” he previously excoriated.35 There are, however, several serious problems with this interpretation.

First, human beings all know that they are going to have to die sometime; a soldier ought to be particularly aware of the danger. Unlike Machiavelli’s protagonist, the historical Castruccio thus arranged to have his son elected captain on the eve of his first great battle with the Florentines—just in case he himself was killed.36 At the very least, in attributing this deathbed speech to Castruccio, Machiavelli suggests that the captain was lacking in foresight.

Second, Machiavelli shows that Castruccio regretted his lack of success and consequent failure to win glory. But it is not at all clear that he disavowed his imperial ambitions as wrong or excessive. On the contrary, Castruccio brags about his having demonstrated his gratitude to his benefactor not only by refusing to marry, lest he have his own natural children who might compete with Pagolo for his affection, but also by leaving Pagolo more than his father did. In other words, Castruccio thinks that more is better. He regrets the fragility of his acquisitions, but he has not become more moderate in his desires. He says that he is happy to have left Pagolo a large state; he is sad only because that state is weak and infirm. All the cities over which he has acquired control are apt to revolt, and his conquests have angered their most powerful neighbors, the Florentines.

Castruccio bequeaths Pagolo an admittedly difficult position, but he also prides himself on telling Pagolo how to deal with it. Because Pagolo is not suited to war, Castruccio advises him to endeavor to use the arts of peace. He should not count on the support of his rebellious subjects or distant allies, but, relying on his own cleverness and their memory of their recent defeat, he should try to make peace with the Florentines. Castruccio concludes, therefore, by informing Pagolo that he will be indebted to Castruccio not only for the state he has left but also for teaching him how to keep it.

But Castruccio’s claim to have benefited his adopted heir, particularly by teaching him what to do in order to stay in power, proves on examination to be hollow. Machiavelli does not explicitly comment on the wisdom of Castruccio’s deathbed advice. He merely informs his readers that neither virtue nor fortune was as friendly to Pagolo as they had been to Castruccio. Pagolo soon lost everything Castruccio had left him, except for Lucca, which remained in his family for two generations.

If readers review the story of Castruccio’s rise to power and Pagolo’s role in it, however, they see that Castruccio was not a good teacher. (No one who knows anything about teaching would believe that he could tell his successor what to do in a brief speech at the end of his life.) Machiavelli tells his readers that Castruccio used Pagolo as his lieutenant both in the conspiracy against Pistoia and in the defense of Pisa and so instructed him by example, if not by precept, in the arts of war. He does not mention any instance in which Castruccio attempted to train Pagolo in the “arts of peace” (which Machiavelli identifies with religion in his praise of Numa in D 1.11) that Castruccio now tells his heir to employ in negotiating with Florence, because Pagolo is not capable of waging war. Having discovered that Pagolo was not warlike by nature, Castruccio had not reversed his own experience and given his heir to a priest to teach him what Castruccio himself had refused to learn from Messer Antonio. Nor had Castruccio imitated Messer Francesco’s prudent policy by finding a young man with a suitable nature to adopt and educate, who would be able to lead his troops when he himself was no longer able to do so. In other words, Castruccio may have increased the estate he passed on to Pagolo, but he had not served as an effective tutor. He had not, because he had not reflected on his own experience and drawn appropriate conclusions from it. Machiavelli thus shows, although he does not explicitly say, that Castruccio lacked self-knowledge.


B. What Castruccio Needed to Know in Order to Succeed, but Did Not


Castruccio’s lack of self-knowledge proves, indeed, to be the implicit theme of the last third of the Life. As Castruccio told Pagolo, he thought that he was on “the path toward glory promised by his many successes.” Unfortunately, Machiavelli shows, Castruccio did not understand what is required truly to achieve the glory he sought.

Castruccio’s failure to educate his heir meant that he would not have an effective successor or succession. Although his description of Castruccio’s birth is reminiscent of the legends associated with Moses and Cyrus, Machiavelli does not present the Lucchan prince as a founder or legislator. In what appears to be a eulogy at the conclusion of his account of the funeral, Machiavelli points to Castruccio’s fundamental misunderstanding. Tall and handsome, Castruccio would appear literally to have embodied the characteristics of an ideal prince.37 As in his youth, so as an adult Castruccio had “so much grace in his bearing and received men with such humanity that nobody who had spoken with him left dissatisfied.” Machiavelli adds that “he was kind to his friends, but terrible to his enemies; just towards his subjects, but faithless to foreigners.” He would never seek to win by force what he could take by fraud; for he said, “it was the victory itself, not the way you won the victory, that brought you glory” (104).

This final “saying” reveals what Machiavelli saw to be Castruccio’s fundamental intellectual error or misunderstanding; he did not know how to attain what he most wanted. In D 3.40 Machiavelli observes that although one can use fraud not only to win wars but also to acquire a kingdom, the use of fraud will not bring anyone glory. In order to acquire glory, Machiavelli argues in both his Prince and Discourses, a leader must not only satisfy the desires of his fellow citizens or subjects to preserve their lives and property but also appear to be merciful, faithful, honest, humane, and religious. But, as the sayings Machiavelli attributes to Castruccio at the end of the Life show, he was not concerned about appearing to be moral or religious. On the contrary, Castruccio used to say that “men should try everything and not be dismayed by anything. God clearly is a lover of brave men, since one sees that the weak are always punished by the strong” (104). Castruccio apparently had not read enough history to have learned that “among all men praised, the most praised are those who have been heads and orderers of religion. Next, then, are those who have founded either republics or kingdoms. After them are celebrated those who, placed over armies, have expanded either their kingdom or that of the fatherland” (D 1.10).

The caustic sayings drawn from Diogenes Laertius’s account of the lives of the ancient Greek philosophers that Machiavelli attributes to Castruccio show that he had no compunctions about openly contradicting widely held moral opinions. Nor did he have sufficient regard for maintaining a dignified public presence. Castruccio should have seen that the thought expressed in the sayings he repeated was incompatible with a political life like his own. His adoption and repetition of these sayings reflected a kind of arrogance that led him to despise the need to keep up appearances. His borrowing of the words of others constituted a pretention to wisdom that would have been condemned by the authors whose words he appropriated. Castruccio thought that he was better and wiser than he really was.

Like his first young Florentine readers, most commentators have simply ignored or dismissed the long list of maxims taken largely from Diogenes Laertius that Machiavelli attributes, in slightly modified form, to Castruccio at the end of his Life.38 As a result, they have missed not only Machiavelli’s critique of the Lucchan prince for his lack of practical wisdom, but also Machiavelli’s indications of what a prudent prince or educator would understand.

All the ancient philosophers from whom Castruccio takes his maxims were students of Socrates: the hedonist Aristippus (the first 16 sayings), the sophist Bion (2 sayings before and 2 after the one saying by Aristotle), and the cynic Diogenes (11 sayings, punctuated by one statement attributed by Tegrimi to Castruccio himself and one from Dante’s Inferno). All these Socratics were critical of the Platonic notion of the ideas. They did not themselves posit such transcendental, purely intelligible objects of knowledge or standards of right and wrong. All of them nevertheless recognized a fundamental difference between nature and convention and criticized conventional morality, customs and laws on that basis.39 Because he attributed the sayings to Castruccio, Machiavelli did not have to cite or explain the source.

In attributing these sayings to Castruccio, Machiavelli adapts them to his times, for example, by substituting celebrations of “saints’ feast-days” for “festivals of the gods.”40 He also adapts the sayings to his protagonist’s position, first, by identifying Castruccio with the tyrant Dionysius rather than with the philosopher Aristippus. According to Machiavelli, Castruccio thus spit on a flatterer rather than, like Aristippus, allowing a tyrant (Dionysius) to spit on him. Likewise, Machiavelli reports, when someone came to ask him a favor and Castruccio appeared to turn a deaf ear, the man threw himself onto the ground; and when Castruccio rebuked him, the man responded, “it is your fault; you have ears in your feet.” Diogenes Laertius says that when Aristippus made a request to Dionysius on behalf of a friend and the tyrant refused to grant it, the philosopher fell down at the tyrant’s feet and responded to a jeering passerby, “It is not I who am to blame, but Dionysius who has his ears in his feet” (2.8.79). Second, where Aristippus said that he would like to die like Socrates, Machiavelli has Castruccio say that he would like to die like Caesar. Both Socrates and Caesar might be said to have acquired fame if not glory by dying as martyrs. But the hedonist Aristippus would no doubt have pointed out that Socrates emphasized that he was seventy years old and apt to die soon of natural causes in any case. The hemlock was, moreover, supposed to be painless. Caesar was killed painfully by stabs inflicted by many of his supposed friends and colleagues. Like Castruccio, Caesar had just acquired his empire. The first Roman emperor was his adopted son Augustus, whose rise was facilitated by the will in which Caesar left his property to the people of Rome (and even he called himself merely princeps rather than imperator).41 As we have seen, Castruccio did not leave his heir such a good example to follow or teach him how to obtain the favor of his people. Nor had he learned to conceal his own imperial ambitions by retaining old titles and forms. (Cf. D 1.25.)

Even though Machiavelli adapts the sayings to fit Castruccio’s particular circumstances, a comparison of Castruccio’s sayings with the original versions indicates not merely that he did not recognize the fundamental tension between his own political concerns and the explicitly apolitical stance taken by the ancient Socratics. He did not understand the requirements of his own political position.

Ancient Socratics like Aristippus insisted that philosophy was a better way of life than politics, and that philosophers should keep their distance from this “disease.” Both in the Apology and in the Gorgias Plato’s Socrates claimed that his refutations constituted a kind of corrective “medicine” for the individuals he interrogated. But Socrates also insisted that his examinations had to be conducted in private. He could not go into a public assembly and oppose the unjust will of the many without losing his life.42

Castruccio went into politics at an early age and expressed contempt for philosophers. When Castruccio told a man who professed to be a philosopher, “You are all like dogs, who always come running to the man who can give them most to eat,” Machiavelli reports that the philosopher retorted, “No, we are like doctors, we go to the houses of those who have most need of us.”43 According to Diogenes Laertius, Aristippus (following Socrates) went even further in observing that “physicians tend those who are sick,” but that “no one for that reason would prefer being sick to being a physician.”

One of the few commentators if not the only one to pay attention to the maxims at the end of the Life, Strauss points out that the last set of sayings drawn from Diogenes begins with a reference to Castruccio’s education by Messer Francesco Guinigi. Asked by a comrade what he would want in exchange for letting himself be slapped, Castruccio replied, as did Diogenes, “a helmet.” As a youth, Machiavelli shows, Castruccio had learned the importance of being able to defend himself from harm inflicted by others. That lesson led him to engage in politics—in contrast to the cynical philosophers whose sayings he had apparently absorbed. The first saying derived from Diogenes is thus followed by the only saying attributable to Castruccio himself (by Tegrimi). When he put to death a citizen of Lucca who had contributed to his greatness, Castruccio was told that it was wrong to kill one of his old friends, whereupon he replied that he had killed a new enemy. As Machiavelli points out in D 1.28–30, it is not possible for a prince to be grateful to those who have served him, because his best “servants” become competitors for rule.

In the next saying borrowed from Diogenes, Machiavelli has Castruccio praise men who take women and do not marry them and those who say that they are going to travel by sea, but do not; that is, he praises adulterers and liars. Castruccio does not go on, however, as Diogenes does in the same maxim (6.29), to praise those who thought about engaging in politics, but did not, those who purposed to rear a family, but did not, and those who made ready to live with potentates (dunastais), but never came near them. Castruccio clearly took pleasure in women he did not marry and often lied about his intentions, but he just as obviously went into politics and associated with potentates. The young Lucchan tyrant understood his political power to be a means of satisfying his own desires and thus bringing him pleasure. He did not understand the way in which political power becomes a burden that requires a ruler to exercise a certain amount of self-restraint. Both Machiavelli and the ancient philosophers whose sayings he steals from did.

To be sure, in repeating the sayings of Aristippus and Diogenes, Machiavelli has Castruccio omit the explicitly antipolitical parts. Castruccio was proud of his political position and certainly did not want to disavow it. He apparently did not understand the connection between the ancient philosophers’ caustic comments about conventional morality and their withdrawal from politics. Having done little reading as a youth, he does not seem to have been aware of the exchange Xenophon reports in his Memorabilia (2.1) between Socrates and Aristippus in which Socrates gets Aristippus to agree that a ruler needs to be virtuous, but Aristippus responds by arguing that he himself does not have to be virtuous, because he does not want to be a ruler, who would have to assume the burden of caring for others. When Socrates objects that if he does not rule, he will be ruled, Aristippus concedes that he does not want to be a slave, but he thinks that he can avoid becoming dominated by anyone else by traveling from city to city. Aristippus may have thus made himself vulnerable to attack, as Socrates suggests, but his stance was clearly antipolitical and thus antithetical to Castruccio’s own position and ambitions. Although Castruccio told Pagolo that it is important to know oneself, i.e., to have an accurate understanding of one’s own circumstances and abilities, Machiavelli suggests that Castruccio himself did not.

By repeating the sayings of these antipolitical philosophers, Castruccio showed not merely that he did not understand the tension between their understanding of the world or nature and his own political concerns. By accepting, without resentment, such caustic statements made to him by others, Castruccio also showed that he did not understand one of the basic requirements of his own position, the need for a prince to maintain a certain kind of public position or front. In P 23 Machiavelli observes: “There is no other way to guard oneself from flattery unless men understand that they do not offend you in telling you the truth; but when everyone can tell you the truth, they lack reverence for you” (93–94). Castruccio accepted the biting statements made by others, because he hated flatterers. He did not understand the need to insist that others revere him any more than he understood the need for a prince to appear to be reverent himself.

In other words, Castruccio did not understand why a prince, who cannot always be merciful, honest, humane, and religious, must nevertheless always seek to appear to be so, especially to be religious. When asked whether, to save his soul, he had thought of becoming a friar, Castruccio said, “No, because it seemed strange to him that Brother Lazarus should go to paradise and Uguccione della Faggiuola to hell” (107–8). Uncharacteristically seeming to recognize political excellence and achievements, Diogenes had said: “Would it not be ludicrous, if Agesilaus and Epaminondas were to dwell in mire, but certain folk of no account live in the isles of the Blessed, because they have been initiated” (6.40).44 In protesting the descent of his former protector and enemy, Castruccio displays the same indifference to distinctions of friend and enemy in the netherworld that Diogenes did by grouping Agesilaus and Epaminondas together. More important, Castruccio expresses the same doubt about the justice, if not existence, of a God or gods who would reward the undistinguished and punish the eminent and active.45 It is not that Castruccio (or Diogenes) thought that social rank per se should be respected. In other sayings both Castruccio and his source recognize the emptiness if not damaging results of conventional hierarchies, e.g., between master and servant, and other forms of pretentious behavior like big gates for small houses or cities. Machiavelli seems to underline the fundamental point in the last saying quoted, in which Castruccio and Diogenes agree that a wise man would not fear death or, therefore, the king who threatens him with death, if that king claims to be good. Neither the Lucchan tyrant nor the cynic philosopher believed that justice would be done or that people should trust that it would be done in the life hereafter.


Machiavelli as Both a Follower and a Critic of Socrates


Strauss suggests that in relating Castruccio’s embrace and restatement of the sayings of these “unsung and undignified” atheistic philosophers Machiavelli is relating his own innermost thought in an ironical manner (TM, 224–25). By attributing the maxims to Castruccio, Machiavelli evades responsibility for restating them while nevertheless repeating them. But the “innermost” thought Strauss attributes to Machiavelli goes beyond a declaration of atheism and a desire to protect himself from persecution for that atheism. By placing the one statement from Aristotle between two pairs of sayings of the infamous atheist Bion, Machiavelli points “to a thought at the center of which Aristotle is kept in bonds or overwhelmed by Bion.” And that thought goes far beyond the atheism of Bion as well as the contempt for convention exhibited by Aristippus and Diogenes (whose sayings surround those taken from Bion). “In contradistinction to Aristippus and Diogenes, Machiavelli is a political philosopher, a man concerned with the good society; but he understands the good society by starting from the conventionalist assumption, from the premise of extreme individualism: man is not by nature . . . directed toward political society.” And Strauss concludes, “Machiavelli achieves a synthesis of the two classical traditions . . . by going over to a new plane from the plane on which all classical thought moved.”46

What was that “synthesis” and “new plane”? In marked contrast to Aristotle, but like Aristippus and Diogenes, we have seen in both the Prince and Discourses, Machiavelli denies that human beings are by nature political. Their fear and consequent desire to acquire naturally bring them into conflict; and when they no longer fight from necessity, they fight from ambition. As Machiavelli emphasizes in his treatment of the early Roman kings in D 3.2–6, both erotic and familial affection give way to a much stronger desire for domination. However, in contrast to Aristippus and Diogenes as well as Aristotle, Machiavelli does not take nature as a standard or guide to the best human life. He is not a hedonist like Aristippus who seeks to maximize his pleasure (or minimize his pain) or an anticonventionalist who, like Diogenes, seeks to live solely in accord with nature. Machiavelli seeks to show his readers how, using their intelligence and experience, they can discover conventions or laws, i.e., a political order, that will enable most if not all human beings to overcome their natural condition of scarcity and weakness and feel secure in their lives, families or honor, and properties. The “new plane” upon which Machiavelli creates a synthesis of the two classical traditions is a new conception of nature, as hostile to human happiness but a source of “matter” (P 6) to be shaped, directed, and trained by means of a human “art,” the political art, to improve the human condition.

Machiavelli’s own words and deeds often appeared to be as irreligious and immoral as Castruccio’s. He once infamously wrote that he cared more about his fatherland than his soul; he was not often seen in church; and he was known to have engaged in many extramarital affairs.47 Unlike Castruccio, however, Machiavelli was keenly aware of the political power and uses of religion. In P 18 he tells his reader that an effective ruler cannot always be religious, especially if he is a new ruler, but that he must always seek to appear to be so. And in D 1.11–15 he praises the Roman Senate’s prudent use of religion to deceive and control the plebs. He suggests (D 2.2) that it is their Christian education that has made modern men unable to establish and defend free political regimes. He is particularly critical of the founders of the monastic orders (D 3.1): by teaching their followers not to expect justice in this world but to seek it only in the next, he argues, the monks have left the world to be plundered and ruled by the wicked. In the case both of the monastic orders and of the teachings they propagated, Machiavelli is especially critical of the combination of Christianity with contemplative philosophy. In D 2.2 he explicitly states that the feminizing results of the Christian religion are products of a particular, pernicious interpretation. As Machiavelli indicated in his description of King Ferdinand of Spain in P 21 (and the fact of the Crusades shows more generally), Christianity could be interpreted differently so that it would be not merely compatible with but supportive of political and military orders.48

The one form of human activity to which Machiavelli consistently shows indifference, if not outright hostility, is contemplative philosophy. As Strauss points out, Machiavelli refers on more than one occasion to Xenophon’s political writings, but never to his depiction of Socrates as the philosophical alternative to the political life. However, Machiavelli’s complete silence with regard to Socrates (as opposed to his admittedly infrequent explicit references to Plato and Aristotle) appears to have a somewhat ambiguous meaning, because Machiavelli himself is in some respects surprisingly like Socrates.49

By attributing the sayings of the non-Platonic Socratics to Castruccio, Machiavelli reminds his more thoughtful readers that like the Socrates depicted by Xenophon and Plato, he concentrates on “the human things.” In the relatively infrequent statements he makes about the cosmos or the order of things as a whole, he sometimes (e.g., D 3.1) appears to be an Epicurean who thinks that everything comes into being and passes away,50 but he also sometimes appears to adhere to a decayed form of Aristotelianism, as when he observes in D 1.Pref. that the heavens, sun, elements, and men have not varied in motion, order, and power from what they were in antiquity.51 For Machiavelli these are neither the most important nor the most pressing questions. Rather than investigating the motions of the heavenly bodies, like Xenophon’s Socrates (Memorabilia 1.1.11) Machiavelli insists that human beings need to learn first and foremost about themselves, by reading history and reflecting on their own experiences. Basic human passions like fear and the desire to acquire cannot be entirely repressed, much less eradicated; but once recognized for what they are and their strength acknowledged, these passions can be redirected to have less destructive if not more productive results.

Further like Socrates, Machiavelli seeks primarily to educate the young. Recognizing that individual human beings have different natural inclinations (like Castruccio for the military rather than the priesthood), but that human beings are also shaped decisively by their experience (P 4–5, 25; D 3.9), he seeks to affect their opinions and behavior before they harden and become unalterable. Like Socrates and his students, Plato and Xenophon, Machiavelli recognizes that politically ambitious young men do not like to be told what to think. Rather than deliver his “teaching” in the form of a straightforward treatise, he thus presents his understanding of “the human things” indirectly and somewhat playfully in a variety of literary modes—advice to a prince, discourses on an ancient text, comedies, poems, a dialogue, biography, and a civic history. Just as Socrates was reputedly able to make up stories to entertain, engage, and thus indirectly instruct his young friends (Phaedrus 275b), so Machiavelli repeatedly showed himself willing to alter history or imagine “new cases” in an attempt to teach his young friends both the harsh truths and the exciting potential of political life.

Machiavelli emphasizes both the fictional and the playful character of his version of the Life of Castruccio Castracani, for example, by returning at the end to the role of fortune that he emphasized at the beginning. Noting that Castruccio died at age forty-four, Machiavelli adds, “since, in his lifetime, he was not inferior to Philip of Macedon, father of Alexander, nor to Scipio of Rome, he died at the same age they both did; and without doubt he would have surpassed the one and the other if, instead of Lucca, his fatherland had been Macedonia or Rome” (109). Machiavelli thus concludes by echoing Castruccio’s self-description and apology, as related by Tegrimi. It is hard to believe, however, that Machiavelli did not know that Castruccio actually died at age 47, Philip at 50, and Scipio at 46.52 As we have seen, Machiavelli falsified the historical record in many ways in order to show the ways in which Castruccio was inferior to these ancient military and political leaders, both monarchical and republican.

Although he resembled Socrates in the focus and mode of his teaching, Machiavelli never mentioned his famous predecessor by name, because he disagreed with Socrates about the answer to the most fundamental question: what is the best form of human existence. According to Socrates, it is philosophy. According to Machiavelli, human beings not merely must but should engage in politics. So if Machiavelli like Socrates sought particularly to persuade the young, the appeal was fundamentally different. Whereas Socrates tried to persuade young ambitious Athenians such as Alcibiades, Critias, and Plato to withdraw from politics in order to seek wisdom with him in private conversations, Machiavelli attempted to show his young ambitious friends how they could and should complete the political project he had begun but did not have the good fortune to be able to complete (D 2.Pref.). His works are not simply or solely calls to action; he saw that his young friends needed to acquire the understanding he had achieved from many years of study and practical experience before they acted. He thus had to observe with some irony that they had not, as yet, acquired such an understanding.
