6


On the Evils Caused by Unchecked Eros


CLIZIA


Although the maxims attributed to Castruccio at the end of Machiavelli’s account of his Life point to both the similarities and the differences between Machiavelli and Socrates, they do not bring out the root of the difference. Because all the students of Socrates whose sayings “Castruccio” modified and quoted dismissed the transcendent ideas, they did not embody or celebrate the eros that, according to Plato’s Diotima, not only moves philosophers to seek wisdom but also leads them to acquire all the other virtues as a result.1 But in a comedy he wrote four years later, Machiavelli indicated the reasons why he thought that eros—not merely sexual, but also in its more transcendent forms—needs to be controlled and disciplined by lower, more worldly concerns for reputation and wealth, if human beings are to live and prosper.

The commission Machiavelli received to write a history of Florence in the fall of 1520 was initially for two years, and later extended. But in 1524 he took a short break or respite from working on his last major prose work. Instead of directing a new production of Mandragola, he volunteered to write a new comedy to be put on at the villa of Jacopo Falconetti (known as “Fornaciaio” [the baker]) where he occasionally supped with a young singer named Barbera Salutati Raffacani. Because that comedy dramatizes the shaming of an old man named “Nicomaco” who falls head over heels in love with a young girl, Machiavelli’s friends understood him to be making fun of himself.2 They did not see the way in which the changes Machiavelli made in his ancient Roman source pointed to the reasons Machiavelli rejected both pagan and scriptural understandings of the best form of human existence.

Although the plot of Mandragola constitutes a comic retelling of the tragic story of Lucretia, in the prologue to that comedy Machiavelli emphasizes that he is presenting a new caso—case or cause—in Florence; and in that comedy he depicts a new kind of “remedy” for the conflicts in private life caused by human desires. Machiavelli begins the prologue to Clizia, however, by emphasizing the continuities in human beings and their behavior over time.3 In this comedy he says that he is presenting a “case” that occurred long ago in Athens, but more recently in Florence, and that he is presenting it in Italian rather than Greek and in Florence rather than Athens so that his audience can understand it. The more learned members of his audience would have recognized that Machiavelli had taken the plot more immediately from a Roman comedy written in the second century BC that had been staged again in Renaissance Florence. They would have known that at the beginning of Casina Plautus explains that he has taken and reworked the plot of a Greek comedy by Diphilus entitled Clerumenoe (The Lot Throwers [which has been lost]).4 Those who had read D 2.5 would also have known that Machiavelli connected changes in language to changes in religion, and that he claimed that the only reason Christians had preserved rather than destroyed all vestiges of pagan religion was that they had continued to use Latin. By referring both to the continuities in human life and the changes he has made in his ancient source, in the prologue to Clizia Machiavelli thus raises the question of what has changed and what has stayed the same—as well as the question of what “remedy” to adopt for a recurring “case” or problem.

Machiavelli brings out the recurrent elements of the story and its denouement in his initial statement of the plot: “There was a gentleman who had no children other than a boy, into whose house there chanced to arrive a little girl who, up to the age of seventeen, was raised by him in a very decent fashion. Then it happened that all at once both he and his son fell in love with her; and in the competition of this love there arose many events and strange accidents, upon whose passing the son took her as a wife and lived with her very happily for a long time” (3). What remains the same, Machiavelli thus suggests, is that there is competition between fathers and sons (or generations), and that that competition can be solved or overcome only by marrying sons to women from outside the family, thus creating the conditions for rearing new generations.5

The changes Machiavelli made to his sources that extend beyond the language and location begin to become evident when he lists the characters in the order of their appearance. The names are derived from ancient Greek, but they do not correspond to the meaning of the names of the characters in his ancient source; and many are clearly ironic.6 The old man’s name, Nicomaco, comes from victory (nikê) and battle (machê). In the play he says that he wants to be victorious (1.1), but we see that he and his plans are defeated by his wife. Likewise his son’s name, Cleandro, refers to a gentleman (anêr, andros) who is celebrated by the muse Cleo or has fame (kleos), but we do not see the son display courage (andreia) or do anything else worthy of acclaim.7 In other words, neither father nor son lives up to his name, which then becomes ironic. The third character, Palamede, is a Machiavellian addition. The resourceful Greek hero Palamedes is said to have tricked Odysseus into coming to Troy. When Odysseus pretended to be mad by plowing salt into the earth, Palamedes placed Odysseus’s son Telemachus in front of the plow; but at Troy Odysseus took his revenge by arranging to have Palamedes killed. Machiavelli’s character listens to Cleandro’s complaints; but, perhaps having learned from his ancient namesake’s experience, he suggests merely that Cleandro try to delay the wedding and departs without offering to devise a “remedy” or any other specific assistance. The next two characters, Pirro, a servant, and Eustachio, a steward, correspond to the two slaves the husband and wife in the original Greek version of the comedy use to promote their respective plans for their son. The fact that Pirro and Eustachio are employees rather than slaves, as in the ancient comedies, points to a significant change that had occurred in the transition from antiquity to modernity; but Machiavelli does not comment on it.8 He simply lists the name of Nicomaco’s wife, Sofronia; yet here the change in the language becomes especially significant. At one point in the play Nicomaco says that she was well named, because in Italian Sofronia sounds like soffiona, which means bellows, and she is full of wind (2.3). In Greek, however, Sofronia would be related to sôphrosunê (moderation or sound-mindedness) and share the same root, -phron, with phronêsis (prudence or practical wisdom); and in the play her calculations of the best means and inventive “remedy” are shown to preserve the family’s reputation and future prosperity. The last characters named are Doria (referring perhaps to a captive of war who would have been a slave in ancient Greece), who is Sofronia’s maid, and Damone and Sostrata, neighbors who agree to help Nicomaco. Damone’s name could refer to daimôn, a demigod or demon; daimones are said in Plato’s Symposium to communicate between gods and men. In any case, he is a decent man who reluctantly assists his friend Nicomaco in his illicit love, but then happily tries to minimize the scandal and helps arrange the marriage at the end. His wife is named Sostrata, a conventional, generic name for a married woman in Italian comedies (and Lucrezia’s mother in Mandragola). The last character remains unnamed in the prologue, because we see at the end of the play that he enters as, in effect, a deus ex machina.

As Robert Faulkner observes, the names of the characters are not determinative, so we have to look at what happens to them, i.e., the plot.9 In both Casina and Clizia a chance revelation at the end of the play concerning the facts of the girl’s birth makes it possible for her to marry the son. In Casina the girl is found to be the daughter of her foster parents’ neighbors and thus a free-born Athenian citizen; in Clizia the girl’s father proves to be a wealthy Neapolitan gentleman named Ramondo, who arrives just in time to claim his daughter and give her in marriage to the son of the family who reared her. By implicitly contrasting the status of a free-born citizen of Athens with the Florentine couple’s stated concerns about noble birth and wealth, Machiavelli may be suggesting that not all the changes from antiquity have been improvements. Even when and where slavery is no longer legal, women can be hired out on terms hardly better; and in “republican” Florence, family background and wealth are deemed more important than common citizenship. No more than Casina is Clizia ever asked or consulted about whom she would prefer to marry (or bed).10 Whether or not she is legally free, the girl is not free to choose her mate.

Machiavelli points to the most significant changes he made on his ancient source, however, when he explains the title. His comedy “is called Clizia because this is the name of the young girl who is fought over.” But she will not appear on stage, “because Sofronia, who raised her, doesn’t want her to come outside for decency’s sake” (4). The absence of the title character could be viewed merely as a convention of the comic form Machiavelli was following. Casina did not appear on stage in Plautus’s play, because, as Ronald L. Martinez notes, “free-born Athenian maidens were not as a rule represented on stage; the unmarried women who do appear . . . are usually slaves or courtesans.” But by bringing the son, who is sent away by his father in Casina, on stage in Clizia, Machiavelli makes the invisibility and ultimate unattainability of the object of everyone’s desire much more pronounced.11 He also changes the motives of the mother in trying to frustrate the designs of her husband on the young girl. In Casina Cleostrata is insulted by Lysidamus’s desire for a younger woman as well as by his trying to take control of the fate of a young girl who is her responsibility, and she takes the part of her son. In Clizia Cleandro accuses Sofronia of opposing his father because she is jealous and envious; but she informs Cleandro in no uncertain terms that she will not allow him to bed their young charge—even if that should mean letting Nicomaco triumph. She nevertheless hopes to frustrate both their desires in order to maintain the reputation and prosperity of their household.

Machiavelli seems to identify himself and his intentions with Sofronia when he states that the author of this comedy is a very well-mannered man who adheres to established customs or conventions (uomo molto costumato). And by invoking the formal requirements of writing a comedy, the prologue to Clizia casts the work in a much different light than Machiavelli’s explicitly unconventional dedications cast his major political treatises. But the content or “message” of his comedy does not appear to be entirely conventional. In the first place, it ends with the man of the house agreeing to be ruled in all things by his wife.12 Because she devises a clever remedy to save the family from the potentially scandalous effects of Nicomaco’s passion, Sofronia appears to be the Machiavellian character par excellence, encompassing the roles of both Ligurio and Lucrezia in Mandragola. Second, when Machiavelli then admits that he may have been forced into some indecency by the need to make his audience laugh, “even if it is said in such a way that the women will be able to listen to it without blushing,” he prepares his audience for the climatic scene in which Nicomaco describes his punishment, which is both hilarious and completely obscene. Because it involves the threat of the rape of one male by another, as punishment for the one who intended to rape a young girl, and the women only hear about it rather than witness the deed, they need not be embarrassed. Yet as one commentator has suggested, Machiavelli leaves his greatest “indecency” implicit in the plot. If a reader describes Nicomaco’s scheme in general terms as the plan of a father who proposes to disown his “chosen” people (by sending his wife and her dowry back) and to sacrifice (the livelihood, if not life of) his only begotten son, in order to bed a virgin purportedly married to another man, the broader, blasphemous implications of Machiavelli’s comedy begin to become evident.13 Consumed by his mad passion or “love,” Nicomaco is also shown to be a tyrant who threatens to destroy those who have been nearest and dearest to him by burning down the house, if they do not obey his commands. In the New Testament it is said that “God so loved the world, that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him shall not perish” (John 3:16). And, as Saint Augustine emphasizes in the City of God (20–21), those who do not believe will be condemned to eternal damnation and torment in the fires of Hell.

In Mandragola Machiavelli showed that the desires of all the characters could be satisfied by devising a clever means or “remedy” that preserved the appearance of conventional morality and religion. Those desires were, however, for goods that are humanly attainable, if transitory—a son to carry on the family name, a young lover and the pleasure that love can bring, a loyal and obedient spouse, food and shelter, money for the poor, maintaining the reputation of the Church, and the satisfaction of seeing the pretensions of the wealthy exposed, if only in private. In Clizia he shows that the old man’s desire to be a young lover—again or, in principle, forever—not merely makes him look ridiculous. It is positively dangerous, because this desire is not only impossible to satisfy; it also undermines the basis of the household and the orderly accumulation and passing on of property. This unrealizable desire for immortality thus needs to be restrained and redirected into the more ordinary forms of living on—at least in name—through one’s progeny and reputation (or fame). That disciplining and redirecting cannot be achieved by the Church, because that institution depends ultimately on a belief in the possibility of eternal life. So when in an implicit reference to Mandragola Nicomaco suggests that he and Sofronia might appeal to Friar Timoteo to mediate their dispute, she dismisses the idea with laughter and scorn. Like Lucrezia, Sofronia talks and acts as if she is extremely pious. But like Lucrezia, Sofronia recognizes that the intensity of her husband’s desire to achieve a kind of immortality threatens to cause him to act in an extremely foolish way, and that he will not be restrained by any piety or fear of God. She perceives the need, therefore, to invent and employ purely secular means of dissuading him.14 In Clizia Machiavelli thus suggests that the potentially unrestrained eros of a male human being can be checked only by the equally fierce attachment a woman forms to the children she has borne and raised as well as to the household goods she seeks to conserve along with the family’s good name. But the “conventional” family order she restores is not based on claims about the physical or intellectual superiority of the male (ancient) or on pure “selfless” love and devotion (Christian) that underlie traditional notions of virtue and the conventions that correspond to them; it is based on a calculation of the arrangements and exchanges that best satisfy the various desires of all the members of the household—husband, wife, children, and servants.15

Insofar as it depends upon the son’s (or slave’s) overhearing the father explain how he plans to wed and bed the young girl that night, the resolution of the conflict between the mother and father in both Casina and Clizia might be said to depend upon chance. Machiavelli never claimed that virtù could entirely conquer God or fortune, however. (See P 25.) And in his comedy he shows that the wife takes action not merely to foil her husband, but to preserve the chastity of the young girl. (In Casina the wife demonstrates no such concern. She is angered by her husband’s denial of her own charms and invasion of her area of responsibility within the household, but she seeks to please her son by enabling him to satisfy his desire.) Sofronia acts more on the basis of her calculations of what is necessary to preserve the family as an economic and social unit and less on the basis of anger or affection. She considers her care for the young girl to have been an investment that she does not want to throw away by having the girl marry a good-for-nothing handsome rascal, any more than she wishes to see her son marry a woman without a dowry. She thus finds her son’s passion as dangerous to the family’s reputation and future prosperity as her husband’s, and seeks to defend the girl from the machinations of both by sending her away. The chance arrival of Clizia’s father Ramondo and the revelation that he is a wealthy Neapolitan gentleman at the end of the play make it possible for Cleandro to satisfy his passion decently by marrying Clizia with his parents’ blessing. But even if Clizia’s origins had not been fortunately revealed, Sofronia would have preserved the family’s reputation and prosperity, as she promised, by finding her son and her charge both suitable mates. In contrast to Casina, the happy resolution of the conflicts between the father and son and the husband and wife does not depend upon chance.

Machiavelli emphasizes the importance of relying on one’s own resources in solving problems in the very first exchange he presents between Cleandro and Palamede (a clear addition to the original plot). Cleandro asks Palamede why he is out and about so early, and Palamede answers simply that he has been taking care of some of his own business. Like Callimaco at the beginning of Mandragola, Cleandro then explains that he, too, is trying to take care of some “business.” However, because he finds that he needs “everyone’s assistance,” he will now reveal the passion that he has been keeping secret. Palamede responds by saying that there are three kinds of men that ought to be avoided: singers who don’t listen to what you have to say because they break into song, old men who duck into church to say prayers (because they are afraid of death), and lovers, because they not merely fill your ears with complaints, but arouse your compassion. He nevertheless agrees to listen to Cleandro, who then provides him and the audience with an explanation of his plight.

In 1494 when King Charles passed through Florence with a great army on his way to attack the Kingdom of Naples, Cleandro explains, a gentleman named Beltramo of Guascogna was billeted at their house.16 Unlike many of the French troops quartered in Florence, he treated his hosts well and they responded in kind. So after the army of King Charles was defeated in Naples and was in retreat, Beltramo sent them a five-year-old girl he had among his spoils for safekeeping. Since his mother and father had no other children, they fell in love with her—as did he. Indeed, when she got to be twelve years old, his parents began to keep their eyes on his hands and prevented him from even speaking to her. But that restriction merely redoubled his love.

Palamede asks: What does he want? To take her as a wife or mistress? And what prevents him from acting, since they are living under one roof? Cleandro explains that his father has also fallen in love with the young girl, everyone in the household knows it, and there is a great scandal. Palamede observes that (in implicit contrast to the Trojan War) the scandal ruins nothing but a household; but Cleandro adds that even if his father were not in love with Clizia, he would never grant her to him as a wife, because his father is avaricious and she doesn’t have a dowry. His father also worries that she may be of ignoble birth. Cleandro would take her any way possible, but his father has arranged for her to be married to a complaisant servant, Pirro, who will share her with him. His mother has forestalled her husband’s plan by sending another suitor into the field, their steward Eustachio; but Nicomaco is now pressing for the wedding to take place this evening. Palamede asks why it matters which servant she marries, and Cleandro explains that Pirro is a scoundrel who has always hated him. The implication is that Pirro will not grant him access to the girl, and that his father’s promise to buy Pirro a house and shop to make him rich threatens Cleandro’s inheritance.

Having listened as he promised, Palamede leaves to take care of his own business. In contrast to his ancient namesake, who was famous not only for snaring Odysseus and bringing him to Troy but also for inventing counting, currency, weights and measures, jokes, and dice, he neither offers nor invents any “remedy” for Cleandro’s plight. He counsels Cleandro simply to delay the wedding as best he can and to let his friend know if he wants something. Given the time pressure, such a request and the promised assistance would clearly come too late.

Forced to rely on his own resources, Cleandro has called Eustachio in from the country. But he discovers that the steward has been in hiding for fear of offending the father. Cleandro orders the steward to clean himself up so Clizia will not reject him, and then to wait in the church. Cleandro has to go home to see what his father is planning. The son recognizes that he alone does not have the resources to withstand his father. The contest between father and son thus becomes subordinate to the contest between father and mother.

Both father and mother initially claim to be acting for the sake of benefiting their young charge. When Nicomaco and Sofronia meet, she tells him that she is going to church, because she believes “that one ought to do good all the time”; and she suggests that they should continue doing the good they have begun—raising a beautiful girl—by not throwing her away. Nicomaco claims that he is benefiting the young girl by giving her to a handsome man, to whom he will also give the means of supporting her. But these claims about the beneficial intentions of both parents soon give rise to charges of wrongdoing. Sofronia accuses Nicomaco of unjustly taking from his son more than is fitting and giving their servant more than he deserves—and suggests that Nicomaco has another motive. He claims to be acting out of love toward two young people he has raised, but she points out that he also raised the steward. Nicomaco responds by asking her whether she wants to give the girl to someone without noble breeding who is accustomed to live in the country with cattle and sheep. She retorts that the girl will die of hunger with Pirro, who does nothing but eat, drink, and gamble, and that “noble breeding of men consists in having some virtù, knowing how to do something, as Eustachio knows, who’s accustomed to business in the markets, to managing the household, to caring for the affairs of others and himself” (2.3). Hers appears to be a very economically based, “middle-class” definition of human excellence; and she concludes by accusing her husband of wasting the money he has spent to feed the girl and his wife’s labor in raising her. She also threatens to raise a scandal. He suggests that her behavior is equally indecent, because she (like the wife in Casina) is favoring her son.

Recognizing that they are both concerned about maintaining appearances, Nicomaco proposes that they come to an agreement lest they become a comedy for the people watching. Since she is going to church, he suggests that they ask their family confessor, the friar Timoteo, to mediate, because he “has already accomplished a miracle. . . . Through his prayers Madonna Lucrezia, wife of Messer Nicia Calfucci, who was sterile, got pregnant.” But Sofronia protests, “some great miracle, a friar making a woman pregnant! It would be a miracle if a nun had made her pregnant!” (2.3). So she goes off to mass while he waits for her at home.

In a soliloquy Machiavelli added to the original plot Sofronia describes the change his passion for the girl has wrought in Nicomaco. He used to be a “grave, stable and respectful man. . . . He got up early in the morning, heard his mass, provided for the day’s food. Then, if he had some business in the public square, at the market, with the magistrates, he did it; if not, either he met with some citizen for honorable discussions or he retired to his study at home, where he balanced his ledger. Later he dined peacefully with his company and . . . held discussions with his son, offered him counsel . . . and, by means of some ancient and modern examples, taught him how to live.” He spent the rest of the day in equally grave and decent pastimes before he returned home, sat by the fire with his family, went into his study to look over his books, and then had a cheerful supper. “This arrangement of his life was an example to everyone else in the household” (2.4).17 After he contracted his fantastic love for the girl, however, Nicomaco neglected his business, went in and out of the house shouting, did not return for meals, and did not answer questions sensibly. The servants began to make fun of him, and his son lost all reverence for him.18

Nicomaco displays his mad rage when he confronts Cleandro in Sofronia’s absence. He threatens to throw his son into prison as well as to return Sofronia’s dowry and send her packing, because he intends to be the lord of his household. If they do not abide by his wishes and the wedding does not take place that night, he will burn the house down. He thus urges Cleandro to go and persuade his mother to come to an agreement. Cleandro bemoans his own plight as a lover who can look for support neither to his father nor to his mother, and shows in passing that he has not been very well educated when he says that he has “never heard it happen that someone had his own father as a rival” (3.2). (He has apparently never heard of Oedipus; if he had, he would know that his problem is not as singular as he thinks.)19 Cleandro then tells his mother about Nicomaco’s threats, and they agree that it is best that Clizia not be married to anyone at present.

Informed about the dangerous potential of her husband’s passion, Sofronia confronts Nicomaco for a second time; and after a bit of risqué bantering, they agree first to try to persuade their respective servants that they do not want to wed the girl. After that tack fails, they resort to drawing lots. Pirro wins, and Cleandro wonders in despair how his mother could have submitted such an important matter to chance. Echoing P 25, he complains that fortune is “customarily” a friend of young men (although he has not shown himself to have the characteristics—impetuosity, ferocity, and audacity—that lead her to love them). However, after he chances to overhear his father explain to Pirro how he plans to arrange the wedding and bedding that evening, Cleandro tells his mother; and she devises a remedy. (Fortune did not desert the young man, it seems, but it is his mother who acts.) She allows the wedding to go forward; but she sends her maid Doria with a report that Clizia is running around crazed with a dagger, threatening to kill both Pirro and Nicomaco. They agree to stay out of sight in the kitchen while she and her women disguise a manservant as the bride and send Clizia away to a convent. When Nicomaco takes the place of Pirro in the dark in the bedroom and tries to embrace his love, he finds himself not merely repulsed with force but threatened with rape by his male servant Siro.

While all the members of his household are convulsed with laughter, Nicomaco tells his neighbor Damone that he does not know how he will ever be able to overcome his eternal shame. Observing that as his wife, Sofronia will share his disgrace, Damone suggests that Nicomaco let himself be governed by her. She assures Nicomaco that she did not want to make him a joke; she orchestrated the tricks so that he would repent. If he does and returns to his old habits, she promises, “the matter won’t be made known,” and even if it is, “it’s customary to err and to be corrected” (5.3). He agrees to be governed by her, and she informs them all that Clizia will not be married to anyone—not to Cleandro, Pirro, or Eustachio. At that point Damone returns with the news that Clizia’s father has just arrived in Florence, that he is a Neapolitan gentleman, and that he is happy to see his daughter wed to the son of the couple who raised her.

Nicomaco’s shaming is the highlight and climax of the plot. But after we stop laughing and recover from our shock at the obscenity, we have to ask: What exactly is Nicomaco punished for? And why in this way? Sofronia assures him that she never wanted him to be a joke, and asks: “Aren’t you ashamed to have raised a young girl in your house with so much decency and in the manner that daughters of respectable people are raised, and then to want to marry her off to a wicked and useful servant just because he was content to have you lie with her? Did you really believe that you were dealing with the blind and with people who didn’t know how to put a stop to the indecency of your designs?” (5.3). She thus claims to be shaming him for endangering the reputation of the family and insulting her intelligence by imagining not merely that he could hoodwink her, but that she would not know how to foil his plans. Sofronia threatened Nicomaco with scandal before, however, and he told her that she was merely fortifying his resolution to have the wedding go forward. He arranged a legitimate cover for satisfying his passion in the sham marriage. Recognizing that she was also concerned about the honor of the household, he suggested that they find a peaceful way of resolving their differences—first by means of a mediator, then by persuading the servants not to go along with their respective schemes, or, finally, when that failed, by chance—and she agreed. The drawing of lots was emphasized in the title of the original Greek comedy; but, as Haig Patapan has pointed out, Machiavelli made a small change from the way in which the lots are drawn that had broader implications. Rather than having one drawing that the father’s servant wins, as in Casina, and resolving the dispute simply by chance, in Clizia the servants’ names are put on two slips for the first drawing, then a slip with Clizia’s name is put into the bowl with a blank for a second chance. Before the first drawing Nicomaco insists on praying to all the saints, in the name of God, for the name of his servant to be drawn—and loses. Then Sofronia prays to God for her husband to lose all hope, but her servant draws the blank, and Nicomaco declares that he has been brought back to life! Neither husband nor wife is favored by God, Machiavelli shows, and neither actually relies upon Him.20 Instead, each claims to have devised a “remedy,” if he or she should lose. We in the audience see that neither the threat of scandal nor piety is sufficient to restrain husband or wife from acting on the basis of their respective desires.

What, then, does each desire? And what restrains them? As Salvatore Di Maria observes, Nicomaco does not merely or simply want to have sex with Clizia. In his first soliloquy he admits that he himself is surprised by his passion and doesn’t really understand it. It does not appear to have been aroused by any of the particular characteristics of the supposed object of his love. In contrast to Callimaco’s praise of Lucrezia in Mandragola, we never hear Nicomaco extol Clizia’s beauty, intelligence, or good character. His concern appears almost exclusively to be in demonstrating to himself above all that he is still as sexually potent and powerful as any youth.21 He does not want to admit that at seventy years old (the expected span of life in the Bible [Psalms 90:10] and the age at which Socrates died), he is old and near to death. And he is willing to use both fraud (his agreement with Pirro and the sham wedding) and force (threatening to dismiss Eustachio and burn down his own house) to get what he wants.

Fearing the destructive consequences of his mad passion, Sofronia punishes Nicomaco by making him see that he cannot realize his desire. He cannot, because it is impossible for any human being to remain eternally young. Nicomaco is not as young or as physically vigorous as the young servant she has secretly put in Clizia’s place; and in struggling with that youth in the dark, he is defeated by force. By enlisting everyone else in the household in her conspiracy, she also shows Nicomaco that he cannot conceal from others either his decrepitude or his illicit desire to deny it. His supposed love for Clizia is shown to be for an illusory fantasy of his imagination (fantasia).

In the song with which the comedy concludes, it seems to be the author rather than the nymphs who tells the audience that through “this decent, humble example, this wise and noble teacher of our human life” has allowed them to “come to know what one ought to shun, what pursue, in order to ascend straight to heaven.” As we have seen, however, the “beautiful souls” who have listened have not learned to rely on God or His providence. And they certainly have not learned to keep faith—with God or each other. On the contrary, they have learned that they need to devise clever remedies to prevent men from acting irrationally on the basis of illusory fantasies or “loves” that would destroy the conventional ties of marriage and economic activities of the household. So, the author suggests, his audience may have heard a great deal more under a thin veil from which he hopes they will reap the profit. The transcendental goals or objects for which some men are willing to sacrifice everything else are the obstacles to gaining security and prosperity here and now.

A final problem nevertheless remains: why does “this wise and noble teacher” name the foolish old man who is the most immediate target of his lesson after himself? Once examined, the parallel Machiavelli’s contemporaries drew between his love for Barbera and Nicomaco’s passion for Clizia does not extend very far. Whereas Nicomaco tried, if unsuccessfully, to keep the means of satisfying his passion hidden beneath a decent cover, in writing Clizia Machiavelli was not merely broadcasting his own passion but mocking it. He had never tried to live the orderly, decent life of a Florentine man of business, and in writing comedies he was trying to provoke the laughter of his audience, not to avoid it. No more than Socrates (Gorgias 471e–474a) did he fear appearing ridiculous. He was not ashamed of living unconventionally, associating primarily with the young, or having been punished by the authorities. Nor, like both his foolish old male characters, Nicia Calfucci and Nicomaco, did he often attend mass. He may have had his “fantasies” or imagined objects of desire. One probable candidate was the unification of Italy, for which he had called in both The Prince and Discourses, and which is imaged, as it were, in the union of Florence with Naples at the end of Clizia.22 If so, Machiavelli also clearly saw that the realization of his dream would occur, if at all, only in the future under the leadership of the youths to whom he addressed his major works. He recognized, in other words, that the realization of his political dream would depend ultimately on chance. He himself did not have the resources or force necessary to bring it about. Serving at most as an advisor (D 3.35), he would not receive the credit or recognition he deserved for the discovery of a new basis and form of political order, whereas those who acted on the basis of his advice would become famous. Understanding, as his more God-fearing characters do not, that all human experience and thus all human knowledge is “worldly” and hence essentially transitory, he could not even be certain that the writings through which he tried to communicate his political understanding to later generations would last, or if his writings did endure, whether anyone in the future would grasp the wisdom he sought to convey “under a thin veil.” But he continued to try.

The first two repetitions celebrate the power of love, and the third the power of the “trick” or “remedy.” The differences occur in songs (at the end of act 2 in Clizia and act 3 in Mandragola) that emphasize the specific kinds of foolishness displayed by the older male protagonists (Nicia and Nicomaco). And there is no concluding song in Mandragola.


15 Martin Fleisher, “Trust and Deceit in Machiavelli’s Comedies,” Journal of the History of Ideas 227 (1996): 372, argues that the conflicts that threaten the order of the family in Clizia arise from three sets of conflicting desires, those of husband and wife, father and son, and mother and son, and that the order which emerges “is constituted by a dynamic set of relations which, more or less, satisfies the desires of its members.”


16 Machiavelli thus dates the beginning of the plot of Clizia at the same time as the beginning of the plot of Mandragola—the time of the French invasion and the destruction in its wake that showed that the military and political condition of Italy had deteriorated to such a point that it clearly needed to be remedied.


17 Because he instructs his son by means of “ancient and modern examples,” in his introduction to the Gallagher translation of Clizia, xiii, Robert Faulkner suggests that Nicomaco’s name refers to Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics. Nicomaco’s habits are not, however, those that produce the virtues Aristotle describes. In the version of “Clizia and the Enlightenment of Private Life” that Faulkner later published in Sullivan, Comedy and Tragedy of Machiavelli, 39–56, he continues to maintain that “the play takes aim especially at Greek philosophy in its Christian version. Consider Nicomaco. He is a respectable Christian gentleman who looks up to ‘ancient and modern examples’ for the instruction of his son. But his ancient virtue and modern religion prove no match for his passions” (42). Thus Faulkner concludes, “Nicomaco’s strange mixture of hypocritical moralism and uncontrolled passion might be Machiavelli’s little comment on the practicability of Aristotelian moral virtue as a disposition to select the ‘mean’” (202n38).


18 Some commentators have compared Sofronia’s account of her husband’s life with Machiavelli’s description of his daily routine in his famous letter to Vettori of December 10, 1513. See Martinez, “Valediction in Clizia,” 134n31; Ezio Raimondi, introduction to Niccolò Machiavelli, Mandragola, Clizia (Milan: Mursia, 1984), 47; Luigi Vanossi, “Situazione e sviluppo nel teatro machiavelliano,” in Vanossi et al., Lingua e strutture del teatro italiano del Rinascimento (Padua: Liviana,1970), 74; and Giulio Ferroni, Mutazione e riscontro nel teatro di Machiavelli e altri saggi sulla commedia del ’500 (Rome: Bulzoni, 1972), 111. The two “days” in the lives of these two men are, however, very different. Whereas Nicomaco led the life of a conventional Florentine merchant, Machiavelli’s day ranged from providing his own bare economic necessities to reading poetry, obtaining information about what was happening abroad from travelers, games and quarrels with “vermin” at the local inn, capped by four hours of study of the deeds of great men of the past—but with no mention of his care or concern for his family. If the old man somehow represents the author, it is not because of his daily routine.


19 The love that father and son feel for the girl who has been raised in their household as a daughter and sister carries overtones of incest, although, strictly speaking, there is none.


20 Patapan, “All’s Fair in Love and War,” 547–49.


21 Salvatore Di Maria, “Nicomaco and Sofronia: Fortune and Desire in Machiavelli’s ‘Clizia,’” Sixteenth Century Journal 14, no. 2 (1983): “Nicomaco himself is bewildered by the extent of his love for the young girl: ‘Is it yet possible,’ he wonders in II.1, ‘that I’m so much in love?’ In view of this confusion Nicomaco’s passion for the foundling cannot be dismissed as simply sensual” (208). “Giulio Ferroni notes that [Nicomaco’s] use of perfumes betrays the old man’s desire to be young. Spicy foods and aphrodisiacs serve the same function. . . . Nicomaco’s weapons, as he himself perceives them, are all meant to characterize him as young and vigorous. Such a—perhaps subconscious—desire is also inherent in the youthful company he is always seeking. . . . The unconscious nature of Nicomaco’s wish to appear young is particularly clear in II.1, when he laments his old age: ‘Oh God, this old age arrives with all (bad) defects! But [‘ma’] I’m not so old that I should not break a lance with Clizia.’ The adversative ma emphasizes Nicomaco’s refusal to succumb to old age and, at the same time, his determination to recover youth. . . . Thus, the girl is not a mere object of Nicomaco’s erotic passion but the symbol of youth, i.e., the real subject of his obsession. Pointedly, the function of Clizia as the abstract characterization of youth is underlined by the fact that she never appears on stage, thus reinforcing in the mind of the reader/spectator her role as a non-physical entity, as the ideal fostering Nicomaco’s desire” (209–10).


22 Patapan, “All’s Fair in Love and War,” 550.


7


The Failed Republic


FLORENTINE HISTORIES


Machiavelli had been attempting to obtain employment from the Medici from the time he was dismissed from office in 1512. In November 1520 he finally succeeded when Cardinal Giulio de’ Medici offered him a commission to write a history of Florence. Once he received the commission, however, he faced a serious problem. How was he going to be able to write a history of Florence that would celebrate the rise and rule of the Medici family, who had deprived his native city of its liberty along with his sage advice?1


Machiavelli’s Rhetorical Strategy


By the time that Machiavelli completed a volume of the Florentine Histories, Cardinal Giulio de’ Medici had become Pope Clement VII; and the letter of dedication with which he presented the volume to the pope in 1525 indicates the brilliant strategy he devised to solve his problem. By noting the pope’s explicit instructions to “write about the things done by [his] ancestors in . . . a mode . . . far from all flattery” (4), Machiavelli reminds his readers of the expectations his official sponsor and others had for such histories. They were to praise the great deeds of the past—and the most notable deeds of Florentines in the recent past were those of the Medici.2 However, recognizing that feigned praise is insulting, Machiavelli states his worry that he may seem to have disobeyed the pope’s injunction in “describing the goodness of Giovanni, the wisdom of Cosimo, the humanity of Piero, and the magnificence and prudence of Lorenzo.” Taking the facts from existing chronicles and narratives, as was the custom, Machiavelli explains that he found his sources full of praise for the Medici rulers. He has, therefore, reported the facts as they appeared to other observers. “If under those remarkable deeds of theirs was hidden an ambition contrary to the common utility, as some say” (4), Machiavelli claims not to know it. By reporting the suspicion of others, however, he raises the question.

As was also customary in the celebratory histories of the time, Machiavelli acknowledges that he has attributed speeches and thoughts to some of the major actors, but he has tried “to preserve the proper humor of the person speaking without any reservations.” After Machiavelli’s death Donato Giannotti wrote a letter in which he reported that Machiavelli had told him that he could “not write this History from when Cosimo took the state until Lorenzo’s death, as I would write it if I were free from all hesitations [respetti]. The actions will be true . . . ; only I shall not tell in what mode or by what means and tricks one arrives at so great a height. And whoever wants to learn this also may note very well what I will make his adversaries say, because that which I will not want to say myself, as from me, I will make his adversaries say.”3 Machiavelli does attribute views he presented in his own name in D 1.33 and 1.52 to an opponent of Cosimo, Niccolò da Uzzano, who warns his colleagues about the dangers of opposing a popular leader (FH 4.3, 4.27). But as Felix Gilbert points out, Machiavelli puts “the severest condemnation of the Medici regime” into the mouth of Piero Medici when he criticizes his own supporters for their arrogance and rapacity.4 One cannot simply equate the speeches of any individual or group with those of the author, because, as he says, he tries to present the relevant actors in character, both in speech and in deed.

Machiavelli indicates his own view of the events he reports not so much by commenting on them as by his selection and organization of his materials. In his letter of dedication he suggests that the volume he is presenting to Pope Clement is the first installment of a history that will bring him up to the present. But at the conclusion of his history, he explains that he has ended the present volume with the death of the Magnificent Lorenzo de’ Medici, because that “brought a change of form in Italy, and because the things that followed afterwards were higher and greater and are to be described in a higher and greater spirit.” By stating that he will describe “the expansion of the pontiffs and of the other principalities that governed Italy afterwards until the arrival of Charles VIII” (20), Machiavelli suggests that the “change of form” to which he refers was a result of the 1494 invasion by the French king. The “higher and greater” things that followed would have included the expulsion of the Medici and the reforms of the republic, first by Savonarola, and then under Soderini, as well as the reinstatement of the Medici in 1512. What the “higher and greater spirit” was with which Machiavelli would have had to describe them is not clear.5

What we do know is that the volume Machiavelli presented to Clement was carefully and tightly organized into eight books. (The division of civic histories into books with general introductions was also customary.) In the preface Machiavelli explains that he initially planned to begin his history in 1434, that is, at the time at which Cosimo de’ Medici triumphantly returned from exile and took control of the government of Florence. But then he discovered that his predecessors, Leonardo Bruni and Poggio Bracciolini, had described Florentine foreign affairs in some detail up until 1434, but that they had not described the civil discords and internal enmities. Yet, Machiavelli protests, it is the number and intensity of the internal divisions in Florence that distinguish it from all other republics, including preeminently Athens and Rome. “Most other republics . . . have been content with one division . . . between the nobles and the plebs. But in Florence the nobles were, first, divided among themselves; then the nobles and the people; and in the end the people and the plebs; and it happened many times that the winning party was divided in two. . . . Had Florence enjoyed such prosperity after it freed itself from the Empire as to have obtained a form of government to maintain it united,” he comments, “no republic either modern or ancient that would have been its superior” (FH Pref.; 7). Unlike his predecessors, Machiavelli will not simply be celebrating the history of his city; on the contrary, he will be showing the reasons why Florence was not able to become as great as Rome. To reveal the causes of the continuing divisions in Florence and the Florentines’ inability to devise a government capable of managing if not overcoming them, in the first four books of his history he will relate what happened inside the city up until 1434 in detail, but what happened outside only when necessary to knowledge of what happened inside. In the last four books he will describe what happened both inside and out.

As a result of this revised plan, Machiavelli makes the rise of the Medici regime the very center and climax of his history, thus recognizing the achievements of his sponsor’s ancestors. He makes that recognition more uniform and less qualified than it would otherwise have to be, moreover, by ending his history with the death of Lorenzo the Magnificent. Because he concludes his narrative in 1492, he does not have to treat the less obviously admirable expulsion of the Medici in 1494 or their reinstatement in 1512 with the support of a foreign army. However, by going back to the beginning of the city rather than the beginning of the Medici regime itself, Machiavelli also presents that regime as a result of antecedent conditions and the actions of others more than as the product of the virtue of its leaders. He suggests that Florence was distinguished, not so much by its wealth or the moderation of its merchant rulers and their ability to maintain the independence of the city in the face of foreign aggression (as Bruni argued), as by its internal divisions.

As in his Discourses, Machiavelli begins his Florentine Histories by emphasizing the connection between foreign and domestic policies and institutions. In FH 1, Machiavelli shows that Florence remained a free and independent city as long as it did not because of the virtue of its leaders or people so much as because of the weakness of the other powers with which it was competing in Italy. In FH 2 Machiavelli then traces the stages of the self-destruction of the Florentine nobility that left succeeding generations without an example of public-spirited, virtuous leadership. After the leaders of the people acquired complete control of the republic, he shows in FH 3, they first divided among themselves and then faced the opposition of the plebs. But after they put down the Ciompi rebellion, the leaders of the people again divided. As he observes in FH 4.1, “cities, and especially those not well ordered that are administered under the name of republic, frequently change their governments and their states not between liberty and servitude, as many believe, but between servitude and license. For only the name of freedom is extolled by the ministers of license, who are the men of the people, and by the ministers of servitude, who are the nobles, neither of them desiring to be subject either to the laws or to men.” To establish a long-lasting republic that truly deserves to be called free, a city needs to have a “wise, good, and powerful citizen” who institutes laws “by which these humors of the nobles and the men of the people are quieted or restrained.” By showing that unlike Rome, Florence never acquired such laws, Machiavelli, in effect, dramatizes the ineptness of its political leaders, both the Medici and their competitors.6

Machiavelli does not explicitly say whether it was virtue or fortune that enabled Cosimo to acquire complete power over the affairs of the Florentine people in 1434. He shows that Cosimo’s opponents made some serious errors of judgment, and that Cosimo acquired his power not by the “public” means Machiavelli argued in D 3.28 are necessary to maintain a free republic, but by the “private” means that enable a seemingly “merciful” leader to become a tyrant.7 In FH 5 and 6 Machiavelli indirectly points out the deleterious effects of Cosimo’s rule by describing the failures of Florentine foreign policy—failures that can, predictably for Machiavelli, be traced to the merchant ruler’s refusal to train and arm his own citizens lest they form an opposition to his control. (Cf. AW 1.58–61.) In FH 7 Machiavelli then shows that the failure of the Florentines to expand resulted in internal degeneration. He writes a eulogy in which he praises the liberality and prudence that enabled Cosimo to acquire and maintain his state for thirty-one years; but he also shows that Cosimo’s heirs began to suffer the effects of that liberality in ways he argued a prince would in P 16.

By relating the failure of three conspiracies to overturn the Medici in FH 7–8 Machiavelli also reminds his readers how difficult it is to reform a corrupt city. It is not sufficient to have noble intentions, like those of Stephen Porcari (FH 6.29), whose efforts were revealed and forestalled, because he publicized his desire to kill the pope and restore a Roman republic, or those of the three schoolboys in Milan, who succeeded in assassinating Galeazzo Visconti (FH 7.33–34) but were themselves caught and killed. As Machiavelli observed in D 3.6, those who conspire against a prince hope that the people will rise up and join them in establishing a new government, once the head of the old is killed. However, he shows repeatedly in his Florentine Histories, once corrupted, people will not fight to free themselves. The Medici acquired tyrannical power in Florence by ruthlessly suppressing all internal opposition and sought to expand their rule by building splendid edifices at home and using mercenary forces as well as money to extend their influence abroad. The French invasion in 1494 should have convinced all observers of the defective character of these policies. Yet no one was able to persuade the Medici, other Florentines, or, more broadly, other Italians to adopt fundamentally different republican “modes and orders.”

Machiavelli had certainly tried. Like the Art of War, Machiavelli’s Florentine Histories constitute a defense of his own proposals, not merely for the necessity of organizing one’s own arms or army, but for a new understanding of the way in which a city can gain and maintain its freedom by dramatizing the defective character of the old in the tragic history of his own city.8 In the first half of that history Machiavelli shows that it is not possible to maintain a republic if either or both of the two humors try to gain complete control of the city. As happened with the Decemvirs in Rome, such attempts culminated—twice—in the rise of a tyrant in Florence. In the second half of his history Machiavelli then shows that a tyrant does not necessarily arise with the use of arms or force. Cosimo de’ Medici and his heirs acquired tyrannical power in Florence by suppressing the opposition and benefiting individuals without the support of any army. But, Machiavelli also shows, it is possible to acquire and maintain control by benefiting individuals and private groups rather than the public as a whole only in the absence of an external threat. The use of such “merciful” means of ruling results not in peaceful coexistence and trade, moreover, so much as in corruption and tyranny. Unlike later modern liberal political philosophers such as Locke and Montesquieu, Machiavelli clearly does not think that commerce can or should substitute for military defense as a basis of republican politics.


Book 1: How the Barbarian Invasions and the Unintended Acquisition of Temporal Power by the Popes Resulted in the Division and Weakening of Italy


Machiavelli begins his history by describing the effects of the withdrawal of the Roman Empire to the east, because the withdrawal of imperial troops created the conditions under which Florence could declare its independence as a free city. By presenting this “general” history of events in Italy after the fall of Rome in 476 BCE, Machiavelli suggests that Florence was able to preserve its liberty less as a result of the virtue of its own leaders and citizens than because of the weakness of the other Italian powers.

Machiavelli first shows that the withdrawal of the empire left Italy open to barbarian invasions from the north. As in D 2.8, he explains that “the people who live in northern parts beyond the Rhine and the Danube rivers . . . often increase to such a multitude that it becomes necessary for a part of them to abandon their fathers’ lands and to seek new countries to inhabit” (9). Forced to seize the lands of others if they are to survive, such peoples make fierce combatants. Yet, as Machiavelli also reminded his readers in D 2.8, under the republic the Romans had withstood such attacks (as had the Germans and Hungarians in his time). At the very beginning of his Florentine Histories Machiavelli thus sets up the contrast between the present weakness of Italy and its more glorious Roman past that runs through the book. At the same time, Machiavelli shows that the problems of Italy stem from the failure of the Roman Empire to perform the first and most important function of any government, protecting its people and their property from external aggressors. No more than in his Discourses does Machiavelli allow his readers to conclude that ancient Rome was a perfect regime. On the contrary, he shows that Rome’s inability to maintain its dominion in the west was the first cause of the current disunion and weakness of Italy. By emphasizing the importance of defense as the first and most fundamental function of any government, he also points to the most obvious weakness of the later governments of Florence.

Responding to the need to defend themselves, the peoples of Italy reorganized into a variety of new polities. “Constrained by necessity,” he reports, the peoples of Aquileia, Monselice, Padua, Vicenza, and Verona all fled from Attila to the reefs and swamps around Rivo Alto. They “left very pleasant and fertile places to live in places that were sterile, deformed, and devoid of every comfort.” However, “because many peoples were brought together at a stroke, in a very short time they made those places not only habitable but delightful.” The Venetians thus demonstrated how much more powerful human industry and art are than nature (as Machiavelli maintained in D 1.1). These refugees “established laws and orders among themselves, and amidst so much ruin in Italy, they enjoyed security”; and they became prosperous and powerful. “As necessity had led them to live in the waters, so it forced them to think of how they could live decently when they had no use of the land; and going in their ships throughout the world, they filled their city with a variety of merchandise.” As long as “they lived in this form their name became terrible on the seas and venerated within Italy, so that in all the controversies that arose, they were most often the arbiters” (FH 1.29; 41).

The other peoples of Italy were not so fortunate. Left without protection, the people of Rome looked to the pope for leadership. And because he was unarmed, the pope sought the assistance of the French king. “Hence-forward,” Machiavelli emphasizes, “all the wars waged by the barbarians in Italy were for the most part caused by the pontiffs, and all the barbarians who invaded it were most often called in by them. This mode of proceeding continues still in our times; and it is this that has kept and keeps Italy disunited and infirm” (20, emphasis added).9

Charlemagne fundamentally altered the relation between the emperor and pope. Previously, the election of the pope had been confirmed by the Roman emperor. Because Charlemagne “judged that the pope as Vicar of God could not be judged by men,” he had the pope and the Roman people make him emperor. From this time forward the emperor needed the support of a pope to be elected. The pontiffs’ acquisition of power was by no means smooth or uncontested, however. Nor was it ever complete. After discords arose among the descendants of the French king, the empire moved from France to Germany; and the emperors began to compete with the popes for control of Italy. The Visconti used the opportunity created by the conflict between the adherents of the pope (Guelfs) and adherents of the emperor (Ghibellines) in Lombardy to establish a duchy in Milan.

The conflict among Charlemagne’s heirs also led some Normans to come to Italy. These Normans first occupied some towns in the Romagna, but their heirs took Sicily from the Saracens and later added it to Naples to form the Kingdom. From its beginning, the Kingdom thus became a prize and prey of foreign conquest.

The barbarian invasions resulted in a change not only in the government and princes of Italy, Machiavelli observes, but also in “the laws, the customs, the mode of life, the religion, the language, the dress, the names. . . . Once Caesars and Pompeys, [they] have become Peters, Johns, and Matthews.” One might suppose that the spread of the Christian religion throughout the empire indicated by these changes in names would have offered solace for the suffering caused by so many other changes. But the introduction of new religious beliefs and practices brought even greater disorder and violence. “Struggles among the Greek Church, the Roman Church, and the Church at Ravenna—and even more, the struggle between the heretical and the catholic sects—afflicted the world” (14–15). The adoption of the Christian religion did not improve the lives of the Italians; on the contrary, it exacerbated the divisions and conflict among them by insisting that there should be one and only one authoritative Church and creed.

Machiavelli shows that the popes had sufficient spiritual power to arouse popular opposition to a prince who defied them and to obtain the aid of external arms in defending them in Rome; but they did not have sufficient temporal power to unify Italy, much less all Christendom. Urban II seemed to be succeeding when he inspired a crusade against the infidels. Many kings, peoples, and private individuals contributed to this noble venture, and the Christians were initially successful in acquiring control of Asia Minor, Syria, and part of Egypt. Within a century, however, they were defeated by their own divisions and the virtue of the Saracen Saladin. And when the popes began trying to use their power to establish hereditary principalities for their “natural” sons, their ability to inflict “spiritual wounds” on their secular competitors for rule in Europe decreased.10

Instead of creating an opportunity for Italian cities to choose their own form of government, the competition between the popes and emperors resulted in the loss of liberty in most. Fearing that he had lost possession of Italy and that Emperor Ludwig might make himself lord there, Pope Benedict XII decided to make friends of all those who had usurped the towns that used to obey the emperor by issuing a decree that the tyrants of Lombardy could keep their towns with just titles. And the emperor, “seeing with how much liberality the pontiff had given away towns belonging to the Empire, so as not to be any less liberal with the things of others than the pope had been, gave to all the tyrants in the towns of the Church” the same just title “by imperial authority. . . . So that of the towns of the Church, few were left without a prince” (FH 1.30; 42).

Machiavelli concludes book 1 by describing the problematic results of the continuing battles over the succession to the Kingdom of Naples and the government of Rome, schisms in the Church, and Visconti murders of their close relations: “Queen Giovanna II held the kingdom of Naples; in the Marches, the Patrimony, and Romagna, some of the towns obeyed the Church, and some were held by their vicars or tyrants. . . . As for Lombardy, part obeyed Duke Filippo [Visconti] and part the Venetians. . . . The Florentines were lords of the greater part of Tuscany; only Lucca and Siena lived under their own laws.” And he emphasizes: “All these principal powers were not armed with arms of their own. Duke Filippo [the Visconti tyrant of Milan] shut up in his rooms and not letting himself be seen, directed his wars through commissioners; the Venetians, as they turned to the land, threw aside the arms that had made them glorious on the seas and, following the custom of the other Italians, administered their armies under the government of others. The pope, because arms did not befit him as a man of religion, and Queen Giovanna of Naples, because she was a woman, did from necessity what the others had done by bad choice.” As he explains in more detail in book 2, “the Florentines also obeyed the same necessities because, having eliminated their nobility by frequent divisions, the republic was left in the hands of men nurtured in trade and thus continued in the orders and fortune of the others.” Instead of being organized and directed by the major political powers, “the arms of Italy, therefore, were in the hands either of lesser princes or of men without a state [mercenary captains]; for the lesser princes, unmoved by any glory, wore them so as to live either more rich or more secure, and the others, nurtured in them since childhood and not knowing any other art, sought to be honored for them” (FH 1.39; 51).

By concluding book 1 with a description of the state of Italian arms that resulted from their relegation to “lesser princes” and men without a state, who seek not glory but wealth and power and have created “a sort of bond and understanding” that has reduced the art of war “to such vileness that any mediocre captain in whom only a shadow of ancient virtue has been reborn would have despised” (50), Machiavelli deflects readers’ attention from the reasons or causes such “arms” were employed.11 A thoughtful reader might agree that it would not have been appropriate for a pope to organize and lead an army (although Julius II did), but she would ask: what prevented one of the other major powers from using the “opportunity” created by the disunity in Italy to expand its dominion to the entire province? The implicit answer seems to be that the Kingdom of Naples and the duchy of Milan were imposed on their people by force, so that their people were not and perhaps could not be organized to defend them. These princes thus had to rely on the mercenary or auxiliary arms of others. And the “spiritual wounds” the popes were able to inflict on governments established by the emperors prevented them from organizing and maintaining the support of their people. Instead, the “liberal” exchanging by the pope and the emperor of towns officially controlled by the other legitimated the rule of tyrants in most. Only Venice, Florence, Lucca, and Siena survived as self-governing republics. But, Machiavelli suggests, the two larger cities were discouraged if not prevented from forming effective land armies by the commercial tastes and experiences of their leading citizens. Venice acquired an empire with the navy she was led to build “by necessity,” but lost it after it imitated the bad examples of its neighbors by employing mercenary forces in its attempt to acquire dominion on land as well as at sea. What then caused the frequent divisions in the Florentine republic that resulted in the elimination of the nobility and therewith its ability to expand its empire to encompass Tuscany, if not all of Italy? That is the question to which Machiavelli turns in book 2.


Book 2: The Self-Destruction of the Florentine Nobility


In book 2 Machiavelli shows how the Florentine nobles destroyed themselves by dividing into factions, each of which sought complete control of the government to the exclusion of all others. First they divided as a result of a private dispute, according to families; then into Guelfs and Ghibellines; next into white and black “Guelfs” after the Ghibellines were exiled; and, finally, into a party of “the great” which sought to deprive the people of all power and was opposed by “popular nobles” or “men of the people” like the Medici. Attempting to quell the violence, the Florentines repeatedly reformed their government; but the institutions they established were not strong enough to establish and maintain order. The selection of a ruling committee by lot for short terms made it difficult if not impossible for an individual leader to establish a government capable of enforcing the law, especially in the absence of public trials in front of popular juries. And the apparently evenhanded requirement that all of the chief magistrates be merchants resulted in the exclusion of the nobles. Like the Roman patricians in the final days of the republic (see D 1.37), the Florentine nobles concluded that they had to seize control of the government by force.

In the introductory chapter of book 2 Machiavelli states explicitly what was only implicit at the beginning of book 1—namely, that ancient republics and principalities protected themselves from barbarian invasions by establishing colonies whereas modern polities do not. These colonies served not only to defend the mother city, as he argued in P 3, but also to distribute people across the land more evenly, so that the population increased and more of the land was cultivated.

In describing the founding of Florence as a colony, however, Machiavelli acknowledges that the dependent status of a colony was not good for it. The Florentines were not able to do anything worthy of memory for the first twelve hundred years of their city’s existence. Because the city was founded as a colony of Rome, its citizens did not learn how to rule themselves. Moreover, they acquired the destructive habit of looking to foreigners to defend them.

The first cause of division in Florence was a feud that arose between noble families about a marriage. When a young noble jilted the woman to whom he was betrothed in order to marry the beautiful daughter of another wealthy family, the Uberti took their revenge by murdering the young man who had dishonored them by breaking his vow. What was initially a private affair thus became a source of public hostility. “This homicide divided the whole city, and . . . since these families were strong in houses, towers, and men, they fought for many years without one dislodging the other” (FH 2.3; 56, emphasis added).12 As Machiavelli argued in D 1.55, it is difficult if not impossible to establish and maintain a republic where gentlemen have their own castles and arms to defend them from the imposition of rule or laws by others.

The Uberti sought the help of the emperor in driving out their opponents, and what had been a local division became an extension of a broader conflict between the Ghibellines and the Guelfs. There were periodic attempts by men in the middle to reconcile the two parties and to institute a government that would provide Florence with a free way of life and the ability to defend itself. But these efforts were repeatedly defeated by members of the two parties, who sought foreign assistance to obtain control of the city. Unlike the ancient Romans in Ardea (D 3.27), neither the Holy Roman Emperor nor the head of the Roman Church was able to reestablish peace in the cities subject to his authority by killing the heads. The conflict in Florence thus continued until the Guelfs eliminated the Ghibellines by exiling them and expropriating their property. After the division between the parties of the nobles was settled, they began oppressing the people, who finally rebelled.

In relating the repeated attempts of “men of the middle who had credit with the people” to reunite the city, Machiavelli seems to agree with Aristotle’s contention in book 4 of his Politics that such “middlemen” seek the common good in a way that those seeking rule for themselves and their party alone do not. However, he also shows that, although these “men of the middle” understood the need to satisfy the opposed interests of the partisans and the people, they did not know how to design institutions that would achieve that goal. Their attempts to reform the government of the city were thus repeatedly foiled by the nobles, who refused to share power.

After the German emperor, who had helped the Ghibellines seize power in Florence, died, some of these men in the middle thought that it would be good to reunite the city by including all parties in the government, so they arranged to bring the Guelfs back. They divided the city into six parts and elected twelve citizens, two for each sixth, every year to govern it. To remove the causes of enmities or vendettas of the kind that had initially divided the city, they appointed two foreign judges (who would presumably not be attached to any particular family or party). And to provide for the common defense, “they established twelve banners within the city and seventy-six in the countryside and enrolled all the young men under them” (FH 2.5; 58). Even though Machiavelli criticized Florence for granting this power to a few foreigners in D 1.49, he praises the foreign policy of this government by observing that under it, the Florentines forced the people of Pisa, Arezzo, and Siena to league with them; they also took Volterra along with some other fortified places, and brought the inhabitants to Florence.13 (They thus followed a policy similar to that Machiavelli attributes to Rome in D 2.3–4, in acquiring the foundation of a Tuscan empire.)

However, because these campaigns were all undertaken at the behest of the Guelfs, the Ghibellines sought the first opportunity to retake the state. With the help of Manfred, who had made himself lord of the kingdom, they defeated the Guelfs and regained control of the city. But after Pope Clement called upon Charles of Anjou to seize the kingdom from Manfred, the exiled Guelfs sought to regain control of Florence. Responding to the Guelf threat, the Ghibellines decided to try to win over the people of Florence by returning some of the honors and authority they had taken from them, allowing them to elect thirty-six citizens to reform the state. Had the Ghibellines done so freely rather than pressed by an obvious necessity, Machiavelli comments, such a move might have been useful.14 As it was, at their first meeting the thirty-six divided the city into guilds, appointed a magistrate for each, and assigned every man to a banner under which to appear armed whenever the city might have need of it. When the Ghibellines decided to try to take back what they had given by using the force, the people were armed and able to repel them.

The armed people then “decided to reunite the city by calling back all the citizens, Ghibelline as well as Guelf” (FH 2.9; 61). But, once again, the “noble” parties could not live content. The Guelfs became so insolent that the Ghibellines fled without being driven out. The Florentines again reordered their state by electing twelve “good men” for terms of two months and creating three councils, one of eighty citizens, another of one hundred and eighty people, and a third of one hundred and twenty citizens from the people and nobles who were to make final decisions with regard to matters debated in the first two. But they destroyed the apparently balanced character of the new constitution by seizing the property of the Ghibellines, who had fled, and so strengthened the Guelfs. Later popes tried to reconcile the parties in Florence, but they were unable to do so.

To deprive the Ghibellines of their part in the government and to keep the powerful in check, in 1282 the magistrates and ensigns of the guild corporations decided to reorder the state again by substituting three citizens called “priors” for the fourteen governors who had been divided between the two parties. These priors were to serve for two months, and they “could be of the people and of the great, provided that they were merchants or practiced an art.” However, this apparently evenhanded requirement that all the chief magistrates be merchants “was the cause . . . of the ruin of the nobles, because through various accidents they were excluded from it by the people and afterwards crushed. In the beginning the nobles consented to it because they were not united”; then, because they “desired too much to take away the [entire] state . . . , they all lost it” (FH 2.11; 64).

The two humors “that are naturally wont to exist in all cities between the powerful and the people” had been repressed in Florence by fear of the Ghibellines. But when the Guelf and Ghibelline parties were almost eliminated, the nobles began injuring people without fear of the magistrates. Giano della Bella, “a man of very noble lineage but a lover of the freedom of the city, then inspired the heads of the guilds to reform the city. On his advice they decided to have the Gonfalonier reside with the Priors and that he should have four thousand men under his command. All the nobles were again deprived of the power to sit with the Signori; the accomplices of an offender were forced to pay the same penalty as he, and they made public report sufficient for passing judgment” (FH 2.13; 65). However, when a man of the people was killed in a brawl in which many nobles had taken part, and the Captain of the People first arrested one of the boldest, Messer Corso Donati, but then absolved him, the people rioted. Responding to the outbreak of violence, the nobles prepared to try to retake control of the government by force; but “some men of the people as well as of the nobles, along with certain men of religion of good repute, placed themselves in the middle to pacify them.” Echoing some of the lessons Machiavelli sought to teach readers of his Discourses, these men

reminded the nobles that their pride and their bad government were the cause of the honors taken from them and the laws made against them, that their taking up arms now to regain by force what they had allowed to be taken from them on account of their own disunion and their evil ways was nothing other than to wish to ruin their fatherland and to worsen their own condition; and they should remember that the people were far superior to them in number, riches, and hatred, and that the nobility by which it appeared to them that they were superior to others . . . would not be enough to defend them against so many.


They then warned the people

that it was not prudent always to want the ultimate victory, and that it was never a wise course to make men desperate [as the Gracchi had made the Roman nobles], because he who does not hope for good does not fear evil. They ought to think that nobility . . . had honored the city in war, and therefore it was neither a good nor a just thing to persecute it . . . ; that . . . the nobles bore easily their not enjoying the supreme magistracy, [but] they could not at all tolerate . . . the orders that had been made . . . to drive them out of their fatherland; . . . nor should they want to try the fortune of battle, trusting in their number, for many times it had been seen that the many were overcome by the few. (FH 2.14; 67)


Because the parties continued to suspect each other, however, they fortified themselves with towers and arms. To weaken the influence of the nobles further, the people reordered the state by restricting the number of “princes.” They also began an extensive building program, including a magnificent palace for the Signori and a public prison. “Never was our city in a greater and more prosperous state than in these times,” Machiavelli exults, “when it was replete with men, riches, and reputation; there were thirty thousand citizens skilled in arms, and those in the surrounding country side came to seventy thousand. All Tuscany, part as subjects and part as friends, obeyed it; and although there was some anger and suspicion between the nobles and the people, . . . everyone lived united in peace” (FH 2.15; 68).15

“If this peace had not been disturbed by new enmities within,” Machiavelli concludes, Florence “would not have had to fear those from the outside.” Once again, however, after a private feud caused a division between two noble families in Pistoia, it quickly spread to Florence.
