Because the heads of both parties—the Cerchi “Whites” and the Donati “Blacks”—were Guelfs, each appealed for help from the pope when the other became dominant. And in each case, the pope sent a legate who angrily interdicted the city after the party in power refused to reconcile with the other.16 (Unlike the armed people, the pope’s representative could not force them to reconcile.) So the internal fighting ceased only after the whites had been exiled and the ambitious leader of the blacks, Messer Corso Donati, was killed.17

But just as their internal divisions had been settled, the Florentines found themselves confronted with a series of new external Ghibelline threats. Following their bad old habits, the Florentines looked to a foreign power to defend them. Learning that Emperor Henry was coming into Italy with all the Florentine rebels he had promised to restore to their fatherland, the heads of the Florentine government asked King Robert of Sicily to help them; and when he refused to do so as a friend, they agreed to give him the city for five years in return for a promise to defend them.

Henry died just as his army reached Florence, so the city was saved from the emperor. But the king’s representatives were not as successful in defending the Florentines from attacks by the Ghibelline tyrants of Lucca; and they were cruel and rapacious in their treatment of the Florentines. So when King Robert’s lordship came to an end, the city revived its old magistracies, and this time “the great fear it had of Castruccio [who had become tyrant of Lucca] kept it united.” After he attacked Prato, the Florentines closed their shops and gathered together twenty thousand on foot and fifteen hundred on horse to help. Frightened by such a large force gathered together so speedily, Castruccio withdrew. The people and nobles of Florence then began to debate about whether they should pursue him, and the delay “gave the enemy time to retire safely” (FH 2.26; 81).

“As happens in all republics,” Machiavelli comments, “always after an unforeseen event some old laws are annulled and others are renewed” (FH 2.28; 82). Popular outrage at the failure of the Florentine army to pursue and defeat Castruccio led the Signoria to change the way in which its members were elected. The names of eligible citizens were put into a bag and every two months a new set of eight were drawn. New baggings had to be held, however, because many citizens doubted that their names had been put in. The Florentines then decided to put the names in for a longer time—every three to five years—to relieve the city of the annoyance and remove the cause of the tumults that arose at the creation of a new magistracy. They “did not understand the defects that were hidden under this small advantage” (FH 2.28; 83). Both the contents of the bags and the selection of the magistrates from them supposedly by lot could be rigged.

The bad effects of this reform did not become immediately evident, because the Florentines were preoccupied with foreign affairs. After Castruccio seized Pistoia in 1325, the Florentines decided to attack him before he acquired complete dominion over that city. They gathered twenty thousand foot soldiers and three thousand cavalry under leadership of Ramondo di Cardona. But having seen the city give itself to King Robert, this captain thought that if the Florentines felt the need, they would make him prince as well. So he procrastinated, while Castruccio built up his forces so that he was able to attack and defeat the Florentine army at Altopascio, where many Florentine citizens were killed along with Ramondo.18

After the destruction of their army by Castruccio, the Florentines were no longer able to man their own defense. Yet they had not “become so vile that they failed to provide large sums of money, hire men, and send to their friends for help.” The price was, however, their liberty. Because provisions alone would not suffice to protect them from a young and daring enemy like Castruccio, “they were forced to elect as their lord, Charles, . . . son of King Robert, if they wanted him to come to their defense.” Since Charles was fighting in Sicily, he sent Walter, a man of French birth and duke of Athens, to take possession of the city as vicar of the lord. During this first visit “his bearing was . . . so modest, and so contrary to his nature, that everyone loved him” (FH 2.30; 84).

The harsh effects of depending upon a foreigner to defend the city began to become evident after Charles had extracted double the fee of two hundred thousand florins to which the city had initially agreed. However, the Florentines again regained by good fortune what they had not been able to achieve with their own virtue. Although Castruccio had expanded his empire by seizing control of both Pisa and Pistoia, Castruccio died when he returned to Lucca, and Charles died in Naples.

In the absence of an external threat the powerful within the city began trying to increase their power. Not content to restrict the names in the bags from which magistrates were drawn and to select judges who would be favorable, they added a foreign Captain of the Guard and gave him authority over all the citizens. That captain injured some other nobles, and they conspired to seize control of the government. The conspiracy was revealed, “as always happens [in] conspiracies that allow an interval of time before their execution.” (Cf. D 3.6.) Many citizens met at the palace and demanded that the Signori call the people to arms; and seeing that they were discovered, the conspirators prepared to defend themselves with force. But one of the judges placed himself in the midst of the fighting; and “reverence for the man . . . made them lay down their arms . . . and listen” (FH 2.32; 88; cf. D 1.54). He convinced the conspirators of the danger they faced if they did not yield to the people and persuaded the Signori that they would not want to prevail with the blood of their citizens. They let the conspirators leave the city and return to their castles; but they later bought those castles and provided by law that no citizen could own a castle nearer than twenty miles to Florence. They thus created the conditions, according to Machiavelli in D 1.55, in which a republic can best be established and maintained.

No one in Florence knew how to take advantage of those conditions, however. Instead, Machiavelli observes, “it was not enough for those who were governing to have overcome the conspirators, but as men do almost always, the more authority they have, the worse they use it and the more insolent they become” (FH 2.32; 88). Rather than acknowledge the mistake they had made by appointing a tyrannous captain of the guard in the city, they elected another in the country. As a result people were so stirred up against all the nobles that they were prepared to sell the city in order to avenge themselves at the first opportunity.

This opportunity arose when the Florentines asked King Robert to help them in a war to acquire Lucca. He again sent them Walter, duke of Athens, who arrived just as the campaign had been lost. Seeing that the people were indignant, the twenty men they had appointed to conduct the war decided to elect a new captain; “and so that the people might still have cause to fear and that the duke of Athens might defend them with greater authority, they elected him first as protector, then as captain of their men-at-arms.” Seeking to subdue the people who had afflicted them, the great offered to help the duke take lordship over everything in the hope that he would then reward them. But rather than accept their support, the duke sought to increase his favor with the plebs by prosecuting those who had directed the war against Lucca and fined or condemned many others to exile. Everyone began to fear him; and he informed the Signori that they should grant him lordship, since the whole city consented to it. Seeing that they had no forces with which to withstand his men-at-arms, the Signori saw no remedy but to pray him to desist and to make his lordship less harsh. But the traditional arguments against tyranny—that he would have to use a great deal of force to enslave a city that was used to living free, that he would have no friends and thus no security, and that he would never be loved—did not move him.19 So the Signori agreed to gather the people in the plaza and by their authority to grant him lordship. The next day when they read the proposal to grant the duke lordship for one year, the multitude shouted, “For life!” (FH 2.35; 93).

As in Rome with the institution of the Decemvirs, Machiavelli shows, so in Florence the attempts of the nobles to seize complete control of the government and of the people to exclude the nobles entirely from it resulted in the creation of a tyrant. The duke dismantled the government of the republic. And “the severity and humanity that he had feigned were converted into arrogance and cruelty, whence many great citizens and popular nobles were either fined or killed, or tortured in new modes” (FH 2.94).

As he showed in the case of the Decemvirs, so Machiavelli shows in the case of the duke of Athens, the tyrant was brought down primarily as a result of his own errors. Unlike Appius, who understood how easily men can be corrupted, the duke “could not believe that the generous spirits usually found in the nobility could be content in obedience to him; so he turned to benefiting the plebs, thinking that with their favors and with foreign arms he could preserve the tyranny” (FH 2.36; 94). Like Appius, the duke did not understand that what particularly made the citizens of Florence indignant was the violence that he and his men did to the women. (Cf. P 19.) To show the people that he believed that he was loved, the duke had a man who “revealed that the Medici family with some others had conspired against him” put to death miserably without investigating the charges.20 He thus discouraged “those who might seek to warn him for his safety” and encouraged “those who might wish his ruin.” The number of the latter grew after the duke had the tongue of a man who complained about the heavy assessments he had levied on citizens cut out so cruelly that he died. “The city was accustomed to do and to speak about everything and with every license and could not bear to have its hands tied and its mouth sealed” (FH 2.36; 95). The great, the people, and the artisans all joined in a conspiracy to recover their freedom, and the duke was frightened by both the quality and the quantity of his opponents. He did not have a sufficient number of armed men to arrest and then put the conspirators to death, so he sent for outside forces while he made a list of three hundred citizens and had his sergeants summon them under color of wanting to consult with them. But his sending for the outside forces and summoning the individual who had first revealed the conspiracy frightened the citizens. The boldest refused to obey the summons, and having read the list of names, they sought each other out. Within three hours they had resolved to take up arms and call the people to freedom the next day. The fighting was fierce, but the duke and his forces were overcome.

The citizens first granted fourteen citizens, half from the great and half from the popular party, along with the bishop, authority to reform the state. They then sent foreign ambassadors to negotiate with the duke, but they would not agree to any settlement until he surrendered three men, two of whom the mob literally tore to pieces. “The multitude having purged itself with the blood of these two,” Machiavelli calmly comments (cf. D 1.7), the citizens escorted the duke and his men out of Florence to Cassentino where he formally renounced his lordship.21 Although he repeatedly shows that the people were willing to share power with the great, whereas the great were not willing to share power with the people, Machiavelli also describes the dysfunctional tendency of the people to riot and to take vengeance unjustly on certain individuals.

After some debate, an agreement was reached to divide the government between the great and the people; and Machiavelli observes: “The city would have settled down if the great had been content to live with that modesty which is required by civil life; but they acted in a contrary way” (emphasis added). The people “lamented that from one tyrant who had been eliminated a thousand had been born.” So they convinced the bishop to propose that the great should be content with taking part in the lower offices and leave the Signori exclusively to the people. When the great refused and withdrew to their homes, the people ran to the palace, armed and shouting. The remaining popular Signori then “reformed the councils so as to put the whole government in the will of the people” (FH 2.39; 100–101).

At that time, Machiavelli explains, Florence suffered from a great scarcity of grain, and in an incident reminiscent of Roman history (Spurius Cassius), Messer Andrea Strozzi thought that he could seize power by selling his wheat at a lower price than others. The Roman Senate had been able to persuade the uncorrupt Roman people to turn against the would-be tyrant (D 3.9); but, Machiavelli reports, in Florence many of its corrupt people gathered at Strozzi’s house to buy it (as he predicted in D 3.8 a corrupt people would). One morning Strozzi dared to mount his horse and call the people to arms. Having amassed more than four thousand men, he rode to the piazza of the Signori and asked them to open the palace. The Signori repulsed them, and Messer Andrea was barely able to save himself from the magistrates. It appeared that the Florentine republic was not entirely corrupt or unable to maintain itself.

However, in contrast to the Roman Senate, which had appointed a dictator to deal with the crises, the Florentine government, solely in the hands of the people, faced and used force against a crowd. And “this unforeseen event . . . gave hope to the great that they could compel the people. . . . They decided to arm themselves with every sort of help so as to regain by force, reasonably, that which had been unjustly taken from them by force” (FH 2.40; 102). But the people also armed, and, led by the Medici, they attacked and defeated the great.

Since he has repeatedly blamed the great for their arrogant attempts to gain freedom for themselves by oppressing others, it is surprising to see Machiavelli conclude book 2 by expressing regret for their demise. “The ruin of the nobles was so great . . . that they never again dared to take up arms against the people. . . . This was the cause by which Florence was stripped not only of its arms but of all generosity” (FH 2.42; 104).22 In book 3 he explains how and why.


Book 3: The Rise and Fall of a New Division between the Popular Nobles and the Plebs


Reflecting on the history he has just related, Machiavelli begins book 3 by declaring that “the grave and natural enmities that exist between the men of the people and the nobles, caused by the wish of the latter to command and the former not to obey, are the cause of all evils that arise in cities.” As he showed in his Discourses (see especially 1.7, 1.37, 3.27), the conflict between the two humors, if not regulated and channeled by laws that enable each humor to check the abuses of the other, always threatens to become a destructive civil war. Explicitly reintroducing the contrast between Florence and Rome he initiated in the preface, he observes that in Rome the enmities were resolved by debates that culminated in legislation, but in Florence the conflict between the two humors ended in fighting that resulted in the exile and deaths of many citizens. In Rome, he now adds, the tumults always increased military virtue, whereas in Florence they eliminated it altogether. However, he also points out that the conflict brought Rome from equality in the citizens to a very great inequality, while in Florence the conflict “reduced it from inequality to a wonderful equality” (FH 3.1; 105). In Rome the conflict thus culminated in the need to replace the republic with the rule of a single “prince,” whereas in Florence the conflict ended in establishing the conditions under which, Machiavelli argued in D 1.55, a republic could most easily be established.

Machiavelli initially seems to attribute the different results of the conflict between the two humors in the two republics to a difference in the desires of the two peoples: “The people of Rome desired to enjoy the highest honors together with the nobles, while the people of Florence fought to be alone in the government without the participation of the nobles; and that is why it came to the blood and exile of citizens, and the laws that were made afterwards were not for the common utility but were all ordered in favor of the conqueror.” For a time the leaders of the people of Rome became more virtuous, because they were competing with the nobles to hold the highest public offices (D 1.60). But in Florence, after the people forcibly denied the nobility any part in the government, “it was necessary for them . . . to be . . . similar to . . . the people in their conduct, spirit, and mode of living,” if they wanted to regain any part. “So the virtue in arms and the generosity of spirit that were in the nobility were eliminated, and in the people, where they never had been, they could not be rekindled; thus did Florence become ever more humble and abject.”23 In book 2 Machiavelli appeared to blame the intransigency of the Florentine nobles, who refused to share power with the people, for the troubled history of that republic. But at the beginning of book 3 he seems to be initiating a damning critique of the character and effects of the entirely popularly based polity and its leaders.

Machiavelli does not simply praise the mixed regime in Rome in contrast to the entirely popular polity of Florence, however. On the contrary, he points out that “whereas Rome, when its virtue was converted into arrogance, was reduced to such straits that it could not maintain itself without a prince, Florence arrived at the point that it could easily have been reordered in any form of government by a wise lawgiver” (FH 3.1; 105–6). The proximate results of the conflict between the two humors had been better in Rome, but the ultimate results could have been better in Florence than they had been in Rome—if anyone in power had known what to do. The problem in Florence was a lack of political understanding on the part of the “men of the people” (including, although Machiavelli does not say so explicitly here, the Medici).

In the Discourses Machiavelli argued that Rome had the good fortune of electing three virtuous kings in succession, and concluded in discussing the third that “if where there are men there are no soldiers, it arises through a defect of the prince and not through any other defect, either of the site or of nature” (D 1.21). Rome also had the good fortune of needing to defend its independence from neighboring cities; as a result both its people and its nobles learned to reward military virtue with honor, and there were many competitors. Because Florence had been established as a Roman colony, Machiavelli suggested at the beginning of Book 2, its citizens had not acquired the experience of governing or defending themselves. When an internal division arose between two sets of noble families, they looked to external arms to assist them; and that habit persisted even after the Ghibellines had been decisively defeated. Even worse, after their army was destroyed by Castruccio, the Florentines sought not merely to defend their own city but to acquire empire over others with foreign troops. There was no prince like Tullus who raised and trained a new army of Florentine citizens. Instead, like the Roman patricians and plebs in appointing the Decemvirs, the nobles and the people of Florence, in seeking to deprive the other humor of any power, made Walter, duke of Athens, a tyrant. However, Machiavelli shows, in contrast to the Roman senators who told the plebs what to demand and what not, and the tribune who persuaded them not to continue persecuting all patricians after they had brought down the tyrannical Appius (D 1.40–45), the Florentine nobles attempted to seize all power for themselves with force. It was not simply the difference in their historical experience or the more decent and just desires of the Roman people that were responsible for the different fates of the two republics. Because they had a superior understanding of political necessity, the Roman senators had preserved the liberty of the city for centuries by “temporizing” in various ways with the demands of the plebs; and the plebs had been able to demand an increasing role in the government because they were armed. Florence experienced a continuing failure of leadership, most particularly in the failure of its leaders to arm the people and to give them a part in the government.

The problem after the destruction of the nobility was not simply that the Florentines lost their arms. In fact, Machiavelli reports, both the city and many of its citizens saw a need to protect themselves from the mercenary soldiers hired by the pontiffs and emperors and then left in Italy at the end of their employment. But the families competing for control of the republic, the Albizzi and Ricci, did not join forces to form a citizen militia. These “men of the people” (the wealthy merchants who called themselves popolari) did not see their arms as means of protecting the republic from its enemies or of acquiring political power for themselves. Like the Roman generals who waged the civil war that brought down the republic, “each sought with greater diligence to acquire partisans. However, because the citizens had already attained such equality through the ruin of the great that the magistrates were more revered than they used to be in the past, they planned to prevail by the ordinary way and without private violence” (FH 3.2; 107).

Machiavelli has an anonymous representative of the people describe the disastrous results: Since Italy “extricated itself from under the forces of the empire, its cities have had no powerful check to restrain them and have ordered their states and governments so as not to be free but divided into sects.” With the fear of foreign domination gone, they no longer look to the pope for help. “Because religion and fear of God have been eliminated in all, an oath and faith given last only as long as they are useful.” And that use is primarily to deceive others, as when “the promoters and princes of parties give decent appearance to their intention and their end with a pious word.” They “are all enemies of freedom, [but] they oppress it under color of defending the state. . . . For the prize they desire to gain by victory is not the glory of having liberated the city but the satisfaction of having overcome others and of having usurped the principality of the city. . . . Hence orders and laws are made not for the public but for personal utility” (FH 3.5; 109–10).

This representative of the people asked the Signori to reform the government in order to rid Florence of these evils, and the magistrates granted fifty-six citizens authority to do so. However, this attempted reform did not work any better than those previously adopted. Echoing his observation in D 1.58 that princes may be better at designing and introducing new laws and orders, but peoples are much better at maintaining them, Machiavelli comments: “it is very true that most men are more apt to preserve a good order than to know how to find one for themselves. These citizens gave more thought to eliminating the present sects than to taking away the causes of future ones; so they achieved neither the one nor the other” (FH 3.5; 112). To put an end to the current conflict, they excluded the three leading members of both the warring families from all magistracies for three years, and forbade all citizens from entering the palace of the Signori unless the magistrates were sitting. The reformers intended to penalize both parties equally, but, in fact, they unintentionally favored the Albizzi at the expense of the Ricci, because the palace of the Guelf party was still open, and their adherents were able to gather and organize there.

Again, Machiavelli shows that the bad results of this reform were not immediately felt, because an external threat provoked the Florentines to take common action and temporarily to create an effective emergency government. When a legate of Pope Gregory XI refused to offer Florence succor in the midst of a famine, and instead sent a great army to conquer the city, “the Florentines, having no better remedy, gave his soldiers one hundred and thirty thousand florins and made them abandon the campaign.” The Florentines knew how to use money to deal with mercenaries; but, Machiavelli points out, “Wars begin at the will of anyone, but they do not end at anyone’s will” (FH 3.7; 113). The legate’s perfidy aroused the indignation of the Florentines, who not only made an alliance with Bernabò of Milan and all the other cities hostile to the Church, but also created a board of eight citizens to administer the war with authority to act without appeal and spend without rendering an account. Once the war had been won, however, the use of the plenary authority by the eight provoked a reaction against it.24

Fighting broke out in the streets of Florence after Salvestro de’ Medici was drawn as gonfalonier. “This man, born of a very noble popular family, could not bear that the people should be oppressed by a few powerful men.” He thus secretly resolved with some friends to pass a law “to renew the Orders of Justice against the great, to diminish the authority of the captains of the [Guelf] Party, and to” restore the hundreds of citizens who had been prohibited from seeking public office the full rights of citizens. To get the law enacted as expeditiously as possible, he had both the college (upper house) and the council (lower, more popular house) meet simultaneously. When the college refused to ratify the law, he excused himself and went to the council, where he threatened to resign. He protested that he had “been made a Gonfalonier not to be a judge of private causes, which had their own ordinary judges, but to watch over the state—to correct the insolence of the powerful and to temper those laws” which would ruin the republic. However, “the malignity of men so opposed his just enterprises that the way to doing good had been taken from him” (FH 3.9; 116). At this point members of the council began fighting among themselves, and, leaning out of the window, one of them called the people to arms.

“No one should make a change in a city believing that he can stop it at his convenience or regulate it in his mode,” Machiavelli warns.25 Salvestro intended to make a law that would put the city to rest, but “the humors set in motion had changed everyone so that the stores did not open, the citizens fortified themselves in their homes, many hid their movable goods in the monasteries and churches” (FH 3.10; 117), and various groups met to discuss what should be done. The next day the guilds brought out their banners and a large number of armed men assembled in the piazza. In the hope of calming everyone down, the council granted the Signori, Collegi, the Eight, the captains of the Party, and the guild syndics a general power to reform the state. But violence erupted almost immediately when “those of lesser quality” sacked and burned the house of one of the leading Guelfs. And once begun, the violence escalated.

“Because it is not enough for men to get back their own but they want also to seize what belongs to others and to get revenge,” Machiavelli explains, “those who put their hopes in disorders pointed out to the artisans that they would never be safe if their many enemies were not driven out and destroyed” (FH 3.11; 119). They appealed to “the hatred that the lesser people had for the rich citizens and princes of the guilds, since it did not appear to them that they had been satisfied for their labor as they believed they justly deserved” (FH 3.12; 121).26

According to Machiavelli, “one of the most daring and more experienced” men of the plebs conceded that if they were deliberating about whether to take up arms, he might favor the acceptance of quiet poverty rather than seek perilous gain. However, since they had already taken up arms and committed many crimes, they needed to think about the best way of avoiding punishment themselves and gaining more freedom from their past oppressors. They should involve as many people and make the rioting as widespread and destructive as possible, “because when many err no one is punished, and though small faults are punished, great and grave ones are rewarded.”27 Nor should they let themselves be restrained by either conscience or reverence for their “superiors.” “For all men, having had the same beginning, are equally ancient and have been made by nature in one mode. Strip all of us naked, you will see that we are alike; dress us in their clothes and them in ours, and without a doubt we shall appear noble and they ignoble, for only poverty and riches make us unequal.” And, he concluded, “where there is . . . fear of hunger and prison, there cannot and should not be fear of hell.” Their present position was neither desirable nor tenable; but they could be assured that “all those who come to great riches and great power have obtained them either by fraud or by force; and afterwards, to hide the ugliness of acquisition, they make it decent by applying the false title of earnings to things they have usurped by deceit or by violence.” The plebs, “therefore, should use force whenever the occasion for it is given to us; nor can a greater occasion be offered us by fortune than this one, when citizens are still disunited.” The speaker admitted that he was advocating a risky course of action, but he promised, either they would be “left princes of all the city” or they would “have so large a part of it” that not merely would their past errors be pardoned, but they would have the power to threaten their former oppressors with new injuries (FH 3.13; 122–23).

Machiavelli does not comment directly on what is the theoretically most interesting and radical argument about the foundations and nature of government to be found in the Florentine Histories. Instead he lets events speak for themselves. The plebs succeeded in seizing control of the republic by force when most of the armed men the Signori had ordered to defend them stayed home and the eighty who showed up quickly retreated when confronted with a thousand or more men with arms in the piazza. Far from demonstrating the equality of all men without clothes, however, Machiavelli reports that a scantily clad wool carder holding the sign of the gonfalonier of justice led the mob into the palace of the Signori and, having reached the audience chamber, turned to ask them what they wanted. They shouted that “they wanted him to be Gonfalonier and lord, and to govern them and the city however seemed best to him” (FH 3.16).28

Machiavelli consistently maintains that individuals are born with different inclinations and talents that are then shaped and hardened by their experience (P 25, D 3.9; 22). So he shows here that, despite his humble occupation and lack of education, Michele di Lando “accepted the lordship,” and “because he was a sagacious and prudent man who owed more to nature than to fortune, he resolved to quiet the city and stop the tumults. To keep the people busy and to give himself time to get in order, he commanded them to seek out one Ser Nuto,” the foreign sheriff appointed by the previous government, who would have punished them, and to bring him to the piazza, where, hung by one foot, his body was literally torn to bits by the crowd. Michele thus gave the people a means of venting their humor (cf. D 1.7), while he took the opportunity to reestablish law and order by having “it publicly commanded that no one burn or steal anything, and to frighten everyone, he had a gallows erected in the piazza.” He also began to reform the city by dismissing all the sitting magistrates of the guilds, both Signori and Collegi, and burning the old bags. Dividing the state into three parts, he redistributed the eight members of a newly created Signoria, taking “four from the lesser plebs as well as allocating two to the greater and two to the lesser guilds,” and made a new bagging. Finally he granted himself, Salvestro de’ Medici, and other friends of the plebs benefits, “not so much to compensate them for their deeds as that they might . . . defend him against envy” (FH 3.16; 127–28).29

However, Machiavelli shows, envy of this clearly extraordinary natural leader who emerged in a crisis could not be so easily overcome. (Cf. D 3.16, 30.) Because Michele had not delivered the state entirely into the hands of the plebs, but had shared power in it with the guilds, the mob took up arms again and came to the palace with new demands. Michele “censured the mode in which they made their demands and urged them to put down their arms.” Becoming indignant, the multitude “withdrew to Santa Maria Novella” where they created their own government. They then sent two envoys to demand that this government be recognized in order to obtain “what they wanted by force if they could not get it by accord.” Angered by their arrogance, and “mindful more of the rank he held than of his own condition,” Michele decided that he had to “check this extraordinary insolence with an extraordinary mode.” So he attacked the two envoys with the weapon at his side and had them imprisoned. Enraged by the treatment of their emissaries, the multitude marched on the palace. “Thinking that it would be more to his glory to attack others than to wait for the enemy within the walls and to have to flee,” Michele “decided to forestall it” (and so acted in marked contrast to the previous Signori who fled before the mob). Taking a different route in going to meet the mob than they had taken going to attack the palace, he turned around to attack them from the rear in the piazza and “conquered them.” Machiavelli concludes that “the tumults were settled solely by the virtue of the Gonfalonier,” who thus “deserves to be numbered among the few who have benefited their fatherland, for had his spirit been either malign or ambitious, the republic would have lost its freedom altogether and fallen under a greater tyranny than that of the duke of Athens. But his goodness never allowed a thought to enter his mind that might be contrary to the universal good; his prudence led him to conduct things in such a mode that many yielded to his party and others he was able to subdue with arms” (FH 3.17; 130).30

Despite his generous spirit, prudence, and goodness, Machiavelli nevertheless shows, Michele was not able to maintain his government for long. Somewhat ironically, his example not only led “the better guildsmen . . . to consider what ignominy it was for those who had overcome the pride of the great to have to bear the stench of the plebs”; it also showed them the means of freeing themselves. “When the new Signori assumed the magistracy, the piazza was found to be full of armed men.” They shouted that “they did not want any of the lesser people to be Signori.” The Signori then deprived the lesser guilds of their right to select or serve as two of the highest magistrates of the city, “except for Michele di Lando . . . and some others of better quality” (FH 3.18; 130).

The state divided between the popular nobles and the guildsmen of lesser quality “lasted for three years [1378–81]. Because those who governed lived with the greatest suspicion” (FH 3.18; 131) of further rebellions and attempts to seize control of the state, many individuals were accused and admonished, exiled, or sentenced to death unjustly and illegally. Following the execution of one of the popular nobles who had been leading the city, many groups thus took up arms.31 Two parliaments and several balìe (committees authorized to exercise all legislative and executive functions) were created to reform the city, and after much tumult, a government was established that deprived the lesser guilds of most of their share and allowed the party of the popular nobles to regain the state.

“This state was neither less injurious toward its citizens nor less oppressive in its beginnings than that of the plebs had been,” Machiavelli comments; “for many popular nobles who had been known defenders of the plebs were banished, together with a large number of the plebian chiefs, among whom was Michele di Lando” (FH 3.22; 135). Michele was not able to maintain his state, Machiavelli indicates, because he did not have enough experience with the perfidy of the “nobles.” He believed that they would protect him in exchange for benefits received and did not retain an organized group of followers in control of part of the government able to force the elite to include them.

New injuries brought new tumults, and the number of malcontents, both inside the city and out, grew. However, when some exiles conspired with some of the admonished living in the city to enter secretly, kill the head of the government, and call the people to arms, they found that no one followed. “Perceiving too late how dangerous it is to want to free a people who want in every mode to be enslaved,” they “despaired of their undertaking and retreated to the church of Santa Reparata,” where they were easily captured (FH 3.28; 143). It was not merely the “popular nobles” who had been corrupted under a government in which laws were passed solely in order to benefit the members of the party in power; the Florentine people had been corrupted by their example. Florence retained its independence, Machiavelli again shows, because of its good fortune, not the virtue of its leaders or citizens. The external powers that threatened to conquer it—Louis of France, Giovan Galeazzo Visconti of Milan, and Ladislas, king of Naples—all died before they could take advantage of their military victories.


Book 4: How a “Popular Noble” Acquired Tyrannical Power in Florence


Machiavelli begins book 4 with a summary reflection on the history he presented in book 3: “Cities, and especially those not well ordered that are administered under the name of republic, frequently change their governments . . . not between liberty and servitude, as many believe, but between servitude and license. For only the name of freedom is extolled by the ministers of license, who are the men of the people (popolari), and by the ministers of servitude, who are the nobles (nobili), neither of them desiring to be subject either to the laws or to men” (emphasis added). Some ancient republics had been fortunate enough to have a “wise, good, and powerful citizen” able to establish laws to quiet or restrain these humors of the nobles and men of the people. Such a “city can be called free and that state be judged stable.” Florence had not been so lucky; and in a republic without good laws, the state can “be maintained only by the virtue and fortune of a single man who can either fail by death or become useless because of his travails” (FH 4.1; 146; cf. D 1.10).

Applying this general observation to the government of Florence after 1381, Machiavelli observes that “the state that had its beginning in Florence with the death of Messer Giorgio Scali . . . was sustained first by the virtue of Messer Maso degli Albizzi, later by that of Niccolò da Uzzano.”32 But he shows that the deeds of the first and the prudent advice of the second served only to postpone the Medici family’s taking effective control of the state.

Taking revenge for the death of his grandfather Piero at the hands of the Alberti, Messer Maso managed to have the families who had headed the popular party—the Alberti, Ricci, and Medici—despoiled of men and riches by banishing, admonishing, and fining them. However, “because the humor of that party was shared by the greater part of the city, it could never be altogether eliminated.” Many men retained “a memory of injuries received and a desire to avenge them.” And “those popular nobles who governed the city peacefully made two errors that were the ruin of their state: one was that they became insolent through unbroken dominion; the other was that through the envy they had of each other, and through long possession of the state, they did not take the care they should have for whoever could offend them” (FH 4.2; 146–47). So it was that “they made the Medici family regain authority” (FH 4.3; 147).

Niccolò da Uzzano warned his colleagues about the dangers of fostering the reputation of Giovanni di Bicci de’ Medici, who, because he was “very rich and . . . of a kindly and humane nature, . . . was brought to the highest magistracy by the concession of those who were governing.” Most of the people were overjoyed, “since to the multitude it appeared that it had gained a defender” from those in power. It would be easy to block the rise of such an individual at the beginning, Niccolò told his party, but difficult to remedy if his rise were left unchecked. More envious of Niccolò’s reputation than fearful of Giovanni, his peers refused to listen.33

Niccolò’s colleagues did not see immediately how shortsighted they had been. Despite Giovanni’s opposition, Rinaldo degli Albizzi was able to persuade an assembly of many citizens to undertake a preemptive war against the duke of Milan. But after the Florentines were defeated, the people blamed the “great citizens” (cittadini grandi) who had argued in favor of war; and the committee appointed to create a new tax levied it primarily on the great. “Many of the first citizens . . . [concluded] that it was a necessity for them to take back the state, because their own lack of care had . . . made bold those who were used to being the heads of the multitude” (FH 4.8; 153). Rinaldo convened a secret meeting of these citizens, and Niccolò da Uzzano agreed that they should attempt to retake control of the government—if they could do so “without coming to an open division in the city” (FH 4.9; 154). That would not be possible, however, without Giovanni de’ Medici’s agreeing to their plans.

Giovanni did not agree. He warned Rinaldo against taking “authority from the people by means of your forces, . . . [because] the people will have become your enemy for this injury.” Instead he advised Rinaldo “to imitate his father, who, so as to get universal good will, lowered the price of salt, provided that anyone whose tax was less than half a florin might pay it or not as he saw fit, and that on the day the councils assembled, everyone might be safe from his creditors” (FH 4.10; 155). In other words, rather than trying to eliminate his competition and risk civil war by seizing control of the state by force, Giovanni advised Rinaldo to act the way Machiavelli had urged his Florentine readers in his Discourses (1.32; 51) to imitate the Romans: to compete for political office by gaining the favor of the multitude and passing laws that benefited them. Instead of joining the great in opposing the tax that weighed so heavily on them, Giovanni openly praised it, since it “placed a partial restraint on the tyranny of the powerful, because they could not strike at lesser persons and by threats make them keep silent in the councils as they were able to do before” (FH 4.10; 159).

Machiavelli does not restrict his criticism to the powerful, however. “As it happens that men are never satisfied and, having got one thing, do not content themselves with that but desire something else,” he observes, “the people, not content with the equality in taxation that arose from the law, demanded that they return to time past to see how much less the powerful had paid” than those who had been forced to sell their possessions in order to pay the tax and make them pay the difference now. Giovanni de’ Medici managed to quiet these humors for the moment by pointing out that “it was not good to go back over things past, but rather to provide for the future; and if the taxes had been unjust in the past, they should thank God that a mode had been found to make them just” (FH 4.14; 159–60; cf. Machiavelli’s judgment of the Agrarian law in D 1.37). But Giovanni died soon thereafter. One virtuous individual is not enough to maintain a state, Machiavelli shows; he needs to establish institutions and laws that will last after he dies.

Feeling himself near death, Giovanni urged his sons Cosimo and Lorenzo to follow his example. With regard to the state Giovanni advised them, if they wished “to live secure, to accept from it as much as is given to you by laws and by men. This will bring you neither envy nor danger, since it is what a man takes himself, not what is given to a man, that makes us hate him.” He had “never asked for honors yet had them all” (FH 4.16; 161).

However, Giovanni was not able merely by means of his example or admonitions to prevent his sons or political allies from seeking to acquire more power or wealth from their enemies. They wanted to enrich as well as to secure themselves by dominating others. So did the Florentine people. After they unexpectedly lost and then regained Volterra, and a mercenary captain employed by them captured two of the fortified places of the Lucchese, a great many wanted a campaign against Lucca to be undertaken. Machiavelli wryly comments: “That people who after ten years of peace had censured the war against Duke Filippo to defend their own city’s freedom now, after so much expense incurred and with such distress in the city, were demanding that a war be started . . . to seize the freedom of others; . . . so much more ready is the multitude to seize what belongs to others than to watch out for its own. . . . Men are moved so much more by the hope of acquiring than by the fear of losing, for loss is not believed in unless it is close, while acquisition, even though distant, is hoped for” (FH 4.18; 164).

Among the great citizens who favored the war were the Medici, who were joined by Rinaldo. He pointed out the profit to be gained from the acquisition as well as the ease of acquiring it. None of the other Italian powers were apt to interfere, since at the end of the last war Lucca had been left to the Florentines as booty by the Venetians and Duke Filippo, and the pope was involved with affairs elsewhere. The citizens of Lucca were not apt to put up much resistance, moreover, because they were slave to one of its citizens. Recounting the injuries done to Florence by that lord, he concluded that no other campaign would be easier, more useful, or more just.

Niccolò da Uzzano objected to their hurting “a Guelf city that had always been friendly to the Florentine people” and reminded his audience that “a free Lucca had never harmed Florence,” only her tyrants had. However, in a speech reminiscent of that Diodotus gives in Thucydides’ history, he appealed to considerations not of justice, which he observed did not have much force in his day, but only of “utility to the city.”34 He conceded that the profit to be gained from the acquisition of Lucca was great, but, he emphasized, success was highly uncertain. “He urged them therefore to refrain from the campaign and to live with the tyrant so that he would make as many enemies as possible within. . . . For if the thing was governed prudently, that city would reach the point where the tyrant could not hold it, and neither knowing how nor being able to govern itself, [Lucca] would necessarily fall into their lap.” However, “he saw that their humors were excited and that his words were not being heard” (FH 4.19; 166). The people, whom Machiavelli observed in D 1.53 are attracted to bold rather than cautious policies and fail to see the long-run costs hidden beneath immediate or promised gains, were too impatient to wait.

Machiavelli shows that things occurred as Niccolò predicted. The Florentines appointed two commissioners to lead the soldiers they hired to attack Lucca. Both acquired territory and booty, but one did so with such cruelty and fraud that he was recalled, condemned, and admonished.35 When Rinaldo heard that he had been slandered by two of Cosimo’s creatures, who claimed that he was “carrying on the war not for the profit of the Florentine people but for his own,” his “sincere and haughty spirit” led him to give up his commission and return to Florence. “Since it was not the custom in Florence to allow citizens a triumph [as in Rome],” he protested, “it might at least be the custom to defend them from false abuse” (FH 4.22; 169).

Because the Florentine people had supported the war, they did not know whom to blame for its failure. They thus readily believed the slanders of the commissioners spread by Cosimo’s creatures. “A very prudent man,” Machiavelli comments, Cosimo “never attempted anything against either the Party or the state but took care to benefit everyone and with his liberality to make many citizens into his partisans. So his example increased the charge against those who were governing, and he himself judged that by this way he would either live in Florence as powerful and as safely as anyone else or, if because of the ambition of his adversaries it came to something extraordinary, he would be superior both in arms and in favor” (FH 4.26; 172–73).

Niccolò da Uzzano and the other heads of the party understood what Cosimo was attempting, but they were unable to find a remedy. Some wanted to unite behind Rinaldo in an effort to drive Cosimo out, but Niccolò responded: “Those who think of driving Cosimo out of Florence must, before everything else, measure their forces” against his. And, he made it clear, Cosimo’s position was stronger.

First, Niccolò called his associates’ attention to the power of relative numbers. They called themselves “the party of the nobles and the opposing side that of the plebs.” Even if that were true, victory would be uncertain, because they would be few opposing many and apt to be defeated the same way the old nobility of the city had been. In fact, they had even more to fear since their party was fragmented, whereas their adversaries were united. Many families at that very meeting were divided; some out of envy of their brothers or relatives did not favor the self-styled “nobles” and favored the plebs. What dignity their party had “arises out of the ancient reputation of this state, which has been preserved for fifty years; but if it should come to a test in which our weakness was uncovered, we would lose it” (FH 4.26; 174).

Second, he pointed out the difficulties they would encounter in persuading others that their cause was just. “The deeds of Cosimo that make us suspect him are . . . [that] he helps everyone with his money, and not only private individuals but the public, and not only Florentines but the condottieri.” We would “have to allege as causes for driving him out that he is merciful, helpful, liberal, and loved by everyone. And although these are all modes that send men flying to a princedom, . . . they are not believed to be so.” Nor would their party be able to persuade others, because their mode of governing had destroyed the people’s faith in them, and “the city, . . . since it has always lived with parties, is corrupt” (FH 4.26; 175).

Third, Niccolò reminded his colleagues that if they succeeded in driving Cosimo out, which they could easily do, since the Signoria at present happened to be favorable, they would find it difficult to prevent his returning. Because he would have so many friends remaining in the city, the next Signoria would be pressed to allow him to return, and they would have “driven out a good man who would return to us a wicked one because his nature would be corrupted by those who recalled him.” And if they aimed to have him killed, they could not do so legally “by way of the magistrates because his money and your own corruptible minds will always save him” (FH 4.26; 175).

Finally, Niccolò objected, even if they succeeded in killing Cosimo or merely preventing his return, they would not gain anything, because if the republic “is freed from Cosimo, it becomes the slave of Messer Rinaldo.” So he counseled them not to take “a course that is harmful in every way or believe that [they], accompanied by a few, can oppose the will of many; for all these citizens, partly out of ignorance and partly out of malice, are prepared to sell this republic, and so much is fortune their friend that they have found a buyer” (FH 4.176).

Once again, things occurred more or less as Niccolò da Uzzano predicted.36 After his death his admonitions to his colleagues had no more effect than those of Giovanni de’ Medici had on his sons. When the war with Lucca was terminated, the proud Rinaldo saw that he was left sole “prince” of his party; so he sought allies in an attempt to drive Cosimo out and take the state by force. He found a gonfalonier he could persuade to summon Cosimo and create a balìa to reform the state. However, because there was disagreement among the armed men assembled in the piazza about whether to kill, exile, pity, or fear Cosimo, no decision about his fate was taken immediately. He was imprisoned, and his jailor, not wanting to be implicated in his death, not merely ate with him (because Cosimo feared that he would be poisoned), but brought a friend to dine with him. Cosimo took the opportunity to pay this man to take a bribe to the gonfalonier, who accepted it and, as a result, banished Cosimo along with many of his relatives and creatures instead of killing him as Rinaldo desired. Cosimo accepted his banishment cheerfully, and in a gesture reminiscent of Julius Caesar (although Machiavelli does not note it), he offered himself and his property, in whatever place he might be, to the city, its people, and the Signori. The gonfalonier invited him to his home for dinner, “and then had him accompanied by many armed men to the borders. Wherever he passed, Cosimo was received with honor; and he was visited publicly by the Venetians, and not as an exile but honored as one placed in the highest rank” (FH 4.29; 179).

“It would have been better for them to have let things be than to have left Cosimo alive and his friends in Florence,” Rinaldo told a group of friends, “because great men must either not be touched or, if touched, be eliminated.”37 But his colleagues refused to follow his advice to ally with the former great against the plebs. A year later, when a gonfalonier and all eight of the Signori whose names were drawn were friendly to Cosimo, Rinaldo again called the heads of his party together and urged them to seize control of the state by force. Again his colleagues hesitated; and when the new Signori assumed their offices, they agreed to bring Cosimo back. Summoned to the palace, Rinaldo “thought that he should delay no longer, and he came out of his house with a great number of armed men” (FH 4.31; 181). But only two other heads of the party joined him; and while Rinaldo was waiting for others, the Signori seized the opportunity to propose a reconciliation. His two associates agreed to the terms. Left entirely alone, Rinaldo accepted Pope Eugene’s offer to negotiate a settlement for him. However, the Signori postponed the negotiation while they secretly sent to Pistoia for infantry, with which they took control of the strongholds of the city. They then called the people into the piazza and created a new balìa to restore Cosimo to his fatherland and to banish Messer Rinaldo along with the associates who had failed to back his efforts. Bemoaning the end of any effective resistance to the rise of Cosimo, Machiavelli concludes, “thus Florence was deprived . . . not only of good men but of men of riches and industry” (FH 4.33; 183).


Books 5 and 6: On the Vileness of Mercenary Warfare


Cosimo’s triumphal return from exile to Florence is the climatic event at the center of Machiavelli’s history. Yet in the two books with which Machiavelli begins his account of the rule of the Medici, he says very little about the actions of its founder. Instead he devotes all but three of the thirty-five chapters of Book 5 and five of the thirty-eight chapters of Book 6 to detailing the shifting alliances and inconsequential battles fought by the mercenary captains who were employed by the equally unfaithful heads of the Milanese, Florentine, and Venetian states.

In FH 5.4 Machiavelli briefly describes the measures Cosimo’s party took to secure their control of the state after his return. Following the pattern of parties that had taken control of the Florentine state previously, they banished their enemies and brought back their friends who had been exiled. But in contrast to the conclusions of the two civil wars in Rome, there was no bloodbath.38 Like the popular nobles who had controlled the government of the republic before them, Cosimo’s party proceeded primarily by making laws that favored them and penalized their opponents. So “in a short time, having driven out or impoverished all the enemy party, they secured the state for themselves” (FH 5.4; 190).

When the duke of Milan later sent Niccolò Piccinino to attack Florence, Cosimo’s party did not have to do much to keep the government steady, because of the goodwill that Cosimo had among the people and “because they had restricted their chief magistrates to a few powerful men, who held firm with their severity” (FH 5.31; 222). But in the one—and only one—chapter Machiavelli describes Cosimo’s foreign policy (FH 5.14), he shows that the head of the Medici party utterly failed to persuade the Venetians to help the Florentines oppose the duke, even though it would have been to the Venetians’ advantage to do so.

Machiavelli explains the surprising shift in the focus of his analysis from the domestic to the foreign policy of the Florentine state in his introduction to book 5. He begins by suggesting that in human affairs nothing ever fundamentally changes (in which case the ascension of the Medici to power in Florence would be of only passing interest and importance). “Usually provinces go . . . from order to disorder and then pass again from disorder to order, for,” as he observed in D 1.6 and 3.1, “worldly things are not allowed by nature to stand still.” Like his incorporation and partial adaptation of Polybius’s argument concerning the cycle of regimes in D 1.2, Machiavelli’s observation here that “as soon as they [worldly things] reach their ultimate perfection, having no further to rise, they must descend; and similarly, once they have descended and through their disorders arrived at the ultimate depth, . . . of necessity they must rise” has convinced some commentators that he has a basically cyclical understanding of history.39 “Virtue gives birth to quiet, quiet to leisure, leisure to disorder, disorder to ruin,” he explains, “and similarly, from ruin order is born; from order, virtue, and from virtue, glory and good fortune.” So the prudent have observed “that letters come after arms and that, in provinces and cities, captains arise before philosophers. For, as good and ordered armies give birth to victories and victories to quiet, the strength of well-armed spirits cannot be corrupted by a more honorable leisure than that of letters, nor can leisure enter into well-instituted cities with a greater and more dangerous deceit than this one.” He thus praises Cato who, recognizing “the evil that could result to his fatherland from this honorable leisure, . . . saw to it that no philosopher could be accepted in Rome” (FH 5.1; 185).

Yet even those who had not read Machiavelli’s Discourses would have known that Rome also fell and not, primarily, as a result of its embrace of philosophy.40 And, in fact, Machiavelli’s explanation of the rise and fall of order here applies better to Florence than to Rome, because the Medici were great patrons of philosophy along with the other arts. In Italy, Machiavelli observes, “men become wise from their afflictions” have not restored order, as did the ancient Tuscans and then the Romans, because they have been “suffocated by an extraordinary force.” As in D 1.2, he thus acknowledges that the cycle does not hold.41 And in explaining how and why it has not, he begins to level an implicit critique of the rule of the Medici that runs through books 5 and 6.

Machiavelli does not state what the “extraordinary force” that has prevented “men become wise from their afflictions” from restoring order in Italy is. He simply observes that “nothing was built upon the Roman ruins in a way that might have redeemed Italy from them, so that it might have been able to act gloriously under a virtuous principality.” The five new cities and empires whose history he has described succeeded (until 1494) in defending the province from invasions by the northern “barbarians.” However, he explains, “if from the virtue of these new principalities times did not arise that were quiet through a long peace, neither were they dangerous because of the harshness of war. For one cannot affirm it to be peace where principalities frequently attack one another with arms; yet they cannot be called wars in which men are not killed, cities are not sacked, principalities are not destroyed, for these wars . . . were begun without fear, carried on without danger, and ended without loss. So that virtue which in other provinces used to be eliminated in a long peace was eliminated by vileness in the provinces of Italy, as will be described by us from 1434 to 1494.” In these disgraceful wars “will be seen how in the end the way was opened anew for the barbarians and how Italy put itself again in slavery to them” (FH 5.1; 186).

As he clearly stated the purpose and audience of the Discourses only in the preface to the second book, so Machiavelli makes the way in which his Florentine Histories are intended to add to his previous work explicit only in beginning the second half. Explaining the way and the reason why his history of the city differs from those of his predecessors, he first observes that “if the things done by our princes outside and at home may not be read, as are those of the ancients, with admiration for their virtue and greatness, they may perhaps be considered with no less admiration when it is seen how so many very noble peoples were held in check by such weak and badly directed armies.” The fact that the leaders of Florence and the other cities of Italy had kept them independent of foreign domination could, in a certain sense, produce wonder or “admiration,” precisely because that independence had not been achieved by the institution of good domestic orders, even in Venice (which in D 1.2–6 was Machiavelli’s modern example of a republic ordered so that it did not need to expand in order to maintain itself). Although these leaders all wished to expand their respective dominions, they had not successfully imitated the necessarily expansive foreign policy Machiavelli recommended on the basis of the Roman example in D 6. On the contrary, “if in describing the things that happened in this devastated world one does not tell about either the strength of soldiers, or the virtue of the captain, or the love of the citizen for his fatherland, it will be seen with what deceits, with what guile and arts the princes, soldiers, and heads of republics conducted themselves so as to maintain the reputation they have not deserved. It may, perhaps, be no less useful to know these things than to know the ancient ones, because, if the latter excite liberal spirits to follow them, the former will excite such spirits to avoid and eliminate them” (FH 5.1; 185–86, emphasis added). The history of the interactions of the five Italian powers whose rise Machiavelli traced in the first book of his Florentine Histories is intended to serve as a negative example to persuade his readers to take a different tack.

The campaigns of the mercenary captains Machiavelli describes in book 5 support the charges he made against such soldiers in P 12 and D 2.20 in great detail. At the same time Machiavelli shows that the leaders of Milan, Venice, and Florence were no more anxious to keep the peace than the mercenaries they employed. In book 5 he describes the repeated attempts of the duke of Milan to expand his influence into Tuscany and Lombardy, and the corresponding attempts of the Florentines and Venetians to foil him.

Machiavelli brings his account of these inconsequential battles to a climax in describing the battle of Anghiari. After the Florentines repelled the attack on their city by the duke’s mercenary captain, Niccolò Piccinino, they thought he would simply withdraw back to Lombardy. So they relaxed their defenses. But Piccinino decided to surprise them. Warned by the dust raised by his troops’ horses on the road, the Florentines hurriedly put themselves in order, and in a battle lasting all day and all night they finally repulsed his troops at the bridge. But the “victory was more useful for Tuscany than harmful to the duke; for if the Florentines had lost the day, Tuscany was his; but having lost it himself, he lost nothing more than the arms and horses of his army, which he could replace with not much money” (FH 5.33; 227).

Instead of celebrating the victory that preserved the independence of the city (as the Florentines themselves did when their commissioners, Bernardetto de’ Medici and Neri di Gino Capponi, returned to the city [FH 5.35; 229]), Machiavelli presents Anghiari as “a great example of the lack of success of these wars” (FH 5.34; 227).42 Never were there “times when war waged in the countries of others was less dangerous for whoever waged it than these. In such a defeat and in so long a battle . . . , only one man died, and he not from wounds or any other virtuous blow, but, falling off his horse, he was trampled.”43 Knights in shining armor might have been thought to be emblematic of nobility, but Machiavelli debunks any such notion by observing the safety with which men then fought: “for they were all on horse and covered with armor, and being secure from death whenever they surrendered, there was no cause that they should die” (FH 5.33; 227).44

After Niccolò and his troops withdrew, the Florentine army showed a complete lack of discipline. The commissioners wanted to follow and besiege the enemy in order “to have a complete victory. But not one condottiere or soldier was willing to obey them. . . . The next day, at noon, without permission or regard for commissioner or captain, they went to Arezzo and, having left their booty there, returned to Anghiari—a thing so contrary to every praiseworthy order and military discipline that any remnant of an army, however ordered, could easily and deservedly have taken from them the victory that they had so undeservedly gained.” Even worse, “when the commissioners wanted the men at arms who had been taken to be held, so as to deprive the enemy of the opportunity of reforming itself, they freed them” (FH 5.34; 227).

As Machiavelli points out in introducing book 6, the mercenary wars of his time were the polar opposites of the Roman model he recommended in his Discourses and Art of War. Roman patricians and plebs both benefited from the wars they fought, especially when the Romans were able to put the spoils into the public treasury and, as a result, did not need to tax citizens in order to support further wars. In the wars he has described, neither the victor nor the vanquished gained much, because both had to pay soldiers to fight, and neither acquired either land or goods, because their soldiers seized the booty they captured as spoils for themselves, did not remain in order to maintain control of the territory, and demanded new wages and equipment in order to fight another battle.

Because neither their victories nor their losses had any lasting effect, Machiavelli shows in book 6, the five major states in Italy were almost constantly at war in shifting coalitions. And, he suggests, these wars were caused by the ambitions of the mercenary captains even more than those of the princes who employed them, because the mercenary captains wanted to become princes themselves.

For example, Machiavelli reports that although he had been defeated at Anghiari, Niccolò Piccinino was soon able to collect more troops in Lombardy where he began attacking Count Sforza and the Venetians on behalf of the duke of Milan. Indeed, Niccolò was so successful that he would have defeated the count, had he not angered the duke by demanding a grant of a small principality as a reward for his service. Vexed by his captain’s insolence, the duke decided to come to terms with the count. Puzzled by his employer’s rewarding an enemy rather than a friend, and threatened with worse punishment if he kept complaining, Niccolò kept fighting; and although he suffered a bad defeat the following year, he again brought the count and his forces to such extreme necessity that he would have conquered them, had he not been recalled to Milan. Told that the duke wanted to speak directly to him and continuing to hope for a proper reward for his services, Niccolò “abandoned a certain victory for an uncertain good” (FH 6.8; 238). In his absence, the count attacked, defeated Niccolò’s forces, and captured his son Francesco. Seeing how he had been deceived, Niccolò died soon thereafter of grief. Machiavelli’s account of the life of this mercenary serves as a perfect illustration of the reasons he presents in D 1.29–30 that no victorious captain should expect a reward from his prince.

Machiavelli shows that Count Francesco Sforza succeeded much better than Niccolò Piccinino in realizing his ambitions not merely by seizing and maintaining control of parts of the Marches, but, more importantly, by becoming duke of Milan. Sforza learned from bitter experience that he should not believe the promises of future rewards offered for his services, whether they came from the leaders of republics like Venice and Florence or solitary rulers. He acquired power on the basis of “his own arms,” which included not only the troops he led and employed but also his understanding of the basis of his power in the needs of others.

After the duke died, the newly established republic of Milan discovered that they needed someone to defend them from the Venetians. So they agreed to employ the count on the same terms the duke had. But when he prepared his troops to attack Pavia, the citizens offered him the town on the condition that he not put them under the empire of Milan. Although he feared that he might anger his new Milanese employers, he agreed. “Nor was he restrained by fear or shame in breaking his faith,” Machiavelli comments, “for great men call it shame to lose, not to acquire by deceit” (FH 6.17; 247).

The Milanese thought (correctly) that the count had revealed his ambition, but they did not feel free to express their outrage, because they needed him to defend them from the Venetians. But knowing that the Milanese feared that the count wanted to make himself their lord rather than merely their captain, the Venetians decided “to make peace with the count and to offer him help in the acquisition of Milan,” because “they were persuaded that as soon as the Milanese saw they had been deceived by the count, in their indignation they would be willing to subject themselves to anyone rather than to him” (FH 6.19; 250). The count was “stung” by the words of the Milanese ambassadors who came to berate him for his perfidy; but he assessed the situation with great astuteness. “When the ambassadors had departed, the count ordered his troops so as to be able to assault the Milanese.” Recognizing that the Venetians were not apt to remain his allies for long, the count also “sought to keep them loyal with a reward.” He let them take Crema, and “this meal set before the Venetians was the cause that their friendship with the count lasted until the count had seized the whole dominion of the Milanese” (FH 6.22; 254). The despairing appeal the Milanese made to the Venetians to save another republic had no more effect than their ambassadors’ reprimands of the count. The Venetians waited to secure Crema before they made an alliance with the Milanese; and the count used the time he was given to accept the peace to persuade his enemies that he had abandoned his ambitions by withdrawing his troops, and so encouraged them to neglect their defenses while he prepared a more effective siege. The next spring the Venetians decided not to risk a battle with the count in order to save Milan, because they thought the Milanese would never cede to the count. But the Milanese decided that if they had to give up their liberty, they would give it to someone able to defend them. The count thus entered Milan as prince on February 26, 1450.

Machiavelli’s history of the struggle for control of Milan supports his contention in P 18 and D 1.59, 3.42 that “princes” (whether solitary or republican leaders) will always find reasons not to abide by their promises, if keeping those promises no longer serves their interests. But he also shows that the wars in Italy did not cease after the count realized his ambition to become duke.

Princes and republics might employ mercenary soldiers to further their ambitions, but as Fabrizio pointed out in the Art of War (1.51–62), mercenaries need wars in order to support themselves. So when “the Venetians, as is customary when peace is made, had dismissed from their hire Jacopo Piccinino, . . . joined by some other condottieri without employment, he came into Romagna and from there into the territory of Siena, where [he] stopped to make war” (FH 6.33; 268–69). Like other mercenary captains, Jacopo frequently switched from one employer to another; and like his father, he was finally deceived and executed by one of them.

Machiavelli shows that the best mercenary captains knew how to fight wars successfully. But he also demonstrates that hiring such men is dangerous for their employers, and that knowing how to fight and win battles does not, in itself, qualify a man to become a ruler.45

Machiavelli ends book 6 by noting that the Florentines had no part in the last war between France and Spain for control of the Kingdom of Naples. But he shows that they played a part in bringing it about by going to France and requesting the aid of the king against Alfonso, son of King Ferdinand of Aragon. In doing so, moreover, they suggested that the French king could use his aid to them as an excuse for taking Naples himself. Machiavelli does not say so explicitly, but he indicates that the Florentines were playing the same divisive role in Italy for which he initially blamed the Church. And for the same reasons: they were too weak to defend themselves and so had to call in foreign forces to protect them and their interests. To be sure, the Florentines were not alone in bringing in foreign troops. Naples was ruled by a son and then a nephew of the king of Spain. The Venetians allied with Alfonso, because they saw that having lost their fear of the duke of Milan, the Florentines had begun to fear them. The duke of Milan and Florence brought in the French to protect them from the Venetian-Spanish alliance. As Machiavelli emphasized at the conclusion of book 1, like the popes, all the other four major Italian powers had to seek assistance from abroad, because they did not have arms of their own. This was true even of the count, because his arms were the mercenary soldiers with whom he had taken Milan, not his citizens or subjects. Once he became duke, he had to pay them; he could not look to a foreign power to do so.

In D 1.6 Machiavelli suggested that a republic that did not find it necessary to defend itself would degenerate internally. And in book 7 of his Florentine Histories he shows that this is exactly what happened in Florence during Cosimo’s rule, when the city was fighting the “vile” inconsequential wars he describes in books 5 and 6 or was, finally, at peace. He begins to point out some of the internal consequences of the weak and ineffective foreign and military policies of the major Italian powers, however, even in book 6.

Although Machiavelli claims in FH 7.2 that Cosimo and Neri were united so long as the latter lived, in FH 6.6 he observed that Cosimo feared Neri’s “reputation more than any other’s because to the great credit he had in the city was added that which he had with the soldiers; for having been at the head of the Florentine armies many times, he had earned it with his virtue and his merits. Besides this, the memory of the victories credited to him and to his father Gino (Gino having taken Pisa and Neri having defeated Niccolò Piccinino at Anghiari) made him loved by many and feared by those who desired not to have him as partner in the government” (236). Some members of Cosimo’s party thus sought to diminish Neri’s reputation by assassinating one of his chief subordinates (and thus deprived Florence of a much needed potential defender). In FH 6.23 Machiavelli also reports that Neri and Cosimo disagreed about whether Florence should help the count seize control of Milan. Neri argued that as head of Milan the count would constitute a formidable challenge to the security of their city. But Cosimo’s colleagues thought that Neri wanted to press the count to negotiate a peace rather than take Milan, because the count had always been a friend of Cosimo, and Cosimo continued to support him privately. So if the count took Milan, his friendship would increase Cosimo’s influence not merely in Florence, but in Italy as a whole. Cosimo justified his position by observing (truly, as Machiavelli shows his readers in FH 7.33–34) that the Milanese people were not capable of sustaining a republic. But Machiavelli also shows that the Florentines did not train a citizen army under a very capable general because Cosimo’s party feared that general would acquire partisans who would enable them to challenge his rule. There was as close a connection between Cosimo’s failures in foreign policy and his party’s attempt to acquire tyrannical control of the Florentine republic as there had been between the arming of the people and the preservation of liberty in Rome. As Machiavelli argued in his Discourses (1.29–30), every successful captain necessarily constitutes a threat to the government, but no republic will survive as such where there are not many princes vying for popular support.


Books 7 and 8: The Medici “Princes”—Cosimo, Piero, and Lorenzo the Magnificent


Machiavelli begins book 7 by apologizing for what might seem to have been a long digression on the condition of Italy as a whole in what was supposed to be a history of the city of Florence. Acknowledging that he never promised to write about the “things of Italy” (and so letting his reader see that he has departed somewhat from the order and contents of the book forecast in the preface), he states simply that without these things his history “would be less understood and less pleasing, since the wars in which the Florentines were compelled of necessity to intervene arose most times from the actions of other Italian peoples and princes” (FH 7.1; 276). Somewhat indirectly Machiavelli thus indicates the point of the preceding discussion of the wars fought in Italy during Cosimo’s reign in Florence.
