His government showed itself to be weak and ineffective outside the city limits. Rather than taking bold initiatives, the Florentines acted only when prompted to do so by others. They were not able to extend their dominion to Lucca. Because they did not have their own arms, they were forced to rely on the self-serving count. And after he achieved his own ambition by becoming duke of Milan and refused to fight any more battles on behalf of others, they made Italy into the battleground between armies of the two emerging national monarchies of France and Spain, by inviting the French, in effect, to invade Italy to prevent the Spanish king from extending his dominion in Naples northward.

By first presenting a detailed account of the weak and undistinguished foreign policy of the Florentine state dominated by Cosimo’s party, Machiavelli casts a dark shadow on the eulogy he gives of the founder of the Medici state. In book 7 he shows not merely that in the last decade of his life Cosimo was unable to maintain control of his own party. Like Cosimo’s weak and ineffective foreign policy, the particular way in which Cosimo acquired (or, in foreign affairs, sought to acquire) political influence contributed to the internal corruption and tyranny that developed within his party. Crudely put, he tried to buy influence by doing personal favors as well as lending or giving money to individual citizens and mercenary soldiers like the count. But “money is not the sinew of war,” as Machiavelli argued in D 2.10. “Truly powerful republics and princes buy friendships not with money but with virtue and the reputation of strength” (D 2.30).

Following the brief explanation of why he devoted two of the four books in the second half of the Florentine Histories to the foreign affairs of Italy as a whole, Machiavelli shifts abruptly to introduce his account of the “travails inside” Florence with another general reflection. For the first time in the Florentine Histories he states unqualifiedly that “those who hope that a republic can be united are very much deceived.” As in his introduction to book 3, he observes that “it is true that some divisions are harmful to republics and some are helpful.” But here he does not distinguish between the nobler desire of the Roman plebs to share offices with the patricians and the destructive desire of the Florentine people to seize all power for themselves. Instead he distinguishes between divisions that are accompanied by sects and partisans, and the helpful divisions that are maintained without them. A founder of a republic cannot prevent the emergence of enmities, but he can prevent the emergence of sects by forcing its leading citizens to “acquire reputation” through public competition for honors rather than through acquiring personal dependents by benefiting them privately as individuals. As in D 3.28, Machiavelli argues that public means of competing for honors and office make it necessary for ambitious individuals “to attempt to exalt the republic and to watch each other particularly so that civil bounds are not transgressed.” In the Discourses he showed that such public competition had beneficial results in Rome until the prolongation of commands made it possible for generals to acquire partisan armies. In Florence, he now observes, enmities “were always accompanied by sects and therefore always harmful, never did a winning sect remain united except when the hostile sect was active, but as soon as the one conquered was eliminated, the ruling one, no longer having fear to restrain it or order within itself to check it, would become divided again” (FH 7.1; 277).

As Harvey Mansfield observes, in the Florentine Histories Machiavelli never defines ‘sect.’46 In the Discourses, he uses the word consistently to describe religious organizations; and in FH 1.5 he observes that after the emperor withdrew from Rome to Constantinople, the people in Italy suffered as a result of the divisions among Christian sects. When he applies the term to Florentine politics, however, Machiavelli appears to have not religious so much as political organizations or parties in mind. What they had in common with the Christian religious sect (to which they all adhered) was their insistence that they alone should prevail; there could be no compromise or sharing of rule with their competitors. Since Machiavelli thinks that all human beings constantly seek to acquire more security, goods, and reputation for themselves, he does not blame the Florentine politicians or people for wanting to satisfy their own desires. Nor does he think that Roman politicians altruistically sought the common good at the expense of their own. Over time, he shows, they devised a set of laws that forced ambitious nobles to compete with one another in seeking the support of the people. The Florentine ‘sects’ as he describes them were composed of men representing both of the humors that Machiavelli contends exist in every city. What distinguished the divisions in Florence from those between the patricians and plebs in Rome was first that the Florentines were not continually united by the necessity of defending the city from foreign aggression. Their political habits were formed when Florence was a colony protected by Roman troops and persisted because there were no powers in Italy that threatened to conquer them if they did not arm themselves. And after the new tyrant of Lucca destroyed the Florentine army, they did not attempt to marshal and train a new one. They looked outside the city for defenders and tried to buy them instead of rebuilding their own defenses. The second and most obvious difference between the enmities between the humors in Rome and the sects in Florence was that, whether they fought in the streets or by means of law, the Florentines sought to destroy their domestic opponents in order to obtain complete control of the state. Their leaders did not compete for popular support in elections, because the Florentines selected their magistrates in an apparently democratic fashion by lot for short terms of office. By controlling whose names went into the bags, first the Guelf and then the Medici party was able to control the quickly changing official government of the republic. Although Machiavelli appears to praise the three Medici princes who in effect ruled Florence from 1434 until 1492, he shows that they imposed a relatively soft form of tyranny, not so much by force as by the destruction of all effective political opposition inside the city and the corruption of its people by means of the private, largely economic benefits they distributed.


A. Cosimo


“The ruling party of Cosimo de’ Medici was left on top in 1434.” However, “because the beaten party was large and full of very powerful men, Cosimo’s party maintained itself united and humane for a time through fear.” (This was the same fear that Machiavelli argued prevented the nobles from oppressing the plebs after Brutus banished the Tarquins in D 1.5.) So long as the party did not give the people any reason to hate it, they were willing to cede to its heads every balià and power that they desired. From 1434 to 1455, Cosimo’s party reassumed the authority of the balìa (to restructure the government) six times ordinarily through the councils.47 Although Neri acquired his reputation by public means (and thus aroused the envy and suspicions of Cosimo’s partisans), whereas Cosimo used what Machiavelli calls private means, and they disagreed to a certain extent about Florentine foreign policy, they agreed about what needed to be done internally and were able to get what they wanted from the people without difficulty. After Neri died, however, some of Cosimo’s “friends” saw no reason not to try to diminish his power. They decided not to use the power of the balìa again, because that would require an appeal to the people, but to lock up the bags from which the magistrates were drawn by lot so that no new names could be added. What had begun as a party headed by “popular nobles” such as Salvestro de’ Medici, who sympathized with the people’s desire to avoid oppression, no longer felt the need or wanted to rely upon popular support.

The people did not understand that they had lost power, because they had no leaders to point it out. Cosimo understood perfectly well what his party had done. But instead of trying to exercise his authority directly by attempting to take back control of the state from his former “friends” with force, he decided to teach them a lesson by allowing them to do what they wished. “Since the city had been brought back to creating magistrates by lot, it appeared to the generality of citizens that they had their liberty again and that the magistrates were judging in accordance not with the will of someone powerful but with their own judgment, so that sometimes a friend of someone powerful . . . was punished.” As a result, “those who were used to seeing their houses full of well-wishers and gifts saw them empty of possessions and men. They also saw that they had become the equals of those whom they were long accustomed to consider inferior.” But “what frightened the great more and gave Cosimo greater opportunity to make them recognize their mistake was the revival of the mode of the catasto of 1427, whereby the taxes were assessed not by men but by law” (FH 7.2; 278).

Fearful of losing their property (more than their political position and so demonstrating the same preference for property over honors that Machiavelli attributed to the Roman patricians in D 1.37), Cosimo’s former friends and party members begged him to call for a parliament to restructure the government so that it would follow their desires. But because he wanted them to learn their lesson about the need to maintain popular support, Cosimo insisted that the law had “to be made in the ordinary way, with the will of the people and not by force” (FH 7.3; 279). The people refused to consent to a parliament, however. And Cosimo, thinking that it was not well to let things go so far that he could not bring them back later with ease, allowed Luca Pitti to press for the change in government, so that Luca would incur the blame if things went awry. They did. After the people repeatedly refused to consent to renew the balìa, Luca threatened the citizens sitting on the councils, and in August 1458, “having filled the palace with armed men, he called the people into the piazza and by force . . . made them consent to that which they had not consented to voluntarily before.” Indicating his own judgment of this government, Machiavelli reports that “to give a beginning of terror to this government that they had begun with force” (FH 7.3; 279), they banished and finally killed Messer Girolamo Machiavelli (one of Niccolò’s ancestors), and deprived many others of honors.

Contrary to his expectations, Cosimo was not able to retake control of the city. Luca Pitti was now in control. And “the other citizens, if they did not build as he did, were not less violent or less rapacious than he; thus if Florence did not have war from outside to destroy it, the city was destroyed by its own citizens” (FH 7.4; 280). The violence and rapacity of Cosimo’s successors made even his enemies lament his death, because they saw that respect for him had made his colleagues less unbearable, and “they feared that without him they would be altogether ruined and destroyed.” So even though he had proved unable to restrain the rapacity of his colleagues, “he died full of glory and with a very great name in the city and outside” (FH 7.5; 281–82).

After an extremely brief account of the thirty-one years in which Cosimo, in effect, ruled Florence, in which Machiavelli emphasizes the swift degeneration of Cosimo’s party’s rule when he became old and infirm, Machiavelli launches upon a two-chapter eulogy.48 In it he shows that Cosimo’s ability to maintain his preeminence was a product of personal virtues that could not be institutionalized and that he was unable to pass on to his successors. He begins by declaring that “Cosimo was the most reputed and renowned citizen, as an unarmed man, of whom not only Florence but any other city had ever had memory” (emphasis added). Without stating it explicitly, Machiavelli thus emphasizes the difference between the rule Cosimo exercised in Florence and that of the Roman republican heroes such as Furius Camillus (who also was brought back from exile), with whom Machiavelli’s humanistic predecessors (Leonardo Bruni and Poggio Bracciolini) regularly compared him. According to Machiavelli, Cosimo “surpassed every other man of his times not only in authority and riches but also in liberality and prudence, because among all the other qualities that made him prince in his fatherland was that, above all other men, he was liberal and magnificent” (FH 7.5; 281, emphasis added).

As evidence of his liberality Machiavelli points not merely to the “abundance” of richly furnished churches, monasteries, private homes that were “palaces not of private citizens but of kings” Cosimo built, in addition to a hospital for the poor and sick pilgrims in Jerusalem. As his son Piero discovered only after his father’s death, there “was no other citizen who had any quality in that city to whom Cosimo had not lent a large sum of money.” Yet, Machiavelli also indicates, Cosimo demonstrated his prudence by exercising a certain kind of restraint in his private life. “Although his dwellings like all his other works and actions were kingly, . . . he never overstepped civil modesty. For in his conversations, in his servants, in riding on horse, in his whole mode of living, and in his marriage alliances, he was always like any modest citizen.” Unlike his son and grandson, “when [Cosimo] had to give wives to his sons, he did not look for alliances with princes” (FH 7.6; 281–82), but arranged for them to marry into other wealthy Florentine families. Although Machiavelli does not say so, Cosimo showed that he understood the main obstacle to becoming a “prince” in a republic better than Camillus did when he rode in triumph (D 3.23).

Machiavelli extols Cosimo’s prudence more generally: “No one in his time was equal to him in his understanding of the states of princes and civil governments; hence, it arose that in such variety of fortune and in so various a city and so changeable a citizenry, he held one state for thirty-one years. For, being very prudent, he recognized evils at a distance and therefore was in time either not to let them grow or to be prepared so that, if they did grow, they would not offend him.” In P 3 Machiavelli praised the same foresight in the Roman republic, especially with regard to the need to wage war. Cosimo was unarmed (and Machiavelli has criticized him indirectly for it). Yet here he observes that Cosimo was able not only to “conquer domestic and civil ambition, but [also to overcome] that of many princes with such prosperity and prudence that whoever allied with him and his fatherland would come out either equal or superior to the enemy, and whoever opposed him would lose his time and money or state.” As he showed in books 5 and 6, the Venetians were able to oppose the dukes of Milan successfully only when they were allied with the Florentines; and now he adds that by using his own credit to empty the banks of Naples and Venice of money, Cosimo forced the Venetians to accept “the peace he was willing to concede to [them].” So Machiavelli concludes, “civil discords always increased his state in Florence, and wars outside increased his power and reputation, in consequence of which he added Borgo San Sepolcro, Montedoglio, the Casentino, and Val di Bano to the empire of his republic. And thus his virtue and fortune eliminated all his enemies and exalted his friends” (FH 7.5; 281–82).

Cosimo “was without learning but very eloquent and full of a natural prudence and was thus kindly to his friends, merciful to the poor, useful in conversations, cautious in advice, quick in executions, and in his sayings and replies he was keen and grave.” He built many churches, but, as the sayings Machiavelli quotes show, Cosimo was not pious. “He said of Pope Pius when he was summoning princes to a campaign against the Turk that he was old and was carrying on a campaign for the young.” Likewise, “when his wife asked him a few hours before his death why he kept his eyes closed, he answered, ‘To get them used to it.’” Most telling, perhaps, “when some citizens told him after his return from exile that the city was being spoiled and that it was acting against God to send away from it so many men of means, he answered that a city spoiled was better than one lost, . . . and that states were not held with paternosters in hand” (FH 7.6; 283). As shown by his deeds, Cosimo recognized the need for a prince always to appear to be “merciful, faithful, humane, honest, religious” (P 18), but the impossibility of his always being so in fact. Like Castruccio, he knew that those in need come to princes in search of favors, but that princes command; they do not beg. Unlike Castruccio, however, Cosimo did not flaunt his disbelief in the Christian god or openly outrage the conventional morality of his fellow citizens, especially with regard to marriage.

Machiavelli reports that “Cosimo was also a lover and exalter of literary men; he therefore brought Argyropoulos to Florence, a man of Greek birth and very learned . . . , so that Florentine youth might learn from him the Greek language and other teachings of his. He took into his home Marsilio Ficino, second father of Platonic philosophy, whom he loved extremely” (FH 7.6; 283). But Machiavelli does not describe Cosimo, as did Argyropoulos and Ficino, as an Aristotelian gentleman or a Platonic philosopher-king.49

Ironically perhaps, Machiavelli’s eulogy provides some of the best evidence for his claim in the dedication that he did not flatter the Medici. Although he describes the liberality, magnificence, and prudence that gained Cosimo favor both at home and abroad, and quotes some of the sayings that reveal his hardheaded insights, Machiavelli does not present this unarmed Florentine citizen as a Roman statesman or a philosopher-king, the way other writers he patronized did. Instead, Machiavelli concludes his eulogy with an account of Cosimo’s own sense of his failure to leave an enduring legacy. He did not have a son healthy enough to take on the burden of his public or private affairs. Nor had he “increased the Florentine empire by an honorable acquisition.” (He seems to have considered the places Machiavelli listed among his achievements to be small and insignificant.) Perhaps because he was a merchant, he did not understand that neither princes nor republics keep their promises. He had therefore been deceived by Francesco Sforza, who had promised to make a campaign against Lucca as soon as he had become lord of Milan, but then changed his mind.50 Cosimo saw “that, because of the infirmity of his body, he could not bring his former diligence to public or private affairs, so that . . . the city was being destroyed by the citizens and his substance by his agents and his sons.” Yet, Machiavelli concludes, “he died full of glory and . . . on his tombstone he was named Father of his Fatherland” (FH 7.6; 284). Machiavelli himself does not call Cosimo father of his country. He has, in fact, shown that Cosimo had not fathered a lasting dynasty and knew that he had not.


B. Piero


Cosimo was correct in thinking that he had not established a firm succession, because his son Piero’s weakness and infirmity would prevent him from managing either public or private family affairs. Shortly after Cosimo’s death, Machiavelli reports, four of his old “friends” conspired to seize control of the state from his son. Cosimo had instructed Piero to follow the advice of his old friend Dietsalvi Neroni in administering the estate. Moved more by ambition than by gratitude or loyalty, however, Dietsalvi gave Piero seemingly good advice that would, in fact, ruin his reputation in Florence. Finding the accounts in disorder, Dietsalvi told Piero that he should call in all the debts owed his father or risk losing his own credit. When Piero did, he lost the support of many of his father’s partisans and made enemies of others, who feared that their businesses would fail.51 Dietsalvi then sought the cooperation of Luca Pitti, Agnolo Acciaiuoli, and Niccolò Soderini in taking control of the state away from Piero. They agreed to do so for different reasons: Luca wanted to resume the power he had abused, Agnolo wanted to revenge a slight he thought he had received from Cosimo, and Niccolò wanted the city to live more freely. In public they all stated, however, that they simply desired to have the city ruled by its magistrates, not the advice of a few. Lacking the prudence of his father in this respect, Piero added to popular resentment by contracting a marriage between his eldest son and Clarice degli Orsini. He thus looked as if he did not think that the daughters of Florentine families were good enough. Deceived by the name of liberty, Machiavelli comments, the greater part of the citizens were ready to follow the conspirators.

The dispute between these citizens and the Medici came out into the open after the duke of Milan died and the question arose whether Florence should continue to pay his son what they had paid his father. Opponents of the Medici argued that the agreement was with the father and that, because Galeazzo did not have the same virtue, he should not receive the same profit. But Piero pointed out that it was not good to lose so necessary an alliance out of avarice and that there was nothing that contributed more to the safety of Florence or, for that matter, all of Italy than for them to be leagued with the duke so that the Venetians would not try to win the youth over to them by means of deceit or force. Piero’s reasoning was not accepted (although Machiavelli subsequently shows that he was correct).

Piero’s opponents were divided among themselves. Some simply wanted to let the balìa end and the magistrates retake control of the state. But the more impatient argued that Piero would continue to exercise influence under these conditions unless they did away with him. When Niccolò Soderini was appointed gonfalonier, many citizens expected him to restore the safety and liberty of the republic. But his brother Tommaso convinced Niccolò that the best way to achieve his goal was to draw up new lists of names of citizens to put into the bags. So Niccolò frittered away his short term of office without objection from his colleagues, because they thought that they would have another opportunity in the future and out of envy did not want him to get credit for renewing the state.

His opponents’ failure to act when they had the opportunity made Piero’s party bolder and more able to gather support. So his enemies decided that they needed to have him killed and then bring armed men to the piazza to force the Signoria to create a government according to their wishes. Informed of his enemies’ plans, Piero decided to take up arms first and to use the coming of the mercenary captain who had been hired by his opponents to justify his move. When the citizens saw Piero armed and his enemies not, they began to think about how to become his friends. Because Piero had not moved his arms from his home, he was able to convince his fellow citizens that he sought only to defend himself. When the balìa ended, he promised, he would be content for the magistrates to rule the city. He then rebuked Dietisalvi and his sons for having so betrayed the faith Cosimo and he had put in their friendship that others would have used arms against them if Piero had not restrained them.

Piero’s party waited until a friendly gonfalonier was elected, who called the people to the piazza where they made up a new balìa composed entirely of members of their party. Many citizens, including the conspirators, were frightened by the evident takeover and left the city immediately. They were banished, others were imprisoned and tortured, and still others killed or exiled. The conspirators sought not merely safety but allies to help them retake the state. Agnolo first wrote to Piero asking his forgiveness; but showing the way in which the Medici did not always adhere to Christian beliefs, Piero responded that the ingrate was receiving his just deserts. Agnolo then went to Rome where with the help of the archbishop he tried to destroy Piero’s credit, but Piero and his friends prevented it. Dietisalvi and Niccolò Soderini had more success with the Venetian Senate. Machiavelli notes that appeals to save another republic from tyranny did not move the Venetians, but when the exiles reminded the Senate how, acting on his own and not according to the desires of other citizens, Cosimo had aided Count Sforza against them, they hired an army to attack Florence. Thanks to a new alliance with Galeazzo and King Ferdinand, however, the Florentines were able to amass a great army to defend them.

Piero’s party had triumphed, but the invalid was no more able to control his subordinates than the elderly Cosimo had been. They continued to harm their enemies any way that they could and terrorized others. He first tried to distract his fellow citizens by sponsoring a magnificent celebration of the marriage of his son Lorenzo to Clarice and two military spectacles. He also tried to shame his colleagues by calling them together at his house and reproving them for despoiling their neighbors, selling justice, escaping civil judgments themselves, and oppressing peaceful men. He was so disgusted by their violence and avarice that he met with Agnolo secretly. “Nor can there be any doubt,” Machiavelli comments, “that if he had not been interrupted by death he would have had all the exiles restored to their fatherland to check the rapacity of those within. But these very decent thoughts were thwarted by death. . . . His fatherland could not entirely know his virtue and goodness, because he had been accompanied almost to the end of life by his father Cosimo and because those few years that he survived him were consumed in civil dissension and by illness.” He left two sons who showed some promise, but “their youth frightened everyone” (FH 7.23; 302).


C. Lorenzo


Because his prudence and authority were known not only in Florence but among all the princes of Italy, Machiavelli reports, after Piero’s death many citizens visited and many princes wrote to Tommaso Soderini as head of the city. “But as he was prudent and best understood his fortune and that of his house, he did not answer the letters of princes and gave the citizens to understand that they should visit not his houses but those of the Medici.” He gathered together all the first men of the noble families at the Convent of San Antonio, including Lorenzo and Giuliano de’ Medici, and told them “that if they wanted those in Florence to live united in peace and safe from division within and from wars outside, it was necessary to follow those young men and to maintain the reputation of their house.” Because “men never complain of doing the things they are used to doing,” he reasoned, “it has always been easier to maintain a power that by length of time has eliminated envy than to raise up a new one that for many causes could easily be eliminated” (FH 7.24; 303).

Despite his youth—indeed, partly because he was young—Lorenzo appeared to be a more promising leader than his father, Piero, had been. In one of the festivals Piero had sponsored to distract the citizens from the political turmoil in Florence, Lorenzo had won a tournament as a result of his own skill in military combat (FH 7.12; 290). The gravity and modesty of his speech of acceptance, as it were, at the convent had given the citizens hope of his becoming the prince they needed.

In his first notable public act Lorenzo gave a clear indication of the character of his future leadership. An alum mine had been discovered outside of Volterra (a Florentine dependent). Because the citizens did not recognize its value at first, some of them sought capital from Florentine citizens to develop the mine privately. However, when the Volterrans saw how profitable the mine was, they began to object vociferously to the private use of public property. They sent a delegation to Florence to protest and were not happy when the Florentines responded: “The people of Volterra [were] not seeking justice in desiring to deprive its citizens of their labor and industry, and that . . . the alum mines belonged to the private individuals and not to the people. But it would be very proper for [those private individuals] to pay a certain quantity of money each year as a sign that they recognized the people as superior” (FH 7.29; 307–8). This response provoked riots in Volterra, after which the Volterrans offered to keep the old agreements if the Florentines wished to do so. Tommaso advised the Florentines to accept the Volterrans on whatever terms they wished to return. But Lorenzo, who saw an opportunity “to demonstrate how much his advice and prudence were worth, . . . decided to undertake a campaign and punish with arms the arrogance of the Volterrans.” The Florentines quickly “put together ten thousand infantry and two thousand cavalry,” who easily seized the countryside around Volterra. Seeing how badly the one thousand soldiers they had hired to defend the city were outnumbered, the Volterrans opened the gates to the Florentine commissioners and their army. But after one of the Volterran priors was contemptuously plundered by a soldier, both those who had been hired to attack and those who had been hired to defend the city joined in sacking it. “The news of this victory was received with very great joy by the Florentines,” Machiavelli reports, “and because it had been altogether Lorenzo’s campaign, he rose to very great reputation from it.” However, when one of Tommaso’s friends reproached him for opposing the campaign, he responded that Volterra “appears to be lost; for if you had received it by accord, you would have had advantage and security from it; but since you have to hold it by force, in adverse times it will bring you weakness and trouble and in peaceful times, loss and expense” (FH 7.30; 308–9).

What Machiavelli shows but does not state explicitly is that Lorenzo’s decision to punish the “arrogance of the Volterrans” demonstrated his own desire to make an expensive show and gain reputation for himself more than a concern for justice, and that the Florentine people’s embrace of his lopsided “victory” revealed their corruption. A reader might wonder, therefore, why Machiavelli thought it prudent for the individual whose sagacity he affirms more repeatedly than that of any other character in this history not to accept the invitation extended by his fellow citizens to lead them. Lorenzo and Giuliano were young, and others were reasonably concerned about their ability to lead what had been an extremely fractious city. Machiavelli suggests that the envy of others, which he argued in the Discourses constitutes a major barrier to the rise of talented leaders in a republic, was one reason. Writing to and with the sponsorship of a Medici prince, Machiavelli might also have been hesitant to argue openly and directly that Tommaso should have accepted leadership of the republic, because Tommaso belonged to the family of the man who had been Machiavelli’s patron and whom Machiavelli had criticized for not eliminating his Medici opponents (D 1.52, 3.3, 3.30). Tommaso’s decision not to accept the petition of his fellow citizens to become head of Florence because of “his fortune and the fortune of his house” could also be taken to refer to Tommaso’s brother Niccolò’s failure to revive a truly free government in Florence, a failure to which Tommaso contributed by advising Niccolò to squander his opportunity to make a change when he was elected gonfalonier, and ended in the failure of every one of his associates to join him in a spirited armed opposition to Piero de’ Medici. As the reaction to the conspiracy against Piero showed, the Soderini did not command sufficient forces nor did they have sufficiently reliable allies to seize control of the state from the Medici, if the Medici objected, as they inevitably would. Prudence may tell a man what to do, but it is not sufficient to enable him to do what he knows should be done.

Without drawing the connection explicitly, Machiavelli demonstrates the truth of Tommaso’s contention that Florence could live at peace internally and defend itself from external aggressors only under the Medici by relating the fate of the Pazzi conspiracy and its aftermath. At the beginning of book 8 Machiavelli reminds his readers that before the victory of Piero’s party in 1466, citizens who were envious of the power of the Medici could openly oppose it without fear of being suppressed. After the Medici took complete control of the state, however, it was possible to oppose them only in secret. The Pazzi were a wealthy noble family to whom Lorenzo denied honors they and others thought they merited. One of the young members of the family thus conspired with the pope and his representatives to take the state away from the Medici by killing Lorenzo and Giuliano. Although more than fifty individuals knew what was planned, no one informed the brothers, as Machiavelli argues in D 3.6 someone usually will in order to gain the favor of the prince(s). The large number of collaborators may testify to the strength of the secret opposition, but, Machiavelli shows, the conspirators failed nevertheless. The first reason was the reluctance of the churchmen and the one experienced soldier involved to commit murder—especially in church. The conspirators were forced to rely on young men who had no experience with killing a man at close range and were not, therefore, sufficiently hardened to perform their assigned task. Although two of the young men appointed to attack the brothers when they entered the church succeeded in killing Giuliano, the other two assassins barely scratched Lorenzo, who fought to defend himself. The second and more decisive reason was, however, that when the head of the Pazzi family rode through the town calling to his fellow citizens to come and aid him in regaining their freedom, no one responded. Opposition had been made costly by the fortune and liberality of the Medici, Machiavelli explains, and liberty “was not known in Florence.” Calling out the name of the Medici, the people sought rather to apprehend and kill the murders.

As Machiavelli makes clear in the speech he attributes to Lorenzo after the attack, the Medici established a tyranny in Florence on the basis of the widespread popular favor that they had, in effect, bought with their liberality (while they eliminated the opposition by exiling or otherwise repressing them). Lorenzo told the three hundred citizens who assembled in the palace with the Signori that he did not know whether to grieve as a result of the fraud and hatred with which he had been attacked, or to rejoice when he considered the promptness, zeal, and love with which his brother had been avenged and he himself had been defended by the united consent of the whole city. He claimed not to know what private offense he had done the conspirators. (However, Machiavelli reports [FH 8.2] that Giuliano warned Lorenzo that in depriving the Pazzi of all honors Lorenzo risked losing everything in wanting too much, but that “Lorenzo, hot with youth and power, wanted . . . everyone to recognize everything as from him” [FH 8.3; 319]. Nor does Machiavelli remind his readers that in D 1.26 he argued that a new prince who “does not want to leave anything untouched in that province, so that there is no rank, no order, no state, no wealth there that he who holds it does not know it as from you,” uses “modes” that “are very cruel, and enemies to every way of life, not only Christian but human” [61–62].) If the conspirators complained about their lack of public honors, Lorenzo suggested, they were offending the public more than the Medici, “by making it appear that for our cause you injured undeservedly your own citizens.” His house had been exalted “with such agreement for no other cause than that it has striven with humanity, liberality, with benefits to surpass everyone” and that it had never risen “to any rank of greatness to which it was not thrust by . . . your united consent.” Now that the conspiracy had failed to overturn their state, the king of Naples and the pope had mounted an armed attack on the city; and, Lorenzo concluded, his fate was entirely in their hands: “it is for you to rule or leave me; you are my fathers, you my defenders; and however much I am commissioned to do by you, I will always do willingly.” Unable to restrain their tears, the citizens appointed a spokesman to reassure Lorenzo that the “city recognized how great were his merits and those of his family” and promised “that they would save his reputation and state for him.” And Machiavelli concludes, “so that their deeds should match their words, they provided publicly a certain number of armed men for the protection of his body, to defend him from domestic plots” (FH 8.10; 330). He does not observe, although most of his readers would know, that such armed bodyguards were the mark of a classical tyrant.52

The Florentines were not the only Italians to have lost their love of liberty, along with any knowledge of what it means to be free. Machiavelli leads up to his account of the failure of the Pazzi conspiracy at the beginning of book 8 by describing the failures of two other conspiracies at the end of book 7. In the first case, a young man whose family had been exiled from Florence decided to seek renown by conspiring to free Prato from Florentine rule. After his co-conspirators fraudulently obtained the key to the gates and let in the young man with his armed group, they seized the citadel and the palace. But they found no one willing to join them in rebelling against the Florentine government. Discovering the weakness of the conspirators, the many Florentines who lived in the town mounted a counterattack that resulted in the young man’s imprisonment and death.

In describing the second “unforeseen event of greater moment, which was the presage of greater evils,” Machiavelli explains that a teacher of Latin to leading youths in Milan convinced them that “all famous men had been nourished in republics and not under princes,” and made three of them “swear that as soon as they were of an age when they could, they would free their fatherland from the tyranny” of the duke. “Galeazzo was lecherous and cruel” (FH 7.34; 315), so he deserved to be overthrown; and he had provoked these young men to try to do so by dishonoring them. They thus deliberated together about the means, place, and time at which they could assassinate him. They settled on the day of San Stefano when the prince was accustomed to visit the church of the martyr and succeeded in killing him. Rather than being joined by many of the nobles and the whole people in regaining their freedom, however, the young men were recognized by some of the bystanders, caught, and killed. As Cosimo had wisely observed earlier, the Milanese were not capable of ruling themselves; they had become accustomed to living under a tyranny for too long. (Cf. P 4.)

Machiavelli concludes his account of the failure of the conspiracy to overthrow the duke of Milan, as he concluded his warnings against conspiracies in both P 19 and D 3.6, by warning a prince to “learn to live in a manner and act in a mode . . . , so that no one can hope, by killing him, to save himself,” and urging those who might consider conspiring against a prince to “know how vain is the thought that makes one trust too much that a multitude, even though malcontent, will either follow you or accompany you in your dangers” (FH 7.34; 316). But the implications of his descriptions of the failures of these attempts to return cities to liberty simply by replacing the current government are much broader. As Machiavelli argued explicitly in D 1.16–18, a corrupt government quickly corrupts the people so that they are no longer able to rule themselves. Those who wish truly to reform a city and its government have to do much more than merely assassinate the current tyrants. They have to assume kingly power and use harsh measures to introduce “new modes and orders” to force the people to learn how to defend themselves from oppression at home as well as abroad.

Lorenzo did not have the resources or desire to do either. After the pope’s first attempt to seize control of the city by means of the Pazzi conspiracy failed, he and the king of Naples attempted to do so by force. Lorenzo sought support from his “allies,” but Milan was then torn apart by the competition between the young Duke Gian Galeazzo’s uncles and widowed mother for control, and Venice characteristically refused to send aid when its immediate interests were not at stake. Lorenzo had to hire mercenary troops, who proved not only expensive but also characteristically unreliable. Tired of both war and the heavy taxes imposed to support it, his citizens finally protested (FH 8.17). Seeing that he could expect no aid from his current allies, Lorenzo thought that he needed to try to come to an agreement with one of his current enemies. Because the pope was supported by higher powers, and no single pope would hold office or could be relied upon for long, he decided to try the king. Ferdinand was impressed by Lorenzo’s daring by coming to Naples and putting himself under the king’s control as well as by the gravity and prudence of his speech. Nevertheless, he held Lorenzo in Naples for three months to test the truth of the rumors that in his absence Lorenzo would be overthrown by his enemies. Seeing that did not happen, he signed a mutual protection agreement with Lorenzo. Meanwhile fear of Mahomet the Grand Turk, who had landed on the coast of Italy and sacked the city of Otranto, forced the pope to adopt a more peaceful approach to his neighbors.

In 1484 all five of the major powers in Italy signed a peace accord that stated not only that “one could ask for the return of things lost but that one could make war on anyone who hindered their acquisition” (FH 8.29; 351). Florence used the opportunity to reacquire the town of Sarzana which had been seized from it by a private citizen of Genoa.53 However, although Florentine troops succeeded in retaking the town, Lorenzo did not live long enough to complete the negotiations for its surrender. At age forty-four he succumbed to the gout that had killed his father. Although Machiavelli does not state the implication of his retelling this incident in some detail, it shows that Lorenzo not merely did not surpass his grandfather Cosimo in adding to the Florentine empire; in fact, he was not even able to keep it all intact.

Like his grandfather, Machiavelli reports in a concluding account of his rule, Lorenzo took advantage of the peace to display both his own greatness and that of his city. Following the model of his father, Piero, rather than that of his grandfather Cosimo, Lorenzo married his eldest son to the daughter of an Orsini knight. He also saw that his second son, Giovanni, was named cardinal at less than fourteen years of age. (This cardinal later became Leo X.) Unlike his grandfather, Lorenzo did not prosper in mercantile trade, because his agents mismanaged his property. So his fatherland had to help him with a great sum of money when he decided to invest in land as a more stable form of wealth. Following his grandfather’s model in this respect, Lorenzo erected buildings in the properties he developed around Prato, Pisa, and the Val di Pesa that had the “magnificence . . . not of a private citizen but of a king” (FH 8.36; 361). He also sought to make his city greater and more beautiful by having new buildings erected. Unlike his predecessors, however, he sought to enhance the security of his own state and fend off enemies at a distance from the city by fortifying the town of Firenzuola and keeping mercenary captains along with an army at Sarzana. Following the example Cosimo had set with Count Sforza, Lorenzo also maintained his mercenary “friends,” the Baglioni in Perugia and the Vitelli in Città di Castello. And expanding upon his father’s attempt to distract the citizens of Florence from politics, he continually sponsored festivities. He embraced anyone who demonstrated excellence in an art and, like his grandfather, favored men of letters.54

Machiavelli seems to end with a panegyric when he states that “Lorenzo was loved by fortune and by God, because of which all his enterprises had a prosperous end and all his enemies an unprosperous one. . . . His reputation grew every day because of his prudence, for he was eloquent and sharp in discussing things, wise in resolving them, quick and spirited in executing them. Nor,” Machiavelli cautions, “can the vices of his be adduced to taint his great virtue, even though he was marvelously involved in things of Venus and he delighted in facetious and pungent games, more than would appear fitting in such a man” (FH 8.36; 362). Lorenzo had obviously acted contrary to Machiavelli’s advice to his nephew in P 20 and 23 about the importance of a prince’s maintaining a dignified appearance. But Machiavelli merely observes, “considering both his voluptuous [private] life and his grave [demeanor in public] life, one might see in him two different persons.” Once again Machiavelli does not state the implication of his observation explicitly, but Lorenzo’s private license would seem to have contributed not merely to his own painful death from the disease he inherited from his father a decade earlier. It would also have set a perfidious example of the misuse of the leisure that peace brings of the kind Machiavelli earlier attributed to the duke of Milan (FH 7.29), and that provoked the moral revolution led by Savonarola a mere two years after Lorenzo’s death. Machiavelli nevertheless ends by emphasizing the regret all Italians felt at Lorenzo’s death and by blaming the disasters that followed shortly thereafter on the ambition of Ludovico Sforza, who planted “seeds” that continued to grow and that “ruined and are still ruining Italy, . . . since the one who knew how to eliminate them, was not alive” (FH 8.36; 363).

Concluding his history with the death of Lorenzo instead of bringing it up to present times as he had suggested in his preface enabled Machiavelli to end with what appears to be a celebration of Medici rule. His immediate readers would know very well, however, that two years later Lorenzo’s son Piero gave up the forts intended to guard Florence from an attack from the north and fled before the invading French army. They could not have forgotten that after Savonarola negotiated a peaceful occupation of the city with the French, he and his party had also taken control of the government of Florence and instituted a program of moral reform. If, as Machiavelli observed in passing, in times of peace the young become idle and develop a taste for luxuries, and if the duke of Milan and his courtiers provided worse examples, what must have been the power of Lorenzo’s voluptuous private life in conjunction with his public magnificence on the Florentine youth? Cosimo had built magnificent palaces for himself, as well as churches, convents, and hospitals (which Machiavelli does not attribute to Lorenzo), with both public and private funds; but, Machiavelli emphasized, Cosimo had been careful not to give the impression that he thought he and his family were better than his fellow citizens, by arranging for his children to marry into Italian aristocratic families in other cities, the way his son and grandson did. Whereas Cosimo “left such a foundation to his descendants that with virtue they could equal him and with fortune surpass him” (FH 7.6; 284), Lorenzo the Magnificent left a city that depended on his personal presence, prudent dealings with other princes, and ability to speak well for its defense. Although he had built fortifications to defend Florence some distance from the city walls, he had done nothing to train an army of citizens serving under its own captains. Nor was it likely that his successors would be able to continue to buy popularity with their liberality, since he had used public funds to finance his magnificent projects. Those public funds would eventually need to be replenished, especially in the case of war, and that would require higher taxes that the citizens of Florence were apt to protest.


What the Florentine Histories Adds to Machiavelli’s Previous Writings


In both his Discourses and Florentine Histories Machiavelli presents Rome as the model of a virtuous republic and Florence as the example of a defective one. In both cases, he shows, the governments of the two cities developed as they did to a considerable extent as a result of their different circumstances.

Constituted by a group of exiles and robbers, Rome found it necessary to defend itself from its neighbors, so its people appointed a king able to organize and lead an army. That king had the foresight, however, to see the necessity of creating institutions that would maintain the order he had established. So he created a senate with whom he consulted and which had the right of electing his successor. When the kings became oppressive, the nobles rebelled and created annually elected consuls to lead the armies while the Senate retained the power of making laws. And when the rule of the senators became oppressive, the people rebelled by refusing to fight in the armies and insisted upon the creation of tribunes with the ability to prevent the nobles from oppressing the people.

Established as a colony of Rome, Florence had no immediate need to defend itself. But after both the empire and the city were destroyed by the barbarians, and the city was rebuilt by Charlemagne, the Florentines remained united and able to defend themselves. The first division in Florence arose from a private dispute between two noble families. That dispute became a contest for control of the state, however, after the two families recruited allies in their fight against each other, not only from other Florentines, but also from foreign powers. In contrast to the Romans, who eliminated the heads in cities when called in to end a civil war, neither the pope nor the emperor was able to impose or reestablish order in Florence. Although the Guelf party initially acquired some popular support because of its association with the Church, its Christian beliefs did not prevent it from oppressing the people after the Florentine Ghibellines were expelled. “Men in the middle” repeatedly tried to establish a government that included members of both parties, Ghibelline and Guelf, noble and popular; but ambitious Florentine politicians were not willing to share power with others. Nor did they, like the Roman Senate, feel themselves impelled to do so by the need to field an army. Like the Romans, the Florentines united internally in the face of external threats. Unlike the Romans, however, the Florentines looked to foreign powers to defend them—first to lead their own troops and, after these were destroyed as the result of the ambition of a foreign captain, to supply them with arms in exchange for money.

Machiavelli does not trace the corruption of Florence primarily to the failure of the republic to train and arm its citizens, however. He presents it as a failure of leadership. (In D 1.55 he argued that a man who knew what to do could found a republic or principality even where the circumstances did not favor it.) In the Florentine Histories, Machiavelli praises the virtues of named individuals: Farinata degli Uberti, who did not allow the Ghibellines to destroy the city after he conquered it for them (FH 2.7); Giano della Bella, who showed the people how to enforce the law on the nobles who were arrogantly flouting it (FH 2.13); Salvestro de’ Medici who tried to revive the laws made against the great, because he did not want to see the people oppressed (FH 3.9); Michele di’ Lando, who emerged from the rioting plebs as a natural leader (FH 3.16–18, 3.22); Giovanni de’ Medici, who sought to moderate the excesses of both the powerful and the people (FH 4.3, 4.10–11, 4.14, 4.16; 147–48, 155–56, 159–60, 161); and Niccolò da Uzzano, who warned his colleagues about the danger of the emerging Medici tyrant (FH 4.2–3). Not surprisingly, Machiavelli shows that neither good intentions nor persuasion is sufficient to maintain a republic. But he also shows that a republic cannot be established or maintained simply with the use of force. A people can retain its freedom only by means of laws that restrain both of the humors that arise in all cities. In Florence, he concludes, there was no “wise, good, and powerful citizen” able to institute and maintain such laws.

Machiavelli first attributes the turmoil in the Florentine republic to the arrogant unwillingness of the nobles to obey the laws and their repeated error in looking to foreign powers to defend the city rather than organizing and maintaining a defensive force composed of their own citizens. The ability of the nobles to flout the law was reduced when the Florentines passed legislation prohibiting anyone from owning a castle within twenty miles of the city. But a second and perhaps even more fundamental problem arose as a result of the change the Signori made in the way the highest magistrates were elected. (As Machiavelli indicates in D 3.49, the way in which elections are structured can determine whether a republic becomes corrupt or not.) By adopting a “mode” whereby the names of citizens eligible to hold the highest offices were put into bags and then drawn out by lot, the Signori enabled the party in power to make sure only its friends or partisans were drawn. In the Roman republic all citizens had eventually become eligible for the highest offices (D 1.60), and there were many competitors for the honor because there were many captains who had demonstrated their ability to lead others in military endeavors (D 1.30). But in Florence the people were not able to elevate either the most meritorious individuals or their own champions by means of elections. There were no public trials of individuals accused of attempting to overthrow the republic, so the people had to resort to the streets. They had no way of protesting oppression except by rioting; they vented their humors and took their vengeance on hated individuals whom they literally tore apart in the streets. And their riots convinced the “popular nobles” who had initially been sympathetic to the desire of the people not to be oppressed that the people, beginning with the plebs and laborers, should be excluded from the government. These nobles did not perceive the threat posed by their elevation of a very wealthy but kind man to the highest magistracy. Giovanni de’ Medici was regarded by the multitude as their champion, and his opposition prevented the noble party from seizing control of the state. He also tried to moderate the people’s desire to be avenged against their oppressors; but Machiavelli again shows that the salutary influence of one man does not last after his death. Cosimo learned from his father’s example that he could not merely secure himself but further his own ambitions, not by seeking to hold public office himself, but by benefiting as many individuals as possible privately with his wealth. But Cosimo was not able to restrain his party’s desire to acquire complete control of the state.

Because the popular nobles did not heed Niccolò da Uzzano’s warning about the danger of allowing a popular leader to arise uncontested, and the electoral laws did not encourage competition among ambitious individuals for popular favor, a new kind of tyranny was established in Florence. In D 3.28 Machiavelli distinguished between public and private modes of acquiring a “reputation,” and argued that the latter are dangerous in a republic because they enable an ambitious man to acquire partisans. But he did not mention a specific example—because in Rome there was no example. He was thinking of Florence, even though he did not say so explicitly. What Machiavelli’s Florentine Histories adds to his other works (in addition to providing more historical information and context for the positions he takes) are specifically his depiction and implicit analysis of this new danger.

The new form of tyranny that can arise in what is nominally a republic does not depend upon military might, as did Caesar’s conquest of Rome or as do many contemporary “authoritarian” military regimes. It will emerge, Machiavelli suggests, only in the absence of an immediate external threat of conquest; and when such a threat emerges, such a tyranny will either collapse or fall prey to a conqueror—or, as in Florence, both. This tyranny is deceptive, because its leaders not merely promise to benefit the people, but actually do so by distributing various kinds of goods to them as private individuals. To most of its subjects, such a tyranny does not appear to be onerous, so they are not inclined to resist or rebel against it. In order to distribute such private goods, however, individuals who seek to acquire tyrannical powers in this way have to be very wealthy. If they do not acquire their wealth by seizing it from others, they have to do so by means of trade. Machiavelli recognizes with the example of Venice that commerce is not simply incompatible with maintaining republican institutions. But as the decision of the Venetians to employ mercenary forces when they sought to expand by land indicates, merchants prefer buying to fighting. In this respect they are like the people they rule. In D 1.5 Machiavelli argued that the people are better guardians of their own liberty than the nobles, and in D 1.42 he used the example of the Decemvirs to show how easily young nobles can be corrupted by giving them a share in the rewards of tyrannical rule. But in the Florentine Histories Machiavelli shows how the people can also be corrupted by appeals to their desires for security of their lives and property. The recipients of individual benefits that a would-be tyrant grants them do not see or, if they do see, do not care that they are being deprived of their liberty. Once established, this form of “soft” tyranny is particularly difficult to uproot—except by means of a foreign invasion—because, as Machiavelli repeatedly shows, a corrupt people will not support those who seek to overthrow the tyranny and reestablish republican rule.

The republics Machiavelli saw (and that we continue to see in the modern world) tend to be based on commerce rather than primarily, as in Rome, on military might. They have to fear not the rise of a virtuous young general, such as Caesar in Rome, and the imposition of a tyranny by force, so much as the emergence of a seemingly beneficent figure like Cosimo who acquires power by means of his many partisans. In the Discourses Machiavelli suggested that modern republics could prevent a foreign power from taking away their liberty by forming a federation to protect them against invasions by other emerging powers with armies recruited from their subjects or citizens. In the Florentine Histories he suggests that their legislators can prevent the rise of a tyrant by what he calls private means internally by making sure that elections of the highest officials in the government cannot become controlled by parties or partisans the way they were in Florence. Such an individual may acquire power by liberally sharing the benefits of his own wealth, but he retains power by having his partisans take control of the state. They then destroy their competitors by means of force, false accusations, and onerous taxes. And although such a figure rises to power with popular support, once established his party seeks to insulate their rule from accountability to the people as well. Since no individual can continue to fund a widespread distribution of goods on his own, his partisans and successors will need to use public funds to buy support (and defenders) of their control of the state. They will, therefore, have to impose onerous taxes. The people will become impoverished and want to rebel, but they will not easily find experienced politicians able to organize an effective opposition. A naturally virtuous and good individual such as Michele di Lando may rise out of the crowd, recognize the need to impose order by means of force, and establish institutions that guarantee the lower classes a part in the government. Precisely because he does not seek control of the state for his own benefit, however, he does not recognize that desire in his allies, who will scheme to take control away from him. Someone who has learned about the two humors that divide every city from studying history needs to teach him the necessity of devising laws that not only reward virtuous individuals for their public service, but also enable the ambitious to check the self-regarding ambitions of others like them. That is the reason Machiavelli addressed all his writings to “princes” in an attempt to educate them.

Machiavelli’s condemnation of “sectarian” partisanship does not mean that he thinks that divisions or partisan conflicts within republics can or should be repressed. On the contrary, what are essential for the establishment and preservation of a free republic are laws that ensure that individuals have to compete for public support in order to realize their ambitions and that ambitious individuals are able to “watch each other particularly so that civil bounds are not transgressed” (FH 7.1; 277, emphasis added.) Unlike the mixed regime Machiavelli’s great student Montesquieu later praised in Britain, Machiavelli’s republic does not depend upon the existence of a landed aristocracy or a hereditary monarch. On the contrary, he argues, the condition for establishing a true republic is the absence of “gentlemen,” who do not have to work and can maintain their own independence from the government by means of their castles and arms. For that reason Machiavelli’s thought continues to apply to political life centuries later when most people consider the only legitimate regimes to be those with popular support.

According to Mansfield, that point is the devastating effect Christianity has had on modern politics. The problem with this thesis is that in the FH Machiavelli writes specifically about the problems caused by the pope’s calling in the “barbarian” invaders, which include the armies of the Christian kings of France and Spain. As in D 1.12, Machiavelli writes about the divisive effect the Church has had in Italy (which would also not be a pleasing topic for a pope), not the effect of Christianity on modern politics more generally. 6 Although I agree with Najemy that Machiavelli’s treatment of the rise of the Medici in a work dedicated to two members of the family is a problem, if not the central problem, raised by the Florentine Histories, I do not agree with his contention that Machiavelli’s concentration on Florentine history in “Discourse on Remodeling the Government of Florence” and Florentine Histories marks a fundamental shift in his thought. Following Najemy, Jurdjevic, Great and Wretched City, argues that in his “Discourse” Machiavelli changes both his historical “method” and his understanding of republican politics. In his “Discourse” and Histories Machiavelli undeniably gives more attention to Florence, both its history and its institutions, than he did in his previous works. But that attention is explained by the circumstances. He was invited to propose a constitutional reform and specifically commissioned to write the history; and in both, he applied the general understanding of politics he had developed earlier; he did not essentially modify it. Both Najemy and Jurdjevic emphasize the lesser role of individual leaders and greater differentiations among economic groups in Machiavelli’s later works. Both are, however, products or reflections of the equality of conditions that Machiavelli saw in Florence and that he explicitly stated in D 1.55 constitutes the condition under which a man who knew what to do could best found a republic. What Najemy sees as a change, Machiavelli presents as a problem. Florence did not have a leader with the knowledge needed to establish institutions and laws that would survive his death. Machiavelli notes that there were more divisions in Florence than there had been in other republics, but he does not present the greater number of divisions as an advantage. He does not try to solve the problems of class conflict or a purely popular (as opposed to mixed or aristocratic) republic by means of an increased number of interest groups the way James Madison later does in Federalist 10.


7 Although Machiavelli distinguished between public and private means of acquiring preeminence in D 3.28, he did not provide an ancient example of the successful use of such private means in Rome. In D 3.8 he acknowledges that both Spurius Cassius and Manlius Capitolinus sought to buy popular favor by providing the people with economic benefits, but in both cases the senators were able to persuade the people that these individuals were seeking to become tyrants and their ambitions were defeated. The successful use of such means appears to be a distinctively modern phenomenon, and Cosimo’s rise to preeminence in Florence the example par excellence. Modern political leaders no longer understand how to counter such a threat nor are they able to do so, because the people have become corrupt.


8 The negative lesson of Machiavelli’s account of Florentine history was not lost on the authors of The Federalist, who cite the history of the Italian republics as examples of the kind of defective politics they hope to avoid, for example in Federalist 10, or on Alexis de Tocqueville, who found Machiavelli’s description of Florentine politics particularly abhorrent. Jurdjevic compares Machiavelli’s four (and only four) uses of ‘generosity’—to describe Urban II’s crusade, the thirteenth-century Florentines’ use of a bell to warn Florence’s enemies to prepare for war a month before they planned to attack, the loss Florence suffered with the demise of its nobility, and the spirit that the duke of Athens thought would prevent the nobility from accepting his rule for long—with Machiavelli’s frequent use of ‘liberality’ to describe the economic munificence of the Medici that enabled them to corrupt and control others without actually using force or serving in public office. And he concludes that by ‘generosity’ Machiavelli means something like martial boldness. Such boldness would seem to be more similar to courage than to “generosity,” however. (Levy, Wily Elites, 18, points out that “originally the word meant ‘of noble birth,’ but Machiavelli distinguishes his meaning from the original one by speaking of generosity of spirit rather than of birth.” In the Discourses “Machiavelli speaks occasionally . . . of the generosity of the nobles and of the senate, but never of the people.”) What the “men of the people” Machiavelli goes on to describe lack is a willingness to organize their followers into an army able to wage war successfully and a desire for public honor if not glory that entails respect for the rules of combat and one’s opponents, as opposed to narrowly seeking their own private advantage, political as well as economic.
