See Gene Brucker, Renaissance Florence (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1983), 157–60.


27 He thus recommended a policy, Machiavelli reports in D 3.32, that some of the ancient enemies of the Romans and the Carthaginians adopted.


28 Noting that there is no historical record of such a speech, Yves Winter, “Plebian Politics: Machiavelli and the Ciompi Uprising,” Political Theory 40, no. 6 (2012): 754–56, suggests that it is especially appropriate for a theoretical speech to be delivered anonymously; it is and should be a general argument, which may thus reflect the views of the author. It is also especially appropriate for a plebian speaker not to be identified by his name or family; he would not be so known to his contemporaries. The problem with Winter’s first argument is that Machiavelli presents more than one anonymous speaker (e.g., the men of the middle in FH 2.14, and the representative of the citizens who loved their fatherland in FH 3.5). By making the speakers anonymous, Machiavelli may indicate that he made up the speeches he attributes to them. He seems to say as much in the dedication. However, even if these anonymous comments represent Machiavelli’s views, the speakers and their comments are sufficiently different that no one can be taken to represent the view of the author as a whole without more explanation. The problem with Winter’s second argument is that Machiavelli names the plebian who actually takes the lead of the rioters, Michele di Lando. Relying on Mark Phillips, “Barefoot Boy Makes Good: A Study of Machiavelli’s Historiography,” Speculum: A Journal of Medieval Studies 59 (1984): 598–603, Winter maintains that Machiavelli’s account of the uprising owes too much to Bruni, who, in contrast to the fourteenth-century chroniclers, inflated the roles of Salvestro de’ Medici and Michele. The chroniclers had emphasized the role of groups, whereas Bruni emphasized the responsibility of individuals. However, although Machiavelli chose to incorporate this aspect of Bruni’s account, as Phillips points out, Machiavelli did not follow it in all respects. Moreover, Machiavelli reminds his readers in FH 7.3 that he himself has a family name and that one of his ancestors was killed because he opposed the tyrannical regime. He is not and cannot thus be simply identified with a nameless pleb. In TM, 131–32, Strauss suggests that the anonymous plebian leader is a “caricature” of Machiavelli, especially in encouraging the plebs not to be frightened by conscience, i.e., by fear of hell. “But the caricature of a man reveals something of the man himself.” According to Strauss, “Machiavelli . . . does not seriously disagree with Livy’s judgment on the multitude. He does disagree with Livy, and with ‘all writers,’ on the status of morality.” He questions “the traditional view of aristocracy or the rule of men of moral worth. But questioning the traditional view of aristocracy is very different from adopting the extremely populist view which he seems to adopt in the 58th chapter [of D 1]. . . . According to Machiavelli, his dissection of the Roman republic entitles him to judge that the ruling class deserving of the name is necessarily superior to the multitude in foresight, but is certainly not morally superior; rather it is morally inferior to its subjects. To the extent to which he ironically accepts the major premise that human excellence is moral excellence, he arrives at the conclusion that the multitude is simply superior to ‘princes.’” But Strauss continues, “this does not mean that the acceptance of that major premise is arbitrary. Machiavelli . . . is a revolutionary, i.e., his adversaries have on their side the laws and everything respected and honored. Compared with the powers which he attacks, he may very well appear as he describes himself, namely, a being of low and abject condition; and, as he teaches, one rises from such a condition through fraud rather than through other means. He is ‘a man of the people’ not only in the literal sense.” However, Strauss concludes, “even a plebeian leader is not simply a plebeian, and a leader of the plebs is not necessarily himself a plebeian.” Having identified the anonymous plebian with Machiavelli, Strauss does not comment on the plebian leader who Machiavelli shows actually took charge. Machiavelli praises Michele for both his “goodness” and the “prudence” that enabled him to institute a new government, but he also shows that Michele did not know how to maintain his and his party’s place in it. Good and honest like the people, Michele did not understand and was not, therefore, able to protect himself and the people from the attempts of the popular nobles to regain control of the government.


29 Phillips, “Barefoot Boy Makes Good,” reports that the contemporary (1378) chronicles by Alamanno Acciaiuoli, Marchionne Stefani, and the Squittinatore explain that a scantily clad wool worker emerged as leader of the mob and took complete charge of the government of Florence for two to three days, but they do not mention or record his speech. Nor do they record that Michele ordered the mob to erect a gallows in the Piazza of the Priors or to search and find Ser Nuto. Machiavelli builds upon Bruni’s later description of Michele as possessing “a certain naïve authority and a character that was not ignoble” (Leonardo Bruni Aretino, Historiarum Fiorentini popoli libri XII, Rerum Italicarum Scriptores 19 [Città di Castello, 1917–34], 224). But none of the sources shows Michele explaining and developing a strategy for seizing control of the city and restoring order the way Machiavelli does. Interestingly, Machiavelli attributes Michele’s ability to do so entirely to his exceptional nature; unlike Bruni, Machiavelli does not attribute Michele’s ability to lead and organize the mob even in part to experience he had as a soldier in Lombardy.


30 Maurice Suchowlansky, “Rhetoric of Violence in Machiavelli’s Florentine Histories,” http://Shakespeare.edel.univ-poitiers.fr/index.php?id=549, thus argues that Machiavelli presents Michele as a hero, an exemplary figure able to channel the ferocity of the plebians, capable of reorganizing the Florentine republic and creating a fairer system of political participation. But some commentators, e.g., Martine Leibovici, “From Fight to Debate: Machiavelli and the Revolt of the Ciompi,” Philosophy and Social Criticism 28, no. 6 (2002): 647–60, continue to celebrate “the boundlessness of the desire for freedom that exceeds all definite developments” (658). Although Machiavelli praises Michele for having brought more of the Florentine population into the government, he also shows that the guilds and their banners, first instituted by a Ghibelline government trying to prevent the resurgence of their Guelf opposition, pressed for most of the changes in the government and were responsible for the final results. The force of the multitude needs to be organized, Machiavelli repeatedly shows, in order to be politically effective.


31 Machiavelli’s listing of the many “diverse humors” each with “a different end”—the “ancient nobles, called ‘great’” who wanted to recover their public honors and “for this would have loved that authority be given back to the captains of the Party,” “the popular nobles and the greater guilds” who “were not pleased with having to share the state with the lesser guilds and the lesser people,” “the lesser guilds” who “wanted rather to increase than diminish their dignity,” and “the lesser people [who] were afraid lest they lose their Collegi from their guilds” (FH 3.21; 134–35)—has led some commentators (e.g., Najemy and Jurdjevic) to argue that in his Florentine Histories Machiavelli moved away from his division of all cities into the two opposed humors of the “great” and the “people” in order to recognize more varied groups and economic interests. However, those humors which Machiavelli maintains exist in all cities constitute dispositions toward the government, not economic classes (even though the grandi are apt to be rich). The varied groups could, moreover, easily be divided into those who were seeking more power for themselves (like the “great”) and those “lesser people” who wanted simply to keep what power and consequent protection they had.


32 In D 1.17 Machiavelli gave Dion and Timoleon as examples of virtuous citizens who kept their city free while each lived, but whose cities returned to tyranny after they died. Here he gives examples of individuals whose virtues maintained the tyranny of the popolari.


33 We see the way in which Machiavelli alters history in order to support the lesson he purports to derive from it when we compare what he says in praise of Niccolò da Uzzano in FH 4.3, 4.19, 4.27 with D 1.33. There in arguing that “when an inconvenience has grown either in a state or against a state, the more salutary policy is to temporize with it rather than to strike at it,” Machiavelli writes: “Niccolò da Uzzano, a man held to be very expert in civil affairs, . . . had made the first error of not recognizing the dangers that could arise from the reputation of Cosimo. [But] while he lived, he did not ever permit the second to be made—that is, of attempting to eliminate him—since he judged that such an attempt would be the entire ruin of their state, as one sees it was after his death” (72).


34 Thucydides 3.41–48. Unfortunately, Machiavelli also shows, Uzzano had less success.


35 Machiavelli here treats the governors of Florence too kindly; the translators report (FH 4.21; 168n2) that Astorre was, in fact, acquitted.


36 For this reason, many commentators take Niccolò da Uzzano to speak for the author. Yet, we have seen, Machiavelli attributes similar views to Giovanni de’ Medici and shows that they both failed to have the effect they desired. Unlike their opponents they either did not desire to organize a following (in the case of Giovanni, whose opposition to the formation of “sects” [FH 4.11] was not shared by his son Cosimo) or were not able to do so (in the case of Uzzano, whose reputation was envied by his colleagues).


37 Since this is a Roman policy that Machiavelli strongly recommends in D 2.23, one should be cautious about simply equating the views of Niccolò Machiavelli with those of Rinaldo’s opponent, Niccolò da Uzzano. Whereas the latter advised his friends to remain neutral (FH 4.27; 176), Machiavelli explicitly argues against such a foreign policy in P 20, and in D 2.23 embraces Camillus’s advice to the Romans not to take the middle way with those they conquered, but either to destroy or to embrace them.


38 To arouse fear of opposition in others, they did behead one man and put to death the four exiles the Venetians returned to Florence as prisoners.


39 Salvatore Di Maria, “Machiavelli’s Ironic View of History: The Istorie Fiorentine,” Renaissance Quarterly 45, no. 2 (Summer 1992): 248–70. He explicitly accepts the reading offered by Gennaro Sasso, Niccolò Machiavelli: Storia del suo pensiero politico (Naples: Instituto italiano per gli studi storici, 1958), 310, and “Machiavelli e la teoria dell’ anacyclosis,” Rivista storica italiana 70 (1958): 333–57, who distinguishes Machiavelli’s understanding of the cycle from Polybius’s, but nevertheless thinks that the former presents a cycle based on human rather than more generally natural causes. Hulliung (Citizen Machiavelli, 152–55), Pocock (Machiavellian Moment, 217), and Kersting (Niccolò Machiavelli, 62–73), also see Machiavelli adopting a version of the ancient cyclical view.


40 In his Discourses Machiavelli also praises Cato, but for his opposition to Scipio, because he saw that such a preeminently virtuous individual was a potential tyrant. See D 1.29, 3.1. He does not mention Cato’s opposition to philosophy, and he attributes the fall of the Roman republic to the greed that produced the civil wars and the prolongation of commands that enabled generals in those wars to acquire partisans.


41 As John M. Najemy, “Machiavelli and History,” Renaissance Quarterly 67, no. 4 (2014): 44–45, also sees, Machiavelli undercuts the cyclical view in both places.


42 In fact, Machiavelli shows (FH 3.34; 228) that the victory had domestic as well as foreign benefits, insofar as it ended any hopes the Florentine exiles had of returning to the city. He downplays these benefits, perhaps because he characterized the hopes of the Florentine exiles earlier as “vain” in the mind of the duke of Milan (FH 5.9; 195) and warned his readers more generally about the danger of believing those who had been banished in D 2.31.


43 As the translators note (227n3), Machiavelli departs here from his source, Biondo, who suggests that at least seventy died in the battle of Anghiari. That’s still a relatively low number of casualties in a daylong battle involving thousands of soldiers; but we see that Machiavelli exaggerates the low cost to support his critique of the military practices of his time.


44 Machiavelli does not explicitly point out that the Florentine troops defeated earlier at Zagora were cavalry (FH 4.6; 151n4), or comment on the fact that Neri specifically offered the Venetians the assistance of “the count with seven thousand cavalry and two thousand infantry” (FH 5.21; 210). But in books 5 and 6 Machiavelli makes it clear that the troops whose “vile” battles resulted in no lasting victories or losses were primarily on horse. Indeed, in these two books he appears to be trying to illustrate, if not, strictly speaking, to demonstrate, with a detailed account of recent Italian history the perfidy and basic ineffectiveness of such troops for which he argued generally in the Prince (especially P 9) and Discourses (especially D 2.10–15, 2.20). (He observed in the preface that the excellence and persuasiveness of a history lies in the details.) He was, in other words, quite well aware of the form of military organization and “technology” that had replaced earlier citizen militias in Italy—and wanted to replace it for political more than strictly military reasons.


45 Christopher Lynch, “War and Foreign Affairs in Machiavelli’s Florentine Histories,” Review of Politics 74, no. 1 (2012): 1–26, rightly emphasizes the importance of both war and foreign affairs, but he goes too far in maintaining that “the relation between the house of Medici and the house of Sforza . . . reveal[s] the fundamental dependence of the former on the latter to be the chief factor determining the narrative line of the work overall” (2). Cosimo’s success in buying support in domestic politics may have prevented him from understanding the ambition of the mercenary captain and his consequent refusal to fight wars on behalf of others after he became duke (FH 7.6). But Sforza’s experience as a mercenary captain did not prepare him to rule as anything but a tyrant; and that was the “legacy” he left his son and grandson. Although Machiavelli brings out the many defects of Cosimo’s rule, the weakness of his son Piero, and the less than magnificent actual achievements of Lorenzo “the Magnificent,” their rule of Florence was certainly better than the treatment Sforza and his progeny gave the Milanese.


46 Mansfield, “Party and Sect,” 138.


47 Jurdjevic, Great and Wretched City, 157, notes that Cosimo’s party thus restructured the state (presumably to maintain its control and squelch any opposition) every 3.5 years, even more frequently than Machiavelli suggested in D 3.1, where he stated that “those who governed the state of Florence from 1434 up to 1494 used to say . . . that it was necessary to regain the state every five years; otherwise, it was difficult to maintain it.” And “they called regaining the state putting that terror and that fear in men that had been put there in taking it, since at that time they had beaten down those who . . . had worked for ill. But as the memory of that beating is eliminated, men began to dare to try new things and to say evil” (211). The perceived need Cosimo and his party saw to retake (and restructure) the state suggests that they did not rule smoothly or uninterruptedly on the basis of simple consent.


48 Machiavelli’s brief account of Cosimo’s rule with Neri for the first twenty-one years occupies less than a chapter; the challenges to his rule by other ambitious party members occupy most of three chapters. By way of contrast, he devotes eleven chapters to Piero’s relatively brief and ineffective reign, and approximately one-third of book 7 in addition to virtually all of book 8 to the reign of his grandson, Lorenzo the Magnificent.


49 He certainly did not compare Cosimo to one of the Roman emperors, as did some of the lyric poets, who were seeking his patronage for their own work. Alison M. Brown, “The Humanist Portrait of Cosimo de’ Medici, Pater Patriae,” Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes 24 (1961): 186–221, presents a useful summary and tripartite categorization of previous humanist eulogies of Cosimo. She begins by noting that Machiavelli asked his readers not to be surprised that he “imitated those who write the lives of princes instead of those who write universal histories,” and “that his description was the source of so much that was later written about him,” but she does not point out the differences between Machiavelli and the earlier humanists’ eulogies.


50 Machiavelli may have thought that as a prudent man Cosimo should have known that princes (and republics) can always find an excuse for not keeping faith. He does not disagree with Cosimo’s characterization of the duke. In the next chapter (FH 7.7) Machiavelli describes the marriages and other alliances the duke and the king of Naples made with each other to “establish their states so that they could enjoy them securely while they lived and leave them freely to their heirs when they died” (285). The king eliminated the barons who had injured him in the war against Jean of Anjou, and when Jacopo Piccinino saw this, he became afraid and sought to reconcile himself with the duke. The duke promised the mercenary captain marriage to his natural daughter, but fearing that Jacopo would attempt to seize power the way he himself had, Sforza arranged to have the king promise to employ Jacopo and bring him to Naples, where the king then imprisoned and killed the mercenary captain. “So much did our Italian princes fear in others the virtue that was not in themselves, and they eliminated it, so that, since no one remained who had it, they exposed this province to the ruin that not long after wasted and afflicted it” (FH 7.8; 286).


51 Rob Hatfield, “A Source for Machiavelli’s Account of Piero de’ Medici,” Studies on Machiavelli (1972): 319–33, reports that neither he nor any other historian had been able to find any evidence of Piero’s calling in his loans. (Hatfield cites R. de Roover, The Rise and Fall of the Medici Bank [Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1963], 359, and N. Rubinstein, The Government of Florence under the Medici (1434–94) [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1966), 140n1], as support.) He then discovered Fra Giovanni di Carlo, Livri de temporibus suis, composed of three books, the first of which, entitled Difensio Cosmi et suorum adversus Philelphum: De bello Dietisalvico et Collionico, contains essentially the same account Machiavelli gives and, Hatfield concludes, must have been his source. Like the end of the Florentine Histories, Fra Giovanni’s three books deal with Florence under the rules of Cosimo, Piero, and Lorenzo de’ Medici. Hatfield observes that Fra Giovanni’s depiction of Piero as an innocent and Dietisalvi as a man who violated the laws of decency and had to pay in the end is more moralistic than Machiavelli’s history, but the overlap leads him to wonder whether the story is not a pure invention and whether Machiavelli was trying to write an apology for the Medici the way Fra Giovanni had. I argue, on the contrary, that Machiavelli is showing that neither the elderly Cosimo nor his invalid son Piero was able to prevent their party from establishing a tyranny in Florence. The problem went beyond personal failures or weaknesses. Because the people had become corrupt under Medici rule, as Machiavelli prescribes in D 1.18, it would have been “necessary to turn it more toward a kingly state than toward a popular state, so that the men who cannot be corrected by the laws because of their insolence should be checked in some mode by an almost kingly power” (51). Lorenzo the Magnificent may have appeared to be establishing a hereditary kingdom, but the demonstrations of his power and wealth took the form of spectacles more than exercises of real force (which he did not have at his command).


52 Thucydides 6.56–57; Plato, Republic 566b; Xenophon, Hiero 2.8.


53 Machiavelli explains that this citizen turned the defense of the town over to San Giorgio, a private group of creditors, who were granted a share of the customs collected in Genoa as repayment, and the palace above the customs house as a place to meet. This group constituted a government for itself with a council of one hundred to deliberate and a magistracy of eight citizens to execute the council’s decisions. As a pledge of repayment of its debts, the commune of Genoa also put most of the towns and cities subject to Genoa under the administration of San Giorgio, which both defended them and had a rector elected in each by public suffrage. As a result, because the government of Genoa often shifted between its own citizens and foreigners, whereas the government of San Giorgio remained constant, the citizens gradually came to regard the government of the Commune as tyrannical and shifted their loyalty to San Giorgio. It merely asked whatever party gained control of the Commune to “swear to observe its laws, which have not been altered up to these times.” Emphasizing the advantages of a stable government under laws established with popular consent over one imposed by force and fraud, Machiavelli comments that it was “an example truly rare, never found by the philosophers in all the republics they have imagined and seen, to see within the same circle, among the same citizens, liberty and tyranny, civil life and corrupt life, justice and license, because that order alone keeps the city full of its venerable customs” (FH 8.29; 352). San Giorgio mounted a spirited defense of the town, but Machiavelli also reports that the Florentines were able to recapture it, after their commissioners came to encourage their troops. However, although Lorenzo came in person to have the affair concluded “with more reputation,” his death prevented him from negotiating a settlement.


54 Machiavelli’s description of Lorenzo here seems to follow his recommendations in the concluding paragraph of P 21 about the ways a prince may become esteemed. There Machiavelli suggests that a “prince” can provide his fellow “citizens” with all the advantages of the “free way of life” he describes in D 2.2 with one exception: they cannot hope for their children to be elevated to the highest offices. The one way in which Machiavelli indicates that Lorenzo the Magnificent may not have followed this model concerns the importance of a prince’s making his “citizens” feel secure in their lives and property, believing that what they have earned with their own industry and intelligence will not be taxed away. Although Machiavelli does not draw this conclusion explicitly, his reporting that Lorenzo had to use public rather than his own private funds to display his “magnificence” and build forts and maintain mercenary troops to secure his state suggests that he or his successors would have had to raise taxes and so make the Florentines feel less secure about keeping the fruits of their own labor.


CONCLUSION


Machiavelli’s Enduring Interest


Machiavelli directed the first production of Clizia in January 1525 and completed his history in March of that year. He did not present the Florentine Histories to Clement VII until May, however, because the pope was trying to negotiate a treaty with Emperor Charles V. The emperor’s troops had defeated the French in February and taken Milan; as a result, the rest of Italy lay open to invasion. Clement was apparently pleased by Machiavelli’s history. He doubled the fee upon which they had initially agreed by paying in gold, and he accepted Machiavelli’s advice to arm his subjects in the Romagna to fight the emperor. However, the pope characteristically changed his mind after Francesco Guicciardini reminded him that the people of Romagna were not friendly and that they could not and would not pay taxes to support the effort.

Although he seems to have acquired a favorable hearing from Clement, Machiavelli never received the appointment to high office he had so assiduously sought from the Medici. The pope did decide to reinforce Florence’s fortifications, and Machiavelli was put in charge of a new magistracy established to supervise the strengthening of the city’s walls. He was also charged to “reorder the militia,” but he found them too corrupt.1 The pope, the king of France, Florence, and Venice formed a Holy League against the emperor in February 1526, but divisions among the commanders prevented them from using their numerical superiority effectively against the ill-supplied imperial troops. In February 1527 they succeeded in deflecting an attack on Florence, but the imperial troops aided by the Colonna went on to sack Rome. In the meantime the citizens of Florence expressed their hatred of the Medici by seizing the Palazzo Vecchio and demanding a restitution of the republic.

Encouraged by his faithful friends Zanobi Buondelmonti and Luigi Alammani, Machiavelli expected to be reappointed by the republic to his former position as secretary. However, the piagnoni (supporters of the party of Savonarola), who controlled the new republic, did not trust Machiavelli, because he had served the Medici pope in the disastrous war against the emperor. On June 10, 1527, Francesco Tarugi, who had served as secretary of the Pratica since June 1515 and was a Medici supporter, was appointed instead. Machiavelli fell ill shortly thereafter and died on June 21. Relying on a contemporary report, his biographer explains:

“Everyone hated him because of the Prince”: the rich thought that his Prince was a document written to teach the Duke “how to take away all their property, from the poor all their liberty, the Piagnoni regarded him as a heretic, the good thought him sinful, the wicked thought him more wicked or more capable than themselves, so that all hated him.” So Busini wrote.2


The fact that Machiavelli confessed his sins to a Friar Matteo before he died (and had composed an “Exhortation to Penitence” to be delivered to one of the confraternities to which he is said to have belonged not long before) has given rise to some debate among the scholars about the author’s own religious convictions. All agree, however, that Machiavelli died reviled more than praised, his hopes of serving not merely his own city, but Italy as a whole, frustrated and defeated.

Machiavelli’s writings had much more influence on later political philosophy and practice than their author had on the leaders of Florence or Italy during his lifetime. The Prince and Discourses on Livy were published five years after his death with papal permission. But, as noted earlier, they had already begun to circulate in manuscript form. And even though Machiavelli’s works were put on the papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559, they continued to be broadly disseminated. “Over two hundred printed editions of his works appeared in the sixteenth century, another hundred in the seventeenth century, and more than one hundred seventy in the eighteenth.”3

Republican political theorists such as James Harrington, Algernon Sidney, and Henry Neville explicitly adopted—and adapted—Machiavelli’s conceptions of political virtue, elections, and the salutary effects of conflict. Although the framers of the Constitution of the United States do not cite Machiavelli as the source of their ideas about the ends of government or how those ends can be achieved, they did look to Montesquieu, who was both an acknowledged student of his Italian predecessor and wary of his influence. It is difficult not to hear the echo of Machiavelli in James Madison’s famous declaration in Federalist 51: “Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. The interest of the man must be connected with the constitutional right of the place.” Machiavelli warned both princes and republican legislators about the “wickedness” of men; and in Federalist 51 Madison observes: “it may be a reflection on human nature, that such devices should be necessary to control the abuses of government. But what is government itself, but the greatest of all reflections on human nature? If men were angels, no government would be necessary.” The author of The Prince and Discourses would have agreed that “in framing a government which is to be administered by men over men, the great difficulty lies in this: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself.” Having argued that elections were a far better mode of acquiring good leaders than hereditary succession or military conquest, Machiavelli also thought that “a dependence on the people is, no doubt, the primary control on the government; but experience has taught mankind the necessity of auxiliary precautions.” He, too, argued that the “policy of supplying, by opposite and rival interests, the defect of better motives, might be traced through the whole system of human affairs, private as well as public.” In addition to the “checks and balances” embodied in the construction of the national government, the framers of the American Constitution proposed to establish a federation that enabled them not only to defend the newly established states but also to expand across the continent and so create a republican empire. That again can be seen to be Machiavelli’s idea, sketched in book 2 of the Discourses, but communicated more directly to the Americans by Montesquieu.

Not all of Machiavelli’s acknowledged followers embraced the republican mode of government he himself had preferred or the gradual way of achieving and maintaining it that he had recommended. Continental European political theorists and practitioners heeded Machiavelli’s insistence upon the need for one man or mind to be at the head of any truly new enterprise; they also saw that the “head” would necessarily have to use force and fraud not only to eliminate the opponents of his new order, but also to keep his own followers in line. In a word, they would have to use terror. According to Robespierre, “the plan of the French Revolution was written large in the books . . . of Machiavelli.”4 Karl Marx was reading the Discourses in 1848 when he composed the Communist Manifesto; and in a letter to Friedrich Engels of September 25, 1857, he recommended study of the Florentine Histories as well as the development of the Italian military system in the fifteenth century in order to understand the “connection between productive forces and social relations.”5 In other words, Machiavelli’s students on the continent saw not only the central importance of the conflict between the classes (even if they tended to define that conflict in fundamentally economic rather than political terms). They also noted the emphasis he put on arms and, more particularly, on the need to order or organize their own followers in quasi-military fashion. Machiavelli’s influence can be observed, in fact, on both the left and the right. According to his biographer, Lenin also read and admired Machiavelli, although he did not name the infamous Italian in public.6 Benito Mussolini, on the other hand, published an essay on Machiavelli’s Prince shortly before he consolidated his dictatorship with the kidnapping and brutal murder of the leader of the parliamentary opposition in 1924. Arrested as part of the opposition to the Fascists, a leader and theorist of the Italian Communist Party, Antonio Gramsci, wrote in prison that Machiavelli’s book “was intended for an entire revolutionary social class, and that its aim was to instruct this class in the need to coalesce around a leader or ‘prince’ capable of acting boldly and not in accordance with the received morality of the time.” Indeed, he argued that the “‘modern prince’ . . . will not be a single man, but rather a political party expressing the interests of the revolutionary class.”7

The influence of ideas on events is notoriously difficult if not impossible to prove conclusively. There are too many factors at work to attribute any particular outcome to any one particular source. It is possible, however, to show simply from reading his works that Machiavelli not merely saw that European states were becoming larger but was able to sketch some of the implications for both the internal organization and foreign policies of those states.8 Internationally his observations concerning the conflict at the heart of all politics and the need to redirect that conflict in order to preserve the liberty of all parties pointed toward the emergence of something like the balance of powers that actually developed in Europe a century or more later. With regard to the internal organization of these states his analysis also pointed toward the two major alternative modes of achieving the popular political ends he endorsed.9

Machiavelli constitutes a “watershed” in the history of Western political philosophy, I have argued, because he was the first to redefine the purpose of government as the satisfaction of popular desires for security of life, family, and property.10 As Strauss notes, “Machiavelli was ‘a man of the people’ not only in the literal sense” (TM, 131). Once political theorists and practitioners accepted that understanding of the end of government, the challenge was no longer to find a way of selecting and educating a few good men to rule for the good of the community as a whole. The challenge was to find and articulate the best means of achieving those popularly desired ends. Machiavelli’s writings pointed in two different directions—republican and “princely” (or, as we might now say, “authoritarian”)—because, as Strauss also observes, Machiavelli differed from later democratic political theorists in arguing that democratic means are not always or in all circumstances the best way of achieving popular ends. Whether they wished to establish and maintain a popular or “princely” single-headed government, Machiavelli clearly thought, those who wanted to become political leaders needed to understand the passions that move human beings and the ways in which those passions can be channeled to support an effective political order. Since those passions put human beings in conflict with one another, these leaders needed to learn to fight both as human beings with laws and as beasts with force and fraud, in order to found and sustain their government or “dominion.”

To see the change Machiavelli wrought in political thought it may be useful briefly to compare his understanding of politics with that of Aristotle. Although some scholars have maintained that Machiavelli writes in a republican tradition stemming from Aristotle, 11 there are at least five fundamental differences. First, whereas Aristotle suggests in book 1 of his Politics that political communities emerge naturally out of the family, Machiavelli maintains that they are formed to defend vulnerable individuals and communities from the aggression of others.12 According to Machiavelli, political organization thus arises out of a natural necessity, self-preservation, but it is artificially constructed by human beings. It is not natural nor does it arise spontaneously.13 Second, whereas Aristotle suggests that the division of labor characteristic of the household as well as the city is and ought to be based on natural differences of inclination and talent, Machiavelli maintains that human nature is basically the same in all. Although he observes that human beings have different inclinations by nature, he sees that those inclinations are either strengthened or changed by individuals’ experience, and that education and training are stronger and more reliable than nature in determining the characteristics of individuals as well as peoples. Machiavelli has been criticized by feminist commentators for not paying sufficient attention to women and treating them negatively when he does. However, although Machiavelli (in)famously declares that “because fortune is a woman, . . . it is necessary, if one wants to hold her down, to beat her and strike her down” (P 25; 101), and purports to discuss “how a state is ruined because of women” in D 3.26, he also observes that when moved by political ambition, women such as Caterina Sforza and Servius Tarquin’s daughter can be as cruel and free from family attachments as their male counterparts. If anything, Machiavelli shows in his comedies, women are even more concerned about their reputation than men; he does not depict them as particularly nurturing or gentle.14 Nor does he try to distinguish political rule from mastery, the way Aristotle does, partly because he does not recognize any such being as a natural slave.15 Third, like Aristotle in book 3 of the Politics, Machiavelli sees that political associations are characterized by conflict. But, according to Aristotle, that conflict concerns the determination of which part of the city has a just claim to rule, and it is a matter of deliberation more than force. Offices or “honors” should be apportioned not only on the basis of the individual or group’s ability to perform the task in question, but also on the basis of the importance and quantity of their contribution to the common good. In making some decisions, Aristotle suggests, a large number of users or those affected are better able to determine the quality of a service or building than those able to provide it. One has to examine the particular characteristics and circumstances of the people in question. According to Machiavelli, however, cities are divided into two humors, one of which wishes to rule and the other not to be ruled; and the outcome is determined by relative strength and institutional design, not justice. Fourth, Aristotle famously categorizes political regimes not only according to the number of people who rule—one, few, or many—but also according to whether they rule for the sake of the common good or merely for their own benefit. Machiavelli reduces the kinds of government or types of “dominions” to two—principalities and republics—ruled by one or more than one. He blurs even this distinction, moreover, by showing that all governments at times need expeditious unitary leadership in cases of emergency but require the support of most of their citizens or subjects most of the time if they are to last. Finally and most fundamentally, according to Aristotle, political order is and ought to be based on nature. According to Machiavelli, political orders emerge as a result of the natural necessity human beings who are weak when isolated from one another feel to come together to defend themselves from others. Human beings do not gather together because they are naturally sociable or attracted to the company of one another, much less to fulfill some natural inclination to govern themselves on the basis of deliberation. On the contrary, political order has to be imposed and is always partly maintained by force, because human beings do not naturally want to be ruled. There is, therefore, always opposition to the government, which will be more or less open or covert, depending upon the circumstances and the ability of those in office to quash it.

In his Discourses and Art of War Machiavelli argues that “training” (esercitato), education (educazione), and art (arte) provide more reliable foundations of political order than nature. In his Nicomachean Ethics Aristotle also emphasized the importance of repeated actions in producing virtuous individuals. But the courageous, moderate, liberal, magnanimous, just, truthful, sociable, and witty actions he described were the deeds of individuals raised in families and guided by laws. He described these virtues, moreover, as a “mean” between two extremes—the “middle way” that Florentine politicians traditionally sought and that Machiavelli emphatically rejects. Instead of leading individuals to form virtuous dispositions, as Aristotle recommended, partly by means of praise and blame, partly by means of laws, and partly as a result of an informed philosophical understanding of what is truly virtuous, Machiavelli uses military training as the primary example of the way in which human beings can be transformed into loyal, ordered citizens. As he describes it in the Art of War, this training includes not merely the ordering of men in small groups that answer to a clear hierarchy of commands and practice the relevant skills. There must also be strict regulation of the spoils or profits of war. But most of all, the formation of an army requires a captain who is able to arouse and maintain the confidence of his troops. Such a captain must be able to speak persuasively to his troops, but words often do not suffice to overcome fear. A captain must, therefore, also know how to arrange their order in battle so that his men will find it necessary to fight for their lives if they are to survive. For the same reason, he will do what he can to encourage a hostile force or captured city to lay down their arms rather than desperately fight until they die. To the extent possible, the captain will enhance the confidence of his troops by leading them into battles and by choosing circumstances where they are apt to win. He will, moreover, follow the Roman example of involving the soldiers in the punishment of those who disobey orders so that the soldiers will identify with the judges who order the executions rather than with the victims.

The military training or “ordering” that Machiavelli recommends might well appear to be suited to make human beings subjects rather than free and equal citizens. As he observes in D 1.16, “a people . . . used to living under a prince . . . is nothing other than a brute animal that, although of a ferocious and feral nature, has always been nourished in prison and in servitude.” If suddenly freed, “not knowing how to reason about either public defense or public offence,” it “will quickly fall back under a yoke.” The “training” necessary to produce citizens of a free republic must therefore encompass more than military service. It must also include the experience of electing its own leaders and judging their possible offenses in trials as prescribed by law, so that rotation in office becomes an expectation, not an exceptional occurrence. As an army needs to attach the passions of the soldiers to their leaders and the order they seek to maintain, so a republic needs to attach the affections of its citizens to the government by promising them or their progeny the possibility of election to the highest offices. The problem is that people tend to take the advantages of free government for granted. No longer perceiving the need or becoming afraid to organize and press for their own interests against those in power, the people become slavish and lose their liberty. People cannot defend themselves from the ambitions of the great, Machiavelli emphasizes, unless they are organized and armed, and that organization and arming require leadership. Popular leaders threaten to become tyrants, however, especially if they appeal to the desire of the people for vengeance against those who have oppressed them and are thus able to eliminate all the leader’s potential competitors for the highest offices.

According to Machiavelli, there is no “common good,” if by common is meant a good that every member of the political community both desires and shares. Because human beings naturally exist in competition and conflict with one another, they form cities to protect themselves from the aggression of others; and once they feel secure from aggression, they attempt to seize the lands and goods of others. Once formed, these cities also divide internally into the two humors of the great, who want to dominate and oppress, and the people, who do not wish to be dominated or oppressed. Every political community is, therefore, always divided into at least two parts or parties (although one may not show itself, because it is oppressed, and the dominant party, as in Florence, may fracture into many competing parts). In D 2.2 Machiavelli can nevertheless write of “the common good that makes cities great” (bene commune è quello che fa grandi le città), which is “without doubt not observed, if not in republics,” because “those for whom the aforesaid [republic] does good are so many that they can go ahead with it against the dispositions of the few crushed by it” (130). The “common good” is thus the good of the vast majority of people who want the security government by law can provide without oppression. It does not include the good desired by “the great,” who seek not merely to preserve what they have but to acquire more, and having tasted how sweet it is to dominate others, want to command and oppress more people. However, Machiavelli also argues that it is possible to design the “modes and orders” of a republic so that the great are able to satisfy their desire to rule only by striving to satisfy the desires of the people. In that way it is possible to achieve an aggregate combination of the two opposed desires that results in a good, liberty under law, which is shared by both, but, strictly speaking, is not desired by either.16 As Machiavelli observes in FH 3.1, people perceive laws and government as restrictions on their liberty, which they mistakenly identify with no-rule or license. The people thus need to be frequently reminded why government is necessary in order to acquire the security they desire. The easiest but most dangerous way this happens is by means of a foreign threat. Machiavelli thus urges legislators to try to find other means of reminding their citizens or subjects of the reasons they need government. Elections are the best way of keeping the individuals in high office responsive to the desires of the people and supplying the different kinds of leaders needed to respond to changing circumstances. But elections are not sufficient, since the people do not always select the best individuals. Sometimes they throw their most distinguished citizens out of office, because they or their leaders envy those citizens. More often people fail to understand the need to adopt cautious or costly policies and so resist or even punish the individuals who advocate such measures. Nor do the people see the threat posed by a popular young leader who uses their support to destroy his competitors. Public trials serve not merely to check the ambitions of popular leaders, but to remind the people that everyone is and ought to be punished for disobeying the laws. By giving the people opportunities within the confines of the law to vent their resentment and envy of those who govern, these trials (or public “executions”) prevent the conflict between the two humors from escalating into a civil war.17 Machiavelli recognizes, however, that “modes and orders” designed for a noncorrupt people no longer work if and after the people become corrupt. He hoped that the emergence of several large states in Europe would prevent their peoples from becoming corrupt, because each would feel the necessity of defending itself from incursions by the others. The resulting “balance of power,” as it came to be called, would operate internationally in a way analogous to the internal checks and balances he recommended for the internal governments of both republics and kingdoms.

In books 1 and 2 of the Discourses Machiavelli thus sketches a solution to the problem of politics as he understands it. That solution is not permanent, however, because Machiavelli explicitly recognizes that it is extremely tenuous. Since each of the opposed humors that arise in every city is constantly trying to diminish if not to dislodge the other entirely, in D 3.49 he concludes that acts of foresight are necessary every day in order to maintain the constitutional checks and balances that moderate the excesses of both sides. In contrast to Plato and Aristotle, he thus dismisses the desirability of having a wise founder like Lycurgus prescribe laws for a city that would remain unchanged for centuries. On the contrary, he argues that “since all things of men are in motion and cannot stay steady” (D 1.6; 23), cities must constantly attempt to grow. To grow, they have to incorporate new peoples, but these peoples come with their own foreign customs. The “heads” of the city thus have to devise new ways of preventing the resultant corruption of their own laws. The problem is that those like Fabius Rullianus, who deserved to receive the honorific title “Maximus” because he knew how to counteract the potential corruption of the Roman polity, do not receive honor or glory as recompense for their service. The people lionize individuals for what appear to be extraordinary acts of self-denial on the part of political leaders such as Manlius Torquatus and Scipio more than they appreciate necessary, but more frequent kinds of public service such as military victories or legislative innovations (TM, 287–90).

Why, then, should talented individuals risk their own lives and fortunes in order to serve the public? According to Machiavelli, there will always be individuals and groups seeking to dominate their cities, because, as he states in D 1.37, “when engaging in combat through necessity is taken from men they engage in combat through ambition.” The human beings moved by the two political humors thus exist on a continuum: although most are initially fearful for their lives and property, once they feel reasonably secure, they seek to take the lives and properties of others. So, he observes, when the Roman plebs secured themselves from oppression by the nobles with the institution of the tribunes, they began “at once to engage in combat through ambition, and to wish to share honors and belongings with the nobility as the thing esteemed most by men” (78). However, in his account of the contention over the Agrarian law in Rome, the specific example he uses to illustrate this point, Machiavelli also shows that, when pressed, the nobles were willing to share their honors or offices, but not the property they had accumulated, with the plebs. Political competition thus begins to look as if it is basically for the sake of acquiring more economic goods. According to Machiavelli, everyone naturally seeks to acquire more, and those who are successful are praised.

Yet, Machiavelli reminds his readers, the greatest and most successful political leaders have risked their own lives and property to serve the public for the sake of winning glory. He distinguishes himself or his political thought from his more “bourgeois” successors, Hobbes and Locke, for example, by the positive way in which he presents the desire to win glory, as opposed to mere dominion.18 In P 8 Machiavelli suggests that it was his lack of glory that distinguished a petty tyrant such as Agathocles from a great founder such as Romulus.19 And he explicitly appeals to the desire to win glory on the part of his readers, both princely and republican, in trying to persuade them to enact his proposals for the unification and liberation of Italy. As Machiavelli shows with his Roman examples, the glory awarded to a successful general, for example, in the form of a triumphal march, can be enjoyed by him during his lifetime. But that glory (gloria) is less than the veneration (venerazione) with which later generations come to view the founders of the political orders from which they benefit; and that veneration is rarely if ever experienced by a leader during his lifetime. Leaders are more apt to confront an armed opposition that they have to try either to coopt (as Camillus did his fellow tribunes) or to eliminate (as Moses did). As Machiavelli argues with regard to Camillus and his ill-advised decision to ride in his triumphal procession behind four white horses as if he were a god, any attempt to win such glory or veneration is apt to arouse the envy of the leader’s fellow citizens; and when it does, it becomes dysfunctional, if not positively dangerous both for him as an individual and for the preservation of his state. Machiavelli recognizes that the Romans used the promise of glory to induce individuals like Cincinnatus to leave their private affairs, devote themselves to public service for as long as necessary, and then return to private life as law-abiding citizens. But he also shows that neither the Roman nobles nor the Roman plebs were willing to accept poverty for long, and that the promise of glory was not sufficient to make consuls such as Fabius Rullianus obey the orders of the Senate when in the field or to prevent an ambitious general like Caesar from seizing the honor he thought he was due by force. It was, moreover, the combination of the desire to increase their wealth and to reward their generals with a triumph that led the Roman Senate to pass legislation prolonging the commands of consuls. And it was the combination of the agitation over the Agrarian law and the prolongation of commands, Machiavelli argues, that led to the fall of the Roman republic. Although Machiavelli appeals to the desire of his young readers to win glory by “imitating the Romans,” he does not, therefore, rely simply or primarily on their yearning for glory to produce good leaders. Like the desire for security that all human beings feel, the desire for reputation or glory that animates the great can never be completely satisfied. It can, however, be enlisted by those who know how to design and maintain institutions that achieve as much peace and prosperity as is humanly possible. In opposition to Hobbes and Locke, Machiavelli shows that it would be a mistake simply to try to eradicate or repress this desire that fuels so much political action, for better as well as for worse.

According to Machiavelli, “peoples are so much superior [to princes] in maintaining things ordered that without doubt they attain the glory of those who order them” (D 1.58). It is the Roman conquest of the world that is remembered and emulated more than the deeds of any particular Roman—founder, general, or emperor. And, Machiavelli regularly reminds his readers, it is not the people so much as the writers who determine the posthumous reputation of individual leaders (P 12, D 1.10, D 2.Pref., FH Ded., FH Pref.; 1, 7–8). Like Homer, Xenophon, and Plutarch, these writers have produced images of successful leaders in the hope that their readers will be inspired to imitate, if not emulate them (P 12). But, Machiavelli also warns his readers, these writers cannot be altogether trusted. Like those who, living under the empire, praised Julius Caesar, they may not state their opinions of the reigning government and its founders openly for fear of persecution (D 1.10). In that case, he urges, a reader needs to look at what the writer says about the opposition, whether that be the praise of Brutus in the case of Caesar or of Niccolò Uzzano in the case of Machiavelli himself. A leader’s posthumous reputation depends upon the deeds of those who follow him; and these are clearly not under the leader’s control. Writers tend to praise those who have succeeded and to attribute their successes to the leaders’ virtue, when, as Machiavelli explains, the desirable outcomes may instead have been largely products of chance (D 2.Pref.). Writers also tend to praise the achievements of past heroes with whom it is no longer possible to compete and to criticize their own contemporaries out of envy.

Machiavelli also reminds his readers that he is one of the writers who describe and determine the posthumous reputations of past leaders. But, we note, he did not produce portraits of successful leaders. His Life of Castruccio Castracani is obviously both ironic and critical. He did write histories, of a sort, of both the Roman and the Florentine republics, but neither is simply celebratory. On the contrary, the purpose of his histories is clearly to enable his readers to do better than the leaders and the peoples he describes.

In announcing that he has discovered “new modes and orders” Machiavelli explicitly states that he worries about arousing the envy of others. He has thus confined himself to indicating the path that others can carry a little way to its end—and receive credit for the innovation. Both as a political theorist and as an advisor, Machiavelli indicates that he has learned the lesson he presents in the example of Camillus. If a leader wants to remain a member of his political community and thus receive its protection (instead of banishment, exile, or death), he must demonstrate his willingness to share both command and credit with others. He cannot seek glory or reputation solely for himself, his ideas, or his achievements. Machiavelli thus insistently and repeatedly dons the modest garb of an advisor. He recognizes that he, like a political leader, needs to persuade others to follow and carry out the orders he proposes; but unlike an “armed prophet,” he cannot force those who fail to believe. Like Socrates, he seeks primarily to educate the young. Unlike Socrates and Epicurus, however, he emphatically does not retreat from public life to live in private. He does not, because he sees that all isolated individuals are vulnerable without political protection. It is, therefore, in the writer’s interest to do everything he can to teach ambitious young politicians how best to rule and to prevent the people from becoming corrupt. Establishing and maintaining a decent political order is the necessary prerequisite for realizing all the other desirable possibilities of human existence.

Machiavelli’s writings continue to engage readers today because he analyzes political problems and phenomena that we still confront. Although he wrote at a time when most people were governed by princes, either hereditary or new, he sought to show why governments need to be placed on a popular foundation. While it was possible for generals such as Severus to rule by means of force and fraud, such regimes are difficult to maintain after the founder dies (or is assassinated). The central lesson of Machiavelli’s analysis of politics is, in fact, that seemingly stable regimes and laws are always under attack, more or less visibly, by dissatisfied individuals and groups. Current institutions and policies also have unintended consequences that, like the admission of “new men” to Roman citizenship, will undermine the checks and balances of a government that preserves liberty, if new “remedies” are not found.

In the last century we have seen Europe change from a “province” ruled by a variety of constitutional monarchies to a continent divided between liberal or social democracies and tyrannies imposed by an external power to a loose federation of republics. Will their dependence on the United States for defense corrupt the Europeans? Or will the reemergence of an external threat in Russia further unite them?

Readers in the United States might not only take particular note of the problems caused by increasing economic inequality in the Roman republic, but also heed his warning that redistributive policies arouse fierce opposition and thus deep divisions. American politics is now characterized by increasingly strident partisan divisions that have threatened at times to shut down the government. In D 1.50 Machiavelli warns legislators against allowing any individual officer or part of the government to have the ability to prevent the government from acting (and thus risk anarchy, revolt, or defeat in war); there must be a constitutional means of getting around any such blockage. In contrasting the Roman and Florentine republics he also suggests that the problems associated with partisanship can be ameliorated if not prevented by changes in the way in which elections are conducted and that economic (and consequently political) inequality can be addressed by changes in the ways taxes are levied and collected rather than an attempt to redistribute wealth per se or directly.

The “postcolonial” governments established in Asia and Africa after World War II face many of the same problems Machiavelli identified in Florence. How do peoples who have no experience defending or governing themselves acquire the requisite habits and skills? After the old government is overthrown, usually by force, Machiavelli emphasizes, a new state cannot be constructed merely by passing laws and hiring police to enforce them. Both the people and their leaders need to learn the advantages of competitive elections, rotation in office, public trials, and sharing power with the opposition, if a republican form of government is to last. The difficulty, which he also notes, is that a people’s political customs or “culture” is a product primarily of their experience. To introduce republican institutions and have them last, a people needs not merely one, but a series of leaders who understand the necessity and means of enforcing such habits and expectations until they become a “second nature.”

Machiavelli is often considered to be a republican, but not a liberal political thinker, because he does not articulate a doctrine of rights. That failure, if it is a failure, is connected to his famous “realism.” Human beings do not want to be ruled by others, he observes, but that does not mean that they are free by nature or that they naturally love liberty. Human freedom like human government is a product of human art. Because Machiavelli saw that the need for government arises from the acquisitive passions that lead human beings to fear and compete with one another, he did not develop such abstract and legalistic notions as the establishment of government for the securing of individual natural rights or a social contract. On the contrary, he emphasized the dynamic, ever-changing character of politics. Laws formulated and imposed on a savage people to establish order no longer have the desired effect once the people have become “civilized,” he observed. Nor do the institutions developed by a people anxious to maintain its freedom continue to work after they feel secure and, as a result, become corrupt. Because human beings naturally do not want to be ruled by others, Machiavelli argues, governments are imposed by some human beings on others—initially, and to some extent always, by force. There is no original contract. No leader can maintain a government solely by means of force or terror, however; at the very least he or she needs assistants. There will, therefore, always be a certain amount of natural resistance on the part of some people to being ruled by others. However, if a government shows that it protects the lives, families, and property of most of its subjects, they will not actively seek to overthrow it (because that would obviously be dangerous); they will not even join or follow the few brave souls willing to take the risks involved in leading a rebellion unless they feel themselves immediately and intolerably oppressed. Although human beings do not naturally want to be ruled, they nevertheless become accustomed to that condition, because they need a government to defend them against the aggression of others. Unfortunately, those who are fortunate enough to enjoy a free way of life tend to take its advantages for granted. Human beings become free, Machiavelli insists, only if they live under a set of laws that enable those who do not want to be ruled to check the excesses of those who wish to rule. Such laws and institutions are acquired primarily on the basis of experience—trial and error—as in Rome. However, later leaders and their peoples can learn from the achievements and mistakes of their predecessors, especially if they are taught by Machiavelli to see what is useful in the histories.

Machiavelli advocates a republican form of government because it secures the most liberty, security, and prosperity for the most people. Never defining or recommending “justice” as the end or purpose of political organization, he maintains that the “common good” consists in what serves the desire of most people to be secure in their lives and property. And he suggests that what may look like the sacrifice of some leading individuals in public trials is not only the equivalent for but also helps to justify the demand made on ordinary citizens to risk their lives in defending the state in war.

The absence of a doctrine of natural or “human” rights in Machiavelli is one, but only one, source of the more general criticism that his teaching about politics is immoral and as such encourages immorality in both leaders and peoples. However, as I observed earlier with regard to Machiavelli’s infamous statement in P 15 that he is going to teach a prince to be able not to be good and to use such knowledge according to necessity, the knowledge Machiavelli promises to convey is not teaching a prince to be evil. On the contrary, he shows in P 19, cruel and rapacious tyrants tend to be overthrown. The knowledge Machiavelli seeks to convey is clearly and explicitly instrumental. Indeed, morality or virtue as Machiavelli presents it in general is instrumental (or “consequentialist,” as some professional philosophers would now say) as opposed to “deontological” (purely for its own sake). The goal for all human beings, princes and peoples alike, is or ought to be preserving their own lives. Political societies are formed for that purpose. The second goal is thus doing what is necessary to maintain that society or “state.” If a prince does what is necessary to preserve the lives and properties of his subjects, he will not merely maintain his state; he will win fame or glory if his deeds appear to be particularly courageous or extraordinary. Machiavelli does not simply identify virtuous behavior with what is praised, however. A prince should always seek to appear to be merciful, faithful, humane, honest, and religious, he insists, although a prince cannot always, in fact, be so. But if he does what is necessary to maintain his state (i.e., protect the lives, families, and property of his fellow citizens or subjects), his people will conclude that he has been merciful, faithful, humane, honest, and religious (if he claims that he has been). They see the effects of his actions, but cannot look into his heart or see his motives.

Machiavelli emphatically insists on the importance of retaining the appearance of what is often called “conventional” morality not only in politics but also, as he shows in his comedies, in the private lives of individuals. Yet, a critic might object, won’t the dissemination of Machiavelli’s cynical views about the self-regarding if not strictly speaking immoral passions that move human beings ultimately undermine the salutary appearances? Machiavelli recognizes that the ancients taught the necessity of using force and fraud in politics covertly. If it is necessary to retain the appearance of morality, isn’t theirs the wiser policy? Machiavelli’s first defense of his explicitly instrumental view of morality is that it is the effectual truth. As Aristotle observes in the Rhetoric, people praise the courage soldiers display in risking their lives in defending the city, because they benefit from that courage. It is not so clear that the soldier himself benefits, especially if he dies. Machiavelli generalizes by observing that people praise the qualities in leaders that enable them to preserve the state that protects the lives and properties of all. He recognizes that popular praise or opinion is not simply or reliably the source of a true understanding of virtue, because it is based on a perception of effects and not of causes. If an individual performs extraordinary acts that are seen to benefit the public, he may receive not merely praise, but glory (and even be venerated after he dies for the benefits later generations enjoy as a result of the institutions and laws he established). Since their reputation or fame is apt to provoke the envy of others, however, Machiavelli also warns ambitious politicians that they should not glory in their triumphs. Nor should they arrogantly seize the property or women belonging to others lest they incite conspiracies against their state. Except in emergency situations (such as war), they should obey their own laws and appoint others to enforce them. Above all, they should not arrogantly claim to be better than others. Machiavelli recognizes that there have been noble individuals such as Scipio in Rome and Giovanni de’ Medici in Florence who genuinely attempted not merely to live virtuously but to serve their people. However, Machiavelli also observes that when there is a conflict between what such individuals believe is virtuous behavior and what is necessary in order to maintain law and order, they may like Scipio seek to maintain their own virtue at the expense of the common good. Like Giano della Bella and Giovanni de’ Medici, such noble individuals may attempt to protect the people from oppression by the powerful, but their moderating policies do not have a lasting effect, if they do not know how to establish and maintain laws that enable the two humors to check each other’s excesses after they die. What is truly virtuous, according to Machiavelli, is knowing what to do in order to achieve the common good, understood to be an aggregation of the desire of most people not to be oppressed and of the ambition of a few to rule. Like Socrates, Machiavelli thus defines virtue as knowledge. The knowledge required is not of something as abstract as the “idea of the Good” or the “good-in-itself,” however; it consists in the explicitly worldly knowledge of how to protect the lives of most people and to enable them to live not merely prosperously, but freely. The philosopher or prudent advisor of the prince is not compelled to rule in Machiavelli’s republic. Insofar as he can be said to rule, he rules by persuasion. He seeks to secure his own life and liberty by showing others how they can best satisfy their desires. Acknowledging that he shares these common desires in seeking to benefit others, he acts on the basis of what can be called his humanity.20
